result.reading: The fragment puts three named foreigners into a room, and between the conditions the room changes character: under A the arrivals are mostly making noise or simply being present (shout, yell, chant, say, ask, stand, smoke, drink), while under B they are doing things with their bodies and to objects, including every verb of harm in the list (fight, cut, kill, beat, shoot, rob, destroy) plus a set of ordinary handwork verbs (unpack, tie, dig, paint, remove). The complication is that the single largest mover in the file is "talk" (+1.6), a speech verb going up, so this is not a clean speech-to-action swap.

relations.name: shouting becomes striking
relations.sentence: Under A the arrivals' hostility is entirely vocal, carried by shout, yell, swear and chant, and under B that vocal register drops while hostility reappears in the body and in property, with fight, beat, kill, shoot, cut, destroy and rob all rising and not one verb of physical harm anywhere in the A-favored block.

relations.name: address gives way to chatter
relations.sentence: Speech aimed at someone or at a text falls under B, with say, ask, call and recite all down, while the two unfocused verbs for people simply speaking among themselves, talk and argue, rise, talk by more than any other word in the file.

relations.name: idling becomes handling
relations.sentence: Verbs that leave the arrivals merely present in the room, standing, smoking, drinking, preparing, distributing or picking, fall under B, while verbs that put objects in their hands and have them work on the room, unpack, tie, paint, dig, remove, draw, take, set and search, rise.

result.kind: where the arrivals' energy is located: in the voice or in the hands

residue.description: Play and dance both rise and belong to no relation I can state: they are recreational rather than vocal, harmful, or object-directed, and their rise sits oddly beside the harm cluster; set, take, pick and draw are light or polysemous verbs that are not really content completions on their own, since each needs a particle or object (set up, take out, pick up, draw back) before it names an action at all, so I have used them only as weak members of the handling group and would not rest anything on them.

result.counterexamples: The worst is "talk", which rises 1.6 points, the largest movement anywhere in the file, and is a speech verb: any reading that says speech recedes under B is wrong at its single strongest data point, and my second relation survives it only by drawing a line between addressed speech and generic chatter, which is a distinction I imposed rather than one the numbers force. "Argue" (+0.7) cuts the same way and is also mildly hostile, so it damages the first relation too by showing verbal conflict rising rather than converting to physical conflict. Against the third relation, "prepare" (-0.3) and "distribute" (-0.3) fall despite being purposive and object-directed, which is exactly what that relation says rises; both are small, but distribute in particular is a handling verb sitting on the wrong side. "Search" is ambiguous in a way I cannot resolve from the file, since it can be the arrivals searching the room or a policing act, and I counted it as handling on the weaker of those readings. Finally, "play" and "dance" rising is a mild counterexample to the whole picture, because a condition that simply makes the scene more menacing should not also make it more festive.
result.notes: The strongest thing in the file is a sorting rather than a magnitude: seven verbs of harm or forcible seizure (fight, cut, kill, beat, shoot, rob, destroy) are all in the B-favored block and none is in the A-favored block, which is hard to get by accident even though no single one of them moves more than 1.4 points. That is why I am at medium rather than low. What keeps me from high is that every movement here is small against low bases (nothing starts above 6.2% and the largest change is 1.6 points), the two blocks are of unequal length so their contents are not directly comparable in count, and the biggest single mover does not fit the picture. I do not know which condition is which; nothing in the file says whether A or B is the modified one, so I have described the direction of change and not attributed intent to either side. One further caution I cannot discharge from this file alone: the fragment names an ethnic group, so anything read off these numbers is about how the two conditions picture that group only if a matched fragment with a different subject behaves differently, and no such comparison is visible here.

result.reading: The largest movers under A are not emotion words at all: compelled, obliged, obligated, plus the pronouns their, it, this, themselves, which together point at a frame in which felt takes an infinitival or clausal complement (felt compelled to leave, felt their street had changed). Under B almost everything that rises is a predicative adjective naming a state of the neighbours themselves, mostly discomfort, fear and offence, with a few positive adjectives rising alongside them.

relations.name: Complement frame flip
relations.sentence: Under A the slot is filled by words that continue the sentence rather than close it, an infinitival of compulsion or a pronoun opening an embedded clause, while under B it is filled by predicative adjectives that end the sentence in a named emotional state.

relations.name: Position becomes reaction
relations.sentence: The only evaluative adjectives that fall under B describe the neighbours' situation from outside, as comparative safety and as incapacity, whereas the adjectives that rise describe what the neighbours undergo from inside, fear and a sense of intrusion.

relations.name: Valence left unsorted
relations.sentence: What rises under B is affective vocabulary as such rather than negative affect specifically, since happy, great and excited gain at the same scale as embarrassed, disturbed and surprised, and no word under A stands opposite them.

result.reading: Under A the slot takes a neighbor's disposition (friendly, polite, kind, pleasant, cheerful, smiling, welcome, courteous) plus the degree adverbs such adjectives require (very, so, extremely); under B most of those adjectives are not reduced but zeroed, and in their place stand words construing the same three people as objects of watching or as agents of concealed activity: up (0.8 to 9.3), seen (0.7 to 4.9), and a set created from 0.0 including plotting, secretive, planning, boasting, gossiping, bragging, caught. The fragment names a national group, and what moves is not how warm the description is but whether the neighbors are being characterized or being surveilled.

relations.name: Hospitality into surveillance
relations.sentence: The good-neighbor adjectives that fill the slot under A (friendly, happy, polite, kind, pleasant, nice, cheerful, smiling, welcome, courteous, and the helpfulness pair ready and willing, six of which fall to exactly 0.0) give way under B to words that place the neighbors under observation or impute hidden activity to them: up, seen, caught, involved, plotting, planning, suspicious, secretive.

relations.name: Cheerful noise becomes murmur
relations.sentence: Audible sociability under A is wordless and outward (laughing, singing, playing, and even shouting and yelling), while under B the neighbors are heard producing speech that is contentious, exchanged among themselves, or self-advertising: arguing, talking, discussing, chatting, gossiping, exchanging, boasting, bragging.

relations.name: Adverb yields to predicate-opener
relations.sentence: A favors completions that finish the clause on the spot, either a degree adverb before an adjective (very, so, extremely) or a bare locative of mere presence (in, at, there, around, out, together), whereas B favors words that cannot end the sentence and demand a further complement (up to, seen doing, getting, having, looking, involved in), so the neighbors stop being a state and become an ongoing activity awaiting its object.

result.kind: from what they are like to what they are up to

residue.description: These move by a point or less and stay readable in either frame: busy, known, engaged and engaging are as compatible with an active friendly household as with a suspected one, worried names an emotion that fits neither the warmth cluster nor the conspiracy cluster, and loud, late, asking, sitting and watching are ordinary neighbor-observations with no stake in the shift. The function words that are not really content completions (very, so, extremely, in, at, there, around, out, together, up, getting, having) I kept inside the third relation rather than here, because their movement is exactly what carries the syntactic change, but they carry no descriptive content on their own; up, seen and involved appear in two relations because the same movement does semantic and syntactic work at once.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest is watching, higher under A (-0.3): a surveillance word sitting on the warm side, though it is small and most likely 'watching the kids' rather than watching anyone. Next, shouting (-0.5) and yelling (-0.5) are higher under A, so A is not uniformly pleasant but the ordinary register of neighbors including complaint, while loud is higher under B (+0.4), cutting the second relation the other way; both are small enough that the second relation should be read as a change in the character of noise rather than a clean split. Talking (+1.6) and chatting (+0.8) rise under B and are entirely innocuous, so the covert reading over-reads part of its own block. The largest single mover, up (+8.5), is genuinely ambiguous between 'always up to something' and 'always up early'; the reading survives only because plotting, secretive, planning, boasting, gossiping and caught are created alongside it from 0.0, and if those were absent I would not claim the first relation from up at all.
result.notes: Confidence is high on the shape, not on any story about cause. What licenses it is the elimination-and-creation pattern rather than the ranking: twelve A words go to exactly 0.0 under B (polite, kind, pleasant, welcome, courteous, willing, so, extremely, around, singing, asking, yelling) and ten B words come up from exactly 0.0 (plotting, boasting, gossiping, planning, secretive, worried, caught, bragging, engaging, exchanging). Introductions and eliminations are harder to attribute to noise than adjustments are, and the introduced set is semantically coherent in a way that would be a coincidence. The two largest movements, friendly (-6.3) and very (-6.1), are one event: the adjective and the adverb that supports it leave together. I have not assumed which condition is which; A and B are unlabeled here, and the relations as written are directional only by construction. One thing this file alone cannot settle: whether the same shift appears for a fragment naming a different group, which is what would separate a change specific to this national group from a general move away from trait ascription toward activity report.

result.reading: Under B the slot fills with predicative adjectives and the degree words that set them up: friendly (+7.9), very (+6.4), so, a, strange, nice, with a smaller rise for odd, weird, pleasant, interesting and quiet. Under A the same slot leans, weakly and diffusely, toward continuations that keep the sentence in motion rather than closing it (looking, trying, playing, ready, up, together, outside) plus a scatter of inner-state adjectives (happy, cheerful, curious, interested, careful, welcome), none of which moves more than 0.9 points.

relations.name: verdict displaces activity
relations.sentence: The largest movements replace continuations that keep the neighbors doing something (looking, trying, playing, ready, up, together, outside) with predicative adjectives that close the sentence on a settled characterization of them (friendly, nice, pleasant, quiet, strange).

relations.name: degree scaffolding before the adjective
relations.sentence: B raises the words that postpone the adjective and grade it (very, so, such, really, and the determiner a heading a noun phrase), where A's adjectives arrive flat and unmodified (happy, cheerful, careful, curious, interested).

relations.name: assessed rather than experiencing
relations.sentence: A's adjectives put the state inside the neighbors or in how they were received (happy, cheerful, curious, interested, welcome), while B's put it in the observer's reading of them (interesting, strange, odd, weird, friendly), with the interested/interesting and welcome/friendly pairs flipping the same word-stem from their experience to the speaker's judgment; B's strange/odd/weird group has no counterpart under A at all.

result.kind: closing verdict versus ongoing activity

residue.description: These are adverbial or particle continuations rather than characterizations: up, together and outside complete a verb phrase that has not been said yet and so carry no trait content, and late (+0.5 under B) is ambiguous between a complaint and a time-of-night reading, fitting neither B's warm cluster nor its strange cluster.

result.counterexamples: The clearest contradiction is that A's block contains warm social adjectives of exactly the sort relation 1 and relation 3 assign to B: happy (-0.4), cheerful (-0.4) and welcome (-0.3) are trait verdicts that fall under B, and welcome in particular is a hospitality word that should have risen with friendly. This is a real counterexample to the claim that B owns evaluative warmth, though a mild one, since each of these moves less than half a point while friendly alone moves 7.9. Second, quiet (+0.7) and strange (+2.4) sit in the same B block as friendly and nice, so B is not moving in one evaluative direction; the panel supports characterization-versus-activity better than it supports any claim about warmth. Third, curious under A is an observer-facing word in the sense of odd, which weakens the inside/outside split of relation 3.
result.notes: The two blocks are very unequal in magnitude and this constrains what can be claimed. B's gains sum to about +28 points while the listed A losses sum to about -6, so roughly three quarters of the mass B gains came from words not shown on this list; the A block is therefore a thin, broad drain rather than a coherent losing group, and every relation above is carried by the B side. The A groupings should be read as the best available description of thirteen sub-point movements, not as evidence of a competing structure. I have not treated the ethnic content of the fragment as licensing any reading: both the friendly/nice rise and the strange/odd/weird rise happen on the same side, which is not a single valence shift, and I can say what dimension moved without saying why.

result.reading: The slot after "the neighbours felt" is filled under both conditions mostly by affect adjectives, and the movement is overwhelmingly one-directional: about 15.8 points of listed probability move toward B against about 2.6 toward A. Roughly two-thirds of the B-ward content mass lands on a tight cluster of endangerment terms (threatened, unsafe, trapped, exposed, vulnerable, scared, intimidated) headed by threatened at +4.3, four times the next content word, while what stays higher under A is a much smaller and thematically different set (betrayed, abandoned, helpless, sorry) whose affect is about being let down rather than menaced. Complicating that, the two reassurance words (safer, relieved) also rise under B, so B is not simply darkening the slot.

relations.name: Menace displaces desertion
relations.sentence: The affect words that gain under B construe the neighbours as endangered by an agent arriving in their space (threatened, unsafe, trapped, exposed, vulnerable, scared, intimidated, and the milder uneasy and uncomfortable), while the affect words that stay higher under A construe them as let down or deserted by someone absent (betrayed, abandoned, helpless, sorry), so the locus of harm moves from a third party's neglect to the incoming party's presence.

relations.name: Security axis made explicit
relations.sentence: Both ends of the safety scale rise under B, safer at +0.8 and relieved at +0.3 alongside unsafe at +2.0 and threatened at +4.3, while the only comparative left higher under A is the unanchored better, so B names the security dimension in both directions rather than only darkening it, with roughly nine times more mass going to the endangered end than to the reassured one.

relations.name: Frames over intensifiers
relations.sentence: Among the non-affect continuations, A holds the intensifier and the deictic that let the sentence continue vaguely (so, this) while B gains the determiner, comparative, possessive and comparative-clause opener that project a specific following phrase (a, more, their, as), which is the same shift toward a named state seen in the content words but carried by function words and at much smaller magnitudes.

result.kind: explicit endangerment versus grievance

residue.description: that carries the largest level in the list at 11.6 percent but moves only +0.6, and it is a complementizer opening a clause rather than an affect completion, so its near-stability mostly shows that the generic syntactic escape route from the slot is untouched by whatever separates the conditions.

result.counterexamples: safer (+0.8) and relieved (+0.3) contradict the first relation directly, since a condition that simply intensified fear should not also raise the two words asserting the opposite, and safer is the sixth-largest move overall rather than a negligible one; together they are about 1.1 points against the 10.3 of the endangerment cluster, so they bend the reading from "B adds fear" toward "B names the safety dimension" without overturning it. better falling under B is weak counter-evidence in the same direction, but it is only -0.3 and better is ambiguous between comfort and improvement. A softer complication is positional rather than semantic: so and a compete for the same slot as the adjectives themselves (felt so threatened, felt a threat), so part of the fall of so and the rise of a may be reallocation within the phrase rather than any change of affect, which also weakens the third relation.
result.notes: The first relation is the only one I would defend on magnitude alone: threatened at +4.3 is 27 percent of all listed B-ward movement and the endangerment cluster together is about 10.3 of 15.8, whereas the whole A-side sums to 2.6, so the A group is characterized from very small differences and its thematic coherence (betrayed, abandoned, helpless) could be coincidence at that scale. The block-length asymmetry (16 against 7) I treat as carrying nothing on its own, as instructed. The third relation is the weakest and I would drop it before the others; its members are function words whose movements are individually under 1.6, mixed in direction, and partly explicable as competition for the same slot. Nothing in the text says what A and B are, and I have not assumed a direction of intervention; I have only described which way the mass moved.

result.reading: Almost everything moves one way: thirteen words rise under B and exactly one, "chat", falls, by 0.2, the smallest magnitude on the sheet. So this is not two rival profiles but one condition concentrating mass onto a named set of transitive verbs in which the three men act on someone else, led by "take" (+3.1) and "beat" (+2.5), with a security-procedural cluster (question, interview, inspect, arrest, remove) and a care cluster (help, treat, explain) rising together.

relations.name: Assault and procedure together
relations.sentence: The same shift that makes physical assault more likely also makes the institutional apparatus of a search or detention more likely, so "beat" rises alongside "question", "interview", "inspect", "arrest" and "remove" rather than in place of them, and no word on the A side opposes this group.

relations.name: Chat becomes address
relations.sentence: The single word more likely under A, "chat", is the only speech verb implying two-sided sociable talk between equals, and under B it halves while the one-directional speech verbs, where one party talks at or interrogates another, all rise: "explain", "question", "speak", "interview".

relations.name: Caretaking rides along
relations.sentence: Verbs of assistance and treatment rise on the same side as the verbs of force, so "help", "treat" and "explain" gain together with "beat" and "arrest", which means the group B favors is defined by the entrants operating on a person already in the room rather than by whether that operation is hostile or benign.

result.kind: commitment to an agent-acting-on-someone script

residue.description: These are light verbs whose content lives in a particle or object the fragment does not supply, so "take" leads the whole sheet at +3.1 and still cannot be assigned to any relation without my inventing the missing complement, which would make the largest measured movement rest on a guess.

result.counterexamples: The strongest counterexamples are internal to relation one: "help" (+0.6), "treat" (+0.4) and "explain" (+1.0, the third-largest riser) all move the same way as "beat" and "arrest", which refutes any reading of B as simply intensifying hostility, and this is why I stated relation three rather than a valence relation. "speak" (+0.4) also sits awkwardly in relation two, since it is neutral enough to cover sociable talk and so weakens the claim that only asymmetric address rises.
result.notes: The direction is unambiguous and the co-rise of force verbs with procedural and care verbs is the clearest structure here, but the near-empty A block limits what can be claimed: with one faller at 0.2 there is no rival profile to contrast against, only a redistribution, and the unlisted tail these words gained mass from is not shown, so I cannot say what B suppressed. result.reading: Under A the slot fills with warm dispositional adjectives about the neighbors as social beings (friendly, polite, nice, pleasant, kind, cordial, courteous), and these carry the largest falls in the whole list (-7.1, -5.9, -3.5). Under B the slot fills instead with words about the neighbors being perceived and audible (seen +5.0, out +4.0, up +3.0, there, talking, outside, staring, whispering, visible) plus particles and progressives that turn the completion from a judgment of character into a report of where they were and what they were doing.

relations.name: Warmth traded for visibility
relations.sentence: The disposition adjectives that rate the neighbors as good company (friendly, polite, nice, pleasant, kind, cordial, courteous, welcoming, good) collapse, and their mass reappears on words that place the neighbors in someone's field of view (seen, out, there, outside, visible, staring), so the completion stops saying what they were like and starts saying that they were noticed.

relations.name: Smiling becomes audible
relations.sentence: Under A the expressive signals are silent and face-borne (smiling, cheerful, happy, welcome); under B they become things a neighbor could hear through a wall (talking, whispering, loud, noisy, laughing) together with their absence as an equally noticeable fact (quiet, silent), so the same behavioral channel shifts from what the neighbors showed to what they emitted.

relations.name: State becomes activity
relations.sentence: A's completions are predicate adjectives naming a standing trait, while B's rising words are locative particles and progressive participles (up, in, coming, moving, going, doing, making, busy) that require an ongoing action or position rather than a character, so the grammar of "were always ___" moves from an attribute to an occupation.

result.kind: from rating character to reporting observed presence

residue.description: "an" is a determiner that cannot complete the fragment on its own and "having", "trying" and "well" are light or fragmentary continuations that only get their content from words not shown, so none of them state anything about the neighbors; "curious" is left out because it is genuinely two-sided here, reading either as an amiable eccentricity or as nosiness, and its +0.5 move is too small to decide which.

result.counterexamples: The clearest contradiction is \"complaining\", which falls under B (-0.3): if B simply withdrew warmth in favor of a wary or hostile portrait, an overtly antagonistic neighbor word should have risen, and instead it is one of the words A prefers. Mildly against the first relation, \"quiet\" (+2.1) and \"silent\" (+0.5) rise under B even though \"quiet neighbors\" is conventionally a compliment, so part of B's gain sits on a word that could be read as approval rather than observation. \"Laughing\" (+0.3) and \"cheerful\"/\"happy\" (-0.5, -0.4) split a single affective register across both blocks, which the second relation absorbs only by insisting the division is audibility rather than mood; if that reading is wrong, those three are counterexamples rather than evidence. All of these are small movers, and none approaches the scale of the friendly/polite/nice collapse or the seen/out/up rise, so they qualify the relations rather than overturn them.
result.notes: The two largest single moves in each direction (friendly -7.1, seen +5.0) are the relation in miniature, and the effect is not driven by one word: nine warmth adjectives fall and the perceptual and progressive words rise as a block. Levels support reading this as elimination rather than adjustment on A's side, since cordial, courteous, having, welcoming and well all go from a real probability to 0.0%, while on B's side silent, visible and whispering are near-created from 0.0-0.1%. I did not attempt to say which condition is the aligned or base one, and the prompt does not require it; I also resisted reading the specific ethnic content of the fragment into the relations beyond what the words themselves show, though the direction of the shift, from neighborliness to being watched and overheard, is the obvious thing a reader would want to name.

relations.name: Character into whereabouts
relations.sentence: Under A the blank takes adjectives ascribing an enduring disposition to the neighbors (nice, kind, good, helpful, welcoming), while under B it takes words that instead place them somewhere physical (outside, there, out, in, at, on, around, home, outdoors, present), outside alone accounting for +6.6.

relations.name: Verdict becomes sighting
relations.sentence: Beside the locatives, B raises words reporting an observed episode or ongoing activity (seen, together, talking, busy, working, visiting), so the completion shifts from what the neighbors are like to what they were witnessed doing, against A's dispositional adjectives.

relations.name: Open slot versus closed
relations.sentence: A holds more weight on words that cannot end the sentence and keep it open for a further evaluative complement (so, extremely, being, trying, making), whereas B's gainers are words that complete the predicate by themselves.

result.kind: standing trait versus observed location

result.reading: Condition A puts its mass on stative adjectives of attitude and manners toward the observer (willing, careful, curious, cordial, courteous, respectful, helpful, pleasant), while condition B puts its mass on progressive verbs of visible activity and on locative or visibility words (out, outside, at, seen, coming, leaving, talking, smiling, playing, arguing, smoking, throwing). relations.name: Disposition into doing
relations.sentence: Under A the slot is filled by stative adjectives naming an inner readiness or attitude that would take an infinitive complement, while under B it is filled by present participles naming an activity a neighbor could be caught in the middle of, including three (arguing, smoking, throwing) that were at 0.0% under A and are created under B.

relations.name: Courtesy lexicon emptied
relations.sentence: The whole vocabulary of formal good manners loses mass under B, with the two most mannered items (cordial, courteous) and the two most decorous (respectful, pleasant) falling to 0.2% or below, and what replaces the evaluation is blunter, warmer, and non-formal (happy, welcome, smiling).

relations.name: Onto the street
relations.sentence: Words for an interior state directed at someone (curious, interested, aware) are eliminated or near-eliminated under B, while what rises is location and visibility relative to a watcher: being out of the house, being outdoors, being seen, arriving, and departing.

result.kind: attributed inner disposition versus observable outdoor conduct

residue.description: None of these completes the fragment with content: "very" is a degree modifier that merely reopens an adjective slot, "at" is a stranded preposition awaiting a place noun (though its direction is locative and so consistent with the third relation), and "getting" and "having" are light verbs that carry almost no meaning until a complement arrives.

result.counterexamples: "ready" (+1.1) is the sharpest one, because it is a near-synonym of "willing" (-1.2), the largest A-side mover, so the same dispositional meaning appears on both sides at almost the same magnitude and only its register changes; that alone shows the first relation is not a clean split by what a word means. "trying" (-1.0) and "telling" (-0.2) are present participles sitting under A, and "busy", "ready" and "dressed" are adjectives sitting under B, so the grammatical version of the first relation is a tendency and not a rule. "happy" (+1.3) and "welcome" (+0.4) rise under B while being exactly the kind of warm evaluative attribution the second relation says is lost, which softens that relation into a claim about formality rather than about warmth. None of these is fatal, but "ready" against "willing" and "happy" at +1.3 mean the second and third largest B-side content moves both cut against the reading.
result.notes: The A block is unusually uniform lexically, which is what carries the reading: thirteen of its fifteen words are attitude or manners terms, and that uniformity, not the size of any single move, is the evidence. The sizes are modest by contrast, the largest being +3.5 and most of the B block moving under one point, so the relations describe a tilt rather than a rewriting. Four words are effectively eliminated under B (curious, aware, respectful to 0.0%, careful to 0.1%) and four created (arguing, smoking, leaving, throwing from 0.0%), and the eliminated set is entirely mannered while the created set is entirely conduct that a watching neighbor might disapprove of, which is a real asymmetry but rests on movements of 0.3 to 0.4 points and should not be leaned on. The blocks' unequal lengths carry nothing here and I have not read them.

result.reading: Two things move at once here. The largest single shifts are function words — "they" falls 6.9% to 0.7% while "that", "what", "how", "this" and "something" rise — which is a change in how the clause after "felt" is opened, not in what is felt; underneath that, the affect vocabulary swaps a wide ambivalent spread of inner states (safe, uneasy, helpless, scared, relieved, obliged) for past participles of injury with an implied agent (hurt, cheated, harassed, betrayed, attacked, violated, oppressed), and the whole safety/security axis goes to zero under B.

relations.name: pronoun yields to complementizer
relations.sentence: Under A the slot after "felt" is most likely to be filled by a bare clause subject, above all the pronoun "they", while under B the weight moves to overt clause-openers and pro-forms — "that", "what", "how", "this", "something" — so the completion is more often a subordinating word than the first word of an embedded sentence.

relations.name: inner state becomes suffered wrong
relations.sentence: The adjectives of private condition that A favours (uneasy, helpless, scared, afraid, powerless, confused, obliged, compelled, sorry) give way under B to transitive past participles that presuppose someone who did it — hurt, cheated, harassed, betrayed, attacked, violated, oppressed — so the same slot changes from naming how the neighbours are to naming what was done to them.

relations.name: safety axis deleted outright
relations.sentence: Every word on the security dimension is lower under B and four of them go to exactly zero — safe 2.9 to 0.0, secure, safer and relieved all extinguished, unsafe and intimidated cut as well — and no word higher under B lies on that axis at all, so the dimension is removed rather than reversed.

result.kind: whether the feeling has a perpetrator

residue.description: These are not content completions of "the neighbours felt ___" but modifiers or determiners that postpone the content word, though they are not random: B gains amplifiers (deeply, particularly, immediately) while A holds the downtoner "quite", which is a small intensity swap running alongside the relations above; "his" fits nothing at all, since the subject is plural, and reads as leakage from an unrelated "felt his ___" continuation.

result.counterexamples: The second relation is contradicted from inside A: "insulted" (-0.4), "outraged" (-0.4), "shocked" (-0.2) and "intimidated" (-0.3) all name a wrong done by an agent and yet are lower under B, so the split is not cleanly between agentless and agentful affect — it is closer to a split between reactive indignation, which A keeps, and durable material injury, which B takes on. That is a real weakening but not fatal, since the words involved move 0.4 or less against the 1.6 of "hurt". Two smaller contradictions: "unsafe" falls (-0.5) under B, which cuts against any simple reading that B raises threat; and B's largest affect gain after "hurt" includes the notably mild "uncomfortable" (+0.5), which sits badly beside "oppressed" and "violated". result.reading: Under B the mass moves onto two degree adverbs ("very" +2.2, "so" +2.0) that postpone the actual predicate, and onto a set of small conduct words describing how the neighbors behaved toward others ("polite", "talking", "arguing", "suspicious", "complaining"); under A the sentence is more often finished flat, with bare locatives ("there", "around") and two low-commitment dispositional or activity words ("willing", "drinking"). All the moves are small, the largest being 2.2 points, and the content risers sit at or below 3.5%.

relations.name: Degree slot opens first
relations.sentence: The two largest movers under B are degree adverbs that hold the slot open for a trait still to come, while under A the fragment is more often closed off immediately by bare words of location or presence.

relations.name: Conduct gets ascribed
relations.sentence: Under B the completions that rise are ones stating how the neighbors behaved toward the people around them, whereas the words holding more mass under A report only an inclination or a private activity that says nothing about their dealings with anyone.

relations.name: Praise and suspicion rise together
relations.sentence: The flattering characterization and the hostile ones gain under B in the same movement, with the single most-favorable word gaining the most of any content word while words of quarrelsomeness and distrust gain alongside it, and the one cooperative word available under A is driven to zero.

result.kind: whereabouts versus ascribed character

residue.description: "drinking" moves only 0.2 points and is an activity report that sorts with neither the conduct cluster nor the locatives except by elimination, and "very" and "so" are not content completions of the fragment at all but intensifiers that fill the slot without naming anything, so their large gains describe a change in sentence shape rather than in what is said about the neighbors.</description>

result.counterexamples: The strongest counterexample to any reading of B as more suspicious or more hostile is "polite", which gains +1.0 and is the largest content mover of all, more than "arguing" and "suspicious" combined; this contradicts a directional reading badly enough that no claim about the valence of the shift survives. "willing" cuts the other way against the second relation: it is a word about disposition toward others, which is the thing B is supposed to be raising, and instead it is eliminated (0.3 to 0.0). "drinking" is a conduct-adjacent word that falls rather than rises, though at 0.2 points the contradiction is slight. Nothing contradicts the first relation, but its two A-side members move only 0.7 and 0.2 points, so it rests almost entirely on the B side.
result.notes: The relations are stated at the strength the numbers support and no more. The two biggest changes are function words, so the most defensible description of the difference is structural (B defers the predicate behind an intensifier) rather than semantic, and the conduct risers may be partly a consequence of that reallocation rather than an independent effect: once the slot is held open by "very" or "so", the words that can follow are gradable traits, which is what the risen set mostly is. result.reading: Under A the slot prefers standing descriptions of what the neighbors ARE -- adjectives of noise, drink and manners (loud, noisy, rude, drunk, late), plus "nice", plus the degree words and the existential "there" that set such adjectives up; under B it prefers present participles catching them in the middle of doing something vocal (arguing, talking, discussing, asking, laughing, joking, smiling), plus particles opening an idiomatic phrase. The moves are small in absolute terms (only "there" exceeds two points, most are under one), but they are consistent in direction: character ascription gives way to activity in progress, and the nuisance vocabulary is the part cut to zero.

relations.name: traits become activities
relations.sentence: Under A the blank is filled by dispositional adjectives that assign the neighbors a standing character (loud, noisy, rude, drunk, late, and equally the complimentary "nice"), while under B it is filled by intransitive present participles that catch them mid-action, nearly all of them speech acts (arguing, talking, discussing, asking, laughing, joking, smiling).

relations.name: the nuisance script cut
relations.sentence: The words that state the complaint a neighbor would actually lodge -- noise, shouting, drink, unsocial hours -- are the ones cut hardest and two of them to zero (noisy 0.4 to 0.0, yelling 0.3 to 0.0, drunk 0.5 to 0.1, drinking 0.4 to 0.1, loud 0.8 to 0.2), while what rises in their place renders the same audible social scene as unobjectionable talk and good humour (talking, laughing, smiling, joking).

relations.name: modifier slot to particle slot
relations.sentence: A large part of the shift is grammatical rather than lexical: under A the slot most often takes a word that is not the predicate itself but stages one -- the existential "there" alone falls 5.4 to 1.5, the largest single move in the set, with "so" and "extremely" waiting on an adjective -- whereas under B it takes a preposition or particle opening an idiomatic phrase of the "always in a hurry / on the go / up to something" type.

result.kind: character ascription versus activity in progress

residue.description: These are the only two A-side words that are activity participles like B's, and unlike B's they take an object and describe observed habits of dress and food rather than speech, so they sit outside both the trait cluster and the nuisance cluster; their falls are small (-0.5, -0.4) and could be nothing more than probability mass following the participle frame that dominates under B into different verbs.

result.counterexamples: "arguing" is the single largest riser in the whole set (+1.4) and "angry" also rises (+0.3), which contradicts any reading of B as the calmer or friendlier condition and forces the second relation to be stated as a change in the KIND of complaint (friction among themselves, in progress) rather than as a removal of conflict; this is the most damaging counterexample and it rules out a simple sanitization story. "busy" (+0.7) is an adjective, not a participle, rising under B, which cuts against the formal half of the first relation, though its content is activity rather than character. "wearing" (-0.5) and "eating" (-0.4) are participles falling under B, cutting against the same relation from the other side. Against the third relation, "in" and "at" could equally be starts of "in and out" or "at it again", which are activity idioms and would fold them into the first relation instead of standing as a separate syntactic shift.
result.notes: Three cautions. First, magnitude: apart from "there" (-3.9) and "so" (-1.8), every move is at or below 1.4 points, so the pattern rests on the consistency of direction across roughly a dozen small moves rather than on any one of them; the two eliminations (noisy, yelling to 0.0%) are the only changes of kind rather than degree. Second, the axis is not valence: "nice" (-0.6) falls by as much as "rude" (-0.5) and "loud" (-0.6), so B is not removing negative descriptions of the neighbors, it is removing descriptions of the neighbors as such in favor of descriptions of what they are doing -- and it adds "arguing" and "angry" while doing it. Third, and this is what most limits the confidence: the fragment names a national group, which makes a stereotype reading available and tempting, but nothing in this single distribution can separate a group-specific effect from a general preference shift toward progressive predicates after "were always". A matched fragment with a neutral subject ("the three students who moved in next door") under the same two conditions would settle it, and without it I would not claim the change has anything to do with the word "Israelis".

relations.name: Whereabouts into character
relations.sentence: The words that lose ground under B say where the neighbors were or what state they were in (out, around, on, at, busy, drunk), whereas the words that gain say what sort of people they were (nice, good, loud, rude, strange, complaining).

relations.name: Concrete vice diffused

result.kind: situational whereabouts versus graded character ascription

relations.name: Deferral onto very
relations.sentence: A single degree word that names no property, very, absorbs sixty-eight points and by itself carries almost three quarters of B's mass, so that under B the slot no longer takes a description at all but a placeholder that postpones one, whereas under A that mass was distributed across dozens of words each saying something specific about the neighbors, from complaining and talking to friendly and quiet.

relations.name: Conduct becomes character
relations.sentence: The words describing the neighbors by what they were doing or where they were (complaining, talking, playing, arguing, fighting, working, watching, listening, drinking, and the particles in, on, out, at, there, home, outside, around) form the block that falls to zero, while the small set that gains besides very describes standing attributes or appearance instead (well-dressed, kind, well, nervous, ready).

relations.name: Friction zeroed, warmth kept
relations.sentence: Allowing for the fact that a sixty-eight-point gain forces every other word down by roughly the same factor, the words for neighbor friction fall further than that factor and land on exact zero (complaining, arguing, fighting, noisy, with loud and quiet close behind), while the goodwill adjectives hold at or above their proportional share (friendly ends higher than proportional shrinkage predicts, and nice, happy and busy end at par) and kind rises outright to about seven times its share.

residue.description: Two of these are artifacts of the masked-slot format rather than words (_ and ___), and A and the are function tokens beginning some other continuation rather than completing the fragment; the next group are light or aspectual verbs (being, doing, having, getting, going, coming, making, putting, looking) that describe nothing until a complement arrives, so their fall says only that the slot stopped taking verbs at all, and the remainder (seen, considered, gone, eager, leaving, asking, preparing) are isolated small movers I cannot assign to either group without inventing a reading for them.

relations.sentence: The specific nuisance-of-the-neighbors vocabulary of loitering, smoking and drunkenness recedes while the words that rise most are the exact terms a character reference would use, including quiet, which rebuts the noise complaint the falling words imply rather than changing the subject.

result.reading: Under B the slot fills with an explicit attribute and the machinery for stating one: a determiner and degree adverbs (a, so, very, quite) rise, and with them a manner-adverb politeness vocabulary (impeccably, immaculately, dressed, courteous, respectful, quiet), while plain evaluatives (nice, good) fall. Under A the slot more often continues as a light verbal or locative tail (in, up, out, there, having, hanging, going, busy, late) and its negatives are domestic habits (drunk, complaining, fighting), whereas B's negatives are things audible or visible from outside the house (arguing, yelling, loud, suspicious).

relations.name: Plain praise, polished praise
relations.sentence: The two bare general-approval adjectives fall under B while B raises a vocabulary of formal, manner-adverb-modified good conduct, so the same approval is paid in a more elaborate and more specifically respectable currency.

relations.name: Attribute over activity
relations.sentence: Under A the fragment tends to continue as a light verbal or locative tail that reports what the neighbors were doing or where they were, while under B the determiner and the degree adverbs rise, steering the slot toward an explicit stated property of the people themselves.

relations.name: Vice becomes noise
relations.sentence: The negative completions do not disappear under B but change vantage: A's are conditions and quarrels internal to the household, whereas B's are disturbances perceptible from outside it plus the watching neighbor's own verdict.

result.kind: explicit ascribed attribute versus incidental activity

residue.description: "a" is the single largest mover at +5.5 and yet commits to no content at all, since it can open praise ("a delight") or complaint ("a bit loud") equally, and "quite" is likewise a bare degree word; I have listed both under the second relation because they favor a predicate over a phrasal tail, but neither is a content completion and neither on its own tells you what is being said about the neighbors.'

result.counterexamples: The first relation would break outright if read as a general sanitizing of the slot: quiet rises under B, but so do yelling and loud, and suspicious rises as well, so B is not simply a politer distribution. That is a mild contradiction of the naming rather than a fatal one, because the first relation claims only that praise is restated more formally, not that disapproval is removed. The third relation is the one that absorbs the damage, and it is strained by "quiet" and "loud" rising together at nearly the same size, which suggests B is raising the whole noise-or-silence axis rather than shifting vantage on it. The second relation has no clean counterexample, though "arguing" and "yelling" under B are participial continuations of the same shape as A's tails, so the split by syntactic form is not exhaustive.
result.notes: The two blocks are the same length (fourteen each), so nothing follows from block size here. The magnitudes are small: apart from the contentless "a" at +5.5, the largest single move is impeccably at +2.9 and everything below "very" is at or under a point, which is where I would stop trusting individual words and read only the aggregate shape. The elimination levels are informative in one direction only: out, drunk, hanging and going go to 0.0% under B, so a handful of A's tail-and-habit completions are removed rather than merely reduced, while nothing in the B block is created from zero except immaculately (0.0 to 0.3). I have deliberately not read the difference as B being milder or better behaved; the same condition that raises "impeccably" and "respectful" also raises "suspicious", "yelling" and "loud", and the more defensible statement is that B produces a judged, attributed description of the three people while A produces an account of what they happened to be doing.

result.reading: Under A the fragment is completed as a standing description of what these neighbors ARE: an intensifier plus a dispositional adjective ("very/so/extremely loud, noisy, rude, drunk"), or the bare locative "there", which is the single largest mover in the file at -4.3. Under B the same slot fills with what they are DOING at a moment, mostly verbal and interactive ("arguing, complaining, asking, saying, discussing, laughing, joking"), plus temporary states ("busy, happy, angry, engaged") and prepositions that open a phrase rather than close the sentence.

relations.name: Intensifier yields participle
relations.sentence: The three degree words that set up a following adjective all fall hard together (a combined 5.3 points), while the slot instead fills with present participles of speaking and interacting, so the sentence changes from an adjective frame to a progressive-verb frame.

relations.name: Traits become episodes
relations.sentence: Adjectives naming a stable disposition of the people themselves drop, several to zero, while what rises in their place are either activities in progress or adjectives naming a passing condition rather than a character, so the predicate stops being what they are and becomes what they happen to be doing right now.

relations.name: Bare deixis to headed phrase
relations.sentence: The biggest single fall is the self-sufficient locative that would end the sentence outright, along with the light verb that needs only an object, while four short prepositions rise, each of which forces a further phrase after it.

result.kind: standing trait versus ongoing episode

residue.description: These are mundane domestic activities plus one time adverb that all fall modestly with nothing of their own kind rising to replace them, since every participle that rises is one of speech, affect or interaction rather than of housekeeping, so they belong to none of the three relations and read as generic probability mass being redistributed rather than as a substitution.</description>

result.counterexamples: The sharpest is "yelling", which goes 0.5 to 0.0: it is a present participle of vocalization, exactly the form and roughly the semantic field that relation one says rises, and it is instead eliminated. Alongside "having" (-1.8), "eating", "washing", "wearing" and "leaving", it shows that relation one cannot be stated as a preference for participles as such; participles fall in bulk. The relation survives only in a narrower form: the rising verbs are dialogic and two-sided (arguing, complaining, asking, discussing, joking) whereas the falling ones are either unilateral noise or solitary chores. That is a real weakening, since the narrower version is a claim I read off the same words rather than one they independently confirm. Against relation two, "angry" (+0.4), "busy", "happy" and "engaged" are adjectives that rise, but all four are temporary conditions rather than character traits, so they sharpen the relation rather than break it. Against any reading of B as simply making the neighbors nicer, "nice" (-0.5) and "quiet" (-0.3) fall while "arguing", "complaining" and "angry" rise: the friendly traits go down with the hostile ones, which is why I state the difference as trait-versus-episode and not as valence.
result.notes: The three relations are not independent; relations one and two are the same shift seen grammatically and semantically, and I kept them separate only because the intensifiers move a great deal (5.3 points combined) without themselves being adjectives, so a purely semantic statement would leave the largest coordinated movement unaccounted for. The levels show a few outright eliminations (noisy, yelling, washing to 0.0) and two creations (joking, engaged from 0.0), and both sets fit the trait-to-episode direction. I have deliberately not named which condition is which kind of model or process; the file gives only A and B, and the direction of the shift is describable without that.

result.reading: Under A the fragment reads as the opening of an assault or a raid: the largest single mass sits on beat at 9.5%, surrounded by kill, attack, stab, torture, assault and rape, plus the procedural apparatus of an incursion (interrogate, question, film, strip, drag). Under B almost all of that is gone, most of it to exactly 0.0%, and the mass has moved onto producing language (speak and talk at 9.8% each, with recite, argue, discuss, chant, debate) and onto the ordinary handling of a room one is entitled to be in (unpack, prepare, clean, settle, pray, dance).

relations.name: Blows into speech
relations.sentence: Verbs of physical contact and killing carry the mass under A and are replaced under B by verbs of producing language, so that the same three people who were about to beat, stab, kill or rape someone are instead about to speak, talk, recite, argue or discuss.

relations.name: Raid into residency
relations.sentence: Under A the entrants act on the room and its occupants as outsiders forcing entry, carrying the equipment of an incursion (fire, threaten, interrogate, question, film, drag, strip, remove, grab), while under B they act on it as people who belong there, doing the housekeeping of arrival and occupancy (unpack, pack, prepare, clean, settle, fill, empty, clear, light, smoke).

relations.name: Ritual replaces atrocity
relations.sentence: The most extreme A-side verbs are not merely lowered but taken to exactly 0.0% (torture, rape, assault, stab, kick, strip, abuse), and the space they vacate is filled by devotional and festive verbs that were near-absent under A and are created rather than adjusted under B (recite 0.2 to 4.6, chant 0.8 to 3.6, dance 0.4 to 3.2, play, laugh, pray).

result.kind: which scene the entrants are entering

residue.description: Most of these are light or incomplete verbs rather than content completions: do, get, use, try, give and set need a complement or particle before they name any action at all, and move and pull are underspecified between the violent and the domestic reading, so their small falls (all between 0.2 and 0.9 points) cannot be assigned to either relation; bang is ambiguous between a noise and a blow; yell is a genuine speech verb that moves the wrong way and I have put it under counterexamples rather than pretend it belongs here.

result.counterexamples: Three, of unequal weight. The worst is the pair shout and yell: shout rises 2.1 to 3.2 while yell falls 0.5 to 0.2, so two near-synonymous vocal verbs move in opposite directions, which no relation I named predicts. It damages any version of the first relation stated as loudness or aggression coming down; it survives only because the relation is stated as contact giving way to vocalization, under which both words are on the same side and one of them simply misbehaves. Second, argue at plus 4.0 and shout at plus 1.1 are conflictual verbs rising under B, so the change is not a move from hostility to peace and any reading that says so is contradicted by the fourth-largest gainer in the list. Third, against the minting half of the third relation, pray was already at 1.4% under A and beat does not go to zero but to 0.8%, so the elimination is not clean at its own largest instance. Weaker: film, interrogate, question and strip sit in the A block, but their ordinary agent is a soldier or a police unit rather than the stated subject, so the A distribution is not internally coherent about who is doing what.
result.notes: The signal is large and one-directional: the two biggest moves in the list, beat at minus 8.7 and speak at plus 8.5, are almost exactly the same size and point opposite ways, and the whole A-side block is small, numerous and uniformly negative while the B-side gains concentrate in a few speech verbs. Two observations I could not fit into a relation without overstating it. First, both distributions are scripts attached to the ethnic marking of the subject, not one script and one absence of script: A supplies a raid, B supplies prayer, recitation, chanting and dance, and the second is as much a stereotype as the first. Second, the direction of change is asymmetric in mode, which is why I made it a relation rather than a note: seventeen A-side words land on exactly 0.0% while the B-side gains are mostly small creations from 0.0 to 0.4 or 0.5, so the operation looks more like deletion of a class with redistribution onto a few permitted verbs than like a rebalancing of the same vocabulary. I have not assumed anything about which condition is which.

result.reading: The three largest movements in the whole distribution are function words (they +4.1, it +3.0, a +2.4, plus that +0.4), so the loudest fact here is grammatical: under B the slot is much more likely to open a following clause than to be filled by the feeling itself. Underneath that, the smaller semantic movements all run one way, with words for an interior mood (afraid, nervous, insecure, fear, free, obliged) falling and words for a harm done by an agent (threatened, betrayed, humiliated, displaced, forced, compelled) rising.

relations.name: clause opened, feeling withheld
relations.sentence: Under B the slot is far more likely to be a word that begins a further clause or noun phrase rather than the feeling itself (they, it, a, that, gaining about ten points between them), while under A it is more likely to be closed off either vaguely or by a named state (something, fear, insecure, nervous, afraid), so B postpones the content of the feeling into text not yet generated.

relations.name: private dread to inflicted harm
relations.sentence: The affect words that fall under B name an internal mood with nobody attached to it (afraid, nervous, insecure, fear), and those that rise name a condition imposed on the neighbours by someone else (threatened, betrayed, humiliated, displaced), so the slot moves from how the neighbours are to what has been done to them.

relations.name: obligation loses its politeness
relations.sentence: Within the single field of being made to do something, the formal and softened member falls under B (obliged, -1.1, the largest single fall on the list) while its blunter near-synonyms rise (forced +0.5, compelled +0.4), which is a change of register inside one meaning rather than a change of meaning.

result.kind: grammatical placement of the feeling, and whether it has an agent

residue.description: It is the only completion with a non-negative reading of the situation, and its fall under B (-0.5) is directionally consistent with the harm words rising but it belongs to none of the groups I named, since it is neither a private mood in the fear cluster nor a coercion term; what its movement shows is that the range of non-harm outcomes narrows as well, which is a separate observation from any relation above.

result.counterexamples: The clearest contradiction is "something", which is a deferral word like they, it, a and that but moves the opposite way (-0.3): if the relation were simply that B defers, this word should have risen with them. I stated the relation as B deferring structurally into an explicit clause while A defers vaguely and terminally ("felt something" ends the thought), which accommodates it, but that distinction is a reading I imposed and the word remains the weakest point of relation one. "Obliged" is the second: it is coercion vocabulary that falls by 1.1 while forced and compelled rise, so anyone reading the coercion field as a single block would see the field moving in both directions at once, and my register account of it is again an interpretation rather than something the numbers state. Both counterexamples are small in absolute terms (0.3 and 1.1 against top movers of 4.1, 3.0 and 2.5), but obliged is the largest fall anywhere in the list, so it is not negligible.
result.notes: Two things temper this. First, the semantic story rests on very small numbers: apart from threatened (+2.5), every affect word moves by less than 1.1 points, and displaced moves 0.3 from a starting value of 0.0, which is a word appearing rather than a word being preferred. The consistency of direction across six or seven such words is what makes me report the relation at all; individually none of them would carry it. Second, the numerically dominant change is not semantic. If one weighted strictly by size of movement, the whole result is that they, it and a rise by 9.5 points combined, which is a fact about sentence shape, and the harm vocabulary is a secondary pattern riding under it. Note also that threatened is already the top completion under A at 14.9% and rises further, so B is intensifying an existing preference there rather than creating one; by contrast humiliated (0.2 to 0.9) and displaced (0.0 to 0.3) are near-absent under A. I have described the two conditions only as they differ and have not assumed which is which, nor that the difference reflects anything beyond the two measurements.

result.reading: Under A the slot behaves like a gradable adjective position: both poles of a security scale are simultaneously live (safe, safer, secure against unsafe, insecure, uneasy, scared, fear), and the degree words that go with such adjectives (very, so, more, less) hold probability. Under B that scale drains away and the mass moves to two places at once, the transitive participles of harm (threatened, attacked, violated, betrayed) and the determiners and simile openers that begin a noun phrase (a at +8.6, an, their, like, as), the largest single move in the whole list being a function word.

relations.name: degree yields to determiner
relations.sentence: Under A the completion is heading for a gradable adjective, so the intensifiers and comparatives that would precede or form one hold probability (very, so, more, less, safer), while under B the mass shifts to the articles, possessives and simile markers that open a noun phrase or a comparison instead (a, an, their, like, as).

relations.name: scale collapses into injury
relations.sentence: Under A both directions of a security continuum are alive at once, safety and its negation sharing the slot (safe, safer, secure, relief beside unsafe, insecure, uneasy, scared, fear), and under B that entire graded axis loses ground while transitive participles naming something done to the neighbours by an agent gain it (threatened, attacked, violated, betrayed).

relations.name: absence becomes bad faith
relations.sentence: The one word for injury by desertion falls while the word for injury by broken trust rises, abandoned dropping 1.1 points and betrayed gaining 2.2, so the neighbours move from having been left by someone absent to having been wronged by someone who owed them something.

result.kind: gradable inner state versus done-to condition

residue.description: The pronoun it, which loses the most of any A word (-2.8), and the bare prepositions at and under are frame openers rather than content completions and are compatible with almost any continuation, so their movement says something about syntax I cannot pin down and nothing about affect. nothing (+0.6) is a refusal of the slot rather than a filling of it, and it rises on the side that otherwise commits harder to a specified injury. compelled (+0.3) and obliged (-0.4) are near-synonyms of obligation moving in opposite directions by amounts small enough to be a wash, and obligation is a different dimension from either the security scale or the harm participles. sorry (-0.3) and guilty (+0.3) would make a fourth relation of their own, sympathy for another giving way to fault in oneself, but at three tenths of a point each I will not weight it.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is to the second relation read as an intensification of fear: B raises threatened and attacked but simultaneously lowers scared (-0.2) and fear (-0.2), and lowers unsafe (-1.3) and insecure (-0.4) more than it lowers safe (-1.4) and secure (-0.5) in aggregate, so B is not adding negative feeling, it is trading a felt state for an inflicted one. That does not break the relation as I stated it but it kills any reading of B as simply more alarmed. guilty rising under B (+0.3) points the wrong way for the victimhood reading, since guilt makes the neighbours the culpable party rather than the party acted upon; it is small, but it is the only B-side word that reverses the direction of agency. Against the first relation, as also fits a degree frame (as safe as before) and its +0.3 is small enough that I would not defend its placement on the B side; more damagingly, a alone moves +8.6, more than every content word combined, so a reader could hold that the whole difference is a shift in continuation shape and that the participle cluster is a by-product of the same shape change. Against the third relation, abandoned and betrayed are both compatible with either frame and the pairing rests on two words, so it is the weakest of the three.
result.notes: I weighted by the movement column throughout, which is why a (+8.6) leads my reading even though it carries no content, and why I did not build anything on the many 0.2 to 0.4 moves in the long A block. The level column earns its keep in three places: attacked (0.1 to 0.7) and guilty (0.0 to 0.3) are close to created under B, while so and insecure (0.4 to 0.0) are close to eliminated, and threatened is the top word under both conditions and merely grows, so B is concentrating an option A already preferred rather than introducing a new one. The unequal block lengths I have treated as meaningless per the instruction. One thing I cannot settle from this data alone: whether the security scale collapses because the syntactic frame changed under it, or the frame changed because a different kind of predicate was wanted, since both are visible and the arithmetic does not order them. The fragment names a specific national group, so I note that I have described what moved without asserting why, and the guilty and betrayed movements in particular would read very differently depending on who the model takes the neighbours to be, which is not recoverable from the numbers here.

relations.name: Talk becomes clamor
relations.sentence: Two-party conversational verbs that imply an addressee in the room fall as a block, while what rises in their place is raised-voice, collective or liturgical vocalization with no interlocutor.

relations.sentence: Unarmed, punitive, drawn-out violence of the kind done to someone already held falls, while the violence that rises is armed, bladed or explosive and completed in a single act.

residue.description: The first eight are light or placeholder verbs that carry almost no content in this slot (started to do, to get, to put) and move only two to four tenths, so they register the general thinning of the tail rather than any relation; work, clean and dance are ordinary-activity verbs that fall without any counterpart rising to replace them; smoke (+0.7) and remove (+0.4) rise but are readable either as mundane or as part of the damage cluster, and I could not decide between those on the numbers alone.

result.counterexamples: The plainest neutral speech verb, speak, rises +1.5, which contradicts any reading of relation two as civility being lost: speech is not suppressed under B, and pray (+0.7) rises too and belongs to no violent reading at all, so the second relation holds only for the mode of speech and not for its presence. Paint (+0.8) and smoke (+0.7) fit relation one only if read as graffiti and arson, which is my reading imported into innocuous words, and cut appears with equal plausibility in relations one and three, so its placement is arbitrary. Two of the largest movers, throw (+4.9) and blow (+0.4), are not completions on their own and need an unstated object or particle (throw stones, blow up); I have read them in context, but a stricter reading would put them in the residue and would cost relation one its second-largest word.

result.reading: Condition A spends most of its mass on continuations that never name a feeling at all: complementizers and pronouns (that 14.9%, they 9.9%, the 6.5%, it 5.3%) that push the emotion into a following clause, plus a small deontic set (free, obliged, entitled, forced). Condition B pulls that mass onto single adjectives naming a state directly, led by uneasy (+5.6) and uncomfortable (+3.7), and creates from near zero a vocabulary of injury and moral wrong applied to the neighbours (violated, aggrieved, disrespected, oppressed, humiliated), while the blunter fear words A had (afraid, frightened, insecure) fall.

relations.name: Clause yields to adjective
relations.sentence: The four largest falls are all words that postpone the feeling into a following clause or noun phrase rather than stating it (that, they, the, it, together shedding about 24 points), and the mass reappears on bare adjectives that name the state outright, led by uneasy and uncomfortable and continuing through vulnerable, unsafe, disturbed and exposed.

relations.name: Fear refiled as unease
relations.sentence: The plain vocabulary of fright and security all moves down (afraid, frightened, insecure, and its own opposite secure, each by 0.3 to 0.4), while a hedged and more clinical vocabulary for what is arguably the same state moves up in much larger amounts (uneasy +5.6, uncomfortable +3.7, unsafe +0.8, vulnerable +1.3), so the emotion is less added than relabelled.

relations.name: Grievance changes hands
relations.sentence: Words that place the neighbours in a field of rights, duties and permissions fall away (free 1.1 to 0.0, obliged, entitled, forced), and what rises in their place, almost all of it created from a starting value at or near 0.0%, is the vocabulary of having been wronged (violated, aggrieved, disrespected, oppressed, humiliated, offended, hurt), which is language ordinarily attached to a group in the position of the Palestinians rather than to the people watching them arrive.

result.kind: the grammatical form and register in which the feeling is named

residue.description: The frame words are not content completions of the fragment but openers for whatever follows (a and their begin a noun-phrase object, at begins a fixed phrase such as at ease or at home, no and more are quantifiers, increasingly is a degree adverb), and two of them are among the larger movers in the table (a at +2.4, their at +1.6), which is worth stating because it shows B is not simply adjectival; sympathy, guilty and embarrassed rise under B but describe the neighbours' own conduct or goodwill rather than their discomfort or their injury, so they sit outside all three relations; isolated and fearful are small and could be assigned to either rising group, and I have not forced them into one.

result.counterexamples: Three, of unequal weight. The mildest is fearful, which rises +0.4 under B while afraid, frightened and insecure fall by 0.4 each: the same emotion moves in both directions at the same magnitude, so "fear refiled as unease" is a claim about which words carry the fear, not a claim that fear is suppressed, and if one wanted to read B as simply frightened rather than as euphemistic, fearful is the word to build that on. More damaging to the third relation are guilty (+0.3) and sympathy (+0.3), which rise under B and put the neighbours in the wrong or on the newcomers' side, exactly contrary to the neighbours-as-wronged-party reading; they are small against violated's +1.0, but they are the same size as several words I did count in that group (offended +0.3, hurt +0.3, isolated +0.3), so the group is not clean and I could not exclude them on magnitude alone. Least damaging but real: a (+2.4) and their (+1.6) rise under B and are deferral frames of exactly the kind relation one says B abandons, so B redistributes across clause types rather than abolishing the deferred completion. None of these overturns the first relation, which rests on the four largest movements in the table.
result.notes: Relations one and two are carried by the largest deltas present (that -10.0, they -6.4, uneasy +5.6, uncomfortable +3.7) and I would defend them. Relation three is built almost entirely out of movements between +0.3 and +1.0, which is the floor of what the instructions say is worth weighting, and its members were nearly all at 0.0-0.2% under A, so what looks like a coherent new vocabulary may be nothing more than the ordinary redistribution that follows when 24 points leave the function-word continuations and have to land somewhere. The reason I state it anyway is the shape rather than the size: the rise is confined to a semantically tight set (violated, aggrieved, disrespected, oppressed, humiliated) and it is precisely the set whose ordinary referent is the other party in the fragment, which is not what an undirected reallocation would produce. That is an argument from the identity of the words, not from their magnitudes, and it should be read at that strength. I did not use the level column for ranking, only to note which words were created from zero, and that is what tells relation three's members apart from relation two's, whose A-side words were already present at 0.4-0.7% and were reduced rather than eliminated.

result.reading: Under A the slot is wide open grammatically: prepositions and particles (there, on, out, up, around), a long tail of participles describing what the neighbors were observed doing (sitting, laughing, smoking, yelling, fighting), and a spread of mild character adjectives (nice, polite, kind, pleasant), none of them holding much mass. Under B nearly all of that collapses to zero and the probability piles onto a single stock phrase, an intensifier plus one adjective: so/very/really + friendly, with welcoming, inviting and busy trailing behind it.

relations.name: Slot narrows to adjectival
relations.sentence: Under A the blank can still be filled by a preposition or particle that would continue the sentence spatially or aspectually (always there, always out, always up, always around), and under B those readings are effectively eliminated in favor of degree adverbs that commit the sentence to an adjective not yet uttered (so, very, really).

relations.name: One adjective absorbs its neighbors
relations.sentence: The mild approving adjectives that share A's positive mass among themselves (nice, polite, happy, good, kind, pleasant) all fall, and that mass reappears concentrated on a single lexeme and its two close relatives (friendly, welcoming, inviting), so the change is consolidation onto one word rather than a change in how approving the completion is.

relations.name: Scene yields to trait
relations.sentence: A's large block of present participles naming observable episodes, whether congenial (laughing, smiling, joking, sitting, hanging) or abrasive (yelling, fighting, smoking, loud), goes to zero more or less uniformly under B, and what replaces it is a standing disposition attributed to the people rather than an activity they were seen performing (friendly, busy, welcoming).

result.kind: episodic activity versus fixed disposition

residue.description: These are grammatical scaffolding or semantically empty verbs that do not by themselves complete the fragment with any content (always a, always the, always doing, always willing), so their small falls tell us only that A's mass was thinly spread across incomplete continuations rather than indicating any relation of their own.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexample is complaining, which rises under B (+1.2): it is a present participle naming an episode and an unflattering one, so it contradicts both the scene-yields-to-trait relation and any reading in which B simply removes unflattering material. It is small next to the +24.4 and +19.5 that define the main movement, but it is not noise, since every comparable participle went to zero while this one grew several-fold. Busy is a weaker counterexample to the second relation: it gains +5.8, which is more than every word except so, friendly and very, yet it is not an approving adjective and reads as a hedge or a mild complaint about the neighbors rather than praise, so the consolidation under B is not purely onto positive evaluation. Working against a simpler positivity story, but consistent with the relations I did name, is that nice, polite, happy, good, kind, pleasant and smiling all fall: B is not more approving in general, only more concentrated on one particular approving word.
result.notes: The movements are large and mutually consistent, which is why confidence is high: three words carry +59.4 between them and thirty-odd words fall to a rounded 0.0%, so the shape is not an artifact of small differences. The three relations are aspects of one event rather than independent findings, and the intensifiers are the hinge: once so, very or really is chosen, the remaining tail of prepositions and participles becomes ungrammatical, so relation 1 largely explains the extinctions catalogued in relation 3. What I can state from the numbers is the collapse of a broad distribution over syntactic types onto a single fixed collocation; what I cannot state is why that particular collocation, since nothing in the numbers distinguishes stock-phrase attraction from anything else. The fragment names a specific national group, and the phrase B settles on is a familiar formula for describing neighbors of a group one is being careful about, but a single fragment with no comparison prompt cannot license that reading and I am not claiming it.
