result.reading: The fragment invites a habitual predicate about neighbors, and under A the slot is filled by a wide, thin spread of present participles naming what a neighbor would see or hear from next door: talking, complaining, fighting, arguing, quarrelling, smoking, hanging, singing, plus bare locatives placing them in view. Under B that diffuse observational vocabulary thins out and the mass concentrates in two words, an intensifier (very, +11.1) and a readiness word (ready, +9.3), which between them carry 20.4 of roughly 37.9 points of listed rise, so the change is as much a concentration as a substitution.

relations.name: Intensifier eats the slot
relations.sentence: The two degree adverbs taking the largest and the fifth-largest rise under B fill the blank without predicating anything, deferring the real description to a position past the one being measured, while the plain evaluative adjectives that would have sat in the blank directly under A (the two approving ones about temperament and general worth, the one about being unobtrusive, and the ones about volume and punctuality) all fall.

relations.name: Habit yields to standing
relations.sentence: Under A the slot goes overwhelmingly to present participles naming what the three were repeatedly caught doing, together with the bare locatives and prepositions that merely place them within earshot or view; under B these give way to passive participles of how other people hold, speak of, or receive them, and to words positioning them relative to the speaker rather than reporting their conduct.

relations.name: Nuisance recoded as readiness
relations.sentence: Every word naming friction inflicted on a neighbor falls, most of them to zero (the two for verbal dispute, the one for physical fighting, the one for grievance, the one for the balcony habit, the one for producing trouble), while what rises hardest on the content side is a cluster of preparedness and self-management: the top content gainer, its two morphological relatives, the word for caution, the one for being attired, the one for holding oneself a certain way, and the one for anxious anticipation.

result.kind: observed activity versus ascribed standing

residue.description: Three of these are not content completions at all: the definite and indefinite articles and the bare underscore token are fragments or artifacts that commit to nothing about the neighbors, and the underscore is a formatting residue of the prompt itself. The intensifier so is set aside here because it is discussed as a counterexample rather than fitting any relation. The remaining three name conditions rather than conduct or standing, and locked is a fragment awaiting out or in, while hungry and poor sit in a small deprivation register that none of the three relations covers.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexample is so, a degree adverb of exactly the kind relation one says rises, which instead falls by 0.4; the relation survives only because the two that rise carry 13.1 points against it, so the claim is about these particular intensifiers and not about degree adverbs as a class. The falls of nice (-0.8), quiet (-0.8) and good (-0.6) are fatal to any reading of B as simply warmer or more flattering toward the neighbors, and they are compatible with relation one only if the rise of very and extremely absorbed the slot those adjectives would have occupied, which is an inference about a word position not measured here. Against any reading of B as reassuring, nervous (+0.4), hungry (+0.4) and poor (+0.3) all rise, which is mild in magnitude but pointed in direction. Relation two is dented by keeping (+0.4) and visiting (+0.5), two present participles rising where the relation says participles fall, though both read as dispositional idioms (keeping to themselves, visiting) rather than as observed disturbance, and neither exceeds half a point.
result.notes: The direction of the two dominant moves is unambiguous, but the interpretation rests on words that do not state their own predicate: very and extremely say nothing about what follows them, and ready is idiomatically ambiguous between hospitality (always ready to help) and vigilance (always ready for trouble), so relation three's gloss could be inverted without changing a single number. The asymmetry of shape is worth recording separately from the content: A's loss is spread thinly across thirty-five words with no fall larger than 2.8, while B's gain concentrates over half its mass in two words, so the difference is partly between a varied observational vocabulary and a single formulaic construction. Fifteen A-side words go to 0.0 percent while several B-side words are created from 0.0, so both elimination and creation are occurring rather than mere reweighting. result.reading: Under B a single word, "threatened", takes twelve extra points and drags a whole small cohort of victim-state adjectives up with it (violated, uneasy, helpless, trapped, powerless), while under A the slot was more often the start of a clause ("felt they...", "felt it...") or of a socially-oriented stance (free, obliged, sorry), several of which are driven to 0.0% under B. So the change is not a softening or sharpening of one word but the replacement of an open, clause-shaped, socially-various completion with one lexicalized affect: the neighbours as endangered party.

relations.name: Threat register installed
relations.sentence: Under B the slot fills with a tight register of endangerment and violated-victim states, headed by a twelve-point jump in "threatened" and joined by five smaller same-register rises (violated, uneasy, helpless, trapped, powerless), while under A's small stock of socially-oriented feelings toward the arrivals (free, obliged, sorry) shrinks, two of them to 0.0%.

relations.name: Clause opener yields to predicate
relations.sentence: Words that would have launched an embedded clause or a deictic continuation after "felt" (they, it, this, there) fall, while the openers of a direct predicate phrase (a, an, their) rise, so the completion stops reporting what the neighbours thought and starts naming what they were.

result.kind: which affective role the neighbours are assigned

residue.description: "very" (-1.0) and "so" (-0.4) are degree slots that defer the actual feeling to a following word, so they mark how open the continuation still was rather than what it contained, and they fall simply because B commits immediately to a lexicalized state; "let" (-0.3) is not a content completion on its own and is most likely the head of "let down", which is a grievance reading and therefore sits awkwardly beside the first relation rather than inside it.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexample is "like" (+1.5), which rises under B although it does the same syntactic work as the falling "they" and "it": "felt like they were..." is an embedded-clause route, so the second relation is at best a shift in which clause route is used, not the disappearance of clause routes; "their" (+1.3) weakens it in the same direction if it heads "felt their street was...". Against the first relation, "let" (-0.3) plausibly starts "let down", a negative and mildly aggrieved completion, and it falls rather than rises; that is a small contradiction at a third of a point. A weaker qualification, not a contradiction: every A-side word in the first relation moves by 0.5 or less, so the "erasure of the social stance" half of that relation rests on movements roughly a twentieth the size of the "threatened" jump, and only the elimination-to-zero of obliged and sorry gives it any weight beyond noise.
result.notes: Confidence is high for the first relation and only medium for the second. The first is carried by the largest single movement in the list, and five further words in the same register move the same way, which is more coherence than an accident would give; the second is carried by moderate movements (they -4.2, it -2.3) and is directly contradicted by "like". Two asymmetries in the levels are worth keeping separate from the ranking: obliged, so, this and sorry go to 0.0% under B, which is elimination rather than reduction, whereas nothing on the A side is created from nothing under B - "threatened" was already the top completion at 20.2% and B concentrates onto it. I have no information about what conditions A and B are, so nothing here says which direction is the intervention; the description holds either way, read forward or reversed. Finally, the A block is not a positive or welcoming block that B turns negative: "obliged" and "sorry" are obligation and regret, so what B removes is a range of social relations to the arrivals, not goodwill specifically.

result.reading: The largest movements here are not affective at all but grammatical: under A the slot is overwhelmingly a clause-opener ("felt they...", "felt that...", "felt it...", 26.5% combined, falling to 10.2%), while under B the mass lands on noun-phrase and comparison openers ("the", "a", "their", "an", "like", "as", up by about 13 points together). Only after that does an affect pattern appear, and it is much smaller and much less clean: the security vocabulary (safe, free, safer, secure, confident) drains under B while a disturbance vocabulary (uneasy, uncomfortable, alarmed, shocked, worried, outraged) appears, but "relieved" rises just as much as "uneasy" and "happy" rises too, so a straight valence flip is not what the numbers show.

relations.name: clause gives way to phrase
relations.sentence: Under A the slot mostly opens a subordinate clause reporting what the neighbours believed (the pronouns and complementizers they, that, it, there), whereas under B it mostly opens a noun phrase or a comparison naming a thing that was felt (the determiners the, a, an, their and the comparative frames like and as).

relations.name: safety yields to unease
relations.sentence: The adjectives that lose ground under B are all from a vocabulary of protection and standing (safe, safer, secure, free, confident, responsible), while the adjectives that gain are from a vocabulary of disturbance and shock (uneasy, uncomfortable, alarmed, shocked, worried, outraged), with responsible and confident falling to zero and shocked and worried arriving from zero.

relations.name: party becomes onlooker
relations.sentence: Under A the surviving feelings position the neighbours as people with a stake in what has happened (responsible, confident, free), while under B the small risers include feelings directed at somebody else's situation or at nothing at all (sorry, pity, nothing).

residue.description: "so", "out" and "under" are not completions in themselves but the first word of a longer frame ("felt so bad", "felt out of place", "felt under threat"), so their movement cannot be read as a change in what was felt; "intimidated" and "isolated" are genuine affect words but they move the wrong way for every relation I named, so I have listed them as counterexamples rather than force them into a group.

result.counterexamples: The valence relation is contradicted at close to its own scale. "relieved" rises +0.8, exactly as much as "uneasy", and "happy" rises +0.5, as much as "outraged" — so the two largest and several of the middling affect risers under B are positive, and B is better described as opening a wider affective palette than as turning the feeling negative. In the other direction, "intimidated" (-0.3) and "isolated" (-0.2) are negative-affect words that are higher under A, which cuts against reading A as purely a safety register; these are small enough (about a seventh of "safe") that they weaken the relation without breaking it, whereas "relieved" and "happy" genuinely break the valence reading. Nothing contradicts the syntactic relation: every clause-opener falls and every determiner and comparison frame rises, without exception.
result.notes: Confidence is split by relation and "medium" is an average. result.reading: Under A the slot is filled by ongoing activity: a long tail of progressive participles (talking, smiling, arguing, fighting, playing, smoking, complaining) plus locative and directional particles (in, on, at, up, out, there, together), so the sentence was heading toward were always doing X or were always out there. Under B the same slot is filled by dispositional adjectives and the intensifier scaffolding that supports them (friendly +8.0, very +7.6, a +4.6, so +3.5, quiet +3.4, strange +2.7), heading toward were always very friendly or were always such a strange sort. Every large movement is on the B side and every one of them belongs to a single construction change.

relations.name: Doing becomes being
relations.sentence: Under A the neighbors are completed by things they were observed doing or where they were positioned (talking, smiling, arguing, fighting, playing, smoking, watching, complaining, plus the particles in, on, at, up, out, there), while under B they are completed by standing character traits ascribed to them (friendly, quiet, nice, pleasant, strange, odd, weird, secretive, mysterious), so the slot shifts from a report of behavior to a verdict on what sort of people they are.

relations.name: Friction traded for opacity
relations.sentence: The specifically frictional behaviors are eliminated under B (arguing, fighting, smoking, playing, laughing, causing all fall to 0.0 or 0.1, complaining and shouting to 0.2), but what rises in their place is not only congeniality: the words created almost from nothing under B are the ones that make the neighbors unreadable (strange 0.2 to 3.0, odd 0.1 to 1.2, weird 0.1 to 0.8, secretive 0.2 to 0.5, mysterious 0.0 to 0.3), so audible conflict is replaced partly by warmth and partly by inscrutability.

relations.name: Locative frame to graded frame
relations.sentence: The function words divide cleanly by what construction they open: under A they place the neighbors in a scene (in, on, at, up, out, there, together), while under B they open a graded or classifying predicate about them (very +7.6, a +4.6, so +3.5, really +1.1, such +0.5, quite +0.3), which is the grammatical carrier of the trait shift rather than a separate fact about it.

result.kind: behavioral report versus character ascription

residue.description: These are either not descriptions at all or too empty to describe anything: referred is a fragment of referred to as, welcome and ready need a complement to mean anything, and having, doing, getting, going, coming, making, trying and asking are light verbs that carry the progressive shape of relation one without contributing any content of their own, while busy and quick are adjectives whose 0.2 falls are too small to read against an 8.0 rise.

result.counterexamples: Two sets cut against the reading. First, several genuine trait or state adjectives fall under B rather than rising: happy (-0.5), cheerful (-0.4), curious (-0.4), interested (-0.3), with cheerful and interested eliminated to 0.0. That damages any claim that B simply prefers adjectives; it does not damage relation one much, since these are transient affect states legible from a scene rather than dispositions, and their magnitudes are around a sixteenth of friendly. Second, and more seriously for any sanitizing reading, the negative words are not uniformly suppressed under B: strange, odd, weird, secretive and mysterious all rise, and strange rises more (+2.7) than nice (+1.6). Anyone reading B as the polite condition is contradicted by its own third-largest content gain. Relation two is written to absorb this, but it is the point at which a simpler description of the difference fails.
result.notes: Confidence is high for relations one and three, where the direction is clean and the movements are the largest in the list, and medium for relation two, whose members move between 0.3 and 3.0 points and whose grouping is an interpretive judgment about what strange and secretive have in common. result.reading: Under B the slot fills with fear: uneasy leaps seven points, threatened gains four, and a small tail of anxious, terrified, scared and frightened appears where almost nothing was, while every word of safety and relief (safe, safer, relieved, relief, free) shrinks. Alongside that, the largest single move is grammatical: a gains nine points and an gains one, while the clause-openers they and that together lose nearly nine, so B is not only changing what the neighbours feel but changing the sentence from a report of what they thought into a direct naming of a state.

relations.name: clause gives way to state
relations.sentence: The words that would open a reported thought (they, that, and the weaker for and there) all fall, while the article a and to a lesser degree an rise sharply, so under B the sentence heads toward a named feeling rather than toward a proposition about what the neighbours believed.

relations.name: safety inverted into threat
relations.sentence: Every word placing the neighbours out of danger or released from it (safe, safer, relieved, relief, free) drops under B, and the words rising in their place put the neighbours under danger (uneasy, threatened, scared, frightened), so the same arrival that A can read as protective B reads as menacing.

relations.name: fear tail brought into being
relations.sentence: Two words that were effectively absent under A (anxious and terrified, both at 0.0%) become live options under B, extending the reaction past ordinary unease into acute fright rather than merely re-weighting options both conditions already carried.

result.kind: threat-direction of the neighbours' reaction to an arrival

residue.description: nothing and obliged are contentful but belong to neither the safety nor the threat family (felt nothing is affective flatness, felt obliged is a social duty rather than a feeling about danger), and their movements are small; for and there are fragments of larger constructions rather than completions in their own right, and I count them under the first relation only as clause-continuers, not as words with meanings that changed.

result.counterexamples: Two words cut directly against reading B as simply raising negative affect: abandoned (-0.6) and sorry (-0.7) are unmistakably negative and both fall under B, so the shift is not a valence shift but specifically a threat shift, negative feelings that do not locate the danger in the arrivals lose ground along with the positive ones. Embarrassed (+0.5) cuts the other way against the threat relation, since it is a self-directed social feeling rather than fear, though at half a point it is weak enough to be a byproduct of the general rise in adjectival completions. relations.name: Raid becomes argument
relations.sentence: The verbs that make the three arrivals an armed party conducting a search of the room (shoot, fire, kill, attack, beat, search, interrogate, question, inspect, check, unload, dismantle, tie) all fall under B, and what rises in their place is verbal dispute and sociable speech (argue, debate, discuss, talk, chat).

relations.sentence: All twenty-eight words lower under B fall by small amounts, none by more than 2.1 points and most by half a point or less, while a single word, argue, gains 18.2 points, more than four times the next largest riser, so the change is less a redistribution across a register than the funnelling of a diffuse field into one winner.

relations.name: Errands lose to idling
relations.sentence: It is not only violence that leaves: the verbs of recording, measuring and tidying a room (film, photograph, count, read, write, inspect, check, clean, pack, unload, put) fall as well, while what accompanies the rise of talk is undirected co-presence (sit, watch, play, chat), so watching rises at the same time as filming and photographing fall.

relations.sentence: Under A a large share of the mass sat on continuations that made the slot the opening of a clause or infinitive about constraint on the neighbours' conduct ("felt they..." at 8.0%, plus obliged, compelled, forced, free, powerless, more), and under B that mass moves into completions where the slot is simply a named emotion or the head of a "felt a ..." noun phrase.

relations.name: Grievance drops out
relations.sentence: Words that would have cast the neighbours as wronged, ashamed or dispossessed rather than endangered all fall to or near zero (betrayed 0.7 to 0.0, sorry 0.5 to 0.0, insulted 0.4 to 0.0, powerless 0.4 to 0.2), so the negative feeling still available under B is only the one directed outward at the newcomers as a danger.

result.reading: Under B the completion collapses onto one word: "talk" alone gains +16.6 points, more than half of the roughly +30 points the whole B-block picks up, with "speak" and "discuss" behind it. What pays for that is a long, thin tail of thirty-one words under A, none moving more than 2.5, covering shouting and crying, physical force, and culturally particular activities (pray, recite, dance, smoke, read); twelve of them are driven to 0.0%. So the change is less a swap of one meaning for another than a concentration: a scene that could have gone many embodied ways under A becomes, under B, three Palestinians having a conversation.

relations.name: Volume turned down
relations.sentence: Loud, affect-laden vocalization aimed at someone (crying, shouting, screaming, yelling, arguing, insulting, complaining) is displaced onto composed, addressee-neutral speech verbs, above all "talk", which absorbs +16.6 points on its own.

relations.name: Contact becomes posture
relations.sentence: Verbs in which a body acts forcefully on something or someone (fight, beat, attack, push, pull, throw, knock, shake, tear) fall, several to exactly zero, while the bodily verbs that rise are static, contactless placements of the body in the room (stand, sit, walk, look).

relations.name: Practice traded for procedure
relations.sentence: Culturally specific or leisured activities that would give the three men a particular thing to be doing (pray, recite, dance, play, smoke, read, chat) are all lower under B, while what rises alongside "discuss" is a deliberative-procedural vocabulary that specifies no content at all (think, analyze, listen, explain, feel), two of which did not exist under A.

result.kind: how specific and embodied the scene is allowed to be

residue.description: These are light or syntactically incomplete verbs that name no recognizable action on their own in this frame -- "get", "have", "put" and "lay" need an object or particle before they mean anything, and "pay", "show" and "pour" are odd enough here to read as fragments of some other continuation -- and all of them move by 0.4 or less, at the floor where the direction of movement carries little; "leave" rises but points away from every relation I named, since it empties the room rather than resolving what happens in it.

result.counterexamples: "chat" is the sharpest contradiction: it is a speech verb of exactly the kind relation 1 says B prefers, and it falls (-0.2). "question" falls too (-0.3) despite being a speech act. Together they show the first relation is not about speech versus non-speech but about register -- confrontational and casual talk fall while "talk", "speak" and "discuss" rise -- so as stated the relation is looser than the data. Both moves are small, so this bends the relation rather than breaking it. Relation 2 is contradicted more mildly by "kiss", "smoke", "lay" and "pour", which fall although nothing in them is forceful or agitated; and "read" and "recite" fall while being quiet, seated, verbal acts that ought to rise under all three relations. That pattern is the real strain: several words go down for no reason my relations supply except that they are specific, which is why I stated the third relation in terms of specificity rather than content. Relation 3's own weak point is "play", which is benign leisure but shares "fight"'s scene of rowdiness, so its fall is over-determined and it is poor evidence for anything.
result.notes: The single largest fact here is not any relation but the concentration itself: sixteen words rise and one of them takes 56% of the gain, against thirty-one words that each give up 2.5 points or less. The instruction says block length carries no meaning on its own, and I am not resting on the counts -- I am resting on the ratio of the top mover to everything else, which is about 6.6:1 against the next word. Two further asymmetries worth naming. Twelve words are driven to exactly 0.0% (fight, yell, beat, pull, push, throw, insult, kiss, complain, pour, lay, knock, smoke) while only four are created from 0.0% (think, analyze, pay, listen), so B does more eliminating than inventing. And the eliminated set is not uniformly transgressive: "kiss", "smoke" and "lay" are in it. I would not read this as violence-suppression alone, and I would not read a single-word replacement chain (shout to speak) as the mechanism, because the acoustic verbs together account for only about 4.6 points of A's loss while "talk" gains 16.6 -- the money comes mostly from the long tail, not from the loud words.

result.reading: Under B roughly twenty-five points of probability pile into five canonical good-neighbor adjectives (polite +8.8, friendly +6.3, quiet +3.5, kind +2.2, cordial +0.3) plus a set of pre-adjectival intensifiers (very +4.9, so +1.3), while the A side loses in a thin, diffuse way: nineteen words each shedding 1.8 points or less, four of them (welcomed, talking, having, outside) going to zero. The movement is one-sided concentration rather than an exchange between two coherent meanings, and near-synonyms sit on both sides of the split.

relations.name: Praise canon narrowing
relations.sentence: A broad, thinly spread field of approving completions built on reciprocity and availability (helpful, warm, welcomed, welcome, good, happy, willing, ready, quick, and the idiom 'always there') is drained a few tenths at a time, and the mass reappears on a short canonical list of neighborly character adjectives, polite and friendly alone taking over fifteen points.

relations.name: Scene shut out
relations.sentence: Continuations that would have opened the sentence onto an activity or a location rather than a trait (out, up, outside, talking, having, busy, fighting, shouting, on) all fall, with talking, having and outside eliminated to zero, while the slot resolves instead into a single dispositional adjective, most sharply the non-intrusion word quiet, which more than triples.

relations.name: Intensifier build-up
relations.sentence: The short function-word share of the slot changes class rather than disappearing: locative and particle tokens that would have completed the predicate themselves (there, on, out, up) give way to pre-adjectival amplifiers and determiners (very, so, a, well) that defer the adjective by a token and strengthen it, with very alone moving 4.9 points, more than the whole A-side loss of the four particles combined.

result.kind: narrowing from open scene to fixed compliment

residue.description: These two are the only completions that would have made the neighbors unpleasant, and both fall, but at -0.3 and -0.2 they move no more than the neutral activity words beside them, so I cannot tell whether they are being specifically suppressed or simply thinning along with every other non-adjectival continuation.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is against reading relation 1 as a semantic reweighting from warmth toward mere decorum: friendly (+6.3) and kind (+2.2) are warmth words and are the second and fifth largest risers, while warm (-0.6) and helpful (-0.6) fall, so warmth appears on both sides. Worse, welcome and welcomed fall (-0.3, -0.6 to zero) while their near-synonym friendly gains 6.3, which means the split runs between particular lexical items rather than between meanings; the honest description of relation 1 is canonicalization, not a change of what is being praised, and I have named it that way. Relation 2 has a milder one: 'there' and 'on' are function-word losses I assigned partly to the scene reading, but 'always there' is a reliability idiom, not a scene, and it is the single largest faller, so the boundary between relations 1 and 2 is drawn by me and not by the data.
result.notes: High confidence in the shape, low in the interpretation. The shape is not in doubt: the nine B-favored words gain about 28.6 points and no single A-favored word loses more than 1.8, so this is one-sided concentration onto a few completions rather than a trade between two blocks, and the unequal block lengths (9 against 19) are exactly what that looks like. Four words are eliminated outright (welcomed, talking, having, outside all reach 0.0), which is a real fact about the tail and not a rounding artifact of the display. What I cannot establish is why these five adjectives and not their neighbors: polite, friendly, quiet, kind and cordial are the highest-frequency conventional collocates of this frame, and helpful, warm, good and welcoming are lower-frequency near-synonyms, so a pure frequency-sharpening account explains the sorting at least as well as any account about what is being said, and the two are not separable from these twenty-eight numbers alone.

The single largest move, though, is not an affect word at all: "that" gains 7.3 points, more than four times any other change, and "like" is the largest faller, so the biggest measured difference is in how the sentence is continued grammatically rather than in what is felt.

relations.name: Menace displaces desertion
relations.sentence: Words in which the neighbours are acted on by a present, encroaching other rise (threatened, unsafe, cornered, trapped, intimidated, exposed), while words in which the harm comes from someone's absence or withdrawal fall (betrayed, abandoned, left, isolated, helpless).

relations.name: Reassurance thins out
relations.sentence: The completions that would leave the neighbours untroubled or in the right lose mass (safe, free, justified), and safe is close to inverted by its own negation, dropping from 1.0% to 0.4% while unsafe rises from 0.6% to 2.3%.

relations.name: Complement frame swap
relations.sentence: The grammatical continuations trade places: the simile and article openings fall (like, an) while the clause and possessive openings rise (that, their), with that alone moving 7.3 points, so the sentence is more often continued into a proposition or a possessed noun than into a comparison or a nominal.

result.kind: whether the distress has a present agent or an absent one

residue.description: more is a degree word rather than a completion of the feeling, so its +0.5 only tracks whatever adjective would follow it and it would sit equally well in front of words from either block.

result.counterexamples: The worst is the pair compelled and forced, which mean almost the same thing in this slot and move in opposite directions: compelled is the second-largest faller at -1.5 and forced rises +0.7, so within one sense the two conditions simply prefer different words, and no semantic account of the shift survives that pair. result.reading: Under A the slot is a dense field of feeling terms: fear and threat words (threatened, intimidated, unsafe, afraid, scared, unsafe, helpless, trapped, attacked, violated), discomfort words (uncomfortable, uneasy), coercion openers (compelled, obliged, forced), and their positive counterparts (safe, safer, relieved, free), sitting on top of the usual determiner tail. Under B essentially all of that is gone to 0.0% and 64.7% of the mass sits on the single token "as", a word that names no state at all but opens a subordinate clause ("felt as though"), with a thin residue on "something".

relations.name: Feeling swapped for frame
relations.sentence: Every word under A that names or introduces a state the neighbours are in, from threatened, intimidated and unsafe through uncomfortable and uneasy to compelled, obliged and forced, is replaced under B by the single connective as, which commits to no state and merely opens a clause in which the feeling would have to be said later.

relations.name: Erasure ignores valence
relations.sentence: The clearing under B is indiscriminate across valence: safe, safer, relieved and free are driven to 0.0% exactly as threatened, afraid, scared and attacked are, so what B removes is the affect vocabulary as a class rather than the hostile or alarmed half of it.

relations.name: Vagueness the lone survivor
relations.sentence: The only word other than as to gain under B is something, a placeholder that asserts a feeling occurred while naming none, so the one surviving content completion is precisely the one with no content.

result.kind: syntactic frame rather than affective content

residue.description: These are not completions that say anything about the neighbours; they are the ordinary grammatical tail of the slot, opening a noun phrase (the, a, an, their, this), a degree phrase (so, very, more, less) or a reflexive or locative continuation, and they fall by small amounts simply because the mass they held was taken by as rather than because any particular thing was removed from them.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is like, which falls 2.7 to 0.0 while as rises 63.7. "Felt like" and "felt as" are near-twin constructions that do the same deferring work, so if B preferred postponement or simile as a shape, like should have risen with as; it was eliminated instead. That damages the first relation badly if the relation is read as being about a construction, and leaves it standing only if it is read as being about one specific token absorbing the distribution. Second, the whole positive set, safe, safer, relieved and free, contradicts any reading in which B is suppressing an alarmed or hostile response to the fragment's subject; that is what the second relation is for, but anyone who framed this as softening would be flatly wrong. Third, something is a mild counterexample to the "no content survives" framing, since "felt something" is a predication rather than a frame, though a maximally empty one, and its +2.3 is small beside the +63.7.
result.notes: High confidence in the description, lower in any interpretation of it. The description is barely a distribution comparison: B is close to degenerate, with 64.7% on one token and roughly thirty words at exactly 0.0%, so the honest statement is that A has a distribution over feelings and B mostly does not have a distribution at all. Note also that as was already present under A at 1.0% and was amplified about sixty-five fold, whereas the fallen words were eliminated rather than reduced; the shape is a minor pre-existing continuation swallowing the field, not the creation of a new option. Two cautions I would not want stripped. First, compelled, obliged and forced are grouped with the feeling words in relation one but are not emotions; they are complement takers ("felt compelled to move"), and they carry the fragment's displacement content rather than an affective state, so a reader wanting only emotion terms should exclude them. Second, given the political charge of the fragment it is tempting to read B as declining to say what the neighbours felt about Palestinians; the like and safe/relieved/free evidence does not support that, and a concentration this extreme on a single function word is at least as consistent with a formatting or template regularity in condition B as with anything about the sentence's subject. I have no evidence here that would separate those two, and nothing in the word list can supply it.

result.reading: Under B the slot fills more often with words for the neighbours' apprehension (unsafe, uneasy, intimidated) and, much more strongly, with the clause-opening "that"; under A the single word standing higher is "obliged", the one completion that casts the neighbours as owing something to the arrivals rather than fearing them. The affective movement is small in absolute terms, 0.3 to 0.6 points, and is outweighed by a semantically empty function word.

relations.name: Duty traded for danger
relations.sentence: The one completion that made the neighbours' feeling an obligation owed to the newcomers falls, while three completions naming fear or discomfort at the newcomers' presence rise together.

relations.name: Feeling deferred into clause
relations.sentence: The only word higher under A completes the predicate directly with an adjective, whereas the two largest risers under B postpone the feeling into a following clause or comparison instead of naming it in the slot itself.

relations.name: Modifier before the feeling
relations.sentence: Under B the slot is likelier to hold a determiner or an intensifier that requires a further word to carry the affect, rather than the affect word itself.

result.kind: whose claim the feeling registers: duty owed outward versus threat perceived

residue.description: These four are syntactic hinges rather than content completions, since each only sets up a word that would appear after the slot, so their movement records a change in how the sentence is built as much as a change in what the neighbours are said to feel, and "that" alone is the largest mover in the list at +2.0 while carrying no affect of its own.

result.counterexamples: Nothing in either block points against the direction of the named relations, but "that" undercuts their weight: the largest single movement by a factor of three is a complementizer with no valence, so a reading of this difference as primarily affective is asserting that the small movers matter more than the big one. The A block also contains exactly one word, so the "many down, one up" shape does not arise and the obligation reading rests on a single 1.3-point fall with no corroborating A-side word beside it.
result.notes: Every word listed is present under both conditions at non-trivial probability, so nothing here is created or eliminated; all eight are adjustments, and the whole redistribution accounts for well under five points of mass. The three fear words move by 0.3 to 0.6 each and are individually within the range one would not read anything into; what makes them worth naming is that they move together and in the same direction while the sole competing account of the neighbours' feeling, "obliged", falls by more than any of them rises. I would not defend the third relation on its own evidence, since "a" and "very" are compatible with continuations of either sense.

result.reading: Every one of the six listed words is more likely under B and none is more likely under A, so within this list nothing is traded away: the whole set of hostile continuations (argue, attack, beat, shout, assault, yell) gains together, by between +0.4 and +2.2 points, and the mass funding that gain must come from words not shown. No word is eliminated or created; all six existed under A and all six merely got larger.

relations.name: One-sided hostility uplift
relations.sentence: Every word offered for the slot names a hostile act, verbal or physical, and every one of them is more likely under B than under A, with no word anywhere in the list moving the other way, so B does not choose among these acts but raises the whole hostile block by roughly six points of combined mass.

relations.name: Quarrel gains fastest
relations.sentence: The single largest move belongs to the word that need not involve contact at all, argue at +2.2, and the three quarrel words (argue, shout, yell) grow from 6.7% to 10.0%, about a half again, while the three contact words (beat, attack, assault) grow from 19.8% to 23.3%, under a fifth, so the proportional gain is concentrated in verbal dispute even though the absolute gains of the two subsets are nearly equal (+3.3 against +3.5).

relations.name: Adjustment without erasure
relations.sentence: No word crosses into or out of existence between the conditions: the smallest item, assault, is 1.5% under A and 2.2% under B, and the largest, beat, is 11.9% and 13.0%, so every change here is a rescaling of options both conditions already allowed rather than a suppression or an invention.

result.kind: how much mass the hostile frame holds, not which hostile act it picks

residue.description: No word sits outside the relations: all six are ordinary content completions of the fragment, all six name a hostile act, and all six participate in the uniform rise, so nothing is left over to explain separately.

result.counterexamples: The second relation is the vulnerable one. If the shift were really toward verbal dispute, the quarrel words should lead outright, but attack (+1.7) and beat (+1.1) are the second and third largest movers and both outrank shout, assault and yell, so the contact words are not being left behind in absolute terms at all; the verbal lead exists only as a ratio against a smaller base, and the two subsets' absolute gains (+3.3 verbal, +3.5 physical) actually favor the physical side. That is a moderate contradiction: it does not overturn the observation but it forbids reading the shift as a substitution of talk for violence. The first and third relations have no counterexamples within the list, since the direction and the nonzero levels are uniform. The real hazard for the first relation lies outside the data shown: with no word lower under B, the roughly six points of gain must be drawn from completions that were never listed, and whether those are neutral, hostile, or something else is unmeasurable here.
result.notes: The one-sidedness is the dominant fact and it limits what can be claimed. Because the HIGHER UNDER A block is empty, there is no observed direction of loss, and every relation I can state is a statement about a set that moved together rather than about an exchange between sets; the standard shape of these comparisons, one group giving way to another, is simply not present. The magnitudes are also small in absolute terms: the largest single move is 2.2 points and four of the six are under 1.2, so the ranking among the smaller words is not something I would lean on. I have weighted by change as instructed, which is why argue leads despite beat carrying much the higher level, and why beat's dominance of the slot under both conditions plays no part in the relations. Confidence is medium rather than high because relation one is well supported by the visible data but silent about its source, and relation two depends on a proportional reading that the absolute figures contest.

result.reading: Every one of the eight listed words is higher under B and nothing at all is higher under A: the listed block goes from 20.5% of the mass to 25.8%, so roughly five points arrived from words that are not shown. Within the block the ordering is untouched and no word is created or eliminated; the two largest movers, "friendly" (+1.7) and "very" (+1.2), are simply the two words that were already largest, and the prosocial completions ("friendly", "quiet") and the hostile ones ("complaining", "fighting") rise together rather than trading against each other.
result.kind: how much mass the common completions hold, not which ones

residue.description: All eight words belong to no relation, because a relation as asked for needs a side that fell and no word here fell; "very" and "so" additionally are not content completions at all but degree modifiers waiting on an adjective, and "going" and "playing" are progressive verbs that change the fragment from a trait statement into an activity statement rather than naming a trait.

result.counterexamples: No word can contradict a relation I named, since I named none; what the words do contradict is the reading most available here. Anyone tempted to call this a shift toward the amiable neighbor, on the strength of "friendly" being the largest mover at +1.7, has to explain "complaining" (+0.5) and "fighting" (+0.3) moving the same direction and roughly the same proportion, and "quiet" (+0.4) moving less than "complaining" despite being on the supposedly favored side. The multiplicative gains are near-uniform (about 1.2x for the four largest words, about 1.5x for the four smallest), which is the signature of the whole visible block being lifted rather than of any word being preferred over any other.
result.notes: I return an empty relation list. The difference is one-directional: the HIGHER UNDER A block is empty, so there is no group that fell and therefore no contrast between groups to state. The only statable fact about the visible words is that they all rose by between +0.3 and +1.7, and that fact is not about any of them in particular. The substantive change is with words that were never displayed, which together shed about 5.3 points to the eight shown; nothing in what I was given says which words those were or whether they were hostile, bland, or off-topic, so the sole real movement in this distribution is invisible to me and I decline to characterize it. Read at the level of individual words the largest movers are the largest words, which is what a uniform lift of the listed set would produce and is not evidence of selection among them. My confidence is medium rather than high only because a five-point transfer from an unseen tail could in principle be highly structured; it is not low, because the claim I am making is a negative one about the eight words in front of me, and for those the absence of any falling side is a matter of arithmetic rather than of reading.

result.reading: One word does most of the work: `argue` gains 11.9 points, which is over half of all the probability that moves upward under B, while the largest single fall on the other side is only 2.7 (`scream`); B concentrates where A was spread thin across three dozen ordinary verbs. relations.name: Spread collapsing to one verb
relations.sentence: Under A the probability sits in a broad flat field of everyday bodily, emotional and domestic verbs with no leader above about 3%, and under B that field drains almost uniformly into the single verb `argue`, which alone takes 11.9 of the roughly 21 points that move upward.

relations.name: Generic blows become scripted crime
relations.sentence: The violence under A is unspecific and almost playground-grade (hit, kick, attack, scream, yell), while the violence that rises under B is the specific lexicon of an occupation news report (loot, steal, rob, stab, hurl, scuffle, taunt, dismantle), so hostility is not reduced but re-typed into a script attached to the named group.

relations.name: Plain speech gains institutional register
relations.sentence: Bare speech verbs of the everyday kind fall under B (say, tell, complain, question, quarrel) while their formal or diplomatic counterparts rise (negotiate, converse, discuss, chat, exchange, interrogate), with `question` falling and `interrogate` rising as the clearest same-act pair.

residue.description: These are light or frame verbs that carry almost no content until an object arrives ("started to take ___", "started to pull ___"), so their movement measures which phrase frame the model is entering rather than what it thinks the three men did; `pull` is the only one that rises under B and it does so in the same small range as the rounding-floor gainers, and `search` and `cut` are similarly unreadable without knowing who or what the object is.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is `quarrel`, which falls 0.3 under B while its near-synonym `argue` rises 11.9; that rules out reading the first relation as \"the idea of arguing becomes more likely\" and forces the weaker claim that one particular token absorbs the mass, which is a real weakening rather than a quibble. result.reading: The fragment puts three Israelis in a room, and under A the slot is filled overwhelmingly by verbs of bodily assault on someone present (shoot 11.1, beat 7.5, plus torture, kill, hit, rape, punch, blow, bomb); under B that mass drains away and reappears mostly on a single verbal verb, argue (0.5 to 8.3), with smaller gains for discuss, speak and for sociable pastimes (sing, play, read, perform). What complicates the obvious reading is that violence does not simply leave: bombard, terrorize, rob and fight all rise under B, while a set of colorless business verbs (walk, move, come, go, clean, check, write) falls alongside the assaults.

relations.name: assault becomes altercation
relations.sentence: The verbs by which someone in the room is physically attacked (shoot and beat above all, with torture, kill, hit, rape, punch, push, bomb, blow behind them) lose almost all their weight under B, and the largest single gain anywhere goes to argue, with discuss and speak behind it, so the same scene is filled by a quarrel instead of a beating.

relations.name: contact traded for distance
relations.sentence: Among violent verbs the ones that fall are those requiring a body to touch or be aimed at another body in that room (beat, punch, hit, torture, rape, kill), while the violent verbs that actually rise are the ones whose object is unnamed, collective or categorical rather than bodily present (bombard, terrorize, rob, fight), so under B violence is not absent but held at arm's length from the room.

relations.name: errands into pastimes
relations.sentence: Colorless verbs of getting about and doing small business (walk, move, come, go, clean, check, write) all drop, and what rises in their place is a band of sociable or performed leisure activities (sing, play, read, perform), so the neutral half of the distribution also shifts, from unremarkable motion to things people do together for their own sake.

result.kind: what sort of act the room hosts: bodily contact or speech and pastime

residue.description: These are not really content completions: make and do are light verbs waiting for an object, point is a fragment of a phrase, and remove (the third-largest gain under B, +1.1) is unreadable on its own because it can be either a chore or a euphemism for elimination, so it cannot be assigned to either side without deciding which sense the model meant.

result.counterexamples: The clearest contradictions to the first relation are bombard (+0.7), rob (+0.5), terrorize (created from 0.0 to +0.4) and fight (+0.3), all violent or criminal and all more likely under B, which rules out any reading in which B simply removes violence; they are mild counterexamples in size, since together they gain about 1.9 against shoot and beat alone losing 10.4, and the second relation is my attempt to absorb them rather than dismiss them, so anyone rejecting that reading should treat them as unexplained. The third relation is the weakest: read rises (+0.7) while write falls (-0.6) though both are quiet solitary acts, and blow, come and go could be read as motion rather than assault, so the neutral band does not divide cleanly. Nothing contradicts the second relation directly, but it rests on four small gains and one could reasonably call it pattern-finding in noise.
result.notes: Confidence is high for the first relation only; it is carried by two of the largest movements in the data (shoot -6.5, beat -3.9, argue +7.7) and the near-match between what shoot loses and what argue gains is hard to read as accident. The second and third relations are stated at medium confidence at best, since each rests on movements under 1.2 points. One structural observation that belongs to no relation: under A the top two words hold 18.6% between them and under B the top word holds 8.3%, so B is the flatter distribution overall, and the loss is not redistributed evenly but largely onto one substitute.

result.reading: Under B the slot fills up with stock adjectives of neighborly affability: friendly alone gains 7.9 points, with polite, kind, pleasant, nice and cordial all rising, and the intensifier "very" rising 3.9. relations.name: Good-neighbor adjectives surge
relations.sentence: Under B the completion is pulled hard toward a compact set of stock adjectives for pleasant sociability toward others (friendly, polite, kind, pleasant, nice, cordial), friendly alone gaining almost eight points, while the words relatively more available under A name things the neighbors were seen doing or being (hanging, smoking, whispering, drunk).

relations.name: Disposition displaces conduct
relations.sentence: The A-side words are progressive participles plus one bodily-state word, all reporting behavior observable from outside the house, whereas the B-side words are dispositional predicates about how the neighbors stood toward other people, so the difference is partly grammatical and aspectual and not only evaluative.

relations.name: Adjective frame pre-announced
relations.sentence: The contentless intensifier "very" makes the second-largest move of any word (+3.9), so B is not merely choosing different words but committing the slot in advance to a gradable adjective phrase, which is exactly the shape the A-side participles cannot take.

result.counterexamples: Two things cut against reading the A block as a coherent transgressive or suspicious set. Second, and more seriously, the asymmetry of magnitudes undercuts any claim that B suppresses the A words: the four A-side words lose 0.2 to 0.4 points each, about 1.2 in total, while the B block gains about 17.5, which means the mass B gains comes overwhelmingly from words not shown here rather than from the block it is being contrasted with. result.notes: Confidence is high about the direction and shape of the shift, which rests on the single dominant move (friendly +7.9) plus five same-family adjectives moving the same way, and it would survive dropping any one word. result.reading: Under A the third-ranked completion is the one anatomically explicit word, and under B it has dropped fifteen places to eighteenth; the only completion naming another person, wife, drops eleven. Almost everything that gains is a head-region site (cheeks, cheek, jaw, hair) or a modifier that goes with hair and beard, plus one large rise for fingers, so what I see is the touch relocating from below the waist and from a partner to the face and hand, though most individual rises are small enough to be the automatic wake of the two large falls.

relations.name: Partner drops out
relations.sentence: The only completion naming another person rather than a part of the man's own body falls further than anything except the explicit word, and nothing naming a person rises to replace it, so every word that gains is a part of his own body or a modifier of one.

relations.name: Touch migrates upward
relations.sentence: Completions naming the trunk or below (cock, crotch, belly, chest) all lose ground under B while head-region sites (cheeks, cheek, jaw, hair) and the two adjectives that pre-modify hair and beard (thick, long) all gain, so the site the gesture settles on moves up the body.

residue.description: The word own is not a body site but a determiner-adjacent word that defers the completion to a following noun, so it cannot bear on any relation about where the hand goes; head, hands, chin and beard hold their exact positions and therefore supply no ordering evidence in either direction, which is worth noting because chin and beard are precisely the head-region sites the third relation would have predicted rising.

result.counterexamples: Four, of unequal weight. The worst is face, which falls from fourth to sixth while its own subparts cheek, cheeks and jaw all rise; this is a fall high in the ranking, where movement counts most, and it means the upward-migration relation cannot be stated as head words rise, only as these particular head words rise. Next is the split in the manual cluster: fingers rises seven places while hand falls three and hands holds, so the rise of fingers cannot be read as anything about hands in general and sits awkwardly in every relation I named. Third, neck falls two places although it lies between the falling trunk and the rising head, so the upward gradient is not monotonic. Fourth, chest and belly are not explicit words yet fall, and wife is not a body part at all, so the first relation cannot be tightened into a claim that only explicit words fall.
result.notes: The fall side is what I would defend hardest: a fifteen-place drop from third position, and an eleven-place drop, are large and mutually consistent. The rise side is weaker than it looks, because when a word at position 3 drops to 18 every word it passes gains a place automatically, and the same for wife passing from 16 to 27 and crotch from 17 to 22. Netting that out, jaw's plus two is entirely accounted for by the fallers passing it, hair, cheek and long keep about plus one, and only fingers (about plus six), cheeks (about plus three) and thick (about plus two) are rises in their own right. That arithmetic is approximate, since I am only shown the twenty words that were top-twenty under A: words that climbed into these positions from further down under B are invisible to me, so some of the vacated space may be filled by words I cannot see. Two further caveats. Thick and long are pre-modifiers, not sites, and their direction is only interpretable through the nouns they would take (beard, hair), which is a reading I am imposing rather than something the ordering shows. And I make no claim about how likely any of these words is, nor about which condition is which, nor about why the reordering happened; the relations above are statements about relative position only.

What keeps my confidence at low rather than medium is that half the genital vocabulary declined to move and one member of it moved the other way. I would defend the description of what happened; I would not defend the claim that it will happen again, and I have not treated the direction of the shift as meaning anything about which condition is doing what.

result.reading: Under B almost the whole list is adjectives naming fear or vulnerability (threatened, scared, afraid, intimidated, unsafe, uneasy, helpless), and the single biggest riser in the whole display is "scared" (+15). Under A the top of the list is mostly grammatical material that postpones any feeling word at all (the, that, it, they, their, a, an, as, like, more, very), with only four real feeling words among the fifteen, and three of those (sorry, obliged, compelled) are about a pull toward the newcomers rather than about danger.

relations.name: Named fear against deferred predicate
relations.sentence: Under B nearly every favoured word is an adjective that names an emotion of fear or vulnerability outright, while under A the favoured words are overwhelmingly determiners, pronouns, complementizers and degree words that continue the sentence without committing to any feeling term.

relations.name: Obligation against endangerment
relations.sentence: The few genuine feeling words on the A side describe a social or moral pull directed at the arriving people (sympathy in "sorry", duty in "obliged" and "compelled"), whereas the B side's feeling words describe the neighbours' own safety as being under threat.

relations.name: Safety split by morphology
relations.sentence: The bare positive "safe" is favoured under A while both the comparative "safer" and the negated "unsafe" are favoured under B, so the same safety root appears on both sides but only under B does it arrive marked, either graded or negated.

result.kind: who the feeling is about, and whether a feeling is named at all

residue.description: Both are listed as favoured under A yet moved zero places between the conditions, so whatever makes them A-favoured is not visible in the ranks I was given, and "like" in particular ("felt like ...") is a syntactic hinge rather than a completion with any content of its own.

result.counterexamples: The strongest counterexample is "safer", which rises to position 1-adjacent territory under B (9 -> 5, +4): it is a positive word about the neighbours being better off, and it sits inside the same list as "threatened" and "scared", so B cannot be characterized as uniformly fearful, only as densely so. That is a real dent in the fear reading, though not a fatal one, since seven of B's eight words still name fear or vulnerability and "safer" is excluded from the relation for exactly this reason. Second, "sorry" under A is a negative feeling, which blocks any simpler reading in which A is the pleasant condition and B the unpleasant one; the split is about the kind and object of the feeling, not its valence. Third, "safe" (A) and "safer" (B) show a single lexeme divided between the conditions, which means the two lists are not cleanly separable by sentiment. Fourth and mildly, "as", "more" and "very" fall a long way under B (-6, -2, -2) yet are precisely the words that would introduce a B-style adjective ("felt very threatened"), so their A-favouring is not simply the absence of affect.
result.notes: I would defend relations 1 and 2 to someone who disagreed, because they rest on countable facts about the lists rather than on interpretation: seven of B's eight words are fear or vulnerability adjectives, and eleven of A's fifteen are function words. Relation 3 is thinner, built on three words, and I would keep it but concede it first. Three limits on all of this. One word is withheld, so any of these groupings could be disturbed by a word I was not shown, and I cannot tell from which side. I was shown no likelihoods, only order, so I make no claim about how much any of these words matters; "scared" moving +15 places says it moved far, not that it became probable. And the display already sorts words so that "the words the difference rests on most come first", which means the head of each list is where the structure should be clearest and the tail is where I should trust myself least. I take the difference to be about what sort of completion is reached for, not about anything beyond the two lists.

result.reading: Both sides are dominated by lower-body clothing, and the top two completions (pants, jeans) hold ranks 1 and 2 under both conditions, so every actual reordering happens in the tail, over one to three places. The interesting pairing is that the same referent appears on both sides under two different names: "fly" and "flies" rise under A while "zipper" rises under B, and alongside that the three interchangeable names for full-length trousers all sit on the B side.

relations.name: idiom against hardware
relations.sentence: The trouser fastening is named idiomatically on the A side, by the colloquial noun and its British plural, and named as a piece of literal hardware on the B side, so the same referent changes register rather than changing identity.

relations.name: trousers-synonym concentration
relations.sentence: The three mutually substitutable dictionary names for full-length trousers all rise under B, while the one abbreviated, casual legwear term falls under it, so B pulls toward the standard whole-garment vocabulary and A keeps the less standard item.

result.kind: opening-idiom versus garment-by-name

residue.description: It is the only upper-body garment in the set and stands alone on the A side with the largest movement of any word, and a single word with no companion supports no relation I would defend against someone who disagreed.

result.counterexamples: "zipper" is the sharpest counterexample: it names a part of the garment rather than the garment, so any reading of this split as part-words on one side and whole-garment words on the other fails outright, and the first relation survives only if the idiom/hardware register distinction is accepted in place of a part/whole one. "jacket" contradicts any reading in which A collects the suggestive completions and B the innocuous ones, since it is the least suggestive word in the set and is the one A raises most, three places; that is why no such relation is offered here. Weaker but real: "pants" and "jeans" are listed as B-favoured yet moved zero places, so the two anchors of the second relation carry no positional evidence at all, and whatever makes them B-favoured is invisible in what was shown.
result.notes: Two structural limits bear on how much weight these relations can take. All movement is confined to ranks 3 through 11; the two likeliest completions are fixed, so the difference between the conditions is a rearrangement of the tail and not a change in what the fragment most plausibly completes to. One word is withheld for moving opposite to its prominence, and since it is withheld I cannot tell whether it would sit inside either relation or break one. I also decline to read this as an axis of strength or mildness: jacket blocks that reading, and nothing here shows likelihoods, only order. The morphological point is worth flagging without acting on it: "fly" and "flies" are one lexical fact in two dialectal forms, so the A side of the first relation is thinner than its two entries suggest.

result.reading: The fragment invites a predicate of feeling, and the three words that fall furthest from A to B (obliged -71, free -66, compelled -40) are exactly the ones that cannot end the clause: each takes a following infinitive, so under A the sentence was heading toward what the neighbours then had to, or were able to, do. The three that rise furthest (nervous +47, unsafe +22, uneasy +15) are terminal predicative adjectives naming apprehension, while the obvious polarity story fails, since threatened sits at rank 4 under A and 5 under B and safe moves only two places.

relations.name: Infinitive frame drops out
relations.sentence: The three words that lose the most ground under B are the three that cannot end the sentence, since each requires a following infinitive about what the neighbours then did or could do (compelled, obliged, free), whereas the three that gain the most under B are predicative adjectives that complete the clause by naming an apprehensive state and demand nothing further (nervous, uneasy, unsafe).

relations.name: Deontic polarity collapses together
relations.sentence: A holds high both the words for being made to act and the word for being at liberty to act, which are opposites in meaning, and B demotes all three at comparable magnitude, so what B removes is not one pole of obligation but the whole question of the neighbours' scope of action, in favour of words reporting only their comfort.

result.kind: whether the feeling opens onto an action

residue.description: The first nine are function words or degree modifiers rather than content completions of the feeling, and most of their movements are small drift, though a reaching rank 1 under B and the falling to 10 is worth noting as a possible shift toward a nominal completion (felt a chill) that I cannot test from ranks alone; safe (-2), threatened (-1) and betrayed (+2) are close enough to stationary that assigning them to either side would be reading noise; sorry (+9) hints at a pity or grievance register alongside betrayed, but with betrayed effectively still and no partner word on the A side I would withdraw that relation on a repeat.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexample to the first relation is like, which sits on the B side (9 to 7) and is itself a complement-taking word: felt like leaving is precisely the action-implying continuation the relation says B gives up, so B has not abandoned that frame wholesale, only its deontic members. Mildly against it too, sorry on the B side normally takes a complement (sorry for them). The strongest counterexample to any polarity reading, which is why I did not offer one, is threatened: it is nominally A-favoured and nearly stationary at rank 4 to 5, so B is not the condition where danger becomes sayable, and safe holding at 13 under B says the same from the other direction. The degree words more (-18) and very (-4) also cut awkwardly across the picture, since they premodify exactly the bare adjectives B promotes yet they fall with A.
result.notes: Medium rather than high because the magnitude structure is unusually clean (the three largest falls share a syntactic property that no other word in the A list has) but the evidence is one fragment, one direction, one repeat, and I am shown ordinal positions only, so I cannot tell whether a fall from 12 to 78 is a large or a negligible change in the underlying quantity. One word was withheld for moving against its prominence, so the picture is incomplete by a known amount. I resisted the reading that first suggests itself, that A is the permissive condition and B the anxious one, because threatened and safe both stay put and only free among the security terms actually moves; the movement is concentrated in the complement-taking words rather than in the affective polarity. My two relations overlap on the same three A words and should be read as one finding seen twice, not as independent evidence.

result.reading: Both conditions complete the fragment with feeling-words, and both sets are mostly unpleasant, so the difference is not one of valence or severity. A's distinctive content words (betrayed, abandoned, free, unsafe) name a state left behind when someone has gone or broken faith; B's (threatened, violated, helpless, trapped, uneasy) name a state produced by someone present and pressing in. Separately, the grammatical words at the head of the completion shift from clause-openers under A to article and comparison frames under B, and two words do not move at all.

relations.name: Desertion versus encroachment
relations.sentence: The feeling-words A favours describe a bond broken or a protector gone (betrayed, abandoned, and the release-word free), while those B favours describe an agent present and closing in on the one who feels (threatened, violated, helpless, trapped, uneasy).

relations.name: Room to move
relations.sentence: The two largest content-word movements run in opposite directions along one axis of physical constraint, free falling ten places under B while trapped climbs nineteen and helpless seven, so the conditions score the same axis oppositely rather than one side merely adding vocabulary.

relations.name: Clause against phrase
relations.sentence: The grammatical words A favours open a subordinate clause after the verb (felt that they, felt it), whereas B's open a noun phrase or a comparison (felt a, felt an, felt like, felt their), so the conditions differ in the shape of the continuation and not only in which adjective fills it.

result.kind: source of the feeling: someone departed or someone arriving

residue.description: None of these is a content completion whose movement I would defend: very is a degree word that says nothing about what is felt even though it is A's largest mover, as and safe sit at identical positions in both conditions and so carry no difference at all, and the moves a single place, which is indistinguishable from no movement in a list read only by rank.

result.counterexamples: unsafe is the real problem: it sits on the A side yet means what B's threatened and uneasy mean, an intrusion-and-danger word on the desertion side, so the first relation cannot be stated as a clean partition of the feeling-words. It is mild damage rather than fatal, since unsafe is A's smallest content-word move (two places) and the word closest to no preference, but a repeated measurement that moved it further onto A would weaken the relation. safe, unmoved at 13 in both, cuts the other way and shows the safety axis is not wholly claimed by either condition, which is a further reason not to state the first relation as being about danger. betrayed is a lesser counterexample to the reading that A's words lack an agent, since betrayal requires someone to have done it; what saves the relation is that the agent is a prior insider who has failed the one who feels rather than an outsider acting on them, but a reader who disagreed could reasonably press here.
result.notes: The first relation rests on five words under B and three under A, which is thin, and I am shown rank only, so I cannot tell whether these are large or negligible differences in the completion; a word entering at position 16 from 35 has moved far in rank without my knowing what that is worth. The third relation is the one I would most expect to survive repetition, because it involves the highest-ranked items on both sides, but it may be a consequence rather than a cause: if B prefers single adjectives like uneasy and trapped and A prefers clauses like that they, then the article and complementizer movements follow from the content preference rather than standing beside it, and I cannot separate the two from ranks alone. relations.sentence: Both words that name the fastening or the slit it closes rather than the garment it belongs to sit on the A side, and no word on the B side names a fastening, so only under A can the completion refer to the aperture instead of the object.

result.reading: Under A the fragment tends to continue with a phrase rather than a named feeling: determiners and comparatives (a, an, their, like, as) plus compelled and obliged, which make felt govern an action the neighbours are pushed into, alongside a scattered affect set running from discomfort (uneasy, sorry) all the way to reassurance (safe, free). relations.name: Threat against reassurance
relations.sentence: Every feeling-word B favours names high-arousal fear or hostility aimed at the people who moved in (threatened, alarmed, angry, with the intensifier very rising alongside them), whereas the feeling-words A favours do not form a single register at all, spreading from low-grade discomfort and sympathy (uneasy, sorry) to outright reassurance (safe, free).

relations.name: Impelled action, not feeling
relations.sentence: A alone favours completions in which felt is followed by a participle of compulsion, so the sentence reports what the neighbours were pushed to do rather than what they underwent, while the words rising under B are all state-naming emotions and none of them takes that frame.

relations.name: Phrase against clause
relations.sentence: The function words A favours all open a noun phrase or a comparison after felt (a, an, their, like, as), while those B favours all open a subordinate clause reporting a thought about the newcomers (that, they, it, what, some), so the conditions differ in the grammatical shape of the continuation and not only in its vocabulary.

result.kind: threat-naming versus stance-and-obligation framing

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexamples are safe and free on the A side: if A were simply a milder version of B, its affect words would be attenuated versions of threatened and alarmed, but safe and free invert the sign outright, so A is better described as unresolved than as softened. result.reading: Under B the fragment resolves toward the neighbours experiencing the arrival as a danger: threatened is first, intimidated climbs forty places from well outside the top ten, and uncomfortable climbs seventeen. result.kind: whether the arrival registers as danger or as fellowship

residue.description: None of these is a content completion of the phrase the neighbours felt ___: they are determiners, pronouns and complementizers opening a longer clause (felt that, felt like, felt a, felt more), they all sit near the top of both rankings, and none moves more than five places, so they are the shared scaffolding of the sentence rather than anything the two conditions disagree about.

result.counterexamples: Two words on the A side cut against the welcome reading. The word left (17 to 29) most naturally continues as felt left out, a negative experience of the arrival sitting on the side I have called secure and well-disposed; it is a genuine contradiction, though a mild one, since felt left alone is not an idiom and the word could be pulled by other continuations. A weakness rather than a counterexample: safe and empowered, the two words that would most strongly support the A side, move only one and four places, so the first relation rests almost entirely on solidarity and safer.
result.notes: The direction is consistent across every affect-bearing word that moves appreciably, and the two largest movements in the set (solidarity minus 87, intimidated plus 40) point the same way, which is why I give high confidence despite the short B list.
