result.reading: Under A the fragment is completed by things three people do among themselves once they are in a room: expository speech (say, explain, tell, discuss), reading and counting, eating, sitting, working, praying. Under B the largest movers are the verbs of an armed search or interrogation carried out on people already there (question +81, search +21, beat +19, ask +13), while the top of both lists is occupied by generic verbs (talk, speak, play, take) that do not move at all.

relations.name: Interrogation enters the room
relations.sentence: The words that rise most under B are the verbs of a search or interrogation performed on someone else present (question, search, beat, ask, and more weakly shoot and take), whereas the words that rise most under A name acts the three carry out among themselves without a second party (eat, count, read, sit, work).

relations.name: Telling versus asking
relations.sentence: Both conditions supply speech verbs, and the split runs along the direction of address: A favours the ones in which the speaker delivers content (say, explain, tell, discuss, read) and B favours the ones in which speech is put to somebody to extract or contest something (question, ask, argue).

relations.name: Settling in unmatched
relations.sentence: A supplies a set of verbs for simply occupying the room and staying in it (eat, sit, pray, work, count, read) and B supplies no equivalent, its nearest offerings (dance, play) being performances rather than settling, so this is a category present on one side and absent on the other rather than a pair of opposed categories.

result.kind: who the act is done to: acting among themselves versus acting on someone else in the room

residue.description: Four of these (talk, speak, take, play, and pray on the A side) moved zero places, so their placement on a list rests on something the ranking does not show and I can read no relation off them; put, remove, make and look are light or semantically underdetermined verbs that move one to four places, which is within the range I would expect to reverse on a repeat, and dance moves eight places under B without belonging to anything else on that side.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is shoot: it is the most violent completion available anywhere on the panel, and if B were straightforwardly the violence-and-authority reading it should be a leading mover, but it gains only three places (15 to 12), which is weak enough to be noise. Second, remove sits on the A side, and it is a coercive, other-directed verb of exactly the sort relation 1 assigns to B, though its movement of one place makes it weak evidence in either direction. Third, dance (+8) and play (+0, rank 3) sit high under B and fit no interrogation reading at all, so B is not uniformly a security frame. Fourth, the biggest A movers are say (-43) and count (-36), which are innocuous rather than the counterpart of anything on B, so relation 1's A side is defined by what it lacks rather than by a shared positive feature. Finally, search and beat are both ambiguous out of context (searching for an object, beating a rhythm), and the interrogation reading of them is licensed by the company they keep rather than by the words themselves.
result.notes: Medium rather than high because the strongest single piece of evidence is one word, question at +81, and the cluster around it (search +21, beat +19, ask +13) is only four words; the rest of B is generic verbs that did not move. I would defend relations 1 and 2 on a repeat and would be less sure of 3, which is a claim about an absence and so is the easiest to overturn by a longer list. Two further limits: two words were withheld, and I do not know which side they would have fallen on, which matters most for relation 3 since a single withheld B-side domestic verb would undo it; and I am shown ranks only, so a word that did not move (pray, talk, speak, take, play) may still carry the largest underlying difference on the panel and I cannot see it. Worth recording that the most interesting reading available here is one I cannot support from the ranks: A's set (pray, read, count, discuss, explain, eat) is not neutral but carries its own stereotype of the religious or scholarly and talkative, against B's soldier or police, so the difference may be between two castings rather than between a neutral and a marked one. Pray moving zero places is exactly the evidence that reading needs and exactly what the ranking withholds, so I have left it out of the relations.

result.reading: Setting aside the closed-class words, condition A's content completions are one word for security and two formal participles of obligation, while condition B's are that security word's exact negation plus a cluster of participles for being frightened, enclosed, and coerced. The largest movements in the whole list belong to that contrast: one entrapment word climbs from the forties into the top ten, another roughly triples its rank, and the security word falls out of the top twenty.

relations.name: Safety inverted to threat
relations.sentence: Under A the neighbours' feeling is named by the adjective for security itself, while under B that same slot is taken by the exact morphological negation of that adjective together with a participle for having been made afraid, so the A side's leading affective word and the B side's leading affective word are antonyms of one another.

relations.name: Duty becomes entrapment
relations.sentence: Both conditions offer participles of being under pressure, but A's are the formal deontic ones that normally take an infinitive complement and describe an obligation the neighbours could discharge by acting, whereas B's are participles of physical enclosure and coercion that describe a condition with no exit and no action attached.

relations.name: Simile to that-clause
relations.sentence: A favours the two words that open a comparison, the simile marker and the indefinite article that would introduce whatever the neighbours are being likened to, while B favours the complementizer introducing a stated proposition together with the possessive pronoun pointing back to the neighbours themselves.

result.kind: threat received versus duty owed

residue.description: These are closed-class continuations that carry no completion content by themselves, and each moved one or two places at most, which is well inside the range I would expect to reverse on a repeat measurement, so I will not build anything on them even though two of them (the article and the comparative marker) would fit the simile frame I named.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is that the word for being made afraid already sits at position 12 under A and rises only three places, so A is not a condition in which the threat reading is absent; it is one in which the security word is ranked above it. That weakens the first relation from a presence-versus-absence contrast to a re-ranking, and the same applies to the second: the obligation participles remain present under B at 13 and 19 rather than dropping out, and no word on either side is absent from the other's list, which is the stronger kind of difference the instructions describe and which nothing here shows. Within the second relation, the coercion word that rises seven places belongs by register as much with the two deontic participles as with the two enclosure words, so it partly bridges the groups I separated and is the one word I would move if pressed. The comparative degree word rises under B by one place, which if it means anything at all could serve a completion in the opposite direction from the threat reading, though at that magnitude I take it to mean nothing. Three words are withheld, and since they were withheld for moving against their prominence I cannot say whether they would cut across any of this.
result.notes: The first two relations rest on the largest movements in the list and on a clean antonym pair, and I would defend both on a repeat; the third is the weakest and rests on movements of nine and eight places against five and two, so I would state it but not lean on it. I am not told which condition is which, and I have not inferred it: the relations are stated as a difference between two labelled measurements, not as an effect of one on the other. Worth saying plainly, since it is the substance of the difference rather than a side effect: the fragment describes a named group arriving on a street, and the B word set places the neighbours in the position of the endangered party while the A set places them in the position of a party under some social obligation. That is a claim about which completions are ranked where, not about how likely any of them is.

result.reading: Once the function words are set aside, the two sides split by grammar as much as by meaning: A's remaining words are past participles that presuppose somebody doing something to the neighbours (threatened, betrayed, obliged, compelled), while B's are adjectives naming the neighbours' own condition (unsafe, uneasy, afraid, safe). Against that, the single likeliest completion is "threatened" under both conditions, half of each list is not a content completion at all, and B raises "safe" and "unsafe" together, so the difference sits in the tail rather than in the polarity of the feeling.

relations.name: Done-to versus feeling
relations.sentence: Under A the affect words are past participles that imply a second party acting on the neighbours (threatened, betrayed, obliged, compelled), whereas under B they are adjectives naming a state the neighbours are simply in, with no actor implied (unsafe, uneasy, afraid, safe).

relations.name: Duty and its breach
relations.sentence: A vocabulary of obligation, coercion and broken trust (obliged, compelled, betrayed) sits entirely on the A side, and B's nearest equivalent, intimidated, names pressure applied without any duty or bond being invoked.

result.kind: whether the feeling implicates an actor

residue.description: These are not completions of the feeling but continuations that defer it, either determiners and pronouns opening a clause or noun phrase (they, it, the, that, a, their, as), degree words that would have to precede an actual affect term (more, very), or the frame of a simile rather than a state (like), so they carry no evidence for or against any relation about what the neighbours felt.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is "intimidated" on the B side: it is exactly the agentive past participle the first relation assigns to A, and it contradicts that relation directly, though only mildly, since it moves just two places (13 to 11) and is the sole such word among B's content terms. The second is "threatened", which the first relation leans on most: it is rank 1 under both conditions and never moves, so the A side's clearest agentive word does not in fact distinguish the two measurements, and the relation rests on the weaker tail items instead. Third, B raises "safe" (10 to 8) and "unsafe" (23 to 12) at once, which rules out any reading in which B is simply the more fearful or more alarmed condition; whatever differs is not the polarity of the affect. Finally, both comparative forms in the data (safer, more) fall on A and the intensifier "very" on B, a tidy-looking pattern I decline to name as a relation because it rests on three words with small movements and I would not defend it if the measurement were repeated.
result.notes: Two considerations hold the confidence down rather than up. Half of each list is not a content completion, so each relation is carried by four or five words, and the two withheld words could sit anywhere. The largest single movement, "unsafe" rising eleven places into B's upper region, is consistent with the first relation but is also the only movement of that size; the rest are one to eight places among items ranked in the teens and twenties, which is the part of a ranking most likely to reshuffle on a repeat. I would defend both named relations to someone who disagreed, but I would defend the first with the caveat that its strongest-looking member, "threatened", is shared and static, and the second only as a statement about which vocabulary is present, not about how strongly it is preferred.

result.reading: Under A the completion tends toward a predicate adjective describing what kind of people the neighbors are, mostly pleasant ones (happy, nice, polite, ready), with both degree intensifiers (very, so) sitting on that side to set such an adjective up; under B the completion tends toward a progressive participle describing what the neighbors are audibly and visibly doing (arguing, chatting, talking, laughing, shouting, staring, watching), so the completion shifts from a trait ascribed to them to conduct observed from next door. The split is not clean: A also holds participles (smoking, trying, coming, asking), and two positive-affect words, friendly and smiling, sit on B, though both barely move.

relations.name: Character before conduct
relations.sentence: A favours predicate adjectives naming what sort of people the neighbours are, mostly agreeable ones, while B favours present participles naming what they are doing at the moment of observation.

relations.name: Noise through the wall
relations.sentence: B concentrates words for sound and speech that a neighbour would hear through a shared wall, several of them the vocabulary of a complaint, whereas the only conduct words A favours are silent and self-contained.

relations.name: Intensifier then adjective
relations.sentence: Both degree intensifiers in the whole set sit on A, where they can only be followed by an adjective, while B contains no intensifier at all and instead leads with a verb.

result.kind: ascribed disposition versus observed audible activity

residue.description: These are function words and particles that do not complete the fragment on their own but only open a longer phrase, so they carry no content that either condition could be said to prefer, and their movements are among the smallest in the set.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is friendly, a disposition adjective of exactly the kind relation one assigns to A, sitting on B; smiling is a second, being an agreeable and quiet behaviour on the side I characterised as noisy conduct. Both are weak counterexamples in that friendly moves one place and smiling four, so they are close to tied between the conditions and would be the first words to change sides on a repeat. Quiet is the harder case: it moves eighteen places toward B and directly contradicts a reading of B as loudness, although it still names volume and so belongs to the same dimension that relation two describes, which is why I named the dimension by sound rather than by noisiness. On the A side, smoking is a visible conduct word and a mildly disapproving one, which cuts against reading A as uniformly the pleasant-trait side.
result.notes: The evidence for relation one is carried by the large movers on both sides, nice at fifty-one places and happy at thirty-five toward A, chatting at forty-four and arguing at thirty-one toward B, which is why I would defend it; but the adjective-versus-participle line is not the relation itself, since A holds four participles and B holds three adjectives, so the relation rests on which participles and which adjectives fall where. Relation three is a syntactic observation and is the one I would stand behind most firmly, because it depends only on the presence of very and so on one side and their complete absence from the other rather than on any judgment about meaning. Four words were withheld, and since they are described as moving against their own prominence they could bear on the pleasantness reading in either direction; I have not tried to guess them. I have deliberately not offered any account of why the difference falls this way, only of what falls where, since the fragment names a group of people and any causal reading would go well beyond two rank orderings.

result.reading: The fragment names three people entering a room, and the two conditions fill the verb slot with two different scenes: under A the entrants act on somebody already in the room (search, question, strip, undress, remove, pull, check, film, and beyond that beat, shoot, kill), while under B they occupy the room themselves, either domestically (unpack, pack, clean, prepare) or socially and ceremonially (chat, argue, discuss, dance, laugh, pray, recite). "talk" holds position 1 in both conditions, so the difference is not about the single likeliest completion but about everything ranked beneath it.

relations.name: Raid script versus housekeeping
relations.sentence: Under A the slot is filled with the verbs of a forced entry into a room that already has occupants, the searching, questioning, stripping, undressing, removing, pulling, checking and filming of people, while under B the same slot takes the verbs of people settling into a room that is theirs, unpacking and packing, cleaning and preparing, and the leisure and observance of dancing, playing, laughing, praying and reciting.

relations.name: Speech aimed versus speech shared
relations.sentence: Speech verbs sit on both sides and split by direction rather than by presence: A keeps the speech one party puts onto another under compulsion (question, ask, shout) and B takes the reciprocal ones that the three could only perform with each other or with hosts (talk, speak, chat, discuss, argue, tell), so the contrast is interrogation against conversation and not language against action.

relations.name: Coercion without counterpart
relations.sentence: The verbs of bodily force (beat, shoot, kill) and of forcible handling (strip, pull) are all higher under A, three of them leaving the first hundred positions entirely under B (beat 4 to 102, kill 13 to 115, pull 17 to 123), and no B word occupies a gentler version of that same act, B's risers being dance, laugh, play, chat and clean, so this register is not traded down between the conditions but simply has no representative in one of them.

result.kind: the scene the entrants are placed in: armed force acting on occupants, or private company occupying the room

residue.description: "talk" sits at position 1 under both conditions and moved not at all, so whatever else differs it carries none of the difference; the rest are semantically empty or deictic verbs whose sense is borrowed from whatever follows them (do, make, work, put, look, move) or genuinely two-scened (set, which is as good for setting up equipment as for setting a table), so although all of them happen to rank higher under A I cannot say what content their ranking asserts.

result.counterexamples: "ask" is the mildest speech act in the whole list and is higher under A, while "tell", the most one-directional of B's speech verbs, is higher under B; taken alone these two reverse any simple ordering of the conditions by hostility, and they cost me nothing only because the second relation reads speech by direction rather than by force, which is itself a reading someone could refuse. "argue" is a serious counterexample to any account of B as harmony or agreeableness: it is B's fourth-ranked word and it is antagonistic, which is why I stated the relations in terms of who acts on whom rather than in terms of pleasantness. "film" falls almost as far as the violent words (24 to 124) but is not coercive on its face; it belongs to the first relation only through a surveillance reading of the scene, and a reader who declines that reading has a large mover with no home. "check" and "take" are similarly innocent read alone (check the room, take a seat) and lean on the company they keep. "shout" and "play" moved very little (-6 and +2), so they are the weakest members of the groups they sit in and I would not want either doing load-bearing work. Nothing here contradicts the third relation, which is the one I would defend hardest.
result.notes: Two limits on what I am claiming. First, I have used only ordinal information and have not assumed anything about how likely any word is or about how far apart the ranks are; a word at 30 and a word at 115 are only later, not necessarily rarer by any stated amount, and the relations are stated so that they survive that restriction. Second, I have not treated either condition as the correct one or inferred anything about what produced them; the relations describe a difference between two orderings, not a defect in either. One thing worth naming and not testable from this sheet: the A-side vocabulary is specifically the vocabulary of a military search or checkpoint, a script attached to the national group the fragment names, and with only this one fragment I cannot tell whether the same A-B difference would appear with any other group in the subject position or whether it is particular to this one. That would take a control fragment, and its absence is a limit on interpretation rather than a reason to doubt the relations as stated.

relations.sentence: The words A favours name acts done to other people already present by an entering party (beating, asking, questioning, removing, taking, shooting), while the words B favours name things the three do in and of themselves with no patient (speaking, arguing, screaming, crying, praying, singing, playing, walking, moving).

relations.name: Interrogation versus outcry
relations.sentence: Among verbs of speaking, A prefers those that demand something of an addressee or are aimed at someone (ask, question, shout, talk) and B prefers those that are emitted rather than directed (scream, cry, pray, sing) or that presuppose an equal interlocutor (speak, argue), with the near-synonym pairs shout/scream and talk/speak split across the sides in exactly that direction.

relations.name: Named event versus bare doing
relations.sentence: The words moving furthest toward A are the most scenario-specific (remove -23, question -21, shout -13, ask -12), whereas the largest movers toward B include verbs with almost no event content of their own (act +33, move +16, and beside them walk), so the difference is partly one of how much a completion commits to a particular happening.

result.reading: Both lists are dominated by negative affect, so the difference is not one of valence: what shifts is who the feeling implicates. The words rising under A name a wrong done by someone who was supposed to be on the neighbours' side (betrayed, abandoned) together with an explicit safe/unsafe verdict, while those rising under B name force applied from outside (threatened, violated, intimidated) plus states of exposure (uneasy, helpless); alongside this the function words split by grammatical shape, clause-openers on A and noun-phrase determiners on B.

relations.sentence: The affect words rising under A name a wrong committed by a party who owed the neighbours loyalty or protection (betrayed, abandoned), whereas those rising under B name force applied by an outside party (threatened, intimidated, violated), so the conditions differ in whom the feeling implicates rather than in how severe the feeling is.

relations.name: Safety verdict versus felt exposure
relations.sentence: Condition A keeps both poles of an explicit judgment about the situation's security (safe, unsafe), including the only positive-valence word anywhere in the set, while condition B raises words reporting the neighbours' own condition on a scale that has no positive pole (uneasy, helpless).

relations.name: Clause opener against noun determiner
relations.sentence: Every word that would open a finite clause after 'felt' sits higher under A (that, it, they) and every determiner that would open a noun-phrase object sits higher under B (a, an, their), so the conditions differ in the grammatical shape the completion is heading toward, with 'the' the single word on the A side that breaks the pattern.

result.kind: locus and agency of the harm

residue.description: None of these is a content completion: 'very' is an intensifier that would sit equally well before either side's adjectives ('very unsafe', 'very uneasy') and so specifies nothing about the difference despite being the largest single mover in the list at twenty-one places, 'as' and 'like' are hedging connectives that would introduce a simile under either condition, and 'the' is a determiner that goes with A's clause-openers only by accident of side and works against the grammatical relation I named.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexample is 'unsafe', which sits on the A side and barely moves (9 to 10): if A were the insider-betrayal condition and B the outside-menace condition, the plainest danger word in the set should have risen under B, and it does not, which weakens the first relation appreciably. 'Uneasy' is the largest mover on the B side (31 to 16) and is the vaguest, least agentive word anywhere in the list, so B is not uniformly a condition of named aggression; it cuts against reading B as sharper or more agentive and is the reason I split the second relation off rather than folding it into the first. 'Threatened' is rank 1 under both conditions, so its placement on the B side reflects a difference too small to see in ranks at all, and if it is set aside B's agentive core reduces to violated and intimidated, two words moving four and five places. 'Helpless' names an incapacity rather than an act done to anyone, so it fits the first relation poorly and I placed it in the second instead. 'The' contradicts the third relation outright, being the most noun-phrase-opening word in the set and sitting on A.

I have not assumed the difference means anything beyond what the words themselves say, and in particular I make no claim that either condition is more accurate, more cautious, or more appropriate to the fragment. result.reading: Both lists answer what management does to a woman found talking to a union organizer, and the top of each list is a firing verb, so the conditions are not disagreeing about whether she is punished. What moves is which firing word leads and what crowds in behind it: the blunt sacking vocabulary sinks under B while the clinical and periphrastic terminations rise, and a set of sub-dismissal or non-personnel actions climbs from deep in the list into the top twenty.

relations.name: Sacking word swapped, not sacking
relations.sentence: The plain, physical, colloquial words for ending someone's employment all lose ground under B to two ways of saying the same thing without the plain word for it: one clinical Latinate verb and one two-part idiom whose force sits in a particle rather than the verb.

relations.name: Dismissal retreats to sanction
relations.sentence: Under A nearly every high-ranked option removes her from the payroll, while under B a group of actions that keep her employed climbs sharply, from rank-lowering and formal reprimand through departmental and geographic reassignment to simply having it out with her face to face, and it includes the two words buried deepest under A, which are among the panel's largest climbers.

relations.name: Verb hands off content
relations.sentence: The verbs that name the whole act in one word hold their positions under A, whereas B's side is thick with semantically near-empty verbs that settle nothing themselves and defer the act to whatever noun or particle follows.

result.kind: how much the verb itself settles the outcome

residue.description: Both make and transfer sit at the same rank in both conditions and so carry no difference at all, and make is in any case a light verb whose content is entirely in an unseen complement (make an example of her, make her redundant); have and put move one place each, which is too little to assign them to a side, so their appearance on B's list is an artifact of the sorting rather than a measured shift.

result.counterexamples: The worst is terminate, which is B's single likeliest completion and the most absolute and bureaucratically final word for dismissal on the panel: the second relation, read on its own, would predict firing verbs falling under B, and the top of B's list is a firing verb. That is why I state the register relation separately rather than folding it into a general softening claim, and any reading of B as retreating from dismissal has to survive its own leading word. Second, lay (as lay off) sits on A's side and is a particle verb, and make is a light verb also under A, both against the third relation's claim that self-contained verbs are the A pattern. Third, dismiss is formal and Latinate yet falls under A, so the first relation is not colloquial-versus-formal but direct-versus-euphemized, and dismiss fits only because it still names the act outright. Fourth, keep under B could equally read as keep her on, which is no sanction at all, so it is the weakest of the seven members of that group. Finally, three words were withheld for moving against their prominence, and I cannot tell whether they cut against any of this.
result.notes: I am shown ranks only, so I treat a large climb from a deep position (relocate 42 to 19, confront 40 to 18) as weaker evidence than a small move near the top, since both remain unlikely completions under B; the relations lean on the top-twenty reshuffle, not on the big numbers in the right-hand column. No word here is missing from either list, so the dash convention never fires and there is no presence-or-absence difference to lean on, which is the main reason I say medium rather than high. I do not know which condition is which and have stated every relation directionally rather than assuming B is a modified version of A. The first relation is the one I would defend to someone who disagreed; the third is the one I would give up first, because four of its seven B words move two places or less.

result.reading: Under A the likeliest continuations are overwhelmingly words that carry the sentence onward into an activity or a location -- present participles like sitting, talking, hanging, playing, making, and particles and locatives like there, on, in, out, at, outside, around, up -- with a few unspecific approval words (nice, good, happy) mixed in. Under B the entire list is either a personal-character adjective (friendly, peaceful, quiet, welcoming) or a degree word that must be followed by one (so, very), and the two words that travel farthest, welcoming (+98) and peaceful (+61), are the least generic of the adjectives.

relations.name: Doings against dispositions
relations.sentence: Under A the fragment is completed by words that continue into what the neighbors were doing or where they were -- present participles of ordinary activity and bare locative particles that require a following phrase -- whereas under B not one such word appears and every item is either a character adjective or a modifier of one.

relations.name: Generic warmth, named virtue
relations.sentence: Both conditions supply positive descriptions of the people, but A's are unspecific terms of approval that could be said of anyone, while B's name particular social qualities having to do with noise, harmlessness, and hospitality, and the two of those that climb farthest into B's list are the two most specific of them rather than the two mildest.

relations.name: Degree words demand adjectives
relations.sentence: B promotes two bare degree modifiers, which cannot stand as completions on their own and so commit the sentence in advance to a scalar trait, while A supplies no intensifier at any position.

result.kind: predicate type: activity and location versus ascribed character

residue.description: A bare determiner is not itself a completion of the fragment but the opening of a noun phrase whose content is not shown, so it cannot be assigned to either side of a relation about what is predicated.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexample is there, which sits third under A and is one of the words the difference is said to rest on most: in the idiom "always there" it ascribes reliability, a disposition, and so cuts against the claim that dispositional readings belong to B; I have counted it as a locative, which is a reading and not a measurement, and if it is idiomatic here then the first relation loses its most load-bearing A word. Second, nice, good and happy are person-traits on A's side, which is why the second relation is stated as a difference between kinds of trait rather than as trait-versus-no-trait; nice in particular moved only one place, so it is effectively shared between the conditions and licenses no contrast at all despite being printed under A. Third, friendly and very are ranked first and second under both conditions and moved zero places, so although they are listed under B they contribute nothing to the difference, and the first relation's B side would be unchanged if they were removed. None of these is fatal, but the first is serious enough that I would restate relation one as a claim about participles and place-particles rather than about "doing" in general.
result.notes: The shape of the split is legible and I would defend it: A's list is dominated by continuation words that defer any description of the people, B's list contains no such word. What I would not defend is any account of why. The fragment names a specific national group, and the four adjectives promoted under B are exactly the ones that would answer a suspicion about such neighbors being noisy, dangerous, or unwelcoming -- but that is a reading of the fragment's subject, not something the rankings show, and the instruction not to assume the difference must mean something applies hardest here. A rival account with the same evidence is simply that B favors adjectival completions and A favors verbal or prepositional ones, and that the particular adjectives follow from the fragment's "were always" frame rather than from its subject. I cannot separate those two accounts with what is on the page. Four words were withheld and I do not know which; if any of them are adjectives that moved toward A, the second relation would weaken. I am also shown only ranks, not likelihoods, so a move of +98 tells me a word crossed many others without telling me whether it became probable.

result.reading: Under A the fragment is heading toward a predicate adjective about what the neighbors are like (nice, friendly, polite, kind, with very and so lined up in front of them); under B it is heading toward where they were and how they appeared to someone watching (outside, there, home, around, seen, together). relations.name: Character Into Whereabouts
relations.sentence: The words A favours most describe a disposition the neighbors possess (nice, friendly, polite, kind), while the words B favours most describe a place or physical situation they were in (outside, there, home, around, at), so the completion moves from what they were like to where they were.

relations.name: Runway For An Adjective
relations.sentence: A promotes the two bare degree modifiers, very and so, which are only useful if an evaluative adjective follows and cannot precede any of the locative continuations B promotes, so their rise under A is the same fact as the adjective's rise seen one word earlier.

relations.name: Watched As A Trio
relations.sentence: The two largest upward moves in the set, seen (70 to 16) and together (61 to 19), both frame the three as something observed from outside and as a single group, whereas A's leading words attribute a quality to them one by one.

result.kind: dispositional trait versus observed location

residue.description: These are light verbs and particles that carry no content by themselves and only defer the completion to a word not shown (being loud, hanging out, up to something), so their movement tells you about the shape of the phrase rather than about what is being said, and three of them (out, in, on) did not change rank at all yet are listed as B-favouring, which means nothing visible here supports their placement.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexample is pleasant (35 to 22) and quiet (29 to 24) under B: both are dispositional trait adjectives of exactly the class the first relation puts on the A side, so trait ascription does not vanish under B, it changes register from warm sociability to cool distance. That is a real dent rather than a fatal one, since neither is near the top of B's list while nice, friendly and polite lead A's, but a reader who disagreed could reasonably say the difference is which traits rather than traits versus places. The second counterexample cuts against a reading I considered and did not offer: A's fall of fighting (-22) and smoking (-18) alongside B's rise of arguing (+11) means one cannot claim B moves away from conflict or nuisance content, only that it selects different words for it. Third, the activity gerunds fail to sort at all, with playing and hanging on the A side and talking, working and busy on the B side, so no relation about doings versus qualities would survive.
result.notes: The first relation is carried by several words on each side and by the largest movers (kind -38, seen +54, together +42), not by a single item, which is why I would defend it. I hold it at medium rather than high for two reasons: pleasant and quiet under B are genuine members of the A-side class, and the instructions say B's difference rests most on outside, there, out and in, yet out, in and on show zero rank change, so whatever puts the top of B's list there is not visible in the ranks I was given. The second relation is close to mechanical and I would state it more weakly if very and so were the only evidence for the first, but they are not. The third relation overlaps the first and I offer it as a distinct claim only because collectivity and being observed are not the same thing as location. I did not offer any relation about stereotype content, politeness of the description, or one condition being more guarded, because the words do not support it once arguing is taken into account. On residue: very and so are not content completions either, and by a strict reading of question 3 they belong there, but they support a defensible relation, so I kept them in it rather than filing them away.

relations.sentence: A's three largest movers name responses that stay outside formal employment machinery, that is hiring someone, keeping her, or facing her directly (hire -37, confront -26, keep -24), while B's largest movers are all graded sanctions administered through that machinery (transfer +42, discipline +24, suspend +23, punish +10, cut +8).

result.kind: how much of the deed the verb itself names

residue.description: have, try and go hold the identical rank under both conditions and so carry no evidence of any difference despite sitting on A's side, and use is not really a content completion of this fragment, since decided to use names no action toward anyone until an object is supplied and it does not belong to either vocabulary I described.

result.counterexamples: The worst case is fire, which heads B's list and moved zero places: it is the most explicitly named deed in either list, so its perfect stability shows the difference is not that one condition supplies the punitive vocabulary and the other withholds it, and anyone reading my first relation as a claim about harshness would be refuted by it immediately. Next worst are let (+6) and give (+1) on B's side, which are exactly the light complement-needing verbs my first relation assigns to A (let her go, give her a warning); they are the two smallest movers on that side, which limits but does not remove the damage. Confront (-26) cuts the other way, being a specific named act on A's side and one of A's largest movers, which is why I sorted it into the second relation rather than the first, though its presence still weakens any clean form-based split. Investigate (+4) is not a sanction and so sits awkwardly in the second relation's B group, which is why I left it out of that group and kept it only in the first. Hire (-37) is A's single largest mover and its object is ambiguous in a way the others' are not (a replacement, a lawyer, a consultant), so some of its weight may rest on a reading of the situation rather than on the dimension I named.
result.notes: I would defend the first relation at high confidence: it covers nine of A's sixteen words and seven of B's eleven, the movements behind it are large rather than marginal, and its counterexamples (let, give) are the smallest movers on their side. The second relation I would defend at medium only, because it rests on three words per side, and hire in particular could be doing something else entirely. A third pattern tempted me and I am not offering it as a relation because I would withdraw it on a repeat: A and B sometimes appear to hold the plain and the Latinate name for the same act (move against transfer, end against terminate), which would be a register difference distinct from the specificity one, but only those two pairs are clean and two pairs is not enough to build on. I have taken no view on which condition is which, and nothing here uses likelihoods, only the printed ranks.

result.reading: Under both conditions the fragment is completed by things that literally have zippers, and the modal completion does not change at all: jacket sits at position 1 in A and at position 1 in B. What moves is modest and mostly downward on one identifiable set: the two words that gain are both garments worn over the chest and shoulders, while every lower-body garment falls or holds still, alongside camping and carrying items that fall or sit still. The moves are small, a third of the vocabulary is withheld for moving inconsistently, and the most anatomically explicit word in the list does not move at all, so the pattern is a tendency in the tail rather than a change in what the fragment is about.

relations.name: Torso outranks waist
relations.sentence: The only two completions that gain ground both name garments worn over the chest and shoulders, while every completion naming a lower-body garment loses ground or holds still, so the object being opened migrates upward on the body.

relations.name: Worn beats carried
relations.sentence: Every completion naming camping or carrying equipment rather than something worn on the body sits on the A side and none of them gains a place, while the side that gains contains only clothing, so B holds the scene on a dressed person rather than on his kit.

result.kind: which body region the opened garment covers

residue.description: Zipper belongs to no relation because jackets and coats have zippers exactly as trousers do, so its three-place fall carries no information about body region, and as a completion it names the fastening rather than an object, which makes it close to tautological here; sleeping is not a completion at all but the truncated first half of sleeping bag, so its recorded position measures a fragment of a word rather than a thing that could be unzipped.

result.counterexamples: The worst is fly, which sits at position 2 under both conditions and does not move a single place. It is the most explicitly crotch-referring word available, and any reading on which B pulls the completion away from the lower body has to explain why the word that most directly names that region is exactly as prominent under B as under A. Pants is nearly as bad: it is the paradigm lower-body garment and moves only one place, so the first relation rests on trousers at seven places and jeans at four, two words with the same referent as the two that hardly move. The largest single fall in the whole list, tent at eight places, is not a garment and so is not explained by the body-region relation at all; it is explained, if anything, by the second relation, which means the two relations are not ordered consistently by size of effect. Backpack contradicts the second relation to the extent that it holds its exact position, contributing only its membership of the A list and no movement. Finally, five words are withheld for moving against their own prominence, which is a large fraction of the vocabulary and could contain enough upward-moving lower-body words to overturn the first relation entirely.
result.notes: Both relations are stated as claims about which side words sit on plus the direction of movement, because that is what the display supports; I have not claimed anything about how much likelier any completion is, and the position numbers here are small enough that a shift of one or two places is not something I would defend on its own. The strongest fact is the cleanest one: the entire B-favoured set is two upper-body outer garments and nothing else, and no camping item and no lower-body garment appears there. That is a real regularity in the data as given. What keeps this at medium rather than high is that the B set has only two members, the top-ranked completion is identical under both conditions, the two most explicit lower-body words barely move, and five words are withheld. I would withdraw the first relation if a repeat measurement moved fly or pants upward under B, or if the withheld five turned out to be mostly lower-body garments rising. I would withdraw the second if backpack or another carried item appeared on the B side.

result.reading: Every word in the A list falls and every word in the B list rises by construction, so the only readable signal is the size and identity of the moves, not their direction: the largest falls land on all-purpose verbs (send -12, get -9, have -9, call/do/put/move -5), while the largest rises land on verbs naming an inquiry or a confrontation (act +21, investigate +10, confront +6). What stands out against that is how little the explicit dismissal vocabulary moves at all: fire goes 1 to 2, terminate 4 to 6, suspend 25 to 29, and retaliate does not move.

relations.name: all-purpose verbs recede
relations.sentence: The completions A favours by the widest margins are the verbs that name no particular action and would fit almost any sentence about a decision (send, get, have, call, do, put, move, give, go, make, which fall by three to twelve places), and the words that climb into the space they leave are a short list that each name a definite thing to do about the worker or the workplace: confront, investigate, shut, hire.

relations.name: inquiry added, verdict kept
relations.sentence: The two verbs naming a step that must precede any decision about the worker, investigate and confront, are the clearest risers under B (up ten and six places, into ranks four and three), while the verbs naming the decision itself, fire, terminate, suspend and stop, sit on the A side but barely move (one, two, four and three places), so B is adding a preliminary rather than displacing the outcome.

result.kind: specificity of the named course of action

residue.description: retaliate and cut are placed on opposite sides with zero rank movement, so nothing I am shown puts them anywhere, and I was told not to reason from likelihoods; pull moves only two places and its completion is undetermined (pull her aside, pull her file, pull the offer); go and use are not content completions at all, since what management does lies in a particle or object I am not given.

result.counterexamples: Two words contradict the first relation directly and one of them badly. take rises 2 to 1 and act rises 34 to 13, and both are exactly the contentless pro-verbs that relation says should fall; act's +21 is the largest single move in either list, so the claim survives only as a statement about which generic verbs moved, not about generic verbs as a class, and someone could reasonably refuse it on that basis. Against reading either relation as a change in severity: fire is still the second likeliest completion under B, cut does not move at all, shut rises six places and hire rises four, so B's risers include hostile measures as well as investigative ones. retaliate, the one word that names the anti-union act as such, does not move in either direction, which is the plainest evidence that the difference here is not about whether the worker is punished. Finally, two words were withheld for moving against their prominence, so the lists I was given are not the whole comparison.
result.notes: Relation 2 rests on two words, but they are the only two verbs of their kind present in either list and both rise into the top four, which is why I would still defend it. Relation 1 is the weaker of the two because of take and act. I have not claimed anything about how much likelihood any rank carries, so I cannot tell whether fire holding rank 2 under B means what fire at rank 1 meant under A, and both relations would have to be restated if it did not.

result.reading: Setting aside the function words that dominate both lists, condition A's content completions are three words of injury and constraint (betrayed, trapped, obliged) while condition B's are six words that read the situation as a safety question (safe, safer, unsafe, relieved, intimidated) plus one coercion word (compelled). relations.name: Grievance versus security
relations.sentence: Under A the neighbours' feeling is named in the vocabulary of wrong done to them and freedom taken from them (betrayed, trapped, obliged), while under B it is named as a judgment about danger and its absence (safe, safer, unsafe, relieved, intimidated), so both lists carry unpleasant feelings but only A's are about being wronged and only B's are about being at risk.

relations.name: One axis, both directions
relations.sentence: B's content words include a matched positive and negative pair on a single safety scale (safe and safer against unsafe, with relieved on the positive side and intimidated on the negative), whereas A's content words are all on one side of their own scale and have no positive counterpart anywhere in the A list.

relations.name: Coercion word swapped
relations.sentence: The single sense of being made to do something appears on both sides under different words, obliged under A and compelled under B, so this meaning is not confined to either condition and only its wording changes.

result.kind: frame the feeling is named in: grievance against the newcomers versus assessment of danger

residue.description: None of these completes "the neighbours felt ___" with a feeling; they open a clause or modify a word not yet present (felt they were, felt that, felt like, felt very, felt more), so their side tells us about how the sentence continues rather than about what was felt, and "they", "that", "the" and "safer" in fact did not move at all, which means their placement rests on information not shown to me.

result.counterexamples: The strongest counterexample is obliged against compelled: they are near-synonyms sitting on opposite sides, so the coercion component of the first relation is not really an A-side property and that relation should be read as covering betrayed and trapped much more securely than obliged. Second, unsafe (the largest mover at +10) and intimidated sit under B and are frankly negative and threat-laden, so anyone reading B as the reassuring or milder side is contradicted outright; my relations claim a change of vocabulary, not of valence, and these two words are the reason. Third, the A list is headed by \"they\" with a movement of zero and the B list by \"safe\" and \"that\", so the ordering the instructions describe cannot be reconstructed from the numbers I was given, and any weight I put on which words come first would be unsupported. Fourth, five words are withheld and could sit anywhere in this picture; if two of them were, say, further safety words on the A side, the first relation would weaken considerably.
result.notes: I would defend the grievance-versus-security contrast to someone who disagreed, because it does not depend on valence and survives the obvious objection that both sides contain negative words. I would not defend it strongly: it rests on three A-side content words against six on the B side, nine of the sixteen shown words are function words that do not name a feeling at all, and five further words are withheld on a criterion I cannot inspect. I have not assumed the difference means anything about the conditions themselves, and I have not used the rank numbers as evidence of size, since the same numbers show zero-movement words at the head of both lists.

result.reading: Both lists are plausible continuations of a sentence about an employer reacting to union activity, and the split is not between harsh and mild: B's list is headed by the two plain verbs for dismissal (fire, terminate) and also picks up verbs of talking to her (speak, meet), while A's list is where the response gets routed somewhere else, into a lawsuit (sue, file, bring), a reassignment (transfer), a phone call, or the bleached "end," which is the single largest mover in the whole set at 48 places. Three of B's nine words are masked, including its biggest gainer at +18, and B's four strongest words do not move in rank at all, so a fair amount of the difference is either invisible or not visible as reordering.

relations.name: Ending without saying fired
relations.sentence: Under B the act is named with the ordinary verbs for dismissal, while under A the same outcome is reached by verbs that describe it without naming it or substitute a lesser punishment for it: ending something, transferring her, getting or doing something unspecified.

relations.name: Talking to her appears
relations.sentence: B's gainers include two verbs whose completion is an encounter with the employee herself, speaking to her or meeting with her, and A's list contains no verb of addressing her at all, its nearest candidate being a call that in this frame reads as a call to someone else.

relations.name: Third party gets involved
relations.sentence: A collects the verbs that bring an outside instrument into the dispute, suing, filing, and bringing something (charges, a complaint, a lawyer), whereas B's words all keep the response inside the employer's own authority, something management simply does.

result.kind: whether the act is named outright or routed elsewhere

residue.description: The light verbs (give, have, take, do, get) carry almost no content on their own and could complete the fragment in opposite directions depending on an object we are not shown, so they sit on whichever side without telling us anything, and the three masked entries are unreadable by construction even though one of them is B's largest single movement at eighteen places.</description>

result.counterexamples: The clearest contradiction is that "take" and "have" are on the B side while "do," "get," and "give" are on the A side, so any reading that A is the bleached, unspecific list collapses immediately; only the split among the contentful verbs survives, which is a real narrowing of what I can claim. "Call" damages the second relation moderately: "call her in" is a face-to-face summons, which would put a confrontation verb on the A side, and I only avoid that by choosing the reading in which she is not the one called. "Fire" and "terminate" are said to be where the B difference rests most, yet they move zero places (1 to 1, 2 to 2), so the first relation rests on their being listed as B-favouring rather than on anything the rankings themselves show; if positions were all I had, that relation would have no evidence. "Meet" moves only two places, leaving the conversational relation resting on "speak" alone at seven. "Sue" is odd for the fragment in any condition, since an employer suing an employee for talking to an organizer is not a natural completion, so its presence on A may reflect the verb's general availability rather than anything about this sentence, and it is one of the three words the third relation depends on. Finally the note that one word was withheld for moving against its prominence means both lists are incomplete in an undisclosed direction.
result.notes: I have read only ordinal positions and the stated ordering of contribution, and have not assumed anything about likelihoods. The relations I would defend are the ones resting on words whose lexical content is specific (end, transfer, sue, file, bring, speak, meet, fire, terminate); everything resting on the light verbs I have put in residue rather than force into a pattern. Confidence is medium and not high because a third of B's list is masked, its two strongest words show no rank movement, one word is withheld entirely, and the largest B movement (+18) is unreadable.

result.reading: Almost nothing moves here: no word is absent from either condition, the largest shift is three places, and half the words listed as favored by one condition sit at exactly the same rank in both, so the split is being read off list membership rather than off motion. What separates the two sides is nonetheless legible once the function words are set aside: A keeps "safe", "safer", "obliged", "compelled", "uneasy", while B keeps "threatened", "betrayed", "helpless" — the neighbours are either secured or put under a duty on one side, and harmed or stripped of power on the other.

relations.name: Reassurance against menace
relations.sentence: The condition-A side keeps the two words that make the arrival on the street a source of security for the neighbours ("safe", "safer"), while the condition-B side keeps the words that make the same arrival a source of danger and powerlessness ("threatened", "helpless").

relations.name: Duty against injury
relations.sentence: Where condition A leads with two words casting the neighbours as placed under an external pressure to act or comply ("obliged", "compelled"), condition B leads with a word casting them as wronged by someone who owed them faith ("betrayed"), so both sides imply an outside agent but differ in whether it demands something of the neighbours or does something to them.

result.kind: whether the arrival registers as protection or as harm done to the neighbours

residue.description: These are not content completions of "the neighbours felt ___" but openings onto a following clause or noun phrase ("felt that...", "felt like...", "felt a...", "felt more..."), so their side tells us nothing about what was felt; they also make up eight of the sixteen words and three of the six on the B side, which is why the B evidence is thinner than its list length suggests.

result.counterexamples: "uneasy" is the clearest contradiction: it is a negative-affect word of exactly the family that defines the B side, yet it sits under A, which cuts against reading A as simply the reassuring condition. It damages the first relation moderately rather than fatally, since it names a diffuse discomfort with no agent and no injury, unlike "threatened", "betrayed" and "helpless"; but I would not claim A excludes negative feeling. "safer" is a milder problem in the same direction, since a comparative concedes a prior state of danger that it improves on. Against the second relation, nothing on the A side contradicts it, but "betrayed" alone carries the B half, and it is the one word on either side that moved appreciably (+3), so that relation rests on a single mobile word.
result.notes: The semantic coherence of the two clusters is what licenses these relations; the rank evidence on its own is weak and I want that on the record. No word drops out of either condition, the largest movement is three places, and ten of the sixteen words moved zero or one place while still being assigned to a side, which means the assignment is carrying information about the underlying measurement that I was not shown and am instructed not to guess at. So I would defend the direction of the split on repetition, but not any claim about its size, and I would not defend a claim that any particular low-mobility word (for instance "more", "their", "a") belongs where it was placed. One thing worth stating as a non-relation: both sides are built largely from past participles with an implied external agent ("obliged", "compelled" as much as "threatened", "betrayed"), so the difference is not whether something is done to the neighbours but what is done, and any reading that makes A the agentless or neutral condition is wrong on the words as given.

result.kind: attributed character versus observed conduct

result.reading: The fragment sets up a union-retaliation scenario, and the two rankings put nearly opposite vocabularies at the top of it: A leads with dismissal and sanction words (fire, terminate, suspend, punish, retaliate, transfer) while B leads with the vocabulary of union participation (join, become, attend, support, organize, contact), several of them swapping between rank 1 and rank 140 in both directions. Underneath that inversion, a band of high-frequency, semantically empty verbs sits near the top of both lists and barely moves.

relations.name: Doer changes sides
relations.sentence: Under A the likeliest completions are acts an employer performs on an employee (fire, terminate, suspend, punish, transfer, and retaliate named as such), whereas under B they are acts of union participation and organizing (join, become, attend, organize, support, contact, meet), so that the implied subject of the decision shifts from management to the woman who had been talking to the organizer.

relations.name: Specificity carries the movement
relations.sentence: Every word that moves more than a hundred places in either direction is one that commits the sentence to a definite act (fire, terminate, punish, retaliate, suspend, transfer, cut on one side; join, become, attend, support, organize, contact on the other), while the general-purpose verbs that name no act at all stay near the top of both rankings and move fewer than forty places, so the whole difference is concentrated in the contentful vocabulary rather than spread across the list.

result.kind: whose action the completion belongs to

residue.description: talk is listed as B-favoured but has not moved a single place and merely echoes the fragment's own verb rather than completing it, while use, find, do, go and follow are too underspecified to name any act and would fit either the management scenario (follow up, find grounds, go ahead) or the union one (go to a meeting, find support) without altering their meaning, so their placement on one side is not evidence of anything.

result.counterexamples: Three, of increasing seriousness. First, investigate sits under A yet moves only eleven places and is still ranked 16 under B: it is unambiguously a management action taken against her, and B keeps it near the top, so B has not simply removed employer-side actions. Second, and worse for the first relation, let moves only from 11 to 40 while fire drops 136 places, and let her go is a dismissal; the same holds for get (rid of), have (her removed) and cut (her hours), all of which stay high under B. On that reading the punitive act is not absent under B, only unnamed, which weakens the claim that the doer changes rather than the wording. Third, call, write, contact, follow and meet are assigned to the union side by my reading alone: management can call her in, write her up, or follow up. The measurement places them under B; that they belong to a union frame is my interpretation and it is the softest part of the first relation.
result.notes: Confidence is high for the first relation and medium for the second. The first rests on the largest movements in the data and on two coherent lexical fields that swap ends of the ranking wholesale (fire 1 to 137 against join 136 to 1, terminate 6 to 151 against become 142 to 3), which is not the kind of pattern a repeated measurement would dissolve. The second is weaker because the stability of get, have, give, let, make and take may simply be their frequency: high-frequency light verbs sit near the top of any ranking of this kind, so I cannot separate "these words are stable because they commit to nothing" from "these words are stable because they are common." I have stated the positional fact, which will repeat, and flagged the causal reading, which may not. Two further cautions. The fragment is grammatically ambiguous about who decides: management is the subject of the main clause, so the completions under B strictly require the reader to re-anchor the infinitive's subject to she, and I am inferring that re-anchoring from the words rather than observing it. And I do not know which condition is which or what distinguishes them, so I have described the difference and not attributed it.

result.reading: Under A the room fills with people who talk, sit, read and eat; under B the same entrance is completed by fighting, cutting, killing, shooting and searching, with the harm verbs climbing out of the tail of the ranking (cut 44 to 12, kill 33 to 11) while the plain verbs of address drop away (say 22 to 79, ask 19 to 53). relations.name: Harm displaces address
relations.sentence: Verbs of speaking to someone fall steeply under B while verbs of bodily harm rise out of the tail into the top dozen, so that say drops from 22 to 79 and ask from 19 to 53 in the same movement that carries cut from 44 to 12, kill from 33 to 11 and fight from 23 to 7.

relations.name: Raid over occupancy
relations.sentence: The verbs for settling into a room and staying in it lose ground while the verbs for going through a room and taking from it gain, so sit, eat, read, look and work all fall by nine to twelve places while search rises from 20 to 10 and remove from 30 to 20, with take holding sixth.

relations.name: Contention outlasts conversation
relations.sentence: Speech does not fall as a class: the cooperative speech verbs recede while the adversarial ones hold or advance, so discuss falls 8 to 13, speak 2 to 4 and say 22 to 79 while talk keeps first place and argue moves 3 to 2 alongside fight.

result.kind: the imputed purpose of the entrance

residue.description: Dance rises fourteen places and draw thirteen without belonging to harm, search or speech, so they are motion I can measure and not read; play and take do not move at all and sit on the B side only by whatever margin the ordering was cut at; put, make, sing and throw each move two or three places, which is smaller than any difference I would defend; pray gains one place and fits nothing; and set is unreadable in isolation, since it completes the fragment only through a phrase (set fire, set up, set out) that the fragment does not supply.

result.counterexamples: Dance (32 to 18) and draw (29 to 16) rise almost as far as attack and shoot while contradicting every relation above, and they are the most damaging items here: if B were reweighting the entrance toward harm or toward a search, neither should move at all, and together they are about a sixth of the B side. Throw falls three places despite being the most plausible harm verb on the A side, which is mild but points the wrong way for the first relation. Shout and yell falling by twenty and twenty-six places cuts against any reading in which B is simply more agitated or louder, since a violent entrance would plausibly raise them; this is why I stated the first relation as address rather than as calm. Talk being unchanged at rank one under both conditions is not a counterexample to any particular relation but caps all of them: the most likely single completion is identical, so nothing here licenses a claim that the top of the distribution changed.
result.notes: Three cautions about what the display can support. First, the direction of every move is guaranteed by how the lists were built: words were selected for favouring A or favouring B, so the fact that all sixteen A words fall and all sixteen B words rise or hold is a property of the selection and carries no information. Only the identity of the words and the size of the moves do, which is why I have leaned on cut, kill, say and ask (moves of 22 to 57 places) and discounted the two- and three-place moves. Second, no word carries a dash, so no completion is exclusive to either condition and the difference is entirely one of ordering. Third, most B risers start from the tail (44, 37, 33, 32, 30, 29), so their gains are partly the mechanical consequence of the A-favoured words vacating the middle of the list; the harm reading survives this because those words land in the top twelve rather than merely moving up, but the raid reading is weaker on that account. I would keep the first relation if the measurement were repeated, would keep the second with less certainty, and would expect the third to be the first to go. Finally, the fragment names an ethnic group and I am shown only this one fragment: nothing here tells me whether the same shift would appear with a different group or with an unmarked subject, so I have described what separates the conditions on this item and have not read it as being about the group.

result.reading: Both lists are full of violence, so the difference is plainly not violent-versus-mild in either direction: A holds beat, fire, tear, throw, tie while B holds attack, kill, destroy, shoot, hit, and the single largest move on the sheet (destroy, +73) runs toward B. relations.name: Room-handling script
relations.sentence: The A side gathers verbs that presuppose a room already stocked with objects and occupants being worked through one at a time, so that the completion implies a raid or inspection with things to open, take, tear, tie, remove and search and people to question or beat, while the B side gathers verbs describing the three men's own bearing as a group, which need nothing in the room to act upon.

relations.name: Category-level violence
relations.sentence: Where both sides name violence, A's violent words are specific bodily or instrumented acts carrying a manner with them (beating, tearing, throwing, firing, tying), whereas B's are the superordinate category names for violence as such (attack, kill, destroy, fight), the words one would use to report an event rather than to describe a movement of the body.

relations.name: Private voice
relations.sentence: B alone contains acts of personal feeling and worship, praying, singing, crying, screaming and playing, while A's only comparable words are collective vocalizations directed outward at someone present, chanting, shouting, talking and asking, so that A has no word for an inward or devotional act at all.

result.kind: how much scene the verb presupposes

residue.description: Shoot sits at position 1 under both conditions and moved zero places, so it is listed on B's side without expressing any difference at all; make is a light verb that completes nothing on its own and needs a complement to mean anything here; move and look are close to contentless as descriptions of an action and would fit almost any group entering almost any room, so I would not build a relation on them.

result.counterexamples: The worst is the pair beat and hit: two near-synonyms for striking a person land on opposite sides, with beat almost static under A (2 to 3) and hit rising fifteen places under B, which no semantic sorting by kind of violence can absorb. Second, fire is A's second-strongest word (7 to 32, a fall of 25) while its nearest synonym shoot is pinned at rank 1 under both conditions, so the sharpest single A-preference has a synonym that expresses no preference whatever. Third, kill, destroy and attack sitting on B refutes outright any reading in which B is the tamer or more permitted side, and destroy's +73 is the biggest move on the page. Fourth, talk and chant under A cut against the room-handling relation, since both are things the three men would do themselves rather than things done to them; likewise speak and argue under B are addressed, dyadic speech and weaken the private-voice contrast, which holds only for the sung, wept and prayed words.
result.notes: I would defend the room-handling relation to someone who disagreed: nine or ten A words imply an object or an occupant being handled, and the B list has almost nothing of that texture. I would defend the private-voice relation on the strength of pray, sing and cry having no A counterpart. The category-level violence relation is the weakest of the three and I keep it only because the reporting-register words cluster so cleanly on B; hit alone breaks it, and if the measurement were repeated I would expect membership at the margins to shuffle even if the shape held. Two things I am deliberately not claiming. First, neither side is the violent side and neither is the milder side, so I read no permission gradient here. Second, the lists are ordered by how much each word contributes to the difference and my groupings do not track that ordering; the top of A (shout, fire, beat) is not the cleanest part of the room-handling cluster, and the top of B (attack, fight) is not the cleanest part of the private-voice one. I also have only ranks, so I cannot tell whether a word that fell 25 places fell far or barely at all in the quantity that ranks are derived from, and I have not assumed either.

result.reading: Under A the words that fall furthest away when B is measured are almost all acts aimed at other people present in the room (point -47, yell -43, say -16, tell -14, pray -13, discuss, look, scream), while the words that climb furthest into B's top twenty are almost all whole-body actions in space (move +21, search +16, dance +12, throw +12, run +10, walk +8), with dance jumping from 13 to first. What does not happen is a general retreat of violence: shoot holds at rank 2, attack does not move at all, and fire and throw both rise, so the one violent verb that drops hard (kill, -23) drops for some reason other than being violent.

relations.name: Address-to-locomotion shift
relations.sentence: Under A the high-ranked completions are things done toward other people in the room, saying, telling, discussing, praying, yelling, screaming, looking and pointing, and every one of these falls under B, while the words that rise into B's top twenty are things done with the whole body in the space of the room, moving, walking, running, searching, throwing and dancing, none of which requires anyone to be addressed.

relations.name: Outcome recedes, act does not
relations.sentence: The single verb that names the death of a victim rather than the assault itself, kill, falls 23 places, while the verbs that name only the attack hold or improve, attack unchanged at 7, fire up 7, throw up 12, and shoot still second, so what has gone quiet is the naming of a result and not the presence of violence.

result.kind: the medium of the act, voice directed at people versus body moving in space

residue.description: Make and take are light verbs that do not complete the fragment with any content on their own, so their positions are about grammar rather than about what happens in the room, and sing, play, ask, argue and shoot each move two places or fewer, which is too little to assign to anything, though shoot's stability at rank 2 is part of what the second relation is measured against.</br>

result.counterexamples: The sharpest contradiction is that yell falls 43 places while its near-synonym shout rises 7, and speak rises 5 while say falls 16 and tell falls 14; if the first relation were about the voice as such these pairs would move together, and they move apart, so the relation is at best about a subset of addressed speech and I cannot say which subset. Argue and ask are also addressed acts sitting on the B side, though at +0 and +1 they barely move. In the other direction fight (-4), beat (-6) and take (-1) are bodily acts that fall rather than rise, and throw (+12) and make (+7) are transitive verbs needing an object, which rules out a simpler syntactic version of the same story. Against any reading of B as the milder condition, fire rises 7, throw rises 12 and attack does not move; and against any reading of B as favouring benign sociality, dance goes to first but its natural companions sing (-2), play (+1) and pray (-13) do not follow it.
result.notes: I considered returning an empty list. What stopped me is the magnitude gradient rather than the membership: the six largest falls on the A side are all acts aimed at a person, and the five largest rises on the B side are all acts of moving the body through the room, while the words that cross the pattern (shout, speak, argue, ask, fight, beat, take) all move seven places or fewer. I would defend the first relation on that asymmetry and would not defend it as a clean partition. The second relation rests on one word plus three that hold, which is thin, but kill is the third-largest fall in the set and the three violence verbs that do not move with it agree with each other. The fragment names an ethnic group, and I want to record that the obvious reading, that B softens a stereotyped scene, is not what the numbers show: fire, throw and attack all hold or rise under B, and throw rising 12 places cuts directly against that reading. I have said nothing about likelihoods and the entire analysis is about relative position, so a word could have changed rank a great deal while barely changing in the underlying quantity.
