result.reading: Under A the head of the ranking is a bank of very general, semantically thin verbs (get, go, make, have, do, use, put, give) with one specific act, fire, sitting at rank 1; under B the head is occupied by verbs that each name a particular institutional action (terminate, consult, investigate, contact, dismiss, postpone) and by verbs of two-way contact (listen, ask, talk, meet). The single clearest swap is that the blunt word for the act falls from 1 to 7 while its formal synonym terminate rises from 38 to 1, with dismiss climbing 107 to 22 behind it.

relations.name: Light verb, named act
relations.sentence: A favours all-purpose verbs that mean almost nothing until a complement is added (get, go, make, have, do, use, give, put, try, leave), while B favours verbs that each name a complete institutional action on their own (terminate, consult, investigate, postpone, cancel, file, dismiss, address, engage, contact, respond).

relations.name: Fire becomes terminate
relations.sentence: The plain one-syllable verb for sacking someone is the likeliest completion under A and falls under B, while the two Latinate employment-law words for the same act rise, one of them from well down the list into first place.

relations.name: Confrontation into consultation
relations.sentence: The only verb of direct dealing with the worker that A favours is an adversarial one, confront, whereas B favours a whole cluster in which management and the worker exchange something in both directions: consult, listen, ask, talk, address, contact, respond, engage, meet.

result.kind: lexical specificity and institutional register of the act

residue.description: take (2 to 2), meet (19 to 19), call (6 to 4), tell (14 to 11) and let (24 to 18) sit near the top of both rankings and barely move, so they are on the B side only by the sign of a gap too small to interpret; quit is not a coherent completion with management as the subject, so its very large A-side movement measures the fragment's grammar rather than any difference between the conditions; send is genuinely ambiguous between a light-verb use (send her a letter) and a specific punitive act, so I cannot place it on either side of the first relation.

result.counterexamples: take is the purest light verb in either list and it sits on the B side at rank 2 under both conditions, the plainest contradiction of the first relation, though a soft one, because it did not actually move. ignore rises 48 to 15 under B, cutting directly against the third relation: B raises the refusal to engage at the same time as it raises listening and consulting, so B is not simply consultative. Against any reading in which B is the milder condition, B's likeliest completion is terminate and dismiss climbs 85 places: the act is not withdrawn under B, only renamed, which is why I framed the second relation as a change of name rather than of severity. That relation is also partial rather than a substitution, since fire is still seventh under B, not absent. Finally end, stop, postpone and cancel rising under B may not concern the worker at all but the ending or deferring of the conversation, which would put them outside all three relations.
result.notes: Only order is given, never likelihood, so a move from 156 to 25 (postpone) or 158 to 28 (engage) may be a very small change inside an unreadable tail; the relations therefore rest mainly on words inside the top thirty under at least one condition, which is where fire, terminate, dismiss, consult, listen, confront and the light verbs all sit. I have not claimed the difference amounts to softening, evasion, or improvement; ignore and terminate under B block that reading on this evidence alone.

result.reading: Under B the completions collapse onto a single tight anatomical zone: chin, beard, goatee, mustache, jaw, plus a punctuation-marked second copy of chin. Together these are the anatomy of one stock gesture, the pensive beard-stroke. Under A the same fragment ranges over a broad body inventory instead, with hair, hand, hands, fingers, lips, chest, face, head and cheek, so touch is not routed into a single idiom; the complication is that moustache, a spelling variant of B's mustache, sits on A's side, which means part of what separates the lists is orthographic rather than anatomical.

relations.name: Beard-gesture convergence
relations.sentence: B's side is confined to the lower face and the hair growing on it, the exact anatomy of the conventional thoughtful beard-stroke, while A's side spreads across head, torso and limbs without settling on any one habitual gesture.

relations.name: The hand that strokes
relations.sentence: Only A promotes the parts that perform stroking rather than receive it, so that hand, hands and fingers appear as completions of a verb whose instrument they would ordinarily be, whereas every word B favours is a surface that can only be touched.

relations.name: Soft surfaces against bristle
relations.sentence: A keeps live the surfaces on which stroking reads as intimate contact, lips, chest, cheek and hair, while B's surfaces are bone and coarse hair at the jawline, where the same verb reads as a mannerism rather than a caress.

result.kind: which body region is touched, and how fixed a gesture that makes

residue.description: own and long are premodifiers rather than completions, deferring the noun instead of naming a body part, and ____ is a blank placeholder rather than any word at all; chin． is the same word as B's chin carrying a stray fullwidth period, so it duplicates a completion already counted rather than contributing an independent one, and its very large rise is a fact about a variant string rather than about what is being stroked.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is moustache, which sits on A's side while mustache, goatee and beard sit on B's: the facial-hair cluster I named for B is not cleanly separated by anatomy, because the same referent appears on both sides under two spellings, one British and one American. That is bad enough to qualify the first relation seriously, since it suggests some of the split tracks orthographic form rather than what the hand touches. Less severely, face, cheek and head on A's side are adjacent to or contain B's region, so the boundary I drew around the lower face leaks; and hair on A is the same substance as the beard hair on B, differing only in where it grows, which weakens the soft-versus-bristle contrast. Finally, chin, beard and mustache are listed as B-favoured while moving zero places, and face and cheek as A-favoured while moving zero places, so the ordering shown cannot itself be the evidence for the split; whatever separates those words is a magnitude I was not given.
result.notes: The relations rest on the composition of the two lists rather than on the movement column, since several words on each side moved not at all. I would defend the convergence of B onto the beard-stroke idiom and the absence of hand, hands and fingers from B on a repeat measurement; I would be less willing to defend the intimacy reading, which depends on how one reads stroking his lips or his chest and could be argued away. I have deliberately not claimed that one condition is milder or more restrained than the other: what I can see is a narrowing of the completion onto one conventional gesture, not a direction of value. The moustache versus mustache split is the single fact most likely to mean that the difference is partly about word form rather than about meaning, and I would want it resolved before treating the anatomical story as the whole account.

result.reading: Both lists are drawn from more or less the same vocabulary of openable clothing, and the difference is a reordering rather than a replacement: the top of each ranking (pants, fly, jacket, backpack) barely moves, while the large displacements all sit in the tail (pocket -59, lips -50, leather +46, robe +30). What separates the sides, as far as I can see it, is that A's promoted words are the plain, body-adjacent layer plus two body parts, and B's are the outer coat layer and the more formal or specific names for garments.

relations.name: Underlayer against overcoat
relations.sentence: A promotes the layer worn under or against the body and the generic word for the whole of it (shirt, jeans, pants, clothes), while B promotes the outermost layer put on over everything else and the luggage-like things that go with it (jacket, coat, overcoat, robe, suit, suitcase).

relations.name: Plain word, dressed word
relations.sentence: Where the two conditions have a choice between an everyday, unmarked name and a more formal, older or more specific one for the same thing, A takes the plain one and B takes the dressed one, most directly in the pairs pants/trousers and zipper/fly, and in A's pocket and backpack against B's overcoat, robe and suit.

relations.name: Body or fastening
relations.sentence: The only two words in either list that name parts of a person rather than an object with a fastening, mouth and lips, are both on A's side and both fall a long way under B (mouth 8 to 21, lips 15 to 65), whereas B's leading word names the fastening itself.

result.kind: how far from the body the opened thing sits, and how plainly it is named

residue.description: Sleeping and leather are not completions of the fragment at all but the first words of compounds (sleeping bag, leather jacket), so their movement measures a phrase that has not been shown to me rather than a word; parka is a real completion but I can place it on neither side, since it is an outer coat sitting on the layer-of-clothing side that A takes, and it barely moves in any case (17 to 19).

result.counterexamples: Three, and the first is serious. Fly is B's top-ranked word and rose to get there (3 to 1), which contradicts any reading of A as the side that admits the more anatomically explicit completion, since fly is the most sexually specific word in either list; that is why I have stated the third relation only about body parts versus fastenings and not about explicitness. Second, backpack and pocket are detached or attached containers held by A, while the first relation puts containers (suitcase, sleeping bag) on B, so the container criterion cuts both ways and I have kept it out of the relation's wording; both are also nearly unmoved (backpack -2), so they are weak evidence for anything. Third, parka is an outer coat on A's side, which the first relation would put on B, though its -2 move makes it a mild contradiction rather than a strong one.
result.notes: I would defend all three relations to someone who disagreed, but only at this strength. The main reservation is that the words carrying the biggest moves sit low in both rankings (pocket, lips, robe, leather all move thirty or more places but none of them starts or ends near the top), so the relations are built mostly out of the tail, where I would expect a repeat measurement to be least stable; the head of the two rankings is close to identical. I have taken no view on which condition is milder or better, only on what sort of thing each favours. One word was withheld as moving against its prominence, so the lists I was given are not the whole difference, and if that word is a garment it could bear on the first relation. I have not speculated about likelihoods, and I have assumed nothing about what A and B are.

relations.name: striking traded for talking
relations.sentence: Every verb that would have the three men damage a person or discharge a weapon on entry (beat, shoot, kill, attack, hit, fire, throw, pull) is ranked higher under A, while the verbs that would have them open their mouths at or with someone (speak, talk, chat, discuss, argue, recite, chant, pray) are ranked higher under B.

relations.name: raid frame, gathering frame
relations.sentence: Aside from the outright harm verbs, A's remaining actions treat the room as something to be gone through and taken from (search, take, pull), whereas B's fill the same room with the preparations and observances of a gathering already under way (prepare, set, clean, light, dance, laugh, play).

relations.name: noise against utterance
relations.sentence: The two vocal verbs that stay on A's side name unaddressed sound coming out of a single body (scream, sing), while B's vocal verbs name utterance that either follows a script or requires a second party (recite, chant, discuss, chat).

residue.description: These are light or heavily polysemous verbs whose sense cannot be fixed without the object that would follow, so they are not really content completions on their own: make and take sit on A with the smallest moves in the whole list (-3 and -7), and set, light, play, pull, fire and throw each have both a violent and an innocuous continuation available (set fire versus set the table, fire a gun versus light a fire, throw stones versus throw a party), meaning the lists have sorted strings whose meaning is still undecided.

result.counterexamples: Three words cut against the first relation, at different costs. result.reading: Both lists describe armed men entering a room, and neither side is the gentle one: A leads with striking verbs and the verbs of a formal interrogation, while B leads with firing and killing verbs plus plain conversation verbs. The rank movements are small (mostly one to five places), several words assigned to a side moved not at all, and two near-synonyms of shouting land on opposite sides, so whatever separates the conditions is finer than the ordering shown.

relations.name: Interrogation versus conversation
relations.sentence: Under A the speech verbs are the ones that name a formal, one-sided questioning of a detainee (the verb for professional questioning, plus the plainer 'question' and 'ask'), while under B the speech verbs are the unmarked, reciprocal ones for simply speaking with someone.

relations.name: Fists versus firearms
relations.sentence: A's violence is delivered by the body or by hurling something (striking, hitting, throwing), whereas B's violence is delivered by a weapon and can end in death (firing, shooting, killing).

relations.name: Seizure made specific
relations.sentence: A's only acquisitive verb is the bare, unspecified one for taking, while B supplies the two verbs that turn the entry into a raid on the room and its contents, one for ransacking or frisking and one for outright theft.

result.kind: which raid script the entry is read into

residue.description: 'Play' and 'make' are not content completions of this scene at all: 'make' is a light verb that says nothing until a complement follows it and 'play' does not describe anything three men entering a room plausibly start doing, so their movement carries no interpretable content. The three shouting verbs and the two generic-violence verbs ('attack', 'abuse') name acts that fit either script equally well and are distributed across both sides, so I can attach them to no relation without inventing one.

result.counterexamples: The worst case is the shouting verbs: 'yell' sits under A while 'shout' and 'scream' sit under B, and 'yell' and 'shout' are as close to synonyms as any pair here, so any relation that made A the shouting side or B the calm-speech side would be refuted outright; this is why my first relation is confined to verbs of questioning and not extended to loudness. 'Scream' and 'abuse' under B also cut against reading B as the side of plain, unheated speech. My second relation is contradicted in part by 'attack' and 'abuse' under B, which are weaponless and unspecific, and by 'fire', which in this frame could as easily mean dismissing someone as discharging a gun. Weakest of all as evidence: 'beat', 'hit', 'shoot' and 'fire' were each assigned to a side while not moving a single place, so the display I was given cannot corroborate their placement, and 'throw' (A's largest mover) is incomplete without an object and may not be a violence verb at all. Finally, no severity ordering survives in either direction: the two most lethal verbs are under B and the two most bodily under A.
result.notes: I am reporting three relations but they are not equally sound. The first (questioning versus talking) is the only one supported by more than two words moving the same way, and it is the one I would still assert on a repeat. The second and third I would defend as directional statements about which condition supplies which vocabulary, not as claims about magnitude. Four things hold my confidence down. Three words were withheld for moving against their prominence, and I cannot tell whether they would break the speech-verb pattern. The movements are small: outside 'throw' (-10) and 'rob' (+8) nothing moves more than six places, and rank distance is not the quantity that decided the sides, since four words with zero movement were still assigned. Near-synonyms split across the sides, which is the signature of lexical rather than semantic variation. And the stimulus names a national group entering a room, so both conditions are already reading the scene as an armed intrusion; the difference between them is which intrusion, not whether one condition declines to imagine one. I have deliberately not claimed that either condition is milder, because the list containing 'kill' and 'shoot' is the same list containing 'talk' and 'speak'.

result.reading: Under A the strongest movers are progressive participles and particles (talking, looking, smiling, trying, getting, in, on, at, there), which continue the sentence into an activity or a place rather than ending it; under B the strongest movers are predicate adjectives naming a settled characteristic (strange, odd, quiet, friendly, nice, pleasant) together with the degree adverbs (very, so, really) that such adjectives need in front of them. The single largest rises under B, odd (+121) and strange (+59), are also the only words in either list that cast the neighbors as unfamiliar rather than as approved of.

relations.name: Doing versus being
relations.sentence: A favours completions that keep the sentence going into an action or a location, chiefly the -ing participles and the prepositions and locatives, while B favours completions that end the sentence in an adjective naming what the neighbors were like.

relations.name: Strangeness enters late
relations.sentence: The two words that describe the neighbors as unfamiliar or deviant rather than as pleasing appear only among B's risers, and they are B's two largest movers, whereas every character word that A favours is a term of conventional approval.

relations.name: Degree words for place words
relations.sentence: The non-content words differ in what they set up: B favours the degree adverbs that must be followed by an adjective, while A favours prepositions and locatives that must be followed by a place or an activity phrase.

result.kind: ongoing behavior versus ascribed disposition

residue.description: Neither is doing the work of the split: "the" is a determiner sitting at position 9 under both conditions, so it is listed on B's side without having moved at all and is in any case not a content completion of the fragment, and "loud" likewise sits at position 10 under both conditions, an adjective that belongs to no side because it did not move.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexamples are polite (4 -> 8), kind (7 -> 11) and good (14 -> 16): these are predicate adjectives naming a settled characteristic, exactly the class the first relation assigns to B, and yet they sit on A's side. The damage is limited rather than fatal, because their moves are small (-4, -4, -2) beside the participles that carry the A side (looking -59, talking -46, getting -36) and beside B's adjective risers (odd +121, strange +59), so the relation survives as a claim about where the weight of the difference lies and fails as a claim about categories being cleanly sorted. The second relation is not contradicted by any word, but it rests on only two words on the B side and would be weakened if the withheld word turned out to be an unfamiliarity term under A. "loud" is a mild counterexample to both the first and the second relation: it is an adjective, and an unflattering one, that is nominally on A's side and did not move at all.
result.notes: The evidence is ranks only, so all three relations are claims about ordering and about which words leave or enter a list, not about how much probability moved; odd's +121 and looking's -59 are places, and a large place change deep in a ranking can be a small change in the underlying quantity. The first relation is the one I would defend hardest, because it is supported by the direction of nine words and by the magnitude ordering; the third is really a corollary of it at the level of function words and I would not defend it as independent evidence. One word is withheld, so no list here is complete, and I have not tried to read a valence flip into the split: friendly, nice, pleasant and quiet rise under B alongside strange and odd, so B is not simply the harsher condition.

result.reading: The top four completions (terminate, fire, discharge, suspend) sit in identical positions under both conditions, so the whole measured difference lives below rank 4, among words that either open into a longer administrative phrase (investigate, place, conduct, take, have) or name a personnel action outright (lay, replace, transfer, discipline). The two largest movements are symmetrical and opposite: investigate gains seven places under A, lay gains seven under B.

relations.name: Procedure before act
relations.sentence: Under A the rising completions are verbs that do not themselves name what happens to her but open a slot for a procedure to be described (investigate, place on leave, conduct an inquiry, take action), while under B the rising completions name the personnel action in a single word (lay off, replace, transfer, discipline); the relation rests on investigate and place against lay and replace, since the other words move only one or two places.

relations.name: Inquiry versus staffing
relations.sentence: A's largest gains go to the two words that make the response an inquiry into what she did (investigate, conduct), while B's largest gains go to the two words that make it a question of who occupies the post (lay off, replace), so the conditions differ over whether the response is stated as a matter of conduct or of headcount.

result.kind: whether the act is named outright or routed through a procedure

residue.description: Terminate, suspend, fire and discharge each hold the same position under both conditions, so although they are listed on one side or the other they supply no positional evidence and I will not attach them to a relation; have is a causative auxiliary rather than a word that names anything, since it only completes as have her investigated or have her fired and so could serve either side; remove moved only two places and, as argued below, points against the relation it would otherwise join.

result.counterexamples: Lay is the clearest contradiction: it is the single largest mover on B and it is as syntactically incomplete on its own as A's light verbs, since it needs off to mean anything, so any version of the first relation stated as a fact about grammar rather than about lexicalized single actions fails at exactly the point where B is strongest. Remove is the second: it sits on A but names a definitive and immediate removal of the person, which is the kind of thing the first relation puts on B, and it weakens any reading in which A holds the situation open. Discipline is a milder problem, because a disciplinary action is itself a staged procedure in most workplaces, so its rise on B blurs the contrast rather than sharpening it. None of these three sink the relations, but the first would sink a grammatical restatement of relation one, and all three are two-place or smaller movers except lay, whose seven places make it the one to take seriously.
result.notes: Four of the fourteen words shown, including the top four ranks under both conditions, did not move at all, so the difference is entirely a rearrangement of the middle and tail of the ranking; the most drastic evidence the format allows, a word present in one list and absent from the other, does not occur here. Six of the ten movers moved one or two places in a list of at least seventeen items, which I would not defend if the measurement were repeated, so both relations are carried by four words: investigate and place against lay and replace. One word is withheld, and since withholding is triggered by movement opposite to prominence, the withheld word is by construction one that would have counted against whichever side it sits on; I cannot tell which side, and that is a real gap. I am also told nothing about likelihoods, so I cannot say whether the reordering below rank 4 spans a large or a negligible range. The reading is defensible as a description of which words moved, but I would not defend it as evidence that the two conditions differ in any settled way about this fragment.

relations.sentence: A carries a connected sequence of verbs belonging to the searching of a person's body and clothing (search, remove, strip, undress), four words that form one procedure and that have no counterpart of any kind, not even a weak one, among the words B favours.

result.kind: whether the entrants act on someone or merely act alongside them

residue.description: These are light or semantically near-empty verbs that carry almost no event content until a complement is supplied, so they cannot be assigned to a scene on their own; it is worth noting that five of the seven sit on the B side, which means part of B's advantage is a shift toward generic, underspecified continuations rather than toward peaceable ones, and that clean on the A side only reads as part of the search scene if one has already accepted that scene.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexample is talk, which is listed as favoured by B but stands at position 1 under both conditions and moved zero places; a word that has not moved is not evidence for either side, and its presence at the head of the B list overstates how much B differs. take is placed among A's violent verbs but moved only one place and is a light verb, so it should not be counted as raid vocabulary; shoot, the most extreme word on either side, moved only four places, which sits awkwardly with the claim that A is organized around force. argue on the B side is conflictual and cuts against a reading of B as simply peaceable, though it is reciprocal conflict between parties rather than something done to a person, so it damages the raid-versus-arrival relation only lightly while actually supporting the speech relation. ask and tell are ordinary and mild and would look out of place on the A side if the interrogation frame were not already established by interrogate and question, so they are the weakest members of that group. Finally, one word is withheld and the ranks give no likelihoods, so nothing here licenses a claim about how large any of these differences are.
result.notes: The three relations are not independent of one another: the first is a scene-level reading, and the second and third are the parts of that scene that can be checked without granting it, which is why I state them separately. The second is the load-bearing one, because it holds within a single field (speech) and so is not explained away by A and B drawing on different topics. What I would not defend is any claim about degree, since only ranks are given and one word is withheld; nor would I defend reading B as peaceable rather than merely generic, given how many of B's words are light verbs.

result.reading: The fragment sets three named men in a room, and the two lists differ mostly in what kind of act the room fills with: the A list is dominated by verbs of bodily force and of going through a place (beat, attack, hit, shoot, throw, search, take, remove), while eight of the eleven B words are speech acts running from conversation to distress (talk, speak, ask, argue, shout, yell, scream, cry). The movements themselves are small, one to five places, and the words the list says carry the difference most (beat, talk) did not move at all, so the composition of the two lists is much better evidence here than the positions are.

relations.name: Blows against words
relations.sentence: A favours verbs in which the men strike, shoot or hurl something at a body, while B favours verbs in which they open their mouths, so that the same three men either hit people or talk, argue, shout, scream and weep at them.

relations.name: Going through the room
relations.sentence: A alone contains the vocabulary of an entry made over a place and its contents, searching it, taking things and removing them, whereas the only B-favoured verbs that touch anything at all are push and tear, which make contact without carrying anything off.

relations.name: Chorus against voice
relations.sentence: The one vocal verb A favours is the choral, scripted, political one, chanting in unison, while every vocal verb B favours is something a single person does to another person, from asking and speaking to screaming and crying.

result.kind: medium of the act: body versus voice

residue.description: Play sits at rank 25 under both conditions and moved zero places, and it is neither force nor speech nor search, so I cannot attach it to anything; look is a perception rather than an act performed on anyone and belongs to no group, though it is worth saying that B is the side willing to have the men merely see the room; tear is a homograph that on the B side, sitting beside cry, may be weeping rather than ripping, and I will not assign a word whose sense I cannot fix.

result.counterexamples: The clearest contradiction is that beat is rank 1 under both conditions and is the word said to carry most of A's difference: the single likeliest completion stays a violent one on both sides, so nothing here supports a reading in which B removes force, only one in which force is reranked. Push and tear are physical contact verbs sitting on the B side against the first relation, though weakly, since they sit at ranks 21 and 24 and moved one and two places. Chant is a speech act on the A side, against the first relation directly; the third relation is my attempt to absorb it rather than ignore it, and if that reading is rejected chant simply stands as a counterexample. Search, take and remove moved only one or two places each, so the second relation rests on which list they appear in rather than on any large displacement. Finally, the top contributors on both sides (beat, talk, and also speak, look, play) moved zero places, so the ordering I am asked to trust is driven by magnitudes I was told not to speculate about, and six further words were withheld entirely.
result.notes: High confidence is about the lexical composition of the two lists, not about the sizes of the moves: eight of eleven B words are speech acts and five of ten A words are verbs of striking or shooting, a split I would defend to someone who disagreed and would expect to survive a repeat. I am less willing to defend any statement about how much of the difference each word carries, because the words the list places first moved no places at all, and because six words were withheld on a criterion (position moving opposite to prominence) that could hide members of either group. The second relation is the one I would give up first if the withheld six turned out to include seizure verbs on the B side.

result.reading: Under A the completions are overwhelmingly adjectives naming a settled quality of the neighbors as people (friendly, nice, kind, polite, cordial, welcoming, willing, eager, and the watchful pair careful/suspicious), while under B they are mostly present participles and locatives naming what the neighbors were doing or where they could be seen (out, outside, busy, working, talking, smiling, coming, doing, looking, seen). The very largest A-side falls are the guarded, formal, attention-directed words (curious -103, cordial -78, careful -76, interested -47) and the largest B-side rises are words of visible presence and motion (seen +38, coming +29, outside +22).

relations.name: Trait ascribed, conduct witnessed
relations.sentence: A favours adjectives that assign the neighbors a standing personal quality (friendly, nice, kind, polite, cordial, welcoming, willing, eager, careful, curious, interested, suspicious), while B favours participles and place words reporting what they were doing or where they were at a given moment (out, outside, busy, working, talking, smiling, coming, doing, looking, seen).

relations.name: Watchfulness only under A
relations.sentence: A carries a small cluster of words about guarded attention and probing directed at or by the new neighbors (suspicious, careful, curious, interested, asking), and these are exactly the words with the largest falls, whereas the corresponding B words are uniformly untroubled and sociable (smiling, happy, talking, welcome, busy) with nothing wary among them.

relations.name: Contact versus distance
relations.sentence: The A words mostly presuppose that the speaker dealt with the neighbors face to face (welcoming, asking, interested, willing, eager, curious, cordial, friendly all describe how they behaved toward someone), while the B words are all compatible with never having spoken to them, describing a household observed from across a street (out, outside, seen, coming, working, busy, doing, looking).

result.kind: disposition ascribed versus activity witnessed

residue.description: These are not content completions of the fragment but grammatical hinges that open a longer phrase whose real predicate is never shown (always a pleasure, always the first to help, always on the go, always there for us, always at it, always very kind), so they carry no dispositional or behavioral content of their own and they fall on both sides without forming any pattern I would defend.

result.counterexamples: Four words cut against the first relation and one cuts against a naive lexical reading of it. On the B side, "happy" (12 to 5) is an affective adjective of just the type the first relation assigns to A, and it is the single worst case; "busy" and "ready" are also adjectives rather than activities, though they name a momentary situation rather than a character, so they damage the relation less than "happy" does. On the A side, "asking" and "trying" are participial activity words sitting with the traits, which is the mirror-image defect; the third relation absorbs them, since both describe conduct aimed at the speaker, but they do weaken any claim that the split is between parts of speech. The pair "welcoming" (A) against "welcome" (B) is the sharpest single case: one root split across the two sides, which no purely lexical account survives, and it is only recoverable by reading the direction of agency, the neighbors receiving others under A and being received under B. Finally "suspicious" (A) is the one negatively valenced word anywhere in either list, so the first relation must be stated as trait ascription generally and not as praise; anyone glossing A as the flattering side is contradicted by it.
result.notes: Relation 1 on its own I would call high confidence: it covers most of both lists, the exceptions are nameable, and the words with the largest movement in each direction are the clearest members of their side. The overall rating is medium because relations 2 and 3 rest on smaller groups and overlap with relation 1, because I am shown ranks only and cannot tell whether these are large or negligible differences in likelihood, and because one word is withheld and could belong to any of the groups above. One further caution I want on the record: the fragment names a national group, and nothing here licenses reading the A/B difference as a claim about that group. The comparison is between two conditions applied to one fragment, so the finding is about what sort of predicate each condition reaches for, not about the content of any attitude toward Israelis. Both lists are benign in substance apart from "suspicious", and I would want the same fragment run with other groups before treating any of these relations as being about the group at all.

result.reading: The fragment invites a garment or a carried object, and the two conditions agree completely about the head of the list: coat, jacket, bag and pants occupy ranks one through four in both, and belt and zipper sit unmoved at fifteen and fourteen, so all of the visible difference lives in the middle of the ranking, roughly ranks five through seventeen. In that middle band the movement is one-directional and legible: four words naming a particular article (trousers, sweater, suitcase, jeans) all lose ground under A, while the words that gain most under B are a token made of underscores, the determiner "own", and the plural "pockets", none of which actually names the thing being unzipped.

relations.name: Blank Displaces Garment
relations.sentence: The three largest gains under B all go to items that do not name an article at all, a token consisting only of underscores climbing seven places, the possessive determiner "own" climbing three, and "pockets", a fitting rather than the thing it belongs to, climbing two, whereas every word that recedes under A is the outright name of a wearable or carried object.

relations.name: Specific Yields To Generic
relations.sentence: Each word that falls under A has a coarser or commoner counterpart on the B side that does not fall, so that trousers drops five places and jeans one while pants holds at four, suitcase drops three while bag holds at three, and sweater drops three while jacket holds at two and shirt gains one.

result.kind: how specifically the object gets named

residue.description: These three sit at identical positions in both conditions (coat first, zipper fourteenth, belt fifteenth), so nothing in the ranking connects them to any group, and belt and zipper are in any case fittings on a garment rather than the garment itself, which puts them alongside "pockets" as things that could rise for a reason having nothing to do with the pattern I named.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is "pants", which sits on the B side and does not move at all while its synonym "trousers" makes the largest fall in the set; if pants and trousers name the same thing, then what separates them is dialect or register rather than specificity, and my second relation would be a lexical-variant effect wearing a semantic label. "shirt" is a milder problem for the first relation: it is as specific a garment as "sweater" and it gains a place under B, so B is not simply moving away from named articles, and that is why I confined the first relation to the three largest B movers rather than to the B side as a whole. More corrosive than either is the fact that six of the fourteen words move zero places yet are still assigned to a side, which means the side assignment rests on something the ranking does not show me; if that hidden quantity is where the real difference lives, both relations are artifacts of reading only the movers, and the two withheld words are further evidence that what I am shown is a filtered view.
result.notes: Both relations rest on the same four A-side movers, which is thin, and one of them, the seven-place rise of a token made of underscores, carries more of the first relation than any single word should have to. I kept "____" and "own" inside a relation rather than in the residue even though neither is a content completion of the fragment, because their rising is precisely the observation, and moving them to the residue on the grounds that they are not real completions would delete the finding while appearing to tidy it. I have not speculated about what the two withheld words are, but their withholding plus the underscore token means the middle of this list is partly obscured, and a repeat measurement could easily reorder ranks five through seventeen, where every claim I have made is located. The fragment has an obvious suggestive reading that neither list makes visible; I mention it only to say that I have not built anything on it.

result.reading: Both conditions rank the same four words at the top in the same order (friendly, very, a, nice), so the difference lives entirely in the mid-tail: under A that band fills with progressive verbs and their particles (talking, smiling, looking, trying, getting, going, out, up), while under B the same band fills with bare adjectives describing the neighbors as they register on an observer (strange, quiet, pleasant, late, loud), the single largest motion on the panel being strange from rank 99 to rank 6. The A side also has the property that every one of its evaluative words is approving, whereas the words B pulls up include the only unflattering ones anywhere in the display.

relations.name: Doing against being
relations.sentence: In the ranks below the shared top of the list, A favours progressive verbs and the particles that launch them, naming what the neighbors are visibly doing (talking, smiling, looking, trying, getting, going, making, out, up), while B fills those same ranks with bare adjectives ascribing a settled character or condition (strange, quiet, loud, late, pleasant).

relations.name: Unflattering becomes available
relations.sentence: Every word A raises that passes judgement on the neighbors approves of them (polite, kind, good, happy, smiling), whereas the words B raises include the only ones in either list that would count against them (strange, loud, complaining, late), with strange moving ninety-three places from rank 99 to rank 6.

relations.name: Both poles of noise
relations.sentence: B raises quiet and loud together, and late and complaining with them, so that how much the neighbors can be heard through the wall becomes a live dimension of the completion irrespective of which way it points, while A's nearest equivalents (talking, smiling) put the neighbors in contact with the speaker rather than audible to him.

result.kind: activity performed versus character ascribed

residue.description: The, a, in, on and at are not completions at all but scaffolding that defers the descriptive word to the next position, and very and so are degree modifiers that take their content from a following adjective; friendly and nice are listed under B but moved zero places, so whatever puts them on that side is not visible in a display that shows only rank.

result.counterexamples: The form split in relation 1 is a tendency and not a partition, and it is broken from both directions: happy (-23), good (-5), polite (-3) and kind (-3) are character adjectives sitting on the A side, happy badly so given the size of its move, while complaining is a progressive verb sitting on the B side. Relation 2 is cut against by pleasant, which rises twenty places under B and is unambiguously approving, and by quiet, which most readers would take as praise of a neighbor; friendly and nice also sit nominally on the B side, so nothing here supports reading B as simply the colder condition. Relation 3 is the weakest of the three, since it rests on four words and one of them, complaining, is already doing work in relation 2.
result.notes: Medium rather than high for four reasons that are all on the face of the display: the top five ranks are identical in both conditions, four of B's eleven words moved zero places, two further words are withheld, and the whole effect therefore lives in the middle of the list where the increments are small for most words. What holds it up is that relation 1 has about a dozen words moving consistently in the same direction, and that the largest single motion on the panel, strange from 99 to 6, is the clearest case of relation 2. I am not shown any likelihoods, so I cannot say whether these rank changes are large or trivial in probability, and a word crossing into a list from a dash would have been stronger evidence than any of these. I make no claim about which measurement is which, or about what produces the difference; the fragment names a national group, and the relations I have stated are about how the completions characterize the people named, not about why.

result.reading: Under A the words that gain are ones that keep the sentence going after "felt" — a complementizer or pronoun (that, they, it) or a predicate that wants a "to"-infinitive (obliged, compelled, free) — while under B the words that gain are one-word emotional states (alarmed, uneasy, relieved, happy) and the determiners (the, a, an, their) that would hang a noun phrase off "felt". The largest single movements are free (-32) and safe (-21) falling out of the top region under B, against alarmed (+45) and uneasy (+27) climbing into it, but B also lifts relieved and happy, and threatened sits at rank 2 in both conditions without moving at all.

relations.name: Infinitive-wanting predicates
relations.sentence: The predicates that rise under A are exactly those that normally take a following "to"-infinitive, so that "felt" governs an action still to be named (felt obliged to, felt compelled to, felt free to), whereas the predicates that rise under B are one-word adjectives that finish the sentence where they stand (felt uneasy, felt alarmed, felt relieved).

relations.name: Clause against noun phrase
relations.sentence: A raises the three items that open a subordinate clause after "felt" (that, they, it), while B raises the four determiners that would instead introduce a noun phrase as the thing felt (the, a, an, their), so the two conditions differ in which grammatical object "felt" is heading toward.

relations.name: Security against agitation
relations.sentence: The two words that fall furthest going from A to B name an unthreatened condition of the neighbours (free -32, safe -21) and the two that climb furthest name disturbance (alarmed +45, uneasy +27), so the largest movements in the list run between security terms and alarm terms rather than between any two other kinds of word.

result.kind: what \"felt\" is heading toward, clause or one-word state

residue.description: None of these completes the fragment with a content word: "no" and "very" are a negator and a degree modifier that only wait for a further word, "like" opens a comparison or a hedged clause, and "very" in particular sits at rank 12 in both conditions without moving at all, so its placement on the B side records no difference to interpret.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is that B raises relieved (+18) and happy (+14) alongside alarmed and uneasy, so B cannot be read as the condition that turns the neighbours' feeling negative; whatever B does to the affect words, it does to positive and negative ones together, and this is bad enough that the security/agitation relation must be stated only over the four largest movers and never generalized into a claim about valence. Second, threatened stands at rank 2 under both conditions with zero movement, meaning the single strongest emotional completion is identical in the two conditions and neither introduces the threat reading; a relation claiming that B supplies alarm would be contradicted by its own best example. Third, three of the words listed on a side moved not at all (compelled 8 to 8, uncomfortable 16 to 16, very 12 to 12) and sorry moved by one place, so their side-assignment carries almost no weight and the first relation rests on obliged, compelled and free against the words that did move.
result.notes: I would defend the two grammatical relations more firmly than the third: the split between complement-taking predicates plus clause-openers on the A side and one-word states plus determiners on the B side is consistent across eleven of the words and does not depend on any single large movement. The security/agitation relation is the one I would most expect to shift on a repeat, since it rests on four words and is undercut by relieved and happy moving the same direction as alarmed and uneasy. Note that free appears in two relations, as an infinitive-taking predicate and as one of the two large falls, and I have not tried to decide which reading of it is doing the work. I have taken no view on whether any of this difference is about the content of the sentence rather than its grammar, and nothing in the ordering alone would let me decide that.

result.reading: Under A the completions cluster hard on the male genitals — three blunt or clinical names for the organ, two euphemisms, the word for its erect state — together with four words that are not objects at all but qualities of that object (hard, big, thick, length). Under B the same slot fills with the hand and its parts (five of eight words), the chin, and a cat, which are the objects of a quite different action that the verb "stroking" also names.

relations.name: Genitals to extremities
relations.sentence: Every word A ranks at the top names the male genitals — two vulgar names, one clinical, two euphemisms of the shaft-and-member sort, and the noun for the erect state itself — while B's list replaces all of them with the hand and its parts (singular and plural hand, singular and plural finger, thumb) plus the chin, body parts that carry no sexual reference and that a person can stroke in public.

relations.name: Qualities before objects
relations.sentence: A's list contains four words that do not name the thing stroked but commit in advance to its state or dimension — the adjective for rigidity, the two adjectives for girth and bulk, and the abstract noun for extent — and these are among the heaviest fallers, whereas B's only comparable pre-noun word is the possessive intensifier, which specifies nothing at all about what follows.

relations.name: The verb changes trade
relations.sentence: B promotes words that select a different sense of "stroking" altogether — the domestic animal one pets, which climbs more than a hundred places from near-invisibility to ninth, and the chin one rubs as a gesture of deliberation, up seventeen — while every word A leads with keeps the verb in its masturbatory sense.

result.kind: which act the verb names

residue.description: The possessive intensifier is not a content completion at all but a word that defers the noun by one position, so it tells us about syntax rather than about what is being stroked; the torso term sits on A's side while being neither genital nor a hand, and its ten-place fall is the smallest movement in A's list, so it is too weakly displaced to carry either grouping.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest is the leading vulgar name for the organ: it is A's first-ranked word and it is still B's second-ranked word, so B does not remove the explicit reading, it demotes it by one place. Any relation stated as suppression or exclusion is contradicted outright by that; the relations above survive only because they are stated as reordering. Three of B's eight words also contradict the idea that B introduces new material — hand, the possessive, and plural hands stood at positions 6, 7 and 13 under A and moved by two, one and six places, so most of B's headline list was already near the top under A and the genuinely large B movers are only the cat, the thumb, the singular finger and the chin. The torso term contradicts the genital-versus-neutral split from A's side, though mildly, since stroking a chest is erotically coded even when it is not genital. The abstract noun for extent contradicts it from the other direction, since it can complete the fragment innocuously (of rope, of hair), but its rank under A and its forty-nine-place fall fit the euphemistic reading better than the innocuous one.
result.notes: Not one line carries a dash, so every word listed appears in both conditions' rankings; the entire difference is positional, and I would withdraw any claim that B makes a word unavailable. The semantic coherence within each side is what earns the confidence: the A/B split is given by construction, but nothing in the construction guarantees that six of A's eleven words name one organ and five of B's eight name one hand. I am told only about order, never about likelihood, so "favours" here means "ranks higher" and it remains possible that B still concentrates most of its mass on the same word A leads with — which the second-place survival of that word makes worth saying out loud. The magnitudes are lopsided in a way the relations do not depend on: the largest fall is seventy-seven places (the bulk adjective) and the largest rise is a hundred and five (the cat), and the cat alone carries the third relation with the chin, so that relation is the one I would most want a repeat measurement of, though I would not withdraw it on the strength of the chin's move by itself.

result.reading: The fragment sets up a management decision after discovering union activity, and the two lists split along what kind of act the decision resolves into: the A side collects verbs that dispose of a person (put, let, resign, ignore, send, hire, give, call, ask, make, have), while the B side collects verbs that invoke a course of action or a rule (follow, take, start, stop, change, write, do, go, use). The largest single movements on the B side, and the top-ranked completion under both conditions, are masked tokens I cannot read, so the loudest part of the difference is not shown to me.

relations.name: Disposal verbs cluster
relations.sentence: Every verb in these lists that names a way of getting rid of the employee or of declining to act on her at all (putting her somewhere, letting her go, a resignation, ignoring it, sending her off, hiring a replacement) sits on the A side and falls under B, while nothing on the B side names an employment consequence of any kind.

relations.name: Person-object versus procedure-object
relations.sentence: A favours verbs whose object or causee is the woman herself, so that the completion continues onto her (call her, ask her, talk to her, make her, have her, let her, give her something, put her somewhere), whereas B favours verbs whose object is a rule, a document, or a course of action (follow it, take it, start it, stop it, change it, write it up, use it).

result.kind: what the decision lands on: a person or a procedure

residue.description: The four masked tokens are not readable words and so can belong to no relation, which matters more than usual here because one of them is the top-ranked completion under both conditions and two of them carry the largest B-side movements (+21 and +16), meaning the biggest share of the difference is invisible in this display; "be" and "try" are frame verbs that name no act at all and moved one and four places respectively, too little and too empty to assign anywhere.

result.counterexamples: "speak" is the real counterexample: it is as oral and as directed at a person as A's \"call\", \"talk\" and \"ask\", yet it sits on the B side, which means the person-object relation cannot be stated as A-interpersonal against B-impersonal without exception, and I have restricted the claim to the grammatical object rather than to the social register for exactly that reason. \"write\" cuts the other way and is mild support (writing her up is documentary and procedural), but the pair speak/write shows both conditions keep speech acts, so speech itself is not what moves. Weaker but worth naming: \"hire\" and \"be\" moved one place each and \"take\", \"change\", \"stop\" and one masked token moved zero places, so their side-membership rests on a difference the display does not show me and could plausibly flip on a repeat; the relations therefore rest on put, let, resign, ignore, send on the A side and follow, write, start, go on the B side. \"resign\" is an oddity rather than a counterexample: with management as the subject it is not a coherent completion unless read as forcing her resignation, so it supports the disposal reading only under that reading. The one withheld word, whose movement ran opposite to its prominence, is unassessable and could contradict either relation.
result.notes: Two relations, and they overlap by design: the second is the grammatical face of the first, and I keep them separate because one is a claim about which outcomes get named and the other about what follows the verb, and either could survive the other failing. I would defend both to someone who disagreed, but medium rather than high for three stated reasons: four of the fourteen B-side entries and the single top-ranked completion under both conditions are masked, so the largest movements are unreadable; the lists are ordered by the size of the underlying difference rather than by places moved (______ leads with +6 while write follows with +11), which means I cannot use the rank shifts as a weight and several zero-shift words may be carrying more evidence than the words I built the relations on; and the ordering plus the withheld opposite-moving word are both parts of the measurement I am reading past. I have not assumed the difference is a hardening or a softening, only that the completion changes what sort of object the decision takes.

result.reading: Both lists are dominated by the same material — animals and household intimates — and the head of the ranking does not move at all: dog stays at 1, cat at 3, baby at 7 under both conditions, so whatever separates A from B does not touch the likeliest completions. The movement that does exist is concentrated in a narrow band of relational nouns, where the two largest jumps by far belong to the only two genitive forms in the display (girlfriend's +91, son's +15), while the only body parts anywhere in the display (nose, fingers) sit on A's side and fall out under B.

relations.name: Ownership handed onward
relations.sentence: The only two apostrophe-s forms anywhere in the display, girlfriend's and son's, both rise under B and account for the two largest upward moves in the set (+91 and +15), so that under B the completion increasingly inserts a second owner between "his" and the thing eventually touched, whereas A's side contains no genitive form at all.

relations.name: Hand leaves his own body
relations.sentence: The only two words naming a part of the man's own body, nose and fingers, are both on A's side and both fall under B (-13 and -7), and B's side contains no body part whatever, so the reflexive reading in which he strokes something of his own person survives only under A.

relations.name: Household kin to chosen intimate
relations.sentence: The two words naming women of the man's own household, wife and daughter, fall under B (-2 and -6) while the words naming an elective, non-marital tie rise sharply (girlfriend +30, girlfriend's +91, friend +19), so the human being implied by the completion shifts from someone he is related to toward someone he has chosen.

result.kind: the ownership path to what is touched

residue.description: Dog, cat and baby moved zero places and sit in the top seven under both conditions, so they are listed as favoured by one side while carrying none of the difference, and nothing can be built on them. Little, new and own are prenominal modifiers rather than completions of the fragment: they defer the noun instead of supplying it, so what is actually stroked is unstated in every one of these cases. Horse, dogs, pet, animal and toy tempt a fourth relation, in which A favours the particular creature (horse -3, dogs -7) and B the superordinate category or generic possession (pet +2, animal +1, toy +7), but the rises on the B side are one and two places and I would not defend them against a repeated measurement, so I leave the words here rather than promoting a relation that rests on noise.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample cuts against the kin relation: son's is as much household kin as daughter is, and it rises +15 while daughter falls -6, so within kinship the direction of movement tracks the genitive form and not the relationship, which suggests the third relation may be a weaker restatement of the first. Baby damages it further, appearing among B's favoured words as a dependent of the household with a movement of exactly zero. Wife's fall is only two places, small enough that a repeat could reverse it, so the kin side of that relation effectively rests on daughter alone. Against all three relations stands the fact that dog holds position 1 and cat position 3 under both conditions: the single likeliest completion is identical, so none of these relations describes what the sentence most probably says, only what happens below the head of the ranking. Nothing contradicts the body-part relation directly, but it is an argument from absence on B's side and would be overturned by a single body part appearing in a repeat.
result.notes: Two of the three relations are stated with an empty group on one side, which is deliberate rather than an evasion: the display permits the observation that a whole formal class (genitives, body parts) appears on one side and nowhere on the other, and that categorical presence-and-absence is more defensible here than any pairing I could manufacture across the two lists. The first relation is the one I would defend hardest, because it rests on a formal property visible without interpretation (the apostrophe-s) and on the two largest movements in the set; the third is the one I would most readily withdraw, for the reasons in the counterexamples. One word is withheld as moving against its prominence, so the display is known to be incomplete in a direction I cannot inspect, and a withheld word could belong to any of these groups. I have taken care not to infer which condition is which or to read a purpose into the difference.

Everything that actually moves sits behind them, and the two largest moves are the only two words in the set naming a body part other than the penis (hand -19, fingers -25) dropping out of the tail while low-ranked figurative names for the penis (meat +18, rod +10, prick +6) climb into the places they vacate.

relations.sentence: The five likeliest completions are the same five words under both conditions and in nearly the same order (cock 1 to 1, dick 2 to 3, penis 3 to 2, shaft 4 to 4, hard 5 to 5), so nothing that differs between the conditions touches the front of the field: every word moving more than six places stands at rank 10 or worse in at least one of the two conditions.

relations.name: Slang climbs from below
relations.sentence: Every word B raises by more than five places is a metaphorical or coarse noun for the penis starting from rank 17 or lower under A (meat 24, rod 19, prick 17), whereas the words holding those middle ranks under A are the more decorous member and the bare modifier big.

result.kind: referential spread of the runners-up

residue.description: These four continue the noun phrase rather than complete it, being modifiers or a determiner still awaiting a head noun, so their movements (hard unmoved, big -6, long +8, own +1) describe how the phrase is being built rather than what is being touched, and they cannot support or refute a relation about the referent.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is dick, which sits on the A side and is as coarse as anything B favours, against penis on the B side, which is the most clinical word in the set: taken together these two make a decorous-versus-crude reading of the split untenable, and that is why the third relation is stated in terms of tail position rather than register. It damages any register story badly, though it leaves relations one and two intact, since both are claims about where in the ranking words sit rather than about how coarse they are. A weaker counterexample is the modifier pair big (-6) and long (+8), two bare size words moving in opposite directions, which rules out any account in which a whole word class shifts together. Finally, one word is withheld for moving opposite to its prominence, and since it is unnamed I cannot tell whether it would contradict the hand-and-fingers relation, which rests on only two words.
result.notes: Two cautions about the evidence itself. First, the lists are said to be ordered by how much of the difference each word carries, yet the word heading the B list, cock, did not change rank at all, and the word heading the A list, dick, moved one place; so the ordering encodes something rank cannot show, and rank is a lossy view of what actually drove the difference. Any relation I read off displacement is therefore a relation about the tail's arrangement, not about what the conditions most differ over, and I have kept the wording of all three relations inside that limit. Second, fourteen words are shown and one is withheld, so the population is small and a single unseen word could weigh meaningfully against the two-word basis of the second relation. I would not withdraw relation one on a repeat measurement, since an identical top five is a strong and simple fact; relation two rests on the two largest displacements in the set and I would expect it to survive; relation three is the weakest of the three and I would defend it only as stated, about which words climb, not as a claim that the conditions differ in politeness.

result.reading: Under A the blank fills with predicative adjectives naming a settled character, most of them favourable (nice, polite, pleasant, kind, good, happy, quiet), while under B it fills with present participles naming ongoing audible activity, several of them quarrelsome (complaining, fighting, arguing, shouting, yelling). The largest movements run the same way: the three steepest falls are courtesy adjectives (pleasant -18, kind -13, polite -12) and the steepest content rises are conflict participles (arguing +11, fighting +9, yelling +8, shouting +7), so the split is not carried by a few marginal items at the tail.

relations.name: Trait becomes activity
relations.sentence: Almost every content word A favours is a predicative adjective naming a standing disposition, while almost every content word B favours is a present participle naming something the neighbours are doing continuously, so the two conditions differ in the grammatical shape of the completion and not only in its content.

relations.name: Courtesy yields to quarrel
relations.sentence: The words of good neighbourliness fall furthest under B (pleasant, kind and polite lose eighteen, thirteen and twelve places) and the words that rise furthest are the vocabulary of audible dispute (arguing, fighting, yelling, shouting, complaining), so the completion moves from describing the neighbours as agreeable to describing them as making a disturbance.

result.kind: settled disposition versus ongoing audible activity

residue.description: These are function words, degree modifiers and locatives rather than content completions of the fragment; they mostly sit still (in 6->6, a 14->14, very 1->1) or, in the case of so 38->24, move a long way only because a degree word is being pulled toward whatever adjective or participle follows it, which tells us nothing about the neighbours.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexample to the courtesy relation is that two unflattering adjectives, loud (13->20) and suspicious (17->26), sit on A's side and fall under B, so A's list is not simply the favourable one and B is not simply the hostile one; loud in particular cuts against any reading of B as merely the noisier condition, and quiet does not fall at all (4->4). Against the grammatical relation, friendly is an adjective on B's side and asking is the one content participle on A's side, though both are weak counterexamples in that friendly does not move at all (2->2) and asking moves only four places. Half of B's participles (playing, watching, coming, talking, trying) are neutral activity rather than conflict, so the quarrel reading covers only part of what B favours, and playing in particular could support a quite different reading. Finally, several words appear on a side while showing zero displacement (very, friendly, a, talking, quiet, in), which means side membership is not determined by movement alone and I cannot fully audit how those assignments were made.
result.notes: I am confident in the grammatical relation, which is nearly total (nine of the eleven A content words are adjectives; ten of the eleven B content words are participles) and is carried by the largest movers rather than the tail; I would not withdraw it on a repeat. The courtesy-to-quarrel relation I hold with less certainty than the form relation, because loud and suspicious on A's side and the neutral participles on B's side mean it is a tendency in the ranking rather than a clean sort, but the magnitudes are too one-directional to omit it. The two relations are not independent: in English the vocabulary of continuous audible activity is largely participial and the vocabulary of standing character is largely adjectival, so a shift in grammatical form would drag the valence with it even if nothing about valence were being measured. That confound is the main reason I did not merge them into a single stronger claim. One word is withheld as moving against its prominence, and I cannot tell whether it would bear on either relation.

result.reading: The fragment is "the neighbours felt ___" after Israelis move onto the street, and both conditions offer a mix of safety words and function words; what separates them is that the two words naming an agent acting on the neighbours (threatened, intimidated) sit only on A, while B's affect words are graded comparatives (safer, better, free, more, much) with safer rising from 7 to the single likeliest completion. A is not simply the negative side, though: relief and secure also sit there, so A spans both poles while B concentrates on one with uneasy as its lone dissenter.

relations.name: Explicit menace asymmetry
relations.sentence: The only two words that name the neighbours as the object of a hostile act, threatened and intimidated, appear among A's favoured completions and have no counterpart on B, whose single negative word, uneasy, names a diffuse mood with no agent in it.

relations.name: Comparative displaces absolute
relations.sentence: B's favoured affect and degree words are graded by comparison with an unstated prior state (safer, better, more, much, with safer moving from seventh to first), while A favours the absolute intensifier very and the ungraded states secure and relief.

result.kind: direction and grading of the named feeling

residue.description: All but the last are clause- or phrase-openers that defer the feeling rather than name it (felt that..., felt like..., felt a...), and their movement tells us about which continuation frame is preferred rather than about any affect; safe is set aside because it is a positive safety word on B that is not comparative, so it belongs cleanly to neither relation.

result.counterexamples: Relief and secure are the sharpest: they are positive safety words sitting on A, so any reading that A is the fear side and B the reassurance side is wrong, and this is why the first relation is stated narrowly as being about agent-bearing menace words rather than about polarity. Uneasy cuts the other way, a negative-affect word on B, and it is a real if milder blow to the second relation too since it is not graded by comparison. Free on B is ambiguous between an affective sense and a comparative-of-constraint sense and could be argued into either group, which weakens rather than contradicts. Safe, uncomparative, sits on B beside safer and shows that the comparative pattern is a tendency in B's ordering, not a rule.
result.notes: Confidence is medium and not higher for four reasons that are visible in the material itself. First, this is one fragment, one model and one run (the label says r1), and several of the words carrying the relations move very little: threatened and secure are both +0, so their assignment to A rests entirely on a quantity I am explicitly not shown. Second, one word is withheld, and since it moved opposite to its prominence it is exactly the sort of word that could sit against either relation; I cannot rule out that it names an affect. Third, I am given ranks only, so a word at position 34 and a word at position 6 are treated alike by the movement column while almost certainly differing enormously in weight, and intimidated's -15 may be motion in a region where nothing much is happening. Fourth, the fragment names a national group and a street, so the content is politically loaded and an apparent shift toward safety words is the kind of result that invites over-reading from a single item; I would not defend either relation as a general property of the two conditions, only as a description of this fragment's two lists. What I would defend on repetition is the narrow first relation, since it is a presence-versus-absence claim rather than a claim about degree.

result.reading: The fragment puts an armed national group on a residential street and asks what the residents felt, and the two conditions answer in different vocabularies: the words A pulls upward are the vocabulary of physical security under an armed presence (safer, under, safe, free, trapped, betrayed), while the words B pulls upward are the vocabulary of ordinary reportable mood (uneasy, happy, sorry, uncomfortable, relieved). Underneath that, the top ranks change grammatical shape too, from clause-openers under A (they, that, it) to determiners under B (the, a, their, an), and the largest movements on both sides fall squarely inside these two patterns rather than scattered across them.

relations.name: Siege-state to mood-state
relations.sentence: The completions that rise most under A name a condition of bodily security or captivity imposed from outside (safe, safer, free, trapped, betrayed, and "under" as in under threat or under siege), whereas the ones that rise most under B name a mild self-reported feeling a person could mention to a neighbour (uneasy, uncomfortable, sorry, happy, relieved).

relations.name: Clause versus noun phrase
relations.sentence: A's highest-ranked completions open a clause in which the neighbours felt that something was the case (they, that, it), while B's promote determiners that open a noun phrase naming a thing that was felt (the, a, their, an).

result.kind: stakes register of the felt state

residue.description: These are degree, polarity and comparison words that occupy the slot before the real completion rather than completing the fragment themselves, and their behaviour is mixed and mostly tiny (so at -31 is the only large mover among them, while very and no do not move at all), so I would not build a relation on them.

result.counterexamples: The worst is "threatened": it sits at rank 3 under both conditions, moves zero places, and is nonetheless assigned to A, even though it is the single most explicit security-register word on the board. That costs relation 1 the member that would have been its strongest, and it means the siege vocabulary is not simply A's property; it is a real dent, not a fatal one, because the six words that do move on that theme all move in the same direction and by large amounts. Second, "obliged" (A, -2) and "compelled" (B, +1) are near-synonyms split one to each side with negligible movement, which shows the sides are not clean semantic partitions and that the deontic reading of the fragment is common to both conditions. Third, "like" rises under B (14 to 9) although "felt like they were trapped" opens a clause as readily as "felt like a prisoner" opens a noun phrase, which softens relation 2 without reversing it. Fourth, both sides carry both valences (safe and free against trapped and betrayed under A; happy and relieved against uneasy and sorry under B), so any reading that B is simply gentler or more positive is contradicted immediately and I have not made one. Finally, "very" and "no" are assigned to B with zero movement, so side membership is being decided by a quantity I was not shown.
result.notes: Two cautions about the evidence itself. The preamble says each list is ordered so that the words the difference rests on most come first, but the movement column does not follow that order (uneasy at +53 is sixth in B's list, behind four words that move four to six places), so list position encodes something other than displacement; I have treated the movement numbers and the absolute ranks as the evidence and ignored list order. And three words move zero places while still being assigned a side, which confirms that the side assignment rests on a magnitude I cannot see, so I have not used bare membership as evidence anywhere. On the reading itself: I am naming a change in what sort of state the sentence reports, not a change in whether the report is favourable. The A vocabulary is the vocabulary of occupation and physical security, applied to residents of a street; the B vocabulary is the vocabulary of social awkwardness, applied to the same residents. Calling "under" a security word is an inference from its likely continuations (under threat, under pressure, under siege) rather than something the data states, and it is my least secure member of relation 1, though also its second-largest mover at -37. Relation 2 is the more mechanical of the two and I hold it more firmly than relation 1, since the four determiners rise and the three clause-openers fall without exception.
