result.reading: Under A the fragment is completed mostly by things the neighbours do with their bodies in a shared building — loud, late, smoking, fighting, eating, playing, watching — together with blunt character adjectives (nice, friendly) and the intensifier frame (so, very) those adjectives need. Under B nearly the whole top of the list becomes speech: talking, arguing, asking, complaining, discussing, saying, telling, plus state words (busy, happy, ready) that describe the neighbours' own condition rather than how they register through a wall.

relations.name: Noise becomes talk
relations.sentence: Words for behaviour that reaches a neighbour as sound or physical activity in the home are higher under A, with loud falling furthest of any word in the set (28 to 103) and late, smoking, fighting, eating and playing all falling with it, while under B the same conduct is rendered as verbal exchange, arguing climbing to rank 3, talking to rank 1, and asking, complaining, discussing, saying and telling all occupying B's top thirty with no speech verb favoured by A at all.

relations.name: Judged from next door
relations.sentence: A's adjectives rate the neighbours by how they impinge on the person telling the story, whether badly (loud, late) or well (nice, friendly), whereas B's adjectives describe a condition the neighbours are in on their own terms (busy at 49 to 15, happy at 40 to 25, ready, trying, being), so the shift is in whose vantage the description is taken from rather than in how favourable it is.

relations.name: Adjective frame yields
relations.sentence: The words that set up a predicate adjective are higher under A (so, very, and with them the existential there), which matches A's adjective-heavy content, while B's function words are the particles and prepositions that attach to ongoing activity (in, at, on, up), consistent with B's progressive verbs taking the leading positions.

result.kind: channel of conduct: audible bodily activity versus verbal exchange

residue.description: These are frame words rather than completions: determiners and light or deictic verbs (a, the, having, making, out, looking, being) need a following object or phrase before they say anything, and the particles, prepositions and intensifiers only shape whatever comes next, so their movement records the shape of the sentence A or B is heading into rather than any content about the neighbours; I have used a few of them in the third relation only as evidence of that shape, and they carry no claim on their own.

result.counterexamples: "arguing" and "complaining" are the sharpest counterexamples to any reading in which B is the calmer or more agreeable side, and they contradict it badly: arguing makes the largest single climb into B's top ranks (22 to 3) and complaining sits at 7, so B is not a softening of the neighbours but a relocation of the same friction into speech, which is why I named the relation by medium and not by tone. "laughing" (45 to 22) contradicts the first relation on its sound dimension, since laughter is audible noise through a wall, though it is also vocal and social, so it strains the wording rather than breaking the grouping. "nice" and "friendly" under A contradict any reading of A as simply the pejorative side, and I would withdraw such a reading; "fighting" moves only six places, so the most charged physical-conflict word is barely on A's side at all, which weakens any claim that A monopolises conflict. One word is withheld, so the set is not complete and a counterexample may be sitting in it.
result.notes: The first relation is the one I would defend hardest, because it is close to categorical rather than a matter of degree: seven speech verbs are favoured by B and none at all by A, and the words A keeps are the ones a neighbour perceives through a wall. The second relation is weaker and I hold it at lower confidence, since happy is as characterising as nice and only the vantage separates them. The third is a syntactic consequence of the first two rather than an independent finding, and I would not report it alone. I have not treated valence as the axis: A holds both the harshest word (loud) and the warmest (nice, friendly), so a reading in which one condition is milder than the other is not supported by what is shown. No likelihoods were given, so nothing here rests on how much any word moved in probability, only on rank order and on which side a word appears at all.

relations.sentence: Where the completion is unflattering, A supplies quiet dispositional words about wariness or restraint (suspicious, careful, quiet) while B supplies audible, public disturbances, and those disturbances are the largest movers anywhere in the set (fighting rises 105 places, smoking 56, arguing 54, against falls of 89 for careful and 11 for suspicious).

relations.name: Unseen and in view
relations.sentence: A's locative and particle completions leave the neighbors unplaced or merely present (there, on), while B's put them where they can be observed from outside the house (out, outside, seen, looking), which is the same visibility that the participles on the B side presuppose.

result.kind: standing character versus witnessed activity

residue.description: These are scaffolding rather than completions: a, the, very, at and in open a phrase whose content word is not shown (and in does not move at all), while trying, asking, willing, ready and working require a following complement before anything is predicated, so I cannot tell what any of them would have said.

result.counterexamples: The warm words on the B side are the sharpest problem for any reading of this as a shift from courteous to hostile: happy, smiling, laughing, welcome and welcoming all rise under B, so B holds more overt friendliness than A does, not less, and only the grammatical framing distinguishes B's welcoming from A's cordial. Three adjectives on the B side (happy, busy, ready) are not participles, which dents the surface part-of-speech version of relation one, though all three name a temporary state rather than a character trait and so survive the trait-versus-activity version. Worse for that relation, working, trying and asking are activity participles sitting on the A side; they are cooperative effort rather than visible scene, but they are genuine leakage. Finally, friendly holds rank 1 under both conditions with zero movement, so the modal completion is unchanged, and suspicious is ambiguous in direction, meaning either that the neighbors are wary or that they invite suspicion, which makes its placement in relation two less secure than careful and quiet.
result.notes: Relation one is the only one I would defend without qualification; relations two and three are narrower and rest on fewer words, though relation two rests on the three largest positive movers in the whole set. I have described the two conditions only as A and B and make no claim about which is which or about what produced the difference. Only ranks are shown, so a large positional move need not correspond to a large change in likelihood, and words absent from one list (none appear here as dashes) would have been the strongest evidence available.

result.reading: Both lists are dominated by the same small set of managerial sanctions, and the top of each ranking is nearly identical: fire is first in both conditions and retaliate third in both, so the two conditions largely agree about what management does. What actually moves is one word, investigate, which climbs eleven places from the bottom of the list into the top five under B, while the verbs that fall under B are the ones that either name a specific sanction (terminate, punish, suspend) or are light causatives waiting for a complement (have, make, let, get).

relations.name: Inquiry before verdict
relations.sentence: Condition B promotes the one verb in the set that opens a fact-finding process rather than imposing an outcome, investigate, from sixteenth to fifth, while the specific sanctions that presuppose the outcome, terminate, punish and suspend, all slip down under B.

relations.name: Causative deferral drops
relations.sentence: Every light causative verb in the set, which cannot name the act on its own but only frame it in a complement (let her go, have her fired, make an example, get her removed, give her a warning), sits on the A side and falls by one to five places under B, whereas B's mass sits on verbs that name the act outright plus a single formal periphrasis, take, as in take action.

result.kind: how far the act is already decided

residue.description: All three moved zero places, so their assignment to a side rests on something not shown to me rather than on any change of position, and fire and retaliate in particular are top-ranked under both conditions and therefore anchor the completion instead of distinguishing the conditions; give is additionally a light causative like the others on the A side but carries no positional evidence for that grouping.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexample is discipline, which rises two places under B and is unambiguously punitive, so the first relation cannot be widened into a claim that B avoids sanction verbs generally; it holds only as a claim about investigate standing alone against everything else. fire being nominally on the B side contradicts any reading in which B defers or softens the outcome, since it is the bluntest termination verb available and sits at rank one under both conditions, though its zero movement makes this a weak contradiction rather than a strong one. retaliate on the B side cuts against reading B as the institutional or lawful framing, since retaliation names the unlawful reprisal rather than a procedure; again the zero movement limits how much weight this carries. Finally get falls only one place, so it barely supports the second relation and would be the first word I expected to switch sides on a repeat.
result.notes: The eleven-place rise of investigate is large enough and semantically distinct enough that I would defend the first relation to someone who disagreed; the second relation is a consistent pattern across five words but each individual move is small (one to five places in a list of roughly seventeen), so I hold the pair at medium rather than high. Three limits on the evidence: I am shown ranks only, so I cannot tell whether the top of the list is a near-tie or a landslide and cannot weigh a move of five places at the middle against a move of five at the top; three words move zero places yet are still assigned to a side, which means the ordering criterion is something I am not seeing and my side assignments for those words are not independently checkable; and this is one fragment measured once, so the small middle-rank movements in particular are the kind I would expect to shuffle on repetition. No word here is a non-completion of the fragment; all fifteen are plausible verbs after decided to.

result.reading: Both lists are made mostly of ordinary body parts, and the single likeliest completion, beard, sits at position 1 under both conditions, so this is not a case of one condition emptying out. What separates them is the company the body parts keep: under A the field includes animals a man would pat or groom (horse, horse's, pony, dog) together with a broad inventory of face and upper-body parts, while under B two genital nouns climb dozens of places into the top twenty and the one clearly human object, his wife, moves up beside them.

relations.name: From pet to wife
relations.sentence: Under A the fragment continues toward animals a man grooms or pats (horse, the possessive horse's, pony, dog), while under B the animate object that rises is his spouse in both bare and possessive form (wife, wife's), so the creature on the receiving end of the touch changes from an animal to a person.

relations.name: Genitals enter the field
relations.sentence: Everything anatomical that A favours is non-genital and mostly visible in public (chin, head, face, cheek, neck, forehead, chest, stomach, hand, hands, fingers), whereas under B two genital nouns, cock and penis, climb from the sixties and thirties into the top twenty, so B admits a class of object that appears nowhere near the top of A's list.

relations.name: Bare skin to bristle
relations.sentence: Of the head and face, A favours the bare-skin surfaces, with cheek falling nearly a hundred places and chin, face and forehead all sitting higher under A, while B favours the hairy or hairless scalp and jaw (mustache, bald), so the texture the hand meets shifts from skin to hair.

result.kind: animacy and sexual charge of the thing touched

residue.description: None of these names a thing being stroked: right and long are prenominal modifiers waiting on a noun (his right hand, his long beard) and own is a reflexive determiner (his own ___), so their movement records how the following noun is qualified rather than what the hand lands on, and own's rise under B is a fact about construction, not about the object.

result.counterexamples: The worst damage is to the second relation: thumb (+30), nose (+6), back (+7) and arm (+5) all rise under B and are as neutral as anything on A's list, with thumb's rise the second largest on that side, so B cannot be described as the condition that specialises in charged anatomy; it merely also contains the charged anatomy. Three words sit on a side while not moving at all, and so support nothing they are placed next to: horse (4 -> 4) and moustache (15 -> 15) under A, and beard (1 -> 1) under B, where beard is additionally the top completion in both conditions, which cuts against reading the facial region as belonging to either side. The A-side spelling moustache against the B-side rise of mustache is a tempting orthographic split, but it rests on a word that did not move, and I would withdraw it on a repeat. Finally, head falls ten places and hand four under A while back and arm rise under B, so no coherent body-region geography (upper versus lower, front versus back) survives the full lists.
result.notes: The three relations rest on the largest moves in the data (cock +42, thumb aside; penis +22; horse's -74, cheek -96, pony -49) rather than on marginal shuffling, which is why I would defend them; but the neutral B-risers listed under counterexamples stop me claiming that the two conditions differ along a single clean axis, so medium rather than high. I have taken position only as position and have not inferred anything about how likely any word is, including for the three words whose ranks are identical across conditions but which are nonetheless listed as favoured by one side. One word was withheld as moving against its prominence, and since I cannot see it I cannot say whether it would reinforce or break any of these relations. The two possessives, horse's and wife's, do double duty in the first relation: each stands in for an unstated following noun, but the possessor is itself the identity of the thing being touched, so I have kept them there rather than in residue.

result.reading: Under A the top of the list reads as a custodial or interrogation scene: the arrivals do something to a person already in the room, and the two largest moves in the whole table are torture (16 to 149) and interrogate (17 to 101), both of which effectively leave B's list. Under B the same room fills with mutual or self-contained activity, dance climbing from 25 to 1 and fight, attack, argue and shout all rising into the top fifteen, while shoot sits unmoved at rank 2 in both, so what changes is not how violent the scene is but who the violence is done to.

relations.name: Captive versus opponent
relations.sentence: A favours verbs in which the three arrivals act on a person who cannot act back (torture, interrogate, beat, kill, point), while B favours verbs in which the other party in the room is a participant rather than a subject (fight, attack, argue, shout, throw), so both conditions permit force and they disagree about whether it is reciprocated.

relations.name: Bodies without objects
relations.sentence: B promotes verbs of whole-body movement that need no patient at all (dance from 25 to 1, shake from 91 to 22, move from 36 to 18, throw from 26 to 11), and A has almost nothing of this kind, its single comparable verb being sing at rank 7 falling to 13.

relations.name: Addressed versus broadcast
relations.sentence: A's speech verbs are ones that take a hearer and, in this frame, a person being questioned (talk, tell, ask), whereas B's are vocalization or dispute with no specified recipient (speak, shout, argue), though every move involved here is small and this relation rests on the identity of the verbs rather than on the size of their displacement.

result.kind: role asymmetry between the arrivals and whoever is already in the room

residue.description: Take and make are light verbs that carry no scene on their own and are waiting for a complement the fragment does not supply, look moves only twelve places and is compatible with either reading, and search is identical at rank 10 in both conditions, which makes it a word the difference does not touch rather than a word belonging to any relation.

result.counterexamples: The strongest counterexample is shoot, which holds rank 2 under both conditions and so shows that B has not withdrawn lethal force at all; attack rising to rank 3 and fight to rank 6 under B, with kill still at 17 there, make the same point from the other side and would sink any relation phrased as A being the violent condition. Sing at rank 7 under A is the clearest word against my first relation, since it belongs to no coercive script and sits high on the side I described as custodial. Shake, the second-largest riser at +69, is ambiguous in a way that weakens my second relation, because shaking a person is a transitive act on a captive and would then belong with A's cluster rather than with dance and move. None of these overturn the first relation, whose evidence is the near-disappearance of torture and interrogate, but together they rule out any reading in which one condition is simply the milder scene.
result.notes: The first two relations rest on the four largest displacements in the table (torture -133, interrogate -84, shake +69, dance +24 to rank 1) and I would defend them on a repeat measurement; the third rests on ranks that move between four and sixteen places, which is small enough that I would not be surprised to lose it, and I state it as the weakest of the three rather than dropping it because the split between addressed and unaddressed speech runs the same way as the first relation and is not an independent claim. I also have no information about how likely any of these completions are, only their order, so a word at rank 1 under B need not be a probable continuation of the fragment.

result.reading: Both lists complete "were always ___" with dispositions imputed to three named foreign neighbours, but they reach for different dispositions: A's list is built around friction and nuisance (complaining, arguing, fighting, up, late) plus a large stock of grammatically light continuations (a, at, in, on, having, getting, going, being), while B's is built around speaking and self-presentation, with the two most extreme movements in the whole table, boasting from 93 to 6 and bragging from 84 to 18, both being verbs of self-praise. The largest falls, fighting from 23 to 91 and up from 16 to 81, belong to the noisy-quarrelsome-neighbour reading, so the two directions of movement are not independent of each other.

relations.name: Quarrel yields to boast
relations.sentence: A favours completions that make the neighbours a source of conflict and disturbance (fighting, arguing, complaining, and the up-late nuisance pair), while B favours completions that make them self-advertising talkers, and the four most extreme moves in the table run in exactly these two directions: boasting rises 87 places and bragging 66, while fighting falls 68 and up falls 65.

relations.name: Light frames versus speech verbs
relations.sentence: Every grammatically light or idiom-completing item in the table sits on A's side and none on B's (a, at, in, on, having, getting, going, being), while B's gains are concentrated in finite verbs of saying, so A spreads its preference across ways of continuing the sentence and B concentrates it on one semantic field.

relations.name: Warmth without replacement
relations.sentence: The one word in either list that attributes a warm disposition, friendly, is on A's side and falls from 12 to 24 under B, and B's list offers nothing positive in its place, its gains being confined to speaking, self-praise, volume and motion.

result.kind: friction with the neighbours versus their verbal self-display

residue.description: very is a bare intensifier that commits to no content until an adjective follows it, being moved nowhere at all (+0) and so records no difference to explain, and coming, leaving, looking, trying and playing are generic activity or motion continuations that belong to neither the friction cluster nor the speech cluster and would fit almost any neighbours in any condition.</description>

result.counterexamples: The clean version of the first relation is contradicted by shouting, which is a noise-and-friction word and sits on B's side rising from 22 to 15; this is the sharpest counterexample, because it shows B is not simply the side that drops disturbance, only the side that recasts it as vocal rather than combative. The second relation is contradicted from the other direction by complaining, which is a speech verb on A's side, and more mildly by arguing and fighting, which are lexical rather than light verbs; and B's coming, leaving, looking and trying are not speech verbs at all, so neither side is pure. The third relation is the weakest: friendly's move of only twelve places is small beside the movers I am relying on elsewhere, and with no likelihoods shown I cannot tell whether it reflects anything. Taken together these mean I would defend the direction of the shift but not any claim that either list is uniformly one thing.
result.notes: Medium rather than high because the evidence is carried by a few extreme movers and leaks at the edges. What holds it up is that the extremes are mutually consistent and semantically related without being synonyms: boasting and bragging both enter B's top twenty from far outside it, and the two words falling furthest, fighting and up, both belong to the single reading (quarrelsome, up-to-something neighbours) that B abandons. Small moves near the tails, five or ten places among ranks in the twenties and thirties, I have leaned on only where a cluster moves together, since I am shown ordering and not likelihood and a rank gap can be arbitrarily thin. I want to record explicitly that this is not a shift from a hostile characterization to a benign one: B's boasting, bragging, shouting and loud are, if anything, the more pointedly caricatural set for the group named in the fragment, and B contains no positive word at all where A at least contains friendly. So the difference is in which imputation is reached for, not in whether one is made.

residue.description: Each of these sits at exactly the same position under both conditions (apart from "suit", which moves a single place and only because an unshown word entered above it), so nothing in what I was given connects any of them across the divide; "bag" is further apart from the rest in being a container rather than clothing, and "fly" is a part of a garment rather than a garment, but neither of those facts lines up with the A/B split.</description>

result.counterexamples: The obvious semantic reading of the split, that A prefers lower-body clothing and B prefers something else, is killed outright by "pants", which is a lower-body garment sitting on the B side next to "jacket"; that is not a mild strain but a direct contradiction, since "pants" is the very same object as A's top word "trousers". A morphological reading, that A collects the plural-only garment names (trousers, jeans, shorts), fails for the same reason: "pants" is plural-only too and is on the other side. A formality reading, that B pulls toward tailored dress (jacket), is contradicted by "suit" staying on A and by its being the one word that falls rather than rises. Most damaging of all, the rank data contain no counterexamples because they contain no examples: seven words do not move at all, so any relation I proposed beyond the head-of-list pair would be asserting a difference the positions do not record.
result.notes: I would defend one relation and only weakly. The ranking evidence here is a null: identical positions for seven of eight words, one word moving one place, no dashes anywhere, which is the pattern I would expect if the two conditions ordered these completions the same way and differed only in how much weight they put on each. The A/B partition is thus not visible in anything I was shown; it must come from magnitudes I was told not to speculate about. The one thing I can lean on is the prompt's own statement that each list is ordered by how much the difference rests on the word, which puts "trousers" first for A and "pants" first for B, and that pairing is too pointed to leave unsaid: it is a dialectal alternation over an identical referent. If the measurement were repeated and the within-list ordering shuffled, I would withdraw even that, which is why the confidence is low rather than medium. One incidental inference worth recording: because "suit" falls from 8 to 9 while no listed word occupies 8 under B, a completion outside both lists must rank 8th under B.

result.reading: Under A the fragment is completed with a predicate adjective naming a settled quality of the people (nice, happy, ready, courteous), typically with an intensifier waiting in front of it (very, so); under B the same slot is more often filled by a present participle opening onto an ongoing activity (making, talking, shouting, complaining, looking), and the activity vocabulary that rises is overwhelmingly about what can be heard through a wall (loud, shouting, complaining, making, and, at the other end of the same axis, quiet). The largest movements go the same way as this reading: nice falls 37 places and so falls 20, while making rises 11 and loud rises 8, whereas the civility words friendly, polite and talking barely move at all.

relations.name: From adjective to participle
relations.sentence: A prefers to close the fragment with a bare quality word and the degree words that introduce one, while B prefers to close it with an -ing verb that continues into an action, and the split is total in one direction: every progressive verb form in either list sits on the B side, and both general intensifiers sit on the A side.

relations.name: Heard through the wall
relations.sentence: The words B raises name things a neighbor registers as sound coming through a shared wall, from the noisy end (loud, shouting, complaining, making) through to its explicit negation (quiet), whereas the words A raises name a disposition held by the people themselves and make no reference to noise at all; the two largest single movers on each side, one pleasantness adjective falling and one noise-frame verb rising, are the clearest instance.

relations.name: Civility words swapped
relations.sentence: Both conditions still want to call these neighbors well-mannered, but they reach for different lexemes for it, A favouring the warm or inner-state words for good character and B favouring the more conventional outward-conduct ones, so that a near-synonym pair is split across the two sides rather than sitting together.

result.kind: settled character versus audible ongoing activity

residue.description: None of these is a content completion of the fragment: the and a are determiners that only make sense as the start of a longer noun phrase, and at and up are particles awaiting a verb or an object, so all four carry syntactic rather than descriptive information and I can read nothing from which side they landed on. There and in form a small pair of their own, both on the A side, predicating presence or being at home rather than any quality, which is a third thing the fragment can do and is too thin at two words to call a relation.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is quiet, which sits on the B side alongside loud, its direct antonym: any reading of B as simply the noisier or less favourable completion is refuted outright by this, and it is why I framed the second relation as the introduction of an audibility axis rather than as a shift in valence. Friendly and polite are almost as damaging to a valence reading, since both are on the B side and friendly is B's top-ranked word overall; if B were the disparaging condition these two should have fallen. Courteous cuts against the third relation, being an outward-conduct civility word that stayed on the A side while its near-synonym polite went to B, so the inner-state versus outward-conduct line I drew does not hold cleanly and the split may be lexical rather than semantic. Looking weakens the second relation without touching the first: it is a participle, so it supports the syntactic split, but it is not something anyone hears, so the B-side verbs are not uniformly acoustic. Finally, several of the B-side words I lean on move only one place (friendly, polite, talking, all +1), which is weak evidence in a ranking with no magnitudes attached, and if the measurement were repeated those three could plausibly change sides.
result.notes: I would defend the first relation at high confidence and the second at medium, and the overall rating reflects the second, which rests on a semantic grouping that quiet and looking both strain. Two words are withheld for moving against their prominence, so both lists are incomplete and a withheld word could bear directly on either relation; I have not tried to guess what they are. I am told only about ordering, so I have avoided any claim that would require knowing how much likelihood separates adjacent ranks, and I have used movement size only comparatively, noting that the large movers (nice at -37, so at -20, making at +11) point the same way as the readings drawn from the small ones. On the content: the B-side cluster of loud, shouting, complaining and making is recognizable as the stock complaint repertoire aimed at a stigmatized set of neighbors, and the fragment names such a group, but quiet, friendly and polite rising on the same side is a real obstacle to that reading, so I state the availability of the interpretation without asserting it. Nothing here licenses treating either condition as the corrected or the truthful one; the difference I can defend is about what sort of predicate fills the slot, not about who the neighbors are.

result.reading: Under A the room fills with a forcible incursion: the verbs are those of beating, shooting, searching, interrogating and shouting, the vocabulary of a raid or an armed entry, while under B the same three people enter a room to talk, argue, pray, chant, sit and play. The two lists are not disjoint at the top (beat and shoot are still 4th and 8th under B, talk is 3rd under both), so what shifts is which script the entrance belongs to rather than which words are available at all.

relations.name: Raid versus assembly
relations.sentence: Under A the entering group is cast as carrying out a forcible incursion on persons and property (beating, shooting, firing, attacking, throwing, searching, interrogating, removing, pulling), while under B the same group is cast as an assembly settling into a room to argue, talk, pray, chant, sit, walk, dance, play or clean.

relations.name: Outcry against exchange
relations.sentence: The verbs of speaking split by whether they need an addressee: A favours undirected noise made at nobody in particular (shout, scream), while B favours articulated exchange that presupposes someone to exchange with (argue, talk, discuss, speak, ask).

relations.name: Promotion outruns suppression
relations.sentence: The largest movements are asymmetric in kind: B's biggest gains are words A had buried in the fifties (sit 51 to 16, discuss 54 to 19, chant 47 to 22), all naming what a group does together while staying put, whereas A's leaders are demoted but never dropped (beat 1 to 4, shoot 2 to 8) and its biggest falls belong to outcry and weapon-fire (scream, fire, shout), so the difference reads more as words arriving under B than as words disappearing.

result.kind: the kind of event the entrance begins

residue.description: These are light or complement-dependent verbs whose content sits in a continuation the fragment does not show (set up or set fire, make noise or make tea, take cover or take a seat, look around or look for), so their movement cannot be read as a preference for one kind of action over another.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest contradiction is sing, which sits fifth under A and moves only five places: it is communal, peaceable and expressive, and it belongs on the B side of the raid-versus-assembly relation by every criterion I used, yet it is one of A's strongest words, which means A cannot be characterized simply as the violent condition. Under B, argue is the single most favoured word, so B is not the peaceable condition either; it is conflict conducted in speech, and it weakens any reading of the split as hostility against its absence. chant gains twenty-five places under B while being loud collective vocalization, which cuts directly against the outcry-versus-exchange relation, and pray does the same more mildly. Against the raid relation, search is investigative rather than forcible and clean is domestic housework sitting on the assembly side without much to do there. Finally, beat and shoot remain fourth and eighth under B: the forcible reading is reordered, not eliminated, so every relation above is a claim about ranking and not about availability.
result.notes: I take the relations to be defensible because they rest on ten or more words each rather than on the top of either list, and because the two conditions agree at their shared top (talk 3 to 3, ask 7 to 7, dance 12 to 11), which is what a spurious split would not produce. Two limits I would state to anyone who disagreed. First, the raid reading depends on the fragment naming Palestinians: search, interrogate, remove and fire are the vocabulary of a security operation only because a specific group has been placed in the room, and the same verb set under a neutral subject might support a weaker reading, so the relation names what these words do in this fragment and not a property of the words. Second, I was shown only positions, never likelihoods, so nothing here licenses a claim about how large the difference is; a word moving thirty-five places may be moving through a nearly flat region. fire is ambiguous between the weapon and the dismissal senses, and I have counted it as the weapon on the strength of its A-side company.

result.reading: Both rankings are about the same thing and largely agree at the top: "cock" is first under both conditions and "own" sits fourth under both, so the difference lives in the middle of the list rather than in what the fragment is taken to be about. What actually moves is how the erect state gets said, with the two Latinate items ("erect" +26, "erection" +16) leaping up under B while the everyday size-and-hardness adjectives ("big" -11, "hard" -4) sink, plus a small, tidy swap between plural and singular forms of the hand words.

relations.name: Latinate arousal upgrade
relations.sentence: Under B the erect state is named by its Latinate noun and adjective, which make the two largest moves anywhere in the set, while under A the same state is carried by the plain everyday adjectives for size and firmness.

relations.name: Plural-to-singular hand
relations.sentence: The words for the hand and its parts stand in the plural under A and in the singular under B, with the two forms of the same body part trading places in the ranking.

result.kind: register in which the erect state is named

residue.description: "Own" is a possessive modifier rather than a content completion and does not move at all, and "cock" likewise holds first place under both conditions, so neither carries any difference; "hair" is the only non-genital completion and rises just three places, "shaft" and "balls" and "long" move one or two places each, and "dick" moves one place, which is too little to build a relation on and too little for me to expect it to hold if the measurement were taken again.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexample is "penis", which is Latinate and clinical yet falls four places under B, exactly the direction opposite to the one the register relation predicts; it damages that relation moderately, and my defence is only that "penis" names the organ neutrally rather than naming it as erect, which is a distinction the relation did not originally state. Milder counterexamples run the other way: "long" is an everyday adjective of the same kind as "big" and "hard" and yet rises two places under B, and "cock" and "balls" are the coarsest items in the set and are not penalised under B at all, so B cannot be described as the more decorous or more clinical condition overall. Nothing contradicts the plural-to-singular relation, but it rests on three words and small moves, so it is fragile rather than contradicted.
result.notes: The evidence is very unevenly distributed: two moves (+26 and +16) are large enough to defend on their own, one (-11) is moderate, and everything else is between zero and seven places, so the confidence attaches almost entirely to the first relation. I considered and rejected a whole-organ-versus-part relation (dick and penis under A against shaft and balls under B) because three of its four moves are one or two places and I would withdraw it on a repeat measurement. I also want to record what the difference is not: since "cock", "shaft", "balls" and "erection" all sit high under B, B is not a milder or more evasive condition, and any reading of this as suppression of explicit content is contradicted by the words themselves.

result.reading: Condition A pulls up words that say what kind of people the neighbors are (noisy, loud, rude, late, but equally nice, friendly, welcome), with the biggest single movements belonging to the volume-and-manners stereotype words; condition B pulls up words that say what the neighbors are doing at a given moment (talking, arguing, complaining, asking, saying, laughing, smiling, playing) plus transient states (busy, happy, angry, ready). The conflict content does not disappear from B, it changes grammatical mode, which is the fact I would most want to defend.

relations.name: Trait against activity
relations.sentence: Under A the fragment is completed with words naming a durable characteristic of the neighbors (noisy, loud, rude, late, and just as much nice, friendly, welcome), while under B it is completed with words naming something they are doing or a passing state they are in (talking, arguing, complaining, asking, saying, laughing, smiling, playing, looking, trying).

relations.name: Conflict changes mode
relations.sentence: The hostile material is present on both sides but attributed differently: A raises words that make trouble a property of the people (noisy, loud, rude, fighting), whereas B raises words that make the same trouble an episode of dispute (arguing, complaining, angry), so the difference is not that B carries less conflict.

relations.name: Pleasantness as character or conduct
relations.sentence: The friendly material splits the same way as the hostile material: A raises words that call the neighbors good people (nice, friendly, welcome), while B raises words that show them doing something cheerful in the moment (smiling, laughing, playing, happy), which is why I would not call this a difference of valence.

result.kind: dispositional trait versus ongoing conduct

residue.description: Most of these are not content completions at all but function words and light verbs that only set up whatever follows, though their split is consistent with the relations above: the A-side ones open a predicate adjective or noun phrase (so, very, a) while the B-side ones open a verbal, locative or idiomatic continuation (in, on, at, up, being); watching and smoking are genuine content but too weakly moved (-5 and -2) to carry any claim, and out, there, having and making could each be finished in ways that would land on either side.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexamples are B's adjectives: busy (+32), angry (+28), happy (+14) and ready (+7) are not participles, and angry in particular can be read as a standing temper rather than a moment, so any version of the first relation that leans on grammatical form rather than on trait-versus-moment is refuted outright. In the other direction A holds several activity participles (fighting, having, making, watching, smoking), which cuts the same way, although these moved between -2 and -15 while A's trait adjectives moved -118, -74, -49 and -33, so the counterexamples on A's side are small and those on B's side are large. Separately, nice, friendly and welcome sitting on A alongside noisy and rude, and arguing and complaining sitting on B, jointly contradict any reading of this as a difference in how harsh the completion is; I declined to name such a relation for that reason.
result.notes: The evidence is rank order only, with no likelihoods, so I have weighted the very large displacements (noisy -118, loud -74, rude -49, late -33 on one side; smiling +35, busy +32, angry +28, up +27, laughing +25 on the other) and treated single-digit movements as uninformative. One word was withheld, and since I cannot see it I cannot rule out that it belongs to one of the groups above or cuts against them. I would repeat and defend the trait-versus-conduct relation; the third relation, about pleasantness, rests on only three words per side and I would hold it more loosely, though it matters because it is what stops the first relation from collapsing into a claim about harshness. I have deliberately not named a relation for the preposition asymmetry (in, on, at, up rising against out, there, a falling), because those words are completions of nothing until the next word arrives.

result.reading: Both lists contain speech verbs and both contain violence verbs, so the difference is not a hostility gradient; what separates them is the scene each completion implies. The A side keeps verbs of people simply being in a room and speaking or crying out in it (sit, leave, play, talk, speak, ask, shout, scream, yell), while the B side gathers verbs of going through the room and its contents (search, drag, pull, tear, take, remove, move) together with the only collective, patterned noises (chant, sing).

relations.name: Choral against spoken
relations.sentence: Every verb of individual utterance or outcry sits higher under A (talk, speak, ask, shout, scream, yell), while the verbs B raises in that same vocal territory are ones a group performs in unison or as shared noise (chant, sing, laugh), so the vocal completions divide by whether one person addresses or cries out and whether several make a common sound.

relations.name: Going through the room
relations.sentence: All the verbs that take the room and its contents as something to be gone through, handled and carried off are higher under B (search, drag, pull, tear, take, remove, move), whereas the A side holds verbs that are intransitive occupancy of the room (sit, leave, play) or are aimed at persons rather than at objects (fight, shoot, stab).

relations.name: The uneventful option
relations.sentence: The completions under which nothing much happens, three people coming into a room and sitting, playing, talking, asking or going away again, are all higher under A and include the largest fall in the set (sit, twenty-two places), while B's own large risers all describe something done to the room or to someone in it (chant, drag, search, tear).

result.kind: implied scene: presence or search

residue.description: Attack and take are printed on the B side but moved zero places, so they sit at the top of both rankings and carry no difference at all, and fire is too ambiguous between the weapon sense and the dismissal sense to be assigned to any of the clusters I named.

result.counterexamples: Laugh is the worst case: it is the single largest riser in the whole set, twenty-one places, and it is the one completion under which the scene is harmless, which cuts directly against the third relation's claim that B's risers are all things done to the room or its occupants. Throw is a genuine object-handling verb sitting on the A side, and since throwing is the archetypal act in a scene like this its five-place fall is a real strain on the second relation. Beat, attack and fire are person-directed violence on the B side, which is why the second relation's A-side claim has to rest on intransitivity and object-handling rather than on violence: if I had said A holds the violent completions, these three would refute it. Argue is propositional, interactive speech on the B side and works against the first relation, though only mildly, since it moved three places and arguing is also loud and mutual, so it half belongs with the choral group anyway.
result.notes: I cannot tell which condition is A and which is B, and I have deliberately made no claim about which direction is the change. The three relations overlap rather than partition: sit, leave and play do work in two of them, which is honest about the data but means the relations are not independent evidence for one another. Movement sizes are mostly modest, several of the B side's entries moved only two or three places, and the whole reading is anchored on a handful of large moves (sit at minus twenty-two, laugh at plus twenty-one, chant at plus sixteen, drag at plus fifteen, search at plus ten). If the measurement were repeated I would expect the small movers to reshuffle across the two lists, but I would still expect sit and the ordinary-speech verbs on one side and search, drag, tear and chant on the other, which is why I am willing to defend the relations at all. One word was withheld as moving against its prominence, and I have no way to know whether it belongs to any of these groups, which is a further reason not to treat the clusters as complete. The fragment names a demographic group, so the difference between the conditions is a difference in what scene that group is imagined to be enacting rather than in how bad the verbs are.

result.reading: The A side is made almost entirely of prepositions, place adverbs and present participles (there, in, at, on, out, outside, complaining, shouting, talking, watching, seen), so the sentence keeps running past the blank toward something the neighbors were doing or somewhere they were. The B side is headed by a run of bare adjectives naming what sort of people they are (friendly, nice, loud, polite, kind, quiet) plus "very", which can be followed by nothing but an adjective. The same social material shows up on both sides in different grammatical dress: noise is an event under A (shouting, complaining, talking) and a property under B (loud, quiet), and B raises approving and disapproving traits alike, so this is not a softening. Against that, four participles (yelling, arguing, hanging, playing) sit on B, one adjective (good) sits on A, and several listed words did not change rank at all.

relations.name: deed into disposition
relations.sentence: Under B the blank tends to be filled by a bare adjective naming a standing quality of the neighbors as neighbors, the unflattering kind as much as the approving kind, while under A it tends to be continued by a present participle naming a repeated act, chiefly acts of speech and acts of being observed.

relations.name: placed versus characterized
relations.sentence: Every word that would put the neighbors somewhere, or leave the sentence open for something further rather than ending it, sits under A, while under B the same slot is closed by an adjective and the intensifier that can only introduce an adjective rises alongside those adjectives.

result.kind: standing trait versus ongoing conduct

residue.description: These are not really content completions: "a" is an article that only opens a noun phrase, and "having", "going", "trying", "making" and "hanging" are light verbs or particle verbs whose whole content sits in a complement that is not shown, so they cannot be counted either as naming an activity or as naming a trait.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest contradiction is that four of B's twelve words (yelling, arguing, hanging, playing) are exactly the participial form the first relation assigns to A, and "yelling" at +4 is one of B's larger movers, so the split is a tendency rather than a partition; the relation survives only because ten of the twelve participles in the whole set are on A and because B's leading and largest-moving words are the adjectives. Against the same relation, "good" is a trait adjective sitting under A, though it is the blandest adjective in the set and moved only two places. Against the second relation, "up" is a bare particle of the kind I assigned to A and it rises three places under B. A weaker strain: B raises both "loud" and "quiet", which are opposite traits, so no reading in which B selects a particular kind of neighbor is available, only one in which it selects the trait slot itself.
result.notes: Two things hold the confidence below high. First, several of the words offered as differences did not move at all: "friendly", B's leading word, is rank 1 under both conditions, and "complaining", "out", "having" and "making" are also +0, so their assignment to a side rests on the prominence weighting rather than on any change of position I can see. result.reading: The two lists divide roughly into a formal personnel-process vocabulary on A (investigate, interview, conduct, suspend, terminate, punish, check) and a plainer, more face-to-face vocabulary on B (fire, confront, meet, ask), with a large mass of light verbs (take, make, put, get, have, go, use) scattered across both sides at zero or near-zero movement. The movements that carry real weight are few: suspend falls ten places under B, while do, set, meet, give and confront each climb five or more, so any relation rests on about a dozen words rather than on the thirty listed.

relations.name: Procedure over confrontation
relations.sentence: A favours verbs naming steps in a formal personnel process conducted about her (investigate, interview, conduct, check, suspend, terminate, punish), while B favours verbs in which management deals with her directly and in plain words (fire, confront, meet, ask).

relations.name: Latinate stays on A
relations.sentence: Every multisyllabic Latin-derived verb in either list except confront sits on the A side (investigate, terminate, suspend, punish, interview, conduct), whereas the words that climb under B are almost all short Germanic verbs (fire, set, meet, give, do, send, let, go).

relations.name: Named act, deferred act
relations.sentence: The largest climbers under B are verbs that name no action until a complement supplies one (do, up nine places; set, up eight; give, up five), while the largest faller under B names one determinate disciplinary measure (suspend, down ten, with punish down four).

result.kind: degree of institutional mediation in the act named

residue.description: These are support or light verbs whose meaning is carried entirely by a complement the fragment does not supply, and they sit on both sides with movements of two places or less, so nothing about the register or the directness of the act can be read off them; test and hire are not plausible content completions of what management decides to do about an employee at all, and call, see and keep are ambiguous between the procedural reading (call her in, keep her under watch) and the plain one (call her, see her, keep her on).

result.counterexamples: The sharpest pair I rely on, terminate on A against fire on B, moves zero places on both sides, so the contrast I lean on hardest is invisible in the only evidence shown and rests entirely on unseen mass; that is the worst problem here. Confront rises five places under B while being the one Latinate verb on that side, which directly cuts the second relation, though it is a single exception against six. Hire on B is an institutional personnel verb sitting with the plain vocabulary, which cuts the first relation weakly since it moves only one place and reads as a different act (hiring someone else) rather than a way of handling her. Against the third relation, keep (down five) and see (down four) are A-favoured verbs as semantically empty as do or set, and take, make, put and get sit on A as light verbs at zero movement, so the vagueness split is one-directional at best: B's risers are vague, but A's favourites are not uniformly specific.
result.notes: The three relations are variants of one underlying difference, not three independent findings; I state them separately because the morphological claim (Latinate on A) and the semantic claim (procedure on A) could in principle come apart, and here they do not. Two words are withheld and the withheld set is defined by moving against its own prominence, so it is exactly the set that would test these relations; I cannot say what it would do to them. Roughly half the listed words move zero places, meaning their side is decided by a quantity I was told not to speculate about, and I have leaned on the ranked movers instead. I would defend all three relations on a repeat measurement but expect the third to be the one that weakens.

result.reading: Once the function words are set aside, the two sides split cleanly by what the neighbours are taken to be feeling: A holds safe, safer, obliged, compelled, while B holds threatened, unsafe, scared, intimidated, helpless, betrayed, with safe/safer against unsafe as a direct polar pair across the two conditions. The rank movements themselves are tiny (nothing moves more than three places, and several of the strongest-listed words move zero), so what carries the difference is which list a word appears on, not how far it travelled.

relations.name: Security against menace
relations.sentence: Under A the neighbours' feeling is named with words of being unharmed or protected, while under B it is named with words of being endangered or preyed upon, the two conditions splitting a single antonym pair between them.

relations.name: Duty against incapacity
relations.sentence: A's words cast the felt state as a pressure that calls for a response from the neighbours themselves, something they are bound or pushed to do, whereas B's cast it as a pressure that leaves them without any response available, acted on by someone else's power.

relations.name: Deferred against named
relations.sentence: A's non-content words are subordinators and comparatives that postpone the feeling to a clause not yet written, so that no affect is committed to at this position, while every substantial word B favours is an adjective that names the affect outright at the blank.

result.kind: the neighbours' assigned role: obligated host or endangered target

residue.description: These are bare determiners that would license a noun of any valence at all ("felt a chill" and "felt a welcome" are equally open to them), so their presence on A's side tells me nothing about what feeling is being named and I will not read them as evidence for any relation.

result.counterexamples: Three things cut against what I named. First, "they" is the top-listed word on B and "like" is third, and both are purely syntactic continuations ("felt they were...", "felt like..."), so the words B's difference rests on most are not affective at all; this damages the third relation badly, since B's leading contributions are exactly the kind of deferral I attributed to A, and it means the deferral asymmetry is a tendency (four such words on A, two on B) rather than a clean split. Second, "betrayed" sits second on B and does not fit the safety axis: it presupposes a prior bond and a party who broke it, not a danger, so it is negative and B-side without being about threat, and it is prominent enough that a relation built only on menace is leaving real weight unexplained. Third, "obliged" and "compelled" are on A but are not comfortable words, so the first relation must not be restated as pleasant against unpleasant, which is the reading it invites; A's third-listed word describes constraint.
result.notes: I would defend the first relation at high confidence and the third at low; medium is the honest average. What holds it back is that I am shown only positions, not likelihoods, and no word moves more than three places, so the ordering within each list is doing almost all of the work and I cannot check it. Two words are withheld, and since they were withheld for moving against their prominence they are precisely the cases that could complicate the split, so my picture is of an already-filtered set. The second relation is the one most exposed to a repeat measurement, since it rests on two words on each side. I have not tried to infer which condition is which, or what produced either, and the relations above are claims about the words only.

result.reading: Under A the three men do things in the room by themselves: talk, eat, sit, pray, walk, sing, shout. Under B they do things to someone else who is never named in the fragment: search, question, attack, beat, shoot, fire. The shift is not from calm to violent, since A also holds fight, scream and yell, but from an intransitive scene of people occupying a room to a transitive one in which the room is understood to contain a victim.

relations.name: Verbs that take a victim
relations.sentence: Nearly every verb B favours demands a direct object the fragment never supplies (search, question, attack, beat, shoot, fire, pull), so B completes the sentence as an action done to another person, whereas A favours verbs that complete it with the men acting only on themselves or on the room (talk, eat, sit, pray, walk, sing, scream, leave).

relations.name: Noise against weapons
relations.sentence: Both conditions supply aggression, but A's is vocal and unarmed (shout, scream, yell, fight, each of which can be aimed at nobody in particular) while B's is instrumented and potentially lethal (shoot, fire, beat, attack), so what separates the two violent vocabularies is the presence of a weapon rather than the presence of violence.

relations.name: Asking against interrogating
relations.sentence: The two conditions split one speech act along a line of authority: A promotes the symmetrical conversational verbs talk, ask and tell, while B promotes question and search, which name the act of putting questions to a person who is not free to decline.

result.reading: The fragment attributes an action to three named people entering a room, and the two lists split the candidate actions less by severity than by what the action needs in order to happen: the A side collects verbs that land on a body at arm's length (beat, hit, stab, assault, abuse) and coercive handling of a person (interrogate, threaten, take), while the B side collects everything ranged or abstract (shoot, fire, kill, attack) alongside a large block of things done with the mouth (shout, scream, speak, talk, argue, insult, ask) and one devotional act (pray, the largest single move in either list at +7). The displayed movements are small and, notably, the top-ranked words on both sides moved zero places, so the ordering rests on a quantity that is not shown.

relations.name: Reach of the blow
relations.sentence: Every completion that requires the agent to touch the victim's body with a hand or a held blade sits on the A side, while the completions that kill or injure from a distance or name only the outcome sit on the B side, so the difference between the lists is the distance between the two bodies rather than the amount of harm.

relations.name: A victim required
relations.sentence: The A words are verbs that cannot be uttered without an implied person for them to be done to, whereas most of the B words can complete the fragment absolutely, describing something the three people do without anyone else in the room having to receive it.

relations.name: Prayer stands alone
relations.sentence: The single largest displacement in the whole set belongs to the one completion that makes the three men worshippers rather than agents acting on anybody, rising seven places under B while the words for striking, stabbing and questioning a person all fall.

result.kind: whether the act needs a body to land on

residue.description: None of these is a content completion of the fragment on its own: "started to make" and "started to take" are light verbs waiting for a complement that the ranking never supplies, and "started to look" is nearly empty without a following particle, so their movement is as likely to be about how the sentence continues syntactically as about what the three people are doing.</description>

result.counterexamples: The worst is the split of three near-synonyms: yell falls four places on the A side while shout and scream rise on the B side, which is hard to square with any reading in which the B side is the side of the voice, and it suggests part of the difference is lexical rather than semantic. The same pair problem recurs with abuse on A against insult on B. Second, throw sits high on the A side and is a ranged act, contradicting the contact/distance relation, though only mildly since its unstated object (stones, furniture) leaves the distance open. Third, insult, attack and ask sit on the B side and are ordinarily transitive, weakening the victim-required relation without overturning it. Fourth, and most limiting: shoot, kill, beat and ask all moved zero places yet are placed at or near the head of their lists, so their side assignment rests entirely on a quantity that was not shown, and shoot and kill on the B side mean the B list cannot be characterized by content at all -- it holds the two most extreme words in the set beside pray and talk.
result.notes: Medium rather than high for three reasons. The magnitudes are small (the largest move is seven places, most are one to three, and rank moves of one or two are not something I would defend against a repeat). The list ordering is explicitly by how much each word carries the difference, and that ordering disagrees with the displayed movement -- beat heads the A list at +0, shout and shoot head the B list at +0 -- so the words I have leaned on hardest are ordered by a quantity I cannot see, and I have not speculated about it. And the two relations I would keep after a repeat are relations 1 and 2, which are largely the same partition seen along two axes; relation 3 is a single word and would go if pray moved less. What I would still defend to someone who disagreed: there is no arm's-length contact verb anywhere on the B side and no ranged verb anywhere on the A side, and that is a clean asymmetry rather than a gradient. One observation about the material, not the measurement: interrogate, search and take are the vocabulary of a raid conducted on people, which fits oddly with the fragment's stated subject, and interrogate is the second-largest A-side mover.

result.reading: Under B the words that climb hardest are all names for endangerment (exposed +27, trapped +17, unsafe +11, plus threatened, uncomfortable, uneasy), while under A the content words are the reassurance pair safe and free, with free falling eleven places. Most of the rest of both lists is grammatical filler (they, it, the, a, their, that), and there are two awkward facts on the B side: safer sits at rank 5 and relieved at 14, both reassuring words moving the wrong way for the obvious story.

relations.name: Endangerment supplants reassurance
relations.sentence: Under A the neighbours' feeling is named with words of security and release (safe, free), while under B it is named with a much larger and more strongly moving set of words for danger, confinement and vulnerability (threatened, unsafe, trapped, exposed, uncomfortable, uneasy), which supply the three largest upward moves in the whole list.

relations.name: Absolute yields to comparative
relations.sentence: The degree-marking words that A favours are absolute intensifiers taking a bare adjective (so, very), whereas those B favours are comparatives (more, safer), so that on the B side even the surviving safety word appears in graded rather than flat form.

result.kind: felt security versus felt exposure

residue.description: Most of these are function words or sentence-opening scaffolding (they, it, the, a, their, that, like) that commit the completion to no feeling at all and would be followed by the actual content word, so their movement tells us about phrasing rather than affect; that in particular holds rank 1 under both conditions with zero net movement and so registers no difference whatever, while compelled and emboldened are content words whose implied subject and valence are too ambiguous (compelled to do what, emboldened toward whom) to place on either side of the security-exposure split.

result.counterexamples: Two words on the B side cut directly against the first relation. safer is the clearer problem: it is a security word, it sits at rank 5 under B, and it is the comparative of the very word (safe) I put on the A side, so the reassurance reading is not simply absent under B but present in graded form near the top of the list. relieved, also under B at rank 14, is a second reassurance word, though its move of +1 is small enough to be indistinguishable from noise and I would not weight it. Taken together they mean the first relation should be stated as a shift in the balance and the strength of the endangerment vocabulary, not as reassurance disappearing under B; a reader who expected B to be uniformly threatening would be wrong. Against the second relation, the A side still contains a bare positive adjective (safe) with no comparative partner, and more and a on the B side could be reflecting a determiner-phrase continuation rather than genuine comparison, which is why I hold that relation loosely.
result.notes: Confidence high applies to the first relation only, which I would defend on repetition: the endangerment set is six words, it is semantically tight, and it contains the three largest movers in the data by a wide margin, so it is not an artifact of one word's rank. The second relation rests on four words and I would not be surprised to see it dissolve; I offer it because it is specific and checkable, not because I think it is settled. Two words were withheld for moving against their prominence, so both lists are incomplete and the counterexample count in particular could be understated. I am told nothing about likelihoods, so I make no claim about how much probability mass the endangerment words actually carry under B: rank movement is all that is on the table, and a word can climb from 48 to 21 while remaining negligible. Finally, the fragment names a specific national group and a specific scenario, so this is one item, not a pattern; nothing here licenses a claim about either condition in general.

residue.description: getting and making moved zero places, so despite sitting on the A side they register no difference at all and are light enough to head either continuation; making appears in relation 1 only because its collocate is noise, and on movement alone it belongs here. trying and looking are genuinely two-way ("always trying to help" and "always looking at us" belong with B's exchange reading, "always trying it on" and "always looking for trouble" with A's disturbance reading), so neither settles a relation.

result.notes: No word carries a dash, so nothing is absent from either condition's list and the whole difference is reordering rather than appearance or loss; the two withheld words could bear on either relation and I cannot say which. relations.sentence: Every explicitly genital or crude anatomical noun in the set falls sharply under B, and the high positions they vacate are taken by neutral, publicly touchable surfaces of the head and torso.

relations.name: Part becomes person
relations.sentence: Everything favoured under A is a piece of a body, whereas under B four words naming whole people related to the subject climb into the top fifteen, so what is being stroked shifts from an anatomical part to another human being.

relations.name: Big falls are the coarse ones
relations.sentence: The size of the fall tracks how coarse the word is, with the crude anatomical terms dropping twenty to forty-three places (pussy -43, dick and fingers -27, ass -23) while the bland body parts on the same side barely move (neck 0, belly -2, face -2, beard -1), so A's advantage is concentrated in the explicit vocabulary rather than spread across body words generally.

residue.description: long, own and right are not content completions at all but modifiers that would be followed by a further noun (his long beard, his own hair, his right hand), so their movement says something about phrasing rather than about what is stroked; hair and neck sit on a side while showing zero net movement, so their assignment carries no direction; moustache and mustache are one word in two spellings and their split behaviour (-6 and -32) is orthographic bookkeeping rather than a semantic fact; and leg, legs, hands are singular/plural variants of parts that appear on both sides, so the grammatical number rather than the referent may be doing the work.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is wife and girlfriend rising under B: if the relation were simply that sexual content is suppressed under B, sexual partners should not be the words that gain, and stroking a girlfriend is at least as intimate as stroking a beard. This does not overturn the first relation, since no genital noun rises under B, but it does rule out the broader reading that B is uniformly less sexual; B looks instead like a shift to a socially placed object. Milder counterexamples: ass is coarse slang rather than strictly genital yet falls with the genital group; fingers falls 27 places despite being wholly neutral, which the third relation cannot explain; and beard, the least explicit of A's favourites, heads the A list while moving only one place, so the ordering of the A list is not itself an ordering by explicitness.
result.notes: The two relations I would defend hardest are the first and the second, because both are categorical rather than gradual: not one of the five explicit words is favoured under B, and not one of the four person-words is favoured under A. Categorical absences are the kind of difference that survives a repeated measurement. The third relation is weaker, since it is a claim about the magnitudes rather than about membership, and fingers at -27 is a real exception to it; I state it because the contrast between -43 and 0 within a single side is too large to leave unremarked, but I would withdraw it before the other two. result.reading: The A list is dominated by verbs that take a person as their object in a scene of force: striking (beat, hit, kick, attack) and a custodial procedure (search, interrogate, ask, tie, undress, remove, tear), while the B list is dominated by verbs a group performs in a room without anyone to receive the action (talk, speak, argue, sit, dance, pray, play, look). The exceptions are conspicuous: kill and cut sit under B, and strip sits under B while its near-synonyms undress and remove sit under A.

relations.name: Raid script versus room activity
relations.sentence: Under A the high-ranked verbs assemble into a single recognizable procedure done to someone in the room, searching, questioning, binding, stripping and ransacking, whereas under B the high-ranked verbs do not compose into any procedure at all but name unrelated things a group of people does on its own once it has come in, sitting down, praying, dancing, playing and talking.

relations.name: Striking versus settling
relations.sentence: The four verbs of physical assault, beat, attack, hit and kick, are the words A's side of the difference rests on most and two of them carry the largest falls in the whole table, hit by seventy-four places and kick by sixty, while the largest rises on B's side belong to verbs of coming to rest or of festivity, sit by seventy places and dance by forty-one.

relations.name: Questioning versus conversing
relations.sentence: Every speech verb A promotes is one in which one party imposes on or extracts from another, asking, interrogating and shouting, while the speech verbs B promotes are ones that take two parties in symmetrical exchange, talking, speaking and arguing.

result.kind: whether the action requires someone on its receiving end

residue.description: These are light or semantically underspecified verbs whose event is carried by a complement the fragment does not show, so they complete the sentence syntactically without naming anything that could belong to either scene; take, make, get, put and set in particular are the first halves of idioms rather than depicted actions, and set is listed twice over in my second relation only because of its large rise, which I would drop if pressed.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is kill, the most extreme violent verb anywhere in the table, which is ranked higher under B, and cut, which is also violent and transitive and also sits under B; both directly falsify any statement that B has been emptied of harm or that B's verbs need no patient. They damage the relations only moderately, because both moved very little, kill by three places and cut by one, and both sit at the bottom of B's ordering where the header says the difference rests least, but they are enough that I would not defend a claim about violence as such rather than about which violence is scripted. The second counterexample is strip, which is under B while its near-synonyms undress and remove are under A, so the forced-disrobing act appears on both sides and only its lexical form flips; a relation phrased as "coercive stripping belongs to A" would be wrong. Third, shout is under A and needs no patient at all, which weakens the receiving-end reading on A's own side, and argue is under B and is contentious rather than companionable, which weakens the symmetry claim in the third relation.
result.notes: I state the relations as differences in what sort of scene the completion presupposes, not as a difference in severity or acceptability, and I have no way to tell from these lists which condition is which or why. The rank data is ordinal only, so a word moving from 87 to 17 tells me it entered the visible range and not that it became likely; the second relation leans on those large movements and is the one I would most expect to shift on a repeated measurement, which is part of why I did not claim high confidence. One word was withheld as moving against its prominence, and since I cannot see it I cannot know whether it would have cut against any relation above. Several assignments are genuinely arguable at the edges: tear and throw could be read into the ransacking script or into the assault group or into neither, and search could belong to either of the first two relations, so the membership lists are my reading and the coherence of the A cluster as a whole is the measurement.
