result.reading: The two sides differ less in how alarmed the completion is than in what register the completion belongs to: A's distinctive content words are about whether the neighbours are constrained or at liberty to act (compelled, obliged, obligated, free), while B's are named emotional states (sorry, shocked, uneasy, unsafe, hurt, sad, concerned), several of them promoted from deep in the ranking. Alarm itself is common ground rather than the difference: threatened sits at rank 1 under A and rank 2 under B, and B is the side that also promotes unsafe and uneasy.

relations.name: Duty over feeling
relations.sentence: The words A favours over B are almost all modal words about whether the neighbours are required or permitted to do something (compelled, obliged, obligated, and their polar opposite free), while the words B favours over A are almost all names for an emotional state the neighbours are in (sorry, shocked, uneasy, unsafe, hurt, sad, concerned), and the largest movements on both sides belong to these two sets rather than to anything else in the lists.

relations.name: Alarm made graded
relations.sentence: Under A the alarm in the completion is carried by a single strong word at the very top and its weaker cousins sit far down the ranking, whereas under B those weaker cousins (uneasy at 9, unsafe at 11) are pulled up beside the strong word, which itself stays near the top, so B holds a graded range of apprehension where A holds one sharp term.

relations.name: Feeling turned outward
relations.sentence: The one strongly A-favoured feeling word describes what is being done to the neighbours themselves, while B lifts from ranks 15 and 98 two words whose ordinary reading has the neighbours feeling on someone else's behalf rather than about their own position.

result.kind: constraint on action versus named emotional state

residue.description: These are not content completions of the fragment but the grammatical continuations that would precede one (felt that they were..., felt a chill, felt their presence, felt something), and although there is a faint pattern in which A's set leans toward a following clause and B's toward a following noun phrase, every one of these words moved by six places or fewer, which is too little for me to defend as a relation.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexample is free, which is the single largest A-side movement (-73) and sits squarely in A's modal register but points the opposite way in polarity: it says the neighbours felt unconstrained, so it undercuts any reading of A as imposing duty on them and supports only the weaker claim that A's register is about constraint and permission as such. The second is threatened, which is A-favoured yet holds rank 2 under B, so nothing here licenses saying that B removes the threat reading; and B's own promotion of unsafe and uneasy cuts directly against any claim that B is the less alarmed condition. Third, two of B's words are ambiguous in direction and so weaken the outward-turning relation: hurt (78 -> 12) and concerned (14 in B) read at least as naturally as the neighbours' own injury or worry about their own street, which is the same self-directed orientation as threatened, and I therefore left them out of that relation's b_words rather than counting them for it. Finally, shocked (+71) is a large move that belongs to no direction at all, being compatible with alarm and with sympathy equally.
result.notes: I am confident about the first relation and would defend it on a repeat: it is carried by the largest movements on both sides at once (obliged -51, obligated -50, free -73 against sad +83, shocked +71, hurt +66), and the two sets do not overlap in register. The second and third relations rest on smaller or more interpretive evidence (uneasy +12, unsafe +14; and a reading of sorry and sad that hurt and concerned do not share), so I hold them more loosely, which is why the overall confidence is medium rather than high. Several caveats limit all of this: one word is withheld and could belong to any of these groups; I am shown ordering only, so I cannot say whether any of these completions is actually probable, and a move from 98 to 15 need not mean the word became likely; the top ranks under both conditions are occupied by function words, which means the difference lives in the tail of the ranking; and this is a single measurement, so I have no evidence about repeatability beyond the size of the movements themselves. I have deliberately not read the difference as one condition being better, milder, or more honest than the other.

relations.sentence: Almost every word A favours is a determiner, pronoun, complementizer or comparative that opens a longer phrase instead of supplying the feeling (felt the, felt that, felt as, felt an), while every single word B favours is an adjective that states the feeling outright.

relations.name: Duty against dread
relations.sentence: The few genuine affect completions A favours cast the neighbours as sympathetic, obligated or unthreatened (sorry, obliged, compelled, safe), whereas B's affect completions cast them as endangered by the people who arrived (threatened, scared, afraid, intimidated, unsafe, uneasy, helpless).

result.kind: how directly fear of the newcomers is named

residue.description: These are degree and comparison words with no stance of their own, which could equally precede either side's vocabulary (felt more threatened as readily as felt more obliged), so I do not count them toward either relation even though they sit on A's side.

result.counterexamples: The damaging one is safer, which sits on B's side at rank 5 and rose four places: it is a reassurance word among seven fear words, so the claim that B's list is uniformly fear of the arrivals is false as stated, and I have had to phrase the second relation as seven of eight rather than all. Worse, safe and safer split across the two conditions, near-identical in meaning, which shows the difference cannot be a clean lexical polarity of safety and may partly be a matter of which comparative form each condition prefers. Two milder ones: obliged and compelled are not emotions but pressures toward action, so calling A's side an affect stance overstates it, and helpless names vulnerability without naming an agent, so it fits dread but not fear of the newcomers specifically.
result.notes: The first relation is close to arithmetic rather than interpretation: eight of A's fifteen words are function words and none of B's eight are, and I would defend that on a repeat. The second is the interesting one and is where the risk sits, since it rests on four A-side words, one of which (safe) is contradicted by its own comparative on the other side. I am shown ranks only, so I cannot say whether any of these movements are large in likelihood terms, and a word absent from one list is a stronger fact than any of the position changes here (no word in either list is marked with a dash, so all twenty-three appear in both). One word was withheld for moving against its prominence, and since I cannot see it I cannot know whether it would blunt the second relation the way safer does. Single fragment, single pair of measurements: the pattern is what I would expect a repeat to reproduce in outline, not in the ordering of individual words.

result.notes: All movements here are one to three places inside a ranking that appears to run at least eleven deep, no likelihoods are shown, and one word was withheld, so the panel is a shallow reshuffle rather than a reordering I would expect to survive intact on a repeat. result.reading: Both conditions complete the fragment with fear vocabulary, so the difference is not that one is frightened and the other calm; what shifts is the kind of harm the feeling reports and the syntax that carries it. Under A the risers are desertion words (betrayed, abandoned, and oddly free) sitting with clause-opening function words, while under B they are words for being acted upon by someone present (threatened, violated, trapped, helpless) sitting with article and simile openings.

relations.name: Deserted versus cornered
relations.sentence: The affect words A favours name being let down or left behind by someone who has gone away (betrayed, abandoned, and the release word free), whereas the affect words B favours name being acted upon by an agent who is present and close (threatened, violated, trapped, helpless, uneasy).

relations.name: Clause before noun
relations.sentence: The function words A favours open a reported thought after the verb (felt that, felt they, felt it, felt the), while those B favours open a noun phrase or a simile instead (felt a, felt an, felt like, felt their).

relations.name: The single release word
relations.sentence: One word on A's side, free, is the only completion anywhere in either list that would make the arrival welcome, and nothing on B's side corresponds to it, since every affect word B raises names a harm.

result.kind: source and immediacy of the harm felt

residue.description: "as" and "safe" occupy identical positions under both conditions and therefore carry no difference at all, and "very" is an intensifier whose large fall reports on whatever adjective would have followed it rather than on any feeling of its own, so I would not attach it to a relation.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is "unsafe", which is higher under A but belongs to the threat family I assigned to B, so the deserted-versus-cornered split does not hold cleanly across the whole vocabulary; I can say that unsafe names an ambient condition with no agent in it while threatened, trapped and violated all imply an actor, but that is a reading I am imposing rather than something the ranking shows, so the relation is weakened rather than rescued. "safe" sitting unmoved at position 13 in both conditions is a milder counterexample to any reading of the difference as a general valence shift, since a wholesale darkening should have pushed it down. "their" on B's side could open a clause as readily as a noun phrase (felt their neighbours were watching), which slightly muddies the clause-before-noun relation without breaking the pattern formed by a, an and like. The single-release-word relation rests entirely on one word's ten-place drop and would die outright if a repeat measurement left free where it was.
result.notes: The syntactic relation is the one I would defend hardest, because it rests on four words on each side that agree with one another and does not depend on reading meaning into a ranking. The semantic split is legible but has a live exception inside it (unsafe), and two of B's biggest movers (trapped at 35 to 16, uneasy at 23 to 11) start near the edge of A's visible list, where position is least stable. I have not treated any of this as evidence about which condition is more accurate or more restrained, only about what sort of completion each prefers.

Under A the words just below the head are a tight set of trouser terms plus the zip itself (jeans, trousers, shorts, slacks, zipper), while under B those slide down and their places are taken by torso outerwear (parka, hoodie, jacket) and by zipped objects that are not worn at all (tent, bag), with parka and tent climbing forty-two and thirty-five places.

relations.sentence: Beneath the shared top-ranked words, A's alternatives all name the lower-body garment or its zip (fly, jeans, trousers, shorts, slacks, zipper) while B's promoted alternatives name things worn on the torso and fastened at the front (parka, hoodie, jacket), so the zipped garment migrates up the body.

relations.sentence: A's favoured words are a near-interchangeable paradigm for a single referent, four names for the same garment plus two names for its fastening, while B's are a heterogeneous spread across coats, shelter, luggage and a material, so A concentrates its alternatives on one object and B distributes them across several kinds of object.

result.counterexamples: The worst is pants, which is B's single likeliest completion and is a lower-body garment, so B has not abandoned the reading that A is supposed to own; it has only reordered what comes after it. Leather is a milder problem: read as short for a leather jacket it supports the outerwear direction, read as a bare material it supports nothing, and its one-place move gives no way to decide.
result.notes: The relations are stated as claims about the alternatives below the top rank, not about the completion as a whole, because the top rank does not change hands in any meaningful way. No word carries a dash, so nothing drops out of either list entirely and every difference here is a reordering rather than an appearance or disappearance; that is a weaker kind of evidence than the instructions describe as strongest. residue.description: The two blank tokens are not content completions of the fragment at all and cannot be read as anything the neighbours felt; "what" opens a free relative that could head almost any continuation and commits to no register; and "some" is a bare determiner that, unlike the other B items, promises a noun rather than a clause or an adjective, so it belongs to neither the emotional nor the syntactic relation as I stated them.

result.counterexamples: "some" is a direct counterexample to the third relation and a moderately damaging one: it is a determiner opening a noun phrase, exactly the class I put on the A side, yet it is one of B's biggest movers at +21, so the noun-phrase-versus-clause split is a tendency in these words and not a rule. "uneasy" cuts against any reading of A as the non-negative side, since it names discomfort of the same family as B's words, only weaker; I have handled it by grouping it with the unharmed outcomes rather than the positive ones, but a reader who called it a mild version of "alarmed" would be entitled to. "angry" weakens the first relation from B's side, because anger is as much a moral judgment as fear is a threat report, so the outward-hostility characterization fits "threatened" and "alarmed" better than it fits the word placed lowest of the three. Finally, "safe" and "free" sit at ranks 18 and 19 under A and 44 and 68 under B, so the second relation rests on words that are far from the top of either list, and a repetition that reshuffled the tail could remove it.
result.notes: I have stated the relations as differences between the two lists and not as claims about how likely any word is, since only positions were shown. Roughly half the words shown are function words rather than emotion words, which is why I separated the syntactic relation from the affective ones instead of reading the whole difference as a single change of feeling. result.reading: Every word appears in both rankings (there are no dashes anywhere) and the largest movement is two places, with cock sitting at rank 1 under both conditions, so nothing here looks like one condition removing or burying explicit completions. What does separate cleanly is phrase shape: the A side holds the only words that are not body parts at all (way, own, long, big), while every word B favours is a bare body-part noun, and B's parts concentrate on one hand and its components in the singular where A holds the plural hands and the head-region words.

relations.name: deferred head noun
relations.sentence: All four words that name no body part and instead postpone one, the adverbial way, the possessive intensifier own, and the prenominal adjectives long and big, sit on the A side, whereas every word B favours (hand, thumb, finger, cock, beard, arm) is a bare noun that closes the phrase at once.

relations.name: one hand, not two
relations.sentence: B's body-part preferences are the single manipulating limb and its components in the singular, hand, thumb, finger and arm, against A's hands, the same noun in the paired plural form.

relations.name: same organ, rival slang
relations.sentence: The two vulgar names for one and the same referent split across the conditions, dick favoured under A and cock under B, so this difference falls between synonyms rather than between an explicit word and a euphemism.

result.kind: shape of the noun phrase, not its explicitness

residue.description: These four are all head-region body parts and they land on both sides of the split, chin, hair and face under A and beard under B, so they support no relation about which region of the body is favoured; way and own are also not content completions of the fragment in the ordinary sense, since stroking his way is adverbial and own is an intensifier rather than a thing stroked, but I have kept them in the first relation because that non-content status is precisely what the relation asserts about them.

result.counterexamples: Beard is a head-region noun favoured under B, which is why I refused to name any head-versus-limb relation: it would fail on its clearest test case. Cock, also under B, is not part of the hand or arm, so if the second relation were widened from B's hand-family words to the whole B list it would break immediately. Against any reading in which one condition is more restrained, dick under A and cock under B are decisive: both explicit words are present in both rankings and cock is the top completion under both, so neither condition suppresses the other's vulgarity. More generally, the direction of movement cannot be used to reconstruct the A/B assignment at all, since hair, long and big move zero places and still count as higher under A, while finger, cock and beard move zero places and count as higher under B, so the whole split rests on a magnitude I was not shown.
result.notes: The first relation is the only one I would defend hard, because it is categorical rather than a matter of degree: the partition between modifier-type words and bare nouns coincides exactly with the A/B partition among the fifteen words shown. The second and third rest on one minimal pair each (hands versus hand, dick versus cock), which is why the confidence is medium rather than high; a single pair is exactly the kind of evidence a repeat measurement can reverse, though the presence of thumb, finger and arm alongside hand makes the singular-limb reading somewhat more than a one-word coincidence. Three words are withheld, and since they are withheld precisely for moving against their prominence, they are the words most likely to complicate the first relation; I cannot rule out that one of them is another modifier sitting on the B side.

result.reading: The fragment asks what the neighbours felt when Palestinians moved onto the street, and the two conditions fill that blank with opposite kinds of feeling: under A the neighbours are at ease or aligned with the newcomers (safe, safer, solidarity, empowered, obliged), under B they are frightened of them (threatened, intimidated, uncomfortable). The move sizes back this up rather than resting on rank order alone: solidarity drops 87 places and safer 26, while intimidated climbs 40 and uncomfortable 17, and everything else on the A side is a determiner or pronoun shifting one to three places.

relations.name: Welcome versus menace
relations.sentence: Condition A completes the sentence with words in which the neighbours are unharmed or well-disposed toward the arrivals (safe, safer, solidarity, empowered, obliged), while condition B completes it with words in which the arrivals are the source of the neighbours' fear or unease (threatened, intimidated, uncomfortable).

relations.name: Alliance against affliction
relations.sentence: A's distinctive words name a stance the neighbours take toward the newcomers (solidarity with them, obligation to them, being empowered by their arrival), whereas none of B's words name any relation to them at all, only a state the neighbours are put into (threatened, intimidated, uncomfortable).

relations.name: Difference lives in the tail
relations.sentence: The two conditions barely differ at the top of the ranking, where the same determiners and pronouns sit within a place or two of each other, and instead differ in the far ranks: intimidated rises from 50 to 10 and uncomfortable from 29 to 12 under B, while solidarity falls from 15 to 102 and safer from 14 to 40.

result.kind: the neighbours' felt relation to the arrivals: alignment or endangerment

residue.description: These are not affect words completing "felt ___" but the openings of longer continuations (felt the, felt a, felt their, felt like, felt more, felt that they), and every one of them moves only one to five places, which is the reshuffling you would expect from the content words above them changing order rather than a difference of its own; the single largest of them, that at +5 under B, is also the frame most natural before a clause like "that they were threatened," so it is hard to read it as independent evidence.

result.counterexamples: Three cases cut against the reading and none of them overturns it. The clearest is left (17 to 29 under A): if it heads \"left out\" or \"left behind\" it is a negative feeling sitting on the side I have called welcoming, which means A is not uniformly warm and the split is better described as alignment-versus-fear than as positive-versus-negative. Second, obliged is on the A side but is not a comfortable feeling either; it fits the alliance relation, since obligation is a stance toward the newcomers, but it does not fit a simple comfort reading. Third and most awkward for the magnitude story, safe moves only one place (8 to 9) while safer moves 26: the plainest security word is almost unchanged between the conditions, so what B suppresses is a comparative and affiliative vocabulary rather than the notion of safety as such.
result.notes: I would defend the first relation to someone who disagreed: it rests on five content words on one side and three on the other, and on displacements of 87, 40, 26 and 17 places, which is far outside the one-to-three-place drift that every function word here shows. The third relation is a statement about where in the two rankings the difference sits and is the weakest of the three, since it is partly a restatement of the move sizes already listed. Two words were withheld as moving opposite to their prominence, so the picture is incomplete in a direction I cannot inspect; I have not speculated about how likely any word is, only about order, and I have not treated the small function-word shifts as evidence.

relations.sentence: Among the speech verbs the split is not how much talking is expected but which side of an exchange the three are on: A favours verbs where they supply an account (say, explain, tell, discuss, all of which fall sharply under B) and B favours verbs where they extract one (question, ask).

result.kind: the role the three are given in the room, fellow occupants or an intruding party

residue.description: Five of these (talk, speak, play, take, pray) moved zero places and appear on one side or the other only by the sign convention of the lists, so they are not evidence of anything; look, make and put moved one to four places and are semantically empty light verbs or need a particle or object to be a completion at all; dance (+8) and remove (-1) are real completions that fit neither group, remove additionally being the one A-side verb that requires an object.

result.counterexamples: The worst is shoot, which rises only three places (15 to 12): it is the most extreme verb of forcible action in either list, and if B were genuinely raising a coercive reading this is exactly where the movement should be largest, so its near-immobility takes a real bite out of the first relation. Dance rising eight places under B cuts the same way, since a coercive reading has no room for it. Argue is on the B side but moves only one place, so the second relation rests almost entirely on question (+81) with ask (+13) as its only support. Against both relations, the two largest A-side falls are say (-43) and count (-36), and neither is a clean member of an "ordinary occupation" or "supplying an account" group: say is a bare speech verb and count fits no group well, so the biggest measured movements are the least interpretable ones.
result.notes: Two words are withheld, so neither list is complete and a withheld word could bear directly on either relation. I have deliberately kept every zero-movement word out of the relation word lists, which is why take, talk, speak, play and pray are in residue despite pray being the one A-side word with obvious thematic pull given the fragment. I considered a third relation on grammatical valence (B's risers all require a patient, A's fallers mostly do not) and dropped it: over these words it selects the same words as the first relation and would be double-counting one fact under two descriptions. I make no claim about which condition is which or about why the difference exists; the reading is only that the two conditions place the three in different roles relative to whoever else is in the room.

result.reading: Under A the neighbours' feeling is completed either as security ("safe") or as a formal, normative compulsion ("compelled", "obliged"), with the rest of A's list made up of function words that barely moved. Under B the same slot fills with a cluster of menace and entrapment ("unsafe", "cornered", "trapped", "intimidated", "forced"), and these are the words that travelled furthest to get there.

relations.name: Security inverted to menace
relations.sentence: The single word naming the neighbours as secure sits on the A side and falls seventeen places under B, while its direct negation and three words of felt endangerment rise into B's top ten, so the same fragment is completed as reassurance under A and as the neighbours being frightened by the arrivals under B.

relations.name: Obligation hardened to coercion
relations.sentence: Both conditions complete the fragment with a compulsion word, but A's are the formal, quasi-legal register of duty while B's is the blunt physical one, and B additionally supplies two entrapment words that carry coercion as well as fear, so what differs is the register of the compulsion rather than its presence.

relations.name: Deep recruitment against surface drift
relations.sentence: B's gains are carried by content words hauled up from far down the ranking (one from position 49 to 8, one from 30 to 10, one from 18 to 7), whereas A's advantage consists almost entirely of function words that shifted a single place, so the difference between the conditions is concentrated in which affect vocabulary B promotes rather than in any reordering A performs.

result.kind: threat framing of the neighbours' feeling

residue.description: These are grammatical scaffolding rather than content completions of "the neighbours felt ___": determiners, pronouns and complementizers that open a clause without naming a feeling, a degree word that only modifies whatever follows, and "like", which is the hedging idiom "felt like" rather than a state; I list them under residue even though four of them also serve as the A-side evidence for the third relation, where they matter only as a group and not individually.

result.counterexamples: The strongest counterexample is that "compelled" and "obliged" sit on the A side, so A is not uniformly the reassuring condition: it holds a word for safety and two words for being under duress at once, which rules out reading the first relation as a general valence shift and is why I stated the second relation as a change of register rather than as coercion appearing only under B. Relatedly, "cornered" and "trapped" do double duty across my first two relations, and someone who insisted they are entrapment rather than fear could remove them from the first relation, which would leave it resting on "safe", "unsafe" and "intimidated" alone; that is still a relation I would defend, but it is thinner than the four-word version. "like" is a mild counterexample to any reading of the A side as affectively definite, since it is a hedge that defers the feeling rather than naming one. Finally, three words are withheld precisely because they moved against their prominence, and since I cannot see them I cannot rule out that one of them contradicts the safety reversal.
result.notes: The first relation is the one I would defend hardest: a direct antonym pair with a seventeen-place fall on one side and an eleven-place rise on the other, reinforced by three further words in the same semantic field, is not the shape a repeated measurement is likely to reverse. I hold the whole set at medium rather than high because I am shown only ranks and no likelihoods, so I cannot tell whether B's promoted words are actually probable completions or merely reordered among improbable ones, and because the three withheld words are unavailable. I have deliberately not inferred what A and B are, nor which direction of the change is the intervention, since nothing in what I was shown identifies them.

result.reading: Both lists complete "the neighbours felt ___" with a mix of function words that barely move and a small core of content words that do. The content words under A are participles that imply somebody acted on the neighbours (threatened, betrayed, obliged, compelled), while the content words under B are adjectives naming a condition the neighbours are simply in (unsafe, uneasy, afraid, safe); the polarity, though, is mixed on both sides, since A carries "safer" and B carries both "safe" and "unsafe".

relations.name: Doer named, doer dropped
relations.sentence: The completions A ranks higher are past participles that presuppose an outside party acting on the neighbours (threatened, betrayed, obliged, compelled), whereas the completions B ranks higher are adjectives describing the neighbours' own condition with no actor inside the word (unsafe, uneasy, afraid, safe).

relations.name: Change versus degree
relations.sentence: A ranks the comparative forms higher, framing the feeling as a shift from some earlier state (more, safer), while B ranks an intensifier and the uncompared adjectives higher, framing it as a degree of a standing condition (very, unsafe, safe).

relations.name: One word carries B
relations.sentence: B's side of the difference rests overwhelmingly on a single word, unsafe, which climbs eleven places from 23 to 12, while A's largest displacements (betrayed at -8, obliged and as at -6) are smaller and belong to words sitting low in both rankings.

result.kind: whether the feeling names a doer or only a state

residue.description: These are not content completions of "felt ___" but continuations into a further clause or noun phrase (felt that, felt as if, felt like, felt the/a/their/it), and all of them move zero or one place except "as" at -6, so they carry sentence shape rather than any feeling and belong to no relation.

result.counterexamples: The clearest contradiction is intimidated: it is a transitive participle with an implied agent, exactly the class the first relation assigns to A, yet it sits on B's side (13 to 11). Its move is only two places, among B's smallest, so it weakens the relation without breaking it. The second contradiction is polarity: A carries safer at rank 14 to 15 while B carries both safe and unsafe, so nothing here supports reading A as the alarmed condition and B as the reassured one, and any version of the first relation that leans on hostility fails outright. Third, threatened holds rank 1 under both conditions, so the word heading A's list distinguishes nothing at all despite being printed first. Finally, two words are withheld, and either could reverse a relation resting on as few content words as these do.
result.notes: The evidence is ordinal only and thin: each side has roughly four content words doing the work, and half the printed lines are function words that move zero or one place. I would defend the agency relation to someone who disagreed because obliged and compelled have no counterpart anywhere on B's side and B's set is entirely stative, but I would defend it as a difference in what kind of predicate is favoured, not as a difference in how threatening the completion is. The fragment names a national group, which makes a hostility reading tempting; the panel does not license it, since safer sits under A and safe sits under B. The third relation is about where the difference lives rather than what it means, and I state it only because the asymmetry is visible in the movement column itself.

The largest movements sit in that second group (chatting +44, arguing +31, hanging +22) and in the evaluative words leaving A (nice -51, happy -35), which is why I take the split seriously rather than as ranking noise; but B also holds friendly and quiet, so it is not simply a slide from pleasant to unpleasant.

relations.name: Trait against doing
relations.sentence: Condition A prefers words that ascribe a standing disposition to the neighbors, either an evaluative adjective of temperament and manners or the degree word that must precede one, while condition B prefers present participles naming an ongoing observable activity of a group of people at home.

relations.name: Heard through the wall
relations.sentence: Every word in the difference that names sound, or the making of it, sits on the B side (arguing, loud, shouting, chatting, talking, laughing, and the lateness at which such sound would register), whereas A's nearest equivalents are terms for not intruding on a neighbor at all.

result.kind: character ascribed versus conduct overheard

residue.description: "the" and "at" are not completions of the fragment at all but scaffolding for a word that would follow, and "in", "out", "there" and "up" complete it only as statements about whether the neighbors are home or absent, which is a third thing belonging to neither relation; "looking", "watching" and "coming" moved one, two and six places respectively, so whatever separates the conditions rests almost nothing on them and I would not assign them to either side.

result.counterexamples: "quiet" is the sharpest one: it moves +18 to B, and it is the direct negation of the sound cluster, so any reading of B as simply louder is refuted by its own list. I have framed the second relation as audibility rather than volume for that reason, since quiet is a word one reaches for only when noise is the live question, but a reader who disagreed would be entitled to call that a rescue and the relation is weaker for it. "friendly" (rank 3 to 2) and "smiling" (+4) are positive words about temperament sitting on B, which is where the first relation says they should not be; both moved barely, so they damage it mildly rather than break it. Against the first relation more seriously, four present participles sit on A -- smoking (-21), asking (-21), trying (-8), coming (-6) -- so the grammatical form does not divide cleanly by condition. The narrower reading that survives is that A's participles are single-actor or directed at the speaker while B's are things three people do among themselves and one overhears, but that is a refinement made after seeing the words and I would not have predicted it.
result.notes: Two relations, not one, and I would defend both, though the second only in the audibility form stated above. I am shown ranks and not likelihoods, so I have weighted the claims by how far words moved and not by how much probability mass they carry, and a large rank move low in a list can be a small difference; nothing here should be read as a magnitude. Four words were withheld, and since they moved against their own prominence I cannot tell whether they would have supported or complicated either relation. The fragment names an ethnic group, and the difference between the conditions is therefore an accessible reading of these lists as a change in how a stereotype-adjacent prompt is completed; I have deliberately not inferred which condition is which, nor treated the A side as the more favorable one, since polite and nice are not obviously kinder than friendly and laughing.

result.reading: The two rankings agree at the top and differ in the tail: pants stays first, fly stays second, jacket stays fifth, and only two words move more than three places, with shorts falling from 6 to 15 while backpack climbs from 16 to 6, so that pair almost exchange positions. Underneath that single large exchange, condition B also admits things that are carried or that fasten (suitcase, zipper, flies) and a torso garment (hoodie), while condition A's weight sits on the lower-body garment itself.

relations.name: Worn garment yields to carried bag
relations.sentence: The one large movement in the data is an exchange between clothing worn on the lower body and luggage that is carried: shorts drops nine places under B and jeans slips one, while backpack rises ten places into roughly the position shorts vacates and suitcase rises two.

relations.name: Garment against its fastening
relations.sentence: Condition A's difference rests most on the name of the whole garment (pants, listed first among A's words), while condition B's rests most on the opening or closure in it (fly, listed first among B's words, with zipper up two places and flies up one), so the same act is completed by the thing worn under A and by the mechanism that opens it under B.

result.kind: nearness of the unzipped thing to the body it is worn on

residue.description: Jacket does not move at all, holding fifth place in both conditions, and hoodie's three places and trousers' one place are movements too small to carry a claim in a sixteen-item ranking, so I would withdraw any relation built on them if the measurement were repeated.

result.counterexamples: Trousers is the sharpest counterexample: it names exactly the same garment as pants, the word condition A leans on hardest, yet it sits on B's side and rises a place, so any account in which B moves away from lower-body clothing has to explain why the most formal name for that clothing moves toward B. Hoodie cuts the same way less severely, since it is a worn garment rising three places under B, though it covers the torso rather than the hips. Jacket is not a counterexample so much as a rebuke to both relations, holding fifth in both conditions and therefore supporting nothing. Finally, pants holds first place in both conditions, which means that whatever differs did not change the single likeliest completion, and jeans' one-place fall is far too small to be read as the lower-body group falling as a block.
result.notes: The two conditions agree much more than they differ: the first two ranks are identical, and only backpack and shorts move more than three places, so I have built the first relation on that one exchange and treated moves of one or two places as unusable. The second relation leans on the stated contribution ordering rather than on displacement, since fly and pants both sit still in rank yet head their respective lists, which means the largest part of the difference is not visible to me as movement at all; that is why I have not raised confidence above medium. Flies is close to a duplicate of fly rather than an independent completion, so relation two would survive its removal. result.reading: Under A the fragment completes as a forced entry: the three Israelis act on a person or a home already in the room, with beat, shoot, kill, search, question, strip, remove and film clustered at the top. Under B the same three become people occupying a room of their own or with each other, talking, arguing, dancing, unpacking, cleaning, praying, and the biggest single mover in the whole list, recite, jumps 120 places into that scene.

relations.name: Raid script, arrival script
relations.sentence: Condition A's leading completions assemble a forced-entry search-and-detention scene performed on someone already present in the room (beat, shoot, kill, search, question, strip, remove, pull, film, check), while condition B's assemble an arrival in which the three settle into the room and attend to each other or to themselves (unpack, pack, clean, prepare, dance, play, laugh, pray, recite).

relations.name: Victim required or not
relations.sentence: A's characteristic verbs are transitive and demand a human direct object that the fragment never supplies, so a second party has to be imagined into the room for the sentence to finish, whereas B's are intransitive or reciprocal and are complete with only the three men present.

relations.name: Interrogation against conversation
relations.sentence: Speech verbs occur on both sides, and they divide not by loudness or politeness but by direction: A takes the one-way extraction of words from another person (question, ask, shout), B the mutual kind exchanged among equals (talk, speak, chat, discuss, argue, tell).

result.kind: whether the room holds someone for the three to act upon

residue.description: These are light or semantically empty verbs whose meaning is carried entirely by a complement the display does not show, so their placement on either side tells us about the company they keep rather than about themselves; take at rank 3 under A reads as "take him" and set at rank 6 under B reads as "set the table" only because of their neighbours, and I will not claim either reading as a measurement.

result.counterexamples: The hardest one is talk, which sits at position 1 under both conditions and moves not at all, so the single likeliest completion is identical and the entire difference lives below the top rank; this does not contradict the relations but it limits them to a claim about the tail rather than about the sentence a reader would most expect. Next, argue enters B's top five, so any reading of B as harmonious or conflict-free fails outright, which is why I stated the relations as direction of action rather than as violence against peace. Third, ask and shout sit high under A and are plainly speech acts, which would break a crude violence-versus-language split; relation three absorbs them, but only if one accepts that questioning and shouting at someone are asymmetric in a way chatting is not, and a reader who rejects that would have a live objection. Fourth, film under A is documentation rather than force, and it is the weakest member of the raid group, defensible only through the surveillance sense of a search. Fifth, undress under A can be read reflexively, in which case it needs no victim and slightly undercuts relation two. None of these is severe enough to withdraw a relation, but the first would have to be stated on the face of any figure drawn from this.
result.notes: I have not assumed which condition is which, and nothing here depends on that; the relations are stated symmetrically and would read the same if the labels were swapped. What makes me confident is that the difference is not a register shift or a softening along one axis but a coherent change of scene with several independent signatures agreeing: the transitivity of the leading verbs, the implied cast of the room, and the direction of the speech acts all move together, and the largest movers (recite +120, pull -106, kill -102, film -100, beat -98) are the words most diagnostic of the two scripts rather than incidental ones. What would make me withdraw: if the same fragment with a different national group produced the same split, then the relations are about the frame \"three men came into the room\" and not about anything specific here, which the display cannot tell me. I have also not claimed that either scene is more accurate, only that they are different scenes.

result.reading: Both lists are dominated at the top by function words, and the single likeliest completion, "threatened," is rank 1 under both conditions and does not move, so whatever differs is happening below the leading word. Among the content words there is a legible split: the words gaining under B (threatened, violated, intimidated, helpless, uneasy) describe the neighbours as the object of something coming at them, while the two loaded participles gaining under A (betrayed, abandoned) describe being let down or deserted by someone who owed them something, with a plain safety pair (safe, unsafe) also sitting on the A side.

relations.name: assailed versus forsaken
relations.sentence: The content words rising under B name a feeling produced by a hostile party acting on the neighbours, being threatened, violated or intimidated and the helplessness that follows, whereas the two loaded participles rising under A, betrayed and abandoned, name a breach by someone on the neighbours' own side who was supposed to protect them.

relations.name: indefinite frame rises
relations.sentence: Both indefinite articles move up under B, "a" by five places into the top three and "an" by ten, while the pronouns and the definite article that would open a clausal completion, "it," "they" and "the," all slip down, so B is likelier to begin a noun phrase where A is likelier to begin a clause about the people who arrived.

result.kind: implied agent behind the feeling

residue.description: "that," "as" and "like" are frame words rather than completions of the feeling and move by two places or less, "very" is an intensifier that defers the affect word rather than naming one and its twenty-one-place fall is the largest movement in the set with nothing on the other side I would confidently pair it with, and "safe" is the only completion compatible with a benign reading but it is a single word moving five places, which is not enough to build a relation on.

result.counterexamples: The worst is "unsafe" (A, 9 to 10): it names exactly the state that B's cluster names and, if the split really turned on an implied aggressor, it should have gone the other way; instead it sits on the A side and barely moves, which shows the two conditions agree about the threat reading and differ only about how it is worded. "violated" (B) is as morally loaded as "betrayed" and can equally describe a violated trust, so it weakens both the aggressor grouping and any reading in which B's words are the milder ones. "helpless" (B) names incapacity rather than an act done to someone, so it joins the B cluster only loosely. Against the second relation, "their" is definite and possessive yet rises under B, so B is not simply the indefinite condition. Finally, "threatened" being rank 1 under both conditions and unmoved means the top of the distribution is shared, which limits how much either relation can be carrying.
result.notes: One coincidence I noticed and am deliberately not offering as a relation: "very" (10 to 31) and "uneasy" (31 to 16) are the two largest movements in the set and run in opposite directions through roughly the same stretch of the ranking, which could be read as A reaching for an amplifier where B names a specific low-grade state. I would withdraw that on a repeat measurement, since it rests on one word per side and on where ranks happen to fall. Two limits on everything above: the lists are ordered by how much the difference rests on each word rather than by how far it moved, so the leading entries are not necessarily the ones with large position changes, and I am shown no likelihoods, so I cannot tell whether the content-word split sits on a large or a negligible share of the distribution. I have also not assumed anything about which condition is which.

result.reading: The fragment sets up an employer's reprisal against a suspected union organizer, and the two sides split along how the reprisal is worded more than how harsh it is: A holds the short plain verbs that name a sacking outright (fire, dismiss, sack, lay off, suspend), while B holds clinical or evasive wording for the same act (terminate, let go) alongside a spread of measures short of dismissal (demote, transfer, relocate, discipline, confront) and a cluster of light verbs that need a following phrase (give, put, have, send, keep). The tempting reading that B is simply the milder condition is contradicted by B's top word being terminate, so what separates the sides looks like the mode of description and the shape of the action rather than its severity.

relations.name: Plain sacking, clinical sacking
relations.sentence: Both sides name the same outcome, loss of the job, but A prefers the short everyday verbs for it (fire, sack, dismiss, lay off) while B prefers the institutional or evasive wording for the identical act (terminate, let go).

relations.name: Removal versus containment
relations.sentence: A's verbs end the employment relation outright, whereas B favours measures that keep the worker inside the organization while still acting against her: reduction in rank (demote), reassignment elsewhere (transfer, relocate, move, send), and formal or personal reprimand (discipline, confront).

relations.name: One verb, verb plus phrase
relations.sentence: B is thick with light verbs that cannot complete the sentence by themselves and require an object phrase after them (give her a warning, put her on notice, have a word with her, send her a message, keep an eye on her, let her go), whereas A's favoured words are self-sufficient action verbs, so the completion under B tends to be a multi-word construction rather than a single word.

result.kind: directness with which the reprisal is named

residue.description: make is the one periphrastic head on the A side (make an example of her, make her redundant), so it neither names an act the way A's other words do nor joins B's cluster of phrase-taking verbs, and its ranking is identical in both conditions (13 to 13), which leaves it with no visible difference to belong to.

result.counterexamples: Three words cut against the relations, at different costs. terminate is the worst: it sits at the top of B and is, if anything, the coldest and most final word in either list, so any reading of B as the gentler or less punitive condition collapses immediately. It survives only under the register reading, where it counts as the bureaucratic form of the same act, and I have named the relation accordingly rather than as severity. suspend is a genuine but mild problem: it sits under A while being a containment measure rather than a removal, exactly the kind of action I have assigned to B, so it weakens the removal-versus-containment relation without breaking it, since B holds five or six such words to A's one. make is a smaller version of the same trouble for the light-verb relation: it is the sole phrase-taking head on the A side, which is why I have left it in residue rather than counting it against the relation. keep is the odd word within B, since read literally it names no adverse action at all and only makes sense inside a fixed phrase, and if it is not idiomatic it belongs to nothing. Finally, fire moves only one place (1 to 2) and is the top or near-top word in both conditions, so the register relation does not rest on the flagship word at all; it rests on dismiss, sack and lay, which move fourteen, fifteen and thirty places.
result.notes: I would defend all three relations, but with two qualifications about what the display can and cannot support. First, two words are listed under a side while showing zero rank movement (make 13 to 13 under A, transfer 8 to 8 under B), so the assignment of words to sides rests on a quantity that is not shown here and that I have been told not to speculate about; for those two words the ranking itself contains no evidence, and I have used transfer only as one member of a seven-word group rather than letting it carry anything. Second, three words are withheld for moving against their prominence, and since they are withheld by a rule about direction, they are not a random sample of the vocabulary; a relation resting on a thin group could be overturned by them. The groups I have named are not thin, which is why the confidence is medium rather than low. I have deliberately not named severity as the dimension, because terminate at rank 1 under B makes that reading indefensible, and I would withdraw a severity claim on a repeat measurement even though I would keep the register and containment claims. The three relations overlap on purpose: the same A words anchor the first two, since what varies is which side of them is being described.

relations.sentence: A favours completions that leave the sentence unfinished and describe circumstance or ongoing activity (bare prepositions like there, on, in, out, at, outside, around, up, and participles like sitting, talking, hanging, playing, making), whereas B favours completions that close the sentence with a permanent character trait (friendly, peaceful, quiet, welcoming).

relations.sentence: Both sides carry approving adjectives, but A's are unspecific all-purpose warmth (nice, good, happy) that barely shift position, while B's are the narrow set that rebuts what the group named in the fragment is commonly accused of being (peaceful and quiet against violence and disturbance, welcoming against hostility), and these are the largest upward movers in the whole display.

residue.description: These are not content completions but scaffolding for whatever follows, so their movement reports a change of frame rather than of meaning: so and very presuppose a gradable adjective and sit on the B side, a presupposes a noun phrase and sits on the A side, and none of the three says anything about the neighbours by itself.

There is no matched fragment with a different or neutral group to compare against, so the difference could belong to the conditions generally and show up identically on any set of new neighbours. result.reading: Every word in the table is ranked under both conditions -- there is not a single dash -- so the whole difference is a reordering inside one shared vocabulary, and the likeliest completion, "fire", holds rank 1 in both. What moves is everything underneath it: the generic English verbs that would need an object before they described anything (get, call, make, take, use, keep, move) sink, while a bloc of Latinate employment-procedure verbs (transfer, discipline, suspend, punish, retaliate, investigate, terminate) climbs, several of them by twenty or forty places.

relations.name: Unnamed act, named act
relations.sentence: The A side collects verbs that name no action until a complement arrives -- get, make, take, do, have, put, use, go, send, call -- while the B side collects verbs each of which already names a complete employment action on its own: terminate, suspend, transfer, discipline, punish, investigate, retaliate.

relations.name: Plain word, procedural word
relations.sentence: For several of the same acts both conditions supply a word and they split by register, with the everyday Germanic term falling under A and its institutional Latinate counterpart rising under B: move (17 to 30) against transfer (55 to 13), end (21 to 29) against terminate (5 to 2), keep (18 to 42) against let (23 to 17), confront (19 to 45) against discipline (35 to 11) and punish (22 to 12).

relations.name: Adding versus acting on
relations.sentence: The largest single movement in the table belongs to hire, the one word that would put a person into the workplace rather than do something to the one already in it, and it falls 37 places (20 to 57), while every word rising under B is an action taken against her employment.

result.kind: how much of the act the verb itself already names

residue.description: Three of these (have 6 to 6, try 15 to 15, go 14 to 14) moved zero places, so their presence on the A side rests entirely on a quantity I was not shown and I will not build a relation on it; do, use and put are pure light verbs that would complete this fragment no differently than a hundred others; and give, let and cut sit under B while being exactly the sort of Germanic light verb the B group is otherwise defined against, becoming employment actions only through an unstated complement (a warning, her go, her hours).

result.counterexamples: The sharpest is fire: it is rank 1 under both conditions and moved zero places, so the most drastic word in the table is not what separates the conditions at all, and any reading of B as the harsher condition has to explain why its flagship word is stationary. Against the second relation, give, let and cut are plain Germanic verbs sitting under B while confront and use are the Latinate members sitting under A, so the register split is a tendency with named exceptions and not a rule. Against any severity ordering, several A words carry readings at least as harsh as the B bloc -- get (rid of her), end (her employment), confront -- while investigate and transfer under B are among the mildest acts available here; this is why I have named the difference as specification rather than force, and a severity claim would be the one I withdrew first. The hire relation is the weakest of the three: hire could read as hiring a union-busting firm, which would make it as institutional as anything under B, so its fall may register implausibility rather than any of the structure I have described. Finally keep, which I placed as retention, reads just as easily as keep an eye on her, which would put it on the wrong side of its own relation.
result.notes: The evidence is ordinal only and the two vocabularies are identical in membership, so everything here is a claim about depth of ranking and nothing about how likely any completion is. What holds the medium rather than low rating is the paired contrasts, since move against transfer and end against terminate are near-minimal pairs for the same act that move in opposite directions by 13 and 42 and by 8 and 3 places, and pairing is much harder to produce by noise than a one-sided list would be. What holds it below high is that three A words did not move at all, one B word moved by one place (give, 11 to 10), and the top-ranked word is common to both, so a repetition could easily reshuffle the small movers without touching the argument.

relations.name: Waist below, torso above
relations.sentence: Under A the completions that gain are the garments covering the hips and legs together with the fastening at their front (pants, jeans, trousers, fly, zipper), while under B the gain goes entirely to garments worn over the torso and shoulders (jacket, coat).

relations.name: Gear alongside garment
relations.sentence: A's side also contains zippered objects that are not worn at all but carried or camped in (tent, backpack), whereas every word on B's side is a piece of clothing, so the widening of the completion beyond apparel happens only under A.

result.kind: which site the unzipping opens onto

residue.description: This is not a noun that completes the fragment on its own but the first half of a compound (sleeping bag), so it is a fragment of a completion rather than a completion, even though the object it points to would sit with the gear group.

result.counterexamples: The most damaging fact is that jacket, the strongest B word, holds rank 1 under both conditions, so the completion the model actually prefers is the same on both sides and neither relation touches it; the relations describe redistribution below the top rank only. Against the first relation, fly is nominally A-favoured yet occupies rank 2 under both conditions and moves zero places, so the second-strongest member of the lower-body group shows no positional evidence at all, and coat rises only one place (4 to 3), a movement small enough that repeating the measurement could plausibly erase it. Against the second relation, backpack also moves zero places and sleeping only two, leaving tent's eight-place fall as effectively the sole positional support for the gear reading, which is thin for a group of three. Nothing here contradicts the relations outright, but five words are withheld and their withholding is defined by moving against their prominence, so an unknown quantity of counterevidence exists that I cannot inspect.
result.notes: I considered a third relation, that A names apertures and fasteners (fly, zipper) while B names only whole garments, and declined to state it: B's side has just two words and both happen to be whole garments, so the contrast could be an accident of how few words B contributes rather than a part-versus-whole difference, and I would withdraw it on a repeat. I have not assumed the two relations are the same relation seen twice, though they may be, since both amount to A's side being broader and B's narrower; the reason for keeping them apart is that lower-body clothing and camping equipment are unrelated to each other except through the shared act of unzipping. Only rank order is shown, so words that moved zero places (fly, backpack) are asserted to differ on evidence I cannot see, and I have weighted them accordingly rather than dropping them.

result.reading: The fragment sets up an employer's response to discovering union organizing, and the two conditions differ in where along that response the verb lands: A's distinctive words are dominated by dismissal and discipline verbs (fire, terminate, suspend, retaliate) plus a large mass of contentless verb heads, while B's gains go to the steps that come before a decision (investigate rises ten places, confront six) and to verbs that name doing something without saying what (act rises twenty-one places, take reaches position 1). Both sides still contain harm verbs, though, and B keeps cut and shut, so this is a shift in what stage of the action gets named rather than a clean split between punishment and restraint.

relations.name: Verdict before inquiry
relations.sentence: Condition A favors the verbs that name the disciplinary outcome itself, dismissal and its cognates, while condition B favors the fact-finding and face-to-face steps that would precede such an outcome.

relations.name: Severing versus keeping
relations.sentence: A's characteristic verbs end or curtail the employee's presence in the workplace, whereas B's characteristic content verbs all leave her in place and describe management doing something toward or about her instead.

relations.name: Unnamed action rising
relations.sentence: The top of the list under A is held by the most specific possible verb, fire, while under B the largest single riser and the new first-place word are verbs that assert an action without specifying which one.

result.kind: point in the disciplinary sequence named

residue.description: Most of these are delexical verb heads that carry no content until a complement follows, so they are not really completions of the fragment and they sit on both sides of the difference; hire and shut are excluded for the different reason that no reading of them is recoverable from the fragment alone, since the fragment says nothing about who would be hired or what would be shut.</br>

result.counterexamples: Two of B's words are punitive actions and cut against any reading that assigns harm to A and restraint to B: cut (position 5 under both conditions, and cutting hours or pay is a standard reprisal) and shut, which rises six places and most plausibly completes as shutting something down. Neither is fatal, because neither names dismissal and both remain compatible with the staging reading, but they rule out a severity-based account. Two of A's own words weaken it from the other side: retaliate does not move at all (17 to 17) and cut does not move at all, so their assignment to a side rests on the prominence ordering rather than on any displacement, which makes retaliate the weakest member of relation one. The mass of light verbs under A (get, have, do, make, give, put) may also be a size artifact, since A's list has sixteen entries against B's eight, and it would be a mistake to read their presence as itself meaningful. Finally, two words are withheld, and either could contradict any relation here.
result.notes: I can defend the first relation to someone who disagreed: fire, terminate and suspend are the three words in the set that name dismissal or its formal equivalents, they are all on A's side, and the two clearest procedural verbs in the set, investigate and confront, are both on B's with the two largest content-verb gains (+10 and +6). The second and third relations are cuts through the same evidence at different angles rather than independent findings, so treat them as refinements, not as three separate confirmations. I have not read the ordering column as a magnitude of anything: the instructions say only that the lists are ordered by how much the difference rests on each word, which is not the same quantity as the places-moved column, and cut and retaliate both appear with zero movement. No likelihood is shown, so nothing here should be read as a claim that the model became less likely to complete with fire, only that fire is less distinctive of B than of A.

result.reading: Under A the emotional completions are all injuries done to the neighbours by someone else's arrival (betrayed, trapped, obliged); under B the emotional completions instead sort onto a security axis, and both of its poles rise together, with unsafe (+10) and relieved (+8) the two largest movements in the whole list. The rest of each side is grammatical scaffolding after "felt" rather than content.

relations.name: Security axis swap
relations.sentence: The affect words rising under A name a wrong suffered in a relationship (betrayed, trapped, obliged), whereas those rising under B all score the same event on a threat-and-safety axis (safe, safer, relieved at one pole, unsafe and intimidated at the other), so the two conditions differ in which axis the feeling is measured on rather than in how strong or how negative the feeling is.

relations.name: No benign outcome under A
relations.sentence: Every affect word that rises under A leaves the neighbours worse off (betrayed, trapped), and the only condition in which completions making them better off rise at all is B (safe, safer, relieved), so the asymmetry is about whether a favourable construal of the arrival is available, not about its intensity.

result.kind: appraisal axis of the feeling: security versus relational wrong

residue.description: These are not content completions but grammatical continuations of "felt" (felt they, felt it, felt there was, felt that, felt like, felt a, felt very, felt more), and they split across the two sides without any pattern I would defend: "that" sits at rank 2 in both conditions and moved zero places, "they" likewise at rank 1, and the degree words "very" and "more" moved one or two places, which is too little to carry a reading, especially since both sides' content words are predicate adjectives and so neither side is more adjective-seeking than the other.

result.counterexamples: Two things cut against the obvious reading, which is that B is simply the reassured or pacified condition. First, unsafe is B's largest single riser (+10) and intimidated also rises under B, so B carries the threat pole as strongly as the safety pole; any claim that B softens the scene is refuted outright by its own top mover, and this is why I stated the relation as a change of axis rather than a change of valence. Second, obliged rises under A while its near-synonym compelled rises under B, the two straddling the divide at almost the same ranks (9 and 11 under A, 14 and 10 under B); this is mild damage rather than fatal, since I make no claim that coercion belongs to one side, but it does rule out reading A as the constraint-and-coercion condition, and it is a reminder that a single lexeme's side can be an accident of near-synonym competition. A third, weaker one: safer moves zero places and sits at rank 8 in both conditions, so it is listed under B on a margin the ranking cannot show me, and relation two would survive its removal only on safe and relieved.
result.notes: Medium rather than high for four reasons that are properties of the data I was given, not of the reading. Five words are withheld because their movement ran against their prominence, and I cannot tell whether they are affect words; if they are, they could reshape both relations, and neither relation should be repeated as though the list were complete. I was shown ranks only, so every "+8" and "+10" is ordinal, and I have no way to know whether the gap between rank 18 and rank 28 is large or negligible, which means I can say the security words moved furthest but not that they moved much. The two relations overlap heavily in their A side and should be read as one finding seen from two angles rather than as independent corroboration. Finally, the fragment names a real political situation, and the finding here is about which vocabulary of appraisal the completion is drawn from, not about a stance toward that situation; the security framing under B is the notable thing precisely because it holds for both of its poles at once, and reading either pole on its own as the result would be the error the withheld-word note and the unsafe counterexample both warn against.

result.reading: Both conditions rank the same four verbs first (fire, terminate, take, have), so nothing that separates A from B lives at the top; the whole difference is a reshuffle of the tail. A's tail fills with verbs needing a document, a court, or a personnel procedure to complete them, plus a scatter of generic verbs moving a place or two; B's tail lifts the two verbs of speaking with her, and three of its nine words are masked, so B's group is only partly readable.

relations.name: Filing against firing
relations.sentence: Under A the completion drifts toward verbs that cannot be carried out without a document, a court, or a personnel procedure standing between management and the woman (lodging something, taking her to law, bringing something against her, moving her to another post), whereas under B it sits on the two verbs naming management ending her employment itself, the blunt one and its formal synonym.

relations.name: Talking to her
relations.sentence: B lifts both verbs that would have management address the woman in person, the one for sitting down with her and the one for addressing her aloud (the latter climbing seven places), while A raises no verb of contact and its one candidate for spoken contact, the verb for telephoning or summoning someone, falls eight places.

relations.name: Scatter against one act
relations.sentence: Four of A's words are among the most generic action verbs in the language, undetermined without an object, and each moves only one to six places, whereas B's gain is anchored on a single named act, dismissal, so this is better described as one specific action standing out against a spread of unspecific ones than as two opposed categories.

result.kind: whether the act is done to her, filed against her, or spoken to her

residue.description: Take and have sit at unchanged positions three and four and are pure light verbs whose act is undetermined without the noun that follows, so they cannot be assigned to either side; the three masked B words and the one withheld word cannot be read at all, which leaves about a third of B's list outside any relation I can defend.

result.counterexamples: The worst is end, A's largest mover at forty-eight places: end her employment is the same act as fire and terminate, only euphemised, so a dismissal verb sits squarely on the side I claimed holds the mediated and procedural ones (it could instead continue as end the union drive, but I cannot tell which reading the ranking reflects, and that ambiguity is itself against me). Transfer is the weakest member of the first relation, since moving her is a direct act on the person even if it runs through a personnel process. Sue and file also cut oddly: they are more naturally what a worker or a union does than what an employer does, so their presence under A may be a shift of implied agent rather than of mediation, which would recast the first relation without refuting it. Against all three relations stands the fact that the top four positions are identical in both conditions, so whatever distinguishes A from B is a matter of what fills the tail rather than of what management is most likely to do.
result.notes: I am shown only rank positions, so I have taken on trust that fire, terminate, take and have are higher under B despite not moving; nothing in the display checks that and I have not speculated about magnitudes. Three of B's nine words are masked and one more is withheld, so B's group is roughly a third unreadable and any relation here could be weakened by what is hidden. The first two relations are the ones I would defend; the third describes the shape of the two lists rather than a semantic contrast, and I state it as such because the instructions allow for one word standing out against scatter. I would withdraw the second relation if a repeat put meet or speak back down the list, since it rests on two words and one of them moves only two places.

result.reading: Only nine of the sixteen words are plausible affect completions at all; the rest ("that", "the", "it", "a", "they", "like", "more", "their") are syntactic continuations that dominate the top of both rankings. Among the affect words the split is clean: every word naming the neighbours as the object of someone else's action or as unable to act ("threatened", "betrayed", "helpless") sits under B, while A holds the two safety words ("safe", "safer"), the two deontic words ("obliged", "compelled"), and one weak disquiet word ("uneasy"). The rank movements themselves are tiny (nothing moves more than three places, ten of sixteen do not move, no word is absent from either list), so the reading rests on which side each word falls, not on how far anything travelled.

relations.name: Menace or reassurance
relations.sentence: B raises words that say the arrival puts the neighbours in danger and strips their capacity to respond ("threatened", "helpless"), while A raises the words that say the opposite happened, that the neighbours were left unharmed ("safe", "safer").

relations.name: Duty against injury
relations.sentence: Apart from the safety pair, the only affect words A raises are deontic ones in which the neighbours feel a pressure to act themselves ("obliged", "compelled"), whereas every affect word B raises casts them as the patient of an aggressor or of their own incapacity ("threatened", "betrayed", "helpless").

relations.name: Weakest distress kept
relations.sentence: A does hold one word of disquiet, but it is the vaguest and least specific one available ("uneasy", a state with no named cause and no named injury), while the distress words B holds each name a specific harm or a specific incapacity ("threatened", "betrayed", "helpless").

result.kind: the role the neighbours are given: harmed party or safe-and-dutiful one

residue.description: These are not completions of the feeling but openings of a clause or noun phrase after "felt" ("felt that...", "felt like...", "felt a..."), so they carry no affect content of their own and their five-to-three split across the two sides supports nothing; that they occupy four of the top five ranks in both conditions is a fact about the fragment's syntax rather than about the difference being measured.

result.counterexamples: "uneasy" is the real counterexample: it is a distress word sitting on A's side, so the first relation cannot be stated as "A carries no alarm" and must be restricted to the safety pair. It damages that relation only mildly, since it sits at rank 15 under both conditions and moved zero places, but it does forbid the stronger version of the claim. A second, more serious problem is internal to the second relation: "felt compelled" and "felt obliged" can be read as coercion by a menacing presence ("compelled to leave", "obliged to keep quiet"), in which case both words belong with the harm cluster and the relation inverts rather than weakens. Nothing in the data settles which reading holds, so that relation is the one I would drop first. Minor: "helpless" is the lowest-ranked word shown (17 to 16) and moved one place, so B's strongest single piece of evidence is really "betrayed" at +3, and a relation resting on "helpless" alone would not survive.
result.notes: What licenses "medium" rather than higher is that the displacement evidence is almost nil: no word is missing from either list, the largest move is three places, and ten of sixteen words do not move at all. What licenses "medium" rather than lower is that the sign of every non-zero move agrees with the side it was assigned to (all six B-side moves are 0 or upward, all four non-zero A-side moves are downward), and that the partition of the nine content words is exact, with all three patient-role words on one side and none on the other. The reading is carried by which side a word falls on, not by how far it travelled. Two cautions. First, "safer" and "more" are comparatives with no stated comparison, so their presence tells us less than the plain words do. Second, the fragment names a national group and an arrival, and the two sides amount to two different accounts of what that arrival is, an incursion felt by its victims or an event after which people feel secure or dutiful; I state that as the content of the split without any claim about how likely either completion is, which the data does not show.
