result.reading: The A side is dominated by adjectives that assign the neighbors a settled character (polite, nice, pleasant, kind, good, happy), while the B side is dominated by present participles reporting what they are repeatedly doing (playing, complaining, fighting, watching, going, laughing), with the largest B gains going to so (+15) and fighting (+11) and the largest A gains to smiling (-17) and pleasant (-14). The split is a tendency among the words that actually move rather than a clean partition: friendly and quiet are character words credited to B, and smiling is a participle credited to A.

relations.name: Trait versus doing
relations.sentence: Under A the blank is filled by adjectives ascribing a standing disposition to the neighbors (polite, nice, pleasant, kind, good, happy), whereas under B it is filled by present participles reporting recurrent activity (playing, complaining, fighting, watching, going, coming, laughing, trying), so the conditions differ in whether the sentence ends in what the neighbors are or in what they are doing.

relations.name: Only B admits friction
relations.sentence: Every descriptor favoured under A is an amiable one, while the only two words on the panel that name conflict, complaining (+2, rising into third place) and fighting (+11), both sit under B, so B allows a kind of completion for which A's list contains no instance at all.

result.kind: standing character versus ongoing conduct

residue.description: None of these describes the neighbors; they fill grammatical slots (particle, determiner, degree word) or say only that the neighbors were present or absent, and most of them barely move (in +0, there +0, a +0, very +0, on -1), so their assignment to a side rests on weighting rather than on any shift I can see, with so (+15) the one large mover and a degree word rather than a description.

result.counterexamples: Friendly is the sharpest counterexample: it is a disposition adjective of exactly the sort relation 1 puts under A, yet it is credited to B, and since it holds rank 1 under both conditions and moves 0 places it also shows that B has not demoted amiable character words at all. Quiet is a second, softer case, a stative descriptor of good-neighborliness that gains under B (+3). Smiling crosses the other way, a participle of behavior that is the largest A mover (-17), though it reads as demeanor rather than as an event, which is why I would defend relation 1 as a tendency and not a partition. Busy (A, -5) is an activity-state rather than a social trait and fits neither side of relation 1. Against relation 2, the presence of friendly and quiet under B means B is not simply the harsher condition; complaining and fighting are additions to B's repertoire, not replacements for warmth.
result.notes: Relations 1 and 2 are confounded and I do not treat them as independent evidence: complaining and fighting are themselves participles, so relation 1 alone could account for their position, and what relation 2 adds is only the observation that no word of comparable valence appears anywhere on A's side. I considered and did not promote a third pattern, that A's locatives are stative presence (in, there, around, on) while B's are motion or absence (out, going, coming); the movements involved are too small (+0, +0, -4, -1 against +2, +9, +2) for me to defend it if the measurement were repeated, so those words are in residue instead. I also declined a degree-modifier relation (very and so both under B), because very moves 0 places and the pattern would rest on a single word. Three words are withheld, and since withheld words are by definition ones whose movement runs against their weighting, any of them could bear on the crossovers I have listed as counterexamples. No likelihoods were shown, so nothing here says how much of the distribution these words hold or whether the A and B completions differ by much at all.

result.reading: Under A the top of the list is a tight set of employer sanctions aimed at the woman in the fragment (fire, terminate, suspend, punish, retaliate, transfer), while under B those same words fall to the 120-160 range and are replaced at the top by verbs of joining and dealing with the union itself (join, become, attend, support, organize, contact). Nothing drops out of either ranking, so this is a near-total inversion of order rather than a loss of vocabulary, and the light verbs that flank both lists barely move.

relations.name: Discipline versus enlistment
relations.sentence: Under A the decision is an employer sanction imposed on the employee for her contact with the organizer, while under B the decision is the subject affiliating with the very union she was talking to.

relations.name: Inquiry against contact
relations.sentence: The one A-favoured verb of finding-out is directed at her as an investigation of her conduct, whereas the B side's corresponding verbs are all two-way approaches to the organizer rather than scrutiny of the employee.

relations.name: Inversion without attrition
relations.sentence: Every word that leads one condition still exists in the other, just at the far end of it, so the sanction words and the affiliation words trade places wholesale (fire 1 to 137, join 136 to 1) instead of either set disappearing.

result.kind: allegiance and target of the decided action

residue.description: These are light or support verbs whose content lies in a continuation the fragment does not show, so a shift in their rank cannot be read as a shift in what the decision is; consistent with that, most of them move only a handful of places on either side.

result.counterexamples: The clearest contradiction is talk, which is listed as B-favoured yet sits at position 18 in both conditions and therefore supports no relation at all; it is presented as a difference and is not one. follow (+74) sits on the B side but reads at least as easily as following her, which is surveillance and belongs with the A-side content, so it cuts against the enlistment reading moderately. take (+2), try (+3) and make (+8) are named as B-favoured on movements small enough to be noise beside the +80 to +139 jumps that carry the relation. On the A side, let (-29) and cut (-108) are ambiguous: let could be permissive rather than punitive, and cut needs an object (hours, pay, her) that is not shown. Finally go (+31) and be (+33) move about as far as some content words while carrying no content, which weakens any claim that magnitude of movement tracks the semantic split.
result.notes: The two leading sets are semantically coherent, mutually exclusive, and separated by 100-plus rank places in both directions, which is why I would defend the first relation to someone who disagreed. Worth stating plainly what the B ranking implies: since the grammatical subject of decided is Management, the top B completions read as management deciding to join, become part of, attend, support or organize with the union. That is a reversal of who the decision serves, not a softening of the same decision, and it is the reason I named the dimension allegiance rather than severity. The third relation is structural rather than semantic and I have kept it because no word is absent from either ranking, so nothing here licenses a claim that any completion was removed. All of this is read off order alone; I have not inferred anything about how likely any completion is under either condition, and a rank gap of 100 places says nothing about how much probability mass separates them.

relations.sentence: Every verb of uttering or of raised voice sits lower under B, with say falling fifty-seven places, ask thirty-four, yell twenty-six and shout twenty, while the verbs of injuring a person or a body sit higher, cut rising thirty-two places, kill twenty-two and fight sixteen.

relations.sentence: The verbs for merely occupying a room and passing time in it fall under B, while verbs that need the room or its contents as something operated on rise, so the entrants stop being people who sit, eat, read, work, look and sing and become people who search, remove, take, set and draw.

residue.description: Put and make are light verbs with no determinate content until an object arrives, and both barely move (two places each), while play, dance and pray sit on the B side without belonging to either relation; a culturally typed reading of the last three is available given who the fragment names, but only dance moves appreciably (+14) and pray and play move one place and none.</description>

result.counterexamples: The worst is talk, which is a speech verb, is listed as favoured by B, and holds rank 1 in both conditions: the most likely completion of all is an act of speaking and it does not fall at all, so the first relation cannot be a fall of speech as a class, only of its middle and tail. Argue is the same defect at smaller scale, a speech verb on the B side rising one place from 3 to 2. Throw contradicts the first relation directly in the other direction, being a physical and potentially violent act that A favours, though only by three places. Shout and yell fall, which fits speech but refutes any restatement of the first relation as aggression rising, since these are the two most aggressive verbal items and they drop twenty and twenty-six places. Beat already stood fourth under A and rises one place, so harm was near the top before B touched it. Sing on the A side against dance on the B side splits two verbs of the same register across the divide, which the second relation does not predict.

result.reading: Both sides carry violence, so the difference is not severity: A leads with shout, fire, beat and B leads with attack, fight, and A's aggressive words name discrete physical operations on things in the room (tear, tie, remove, search, open, take) while B's name the episode under a category label (attack, destroy, kill, hit). Alongside that, B admits a set of actions that make the three men ordinary occupants of a room (pray, sing, play, cry, look) which has almost no counterpart on the A side, whose vocal words are demands and addresses (ask, question, talk, shout, chant).

relations.name: Step, not episode
relations.sentence: A favours verbs that name one discrete physical operation carried out on something already in the room (tearing, tying, removing, searching, opening, seizing, striking, discharging), while B favours verbs that name the whole event under its category label, the words a report would use for it (attack, destroy, kill, fight, hit).

relations.name: Demand versus outcry
relations.sentence: Among the words for using the voice, A favours ones addressed to someone present and seeking an answer, compliance or collective assertion (asking, questioning, talking, shouting, chanting), while B favours ones that are emissions requiring no addressee at all (screaming, crying), the sharpest evidence being that shout falls fifteen places under B while its near-synonym scream rises six.

relations.name: Occupants, not operatives
relations.sentence: B alone carries actions that presuppose no antagonist and no object to be handled, making the three men ordinary people in a room (praying, singing, playing, looking about, moving), whereas the nearest thing A offers is chant, a collective and political vocalization, and every other A word presupposes either something to be handled or someone to be answered.

result.kind: how specifically the action is named, and whether it presupposes an object or an antagonist

residue.description: Shoot sits at position 1 under both conditions and moved zero places, so nothing shown here explains why it is listed on the B side and it can support no relation; make is not really a completion at all, since "started to make" waits on a complement that would carry the whole meaning; move is bleached to the point of naming no action the scene could turn on, and its +15 is a rise in a word that describes nothing.

result.counterexamples: The severest thing to say first: any reading on which one side is the harsher or the other the tamer collapses at once, since B holds kill, attack, destroy, hit and shoot while A holds talk, ask, open and chant. Against the first relation, beat sits under A and hit under B, and they name the same act at the same grain, so that pair is pure noise against the claim; throw is likewise an unremarkable physical act rather than a raid step. Against the second, argue is under B and plainly requires an interlocutor, and speak (B, +2) is no less addressed than talk (A, -6), a near-synonymous pair split across sides with almost no movement, which is why I rest that relation on shout against scream rather than on the vocal words as a class. Against the third, chant is collective and no less civilian than sing, so the line between the two rosters there is political versus devotional rather than antagonist versus none.
result.notes: The relations rest most on the words the ordering says they should: on B's side the two largest gains are destroy (96 -> 23) and play (36 -> 10), one from each of the first and third relations, and the head of the B list runs attack, fight, then argue, pray, play, which is exactly the category-naming and civilian-register split; on A's side the largest fall is fire (7 -> 32) and the deepest coherent block is the operation cluster question, remove, tear, open, tie, search. I am treating fire as discharging a weapon rather than dismissing someone; if that reading is wrong the word leaves the first relation, though the relation survives without it. I have used only the positions given and have not speculated about how likely anything is. Medium rather than high because two near-synonymous pairs (beat/hit, talk/speak) fall on opposite sides and the top-ranked word under both conditions is on the B side with no movement at all, so a repeat measurement could reasonably reshuffle those without touching the operation cluster or the pray/sing/play block, which are what I would defend.

result.reading: Under A the top of the list is a raid: shoot, talk, fight, beat, kill, with point and look for aiming and watching. Under B the likeliest completion is dance, and a block of verbs for moving around a room (move, walk, run, search) climbs sharply, while violence does not retreat: shoot slips one place and still sits second, attack holds its position exactly, and fire and throw both rise.

relations.name: Bodies begin to move
relations.sentence: Verbs for moving a whole body around the room (dance, move, walk, run, search, play) all rise under B, several of them from far down the list, while under A the non-speech verbs are stationary and directed at others present (point, look, pray), so that no locomotion verb at all favours A.

relations.name: The killing word recedes
relations.sentence: Among the harm verbs it is the explicit and lethal ones that fall under B (kill by twenty-three places, and with it point, beat and fight) while harm verbs that name an act without spelling out its result hold or climb (attack unmoved, fire and throw up), so what changes is the word the violence is said with rather than whether violence is said.

result.kind: scene script rather than severity

residue.description: make and take are light verbs that name no action until a complement arrives, so their positions say little about what the completion depicts, and the whole conversational field sits on both sides at once (tell, say, discuss, talk favouring A; speak, ask, argue favouring B) with no line between the two sets that I would defend to someone who disagreed; sing falls two places while dance rises to first, which is too small and too isolated to attach to anything.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest contradiction is shoot: it is the top completion under A and still the second under B, having moved one place, so any reading in which B withdraws from armed violence is false as stated, and the second relation has to be confined to the specific word kill. Almost as bad is the pair yell and shout, near synonyms that move in opposite directions, yell down forty-three places (the second largest fall in the set) and shout up seven, with scream between them at minus four; no meaning-based relation I named predicts that, and it suggests part of the difference tracks the particular word rather than what it denotes. Search rising sixteen places also cuts against reading B as the calmer scene, since three men searching a room is an intrusion rather than an activity; and fight falling while attack holds and fire rises shows the aggression vocabulary does not move as a block.
result.notes: Medium rather than high because only the first relation is carried by a real block of words with large moves and a clean absence on the other side; the second rests on kill alone once shoot is accounted for, and the speech verbs, a third of the set, form no relation at all. Two facts about the data itself are worth flagging: argue and attack are listed under B while their ranks are identical in both conditions, so their placement rests on something the ranking does not show and I have not reasoned from it; and point carries the largest single move in the set, fifteen to sixty-two, which is doing more work in the first two relations than any other word. The most compact statement of the change is that the modal completion goes from shoot to dance without the violent vocabulary leaving the list, which is why I called the dimension a change of script rather than of severity.

residue.description: ____ is a blank rather than a completion, own and long are prenominal modifiers that would precede the object rather than be it, chin． is chin followed by a fullwidth period and so repeats a word already present instead of adding a completion, and face and cheek sit in A's list while occupying identical positions under both conditions, so there is no difference in them for a relation to explain.

result.counterexamples: The worst is moustache against mustache: the same referent appears on both sides, distinguished only by British and American spelling, with moustache at 4 to 7 under A and mustache steady at 3 under B, so no relation can claim facial hair as B's property, and the beard-line relation has to be read as a shift in which spellings and which nearby parts are recruited rather than as a shift in subject matter. Nearly as bad, chin, beard and mustache are printed under B but hold ranks 1, 2 and 3 in both conditions, so the canonical beard-stroking gesture is already at the top under A and B intensifies a shared preference rather than substituting for A's. Also cutting against the first relation, face and cheek are head words that stay in A and do not move at all, and lips, the biggest faller of any word, is anatomically adjacent to chin and jaw, which is why the second relation is stated separately rather than folded into the first.
result.notes: All three relations rest on the words that actually move. The fallers under B are lips at fourteen places, hair and chest at twelve each, fingers at nine, hands at eight and hand at five; the risers are chin． at seventeen, goatee at fourteen and jaw at eight. result.reading: The fragment is completed on both sides by clothing, so the split is not garments against non-garments but a split inside the garment vocabulary: A takes plain, casual, close-to-the-body words (pants, jeans, shirt, clothes, and the redundant zipper) plus two body parts that cannot literally be unzipped (mouth, lips), while B takes more tailored or idiomatic names for much the same scene (trousers, fly, suit, coat, overcoat, robe) along with luggage and gear. The word that cuts against the tidiest reading is fly, B's top-ranked completion and the most anatomically pointed word in either list.

relations.name: Casual versus tailored naming
relations.sentence: The same lower-body garment and its opening get a plain, casual, mechanically generic name under A (pants, jeans, the tautological zipper, the catch-all clothes) and a tailored or idiomatic name under B (trousers, fly, suit, robe), with trousers against pants and fly against zipper standing as near-exact minimal pairs for one referent.

relations.name: Body admitted only under A
relations.sentence: Two parts of the body that cannot literally be unzipped, mouth and lips, are ranked among A's completions and have no counterpart anywhere in B, every one of whose favored words names an object that actually carries a zip.

relations.name: Layers put on over
relations.sentence: B favors garments worn as an outer layer over other clothing (jacket, coat, overcoat) where A favors the layer beneath or the undifferentiated whole (shirt, jeans, pants, clothes), with parka sitting on A's side as a straightforward exception.

result.kind: plain-bodily versus tailored-idiomatic naming of one scene

residue.description: Sleeping and leather are not completions at all but the first halves of compounds (sleeping bag, leather jacket or trousers), so they name nothing on their own; pocket, backpack and suitcase are carriers rather than worn garments and they fall on both sides with no principle separating them, and parka is an outer garment stranded among A's inner ones by a movement of only two places.

result.counterexamples: Fly is the worst, and it is bad enough to have stopped me writing a fourth relation: the obvious reading of this data is that A takes the intimate or sexual completion and B the innocuous one, but fly ranks first under B and is the most explicitly bodily word in either list, so that reading dies on B's own top word. Parka contradicts the outer-layer relation directly, since it is unambiguously an outer layer and sits under A, though it moved only two places (17 to 19) and is near the boundary of the list. Backpack under A against suitcase under B splits the carriers with nothing to distinguish them, which is why I left both in residue rather than build on either. Jacket, coat and overcoat under B are neither more nor less formal than parka under A, so the register relation and the layering relation cannot both be pushed onto the whole outerwear group.
result.notes: Confidence is medium rather than high for three reasons. Several of the movements are tiny (pants -3, backpack -2, parka -2) and I would not expect their side to be stable if the measurement were repeated, so no relation above rests on them alone; the relations I state lean on the large, unambiguous moves (lips -50, pocket -59, robe +30, leather +46) and on the categorical fact that mouth and lips have no counterpart under B. One word is withheld, and since it moved against its own prominence it is exactly the kind of word that could complicate the register reading. I am also shown only positions, not likelihoods, so I cannot tell whether B's promotion of robe and leather from ranks 42 and 59 reflects a real preference or merely the reshuffling of a long tail; both are far enough down under A that their absolute standing under either condition may be slight. The relation I would defend hardest is the second, because absence from a list is stated in the data as a stronger difference than any movement, and the anatomical words are present on one side only.

result.reading: The fragment puts three men into a room, and both conditions complete it overwhelmingly with verbs of coercion, so the difference is not violence against non-violence but which coercive scene is being written: A's leading words gather the verbs of a questioning (interrogate, question, ask, with beat and hit as the physical means of one), while B's gather the verbs of a search-and-shoot raid (search, rob, shoot, kill, fire) plus a set of plain speaking verbs. Against that, several near-synonyms split across the two sides (yell under A, shout and scream under B), and four of the words carrying the relation moved no places at all, so whatever separates them is a quantity this display does not show me.

relations.name: Questioning versus seizure
relations.sentence: Under A the room is completed as a scene where an answer is being extracted from someone present, by the three verbs meaning to put questions to a person, while under B it is completed as a scene where the room and its occupants are gone through, stripped or shot, by the verbs of searching a place, taking property by force, and discharging a weapon at a person.

relations.name: Fists against firearms
relations.sentence: The hands-on, unarmed striking verbs fall under A while the verbs that presuppose a weapon or an actual death fall under B, so that hitting and beating with the body go one way and shooting, firing and killing go the other, even though none of these four words changed rank at all between the conditions.

result.kind: which coercive script the intruders are made to enact

residue.description: Take, throw and make are bleached transitives whose sense depends entirely on an object the display withholds, so they cannot be assigned to either script even though throw is A's largest mover at ten places; play is not a plausible content completion of this fragment under either condition and reads as generic filler that would follow almost any subject entering a room; attack and abuse name violence without specifying manner, instrument or victim, so they are compatible with both scripts and discriminate nothing.

result.counterexamples: The worst is the loud-vocalization set, which splits: yell sits under A and moves five places that way, while shout and scream sit under B. Since the three are near-synonyms differing at most in register, no account of what A prefers about speech survives them, and this is the main reason I did not offer the tempting third relation that B favours speaking without an interrogative demand (talk, speak, shout, scream) against A's answer-seeking verbs. Search is a second, milder problem: it belongs to the same raid-and-detention script as interrogate, and I have had to read it as handling the room rather than the person to keep it on B's side, which is a distinction the word itself does not force. Abuse under B is hands-on and weaponless and so pulls against the second relation, and attack under B is silent about instrument, so between them they leave that relation resting on five words, four of which did not move. Finally, beat and hit are ranked 1 and 5 under both conditions and shoot and fire are ranked 2 and 18 under both, so the second relation is a claim about a quantity I was not shown; if that hidden quantity is what the ordering encodes, the relation is real, and if the ordering is noisy at zero movement, it is nothing.
result.notes: The two relations are not equally strong and I would report them at different confidences: the questioning-versus-seizure split is medium, since all three interrogation verbs land on A and all five search-and-shoot verbs on B with no member on the wrong side, whereas the fists-versus-firearms split is low, because its five words include four with zero rank movement and it is contradicted from within by abuse. Three words were withheld for moving against their prominence, and I cannot tell whether any of them belong to the vocalization set that already splits, so the counterexample above may be understated rather than overstated. I have not assumed which of A and B is which kind of condition, and neither relation depends on that: read in one direction A questions and B shoots, in the other B questions and A shoots, and the dimension named is the same either way. Rank movement is plainly not the measure of contribution here, since beat leads the A list at +0 while throw at -10 is sixth from the top, so I have weighted list order over the movement numbers throughout and would not defend any claim that rests on the size of a move.

result.reading: Under A the fragment tends to continue as an event: five progressive participles (talking, looking, smiling, trying, getting) and four locative particles (in, on, at, there) sit high and then fall hard under B, looking by 59 places and talking by 46. Under B the blank fills instead with single-word character adjectives and the degree adverbs that bracket them, most sharply odd (134 to 13) and strange (66 to 7) arriving from outside contention, while the head of the list, friendly at rank 1, does not move at all.

relations.name: Event tail to trait tail
relations.sentence: Words that would make the blank part of an ongoing activity (talking, looking, smiling, trying, getting) fall between twenty and fifty-nine places under B, while single-word descriptions of settled character (quiet, nice, pleasant, strange, odd) rise into the top fourteen, so the same slot shifts from what the neighbours were doing to what they were like.

relations.name: Particles out, intensifiers in
relations.sentence: The non-content words A ranks highest are locative particles that would extend the clause (in, on, at, there), each falling nine to seventeen places, whereas the non-content words B ranks highest are degree adverbs that require an adjective after them (very, so, really), with really rising sixty-one places, so the grammatical scaffolding switches from continuing a predicate to modifying one.

relations.name: Stationary stereotype, surging strangeness
relations.sentence: The one A-side word carrying an unflattering group stereotype, loud, holds rank 10 under both conditions and does not move at all, while strange and odd climb from ranks 66 and 134 to 7 and 13, so the unfavourable material B admits is of inscrutability rather than of the noise stereotype, which is unchanged.

result.kind: conduct in progress versus ascribed character

residue.description: "the" is not a content completion at all, it merely opens a following noun phrase, and it holds rank 9 under both conditions, so its side assignment rests on something not shown here; "friendly" is a genuine completion but sits at rank 1 under both conditions with zero movement, so it belongs to no difference even though it is listed on the B side.

result.counterexamples: The clearest contradiction to the first relation is that A also favours three plain character adjectives, polite, kind and good, which is exactly the kind of word the relation assigns to B; the damage is mild, because their movements are the smallest non-zero ones in the list (-4, -4, -2) and all three remain inside the top sixteen under B, so what B does is repopulate a trait slot that already existed rather than create one. That friendly is the top completion under both conditions makes the same point more strongly: the relation describes the tail of the ranking, not its head, and anyone who read it as B introducing character description would be wrong. A separate contradiction cuts against any evaluative reading: B raises quiet, nice and pleasant alongside strange and odd, and A holds polite, kind and good alongside loud, so neither side is the warmer or the harsher one, and this is why I offer no relation about valence. Finally, "so" is on the B side and is arguably a clause continuer ("were always so busy") as much as a degree adverb, which weakens but does not break the second relation, since very and really admit no such reading.
result.notes: The three relations rest on movements large enough that I would not expect them to reverse: five participles falling in the same direction by 20 to 59 places is a pattern rather than a jitter, and 121 and 61 place gains are not noise. I hold back from high confidence for four reasons. This is one fragment under one pairing with no likelihoods shown, so I cannot tell whether the top of the ranking carries almost all the mass and the reordered tail is negligible. One word was withheld, and a single withheld word could belong to any of these groups. Three of the twenty-three words shown moved zero places yet are still assigned to a side, which tells me the side assignment is not purely a function of rank movement and that I am reading only part of the measurement. And the fragment names an ethnic group, which makes an evaluative story about strange and odd very tempting; I have deliberately confined myself to the claim that those two words arrive from outside contention and that loud does not move, because the direction-of-valence reading is contradicted by nice, pleasant and quiet rising on the same side.

relations.sentence: Under A the fragment is completed as an armed or official entry in which the three act on people already in the room, by shooting, beating, searching, interrogating, inspecting and questioning them, while under B it is completed as a verbal exchange the three conduct among themselves, by arguing, debating, discussing and chatting, and the two largest single moves in the data belong to this pair of clusters (debate up 108, interrogate down 32).

relations.name: Object required, object dropped
relations.sentence: A's list is dominated by verbs that need something or someone in the room to be acted upon before the sentence is finished (take, put, clean, search, inspect, work), whereas B's leading verbs complete the fragment with no object at all, naming posture, motion or mutual exchange (sit, walk, argue, chat).

relations.name: Violence keeps, victim goes
relations.sentence: Aggression does not leave the completion under B so much as change who receives it: the one-sided violence of shoot and beat falls seventeen places each, while fight, whose violence is mutual and needs no third party present, rises forty-one places into B's list.

result.kind: who the action is done to

residue.description: make moved zero places and so records no difference at all; set and look are light or near-static verbs that read as the first word of a longer phrase rather than as a content action; sing and dance name a performance that fits neither the raid reading nor the conversation reading and sit oddly on the A side; watch is genuinely ambiguous between idle spectating, which suits B's posture verbs, and surveillance, which would put it with A.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest is fight, which is unmistakably violent and sits on B, rising forty-one places: it defeats any reading of the difference as violence under A and calm under B, and I have had to fold it into a relation rather than ignore it. Next is ask, a verbal act on the A side, which cuts against the first relation's verbal/nonverbal division; it survives only because ask reads as questioning someone present, and its move of two places is small enough that it carries little weight either way. The mundane block on A (take, put, work, clean, make) contradicts the raid reading directly, since cleaning and working are not what a raiding party does, and it is the single largest reason to distrust a clean semantic story about A. sing and dance do the same damage more mildly. result.notes: The first relation I would defend to someone who disagreed: the top of each list is coherent and the largest movements in the data (debate +108, sit +43, fight +41, interrogate -32) all fall inside it. What holds me at medium rather than high is the mundane block on A, which no version of the raid reading explains, and the fact that I am shown only orderings, not any indication of how far apart the words actually are, so a small reshuffle at the bottom of either list could be indistinguishable from a large one. relations.sentence: Among the words that actually change rank, A raises verbs that begin a process whose content is still unnamed and that cannot end the sentence on their own (investigate, conduct, place), while B raises verbs that dispose of the employee in a single completed act (fire, discharge, replace, transfer, discipline, lay off), the largest fall belonging to the one word that decides nothing and the largest rise to a form of separation.

residue.description: "Have" and "take" are light verbs that contribute no content by themselves, since whatever completes the fragment would be the noun after them ("take action", "have a word"), and both move only two places, so I would not build anything on them; "remove" sits awkwardly because it is a disposal like B's words but needs a from-phrase like A's, and at two places of movement it is too small to adjudicate.

result.counterexamples: The worst is "terminate": it stands first in A's own ordering, which the instructions say marks it as the word the difference rests on most, and it is the most final verb in the entire set, so the leading A word directly opposes the claim that A prefers unfinished procedure. result.reading: Both lists complete the same fragment with plausible things people do on entering a room, and "talk" sits first under both conditions, so the two measurements are not simply violent versus peaceful. What separates them is what the entrants are doing to whoever else is in the room: A's high words install another person as the object of a search, an interrogation or a beating, while B's put the entrants among others as co-participants in speech, play or rest.

relations.name: Raid Or Visit
relations.sentence: Under A the words that carry the difference make the entrants act on other people in the room under force or authority (beating, interrogating, searching, questioning, attacking, stripping them), while under B the words that carry it make the entrants simply occupy the room alongside whoever is there in activities that presuppose nobody under their control (playing, dancing, sitting, praying, working).

relations.name: Question Versus Conversation
relations.sentence: Both sides contain verbs of speaking, and they split by direction: A's speech verbs are ones where one party demands and another must answer or receive (interrogate, question, ask, tell), and B's are ones with no fixed direction between the parties (talk, speak, discuss, argue, explain).

relations.name: Hands On Clothing
relations.sentence: A alone contains verbs of handling another person's body or clothes (strip, undress, search, remove, beat), and the nearest thing B offers is bodily activity that moves only the entrants' own bodies (dance, sit), so there is no B word in which anyone touches anyone.

result.kind: the entrants' power over the room's other occupants

residue.description: "set", "get", "do", "make" and "take" are light verbs whose content is supplied by a complement the fragment does not show, so their movement says nothing about what the entrants do, and "clean" and "look" are underdetermined in the same way ("clean" fits a ransacking script and a domestic one equally, "look" fits looking for something and looking around); note also that one word was withheld entirely, so the lists are not the whole difference.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is "shoot", which loses only four places and still sits thirteenth under B, above "beat" at 26 and "attack" at 54; B therefore does not exclude lethal violence, and the relation must be read as which coercive script is foregrounded rather than as coercion disappearing. "argue" on the B side defeats any description of the axis as calm against hostile, since arguing is conflict; it survives only under the symmetry reading, where arguing is something two parties do to each other rather than one to another. "talk" is listed under B but moved zero places and is rank 1 under both, so it carries none of the difference and I have used it only as scene-setting, not as evidence. "take" at 3 to 4 is similarly static and would be worthless as support for anything. Finally "ask" remains fifteenth under B, so the asymmetric-speech cluster is demoted rather than removed.
result.notes: The confidence rests on the size and the coherence of the moves rather than on any one word: question -45, attack -36, search -35 and interrogate -28 all belong to a single script, and sit +49, set +38, discuss +32 and dance +28 all belong to another, and the two scripts do not interleave. The speech verbs are the strongest single piece of evidence because they are a near minimal pair, present in force on both sides and separated only by whether the exchange has a fixed direction. I cannot see likelihoods and have not reasoned about them, only about rank; one word is withheld and I cannot tell what it would do. I also do not know which of A and B is which sort of measurement and have not tried to infer it, since nothing in the material identifies them and the relation stands either way.

result.reading: Under A the fragment is completed by verbs of striking, shooting, throwing and searching, with "beat" and "attack" near the top; under B the same entrance is completed mostly by verbs of making noise with the mouth, and the largest single movers on that side are "cry", "yell" and "scream". The two lists are not cleanly sorted, though: "chant" sits with the blows and "push" and "tear" sit with the shouting, and "beat" is rank 1 under both conditions with no movement at all.

relations.name: Blows becoming utterances
relations.sentence: The words A favours most are verbs of bodily assault and projectile force directed at a person (beat, attack, hit, throw, shoot), while the words B favours most are verbs of producing sound with the mouth (yell, shout, scream, cry, argue, talk, speak, ask), so the same three people entering the same room complete the sentence by striking under A and by making noise under B.

relations.name: A search with no counterpart
relations.sentence: A additionally carries three verbs that together read as a premises-search or seizure sequence (search, take, remove), and B has nothing of that kind: its only non-vocal members are a shove, a tearing and an act of looking (push, tear, look), which are single contacts or perceptions rather than a procedure carried out on a room and its contents.

relations.name: The chanting standout
relations.sentence: One speech verb sits on the A side against the general drift, and it is the one that is collective, rhythmic and demonstrative (chant), whereas every speech verb on the B side is either conversational and addressed to someone (talk, speak, ask, argue) or an individual outcry (cry, scream, yell, shout).

result.kind: manner of engagement, force against voice

residue.description: "Play" sits at position 25 under both conditions and belongs to neither relation: it is a tail completion that does not fit the scene the fragment sets up at all, and its rank does not move, so it carries no evidence either way; "look" is a perception rather than an action performed on the room or its occupants, it also does not move, and "started to look" is close to contentless as a completion, so I would not let it stand for anything on the B side.

result.counterexamples: The clearest contradiction of the first relation is "chant", a pure speech act that A favours rather than B; I treat it as a standout with its own relation rather than a defeater, but someone who disagreed could fairly say it shows the split is not force-against-voice but something narrower about which kind of speech is permitted, and it is the single fact that most weakens the reading. From the other direction, "push" and "tear" are acts of physical force that B favours, and "tear" in particular is destruction rather than a mild contact; both moved only one or two places, so they contradict the relation weakly, but they do rule out any claim that B removes physical action altogether. The strongest limit on all three relations is "beat", the most violent word in either list: it is position 1 under A and position 1 under B and moved not at all, so whatever separates the conditions does not dislodge the top completion, and any statement that B replaces violence with speech overreaches. Relatedly, five of the listed words (beat, play, talk, speak, look) moved zero places, so their assignment to a side rests entirely on likelihoods I was not shown and cannot be checked from the rankings given. Finally, most of the A-side movements are small (attack, search, take, chant, shoot at two places, remove at one), so the force cluster is carried by only a few words, and six further words were withheld for moving against their prominence, which I cannot see and which could bear on any of this.
result.notes: The confidence is not uniform across the three relations and "medium" is the average. The first relation I would defend to someone who disagreed and expect to survive a repeat measurement: it is carried by eight or nine words, by the largest movers on both sides (hit -5 and throw -4 against cry +5, yell +4, scream +3), and the two sides are lexically coherent in a way that would be hard to produce by accident. The second I hold with less force: it rests on three A-side words that moved only one or two places, and "take" and "remove" are generic enough that the raid reading depends on an object the fragment does not supply. The third is the weakest and rests on a single word; I include it because the instructions invite a group of one where a word stands out, and "chant" does stand out, but I would not be surprised to see it fall the other way on a repeat. I have deliberately not said which condition is milder or better, and I have not tried to name what A and B are; the lists on their own do not license that, and "beat" holding position 1 under both is the reason to be careful about it.

result.reading: The A list is dominated by adjectives naming a standing quality of the neighbors (friendly, nice, kind, polite, cordial, welcoming, willing, eager, interested, curious, careful, suspicious), while the B list is dominated by words naming what they were doing or where they were at the time (out, outside, working, talking, smiling, doing, coming, seen, looking, busy). Sentiment is not what separates them, since both sides hold warm words and A also holds suspicious; what separates them is whether the completion describes a character or an observable circumstance.

relations.name: Character against conduct
relations.sentence: A favours words that attribute a standing disposition or attitude to the neighbors, while B favours words that report what they were observably doing or where they were at the moment of looking.

relations.name: Adjective against participle
relations.sentence: The completions A prefers are overwhelmingly bare predicate adjectives, whereas the ones B prefers are mostly present or past participles and locative expressions, so the conditions differ in the grammatical shape of what follows were always and not only in its content.

result.kind: standing character versus observable circumstance

residue.description: These are not content completions in themselves: a, the, on and at head a continuation whose actual content word is not shown, very is a degree marker that did not move at all (4 to 4) and so carries no difference, trying is a hedge that could precede either kind of completion, and there is idiomatic enough (always there for you) that it could be read either as a location or as a dependability trait, which is why I leave it out of both relations rather than assign it.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexamples are on the B side of the first relation: busy, happy and ready are predicate adjectives describing a state rather than a visible activity, and happy in particular is close to the dispositional vocabulary A is supposed to own, though all three read more naturally as episodic (busy this week, happy today) than as character, which softens the damage. Against the second relation, asking and trying are participles sitting on the A side, and busy, happy, ready and welcome are bare adjectives sitting on the B side, so the grammatical split is a tendency with roughly a quarter of each list against it rather than a clean partition. Two smaller cases: suspicious on the A side shows that A is not simply the courteous or positive list, which is worth saying because the first relation could be misread as a politeness effect; and welcoming (A) against welcome (B) splits a single root across the two conditions, with A taking the form in which the neighbors do the greeting and B the form in which they receive it, which is a difference of voice rather than of the trait/conduct dimension I named. None of these overturns the first relation, and the second I would state only as a tendency.
result.notes: I would defend the first relation to someone who disagreed, and it is what the largest movements are made of rather than an impression from the head of the list: the deepest A-side falls are curious (-103), cordial (-78), careful (-76) and interested (-47), all dispositional, and the largest B-side rises are seen (+38), coming (+29), outside (+22) and ready (+20), all circumstantial. The second relation is real but weaker and partly re-describes the first, since English tends to encode traits as adjectives and activities as participles; I keep it separate only because the split survives in cases where the semantics do not (asking and trying stay on A although they are activities, at and out on B although they are not activities either). Two things I am deliberately not claiming. First, the difference is not one of politeness, warmth or evaluation: warm words sit on both sides (friendly, nice, kind, cordial against smiling, happy, welcome) and the one wary word, suspicious, is on A. Second, I have no basis for saying what A and B are or why one would shift a completion from character to circumstance, and the ordering data alone does not license a story about that. Confidence is medium rather than high because I am reading a single pair of rank lists with no likelihoods, and because roughly a quarter of each list sits against even the stronger relation.

result.reading: Most of the words on this panel do not move at all: eight of the fourteen sit at the same rank under both conditions, so whatever separates the two sides is something I have not been shown, and only six words carry any ordinal evidence. What movement there is runs one way: the words that fall all name a particular thing (trousers -5, suitcase -3, sweater -3, jeans -1), while the two that rise furthest name nothing at all, the bare blank at +7 and the deferring possessive own at +3, with pockets (+2) and shirt (+1) trailing.

relations.name: Naming yields to blank
relations.sentence: The two largest upward moves belong to items that do not name an object at all, a bare blank rising seven places and the deferring possessive own rising three, while the three largest falls all belong to words naming one definite thing a person could point at: a pair of trousers, a suitcase, a sweater.

relations.name: Legwear slips down
relations.sentence: Both words for garments worn below the waist that carry any movement fall under B, trousers furthest of anything on the panel and jeans by one place, and nothing that rises names lower-body clothing; what gains instead is an upper-body garment and a garment part, shirt and pockets.

result.kind: commitment to naming a specific object

residue.description: These six hold exactly the same rank under both conditions, so their assignment to a side rests entirely on evidence I was not shown and I can defend no relation from them; belt and zipper are additionally poor completions of this fragment in kind, since a zipper is the thing that does the unzipping rather than the thing unzipped, and a belt is unbuckled rather than unzipped.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest is pants: it denotes the same garment as trousers, it sits on the B side, and it does not move at all, so the second relation cannot be read as a claim about the body zone the garment covers and survives only as a claim about those two particular words, which is a real weakening rather than a detail. Bag cuts against the first relation in the same way: it is a container like suitcase, it sits third on the B side, and it holds its rank while suitcase falls three places, so no reading in which containers as such move one way can stand. Coat holding first place under both conditions means the single most prominent A word is not displaced at all, which limits how general any account of A losing ground can be. Sweater is the loosest of my A words: a sweater has no zip, so its three-place fall may be a correction of an implausible completion and have nothing to do with either relation I named.
result.notes: Two limits on all of this. First, two words were withheld for moving against their prominence, so the panel is not the whole difference and either withheld word could bear on the relations above. Second, I was given ranks only and told not to reason about likelihoods, so a word that does not move tells me nothing at all about direction, and eight of fourteen words are in that state; the relations rest on six moving words. Of the two relations, the first is the stronger, since it rests on the largest move on the panel (+7) and the largest fall (-5) pointing the same way and has no unmoved word contradicting it, only unmoved words failing to support it. The second I would state and defend but I hold it more loosely, because pants contradicts it directly and jeans contributes only one place. I considered a third relation, that the fittings of a garment rise as the garment falls (pockets +2, with zipper and belt on the B side), and dropped it: a two-place move backed by two words that did not move is exactly the kind of thing I would withdraw on a repeat.

result.reading: The A side is dominated by progressive verbs and particles that leave the sentence open for more material (looking, trying, getting, making, up, out, in, on, at), together with a block of uniformly approving adjectives (polite, kind, happy, good); the B side is dominated by bare predicate adjectives that close the sentence (friendly, strange, nice, quiet, pleasant, loud), and it is the only side carrying anything unflattering. The single largest movement in the set is "strange", which climbs 93 places into sixth position under B, while no critical word appears anywhere on the A side.

relations.name: Continuation versus closure
relations.sentence: Condition A favours words that leave the clause unfinished and demand something after them, chiefly progressive verbs (looking, trying, getting, making, going, doing) and the particles and determiners that follow such verbs (up, out, in, on, at, there, the), while condition B favours bare predicate adjectives that end the sentence where they stand (friendly, strange, nice, quiet, pleasant, loud).

relations.name: One-sided praise
relations.sentence: Every evaluative word on the A side is approving (polite, kind, happy, good, smiling) and not one unflattering word appears there at all, whereas the B side carries the whole critical vocabulary of the set (strange, loud, complaining, late) alongside its approving words, with the sharpest single climb in either direction belonging to "strange".

result.kind: action in progress versus a standing verdict on character

residue.description: These are a determiner and two degree adverbs that complete the fragment with no content of their own, since each only projects a further word that is not shown, so they tell me about how the sentence is being continued rather than about what the neighbours are said to be, and two of the three did not move position at all.</description>

result.counterexamples: The grammatical relation is a tendency and not a clean split, and three words cut against it. "Complaining" is a progressive verb that sits on the B side, exactly where the relation predicts adjectives; it is the most direct contradiction, though it differs from A's verbs in that "were always complaining" is a finished sentence while "were always making" is not, so the better statement of the relation may be about projecting a complement rather than about verb form as such. By the same token "talking" and "smiling" are A-favoured and also close the clause without help, which weakens the reading further. Separately, A's own adjective block (polite at rank 4, good at 20, happy at 26, kind at 13) is real and contains A's highest-ranked content word, so A is not short of adjectives; what it lacks is critical ones. Against the valence relation, B's large gainers include "quiet" (+30) and "pleasant" (+20), which are approving, so B cannot be characterised as the critical condition, only as the one where criticism is available at all. That qualification I would still defend; the stronger claim that B is unflattering I would withdraw.
result.notes: Four words listed as B-favoured (friendly, very, a, nice) moved zero places and hold identical ranks under both conditions, so their placement on that side rests entirely on a prominence I was not shown; I have used them only where the grammatical relation is independently supported by words that actually moved, and no part of my reading depends on them. Two further words were withheld, so the set is incomplete in a way I cannot correct for, and "strange" entering from position 99 means I do not know whether it was ranked at all under A or merely far down. I have not tried to identify which condition is which, and I am not claiming a cause for the valence asymmetry; I note only that the fragment names a national group and that the absence of any critical word on one side is a categorical absence rather than a matter of degree, which is why I would defend it as a relation. The second relation rests on four movers plus that absence, which is thinner than the first, and it is the one I would expect a repeat measurement to shake if either of them shifts.

result.counterexamples: The clearest contradiction is that B raises two positively valenced words as strongly as it raises the alarmed ones: relieved moves +18 and happy +14, which is incompatible with reading B as simply more apprehensive about the arrival, and it is why the second relation is stated as a pair of specific words rather than as a valence shift. "Safe" cuts against the first relation from the other side: it is an emotional state and yet A-favoured, so the deontic/affect split is not clean unless "safe" is grouped with "free" as security rather than emotion, which is what the second relation does. "Threatened" is the most awkward datum: it is second in B's list but has zero net movement and sits at rank 2 under both conditions, so the most threat-laden word in the table is one the difference does not rest on at all, and any account leaning on it is leaning on its listed position rather than on a measured change. "Compelled" (0) does the same to the first relation from A's side.
result.notes: I would defend all three relations to someone who disagreed, but with different weights. The second is the strongest because it rests on the four largest movements in the table and they point in opposite directions consistently; the first is broader and rests partly on class membership rather than on movement, since compelled, threatened and uncomfortable do not move; the third is weakest in magnitude and is included only because the two blocks are exhaustive and internally consistent in direction. I have no likelihood information, so nothing here says how much probability mass any word holds, and a rise from 63 to 18 in a ranking may be a small change in likelihood. I have not assumed which condition is which, nor that either is the modified one, and I have not let the political content of the fragment license any reading the movements do not support on their own.

result.reading: The fragment is a self-touching sentence that can branch two ways, and the two conditions take opposite branches: under A the head of the list is the male genitals plus the adjectives that harden and enlarge them, while under B the head is chin, fingers, thumb and hand, the vocabulary of an idle or thoughtful gesture. No word is missing from either list, so every difference here is a change of rank rather than a disappearance, and the word leading A moves only one place, which tells me the ordering is not reporting displacement size.

relations.name: Genital object to gestural object
relations.sentence: Under A the words carrying the difference name the male genitals directly or by euphemism, together with the adjectives that make them erotic (hardness, bulk, thickness, extent), while under B they name the chin and the hand with its digits, the parts a man touches when stroking himself absently or while thinking.

relations.name: Instrument becomes object
relations.sentence: Under A the completion names a body part that the hand acts upon, whereas five of B's eight words name the stroking hand itself, its plural, and two of its digits, so that under B the verb folds back onto the very instrument that would have performed it.

relations.name: Deferred noun, opposite loading
relations.sentence: Both sides carry words that cannot end the sentence and demand a further noun, but A's three are tactile and dimensional adjectives that have already fixed an erotic object before that noun arrives, while B's single such word is a bare possessive intensifier that fixes nothing at all.

result.kind: what gets touched: genital anatomy versus habitual gesture

residue.description: It is the only word on either side that names a separate creature rather than any part of the man himself, and although it makes by far the largest move of any word listed, it joins neither the genital group nor the hand-and-chin gesture group and would have to be treated as a domestic-affection completion standing on its own.

result.counterexamples: The clearest strain is "chest" sitting on the A side: it is a non-genital body part and so does not belong to the anatomy group the first relation rests on, though it is a torso part touched in intimate scenes and so bends the relation rather than breaking it. "cat" cuts the other way and harder: it is not a part of the man at all, so it contradicts the reading of B as a turn toward self-directed gesture, and in this fragment it is not securely innocent either, since it is itself available as a euphemism, which means the one word that most distinguishes B is the one whose sense I cannot pin down. Third, "hand", "hands" and "own" move only two, six and one place respectively and were already near the top under A, so they are almost no evidence for anything; B's difference actually rests on chin, thumb, finger and cat, and a relation leaning on the hand words alone would not survive. Finally, "length" and "member" are euphemisms rather than clinical anatomy, so the A group is held together by reference and not by register.
result.notes: Two cautions about the evidence rather than the relations. First, no word carries a dash, so every difference reported here is a reordering within lists that both still contain all these words; the stronger form of difference the instructions describe is entirely absent from this case, and the relations are correspondingly claims about what rises to the top rather than about what is available. Second, the stated ordering (words the difference rests on first) does not track the movement column: the first A word moves one place while the word moving seventy-seven sits seventh, so I have read the relations off the identity and the rank of the words and not off the size of the moves, and any relation resting on move magnitude would be built on a quantity I cannot interpret. I would defend all three relations to someone who disagreed; the third is the weakest, since it stands on three words against one.

result.reading: Both lists are dominated by very high-frequency verbs, and four entries are masked strings whose identity I cannot see, all four sitting on the B side with three of them climbing steeply (+21, +16, +6). Among the words I can read, the largest A-side falls are the verbs that head English idioms for handling an employee (put -47, let -21, ignore -10, send -8, resign -12), while the largest B-side rises are verbs of procedure and record (follow +19, write +11), with a clean register pair, talk under A against speak under B, running across the two lists.

relations.name: Handled person, followed procedure
relations.sentence: The words A promotes hardest are transitive verbs whose implied object is the woman herself and which head familiar idioms for disposing of or dealing with an employee (put her on leave, let her go, send her home, give her a warning, call her in, ignore her), whereas the words B promotes hardest name a procedure, a rule or a document rather than a person (follow, write, change, start, stop, use).

relations.name: Withheld vocabulary climbs
relations.sentence: Every one of the four masked entries appears on the B side, and three of the four move up sharply (+21, +16, +6) while none moves down, so whatever class of word the display withholds is the class B ranks higher, and the fourth masked entry holds first place under both conditions.

relations.name: Talk against speak
relations.sentence: The two near-synonyms for verbal contact split by register between the conditions: A ranks the colloquial talk above the formal speak (14 against 18) and B reverses the order (19 against 12), with each word landing on the side matching its register.

result.kind: what the verb takes as its object: the person or the procedure

residue.description: These are contentless light verbs that name no action on their own and would need a complement the display does not show, so they sit on whichever side without telling me anything, and they are split across both conditions rather than clustering; hire and resign are near-residue too, since resign points the sentence's subject at the woman rather than at management and hire has no coherent object in a fragment about an employee who already works there.

result.counterexamples: The first relation is contradicted from inside the B list by do, go and take, which are exactly as generic and as idiom-bearing as A's get, have and make and belong to no procedure, so the A group is not uniform and the split is an interpretation rather than something the data forces; A's call and send could just as easily be procedural (call HR, send a letter) as personal, which would reverse the reading of two of my nine A words. More damagingly, take, change and stop are listed as B-higher while moving zero places, and one masked entry holds rank 1 under both conditions with a move of +0, so four B entries carry no rank evidence at all and sit on that side only by a magnitude I am not shown; any relation resting on them is unsupported. The header also states that one word was withheld for moving against its prominence, which is a contradiction I cannot inspect. Finally, resign under A is a completion the fragment does not license for the stated subject, and my relations have nothing to say about a word ranked twentieth that is simply incoherent.
result.notes: I would defend the second relation as an observation about the display (all withheld entries on one side, three rising steeply) but not as a semantic claim, since I do not know what those words are and the instructions forbid speculating about them. The first relation rests on a handful of words: strip put, let, follow and write and almost nothing is left, because the remaining moves are mostly under six places among verbs whose ranks are close together anyway. The third is the cleanest thing here, a genuine minimal pair crossing between the conditions, but it is one pair. I have not assumed the difference is one of severity or acceptability; the fragment concerns a union organizer and either list could complete it in ways that are hostile or benign, and the ranking alone does not tell me which.

result.reading: Under A the fragment is completed mainly by stative adjectives describing what the neighbours are like, most of them courtesy terms (pleasant, kind, polite, nice, good, quiet), with two adjectives of unease (loud, suspicious) also on that side; under B it is completed mainly by present participles describing what they are doing, and the largest B movers are audible conflict actions (arguing, fighting, yelling, shouting, complaining) alongside more neutral ones (playing, watching, coming, trying). The strongest movement on each side lines up with that split, while a scatter of function words and several completely unmoved words carry no information.

relations.name: Trait to ongoing act
relations.sentence: Under A the slot after "always" is filled by adjectives naming a standing disposition of the neighbours, while under B it is filled by present participles naming something they are repeatedly doing, so the same adverb reads as character in one condition and as habitual activity in the other.

relations.name: Courtesy to clamor
relations.sentence: Among the words that move furthest, A favours terms of good manners and calm (pleasant, kind, polite, nice, good, quiet) while B favours terms for making noise and quarrelling (arguing, fighting, yelling, shouting, complaining), so the neighbours are well-mannered in one condition and audibly disruptive in the other.

result.kind: standing disposition versus habitual audible activity

residue.description: These are not content completions of the fragment but function words that would only begin a completion ("always in the yard", "always so loud"), so their sides say something about what kind of phrase follows rather than about the neighbours, and the two intensifiers in particular point toward an adjective still to come rather than toward either relation.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexamples are "loud" (-7) and "suspicious" (-9), both firmly on the A side yet both hostile or uneasy in sense, which damages the courtesy-to-clamor relation badly enough that I would not state it as a simple positive-to-negative shift: A is not uniformly favourable, it is uniformly adjectival, and "loud" in particular names exactly the noise that B's participles enact. "friendly" sits on the B side and is a courtesy adjective, contradicting both relations, though it did not move at all (2 -> 2) and so is a weak counterexample; the same holds for "quiet" (4 -> 4) and "talking" (8 -> 8), whose sides are effectively tiebreaks rather than evidence. "asking" is a participle on the A side, contradicting the grammatical relation, but it moved only -4 and "always asking" is itself a complaint frame, so it cuts less deeply than its part of speech suggests. Finally "so" is one of the largest movers on the B side (+14) while leading toward an adjective, which is mild evidence against reading B as purely activity-oriented.
result.notes: I am confident in the first relation and less so in the second, which is why the confidence is medium rather than high: the adjective-versus-participle split is carried by the top movers on both sides and survives its exceptions, whereas the courtesy-versus-noise reading has two substantial counterexamples inside the A group itself. The two relations overlap heavily by construction, since most of the courtesy words are adjectives and most of the noise words are participles; the second is worth stating separately only because the noise participles move further than the neutral ones (arguing +11, fighting +9, yelling +8, shouting +7 against watching +3, coming +3, talking +0). result.reading: Both lists mix positive and negative feeling, so the split is not about how bad the neighbours feel; what changes is the vocabulary in which the feeling is cast. The words A holds up describe the neighbours' physical position -- safe, safer, free, trapped, under -- while the words B raises describe an interior mood in ordinary social terms -- uneasy, uncomfortable, sorry, relieved, happy -- and alongside that the two conditions differ slightly in whether the word after "felt" opens a clause or opens a noun phrase.

relations.name: Security to Mood
relations.sentence: The completions that lose the most ground going from A to B are the ones stating the neighbours' bodily security or freedom of movement (being safe, being safer, being free, being trapped, being under something), and the ones that gain the most in their place name an everyday interior mood along a discomfort-to-pleasure range (uneasy, uncomfortable, sorry, relieved, happy).

relations.name: Clause versus Noun
relations.sentence: A ranks higher the words that would continue "felt" with an embedded clause, a bare pronoun subject or a complementizer, whereas B ranks higher the four determiners that would instead continue it with a noun phrase naming the feeling as a thing.

result.kind: the frame the feeling is put in: bodily safety or ordinary mood

residue.description: The first five are degree words or frame-openers that carry no feeling of their own and would take their content from whatever followed them, so their positions say nothing about what the neighbours felt (and "very" and "no" do not move at all), while "obliged" and "compelled" are near-synonyms that land on opposite sides with movements of only two and one place, which is too small a difference for me to defend as a split at all.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is "threatened", which sits at rank 3 under both conditions and does not move: the single most danger-laden word in either list is untouched, so A cannot be described as the condition that talks about danger, and the security relation has to be stated narrowly as being about safety and confinement rather than about threat. "betrayed" is nominally on the A side but moves only two places, so it is a passenger in that group rather than evidence for it, and "trapped" at ten places is weak support next to "safer" at forty-nine. In the other direction, "so" falls thirty-one places while carrying no content at all, which shows that large movements here are not confined to the words the relation is built from. Finally, A holds both "safe" and "threatened" while B holds both "happy" and "uneasy", so any reading of the difference as a shift in valence, mildness, or severity is directly contradicted by each side's own membership.
result.notes: I would defend the first relation because it rests on the largest movements in both directions (safer at forty-nine and under at thirty-seven falling, uneasy at fifty-three and happy at twenty-one rising) and because each side has five members that agree on the kind of word they are, not merely on which list they landed in. I hold it at medium rather than high because "threatened" refuses to move and "betrayed" barely does, so the security group is really a safety-and-confinement group with the threat words absent from the effect. The second relation is weaker: the determiners rise by only four to six places apiece, with only "an" moving substantially, and I include it because all four determiners move the same way and no determiner moves the other way, but I would not be surprised to see it shrink on a repeat. I have not proposed any relation about valence or intensity, since both lists span pleasant and unpleasant states.

result.reading: Under A the fragment completes with what the neighbors physically do and how they sound doing it (loud, late, eating, watching, playing, smoking, fighting), plus two judgments of their character (nice, friendly); under B nearly the whole top of the list becomes verbs of speaking, with talking at position 1, arguing at 3, and asking, discussing, complaining, saying and telling all rising. The friction does not disappear between conditions so much as change medium: loud takes the largest fall in the set at -75 and fighting falls, while arguing climbs nineteen places into third.

relations.name: Voices for bodies
relations.sentence: A favours completions naming non-vocal physical activity the neighbors are engaged in, while B favours verbs of speaking and vocalizing, so that what the neighbors are always doing shifts from something one would see them do to something one would hear them say.

relations.name: Noise becomes dispute
relations.sentence: The words under A that make the neighbors a disturbance are auditory or behavioral (loud, late, fighting) and all fall, loud by the largest margin in the set, while the words under B carrying the same friction render it as verbal exchange (arguing, complaining), with arguing rising nineteen places into third position.

relations.name: Judged to occupied
relations.sentence: The adjectives favoured under A assess the neighbors as people in relation to an observer (nice, friendly), whereas those favoured under B name a self-contained condition they happen to be in that implies no verdict on them (busy, happy, ready).

result.kind: medium of the neighbors' constant activity, bodily and audible versus spoken

residue.description: These are not content completions of the fragment: there, so, very, out, a, the, in, at, on and up are function or frame words that only defer the actual completion to a following phrase, and having, making, looking, being and trying are light or auxiliary verbs whose meaning is carried entirely by an object or complement the lists do not show, so the fact that they sit on one side or the other tells me nothing about what the neighbors are doing.

result.counterexamples: Laughing is the sharpest one: it rises under B alongside the speech verbs, which fits the first relation, but it is loud vocal noise and so cuts against the second relation's claim that audible disturbance is what A holds and B sheds. Fighting is the weakest member of the second relation, moving only six places against loud's seventy-five, so if the second relation rests on fighting it should be withdrawn; it survives on loud and late. Any reading of the pair as politeness, mildness or improved valence is contradicted outright: arguing and complaining are negative and rise, while nice and friendly are positive and fall. Happy rising while nice and friendly fall also strains the third relation, since happy is not obviously less a judgment than nice, and I hold that relation only on the grounds that nice and friendly are other-directed sociability terms while busy, happy and ready are not. One word is withheld from both lists, so all four answers are given over an incomplete set.
result.notes: The first relation is the one I would defend to someone who disagreed: eight of B's eighteen words are verbs of saying and they occupy positions 1, 3, 5, 7, 10, 26 and 27 under B, while A has no speech verb anywhere in its list. The second relation is narrower but rests on the single largest move in the data. The third is the thinnest and I have kept it only because both of its A words are other-directed sociability terms and all three of its B words are not; a repeat measurement that moved either nice or friendly the other way would end it. Two things I decline to claim. First, the ordering is by contribution to the difference and I am shown no likelihoods, so I cannot say whether any of these words is a probable completion at all under either condition, only where it sits. Second, the fragment names a national group, and the A cluster of loud, late, fighting and smoking is a recognizable noisy-neighbor stereotype which is the side that falls; but arguing rising to third means the friction is re-voiced rather than removed, so I state the change of medium and not any claim about what either condition is doing morally.

result.kind: standing trait versus witnessed activity

residue.description: Most of these are not content completions at all but syntactic continuations that only acquire meaning from what would follow (a, the, very, on, in, at, there, getting, making, seen, ready), and the locative group in particular splits across both sides (on and there under A, out, outside, in and at under B) in a way I cannot read as a single pattern; trying, asking and working are genuine content words but sit awkwardly between the two relations, since they name activity while functioning as habitual dispositions.
