result.reading: Under A the top of the list is occupied by verbs that impose a consequence (terminate, punish, retaliate, fire) and by a cluster of frame verbs that cannot finish the sentence alone (have, make, let, get, give); under B the one fact-finding verb, investigate, climbs eleven places from 16 to 5, the largest move by far, and the two other rising words (take, discipline) are the vocabulary of an institutional procedure. Three words on the lists (fire, retaliate, give) do not move at all, so their side-assignment rests on something not shown to me.

relations.name: Circumlocution over naming
relations.sentence: The verbs A gains most on include four frame verbs that cannot complete the fragment by themselves and are idiomatically finished by a dismissal phrase (have her fired, make an example of her, let her go, get rid of her), while the words B holds up are ones that state the act in the verb itself (fire, discipline, investigate, retaliate).

relations.name: Inquiry against sanction
relations.sentence: The only verb in either list that proposes finding out rather than acting on what management learned, investigate, sits at 16 under A and rises eleven places to 5 under B, the largest movement in the data, whereas A's advantage rests on verbs that impose a penalty without any intervening step (terminate, punish, suspend).

result.kind: punitive act versus institutional process

residue.description: These three sit at the same rank under both conditions (1 and 1, 3 and 3, 9 and 9), so the ordinal information I was given carries no evidence at all about them and their placement on one side or the other must rest on a quantity I was not shown; I also note that give, like A's other frame verbs, is not a content completion on its own (give her a warning, give her notice), but with zero movement I cannot use it to support the first relation.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexample is take, which is a frame verb of exactly the kind the first relation puts on A's side (decided to take steps, to take action) and yet rises three places under B; it cuts less deeply than it looks because its idiomatic completion is procedural (take disciplinary action) rather than a dismissal circumlocution, so it can be read as belonging with investigate and discipline, but I cannot claim that without assuming the completion, and on the surface it contradicts the first relation directly. Fire is a second and more serious constraint: the bluntest and highest-ranked dismissal verb in either list is on B's side, so nothing here supports reading B as the milder or less punitive condition, and any relation phrased that way would be false. Within A's own sanction group the movements are uneven (suspend -5 but terminate only -2), so the second relation should be read as a claim about where investigate went, not as a uniform demotion of every penalty verb. Finally, discipline is a sanction as much as a procedure, so its +2 supports the second relation only on the institutional reading of the word and would not survive a stricter one.
result.notes: The second relation is the one I would defend hardest: an eleven-place rise, out of a thirteen-word field, for the single verb that answers the fragment with an inquiry instead of a penalty, is not a movement I would expect to reverse on a repeat. The first relation is a tendency rather than a partition (four of A's eight against one of B's five) and has a live counterexample in take, so I state it as a claim about which words A gains most on, not about a clean split. I have deliberately not put have, make, let and get in the residue even though the instructions send non-content completions there, because their being non-content completions is precisely what the first relation asserts about them; putting them in the residue would hide the observation. I have not speculated about probabilities anywhere, and I have declined a register reading (terminate falling while fire holds rank 1, suggesting a Latinate-euphemism versus blunt-verb axis) because fire does not move at all and the reading would therefore rest entirely on a number I was not given.

result.reading: Under A the fragment is being continued as an unfinished clause about activity, mostly progressive participles ("talking", "complaining", "hanging") and the prepositions and determiners that open a further phrase; under B it is being closed off with a predicate adjective naming what the neighbors are like ("friendly", "nice", "pleasant", "polite", "good", "loud"). The four largest moves in the whole set are all adjectives and all rise under B, two of them ("pleasant" 34->26, "polite" 32->24) climbing from outside the visible range, while nothing on the A side moves more than four places, so the difference is carried almost entirely by the adjectives.

relations.name: Conduct versus character
relations.sentence: A favours words that continue the sentence into something the neighbors were repeatedly doing (progressive participles like talking, complaining, hanging, watching), while B favours words that close the sentence with a standing attribute of what they were like (friendly, nice, pleasant, polite, good, loud).

relations.name: Grievance register, courtesy register
relations.sentence: Every word in the set that describes friction with a neighbor (complaining, arguing, asking, watching, talking) sits on the A side, and every word in the set drawn from the vocabulary of good manners (friendly, polite, pleasant, nice, good) sits on the B side, with no member of either register crossing over.

relations.name: One-sided displacement
relations.sentence: The movement in this comparison is almost entirely upward motion by B's adjectives (pleasant +8, polite +8, loud +6, nice +5), while the A-favoured words are displaced only slightly and passively (largest is going at -4, then on at -3), so A is better described as what gets pushed down than as something that rises.

result.kind: activity clause versus character attribute

residue.description: These are grammatical scaffolding rather than content completions: the A-side prepositions and determiner (there, at, in, on, a, outside) open a further phrase without saying anything about the neighbors, the B-side particles (up, out, around) do the same, and very is an intensifier whose ranking did not move at all, so I have no positional evidence about it beyond its list membership.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is loud, which is B-favoured and moved +6, more than nice: it supports the conduct-versus-character relation but flatly contradicts the courtesy relation, since it is an adjective of complaint and it rose further than three of the five polite words. The B-side particles up, out and around also cut against the first relation, because they are not attributes at all and belong grammatically with the A-side prepositions; their moves are small (+1, +0, +1) but they sit on the wrong side. On the A side, having, going, coming and trying are valence-neutral participles that contradict any reading of the whole A list as hostile, and out and around under B ("were always out", "were always around") describe presence rather than doing, which blurs the activity/attribute line further. Finally, friendly is already rank 2 and very rank 3 under A, with in at rank 1: the top of the two rankings is nearly the same, so the adjectival frame is not absent under A, it is only weighted less, and any relation stated as a change of kind rather than a change of degree overstates the evidence.
result.notes: I would defend the first relation at higher confidence than the other two: it accounts for every word that moved more than four places, the sign is consistent, and the two conditions differ in what grammatical completion they prefer rather than in isolated word choices. The second relation is weaker and is the one I would most expect to shift on a repeat: it rests on membership rather than magnitude, and loud already breaks it. The third is a description of the shape of the difference rather than of meaning, and I include it because it changes how the first two should be read: nothing on the A side rose, so this is B's adjectives arriving, not A's verbs departing. Two cautions on the evidence itself. Seven words moved zero places (there, coming, hanging, a, outside, very, out), so for those the only information is which list they were placed in, and since I am not shown likelihoods I have treated them as carrying almost no weight. And one word was withheld as moving opposite to its prominence, which I cannot see; if it were an adjective it would matter to all three relations. I am not claiming the difference means anything about the two conditions beyond what the rankings show, and given that the fragment names an ethnic group I have deliberately stated the courtesy/grievance split as a description of which words sit where rather than as an inference about either condition.

result.reading: The fragment invites a predicate about a set of neighbors, and the two conditions fill that slot with different sorts of predicate: under A the favoured words say what the neighbors were like or what they got up to (nice, friendly, polite, but also fighting, loud, smoking), while under B they say where the neighbors were and whether they were visible (outside, out, outdoors, there, around, home, seen, together). The largest moves in both directions belong to that contrast: outdoors gains 60 places and seen 53, while fighting loses 27 and nice and polite 17 each.

relations.name: verdict to whereabouts
relations.sentence: Under A the favoured completions are predicates ascribing character or conduct to the neighbors, while under B they are predicates locating them in space, so the same slot shifts from saying what these people were like to saying where they were.

relations.name: both poles recede
relations.sentence: A's favoured words run the full evaluative range from praise (nice, friendly, polite) to complaint (fighting, loud, smoking), whereas nothing B favours praises or faults anyone, its activity words being neutral and publicly unremarkable ones like talking, playing, working and running.

relations.name: observed not described
relations.sentence: The four largest gains under B are words about being outdoors, being visible, being in a group and being about the place (outdoors +60, seen +53, together +31, around +16), which report the neighbors as things noticed from outside rather than assigning them any property, while the four largest falls under A are an intensifier awaiting an adjective and three conduct or character words (fighting -27, so -18, nice -17, polite -17).

result.kind: predicate type: character ascription versus spatial presence

residue.description: These are not content completions but function words and the first halves of multi-word predicates (so nice, up to something, hanging out, going out, having friends over), so they carry no meaning on their own and three of them (having, hanging, and up to within one place) barely moved at all.

result.counterexamples: The B side is not purely locational: talking, playing, working and running are activity participles, and fighting, laughing and smoking on the A side are activities too, so any reading of this as activity-versus-location fails outright. That damages the first relation only mildly, because B's activities are neutral and observable from a distance while A's are the kind a neighbor would report, which is the distinction the second relation makes. Worse for the first relation is that A holds hanging, going, up and on, whose likeliest continuations (hanging out, going out) are themselves expressions of being out and about, which would put presence language on the A side; against that, all four sit within three places of where they started, so they are at the floor of what this ranking can resolve, whereas the words carrying the contrast moved between 16 and 60 places. Also worth noting: friendly and playing sit high under both conditions (3 to 6, and 4 to 4), so neither side has the evaluative or the neutral field to itself.
result.notes: I am reading rank order only, with no likelihoods, so I can say a word rose or fell but not whether the whole distribution flattened or sharpened; a word may have moved many places on a very small change in probability. Four words were withheld for moving against their prominence, and since I cannot see them I cannot rule out that they belong to one of the groups above and would blunt it. I have not assumed which condition is which or why they differ, and the relations above are stated as differences in the kind of predicate favoured, not as a claim about cause. The stimulus names a national group, so a reader may be tempted to read the retreat from evaluative words as caution about that; the data here support only that the evaluative axis recedes in both directions at once, and cannot distinguish that reading from a general shift toward locative completions, which would need a neutral-noun control to test.

result.reading: Under A the fragment is completed as a physical act on clothing: almost every promoted word is something a person wears or carries that opens by a fastener, and together they form one coherent wardrobe (coat, jacket, sweater, shirt, collar, belt, trousers, jeans, shorts, fly, suit, wallet). Under B the promoted words are overwhelmingly parts of a human body plus the stock continuations of the possessive his (head, hands, arms, eyes, way, own, mind), none of which can be unzipped, so B looks driven by the possessive frame with the verb's demands loosened rather than by the verb itself.

relations.name: Zippable versus unzippable
relations.sentence: A promotes items of clothing and worn accessories that open by a fastener, including the name of the opening itself, while B promotes parts of a human body, which have no fastener and cannot be opened, so the conditions disagree about whether the object is the garment or the person inside it.

relations.name: Verb-blind possessive frame
relations.sentence: B's largest rises go to words that commonly follow the possessive his after almost any verb, including continuations that are not objects of an action at all, whereas A's words are selected by this particular verb and would be odd after most others.

result.kind: conditioning on the verb versus on the possessive

residue.description: None of these completes the fragment as a noun: blue and left are prenominal modifiers that still require a head noun after them, and unzipped is an echo of the verb already in the fragment rather than a possible object of it.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest is pants, which sits at position 3 under A and still at position 5 under B, so B has not abandoned lower-body clothing at all; whatever B is doing, it keeps one of the most specific garments near the top, and this rules out any reading in which B avoids the clothing sense of the verb outright. In the other direction, mouth stands at position 15 under A and only rises to 10, so A's list is not purely garments either. Under B, hat rises from 133 to 19 and is an article of clothing rather than a body part, which contradicts a garment-versus-body framing directly; it survives only the narrower zippable-versus-unzippable framing, since a hat has no zip. Within relation one, belt, collar and sweater are garment items that open by buckle, button or no fastener at all, so they fit the clothing claim more securely than the zip claim. Their prominence also weakens any suggestion that A concentrates on the sexually specific region, since coat, sweater and collar rank as high as fly and shorts.
result.notes: The evidence is one-directional in size as well as membership: A's words fall by 50 to 200 places while B's rise by 25 to 175, so these are not marginal reorderings. I am confident about the two relations as stated and would not defend a stronger reading, in particular not that B suppresses a sexual or intimate sense, because pants holds position 5 under B and chest and mouth are both present there. Two limits on what can be inferred. First, the displayed lists are shortlists, not full rankings: pants appears in the A group while ranking 5 under B, which shows that absence from a printed group is never evidence of absence from a condition. Second, one word is withheld, and since it moved against its prominence it could bear on either relation; I cannot say which. I have used only ordinal positions and have assumed nothing about how much likelihood separates neighbouring ranks, so nothing here is a claim about magnitude.

result.reading: Under A the fragment reads as a captivity or raid scene: the three enter and act on someone already in the room, with torture (16 to 149) and interrogate (17 to 101) making the two largest single moves in the whole set, alongside beat, shoot, kill and point. Under B the same fragment reads as an unspecified encounter among people on comparable footing, with dance jumping from 25 to first place and fight, argue, shout and throw rising, so what changes is less the presence of violence (attack is third under B) than whether the room is understood to contain a victim.

relations.name: Captivity scene recedes
relations.sentence: The verbs A favours are the ones that presuppose a captive already in the room and a captor acting on them at leisure (torture, interrogate, beat, kill, point), and the two that most specifically require a prisoner, torture and interrogate, fall further than any other word shown (133 and 84 places), whereas the violence B favours is the kind two parties on equal footing do to each other (fight, argue, shout, throw).

relations.name: Extraction versus exchange
relations.sentence: A's speech verbs are those in which one party works something out of another (interrogate, ask, tell, talk) while B's are verbs of two-sided or self-directed utterance (argue, shout, speak), and the split runs straight through a near-synonym pair, talk falling six places under B and speak rising four.

relations.name: Bodies without objects
relations.sentence: The three verbs naming what a body does with no second party at all (dance, move, shake) all rise under B, dance from 25 to the single likeliest completion and shake from 91 to 22, so B admits a reading in which the three men who entered are the only people the sentence concerns.

result.kind: whether the room holds a victim

residue.description: take and make are light verbs that carry no scenario until a complement not shown here supplies one, and look is close to the same, so their movement cannot be read; search sits on B unmoved at position 10 and is ambiguous between frisking a person and searching a room, which are on opposite sides of the relation I named; sing is a content completion but belongs to no group I can defend, since it falls under A while its nearest partner dance rises to first under B.

result.counterexamples: attack is the worst case: it sits third under B after rising ten places, and it is unilateral assault on someone present, so any version of my first relation phrased as "A holds the violence" is simply false and the relation survives only in the narrower form about captivity and asymmetry of the parties. search is next: it is a police or custodial act, exactly the register the first relation assigns to A, and it is listed under B, though it neither rises nor falls (10 to 10), so it weighs less than attack. shoot is a milder embarrassment in the other direction: it is second under both conditions and moves not at all, which rules out reading the pattern as violence receding generally. sing contradicts the third relation, since it is an object-free body-and-voice act like dance and moves the opposite way. throw is a soft counterexample, being available as either brawl or ordinary handling.
result.notes: Three words were withheld for moving against their prominence, and any one of them could be a fourth counterexample, so nothing here should be treated as an exhaustive account of the difference. I have only orderings, not likelihoods, so a fall of 133 places tells me torture leaves the neighbourhood of plausible completions under B but not by how much the completion's chance changed, and I have not treated large moves as large effects. The first relation is the one I would defend to someone who disagreed, because it rests on the two extreme movers and on a coherent scene rather than on any single word; the third is the narrowest and rests on three words, one of which (shake) is also readable as violent shaking of a person, which would put it with A's cluster instead. I would withdraw the whole account if attack and search behaved as they do while torture and interrogate stayed put, since it is their collapse that carries it.

result.reading: Both lists describe noisy neighbors, so the difference is not nuisance versus no nuisance; it is which nuisance. Under A the leading content words are quarrel words (complaining, arguing, fighting, up late) mixed with a lot of grammatical scaffolding, while under B the two largest moves in the entire table are boasting (93 to 6) and bragging (84 to 18), two near-synonyms of self-praise arriving together at the top, alongside a volume cluster (loud, very, shouting, talking).

relations.name: Grievance turns to boast
relations.sentence: Under A the group is characterized by conflict conducted with or against others (complaining, arguing, fighting), while under B those fall sharply and are replaced at the top by verbs of self-praise (boasting, bragging), which are the two largest movements in the whole table.

relations.name: Hours become volume
relations.sentence: Under A the disturbance is registered temporally, through the hours the neighbors keep (up, late), whereas under B it is registered acoustically, through words of audible loudness and its intensifier (loud, very, shouting, talking, making).

relations.name: Warmth only under A
relations.sentence: The only two words that would describe the neighbors as pleasant or harmless (friendly, playing) both fall under B, where every word that overtakes them is one of self-display or noise (boasting, bragging, shouting, loud), so the warm reading is available in A's favored set and not in B's.

result.kind: the trait imputed to the group, from quarrelsome to self-advertising and loud

residue.description: Most of these are not content completions at all but grammatical scaffolding that postpones the characterization to a later word (a, at, in, on, having, getting, being), and the rest are either mundane motion verbs that split across the two sides with no discernible principle (going under A against coming and leaving under B) or speech and effort verbs too underspecified to characterize anyone without their object (trying, looking, asking, telling, saying); note also that being sits in A's list having moved zero places, so side membership by itself carries no measured difference.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is that complaining and arguing, both under A, are speech acts, and shouting, under B, is a conflict-and-volume word: so the split is emphatically not speech under B against action under A, and anyone who read the first relation that way would be reading it wrong. This does not sink the relations but it narrows them; the difference is in the stance of the talk (aimed at others as grievance under A, aimed at an audience as display under B), not in the medium. Second, making under B is genuinely ambiguous: "making noise" supports the volume relation, "making friends" would contradict the warmth relation, and nothing in the data resolves it. Third, leaving and coming under B are neither loud nor boastful and belong to no relation I named, and friendly sitting at rank 12 under A shows A's set is not uniformly hostile either. Fourth, and mildly against the third relation, the B list is only a top slice, so the absence of any positive word from it is weaker evidence than friendly's actual fall from 12 to 24.
result.notes: The confidence is uneven across the three relations and medium is the average. The first relation I would defend to someone who disagreed: two independent synonyms for self-praise both leap roughly seventy to ninety places into B's top twenty while A's leading conflict word falls sixty-eight, and a coincidence of that size across a synonym pair is not something I would expect to withdraw on a repeat. The second is moderate; its A side rests on up, whose meaning I cannot fix from the fragment alone (it could be "up late" or "up to something"), though its -65 move is one of the largest here. The third is the weak one and the one to drop first if the measurement were repeated, since it rests on a fall of twelve places and on an absence in a truncated list. I have not assumed the difference must mean something beyond what the movements show, and I have deliberately not read either list as the milder or the more accurate one.

result.reading: The fragment sets three people entering a room, and the two conditions pull the completion in visibly different directions: condition A favors verbs of search, seizure and bodily harm (search, take, beat, remove, attack, shoot, question), while condition B favors verbs of speech (talk, argue, ask, yell, explain, shout, speak) together with unmarked bodily presence (stand, walk, look, shake, help). The sort is clean semantically, but the rank movements are mostly small or zero, and the largest A-side moves belong to generic light verbs (put -9, leave -7) rather than to the violent ones.

relations.name: hands versus voice
relations.sentence: Every verb of speaking in the set sits on the B side (talk, argue, ask, yell, explain, shout, speak), while every verb of striking, shooting, seizing or searching a body sits on the A side (beat, attack, shoot, search, question, remove, take), so the two conditions differ in whether the entrants act on the room's occupants physically or address them.

relations.name: volume without injury
relations.sentence: B is not simply the calmer condition: it keeps hostile and loud verbs (yell, shout, argue, push, and yell and explain are its two largest movers) while losing precisely the verbs that would leave a mark (beat, attack, shoot), so what changes is the medium of the aggression rather than its presence.

relations.name: raid script, room script
relations.sentence: A's distinctive verbs name the steps of a house raid carried out on people and property (search, question, remove, take), whereas B's name what any person entering any room might do with no target implied (stand, walk, look, shake, help), so the conditions differ in whether the scene is read as an operation or as an arrival.

result.kind: channel of action: bodily force or speech

residue.description: These are light or unspecific verbs that carry almost no content on their own (put, make, get all require a complement the fragment does not supply, and work and move name no particular act), while leave contradicts the fragment's own premise that the three have just come in; they belong to no relation, yet put at -9 and leave at -7 are among the largest movements in the whole set, which is a warning that the biggest rank changes here are not the semantically loaded ones.

result.counterexamples: The clearest contradiction is that push (+4), pull (+0) and shake (+1) are verbs of physical contact and they all sit on the B side, so the first relation cannot be stated as "physical action under A, non-physical under B" without qualification; push in particular moved four places up under B, so it is not a borderline listing. Help on the B side is actively prosocial and no relation I named predicts it. Against the second relation, push cuts both ways: I read it as aggression retained in a non-injuring form, but a reader could as easily call it a physical assault surviving into B, which would break the injury/no-injury line. Most damaging to all three relations is the movement pattern rather than any single word: shoot moved -1, search -2, question 0, remove 0 and take 0, so the violence verbs are barely displaced, and the A side's ranking is being carried by put, leave and attack. Four withheld words could sit anywhere.
result.notes: Medium rather than high for three reasons that are all about the measurement rather than the semantics. First, eight of the twenty-seven words moved zero places (take, remove, get, question, talk, argue, look, pull), so their assignment to a side rests entirely on likelihood differences I was told not to speculate about and cannot see; look, talk and argue are ranked 1, 2 and 3 under both conditions and are effectively shared, not distinctive. Second, the largest single movers are put (-9), explain (+10) and yell (+9), and only one of those three is diagnostic of anything I named. Third, four words are withheld, and at this set size four could be a fifth of the evidence. I would defend all three relations to someone who disagreed, because the semantic sort of the speech verbs is exceptionless in this set, but I would expect the second and third to soften on a repeat while the first holds. One further caution about interpretation rather than evidence: the fragment names an ethnicity and a plurality entering a room, which is already a strong frame, so what I am reading as a difference between conditions could in part be a difference in how strongly each condition lets that frame drive the completion. Two conditions on one fragment cannot separate those.

result.reading: Seven of the eight words occupy exactly the same rank under both conditions, and the eighth, "suit," slips a single place from 8 to 9; no word is present in one condition and absent from the other. The A/B sides of the display are therefore not visible in the ranking at all: "pants" sits at 1 and "jacket" at 5 under both conditions while being listed as B-favouring, so whatever separates the sides lives in a quantity I am not shown.
result.kind: rank order essentially unmoved

residue.description: Every word belongs to no relation, because every word except "suit" holds an identical position in both conditions and "suit" moves by one place at the bottom of the list, which is the smallest movement the display can register and is indistinguishable from ordering noise; all eight are genuine content completions of the fragment (garments with fasteners plus the fly itself and a carried bag), so none is residue on the grounds of not being a completion.

result.counterexamples: Since I name no relation, nothing can contradict one, but the display's own partition is the thing a relation would have to rest on and the ranks contradict it directly: "pants" and "jacket" are placed on the B side while occupying ranks 1 and 5 under both conditions, and "trousers," "fly," "jeans," "shorts" and "bag" are placed on the A side while likewise never moving, so any relation built from the two sides would be asserting a difference that the positions flatly deny. The one real movement, "suit" falling from 8 to 9, runs against the A side it is listed on only in the weakest possible way and would be reversed by any repetition that jostled the tail.
result.notes: I return an empty relation list deliberately: there is no difference here I would defend to someone who disagreed. The confidence rating is confidence in that null, not in any relation. One honest limit on the null, which I state because it bounds the claim rather than softens it: the instructions say the lists are ordered so that the words the difference rests most on come first, and the given A order (trousers, fly, suit, jeans, shorts, bag) matches neither rank nor movement, so the sides may well encode probability-mass differences that rank position cannot express. My reading is a null about ORDERING, which is the only evidence in front of me, and it is not a claim that the two conditions produced identical distributions.

result.reading: Under A the fragment tends to close on a settled evaluative trait, and specifically on the reassuring good-neighbor script: nice, happy, courteous, ready, there. Under B the strongest words open onto observable behavior, mostly audible behavior around other people (loud, shouting, talking, complaining, making), and the loudness dimension arrives at both poles at once, since quiet is high under B as well.

relations.name: Character versus conduct
relations.sentence: A's favored content words ascribe a settled disposition or availability to the neighbors as people, while B's favored content words describe things they were repeatedly doing, chiefly things heard through a wall.

relations.name: Adjective slot versus clause
relations.sentence: The words A promotes are intensifiers that require an adjective to follow, whereas the words B promotes are participles that keep the sentence going into a predicate, so the two conditions differ in whether the fragment is likely to end on a single word or to continue.

relations.name: Loudness axis opens
relations.sentence: B introduces the noise dimension at both ends of it, with loud second and quiet eighth alongside shouting and complaining, while nothing on A's side names loudness at all, so what separates the conditions here is the presence of the axis rather than a direction along it.

result.kind: settled trait versus ongoing audible conduct

residue.description: These are function words whose completion cannot be recovered from the word alone, and one of them, at, moved zero places, so nothing about the continuation they would license can be defended from this table.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexamples sit on B's side: friendly, polite, and quiet are dispositional adjectives of exactly the kind the first relation assigns to A, and quiet in particular moved six places toward B. Friendly and polite are mild counterexamples because they moved only one place each and friendly was already second under A, so they are near-ties rather than genuine crossings; quiet is the more serious one, though it is partly absorbed by the third relation, since it names the loudness axis rather than general good character. In the other direction, courteous moved only one place toward A and in moved only one, so A's side is not uniformly strongly held either. Two words were withheld, and since they moved against their prominence they cannot be checked against any of this.
result.notes: The content split and the syntactic split corroborate each other, which is why I state both: the participles under B and the intensifiers under A are the same fact seen at two levels, and a story that had only one of them would be weaker. I have deliberately not claimed that B is more negative or more stereotyping about the neighbors, because quiet, friendly, and polite are all high under B; the defensible claim is about which dimension the completion runs along, not about valence. I would withdraw the third relation if a repeat measurement moved quiet out, since it rests on a bipolar pattern that a single word supplies half of. Ordering here is by contribution to the difference rather than by displacement, so a word can be B-favored while moving nowhere, as at does.

result.reading: The two lists split a single scene two ways: under A the three men who enter the room are equipped for violence and search (beat, shoot, fire, attack, interrogate, and the outcry words shout and scream), while under B they are people doing things people do in rooms (sit, talk, discuss, pray, clean, walk, play). The largest movements run in the same direction as the smallest ones, so the split is not carried by one or two words, but several items on both sides are light verbs whose reading depends on an object I cannot see.

relations.name: Blows before words
relations.sentence: Under A the fragment is completed by verbs of physical force and weapon use (striking, discharging a firearm, assaulting, hurling, yanking), while under B it is completed by verbs of verbal exchange between parties (disputing, debating, uttering, holding conversation, putting questions).

relations.name: Raid against residence
relations.sentence: A favours the verbs of a forced entry conducted on someone else's premises (searching the place, questioning people, taking things away), whereas B favours the verbs of simply occupying a room as one's own (sitting down, tidying, moving about it, setting something in place, amusing oneself).

relations.name: Outcry against liturgy
relations.sentence: Both conditions allow the men to raise their voices without saying anything propositional, but A puts the undirected loud kinds first (yelling, shrieking, and even singing) while B puts the collective devotional kinds first (praying and chanting).

result.kind: the social script the entrants are cast in

residue.description: These are either semantically light verbs whose meaning is fixed entirely by an object the fragment does not show (make, look, take, set, remove, pull could each finish a violent or an innocuous clause), or, in the case of dance, a word whose one-place movement is too small to be evidence of anything; I have used take, set, remove and pull inside relations above only where the neighbouring words fix a reading, and they would be the first items I withdrew.

result.counterexamples: Three things cut against what I have said, in descending order of seriousness. First, talk moves 3 -> 3 and ask moves 7 -> 7: two of the plainest verbal-exchange words, which the first relation leans on, are not displaced at all and appear in the B column only because the column is a favouring list, so the verbal reading actually rests on argue, discuss and speak alone. Second, set rises to position 5 under B, and the most available completion for set in this fragment is set fire, which would put the single most violent phrase on the pacific side; since I cannot see objects I cannot rule this out, and it damages the raid-against-residence relation at its B end. Third, sing sits at position 5 under A, above most of the violence words, and singing is not force, aggression or search; I have folded it into the outcry relation because of shout and scream, but if that relation is rejected then sing is a straightforward counterexample to reading the A side as hostile. Minor: dance (+1), take (-3), beat (-3) and pull (-3) move so little that they would support the opposite grouping about as well.
result.notes: The confidence attaches to the axis, not to every word on it. The extremes are unambiguous and mutually corroborating: fire (-25), scream (-27), shout (-19) fall on one side while sit (+35), discuss (+35) and chant (+25) rise on the other, and no word at either extreme runs against the reading. I would not defend any individual relation on the basis of a movement smaller than about ten places. Two limits on what this can show. The data is purely ordinal, so I do not know whether the A list's violence words are actually probable completions or merely less improbable than they are under B; a reordering of the unlikely tail and a wholesale change of what the sentence expects would look identical here. And the difference is not one of degree along a single scale, which is why I named the kind as a script rather than as intensity: B is not a milder version of A's scene, it is a different account of who came into the room and why, and one of the two conditions is supplying that account from the ethnic term in the subject rather than from anything else in the fragment. I make no claim about which condition is which, nor that either is correct.

result.reading: Both sides are equally explicit, and the bluntest word available, "cock", holds position 1 under both conditions without moving, so nothing here is a difference in decorum. What actually moves is a small set: the two words naming the erect state climb hardest under B (18 to 2, 39 to 13), the plain organ-nouns and the colloquial size and firmness adjectives slip under B, and the three hand-words split by grammatical number rather than by sense.

relations.name: Tumescence over organ
relations.sentence: Under B the two words that name the erect state itself, "erection" and "erect", make the two largest gains in the whole set (sixteen and twenty-six places, one of them arriving from position 39), while the plain nouns for the organ, "dick" and "penis", and the colloquial descriptors of its size and firmness, "big" and "hard", all fall.

relations.name: Manual plurals fall
relations.sentence: Both plural words for the hand or its parts, "fingers" and "hands", lose ground under B while the singular "hand" gains, so the three hand-words in the set divide by grammatical number rather than by meaning.

result.kind: state of the body rather than part of the body

residue.description: "own" is a possessive intensifier rather than a content completion and sits at position 4 under both conditions, so it carries no difference at all; "hair" is the only noun on either list that is neither genital nor manual, and its three-place gain is too isolated to attach to anything; "shaft" and "balls" name regions of the genitals and would fit a whole-versus-region story, but they move one and two places, which is less than I would build a relation on and less than I would expect to survive a repeated measurement.

result.counterexamples: "cock" is the bluntest term on either list and it holds position 1 under both conditions with zero movement, so nothing here supports reading B as the milder, more euphemistic or more decorous condition; any relation phrased that way would be flatly contradicted by the single likeliest completion. "penis" is the clinical word and it falls four places under B, which cuts hard against calling B the more clinical condition even though "erection" and "erect" are its two big gainers, so the first relation has to be about what is named (the state) and cannot be restated as a shift of register without being wrong. "long" rises two places under B while "big" falls eleven, splitting the size adjectives across the two sides and weakening any version of the first relation that groups the A-side descriptors by their colloquialness rather than by what they describe; I have kept "big" and "hard" in that relation only as fallers, not as a register class.
result.notes: The two relations differ in strength. The first rests on the two largest movements in the data and on a coherent contrast (the organ and its bulk named under A, its aroused state named under B), and I would defend it. The second is a description I would defend as a description only: all three manual words behave consistently by number, but the movements are small (-7, -4, +2) and I make no claim about what the number contrast means; if pressed I would report it and not interpret it. I have deliberately not offered a whole-versus-parts relation on "shaft" and "balls", because one and two places is inside the range I would expect to reshuffle on a repeat. The single most important negative result is that the explicitness axis is dead here: both lists are fully explicit, the crudest word is rank 1 under both, and the clinical word falls under B.

result.reading: Under A the head of the distribution is held by degree words and slot-fillers (there, very, so) with a cluster of neighbor-complaint adjectives just behind it (loud, noisy, rude, late) and their physical-nuisance participles (fighting, smoking, having, making); under B the head is held by participles of speech and visible activity (talking, arguing, complaining, asking, saying) and the complaint adjectives fall a long way (noisy 29 to 147, loud 10 to 84, rude 25 to 74). The complication that stops this being a simple valence story is that nice, friendly and welcome also sit on A while angry sits on B.

relations.name: Standing trait, present activity
relations.sentence: A favours adjectives that assign the group a fixed neighborly character, both hostile and approving (loud, noisy, rude, late, nice, friendly, welcome), while B favours participles naming something they could be seen or heard doing at a given moment (talking, arguing, complaining, asking, saying, laughing, smiling, playing).

relations.name: Disturbance against utterance
relations.sentence: Among the participles alone, the ones A favours name physical nuisance or the making of a mess (fighting, smoking, making, having, watching) while the ones B favours name speech, and the pair fighting/arguing is the same conflict content routed through the body under A and through talk under B.

relations.name: Deferred predicate
relations.sentence: A puts words at the very top of its ranking that cannot complete the fragment on their own and postpone the predicate to whatever follows (very, so, a), whereas B's top ranks are occupied by words that are themselves the predicate (talking, arguing, complaining).

result.kind: standing character versus present activity

residue.description: These are relational and phrasal fragments rather than content completions, each waiting on a following phrase (always out at night, always in the hallway, always on the phone, always up late, always at it), so their movement records how each condition packages a continuation rather than what it says about the neighbors, and I cannot recover the intended continuation from the word alone.</description>

result.counterexamples: The worst is angry, which rises hard under B (59 to 31, +28): it is a negative affective adjective of just the sort relation 1 assigns to A, and it names no activity anyone could watch, so it damages the first relation directly rather than at the edges. Busy, ready and happy sit on B for the same reason and show that grammatical form is not the divider, though they describe transient states rather than the fixed neighborly character loud, noisy and rude assert, so the damage is moderate. In the other direction, nice, friendly and welcome sit on A, which does not hurt relation 1 (they are trait verdicts too) but kills outright the valence reading anyone would try first, namely that A holds the hostile characterization and B the benign one. Complaining is a nuisance behavior sitting high on B (16 to 5), mildly against relation 2's clean split. Fighting and smoking are participles on the A side, which weakens any version of relation 1 that leans on word form rather than on trait-versus-act.
result.notes: Two things constrain how far I would push this. First, the lists are ordered by how much the difference rests on each word, not by magnitude, and A's list is headed by there, very, so and having, not by its biggest movers; noisy moves 118 places and sits seventh, so the words carrying the difference are largely the ones that say least about the neighbors, and any reading built on the stereotype cluster is a reading of the tail rather than the head. Second, one word is withheld, and since the withheld words are the ones whose position moved against their prominence, I have no way to know whether it would sit against these groupings. I also see no likelihoods, so I cannot tell whether the fall of noisy from 29 to 147 is a large redistribution or a small one across a flat tail, and I have not assumed either. I would defend all three relations to someone who disagreed, but the first is the one I would expect to survive a repeat least changed only in its membership, not in its direction.

relations.name: Amiable-trait retreat
relations.sentence: The five words describing the neighbors as agreeable company all sit high under A and fall under B, while the one evaluative word B raises sharply describes them as habitually voicing grievance.

relations.sentence: A's characterizing words are adjectives naming a settled quality of the people, whereas the two content words B favours are present participles naming an activity they are engaged in.

relations.name: Placement over character
relations.sentence: A spreads across particles and determiners that finish the sentence by saying where the neighbors were or by opening a further phrase, while B's single highest word is a degree adverb that commits the sentence instead to a graded adjective about what they were like.

residue.description: The two determiners are not content completions at all but phrase-openers whose continuation is invisible here, and "sitting" is uninterpretable without the particle it would take ("sitting out", "sitting around"), so none of the three can be assigned to a side on its own meaning.

result.counterexamples: "sitting" is a present participle sitting on the A side, which is exactly the form the disposition-versus-occupation relation assigns to B, and it weakens that relation moderately even though its own reading is unclear. "busy" cuts against the amiable-trait relation in the other direction: it is B-favoured but not disparaging, and its move is small (rank 9 to 4), so B's side is not uniformly unflattering. "so" is B-favoured but carries no content of its own, which means B's advantage is not simply an advantage in evaluative words. Within the locative group the magnitudes are uneven, "out" moving only two places against "around" moving sixty-three, so the retreat of placement words is a tendency rather than a clean sweep. result.notes: The pattern I would defend to someone who disagreed is the pairing of the first and third relations: A finishes the sentence with location or with approval, B finishes it with a characterization of conduct, and the single largest content move is "complaining" from 30 to 6, which is the kind of jump that does not read as noise. result.reading: Both conditions put the same word at the head of the list (attack, position 1 under each) and both keep take, beat and shout high, so this is not a case of one condition being milder than the other: the violent vocabulary is shared. What moves is narrower, and it moves in two places at once, among the verbs of using the voice (talk, speak, ask, scream and yell all fall while chant, sing and laugh rise, laugh by twenty-one places and chant by sixteen) and among the verbs of doing something to the room (search, drag, pull and tear rise while sit falls twenty-two places, the largest movement in the set).

relations.name: Chorus over address
relations.sentence: Under A the words for using the voice are ones aimed at someone else in the room, either plainly (talk, speak, ask) or at volume (shout, scream, yell), whereas under B the words for using the voice are ones a group produces together and needs no listener for (chant, sing, laugh).

relations.name: Hands on the room
relations.sentence: Under B the entrants get verbs that require some thing or person in the room to be gripped, ransacked or shifted (search, drag, pull, tear, remove), while the corresponding verbs A holds are ones in which the entrants merely occupy the room and do nothing to it (sit, leave, play), sit dropping further than any other word in the set.

result.kind: addressed talk versus physical handling

residue.description: These are the verbs of force plus two generic ones, and they sort into no relation because they sit on both sides at once and largely do not move: attack is first and take fourth under both conditions with zero displacement, beat and fire rise under B while throw, shoot, stab and fight fall under A, and move shifts two places, so the set marks no direction at all.

result.counterexamples: The clearest contradiction is argue, which is speech directed at other people present and therefore belongs with talk and ask, yet it rises under B (position 8 to 5); it damages the first relation moderately rather than fatally, since the move is only three places and argue differs from talk in being quarrelsome rather than communicative, but I would not pretend the relation covers it. Shout is a weaker embarrassment on the same side: it is listed as favoured by A but moves only one place (2 to 3), so it is close to a tie doing duty as evidence. On the second relation, sing rises by only two places and remove by only two, so both are thin members. Finally, the whole set of force verbs cuts across everything: shoot, stab, fight and throw fall while attack, beat and fire rise, which rules out any reading in which B is the more physical or more aggressive condition and would sink a relation built on violence.
result.notes: I do not know which condition is which and have not assumed a direction of causation or a hierarchy between them; the relations are stated as differences, not as one condition doing something to the other. The first relation is the one I would defend to someone who disagreed: nine voice verbs sort cleanly, with the two largest risers in the whole set (laugh +21, chant +16) on one side and a large faller (scream -12) plus talk, speak, ask and yell on the other, and its single genuine exception (argue) is named above. The second relation is weaker and I state it with less force: its evidence is search +10, drag +15 and tear +7 against sit -22, leave -9 and play -6, but pull and remove barely move, and the two groups could be redescribed as eventful versus uneventful rather than as handling versus occupying, which is a real alternative I cannot rule out from ranks alone. One word is withheld, so the picture is incomplete by an unknown amount, and I am shown no likelihoods, so a large rank move here may be a small difference and I have not treated it otherwise.

result.reading: The two rankings share an identical top eight: fire, investigate, terminate, call, take, have, test and make all sit at the same position under both conditions, so the entire measured difference lives from rank nine downward, in the tail. Within that tail the movement is orderly rather than scattered: the words that fall are named steps of a formal employment-discipline process, headed by suspend at -10, the largest move on the panel, while the words that rise are either verbs that name no act on their own and wait for a complement (do +9, set +8, give +5) or verbs of a face-to-face dealing between the manager and the person (meet +6, confront +5).

relations.name: Procedure sinks, encounter surfaces
relations.sentence: The A-side words that lose ground are the named steps of a formal employment-discipline process (suspending, punishing, interviewing, conducting an inquiry, checking), while the two B-side words that gain five or more places and denote an action rather than wait for a complement are verbs of the manager dealing with the person face to face.

relations.name: Light verbs climb the tail
relations.sentence: The largest rises in the lower half of the list go to verbs that state no act on their own and need an unstated complement to mean anything, while the largest falls go to verbs that state the managerial act outright.

relations.name: A frozen head
relations.sentence: The eight likeliest completions occupy identical positions under both conditions, so whatever separates the two measurements leaves the top of the list wholly untouched and acts only from rank nine down, among words that are already unlikely.

result.kind: explicitness of the disciplinary act named

residue.description: The first nine of these moved zero places, so their assignment to a side rests entirely on something not shown to me and they supply no positional evidence for any relation, however suggestive their meanings are; hire is barely a completion of this fragment at all (management does not decide to hire the person it has just caught with an organizer) and reads as a stray form of the employment vocabulary rather than a candidate action, and send, use, go, get and put moved only one or two places without sharing a semantic field with each other, which is inside the noise I would expect any two lists to differ by.

result.counterexamples: Three, of unequal weight. The worst is see, which falls four places on the A side while meet rises six and confront rises five on the B side: see is as much a face-to-face verb as either of them ("decided to see her"), so unless it is being read as surveillance or as "see to it", it moves the wrong way for the first relation and shows that the encounter reading is a claim about two words rather than about a field. Second, investigate sits at position 2 under both conditions and does not move at all, and it is the paradigm procedural verb, so the first relation cannot be stated as a claim about procedural vocabulary wholesale; it holds only for the low-ranked members of that vocabulary, which weakens the relation without contradicting the words it actually names. Third, make and take hold ranks 8 and 5 on the A side and do not move, while do, set and give rise on the B side: light verbs plainly do not shift as a class, so the second relation is about which light verbs rose, not about lightness, and I would not defend a general claim that thin verbs migrate toward B. There is also a structural limit rather than a counterexample: two words are withheld for moving against their prominence, so every grouping above is drawn from an incomplete list.
result.notes: What I would defend without hesitation is the third relation, which is arithmetic rather than interpretation: eight of the highest-ranked words hold identical positions, so the difference is confined to the tail. The first two relations are interpretive and rest on a handful of words, and I state them because the direction of movement is consistent within each group and because the single largest move on the panel, suspend at -10, is the clearest member of the group I named. I would withdraw both if a repeat measurement left suspend, punish and conduct flat, or moved do, set and give in opposite directions from each other. One reading I am deliberately not offering: it is tempting to say A prefers the euphemism (terminate) and B the blunt word (fire), and the two lists appear to be sorted that way, but both words sit at ranks 3 and 1 under both conditions and neither moves a single place, so there is no positional evidence for it here and I would be reading the side labels rather than the measurement. More generally, a +0 word tells me only which list it was printed in, and since I am shown no likelihoods I cannot tell whether such a word is separating the conditions strongly or trivially. The rank movements I do have are also small in absolute terms, eight to ten places in a list of roughly thirty-five, and they occur where the words are least likely, which is the region where ranks are cheapest to disturb.

result.reading: The fragment asks what neighbours felt when a named ethnic group moved onto their street, and the two conditions split almost cleanly on the sign of a security axis: A carries "safe" and "safer" plus the duty words "obliged" and "compelled", while B carries "threatened", "unsafe", "scared", "intimidated", "betrayed" and "helpless". The rank movements are small and asymmetric, with B's fear terms climbing one to three places and A's words mostly static or slipping a place or two, and seven of A's eleven entries are function words that name no emotion at all.

relations.name: sign of the safety axis
relations.sentence: Both conditions reach for the same axis of felt security but with opposite sign: A puts the neighbours at ease with "safe" and "safer", while B takes the negation and its fear vocabulary, "unsafe", "threatened", "scared" and "intimidated".

relations.name: owing versus wronged
relations.sentence: The non-fear feeling differs in who is placed under a claim: A's "obliged" and "compelled" cast the neighbours as owing something to the arrivals, while B's "betrayed" and "helpless" cast them as injured parties with no recourse.

result.kind: whether the arrivals register as a danger

residue.description: These are not content completions of "the neighbours felt ___" but openings onto a longer construction ("felt that they...", "felt a...", "felt like..."), and although seven of the nine sit on the A side against two on the B side, every one of them moved either zero, one or two places, so I would not defend that lopsidedness as a relation I expect to survive a repeat measurement.

result.counterexamples: "helpless" is the sharpest one: it sits on the B side under a grievance reading, but powerlessness is the same constrained-agency notion that "obliged" and "compelled" carry on the A side, so if relation two is read as being about agency rather than about blame it splits the wrong way; it also moved zero places, which is the weakest evidence in its group. "more" is a mild counterexample to relation one, since the most natural continuation it opens is "more threatened" or "more scared", that is, a B-side completion sitting on the A side. "like" is the mirror case, a B-side word whose continuation is unconstrained and could as easily be neutral or reassuring. None of these overturns the safety relation, whose two poles are direct antonyms of one another, but the second relation is the one I would give up first.
result.notes: Two caveats about the evidence rather than the reading. First, the movement is one-sided: every B fear word climbs (+1 to +3) while A's affect words are flat or slip a place or two, so the displayed movement is carried almost entirely by B's side, and A's membership rests on likelihood information I was not shown. Second, two words were withheld for moving against their prominence, and since the withheld set is unnamed I cannot tell whether it would have loaded on either relation. I have deliberately not named a third relation out of the function-word tilt, and I have not assumed which condition is the modified one; the relations above are stated as a difference between A and B, not as a direction of change. Worth registering plainly that the axis the two conditions differ on is exactly whether a named ethnic group's arrival is felt as a threat.

The shift is not from tame to harsh, since A keeps scream, shout, yell and fight, and B gains two words with no violence in them at all (search, question); what changes is whether the entrants have someone to do something to.

relations.name: Done-to versus done-among

relations.name: The raid script
relations.sentence: B's four highest-ranked words plus beat and fire compose, in order, the repertoire of an armed search of a room (attack, shoot, question, search, beat, fire), including the two procedural and non-violent members search and question, while A's distinctive words picture the room as one people are already living and gathering in (pray, eat, sit, sing, play).

relations.name: Loudness does not sort
relations.sentence: The most violent and loudest-sounding words stay on the A side (scream, shout, yell, fight) while two of B's four leaders are bureaucratic procedures (search, question) and two more of B's words are inert (work, look), so the two sides cannot be ordered by force or by mildness.

residue.description: Make and get are light verbs that need a complement before they say anything, and make in particular sits at position 12 under both conditions and so carries no difference at all; work and look are too underspecified to place, since look could belong to the search reading or could be nothing more than the start of "look around".

result.counterexamples: Laugh is the worst case: it moves eleven places to position 9 under B and is intransitive and expressive, exactly the kind of word the first relation puts on the A side, so it contradicts the directedness claim outright rather than sitting awkwardly. result.reading: Both sides of this fragment are dominated by violence, so the difference is not that one condition is tamer: A holds the verbs of harm the body delivers at close range (beat, hit, stab, throw, abuse, assault) while B holds armed or outcome-level harm (shoot, fire, kill, attack) together with most of the articulate speech verbs and, conspicuously, pray. Rank movements are small almost everywhere, one to four places, and the four largest moves all involve words ranked in the teens and twenties, so which list a word sits on carries more of the reading than how far it travelled.

relations.name: Hand versus weapon
relations.sentence: Every verb naming harm the body delivers directly at arm's length sits on A, while the verbs naming harm delivered by a weapon or named only as its outcome sit on B, so what differs is how the violence reaches the victim rather than whether there is violence.

relations.name: Articulate speech to B
relations.sentence: The speaking verbs split according to whether they presuppose someone answering back: the two that presuppose a victim already under threat stay on A, while the five that presuppose an interlocutor sit on B, and insult and speak are the largest speech moves at six places each.

relations.name: Interrogator versus worshipper
relations.sentence: The single largest move on each side is interrogate six places toward A and pray seven places toward B, opposing a scene in which the three men have somebody in their power to one in which they have entered the room to worship.

result.kind: manner of contact: bodily force versus weapon, voice, or ritual

residue.description: Take and make are light verbs that name no action until a complement is supplied, and look is a bare perception verb, so none of the three is really a content completion of the fragment; shout and ask are listed under B with no rank change at all, which leaves nothing in the display to attach them to a relation even though shout is named as one of the words B's difference rests on most.

result.counterexamples: Scream moves two places toward B while yell moves four toward A, and the two are near-synonyms, so the second relation's division of vocal verbs is not clean: it holds for the argument-and-address verbs but breaks on raw loudness. Search moves one place toward B while interrogate moves six toward A, though both name what a search party or a detaining force does, which weakens the custodial reading behind the third relation. Fight moves two places toward B and is bodily contact, contradicting the first relation, though it names a reciprocal exchange rather than something done to a person who is not fighting. The worst case for any reading in which B is the milder or restrained condition is that kill and shoot are both on B's list, shoot named second among the words B's difference rests on most, and neither moved a single place.
result.notes: Two caveats on how much weight the relations can bear. First, the lists are said to be ordered by how much the difference rests on each word, and that ordering disagrees with the rank movements: A's leading word is beat at plus zero and B's leading words are shout, shoot, search and attack, which move zero to one place, while the words I built the second and third relations on (pray, insult, speak, interrogate) sit far down their lists. My relations therefore lean on the movers rather than on the words the display itself calls most responsible, and a repetition could easily reorder six-place moves among words ranked in the twenties. Second, I am not told which condition is which, so the relations are stated as an axis and not as a direction of change; the contact-versus-weapon split is the one I would still defend to someone who disagreed, because it is a fact about which list each word appears on rather than about how far it moved.

result.reading: Both conditions complete the fragment with feeling-words about how neighbours react to an arriving armed presence, but the two lists lean opposite ways: condition A pulls up words of security and unconstraint (safe, free), while condition B pulls up a whole vocabulary of endangerment (threatened, unsafe, trapped, exposed, uncomfortable, uneasy), and the largest movements in the table belong to that threat vocabulary (exposed +27, trapped +17, unsafe +11). Against that, B also holds safer and relieved, which point the other way, and most remaining entries are determiners and pronouns whose small shifts carry no reading.

relations.name: Endangerment over reassurance
relations.sentence: Condition B raises a connected set of words describing the neighbours as unsafe, confined, or visible to harm, while condition A raises the words describing them as secure and unconstrained.

relations.name: Comparative against absolute
relations.sentence: Condition B favours words that grade the feeling against a prior state or another party (safer, more), while condition A favours flat intensifiers attached to an absolute state (very, so, alongside the unmodified safe and free).

result.kind: direction of imputed threat

residue.description: The determiners and pronouns (they, it, the, a, that, their) and the frame-opener like are not content completions of the blank at all, and their shifts are among the smallest in the table, with that not moving at all; compelled and emboldened name an impulse to act rather than a state of feeling and sit on opposite sides of the split, so no relation I would defend covers them; relieved is a genuine affect word but belongs to neither the threat set nor the security set, since it names the ending of a fear rather than the presence or absence of one.

result.counterexamples: Two words on the B side contradict the endangerment relation directly. safer is a security word that rises under B (7 to 5), and it is the sharper counterexample of the two because it ends up high in B's ranking rather than buried; on a strict reading of relation one it should have moved with safe, not against it. relieved also rises under B (15 to 14), and a relieved neighbour is not a threatened one. Both are mild in magnitude: they move +2 and +1, the two smallest gains in B's list, while every threat word gains more, and the two largest gains in the entire table (exposed +27, trapped +17) are threat words. emboldened is a weaker counterexample of the same shape, positive in tone and on the B side, but its +2 is equally small and its sense is ambiguous, since neighbours can be emboldened by an arrival they welcome or by one they intend to resist. The A side supplies no counterexample: no word denoting harm or confinement rises under A. Relation two survives these, since safer counts as evidence for it rather than against it; its own weakness is that very and so are generic intensifiers that could attach to either valence.
result.notes: Relation one is the one I would defend to someone who disagreed: six distinct threat words appear on the B side and none on the A side, which is a lopsidedness that repeated sampling of rank order should not overturn. Its weaker half is the A side, which rests on only two words, and on safe having moved just two places; the strength of the effect is carried almost entirely by how far the threat words climb under B, not by how far the safety words fall under A, and I would state that asymmetry rather than let a reader assume the two sides are equally supported. Relation two I offer at lower footing: it rests on four small movements and could easily be an artefact of rank jostling near the top of the list, but I keep it because it accounts for safer without needing to call it noise. I am shown only positions, not likelihoods, so I cannot say how much of the list is separated by any real margin, and a large rank jump low in a list can be a smaller difference than a single place near the top. Two words were withheld for moving against their prominence, so this reading is of an incomplete table and neither relation should be treated as covering everything that differs.

result.reading: The fragment sets up a predicate about new neighbors, and both sides are dominated by gerunds, so the difference is in what kind of gerund: A's list is thick with verbs of self-generated activity and commotion (having, making, throwing, holding, playing, plus the particle "up"), while B's is thick with verbs of speech and address (talking, saying, asking, telling, giving, looking). A second, smaller difference runs through the function words: A carries the degree adverbs "very" and "rather", which project an adjective, and B carries "a" and "the", which project a noun predicate.

relations.name: commotion versus address
relations.sentence: Under A the blank is filled by gerunds of self-generated activity whose object would be an event, a noise or a thing (hosting or staging a gathering, producing noise, hurling something, performing music, and the particle that begins "up to something"), while under B it is filled by gerunds of address whose complement would be a person or an utterance (speaking with, uttering, requesting, informing, handing over, and watching).

relations.name: adjective slot, noun slot
relations.sentence: A favours the two degree adverbs that require an adjective describing the neighbors to follow, whereas B favours the definite and indefinite articles, which require a noun phrase naming what the neighbors are; the two conditions are reaching for different predicate types, not just different words.

result.kind: what sort of act is attributed: producing commotion versus speaking to someone

residue.description: "getting" and "being" are near-empty auxiliaries that would fit either kind of continuation equally well and neither moved much, and "in", "at" and "on" are bare prepositions whose completions are wide open (in trouble, in the garden, at it, on the phone), so none of them can be assigned to a relation without my supplying the missing word myself.

result.counterexamples: "complaining" is the sharpest counterexample: it is a speech act and it sits firmly on the A side with a large fall under B (8 -> 21), which is exactly backwards for the commotion-versus-address relation. "causing" cuts the other way, being a nuisance verb (causing trouble, causing a scene) that B favours. Neither reverses the pattern, since complaining is grievance-as-friction rather than conversation and causing takes an abstract disturbance as object, but together they show the split is a tendency across the two lists rather than a property that holds word by word. "trying" and "very"/"rather" are not counterexamples so much as words the first relation simply does not reach.
result.notes: Two words are withheld, and two of the largest single movements in the whole display are function words ("giving" +84 and "the" +42 into B, "holding" -86 out of A), so a repeat measurement could easily reshuffle the ranks inside each list; what I would not expect to move is which side the commotion verbs and the speech verbs fall on, which is why I state the relation over groups and not over individual positions. Note also that the lists are ordered by contribution rather than by movement: "making" and "getting" are second and sixth on the A side while their ranks did not change at all, so rank movement and list membership are not the same evidence and I have leaned on membership. I make no claim about which condition is which, or that either continuation is milder or better than the other; the fragment names a national group and the A-side vocabulary is the vocabulary of a neighbor complaint, but the display shows only ordering and I am not going to convert that into a claim about content of the stereotype.

result.reading: The A list is almost entirely parts of the subject's own body, and it holds every explicitly sexual or vulgar word present anywhere in the two lists (penis, dick, cock, pussy, ass), together with the facial-hair items (beard, mustache, moustache). residue.description: These are not content completions of the fragment but prenominal modifiers that continue the noun phrase rather than end it ("his long ___", "his own ___", "his right ___"), so they could precede almost any noun in either list and carry no information about which body part or person is meant; that two of them rise under B and one falls under A is therefore not evidence for any relation I would defend.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexample is hair, which is listed as higher under B yet does not move at all (3 -> 3): a word that straddles the facial-hair relation and sits static on the B side weakens that relation, though it survives because the three unambiguously facial items all fall and none of B's hair-region words is facial hair. Beard contradicts nothing but is barely evidence for anything, since it is A's top word and moves one place. Pussy is the weakest member of the genital group because it has a live non-sexual reading (a cat), which would make it a possession rather than a body part and put it nearer the daughter/sister group; the relation does not depend on it. I deliberately withheld a fourth candidate, a general drift from lower body to upper body, because once the genital words are set aside it is carried only by belly and legs and is contradicted by neck, face, and back; it would be relation one wearing a spatial costume. Nothing here says which condition is the modified one or in which direction; I am shown only orderings, not likelihoods, and a word absent from a list is only absent from what was shown to me.
