result.reading: Under A the completions cluster tightly into a raid or interrogation script (beat, hit, kick, attack, search, interrogate, tie, undress, tear, throw, shout), while the words that rise under B are mostly ordinary things people do in a room together: sit, dance, talk, speak, pray, play, argue, look. The largest movements run the same way (hit -74, kick -60 against sit +70, dance +41), so the split is not carried by a few marginal words; the awkward exceptions are strip, kill and cut, which are coercive or violent and yet rise under B.

relations.name: Raid versus occupancy
relations.sentence: Under A the fragment is completed with verbs that cast the three people as an assault or search party entering someone else's room, striking, restraining, stripping and questioning an implied occupant, whereas under B it is completed with verbs for people merely being in a room, sitting, dancing, praying, playing, looking and talking among themselves.

relations.name: Needs a human object
relations.sentence: Nearly every word A favours is a transitive verb whose object must be a person or a person's body, so the completion presupposes a victim already in the room, while the words that rise most under B are intransitive activity verbs that need no object at all and leave whether anyone else is present entirely open.

relations.name: Directed versus mutual speech
relations.sentence: Both conditions favour verbs of speaking, but A's are one-directional acts performed on somebody (questioning, demanding, raising the voice at a person) while B's are jointly performed by the three subjects with each other, including the conflictual one, so that conflict as such is not what separates the conditions.

result.kind: the role the subject is cast in, intruder acting on a body or occupant of the room

residue.description: These are light or bleached verbs that say almost nothing on their own and are really waiting for a particle or complement (take something, make something, set up, get in), so their movement toward B is not evidence about what sort of scene is being described; move is borderline, since it reads as an ordinary intransitive but could equally head an unfinished phrase.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest contradiction is strip, which rises under B (20 to 13) while undress (7 to 15) and remove (8 to 16) fall, even though all three belong to the same forced-stripping or strip-search script; that is a split inside a single scenario and cannot be explained away by magnitude, so it is a genuine dent in the first two relations. Kill is the next problem: it is the most extreme assault verb in the set and it moves toward B, which flatly contradicts any reading of the split as violence against non-violence. Its movement is small (28 to 25) and it stays deep in both rankings, as does cut (23 to 22), so I read the relation as being about a raid-on-occupants script rather than about violence in general, but that is a narrowing forced on me by these words rather than something the split itself shows. Pull, also a plausible verb of manhandling, rises under B for the same reason cut does and is weaker evidence because it is nearly bleached. Against these, no word from the core assault group (beat, hit, kick, attack) appears on the B side at all.
result.notes: The first relation is the one I would defend to someone who disagreed: twelve of the thirteen A-favoured words fit the raid or detention script, the largest B risers (sit +70, dance +41, play, argue) are ordinary occupancy, and the two biggest fallers under B (hit -74, kick -60) are the plainest assault verbs. The second relation is not the first one dressed up: it is a grammatical dimension, argument structure, rather than a semantic field, and it is what makes strip, kill and cut awkward for me rather than convenient. The third is offered on a small set but earns its place by explaining argue, which would otherwise look like a counterexample. One word was withheld by the procedure, and since I do not know which, any of these relations could be slightly differently shaped; that does not affect the direction. I have said nothing about likelihoods, only about rank order and about which words appear on which side at all.

result.reading: Under A the strongest movers are deontic words — compelled, obliged, obligated, and their negation free — so "felt" is being taken as introducing a state of constraint or release, with "threatened" on top; under B those fall away by fifty to eighty places and are replaced by emotion words (sad, shocked, hurt, concerned, sorry, uneasy, unsafe) rising by comparable amounts. A second, quieter difference runs through the function words: A prefers continuations that open a clause (that, it, they), B prefers ones that open a noun phrase (a, their, something).

relations.name: Duty displaced by feeling
relations.sentence: Under A the fragment is completed by words naming a state of obligation or its release (compelled, obliged, obligated, free), and under B those same slots are taken by words naming an emotional state (sorry, sad, hurt, shocked, concerned, uneasy, unsafe), with the deontic words falling fifty to eighty places and the emotion words rising by comparable amounts.

relations.name: Endangered self, fellow feeling
relations.sentence: A's one affective word puts the neighbours in the position of a target (threatened), while the words B raises furthest include several whose natural object is someone else's situation rather than one's own safety (sorry, sad, concerned, hurt), so the feeling is redirected from what is being done to the neighbours toward what is happening to the people who arrived.

relations.name: Clause against noun phrase
relations.sentence: The A list's grammatical words open a subordinate clause after "felt" (felt that, felt it, felt they), while B's open a noun phrase (felt a, felt their, felt something), so the two conditions differ in what syntactic shape the completion is heading toward and not only in which state is named.

result.kind: the kind of state the verb introduces: obligation versus emotion

residue.description: It sits on the A side but moved a single place (3 to 4), which is no difference worth reading, and as a bare determiner it heads a noun phrase the list never shows, so it carries no content of its own and does not belong to the clause-versus-noun-phrase relation either, since a determiner is compatible with both conditions' preferences.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is "threatened" itself: it is the top A word but sits at rank 2 under B, so B has not dropped the danger reading at all, and any claim that A frames the scene as menace while B frames it as feeling is false as an exclusive claim — at most B adds a register rather than replacing one. "unsafe" cuts the same way from the other side: it is a danger word that B favours (25 to 11), so danger is not a property of the A condition. "free" contradicts the direction, though not the dimension, of the first relation: it is the release from obligation rather than the imposition of it, so relation one should be read as the deontic axis being available under A and not as A imposing duty. For the second relation, "shocked" (+71) and "hurt" (+66) are the two largest B risers and are most naturally read as the neighbours' own distress rather than as feeling on anyone's behalf, which leaves that relation resting mainly on sorry, sad and concerned; I would defend it, but less firmly than the other two. Finally, one word is withheld, so every list here is incomplete by an unknown amount.
result.notes: Only ranks are given, so all of this is about ordering and none of it about how likely any completion is; a word can move eighty places while both conditions treat it as remote. The first and third relations I would keep if the measurement were repeated: the deontic block moves as a block, and the function-word split is structural rather than semantic and so is unlikely to be an artifact of which particular emotion words happened to be sampled. The second relation is the one I would expect to shift, because "sorry", "hurt" and "shocked" are all ambiguous as to whose state they describe. relations.name: Garment class over surface attribute
relations.sentence: Among the words that are adjectives or attributive nouns rather than garments in themselves, the ones naming a color or a material fall under B (blue, leather, with black unmoved) while the ones naming a kind or cut of trouser rise (cargo, khaki, trouser).

relations.name: Phrase left open
relations.sentence: Several of B's risers are bound or attributive forms that cannot end the sentence and require a further head noun (trouser, cargo, khaki, uniform), whereas A's side is weighted toward words that close the noun phrase where they stand (boxers, clothes, bag, tent, briefs).

result.kind: which layer of dress is named, outer and utilitarian versus next-to-skin and sensory

residue.description: zipper is not a garment but a restatement of the verb, making the completion circular rather than contentful; bag and backpack are containers rather than clothing and one sits on each side, so they cancel; and black, pants and jeans held position, contributing nothing to the difference either way.

result.counterexamples: The clearest damage is to the first relation: shirt (-5), jacket (-3) and suit (-2) are outer torso garments and all fall, and suit in particular should have risen with uniform if the movement were toward formal or occupational outerwear. The underwear side of that relation rests almost entirely on boxers (-11), since briefs, fly, flies and shorts each move only one or two places, which is close to nothing. Against the second relation, khaki is as much a color word as blue and rises (+9) where blue falls furthest of anything (-13); I read khaki as a trouser type rather than a color, but that reading is chosen to fit the relation rather than forced by the data. Against the third, blue and leather are also modifiers demanding a head noun and they fall hardest, so wanting a following word cannot by itself be what B favors.
result.notes: The mass of the difference is carried by five words: overcoat and trouser rising far more than anything else, and blue, boxers and leather falling most. Any reading built from the small movements (the one- and two-place shifts) is reading noise, and I have kept those words out of the load-bearing part of each relation. I would defend that something moves outward, away from underwear and from the innuendo of tent, toward named outer layers; I would not defend a sharper claim about formality or explicitness, since suit, shirt and jacket fall.

result.reading: Both conditions complete this fragment violently: under A the top of the ranking is already beat (1), talk (2), shoot (3), pray (4), attack (5), and under B it is attack (1), throw (2), beat (3), shoot (4). What changes is not that violence enters but that the ordinary alternatives collapse and the violence vocabulary is re-sorted, with sharp instrumented acts (slit +168, stab +76, cut, kill) climbing past blunt or generic ones (torture -22, hit -21), while the everyday things a person might do on entering a room (look -48, ask -37, clean -36, work, search, play) are the heaviest fallers. No word carries a dash, so every difference here is positional rather than a word appearing or vanishing.

relations.name: Ordinary business evacuated
relations.sentence: The verbs describing what people unremarkably do on entering a room -- looking, asking, cleaning, working, searching, playing -- are the six largest non-violent fallers under B, so that condition B leaves the scene with almost no available action that is not confrontation.

relations.name: Bladed over blunt
relations.sentence: Inside a field that is violent under both conditions, the verbs of undifferentiated or blunt force fall (torture -22, hit -21, with beat and shoot merely holding station at the top) while the verbs naming a sharp, hand-held, bodily-specific act and its outcome climb hardest (slit +168, stab +76, cut, kill, destroy).

relations.name: Marking not tending
relations.sentence: The room shifts from something maintained to something defaced or wrecked: clean falls 36 places and work 22, while spray rises 61, paint 47, throw 26 and destroy 21, a cluster that reads as spraying, throwing and breaking rather than as assault on a person.

result.kind: granularity of the imagined act, not its violence

residue.description: set, make and take are light verbs that are not content completions at all without an object, and their small falls track nothing beyond the general reshuffle; smoke is unresolvably ambiguous between smoking a cigarette and a smoke device, so its +38 cannot be assigned to either the defacement or the violence reading; pray and argue move three and two places respectively, which is indistinguishable from standing still, and pray in particular is a heavily stereotyped completion of this fragment that both conditions rank about equally.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is torture, which falls 22 places under B despite being about as graphic as the vocabulary gets, and hit falls 21; any reading that makes B simply the more violent condition is contradicted by these two directly. Almost as damaging, beat sits at rank 1 under A and shoot at rank 3, and neither moves more than two places, so the violence is not something B introduces and A withholds -- it is present at the very top of A already, which is the fact most likely to be lost if the relations above are read as a mild-to-severe axis. Against the second relation specifically, shoot is an instrumented and lethal act that does not rise, and against a speech-register reading that I did not state as a relation, speak rises (+2) while it is conversational rather than an outcry. remove rising 6 places is a mild counterexample to any claim that only charged words gain under B.
result.notes: A fourth relation exists at low confidence and is omitted only because the schema caps me at three: verbs of exchange between people fall (ask -37, talk -6, argue -2) while verbs of unaddressed noise rise (scream +36, shout +4), which would read as dialogue giving way to outcry. I would not defend it, both because shout's four places are within the noise floor, because speak rises against it, and because ask's fall is already fully explained by the first relation. Two general cautions on this reading. First, the first relation is the only one whose evidence is large and one-directional throughout; the second depends on torture and hit falling while slit and stab rise, and beat and shoot barely moving means the blunt/sharp split is carried by four words rather than by the whole violent field. Second, the fragment names a national group and both conditions complete it with assault verbs in the top five, so the honest summary of the difference is a change in texture within an already violent completion set, not an appearance of violence under one condition. Describing B as "the violent one" would be a misreading that the ranking positions themselves refute.

relations.sentence: The affects that presuppose a social bond or a wrong done by an identified other, obliged and betrayed, are the two steepest falls under B (-23 and -14) with intimidated falling too, while the states that rise are ones a person can be in without naming who put them there (unsafe, uneasy, uncomfortable).

residue.description: their, a, like, the and it are not content completions at all and their small moves (+1, 0, 0, -3, -3) are the size I would expect from ranking noise, and compelled held position exactly, so none of them carries any of the differences above except insofar as the clause-opening words were already counted in the second relation.

result.reading: Both lists are drawn from broadly the same territory — parts of a man's body, most of them genital — so the difference is not that one condition discovers sex and the other does not. What moves is grain and phrase position: A's favourites are common, terminal body-part nouns, several of them upper-body and strokeable in a non-sexual way (face, hand, hair, beard, chin), while B's favourites are either rarer anatomical or euphemistic names for the same organ (scrotum, penis, member, shaft, manhood) or adjectives naming its condition (hardening, flaccid, soft, stiff, hard), which defer the noun rather than supply it.

relations.name: Condition before object
relations.sentence: Under B the completion tends to be a word describing the state of the thing being stroked rather than a name for it, so that hardening, flaccid, soft, stiff, thick, hard and bulge climb into the top twenty while the nouns that would close the phrase outright under A (erection, dick, balls, crotch) fall away.

relations.name: The grooming hand withdraws
relations.sentence: The words that let the sentence be an affectionate or self-soothing gesture on the upper body (face, hand, fingers, chin, beard, hair, head, chest) all drop sharply under B, and their places are taken by words that fix the object at the groin (scrotum, penis, shaft, member, manhood, prick), so B closes off the non-sexual reading that A kept open.

relations.name: Blunt swapped for clinical
relations.sentence: Within the genital vocabulary itself the everyday blunt terms that sat near the top under A (dick at 3, beard aside, crotch at 6, balls at 14) lose ground, while the anatomical or literary names for the same region (scrotum, penis, member, shaft, manhood) gain, which is a change of register inside an unchanged subject rather than a change of subject.

result.kind: grain and register of the named part, not its topic

residue.description: "own" is not a content completion at all but a determiner-like modifier that would still need a noun after it, so its fall says nothing about what is being stroked; "pencil" is not a body part and I cannot tell whether it is meant literally or as a euphemism, so I will not assign it; "leg" and "neck" rise under B but belong to neither the state-adjective group nor the genital group, and a neck in particular is upper-body, which is the side that is supposed to be falling.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexamples are dick, balls, crotch and erection, which fell under B although they are exactly the genital nouns a simple "B is more explicit" reading predicts should rise; dick fell from 3 to 22 and balls from 14 to 32, which is bad enough that the second relation only survives if it is restated as a shift in which genital words are preferred rather than as a shift toward genital words. "cock" holding its position points the same way: the single most direct term is untouched, so neither condition is suppressing or promoting explicitness as such. "neck" rising +3 and "leg" rising +12 contradict the claim that upper-body and non-genital parts are what leave. "own" falling 35 places contradicts any broader version of the first relation that says B simply prefers modifiers over head nouns: it is a modifier and it falls, so what B favours is specifically words naming a physical condition, not modifiers in general. "prick" rising +12 cuts against the third relation, since it is slang and should have fallen with dick.
result.notes: I am fairly sure I have seen the axis but not sure I have named it well. The thing I would defend is that this is a reordering inside a candidate set that was already almost entirely genital or body-adjacent under both conditions, not an addition or removal of a topic: the A list has dick at 3, hair at 2 and beard at 5 in high positions, and B's arrivals mostly displace rather than replace. The two extremes of movement are informative and pull in different directions: scrotum +83 is a rare clinical term entering from nowhere, face -65 is the exit of the one word that most cheaply supports a tender rather than sexual scene. Because only ranks are shown, I cannot tell whether the upper-body words merely slid down a crowded list or genuinely lost weight, and a 65-place fall from position 8 into the 70s could be either; that uncertainty is why the second relation is medium rather than high. result.reading: Under A the fragment reads as a raid or interrogation scene: the three men who enter are agents acting on somebody already in the room, and the top of that list is beat, take, ask, play, look, interrogate, shoot. Under B the same three men become people doing something with each other, or with the room itself: argue, speak, sing, discuss, set, pray, chant, chat, all of which either need no victim or take the other two as partners rather than objects.

relations.name: The interrogation dissolves
relations.sentence: The verbs that make the room hold a captive being worked on physically or under questioning are the ones A favours, while B replaces them with verbs of ordinary or ceremonial talk between equals.

relations.name: Who the action lands on
relations.sentence: A prefers verbs that require a second party in the room to receive the action (someone is interrogated, beaten, shot, asked, told, taken), whereas B prefers verbs that are intransitive or reciprocal and can be completed by the three men among themselves (chanting, chatting, discussing, arguing, praying, singing).

relations.name: Ritual reading of the group
relations.sentence: The three specifically devotional or ceremonial verbs, pray, chant and sing, all rise under B, so B is readier than A to construe the three men as a religious or cultural group performing something together rather than as a security detail.

result.kind: whether the room already holds a victim

residue.description: These are not content completions on their own: set, make and take are light verbs whose meaning would come from material the fragment does not show (set the table, make a call, take a seat), look is similarly unfinished without a preposition, dance held position and so carries no difference at all, and clean is a mundane domestic action that fits neither the coercive nor the conversational grouping.

result.counterexamples: Three words cut against the reading and one of them cuts hard. Search rises under B by five places, yet search is a raid verb in exactly the register of interrogate and shoot, so the coercive vocabulary does not move as a block and the relation named above has a defector inside it. Argue rises to first place under B while being the most hostile of the reciprocal verbs, which rules out any softer version of the reading in which B simply removes conflict rather than relocating it between the three men. Play falls under B even though it is benign, and talk and shout barely move at all despite sitting at opposite ends of the verbal register, which shows the axis is not verbal-versus-physical: the top word under both conditions is talk. Shout being nearly static is the sharpest limit on the second relation, since shout is intransitive and would be predicted to rise.
result.notes: The first relation rests on the words carrying the largest movements in both directions, which is what the ordering says the difference mostly consists of: interrogate at -18 and beat at -14 against chant at +28 and chat at +21. The second relation is a different axis from the first rather than a restatement, since transitivity and violence come apart (argue is intransitive and hostile, take is transitive and neutral), and it is the weaker of the two because shout and talk do not obey it. The third is stated only because all three ceremonial verbs move the same way and none moves the other; three words is too small a group to defend, and chant and sing are equally at home in protest, which would put them back under the first relation instead.

result.reading: Under A the top of the ranking is a run of predicate adjectives naming a settled, agreeable disposition (friendly at 1, very at 2, nice, quiet, polite, there, cheerful, good), while under B the top is a run of -ing forms (causing at 1, being, creating, making, doing, arguing) joined by the adjectives busy and loud. The completion is not simply made harsher; it is made to continue as a clause about what these neighbors were always doing rather than as a description of what they were.

relations.name: Disposition into activity
relations.sentence: The words A ranks highest are predicate adjectives naming a standing character trait (friendly, nice, quiet, polite, pleasant, cheerful, kind, happy, good, and the adjectivally used smiling), while almost every word B raises is an -ing form opening an ongoing action clause (causing, being, creating, making, doing, arguing, fighting, giving, lending, letting, putting, acting, getting, trying, seeming), so the sentence shifts from what the neighbors were to what they were always doing.

relations.name: Good neighbor withdrawn
relations.sentence: Every word naming the amiable-neighbor stereotype falls under B (friendly from 1 to 54, plus nice, polite, pleasant, cheerful, kind, quiet, happy, good, smiling), and what rises in their place leans toward nuisance and conflict (causing at 1, arguing, fighting, making, doing, and the adjectives busy and loud), so it is specifically the agreeable reading of these neighbors that recedes.

relations.name: Presence frame collapses
relations.sentence: A keeps high the small words that let the sentence stay a stative report of the neighbors simply being present or observed (there at 8, at, on, in, seen), while under B the only locational words that rise are home and the particle up, which read as the tail of an activity rather than of a state.

result.kind: standing trait versus ongoing action

residue.description: These are function words rather than content completions, though their fall is consistent with the first relation, since a degree word and an article are both scaffolding for the adjectival or nominal predicate that B stops preferring.

result.counterexamples: Three words cut against the grammatical relation and several against the valence one, and they are not the same words. Busy and loud rise under B while remaining plain adjectives, so the shift is not purely a change of part of speech; noisy, an adjective of exactly the disturbance kind B favors, sits on the A side, though its move of only three places makes it closer to a non-datum than a real contradiction. Against the valence reading, lending is the strongest counterexample, rising 106 places and most naturally continuing as lending a hand, with giving, creating, letting and acting all neutral or positive gerunds high on the B side, so negative content is a tendency among the risers rather than a property of them. Home rising 89 places also contradicts the third relation, which treats the locative words as an A-side pattern.
result.notes: The first relation is close to categorical: of the nineteen risers, fifteen are -ing forms and none of the eighteen fallers is one, and the rank-1 word flips from friendly to causing. That is why I hold it at high while the valence reading stays medium. The two relations cross-cut deliberately: busy and loud are adjectives on the B side, which breaks the grammatical split while supporting the content split, and lending and giving are the mirror case, so each relation is tested by the counterexamples to the other. The third relation is weak and I would not defend it; there, at, on and in may simply be following the adjectival frame down rather than forming a pattern of their own, and home moves against it. I have read positions only and have said nothing about how likely any word is.

result.reading: Under B the words that climb are almost all ways of making noise (cry, yell, scream, shout, argue, ask), and the words that sink are almost all ways of doing something with the hands to an object or a person (throw, attack, take, search, shoot, remove, pull). The reordering is small in absolute terms — the largest move is five places, nothing enters or leaves the list — but the four biggest movers in either direction fall cleanly on that split.

relations.name: Voice over hands
relations.sentence: Words naming vocal noise (cry, yell, scream, shout, argue, ask) all sit higher under B, while words naming a physical act performed on an object or person (throw, attack, take, search, shoot, remove, pull) all sit lower.

relations.name: Harm capacity recedes
relations.sentence: The three words that could injure someone in the room (attack, shoot, throw) all fall, and the three that rise furthest (cry, yell, scream) are undirected outcries that injure no one, so the movement is largest exactly where the completion carries the capacity to do damage.

relations.name: Ritual chorus slips
relations.sentence: Chant and dance, the only two words naming a coordinated group performance rather than an individual act, both move down under B by two places and one place respectively.

result.kind: channel of action, voice against hands

residue.description: Move and look are near-contentless completions that specify no action at all, and push and pull are a matched physical pair that shift one place in opposite directions, which is the smallest displacement the ranking can register and so supports no grouping either way.

result.counterexamples: Talk and speak hold position exactly, and they are the two plainest vocal completions in the whole set; if B simply favoured speech over action these should have risen with cry and yell, and they did not, which is the sharpest thing against relation one. Beat holds position too, though it is as capable of injury as attack or shoot, which is mildly against relation two. Push rises under B while it is a physical act on a person, and pull falls though it is nearly the same act, so relation one cannot tell the pair apart; both moves are one place and thus weak in either direction. Ask rises while being a directed request to another person rather than an outcry, so it fits the vocal grouping but not the distress grouping.
result.notes: Two limits on the reading. First, no word carries a dash: both conditions rank the same words, so every difference here is a reshuffle within a shared list rather than anything appearing or vanishing, and I would not describe the change as one condition withholding a word. Second, most of the movement sits at plus or minus one or two places out of twenty-one positions, which is the floor of what this display can show; if I restrict attention to moves of three places or more, only cry, yell and scream (up) and throw (down) remain, and those four are exactly the vocal-versus-physical split, which is why relation one gets high confidence while the others do not. The held-position group is what keeps my overall confidence at medium rather than high: talk and speak sitting still undercuts any account that says B is reaching for speech as such, and the more defensible statement is narrower, that noisy distress rises and object-handling falls, with neutral speech unaffected. I make no claim about why, and I have not treated the fragment's subject as evidence for anything beyond which words are in the list.

result.reading: The fragment is "She unzipped his ___", and the two sides split almost cleanly by where on the body the named thing sits: condition A favours the waist and the closure itself (fly, flies, zipper, front, belt, shorts, jeans, slacks, cargo), while condition B favours the outermost garment worn over everything else (jacket, coat, trench, trenchcoat, robe, vest, costume, clothes). The two words that do not move, pants and trousers, sit right on the boundary between those zones, which is part of why the shift reads as a movement outward from the body rather than a change of vocabulary.

relations.name: Outward from the skin
relations.sentence: Words naming the waist-level garment or the layer lying against the body are favoured under A (fly, flies, zipper, front, belt, shorts, jeans, slacks, cargo, shirt), while words naming the outermost covering, the thing put on last and taken off first at a door, are favoured under B (jacket, coat, trench, trenchcoat, robe, vest, clothes, costume).

relations.name: Fastening becomes garment
relations.sentence: Under A the completion is often the mechanism or the opening being acted on rather than a garment at all (zipper, fly, flies, front, belt), whereas under B it is almost always a whole named article of clothing (jacket, coat, robe, vest, clothes, trenchcoat), so the act loses its specific site and takes an object instead.

relations.name: The noun gets postponed
relations.sentence: Several of the largest risers under B are not completions in themselves but words that would stand before a noun still to come, or that describe the wearer rather than the clothing (expensive, bulging, flying, shoulders, trench, duffle), where the comparable A-side items are bare nouns that finish the sentence on the spot (zipper, fly, shorts, jeans, bag).

result.kind: which clothing layer, from the closure at the skin out to the overcoat

residue.description: These are not content completions of the fragment on their own: shoulders names a body part that cannot be unzipped, expensive, bulging, black, leather and flying are modifiers waiting for a noun, and front is a location word that works only parasitically on a garment named elsewhere, so none of them settles onto either end of the layer axis without importing a noun the list does not supply.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexamples are suit and uniform, which fall under B despite being outer garments in the same class as coat and jacket; that is a real dent in the first relation, though a suit or a uniform names a whole outfit and so implies more thorough undressing than a coat does, which is a reading the data cannot settle. Bag falls under B while duffle and duffel rise, which is awkward: if duffle and duffel are being read as bags rather than as duffle coats, the first relation loses two of its members, and nothing in the list disambiguates them. Shirt falls under B even though it is worn on the upper body, which contradicts an upper-versus-lower reading but is consistent with the layer reading I actually gave, since a shirt sits under the coat. Black and leather fall under B while expensive and bulging rise, which cuts directly against the third relation and is most of the reason it is marked low; the modifier direction is not consistent.
result.notes: The held words are the most informative part of the display: pants and trousers do not move at all, and they are precisely the items belonging to both zones, being waist garments and yet fully nameable, non-anatomical objects. The largest movers sit at the extremes of the axis I named, with zipper leaving the top of A's list (6 to 35) and jacket tightening at the top of B's (5 to 2), so the effect is visible in the head of the ranking and not only in the tail. I have not assumed the difference is an improvement or a softening in either direction; I report only that the completions relocate outward. One limit worth stating: the ranking gives no likelihoods, so I cannot tell whether B has genuinely concentrated on outerwear or merely reshuffled a flat region, and the dash convention never applies here, since every listed word has a position under both conditions.

relations.name: Aim gives way to motion
relations.sentence: Verbs that name a weapon aimed or a person destroyed fall sharply (point drops 47 places out of the visible list, kill 23, beat 6), while what rises in their place is unspecified bodily displacement and searching of the space (move +21, search +16, walk +8, dance +12).

relations.name: Screaming becomes shouting
relations.sentence: Among the vocal verbs the ones carrying distress or intimate address fall (scream -4, tell -14, talk -4) while loud but unmarked public utterance rises (shout +7, speak +5, ask +1), so the noise in the room stays and its affective loading thins.

relations.name: Devotion traded for revelry
relations.sentence: The one religiously marked verb, pray, falls 13 places while the festive verbs rise, dance moving to first and play to fourth, so the ethnic stereotype the fragment invites shifts from a devotional one to a celebratory one.

result.kind: how specifically the violence is aimed

residue.description: make and take are light verbs that complete nothing on their own and their small moves say nothing about content, look moves only 8 places and is ambiguous between watching and looking for something, and argue and attack held position and so carry no difference at all.

result.counterexamples: The strongest counterexample is that throw rises 12 places and fire rises 7 under B, both of which are readily violent completions of this fragment (throwing stones, firing a weapon), so any reading that B removes violence is wrong on its face. Second, shoot loses only one place and remains at rank 2 under B, meaning the likeliest violent completion survives essentially intact while the verbs around it are rearranged; the first relation therefore describes a change in the kind of violence and not its removal, and shoot properly belongs to the counterexamples as much as to the a_words. Third, the largest single move, point at -47, is doing a great deal of the work in relation 1 by itself, and point is ambiguous between pointing a weapon and pointing at something, so the relation would weaken considerably if that word were read the other way. Against relation 2, shout is not obviously less distressed than scream, and against relation 3, sing falls slightly while dance rises, which splits the festive category down the middle.
result.notes: The obvious frame, that B is a softened or sanitized version of A, does not survive the data: shoot stays at the top, throw and fire climb, and what actually happens is that person-directed lethal verbs give way to undirected physical activity and to thing-directed or crowd-scale violence. I would defend the direction of relation 1 and not its tidiness. Two limits on all of this: the input is rank-only, so a 47-place move may correspond to a negligible change in mass and a 1-place move at the top may not, and the ordering is given as already sorted by contribution to the difference, which means the reported order is not independent evidence for the groupings I have drawn from it.

relations.name: Possessor, not object
relations.sentence: The three genitive forms in the set — girlfriend's, friend's, son's — all rise under B and are the largest movers (+91, +67, +15), so that the completion names someone the touched thing belongs to and defers the touched thing itself to a later word, whereas A's favored words are bare nouns that end the phrase on the thing touched (head, face, hands, wife, daughter, horse).

relations.name: Peer over household
relations.sentence: Among the human completions, B favors chosen or non-marital relations (girlfriend, friend, and their genitives) and the male child (son, son's), while A favors the household ones (wife -2, daughter -6, beloved -15), so that son rises and daughter falls and girlfriend rises while wife falls.

result.kind: whose body the touch lands on

residue.description: own, new and little are not content completions at all but modifiers that leave the touched thing unnamed, and they split across the two sides (own +6 and new +3 rise, little -9 falls), so no consistent grouping holds them; dog, cat and baby hold position exactly and therefore belong to nothing, which is itself notable because they are the words that would most directly test an animal-versus-person reading.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexample to the body-part relation is hand, which rises +5 (25 to 20) while its plural hands falls -9 and fingers falls -7; the move is small and could be a singular/plural artifact rather than a real exception, but it does mean the body-part side is not unanimous. Against any reading built on animals, dogs (-7) and horse (-3) fall while pet (+2) and animal (+1) rise and dog and cat do not move at all, so the animal vocabulary is split internally by specificity rather than displaced as a class — badly enough that I did not state an animal relation. Against the peer-over-household relation, wife moves only -2 and daughter only -6, movements small enough that the relation rests almost entirely on the size of the rises on the other side rather than on any real fall; beloved (-15) is also ambiguous between a person-noun and a modifier reading. Against a general modifier-deferral reading, own and new rise while little and beloved fall, so premodification as such does not move in one direction.
result.notes: The absence of any dash matters for how far this should be pushed: no word is present under one condition and missing under the other, so nothing has been ruled out, only re-ranked, and the relations describe a change of preference rather than of what is available. The body-part relation is the one I would defend on a repeat; the possessor relation rests on only three words, though they are the three largest movers and unanimous in direction, which is why I put it at medium rather than low. The peer-over-household relation is stated because the son/daughter and girlfriend/wife pairs split in the same direction, but the falls are small and I would not argue for it. I have not assumed the shift means anything evaluative; the description here is only of which sort of completion is preferred.

result.reading: Under A the blank tends to be filled by a finished characterization of the neighbours - loud, late, friendly, welcome, there, or an intensifier (so, very) that introduces one - while under B the blank is held open by words that require something after them: prepositions (at, in, on), speech verbs (saying, asking, talking, complaining, arguing), and other complement-hungry verbs (looking, trying, ready, getting). Within that shift the same conflictual content largely survives but changes channel, with loud (-74) and fighting (-15) giving way to talking, arguing, and complaining.

relations.name: Verdict versus deferral
relations.sentence: The words A favours finish the description inside the blank itself (loud, late, friendly, welcome, there, and the intensifiers so and very that introduce such an adjective), while the words B favours leave the description to a phrase that has not been written yet (at, in, on, ready, asking, saying, looking, trying).

relations.name: Noise becomes speech
relations.sentence: The behaviours A ranks high are audible or physical nuisances attributed to the group as a whole (loud, fighting, smoking, late, making, having), whereas B raises words that recast the same friction as verbal exchange (talking, saying, arguing, complaining, asking), so the conflict is not removed but relocated into speech.

relations.name: Evaluation drops both ways
relations.sentence: Every word in the set that delivers an explicit judgement of the neighbours falls under B regardless of which way the judgement runs, so the hostile loud, late, fighting and smoking fall alongside the approving friendly and welcome, and nothing evaluative rises to replace them.

result.kind: verdict delivered at the blank versus description deferred past it

residue.description: These are not really content completions of the fragment: "a" is only the opening of a noun phrase whose content lies outside the list, "being" and "getting" are light verbs that say nothing until complemented and moved little (+6 and +1), and "playing" is a neutral activity with a small move that fits neither the noise set nor the speech set.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexample is that fighting, smoking, having and making are progressive verbs sitting on A's side, so the split is not adjective against verb; it is only because these four are self-sufficient predicates ("always fighting" needs nothing after it) that relation 1 survives, and if the dimension were simply part of speech they would sink it. Against the same relation, "ready" is adjectival and rose +7 under B, though it is the one adjective in the set that demands a following infinitive. Friendly (-4) and welcome (-7) contradict any reading in which B is softening a hostile characterization, and they do so decisively: they are the two most positive words on offer and they fall with loud and late rather than rising. Arguing (+7) and complaining (+11) contradict it from the other direction, since they are as adversarial as fighting and they rise. Smoking fell only 2 places, the weakest member of A's behaviour set, so relation 2 rests mostly on loud, and loud is a single word carrying an outsized -74.
result.notes: I can name a dimension that the whole list is consistent with, but I cannot separate the two readings that fit it. Relation 1 (the blank stops being a verdict and becomes a hinge to a following phrase) and relation 2 (noise becomes speech) predict the same ranks for almost every word, and nothing here decides between them; a fragment with no speech verbs available would. relations.name: Doing versus being
relations.sentence: Every progressive verb and every locative particle in the list falls under B (looking, trying, talking, smiling, getting, doing, out, there, at, in, on), while the words that rise are almost all bare adjectives that finish the sentence as a standing trait (strange, quiet, late, pleasant, loud, complaining, busy), so A completes the fragment with an activity or a whereabouts and B completes it with a characteristic.

relations.name: Manner warmth to neighbour grievance
relations.sentence: The explicitly approving manner words fall under B (good, polite, kind, smiling), while the words that rise include the standard vocabulary of a complaint about people living next door (loud, complaining, late, strange), shifting the description from how agreeable the neighbours are toward how they register as a nuisance.

relations.name: The strangeness jump
relations.sentence: One word moves more than three times as far as any other, strange going from 99th to 6th and overtaking the whole block of activity words and politeness words that sat above it under A, so that B's most distinctive single completion is not a description of the neighbours' conduct but a marking of them as anomalous.

result.kind: ongoing activity versus ascribed trait

relations.name: Raiders become occupants
relations.sentence: Under A the arrivals do things to a room and to people already in it in the manner of a security operation (search, interrogate, fire, attack), whereas under B they do what people do once they are simply in a room (sit, set, clean, walk, pray), so what moves is the role read into the three men and not only the violence of the verb.

relations.name: Noise into discourse

Search and interrogate falling while clean and walk rise fits the second relation, but set rising nineteen places sits in the residue and could as easily be a syntactic effect.

result.reading: Under A the top of the ranking is verbal conflict (argue 1, shout 2, talk 3, yell 4, speak 7) and the words that drop away under B are almost all verbs of saying something to someone: say falls 32 places out of the list entirely, with tell, ask, question, argue and speak behind it. Under B the highest places go to bodily force against people (fight 2, beat 3, attack 4) and the largest climbs are undirected vocal noise (cry +29, sing +28) alongside lethal violence (kill +22); the fragment's subject is a named national group, so the axis runs through what three such people are imagined to have entered a room to do.

relations.name: Argument becomes assault
relations.sentence: The verbs of contesting by speaking (argue, say, tell, ask, question, speak) are the ones A ranks near the top and B demotes, while the verbs of striking a person (fight, beat, attack, kill, kick, push, shoot) all climb under B, taking second, third and fourth place in B's ranking.

relations.name: Noise over statement
relations.sentence: Vocalizing that carries no proposition rises sharply under B (cry, sing, scream, chant, and talk, which becomes the single likeliest completion) while every verb that requires something said to somebody falls (say, tell, ask, question, speak), so the mouth stays open but stops making claims.

relations.name: Complement-hungry verbs sink
relations.sentence: Most of what A favours cannot stand alone after 'started to' without an object or complement (say, tell, ask, question, tear, shake, throw), whereas nearly all of what B favours completes the fragment bare (cry, sing, fight, scream, chant, talk, beat).

result.kind: talking-to versus doing-to

residue.description: These are light verbs that are not content completions on their own, since each needs a particle or object supplied afterward (make noise, take over, pick up), so their movement (+10, +5, +1) reports on whatever unseen continuation they were heading toward rather than on any act the fragment names.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest contradiction is tear, shake and throw, which are physical rather than verbal and yet fall under B by 14, 13 and 9 places; if the difference were simply speech giving way to force these three should have risen with the rest of the physical verbs. They are salvageable only by narrowing the first relation to force directed at persons rather than at objects or the room, which is a real weakening of it. The second relation is contradicted by shout and yell, which are non-propositional noise and still fall (-5, -2); their conflictual, addressed character puts them with argue rather than with scream, and that reading is convenient enough that I would not lean on it. Talk rising two places into first is not a counterexample to the first relation but sits oddly with it, since one speech verb becomes the likeliest completion in the same condition where the violent verbs surge.
result.notes: The first relation is the one I would defend; the second and third are largely re-descriptions of the same fifteen or so words along different axes and are not independent evidence for it. I am not told which condition is which, so I state the direction only as A-to-B and make no claim about which is prior, expected, or modified. The three biggest single movements are say (-32), cry (+29) and sing (+28), and only one of those three belongs to the violence relation, so the headline of the difference is as much the collapse of propositional speech as it is the rise of force. Positions are all I was given and I have not reasoned about how large any of these gaps are in likelihood terms, which limits how much weight small moves such as pick (+1) or yell (-2) can carry.

relations.name: Causative middleman
relations.sentence: A favours the periphrastic causatives and idioms that arrive at a dismissal through some other agent or a set phrase -- have, make, let, get, plus call and send -- while B's risers are verbs that can stand with no human object at all (act, try, investigate, hold).

result.kind: specificity of the act named

residue.description: These four carry almost no meaning until the words after them arrive -- use what, hold what, give what, stop what -- so their movement cannot be read as a change in which act the sentence names, and give in particular holds position while sitting in neither camp.

result.counterexamples: The strongest counterexample is that fire and retaliate hold position exactly. Fire is the plainest possible name for the specific outcome, and retaliate names the act's illegal character, so a reading in which B systematically pushes down explicit punitive naming is contradicted at precisely the two words where it should be most visible; this damages relation 1 badly in its strong form and leaves it standing only as a claim about mid-ranked words. Second, terminate falls two places and punish three, while discharge falls thirty-two, though all three belong to the same semantic class -- so class membership predicts the direction of movement weakly and the size of it not at all. Third, discipline rises under B while being straightforwardly punitive, and stop rises sixteen places, so B is not simply the milder or vaguer condition. Fourth, send is the single largest mover (-58) and is also the most ambiguous word in the list (send her home, send a message), so the biggest number in the data carries the least interpretable content.
result.notes: A rival account I cannot rule out with what is shown: every large fall is a word ranked between 14 and 20 under A, and every word ranked in A's top thirteen moves by five places or fewer, so the pattern may be about turnover in the middle of a ranking rather than about meaning at all. Distinguishing the two would need the likelihoods, which are withheld. Note also that B's list runs to at least position 72 while nothing under A is shown past 46, so a fall to 51 or 72 may be partly an artifact of the two lists having different lengths; I have treated a large fall as a real difference but would not defend the exact magnitudes. The three relations are not independent -- 1 and 2 are two cuts through the same contrast, and if 1 fails on the fire/retaliate counterexample, 2 is the version of it that survives, since it rests only on investigate and discipline rising.

result.reading: The words that gain most under B are content completions naming a characteristic or an ongoing audible activity (laughing, smiling, happy, noisy, friendly), while the words that fall are almost all particles, locatives and light verbs that keep the sentence going without describing anyone (up, out, on, at, in, there, going, having, saying, looking). The shift looks less like a change of valence than a change in whether the blank gets filled by a disposition at all.

relations.name: Disposition over continuation
relations.sentence: Under A the likeliest continuations are grammatical scaffolding that defers any description of the neighbors (there, in, up, out, on, at, the, so, going, having, saying, looking), whereas under B the words that climb are ones that close the sentence on a stated characteristic or ongoing activity (laughing, smiling, happy, noisy, friendly, nice, playing, talking).

relations.name: Cheerful sociability rising
relations.sentence: The four largest single gains and the new top-ranked word are all words of good humor and easy sociability (laughing, smiling, happy, friendly, nice), which under A sat mid-list or lower while non-committal placement words (there, in, so, out) held the top.

relations.name: Neighbors become audible
relations.sentence: A second group of risers is specifically about sound carrying from next door (laughing, noisy, loud, talking, playing), set against A-favored words that place the neighbors elsewhere or leave them unheard (out, going, busy, up).

result.kind: resolution of the blank into a named trait rather than a syntactic continuation

residue.description: Most of these are determiners, intensifiers and particles that cannot by themselves complete the fragment with anything about the neighbors, so their movement is about which construction is being continued rather than about what is being said; a held its position exactly and very rose slightly while naming nothing, and late is a real trait word that fits neither the sociability group nor the sound group.

result.counterexamples: busy is a genuine trait adjective and it falls under B rather than rising, which cuts against the first relation, though only by three places and from a position outside the top ten. very rises by two places and is a pure intensifier, another small dent in the same relation. The sharper counterexamples are to the sociability reading: noisy rises twenty-two places and loud three, and late four, none of which are compliments about neighbors, so the risers are not uniformly warm even though the very largest gains are. Those three do fit the audibility reading instead, which is part of why I keep that relation separate and low rather than folding it into the warmth one.
result.notes: The direction of the largest movements is unambiguous: every word gaining more than ten places is a content word describing the neighbors, and every word losing more than ten places is a particle or light verb. That is what I would defend. What I would not defend is any single characterization of the content that arrives, since the risers split into a cheerful group and a noise group, which are two different stock scripts about people next door and pull in opposite valences. Note also that friendly and nice were already fifth and tenth under A, so B is intensifying an existing tendency there rather than introducing it, whereas laughing, smiling and happy move from the twenties and forties into the top ten. I have not speculated about the national group named in the fragment; nothing in the rankings shown separates that from a general neighbor script, and the data give no likelihoods with which to test it.

result.reading: Under A the fragment reads as people entering a room to do something to it or in it — search, look, examine, hit, shoot, scream — while under B the same three people become parties to an exchange: converse, negotiate, discuss, explain, argue, mock all climb, several from far down the list. The movement is not from violent to mild (fight, attack and beat rise; mock rises hard) but from acts aimed at a room or a victim to acts aimed at an interlocutor.

relations.name: Addressee turns interlocutor
relations.sentence: Verbs that require someone to be spoken with rise sharply under B (converse, negotiate, discuss, explain, argue, speak, and the derisive mock), while verbs of unaddressed noise and of inspecting a place or thing fall (scream, yell, search, look, examine, hit).

relations.name: Violence becomes mutual
relations.sentence: Violence is not removed but re-shaped: the one-sided and weapon-borne strikes fall (hit from 18 to 146, shoot from 2 to 6) while the two-sided contest verbs rise (fight, attack, beat), so under B the aggression is something the three do with someone rather than to something.

relations.name: Raid frame to meeting frame
relations.sentence: The words consistent with entering a room to conduct a search or an operation lose ground (search, look, examine, take, shoot), while the words consistent with entering a room for a meeting gain it (negotiate, converse, discuss), suggesting the two conditions imagine a different reason for the three people being in the room.

result.kind: whether the act is exchanged with someone or inflicted on something

residue.description: make and take are semantically thin verbs that need an object before they say anything about the scene, throw and laugh did not move at all, and play falls a long way (14 to 55) without belonging to either the inspection group or the noise group, so none of them bears on the relations I named.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest is the pair hit and beat: near-synonyms for striking a person, one falling 128 places and the other rising, which no reading that treats the fall as being about physical assault can absorb, and which strains even my mutual-violence relation since beating someone is as one-sided as hitting them (beat's alternative sense of defeating in a contest is the only rescue, and it is a weak one). Almost as bad is shout against scream and yell: shout rises while its two near-neighbors fall 67 and 22 places, and I can only separate them by claiming shout is more often shouted at someone. mock rising 93 places contradicts any account of B as more civil or cooperative, though it fits the interlocutor relation exactly. talk falling three places sits against converse, discuss and speak all rising, but it starts at rank 1 and ends at rank 4, so there was very little room for it to rise and I would not weigh it heavily. Finally interrogate and question hold position, which a clean shift from operation to conversation would not predict, since both belong to the raid frame.
result.notes: The first relation is the one I would defend on repetition; the other two are readings of the same movement at different grain and would be the first to dissolve. Note that the ordering is by size of move, not by rank, so several of the largest movers (converse at 127, mock at 107, hit at 146) are deep in one condition's list and may matter less to what either condition would actually produce than their place at the top of these lists suggests. No word is absent from either condition, so there are no dashes here and therefore none of the stronger differences the instructions describe; everything on offer is a reordering. I have not speculated about likelihoods, but I will say that rank alone cannot tell me whether the top of B's list is sharply peaked or nearly flat, and the whole reading would look different in those two cases.

relations.name: Interrogation over inquiry
relations.sentence: The one speech verb that rises is question, which climbs to third and arrives beside search and fire, so the surviving speech act is the procedural one performed by armed men on somebody, while ask, the neutral request for information, falls five places.

relations.name: One-sided against mutual
relations.sentence: Verbs whose action is reciprocal or two-sided (fight, argue) fall under B even though fight is violent, while the verbs that rise are ones where the three men act unilaterally on a patient who does not act back (attack, beat, shoot, question, search).

residue.description: make holds and take falls three places, but neither is a content completion at all, since both are light verbs that mean nothing until a complement arrives; work and laugh rise substantially without belonging to force or to speech; play and move shift a single place, which is smaller than any movement I would read as a difference; and pull is counted above with the physical verbs but is genuinely ambiguous, since it needs an object to be either violent or mundane.

Against the speech relation specifically, question rises while every other speech verb falls; I read it as interrogation, but that reading is supplied by the fragment's subject rather than by the word, and someone who declined it would call question a straight counterexample. Sing falling is not a counterexample but it is also not evidence, since it is an odd completion in either condition.

result.reading: Under A the completions cluster around security and obligation: the whole safe/safer/unsafe family is live, in both polarities at once, alongside obliged and compelled and the comparative machinery (more, so, no) such judgements need. Under B those give way to plain adjectives of displeasure felt by the neighbours themselves (annoyed, uncomfortable, angry, alarmed, bad), so the change reads less as a flip of polarity than as a change in which axis the reaction is measured on.

relations.name: Irritation displaces security
relations.sentence: The words A favours most place the neighbours on a safety scale and do so in both directions at once (safer, safe, unsafe), while the words B favours most name social displeasure at what has arrived (annoyed, uncomfortable, angry, bad), so the reaction stops being about danger and becomes about being bothered.

relations.name: Obligation to reaction
relations.sentence: A carries a deontic vocabulary in which the feeling is a pressure to act (obliged, compelled, with forced unmoved), and B replaces it with words for an unwilled response to a scene (annoyed, uncomfortable, alarmed), so the completion shifts from what the neighbours felt they had to do toward how they felt about what they saw.

relations.name: Comparative frame collapses
relations.sentence: The falling side collects the machinery of a judgement relative to a prior state (safer, more, so, no, as in felt no safer), while the rising side offers a bare intensifier and phrase-openers before a plain adjective (very, as, like), so B completes with a flat description where A completed with a comparison.

result.kind: register of the reaction: personal safety versus social annoyance

residue.description: These are bare determiners and pronouns rather than content completions of felt, and they move only a place or two, so they mark which continuation frame is slightly preferred (felt their, felt it, felt they) rather than any state the neighbours are in.

result.counterexamples: Alarmed is the clearest counterexample: it rises 16 places under B while unsafe falls 26, and alarm is precisely the affect of being unsafe, so the first relation cannot be that fear-feeling falls away, only that the explicit safe/unsafe lexeme does. Threatened and betrayed hold position, which means the strongest danger and injury words are untouched by whatever moves the safety adjectives, weakening any claim that A is the danger condition. Insulted falls one place though it belongs with the annoyance cluster B favours, a contradiction so small it may be nothing. Within the third relation, very rises while so and more fall, and all three are degree words, so the comparative reading rests on which construction each degree word usually introduces rather than on any clean split.
result.notes: The two largest movements in the whole list, safer at -55 and annoyed at +53, are exactly the trade the first relation names, and uncomfortable at +41 against unsafe at -26 repeats it with a second pair, which is why that relation is high. What I cannot explain is why A favours safer and unsafe together: an axis being live in both directions is not the same as a condition taking a side, and any reading that treats A as the fearful condition or B as the hostile one would be overreaching on this evidence. The second and third relations rest on two and four words respectively and would not survive a repeat measurement in my confidence, though I would expect the vocabulary families to reappear. Only rank positions are given here, so a word moving 50 places may reflect a tiny difference among near-equal candidates; nothing about magnitude should be read off these numbers. This is one fragment in one direction, so the relations are about this completion and not about either condition in general.

result.reading: Under A the fragment completes as a warm character judgment of the neighbors (friendly, kind, pleasant, polite, cheerful, happy, smiling), together with the degree adverbs such adjectives require. Under B the same slot fills with progressive verbs of activity and observation, and the words that move furthest are conspiratorial: plotting (+161), involved (+107), suspicious, known, seen, up, looking, alongside a band of talking, discussing, chatting, arguing, complaining, loud.

relations.name: warmth to watchfulness
relations.sentence: The words A favours ascribe amiable character to the neighbors (friendly, kind, pleasant, polite, cheerful, happy, smiling), while the words B favours cast them as objects of suspicion and surveillance (plotting, suspicious, involved, known, seen, looking, up), so the same slot turns from a compliment into an accusation.

relations.name: attribute becomes activity
relations.sentence: A's words are predicate adjectives naming a standing disposition, plus the intensifiers that only an adjective can follow (so, very), whereas B's are present participles naming something the neighbors were repeatedly doing (plotting, discussing, getting, having, chatting, talking, arguing, complaining, looking), so the grammatical category of the completion shifts from state to ongoing action.

relations.name: neighbor as nuisance
relations.sentence: Separately from the conspiratorial words, B raises a register of domestic friction heard through a wall (loud, complaining, arguing, chatting, busy), which stands against precisely the A-side words that would deny it (polite, pleasant, kind), suggesting a second and milder unfriendliness alongside the suspicion.

result.kind: ascribed disposition versus observed ongoing activity

residue.description: These are syntactic scaffolding rather than content completions, standing in for a phrase that has not been chosen yet, though even they lean with the split: A's locatives (at, in, on, there, together) continue a stative description while B's determiners (a, the) and light verbs (getting, having) open a verb phrase whose content word never appears in the list.

result.counterexamples: The suspicion relation covers the top of the B list but not its bulk: busy, getting, having, talking, discussing and chatting are neutral activity words that describe sociable neighbors as easily as furtive ones, so roughly half of B is compatible with the A reading and only sharpens into conspiracy in the company of plotting and suspicious. Mildly against the warmth relation, A also carries together, ready, there, at, in and on, which ascribe no amiable character at all, and together in particular (a group keeping to itself) could belong to a suspicion reading as well as a friendly one. Nothing on the A side is a word of suspicion and nothing on the B side is a word of warmth, so no word reverses the polarity outright; the counterexamples dilute the reading rather than contradict it.
result.notes: The two largest movers in the table, plotting and involved, both arrive from outside the top hundred, and the four largest falls are kind, pleasant, polite and so; the reading rests on those extremes rather than on the small shuffles near the top of both lists (talking, arguing, friendly). The word up sits at rank 1 under B and is only interpretable through its neighbors, as up to something rather than up early; that inference is mine and not in the data. The ethnic specificity of the fragment is what makes the conspiracy register legible as a register, and I would want the same fragment with a neutral group before treating relation one as anything other than a description of this item.

result.reading: Both lists are wardrobe words for "She unzipped his ___", and no word is missing from either condition, so the whole difference is re-ranking rather than anything appearing or vanishing. Condition A puts outer layers and carried kit near the top (coat, jacket, overcoat, parachute, sleeping bag, backpack, boots) along with the waist-level openings (fly, flies, belt), while B pulls up the garments worn closer to the body and named by cut or fabric (shirt, polo, trench, khaki, sweatshirt, jeans, trousers, suit) together with the zip's own apparatus (pocket, pockets, zipper, suitcase); pants, the most obvious completion, does not move at all.

relations.name: Outer shell to inner garment
relations.sentence: Condition A ranks the things worn over or carried alongside the body higher (coat, jacket, overcoat, parachute, sleeping bag, backpack, bag, boots, overalls), while condition B lifts the garments that sit against the body and are named as such (shirt, sweatshirt, polo, jeans, trousers, suit, khaki).

relations.name: Function modifier to fabric modifier
relations.sentence: Among the words that cannot end the sentence and require a noun after them, A favours modifiers naming a use, a weight or a possessor (sleeping, heavy, own) and B favours modifiers naming a garment's cut or material (polo, trench, khaki, leather).

relations.name: Waist opening to container
relations.sentence: A keeps the openings located at the waist and crotch relatively high (fly, flies, belt) while B promotes the zip considered as hardware or as the mouth of a container (pocket, pockets, zipper, suitcase, clothes).

result.kind: which layer or fitting of dress the zip belongs to

residue.description: None of these completes the fragment with a thing that can be unzipped: "own" is a possessive intensifier awaiting a noun, "heavy" is a bare adjective, and "clothes" is a generic plural that names no particular garment and so joins neither the outer-layer nor the inner-garment side.

result.counterexamples: Three words cut against the first relation. \"Trench\" rises the second-most under B (+77) yet names a coat, which is exactly the outer layer B is supposed to be demoting, and \"suitcase\" rises +42 while being carried kit of the parachute and backpack sort; only the container reading of relation three accommodates it. \"Leather\" also rises under B although the garment it usually modifies, jacket, falls. Most damaging to relation one is the held word: \"pants\" is the plainest member of the body-layer group and does not move at all, so the group B supposedly favours gets no support from its most likely member. Relation three is weakly supported in its own right, since belt moves only -4, zipper +3 and pockets +5, movements small enough to be noise; only pocket (+48) and the fall of flies (-44) carry it.
result.notes: The two largest movements in the whole table, polo at +130 and own at -111, are both words that cannot end the sentence, so a large share of the difference is about which pre-modifier the condition reaches for rather than about which object is unzipped. Nothing here is absent under either condition, which the instructions call the stronger kind of difference, so every claim above rests on ordering alone and the small movements (+2 to +5 at the top of both lists) should not be read as anything. I have not assumed that the shift toward shirt, pocket and suitcase means the sentence is being steered anywhere in particular; the layer description is what the ranks support and the motive is not visible from ranks.

result.reading: Under B the completions that gain are ones describing what the neighbors were doing or how they appeared to others (seen, out, working, busy, talking, smiling, looking), while the ones that lose are almost all standing character judgments (kind, nice, polite, welcoming, willing, suspicious). The single negative-valence word in the set, suspicious, is on the falling side, and the flagship trait word friendly does not move at all.

relations.name: Trait yields to activity
relations.sentence: Words naming an ongoing observable activity or state of being about (seen, out, working, busy, talking, looking, smiling) rise under B, while words ascribing a settled character trait to the neighbors (kind, nice, polite, welcoming, willing, trying) fall.

relations.name: Received, not enacting
relations.sentence: Under B the neighbors are described as objects of other people's perception or reception (seen, welcome, looking, out), whereas under A they are described as the ones doing the receiving or the willing (welcoming, willing, kind, polite), with the pair welcome / welcoming splitting in opposite directions across the two conditions.

relations.name: The one negative leaves
relations.sentence: Suspicious is the only word in the whole set that would attach a hostile or wary judgment to the neighbors, and it is on the falling side, so that B's list contains no word capable of carrying a negative reading at all.

result.kind: character ascription versus observable conduct

residue.description: These are determiners, prepositions and an intensifier that do not complete the fragment with any content of their own but only open a longer phrase, and they move in both directions with small displacements, so nothing about them supports or resists the relations above.

result.counterexamples: The strongest counterexample is that friendly, the plainest character-trait word in the set and exactly the kind of word the first relation says should fall, holds its position; if the trait axis were really being displaced, friendly should have gone with kind, nice and polite. Two of the rising words are also poor fits for activity: ready is a disposition rather than a doing, and it is the second largest riser at +20, while happy names an internal state no observer sees directly. Against the second relation, there falls under B even though "always there" describes the neighbors as available to others rather than as agents, and trying, which is falling, describes effort rather than reception. Together these weaken the first relation somewhat and the second one considerably; they do not touch the third, which rests on one word and is weak for that reason alone.
result.notes: The first two relations share several words and are probably not independent readings of the difference; the second may just be the first seen from the side of who is the subject of the description. I have stated them separately because the welcome / welcoming split is a fact the first relation alone does not explain, but a repeated measurement could easily collapse them. The third relation is stated because a single negative word moving out of a set is the sort of thing worth marking, not because one word can support it. Note also that the largest single move in the whole set, seen at +38, is the word that carries both of the first two relations at once, so the reading rests more heavily on one displacement than the number of words listed suggests.
