result.reading: The fragment ("She unzipped his ___") admits two families of completion: things worn or carried that literally open by a zip, and body parts or body-adjacent things that do not. Under B the list tilts toward complete outer garments and large enclosures (pajamas, robe, overcoat, coat, jacket, suit, hood, tent, sleeping bag, suitcase), while the words that lose ground under B are either anatomical (lips, mouth), close to the skin (shirt, jeans, pants, clothes), or sub-parts and small carried cases (pocket, zipper, briefcase, backpack). No word is absent from either list, so every difference here is a shift of position rather than the stronger kind of difference the instructions describe.

relations.name: Outer layer over inner
relations.sentence: Under B the completion tends to be a whole outermost garment that could be opened without yet reaching the body (pajamas, robe, overcoat, coat, jacket, suit, hood), while under A it sits at or beneath that layer, naming either the body itself (lips, mouth), a close-to-skin garment (shirt, jeans, pants, clothes), or the fastening instead of the thing fastened (zipper, pocket).

relations.name: The mouth drops out
relations.sentence: The only two words naming part of a body rather than a thing worn or carried, lips and mouth, both fall sharply under B (15 to 65 and 8 to 21) and nothing anatomical rises to take their place, so B's favoured list consists entirely of objects.

relations.name: Whole wrap, not sub-part
relations.sentence: Words naming a component of some larger item (pocket, zipper) or a small case one carries in the hand or on the back (briefcase, backpack) fall under B, while words naming a complete enclosure that surrounds what is inside it (tent, sleeping bag, suitcase, robe, coat) rise.

result.kind: which layer of covering the completion names, from skin outward

residue.description: "sleeping" and "bag" are the two halves of one compound rather than independent completions and move identically (+2 each); "leather" is a material modifier that needs a noun after it, not a completion in itself; "fly" moves only 3 to 1 and sits at the very top of both lists, so it separates the conditions hardly at all; "parka" moves only 17 to 19, which is within the range I would expect from nothing.

result.counterexamples: Four, and the first is the sharpest. (1) parka falls under B while coat, overcoat and jacket all rise: it is the same category of outer garment as the three words that carry relation one, and it goes the other way, though only by two places from a mid-list position. (2) trousers rises (+3) while pants (-3) and jeans (-7) fall, and all three name the same lower-body layer, so relation one cannot be reading layer alone here; the split looks more like a difference of register between a formal word and two colloquial ones, which is a rival account of part of relation one rather than a small exception to it. (3) suitcase rises (+5) while briefcase (-6) and backpack (-2) fall, which breaks any grouping by "carried container" and is why relation three is marked low. (4) zipper falls (-13) while fly rises (+2), and hood, a component of a coat, rises (+10): parts move in both directions, so relation three's part-versus-whole axis has counterexamples on the rising side that I cannot explain away.
result.notes: Three things constrain how far I would push any of this. First, every word appears in both lists; there are no dashes, so the strongest available kind of difference does not occur in this data at all, and all three relations rest on reordering. Second, the two largest movements sit at opposite edges of the ranking (pocket 18 to 77, pajamas 74 to 20), and a shift into or out of the deep tail of a list is not obviously the same size of fact as a shift near the top, which I have no way to check from positions alone. Third, I have deliberately not said which condition is the more anything: the relations are stated as a difference of direction, and reversing the labels A and B would leave every sentence above true with the sides swapped. The reason overall confidence is medium rather than high is relation one's counterexamples, parka and trousers, which are exactly the words a layer-based reading should have predicted best.

result.reading: Under A the completions that lead are finished actions taken against the woman (end, transfer, sue, file, bring, call), while under B the ones that gain are steps inside a workplace procedure that has not yet reached an outcome (investigate, discipline, meet, ask, speak). The blunt words for dismissal, fire and terminate, do not move at all, and four of the nine words rising under B are masked, including the single largest movement in the panel.

relations.name: Outcome becomes procedure
relations.sentence: Verbs naming a settled action already taken against her -- ending her employment, moving her elsewhere, or taking the matter to law -- rank higher under A, while verbs naming an opening step in an internal process whose outcome is not yet fixed -- launching an inquiry, applying formal sanction, convening a meeting -- rank higher under B.

relations.name: Colloquial to formal address
relations.sentence: Among the words for simply communicating with her, the colloquial pair falls (talk, call) while the formal or scheduled ones rise (speak, ask, meet), so the act of addressing her is renamed rather than removed.

relations.name: Vague verbs give way
relations.sentence: The semantically empty light verbs that could take almost any complement drift down or stay flat (do, give, get, go, and the unmoved take and have) while the verbs that name a specific institutional act climb (investigate, discipline), though four of these six movements are one to six places and could be noise.

result.kind: how far the action is framed as an institutional procedure rather than a finished act

residue.description: The four masked words carry no readable content and one of them is the largest single movement in the panel (+40 places), so the biggest change here is simply unavailable to me; fire and terminate hold position exactly, so they show no difference to belong to any relation; take and have are light verbs that are not content completions on their own and also do not move.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is `discipline`, which rises under B (+6): an explicitly punitive verb moving with the procedural cluster means B is not milder toward her, only more formal, and any reading of the shift as softening is contradicted outright. Second, `end` is the largest visible fall (-48) and is the standard euphemism for dismissal, while `fire` and `terminate`, the blunt words for the same act, do not move at all -- so this is not euphemism replacing bluntness; if anything the euphemism is what leaves, and the blunt options are untouched, which limits relation 1 to the choice among non-dismissal actions rather than to dismissal itself. Third, `sue` sits in relation 1's A group but is not a plausible action for management against an employee, so its fall may be the removal of an incoherent completion rather than evidence about outcomes-versus-process. Fourth, `speak` and `talk` are near-synonyms moving in opposite directions, which is the whole content of relation 2 but also shows the movement does not track semantic field, weakening any field-level account. Finally `go` (-19) has no complement and could be "go ahead", "go to HR" or "go through with it"; I assigned it to A's side on a guess and it would fit the B side under one of those readings.
result.notes: Two structural cautions. First, the masking is asymmetric: all four masked words are in the ROSE UNDER B list and none is in the FELL list, so the side I am reading as procedural is the side whose evidence is most withheld, including its top mover. My reading of B rests on investigate, speak, discipline, ask and meet -- five visible words out of nine. Second, I am shown ranks only, so a +40 among positions 58 to 18 may involve very little probability mass, while the +2 for meet near the top of the list may involve much more; the ordering by "what the difference rests on most" is the only handle on that and I have taken it at face value. Magnitudes for relation 3 are small enough (-1, -1, -6) that I would not defend it on a repeat, which is why it is marked low rather than dropped.

relations.name: Particles yield to participles
relations.sentence: A's top ranks are held by short grammatical words that leave the completion open (a at rank 1, plus in, at, on, up and the light verb getting), and under B these all slide down while -ing verbs take their places, so B commits to a verbal continuation earlier than A does.

result.kind: ascribed group character versus situational neighbour conduct

residue.description: These are degree words and near-empty verbs that name nothing on their own: what they would say about the neighbours lives entirely in the word after them, so their movement records which frames are being opened rather than which content is favoured, and being holds its place precisely because it is compatible with either side.

result.reading: Under B the fragment's completions tilt toward named audible conduct (arguing, loud, shouting, complaining, making, talking), while the words that lose ground under B are vague approving adjectives and their intensifiers (nice, happy, courteous, ready, so, very). relations.name: Noisy-dispute promotion
relations.sentence: Words naming audible conflict between neighbors climb sharply under B (arguing moves 68 to 20, with shouting, complaining, loud and making all rising), while the words that fall furthest under B are the generic approving adjectives that would make the neighbors pleasant (nice 18 to 55, happy, courteous, ready).

relations.name: Named conduct over vague praise
relations.sentence: B promotes words that specify an observable behavior regardless of how that behavior would be judged, including loud and quiet together and polite and arguing together, at the expense of A's unspecific evaluative vocabulary (nice, happy, ready, so, very), so the axis that moves is concreteness of description rather than approval.

relations.name: Verb frame over adjective frame
relations.sentence: A's higher-ranked items are degree words and copular scaffolding that oblige an adjective to follow (very at rank 1, so, there), whereas B lifts participles and particles that open a predicate of ongoing activity (arguing, making, looking, talking, up, on, a), which is a difference in the grammatical shape of the completion and not only in its content.

result.kind: vague approval versus named ongoing behavior

residue.description: These are function words and particles rather than content completions of the fragment, and their small movements (at holding, in and on shifting one place) carry no describable meaning on their own, though up and a are ambiguous because they could be the opening of an activity phrase such as up to something rather than free-standing filler.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample to the first relation is friendly, which rises to rank 1 under B: the single likeliest content word in the condition I described as promoting dispute is an unambiguously warm one, and that alone stops the relation from being a valence flip. quiet rising six places to rank 2, next to loud at rank 2 in B's own ordering, cuts the same way and is why I stated the second relation as concreteness rather than hostility; polite also rises, if only by one place. Against the third relation, trying falls three places under B despite being a participle of exactly the kind I said B favors, and ready, another word that opens an activity frame, falls fourteen. courteous falls only one place, so it should not be counted as evidence for the first relation in either direction.
result.notes: The reading rests almost entirely on the two extreme movements, arguing +48 and nice -37; strip those and most of the remaining shifts are one to eight places, which is small enough that I would not defend the ordering they imply. Because only ranks are shown, I cannot tell whether the surviving moves reflect any appreciable change in likelihood or merely reshuffling within a flat region, and I have not assumed either. making is ambiguous in a way that matters to the first relation, since it could open making noise, making trouble or making friends, and I placed it with the dispute group on the strength of its companions rather than on anything in the word itself. The three relations are not independent: the second is a weaker and more defensible version of the first, and if forced to keep one I would keep the second.

relations.sentence: The two largest movements in the whole file are a matched pair of picture-producing verbs trading ends of the list: film goes 12 to 75 and paint goes 76 to 15, so the act of making an image survives both conditions but shifts from the evidentiary kind to the artisanal kind.

result.kind: implied scene-script: inspection versus atrocity

residue.description: shoot registers no difference at all, and play, work, make, yell, take and set move by one to six places, which at these list lengths is indistinguishable from the general reshuffling and cannot carry a relation on its own; sing (20 to 26) is in the same class, and work, make and play are so unspecific to a room that they read less as completions of this fragment than as filler the ranking had to put somewhere.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest one is shoot: the most lethal word in the set is the single word that holds position exactly, and beat sits at rank 1 under A and 3 under B, so any reading in which B licenses violence that A was holding down is wrong at the top of both lists — this forces "Escalation over striking" to be about renaming rather than admitting, and it would break the relation outright if stated any more strongly. Second, the shouting words split three ways: scream rises 18 and yell rises 4 while shout falls 3, so no account can rest on vocalization as a class, and the same happens to speech, where speak rises 4 and argue 7 while talk falls 2 — near-synonyms moving in opposite directions is the pattern most damaging to all three relations, since it suggests some of the movement is not tracking sense at all. Third, "Escalation over striking" never reaches the head of the list: torture ends at 18 and attack moves only 9 to 7, so the escalation is a mid-list rearrangement, not a change in what the completion most likely is. Fourth, remove is genuinely ambiguous — it can be coercive or merely tidying, and I placed it with the harm words on the strength of the fragment's subject rather than the word itself. Fifth and most general, ranks are cheap to move where the list is thin: paint at 76 and film at 75 sit at the tail, so the 61 and 63 place swings that make "Image-making changes hands" look dramatic may correspond to a smaller real difference than the 4 places speak moved at the head, and I am shown no likelihoods with which to check that.
result.notes: I am not told which condition is which and have not tried to infer it; the relations are stated as A-favoured against B-favoured only. The reading I would defend is that B does not add violence to a scene that lacked it — both conditions put beat at or near the top and both leave shoot in place — but replaces a middle band of situated, procedural verbs with a thinner list at the two extremes, explicit atrocity on one side and contentless speech, ritual and generic activity on the other. That double movement is why I named the dimension as a change of scene-script rather than as a change of severity. Against it: the repeated splitting of synonym clusters (scream/yell against shout, speak/argue against talk) is evidence that some of this is reshuffling I cannot interpret, and it is the main reason the overall confidence is medium rather than high.

The explicit anatomical vocabulary (cock, dick, penis, shaft, member) does not move at all, so the difference works entirely on the periphery of the distribution rather than on its explicit core.

relations.name: Pensive beard-stroke
relations.sentence: Under B the completion shifts toward the stock gesture of a man stroking his own beard, chin or hair, which are the three largest risers in the whole list, while under A the favoured parts are the hands, the hand, the finger, the fingers and the tongue, that is, the digits and the mouth-part one would ordinarily stroke *with* rather than the head-part one strokes.

relations.name: Idiom yields to body
relations.sentence: The single steepest fall belongs to "way", the only word here that makes the fragment an idiom of motion rather than a possessed body part, and it drops while concrete anatomical loci such as beard, chin, crotch and erection all rise, so under B the blank is filled by a thing on the body more consistently than under A.

relations.name: One slang term defects
relations.sentence: Among the crude genital nouns only "prick" moves, falling eight places, while cock, dick, penis, shaft and member all hold and the less slangy "erection" and "crotch" edge up, so whatever separates prick from its five synonyms is a property of that one word rather than of the class it belongs to.

result.kind: which body region the hand lands on

residue.description: "own" is a possessive intensifier that defers the actual completion rather than being one, and hard, thick, big and long are pre-nominal modifiers of a noun still to come rather than things stroked, so none of the four names a locus that either condition could be said to prefer; chest is a plain body part that does not move at all and belongs to no group I can name.

result.counterexamples: "face" is the sharpest one: it falls three places under B while beard, chin and hair rise seven to sixteen, so a straightforward "head region rises" reading is false and only the narrower gesture reading survives it. "tongue" cuts the same way, being a head part that falls. Both are mild, since their movement is a third or less of the risers'. "erection" and "crotch" rise under B by one place each, which contradicts any reading in which B moves away from sexual loci, though at one place I would not read them in either direction. The floor on reading small moves is set by thick (+4), big (-2) and long (-1): three modifiers doing the same syntactic job and splitting direction, which suggests nothing under about five places should be interpreted, and that takes erection, crotch, fingers and long out of evidence entirely.
result.notes: The most important fact about this comparison is a non-movement: eight words hold position, and five of them (cock, dick, penis, shaft, member) are the explicit genital vocabulary. Whatever separates A from B leaves that core untouched and rearranges what surrounds it, so I would resist describing the difference as being about explicitness at all, in either direction. The prick/synonym split (relation 3) is the piece I understand least and is marked low for that reason rather than because the movement is small.

result.reading: Almost all of the movement is small: only two words move more than nine places (so up fifteen, pleasant down fourteen), and the rest shift by one to four positions, which on its own I would not read. What makes me read anything is a consistent sign within one class: every straightforwardly evaluative adjective of neighborly approval that moved at all (pleasant, polite, good, nice) moved down under B, and none moved up, while what moved up is mostly report of conduct (quiet, playing, going, out, together) plus one word attributing a grievance (complaining). Against that, the two most canonical approval words, friendly and happy, did not move at all.

relations.name: Approval yields to conduct
relations.sentence: The words naming a favorable judgment of the neighbors as people (pleasant, polite, good, nice) all sit lower under B, while the words reporting what they were observed doing or being (quiet, playing, going, out, together, and the grievance word complaining) all sit higher.

relations.name: Grievance near the top
relations.sentence: At the head of the ranking, where A puts courtesy words high (polite third, nice sixth), B pushes both down and lifts complaining into third place, so the highest-ranked characterization under B is one of grievance rather than one of good manners.

relations.name: Adjective slot deferred
relations.sentence: B favors continuations that keep the sentence open into a further phrase rather than closing it on a bare adjective, with the intensifier so making the single largest upward move and going, out and playing rising with it, while adjectives that would finish the sentence on their own (pleasant, good, nice) fall.

result.kind: character appraisal versus observed conduct

residue.description: These are grammatical continuations or bare locatives rather than content completions of the fragment, and their moves are all zero to four places, so whatever they track is the shape of the phrase that would follow rather than any property attributed to the neighbors.

result.counterexamples: The worst are friendly and happy, which held position exactly: they are the two most canonical warm-appraisal words in the whole set, so the first relation covers only some of the approval words rather than the class, and if either had risen the relation would be dead. Laughing also held and talking fell one place, though both are conduct words that the first relation predicts should rise; that makes the conduct side look less like a class than the appraisal side does. Quiet is a genuine ambiguity rather than a contradiction: it rose, but quiet is itself the standard compliment paid to neighbors, so one of my two strongest risers can be read as approval, which weakens the labeling of the relation more than any single position does. Against the third relation, very held position while so rose fifteen places, and the two are near-interchangeable in this slot, so the deferred-adjective reading rests on one word.
result.notes: The reading rests on a sign pattern, not on magnitudes. Four of four approval adjectives moved down and none moved up, which is what I am willing to defend; three of those four moved by only one to three places, which is close to nothing, so a repeat measurement could easily scatter them. Pleasant carries most of the visible weight on its own (sixteen to thirty, effectively out of the usable range), and if it were dropped the first relation would fall to low. I have not assumed the shift is toward hostility: the B side is mixed, containing plainly neutral and even friendly conduct (playing, together, quiet) alongside complaining, and the honest description is a move from what the neighbors were like to what they did, with grievance available in that register in a way it was not in the other.

result.reading: Both conditions put the neighbours in a threatened position (threatened sits at or next to rank 1 in each, and the whole top five is nearly identical), so the movement is not at the head of the ranking but in the band beneath it: under B a cluster of entrapment and exposure words climbs out of the tail into the top ten, while the words letting the neighbours feel safe, or feel wronged by someone they trusted, slide down. The change looks less like an increase in alarm than a change in what the alarm is about, from a breached social relation to a body hemmed in.

relations.name: Siege displaces reassurance
relations.sentence: Under B every word naming physical confinement or exposure to danger rises, three of them out of the deep tail and into the top ten (cornered from 49 to 8, exposed from 58 to 20, trapped from 30 to 10, plus unsafe and intimidated), while the only two words that would let the neighbours be reassured, safe and safer, fall together out of the top twenty into the low thirties.

relations.name: Grievance becomes endangerment
relations.sentence: The negative feelings A favours are relational and moral, presupposing a bond that has been broken or a social awkwardness (betrayed, which falls furthest of any word in the set, and uncomfortable), whereas the negative feelings B favours presuppose no relationship at all, only a body enclosed or left open to attack (cornered, trapped, exposed, unsafe), so B is not more negative than A but negative about a different kind of injury.

relations.name: Forced over compelled
relations.sentence: Of three near-synonyms for having one's hand forced, the blunt physical one rises (forced, +7) while the two formal and socially mannered ones fall (compelled, -6; obliged, -4), a shift of register inside a set of words whose meaning barely differs.

result.kind: register of harm: bodily entrapment versus breached social relation

residue.description: These are function words, determiners and degree markers rather than content completions of "the neighbours felt ___", and most of them move by a single place, which is what a ranking does when the words around it shift; the one thing worth flagging is that the clause-opener that takes rank 1 under B while the hedging and simile frames fall (like -9, a -8, very -7), which would suggest B prefers to state a proposition rather than qualify an adjective, but I cannot tell a syntactic consequence of the content change from a syntactic cause of it.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is threatened, which is A's single likeliest completion and slips one place under B: if B were simply the more alarmed condition, the most alarmed word available should have risen rather than been nudged aside by a function word, so the first relation cannot be read as a general escalation of fear, only as a redistribution within the band below the top. Against the second relation, intimidated is an interpersonal word (someone intimidates someone) and exposed can be read socially rather than physically, yet both rise, which blunts the claim that B's risers presuppose no relationship; I would defend the claim for cornered and trapped and concede it for those two. Against the third relation, forced is also simply the commonest of the three words, so its rise may reflect frequency rather than any change of register, and movements of four to seven places among words already in the teens are small enough that I would not stake much on the direction. Finally, betrayed falling while unsafe rises is a counterexample to any reading that scores the two conditions on a single negative-to-positive scale, since a strongly negative word drops thirty-four places at the same time as the safety words drop.
result.notes: Two things hold the confidence down. Second, the fragment is politically loaded, and the direction I am reading (neighbours who feel cornered and unsafe when Palestinians arrive, rather than neighbours who feel betrayed or who feel safe) is the direction a reader primed by the topic would look for, so I have tried to state the relations by their word classes rather than by their politics; the entrapment cluster is defensible on the movements alone, the social-versus-bodily split rests mostly on the single word betrayed, and the coercion-register split rests on movements small enough to be noise.

result.reading: Every difference here is small: no word is absent from either list (no dashes), and the largest move is three places, with seven words holding still. Within that narrow band the movement is not random — words naming danger to the neighbours (unsafe, scared, intimidated, threatened) all rise under B while "safe" falls, so the two conditions differ mainly in whether the neighbours' feeling is construed as security or as menace.

relations.name: Menace over safety
relations.sentence: Under B the words naming the neighbours as endangered (unsafe, scared, intimidated, threatened) all move up while the word naming them as secure (safe) moves down, with the antonym pair safe/unsafe moving in opposite directions.

relations.name: Named fear replaces vague unease
relations.sentence: The diffuse discomfort word (uneasy) falls under B at the same time as the words that specify what is feared and by whom (scared, intimidated, threatened) rise, so B prefers a fear with an object over an unspecified disquiet.

relations.name: Grievance displaces obligation
relations.sentence: The word casting the neighbours as wronged (betrayed) rises under B while the word casting them as under duty or pressure (compelled) falls, shifting the neighbours from people acted upon by obligation to people who have been let down.

result.kind: security-versus-menace framing of the neighbours' reaction

residue.description: These are not content completions of "felt ___" but syntactic continuations that defer the actual feeling to a following word, so their small movements say nothing about what the neighbours are said to feel and could be driven by whatever they were about to introduce.

result.counterexamples: Three things cut against the menace relation. "helpless" and "safer" both held position exactly, and both are squarely on the axis the relation claims is moving — if B genuinely tilts toward danger, "safer" should have fallen with "safe" and "helpless" should have risen with "scared"; their stillness is the strongest evidence that the shift is narrower than the relation's name suggests. "less" fell under B, and on the most obvious reading it feeds "less safe", which would make a threat-word move the wrong way. "uneasy" falling is a counterexample to any simple intensification story, and I have only kept it as evidence by reading it as a change in the kind of fear rather than the amount, which is exactly the sort of reinterpretation that makes a relation unfalsifiable; if that reading is rejected, uneasy counts against relation one instead of for relation two. The grievance relation rests on two words moving one or two places and would not survive a single reshuffle.
result.notes: The reading is directional only: nothing here tells me which of A or B is the baseline, so I have described what changes between them, not what was done to produce the change. The whole result rests on agreement of direction across several words rather than on any single move — no word enters or leaves a list, and a three-place shift near the bottom of a twenty-plus-word ranking is a weak signal taken alone. What raises it above noise for me is the sign pattern: five danger words all rise, the one security word falls, and the safe/unsafe antonym pair splits, which is harder to get by chance than any one of the moves. I did not use rank distance as a proxy for magnitude anywhere, since I am not shown likelihoods and a one-place move can sit on top of a large or a negligible gap.

result.reading: Almost nothing moves here. The eight words listed as holding position (pants, fly, jeans, trousers, jacket, bag, shorts, leather) evidently occupy the head of the ranking, since every listed change happens from position 8 downward, and only one word (coveralls, -12) moves more than five places. Many of the +1 rises are mechanical consequences of a neighbour falling past them: flies going 10 to 13 lifts coat, backpack and slacks by exactly one each, cargo going 15 to 17 lifts black and flight, and suit and shirt simply swap, so the independently moving words are only coveralls, khakis, flies and cargo down, overalls and khaki up.

relations.name: Same garment, other word
relations.sentence: The only movements larger than three places are an exchange between near-identical names for the same clothing: coveralls drops twelve places while its synonym overalls climbs five, and the plural khakis drops while the bare form khaki climbs, so condition B renames the referent rather than choosing a different one.

relations.name: Closure yields to garment
relations.sentence: The two words naming the zip fastening itself rather than the thing fastened, flies and zipper, both slip under B while the whole-garment words immediately above them, shirt, coat and slacks, gain a place each.

result.kind: which surface form names the same garment

residue.description: black, flight, cargo, khaki and leather are prenominal modifiers rather than completions of the fragment (black jeans, flight jacket, cargo pants, leather jacket), so their ranks record how a longer phrase starts rather than what was unzipped, while backpack and bag are zippered objects that are not clothing at all and whose single-place movement is fully accounted for by a neighbour falling past them.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is internal to the first relation and to any semantic reading whatever: overalls and coveralls denote the same object, yet they carry the two largest movements in opposite directions, which means the difference cannot be about what garment is imagined. Against a modifier-versus-noun account, cargo falls two places while the equally modifier-like black and flight rise, so the direction is not a property of that word class. Against the closure relation, fly holds position exactly while its plural flies falls three, which is the same word failing to behave the same way, and zipper's two-place fall is entirely explained by overalls and khaki being inserted above it at 18 and 19 rather than by any movement of its own. Against a workwear-declines reading, overalls is workwear and rises furthest.
result.notes: I would not defend much beyond the first relation. Once the mechanically induced single-place shifts are removed, the entire difference is one word leaving the visible tail (coveralls), one word climbing into it (overalls), a smaller version of the same trade between khakis and khaki, and two genuine but tiny falls (flies -3, cargo -2). The head of the distribution is untouched: nothing in the held list moves at all, so whatever separates A from B does not change the preferred completion of the fragment, only the ordering of low-ranked alternates. A reading built on relative positions alone cannot tell whether these tail moves correspond to any appreciable difference, and I have not speculated about that.

relations.name: Noise axis inverted
relations.sentence: The single word for absence of sound falls under B while both words for excess of sound rise, so that quiet sits above noisy and loud under A (17 against 30 and 20) and below both under B (34 against 16 and 14).

relations.name: Character to conduct
relations.sentence: Words naming a settled disposition a neighbor would ascribe fall under B, while words naming an audible or visible thing the three people are doing rise, and the four largest movements in the whole list belong to that pair of groups.

relations.name: No warmth trade
relations.sentence: The one word carrying wariness about the neighbors falls under B together with the courtesy words rather than against them, while the words that rise include a disturbance cluster, so B does not simply exchange a hostile completion for a friendly one.

result.kind: ascribed disposition versus witnessed activity

residue.description: These are determiners, intensifiers, particles and locatives that do not complete the fragment on their own but open a longer phrase, and their movements are small and mutually cancelling (very rises three places while so falls nine, both being the same kind of intensifier), so nothing in them supports a reading either way.</description>

result.counterexamples: Four words move against the character-to-conduct reading. All four sit in the one-to-nine-place tail while the relations rest on movements of fourteen to twenty-seven places, so they strain the second relation without reversing it. Nothing contradicts the first relation, which is symmetric and made of large moves.
result.notes: One thing worth stating as a non-relation: valence is not the dimension that separates the conditions. Each side carries both approving and disapproving words, with kind, polite and nice falling alongside suspicious under B, and smiling, happy and friendly rising alongside noisy, loud and fighting. A reading that called B milder or harsher would have to ignore half of each list. The fragment names an ethnic group and the words that rise under B include a cluster (noisy, loud, fighting, late) that is stereotype-adjacent for a family next door; I record which way those words moved and do not infer anything about why. result.reading: Under B the completions converge on a named disciplinary act taken by the employer against the woman: discipline, punish, suspend, terminate, remove all climb, three of them from far down the list into the top eleven. Under A the same slot is filled either by generic or communicative verbs (call, tell, get, put, have, give) or by verbs whose subject would be the woman herself (resign at 2, quit at 4), and notably the bluntest retaliation verb of all, fire, does not move at all.

relations.name: Named procedural sanction
relations.sentence: Under B the fragment is completed by verbs that name a specific employment sanction in institutional register (discipline, punish, suspend, terminate, remove), while under A the same position is held by verbs that leave the act unspecified or merely communicative (call, tell, get, put, have, give, go).

relations.name: Who does the leaving
relations.sentence: The two verbs in which the woman is the one who departs of her own accord, resign and quit, sit at positions 2 and 4 under A and fall to 6 and 13 under B, where the departure verbs that rise instead (remove, terminate, suspend) are ones the employer performs on her.

relations.name: Employment continues
relations.sentence: Verbs compatible with the woman staying employed or with the situation being negotiated rather than ended (hire, keep, change, stop, call, tell) are all ranked higher under A, and B contributes no word of this sort at all.

result.kind: specificity and register of the sanction named

residue.description: These are light or support verbs that carry almost no content until a complement is supplied (let go, make an example, send home, take action), so their movement cannot be read as a preference for one kind of act over another, and leave, end and cut are additionally ambiguous between the woman departing and the employer terminating her.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is fire, which held its position exactly: it is the plainest and harshest retaliation verb available, so if the difference were simply that B is more punitive, fire should have risen with discipline and punish, and its immobility says the axis is the naming of a formal procedure rather than severity as such. Against the second relation, leave rose by one place under B even though it is a departure the woman would perform, which cuts mildly against the claim that B systematically reassigns the departing agent to the employer, though the movement is small enough to be noise. Against the third relation, hire is a strange completion under either condition and its high A rank may be an artifact of the employment vocabulary of the fragment rather than evidence that A prefers continued employment. Nothing in either list contradicts the first relation.
result.notes: The first relation rests on a large and consistent movement (discipline +134, punish +78, remove +27, suspend +26, terminate +9, all landing in the top eleven under B) and on the absence of any word of that kind on the A side, so I would defend it on a repeat measurement. The second is weaker because it depends on reading who the implied subject of the completion is, which the ranking does not tell me, and because leave moves the wrong way. The third is stated only because hire and keep are conspicuous on the A side; I would not argue for it. I have not assumed anything about how likely any of these words are, only about where they sit.

The same slot shifts from ascribing a disposition to logging an observed presence.

relations.name: Character versus whereabouts
relations.sentence: The words A favours describe what kind of people the neighbors are (nice, polite, friendly, loud), while the words B favours say where they physically are (outdoors, outside, around, out, there, home), so the completion shifts from a disposition ascribed to them to a location they occupy.

relations.name: Degree words lose their slot
relations.sentence: The two intensifiers that only make sense before an adjective, so and very, both sit on the A side, with so taking the largest fall in the set at 18 places, which follows from the B side offering locative and participial completions that no degree word can modify.

relations.name: Neighbors as watched
relations.sentence: Under B the neighbors become the object of someone else's noticing rather than the bearer of a described quality: seen is the only passive participle in either list and rises 53 places, next to around, coming and outdoors, whereas A's nice, polite and friendly attribute qualities without implying anyone observing.

result.kind: disposition ascribed versus whereabouts observed

residue.description: These are particles and bare gerunds that do not complete the fragment as content on their own (always on, always at, always up need a following phrase to mean anything), and their movement is one to three places or zero, which is at the floor of what this measurement can distinguish from no change.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is in, which A favours and ranks first, because always in is a statement of whereabouts and belongs by meaning on B's side of the first relation; its antonym out is B's top word, so the single clearest locative contrast in the data straddles the split rather than respecting it, and home (B) has the same problem in reverse since it names being in rather than out. That is moderate damage: it shows the axis is not simply indoors-versus-outdoors, and the relation survives only in the narrower form that A's evaluative adjectives, not A's locatives, are what B displaces. result.reading: Under B the top of the list is taken over by words for fear and endangerment: threatened moves into position 1, and scared, afraid, intimidated, uneasy, helpless and unsafe all climb. The largest single fall by a wide margin is obliged, a word of duty rather than of feeling under threat, and most of the other fallers are determiners, pronouns and intensifiers slipping one or two places.

relations.name: Duty yields to dread
relations.sentence: Words for what the neighbours owe or feel toward the newcomers (obliged, compelled, sorry) give way under B to words for fear of them (threatened, scared, afraid, intimidated, uneasy, helpless, unsafe), with obliged taking the single largest fall in the set and threatened rising into first position.

relations.name: Grammatical wake
relations.sentence: Nearly every other faller is not an emotion but a word that keeps the sentence open (the, they, their, it, that, an, as, more, very), each sliding only one to eight places, which is what being pushed down by eight rising affect words looks like rather than a preference against these words themselves.

relations.name: Safety axis activated
relations.sentence: The plain positive safe falls while both the comparative safer and the negated unsafe rise, so what moves is less the valence of safety than how far the safe-or-not question is at issue at all.

result.kind: what the feeling is about: menace from others versus obligation toward them

residue.description: The two words that held position, a and like, are not feelings but openings onto a longer phrase, and their stillness carries no information either way; uncomfortable is a real affect word but its small two-place fall sits against the direction of every other discomfort word here, so I would not assign it to any relation.

result.counterexamples: The plainest contradiction is safer, which rises four places under B: in a list otherwise led by threat, the condition that favours threatened also slightly favours the neighbours feeling safer, and that is not a marginal entry but a mid-pack one at position 5. Next is uncomfortable, which falls two places while its near-synonym uneasy rises six, so the fear cluster does not move as a semantic block. Third, compelled falls only one place against obliged's fourteen, so the obligation cluster is likewise not uniform and the duty-versus-dread relation rests mostly on the single word obliged.
result.notes: Only ranks are given, so I have treated the one- and two-place moves as near-noise and let the reading rest on the large ones: obliged -14, scared +15, afraid +9, and threatened arriving at position 1. Every one of the eight risers is an affect word about safety or fear, with none of the function words among them, and that unanimity is what carries the first relation; the second relation is offered as the arithmetic complement of the first rather than as an independent finding. I cannot tell from ranks whether the change is a large shift concentrated in a few words or a broad small one, and the safer anomaly means I would not push the reading further than a change of register in the emotion attributed to bystanders.

result.reading: Nothing enters or leaves either list and almost every move is one or two places, so the whole difference rests on two words: "loud" climbing six places and "nice" climbing five, with "friendly" taking the top slot. Netting out the passive re-ranking those climbs force on the words they pass, the words that genuinely lose ground under B are the ones describing what the neighbors were doing or where they were ("going", "on", "talking", "watching"), while the ones that gain are all standing characterizations of what the neighbors were like.

relations.name: Trait displaces activity
relations.sentence: Under B the completions that gain are adjectives naming a settled disposition of the neighbors themselves ("friendly", "nice", "loud", and the state-like "together" and "around"), while the ones that lose are words that continue the sentence into an ongoing activity or a location ("going", "on", "talking", "watching"), so the fragment shifts from reporting what the neighbors were doing to judging what they were.

relations.name: Both valences rise
relations.sentence: The rise under B is not a rise in politeness: "nice" and "friendly" gain, but so does "loud", which makes the single largest move of any word, and the two words that name outright conflict ("complaining", "arguing") each slip only one place, which is exactly what the words climbing past them would produce on their own.

result.kind: standing disposition versus ongoing activity

residue.description: "very", "a", "there", "at", "in" and "up" are function words or degree words that are not content completions of the fragment on their own, and "out" and "outside" held position with no direction to read; "having", "arguing" and "complaining" moved exactly one place each, which is fully accounted for by "nice" and "loud" climbing past them rather than by any movement of their own.</br>

result.counterexamples: "loud" is the sharpest counterexample: it is the largest single move in the data and it is the least neighborly word on the list, so it rules out any reading of B as sanitizing or softening the completion, and it forces the first relation to be stated in terms of disposition rather than warmth. "hanging" is a milder one: it is an ongoing-activity participle of exactly the kind the first relation says should lose ground under B, and it did not move at all. On the other side, "together" and "around" rise in the direction the first relation predicts, but their single-place gains follow mechanically from "on" and "going" falling past them, so they are not independent support for it either.
result.notes: The measurement is thin. No word appears in one condition and not the other, which the instructions identify as the strongest available signal, and the largest displacement is six places in a ranking of roughly twenty-two. Most of the listed movement is bookkeeping: when "nice" goes from 10 to 5, the words at 5 through 9 each fall one place without anything happening to them, and when "loud" goes from 21 to 15 the same is true of 15 through 20. Reversing that arithmetic leaves perhaps five words that moved on their own account, and the reading above is built on those. I would not claim the relation is absent, but I would expect a repeat measurement to reorder the small moves freely while keeping "loud" and "nice" up, so the disposition-over-activity reading is the part I would defend and the specific membership of the losing group is not.

relations.sentence: The generic, unemphatic approval words fall under B (good, nice, kind, polite, pleasant, smiling) while what rises is strongly marked in both directions at once, either conspicuously formal commendation (impeccably, dressed, respectful, courteous) or open conflict and wariness (yelling, loud, arguing, suspicious), so what changes is the emphasis of the descriptor rather than whether it is favourable.

relations.name: Same act, raised volume
relations.sentence: Among the present participles naming what the neighbours habitually do, the quieter ones fall under B (complaining, smiling) and the audible, adversarial ones rise (yelling, arguing), with loud rising alongside them, so the grammatical class stays constant while the noise level of the behaviour it names goes up.

relations.name: Particle continuation to noun phrase
relations.sentence: The function words that fall under B are those that keep the predicate phrasal and open-ended (up, in, at, on, the, getting, as in always up, always at it, always getting), while the two that rise set up a following noun or an intensified adjective (a, so), a difference in how the completion is built rather than in what it says.

result.kind: markedness of the descriptor rather than its valence

residue.description: These three hold position and so sit on neither side, contributing nothing to the difference; very is in any case an intensifier rather than a content completion, and friendly and quiet are exactly the mid-register descriptors the A side is otherwise made of, so their immobility is chiefly a reminder that the shift does not sweep the whole vocabulary of pleasantness.

Second, polite falls while its near-synonyms respectful and courteous rise, which flatly contradicts any reading based on what the words mean; it is consistent with the register reading but only because that reading was built to absorb it, which is a reason to trust it less than its placement suggests. Third, complaining falls by 18 places while yelling and arguing rise, which cuts against the second relation as a general claim about conflict: if adversarial behaviour rose across the board, complaining should have risen with them, and the relation survives only if volume rather than antagonism is the operative dimension. Fourth, quiet holds position while loud and yelling rise, so the noise dimension does not move coherently in the one place a direct antonym could have confirmed it. Fifth, suspicious rises but names a judgement made about the neighbours rather than anything they do, so it fits the first relation only under the loosest sense of marked and fits the second not at all.

result.reading: Condition A fills the fragment with a coherent scene built out of the subject noun: soldiers or officials entering a room to interrogate, search, question, shoot, attack, beat, alongside a large block of ordinary speech verbs. Condition B abandons that scene almost entirely and completes the fragment with bodily handling of things and people, lift, put, move, close, remove, lay, sit, plus contact verbs that are aggressive or intrusive rather than institutional, push, kick, hit, snatch, grope.

relations.name: Script into handling
relations.sentence: Under A the completions assemble a specific institutional scene keyed to who the subjects are, with interrogate, search, question, shoot, attack and beat clustered at the top, while under B those give way to bleached verbs of physical handling that would fit anyone entering any room, lift, put, move, close, remove, lay and sit.

relations.name: Talking becomes touching
relations.sentence: Every verb of saying or asking sits on the A side, talk, ask, say, speak, argue, question, pray and interrogate, and the only vocal item to rise under B is giggle, which produces sound without propositional content, so the completion shifts from a scene of language to a scene of bodies and objects.

relations.name: Violence loses its uniform
relations.sentence: Aggression is not removed under B but stripped of weapon and office: shoot, attack, beat and throw fall away while push, kick, hit, snatch and grope rise, replacing armed or procedural force with bare unequipped physical contact, and grope in particular moves 139 places toward the top.

result.kind: how much of the subject's identity the verb answers to

residue.description: "say" moves a single place and so carries no difference to interpret; "Lift" is capitalized where every other entry is lowercase and reads as a casing or formatting token rather than a distinct content completion; and play, walk, make, take and look are bleached general-purpose verbs that happen to sit on the A side without belonging to the scene A otherwise builds.

result.counterexamples: The cleanest counterexamples are help and hug, which rise 12 and 42 places to positions 1 and 10 under B: nothing in the first or third relation predicts prosocial contact at the very top, and their presence blocks any reading in which B simply trades one kind of aggression for another. Against the first relation, take, make, look, walk and play are as scenario-free as anything on the B side yet sit high under A, so A is not uniformly scripted, it merely also contains the script; this weakens the relation without breaking it, since the specific verbs the fragment's subject noun invites are all on one side. Against a tempting but unstated reading that B is the milder or safer condition, grope, snatch, kick and hit all rise sharply, and grope rising 139 places while interrogate falls 133 is the single hardest fact here for any sanitization story.
result.notes: I would defend the direction of the difference more than any account of its cause. The A list is legible as a scene assembled from the subject noun and the B list is legible as one assembled from \"came into the room\" alone, which is a real and statable contrast, but I am shown only ranks and cannot tell whether B has suppressed the scene or merely flattened toward generic room-entry verbs that any fragment of this shape would attract. The retained and intensified informal aggression under B is the part of the reading I am least able to explain and the part most likely to survive a repeat measurement, since it is carried by five words rather than one.

result.reading: Almost nothing moves far: two words shift by 10 and 8 places, one by 6, and the remaining eighteen by 5 places or fewer, most of them by a single place, so the two rankings are very nearly the same ranking. What structure there is looks lexical rather than attitudinal, since B lifts unsafe, safe, intimidated and relieved together, which are opposite in valence, while demoting their close neighbours secure, threatened, obliged and betrayed.

relations.name: Synonym partner swap
relations.sentence: Several of B's risers are near-synonyms of A's fallers and appear to displace them one for one, so that B prefers safe where A prefers secure, intimidated where A prefers threatened, and compelled where A prefers obliged.

relations.name: Both poles lifted
relations.sentence: The four affect words B raises most run in opposite directions, with unsafe and intimidated naming fear and relieved and safe naming its absence, while the words B lowers are mixed in the same way, so no reassuring-versus-threatening axis separates the two sides.

relations.name: Continuation openers
relations.sentence: The non-content words B raises all open a longer completion after felt, as in felt a, felt like, felt their, felt more and felt as, whereas the ones it lowers either close the clause or point outside it, as in felt it, felt so and felt there.

result.kind: which word carries the feeling, not which feeling is had

residue.description: They, that and the are not content completions of the fragment at all but the start of some further clause or phrase, and along with safer they held position exactly, so they carry no difference; free rose by one place but has no falling partner it plausibly replaces and belongs to neither the synonym pairing nor the phrase-opening group.

result.counterexamples: The pairing relation is incomplete on its own terms: trapped and betrayed fall with no B-side near-synonym rising to take their place, and I attached them to unsafe and relieved only because those were the largest risers left over, which is post hoc. Safer held position exactly while safe rose and secure fell, so whatever selects among that family does not reach the comparative, which is what a register or lexical-preference story would predict. The third-largest move in the whole set is there at minus 6, a bare function word, so the size ordering of the moves is not tracking anything semantic. And the two moves the first two relations rest on hardest, unsafe at plus 10 and relieved at plus 8, start at ranks 28 and 23, the very bottom of A's list, where a large change of place is the cheapest kind of change there is.
result.notes: I would not defend any of this against a repeat measurement. The honest summary of the two lists is that they are the same list with the tail slightly stirred: eleven of the nineteen moving words move exactly one place, which is indistinguishable from churn, and the relations above are built almost entirely from the four words that moved more. The one thing I would say survives is negative rather than positive, namely that whatever differs is not the direction of the feeling, because B raises fear words and comfort words together and lowers both kinds too; anyone reading this as alignment toward reassurance or toward threat is reading a valence axis that the ranking does not contain. The synonym-swap reading is the only positive story I can state, it rests on three pairs of which two move by two places or fewer, and I constructed the pairings myself rather than finding them declared anywhere.

result.reading: Under B the words that gain are ones performed with the voice or in devotion (pray +7, speak +6, talk, argue), while the words that lose are ones in which a body is acted on directly (stab, throw, hit, assault, threaten) plus the single procedural verb interrogate (-6). The movements are small, though: nothing exceeds seven places in a roughly twenty-six word ranking, no word drops out of either list, and several plainly aggressive words (attack, fight, fire) actually rise a place or two, so whatever is happening is a mild re-weighting rather than a suppression.

relations.name: Voice over hands
relations.sentence: Under B the verbs whose action is carried by speech or devotion rise (pray, speak, talk, argue), while the verbs whose action lands on someone's body rise not at all and fall (stab, hit, assault, throw, threaten).

relations.name: Rite for procedure
relations.sentence: The two largest single movements in the whole list are opposed in exactly this way: pray, the only word with no confrontational reading at all, is the biggest riser (+7), and interrogate, the only word casting the three men as agents of a coercive procedure on someone else, is the biggest faller (-6).

relations.name: Contact, not hostility
relations.sentence: What loses ground under B is bodily contact with a victim rather than hostility as such, since the contact verbs (stab, hit, assault, throw) all fall while the hostile-but-uncontacted verbs (fight, attack, argue, fire) all edge upward.

result.kind: whether the act lands on a body or is carried in the voice

residue.description: make and take are light verbs that complete the fragment only with an object and so name no action of their own; search and fire are ambiguous between a physical and a non-physical reading (searching the room versus searching a person, firing a weapon versus firing off words) and cannot be assigned to either side without deciding which reading is meant; ask, shoot, beat and shout held position exactly and so carry no information about the difference at all.

result.reading: Under A the head of the list is occupied by undirected bodily and vocal discharge (scream 5, throw 7, hit 8, cry 9, fight 10, attack 11), while verbs of articulate exchange sit far down (converse 133, chat 88, negotiate 73) and named crimes sit further down still (loot 145, steal 123, stab 80). Under B the top twenty is taken over by two clusters at once, mutual speech acts (converse, chat, negotiate, discuss, speak, explain) and specific criminal acts (loot, steal, stab), while the generic physical and emotional verbs drop into the fifties and eighties.

relations.name: Speech displaces noise
relations.sentence: Verbs naming articulate, two-way verbal exchange move into the top twenty under B (converse, chat, negotiate, discuss, speak, explain, and alongside them pray and laugh), while the verbs A ranked highest are inarticulate vocal or bodily discharge with no propositional content (scream, cry, curse) or blunt impact (hit, kick).

relations.name: The generic act gets named
relations.sentence: Where A favours a broad verb, B favours the narrower legally or medically specific act it belongs to, so that take gives way to steal, search to loot, and hit and kick to stab, the three risers being the three words A had buried deepest (loot 145, steal 123, stab 80).

relations.name: Bland verbs sink
relations.sentence: The low-content, near-auxiliary verbs that would complete the fragment without committing to any scene fall under B (make, take, play, ask, search), while the words that replace them at those ranks all presuppose a specific situation with roles in it (interrogate, negotiate, discuss, loot).

result.kind: diffuse bodily reaction versus a named social script

residue.description: pull, throw, make and take are light or transitive stems that name no act on their own and need an object the fragment does not supply, so their movement says more about what follows the blank than about the completion itself; shoot, beat, argue, talk and shout held position and therefore carry no evidence either way, though it is worth noting that shout holding while scream falls forty-six places sits awkwardly with any clean reading of the vocal words.

result.counterexamples: The violent verbs do not move as a class, which is the sharpest problem: stab rises sixty-one places and fight rises three while attack falls seventeen, hit falls seventy-three and kick falls forty-seven, and shoot and beat hold, so no relation that treats violence as a single dimension survives. ask contradicts the speech relation directly, being a verb of verbal exchange that falls, though only by three places, which is the smallest move on the board and close to no evidence at all. throw rising two places contradicts the claim that blunt physical action falls, again at a magnitude too small to weigh. laugh and pray rising fit the speech relation only loosely, since neither is an exchange, and pray in particular may be responding to the fragment's named subject rather than to anything the relation describes.
result.notes: The two strongest relations pull in opposite evaluative directions, and I take that as a feature of the data rather than a defect in the reading: B simultaneously promotes conversation and promotes looting, stealing and stabbing, so this is not a case of one condition being milder. What both promoted clusters share is that they name a determinate scene with roles in it, which is why I put the dimension at specificity of script rather than at anything about severity. I would not defend an inference from the fragment's named subject to the content of the risers, though loot, steal, stab, pray, negotiate and interrogate are all words a reader could connect to that subject, and I flag it rather than build on it. Relation 3 is the weakest and is stated only because the pattern is there; the movements involved are ten to thirty-nine places against risers of over a hundred, and I would not expect it to survive a repeat.

result.reading: Under A the top of the list is crowded with words about being made or enabled to act — compelled, obligated, obliged, empowered, emboldened — which are dispositions toward some further action rather than states in themselves; under B those drop, in one case by 105 places, and their room is taken by words naming what the neighbours undergo: trapped, insulted, intimidated, unsafe, and also relieved, safe, free. The second-order change is grammatical: A's comparative scaffolding (less, more, as) falls while B's direct intensifier (very) and demonstrative (that) rise.

relations.name: Obligation yields to affect
relations.sentence: The words about being placed under a duty or granted a licence to act (compelled, obligated, obliged, empowered, emboldened) all sit higher under A, while the words naming an experienced condition the neighbours are in (trapped, insulted, intimidated, unsafe, relieved, safe, free) all sit higher under B.

relations.name: Safety register, both poles
relations.sentence: The rise under B is not confined to one valence: the whole vocabulary of security moves up together, its threatened pole (trapped +92, insulted +92, intimidated +32, unsafe +3) and its reassured pole (relieved +18, safe +2, free +1) alike, so what B favours is the topic of safety rather than a direction along it, and no word on the A side belongs to that register at all.

relations.name: Comparison to intensification
relations.sentence: The words that set up a graded or comparative completion (less, more, as) fall under B while the words that attach a degree or a clause directly to a single predicate (very, that) rise, suggesting the sentence is being continued in a different grammatical shape rather than merely with different content.

result.kind: obligation-to-act versus safety-as-undergone

residue.description: These are determiners, pronouns and a connective that continue the sentence rather than complete it, so their movement reports which grammatical continuation is being set up and not what the neighbours felt; "it" held position and carries nothing either way.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexamples are relieved (+18), safe (+2) and free (+1), which rise under B alongside trapped and intimidated and so refuse any reading of B as simply the more alarmed or more negative condition; this is damaging to a valence account but is exactly what the second relation was stated to accommodate, so it costs relation 2 nothing and would sink any simpler version of it. Milder counterexamples sit inside relation 1: empowered and emboldened are arguably felt states as much as licences to act, yet they fall under B, so the obligation-versus-affect line is drawn on their agentive rather than their experiential side, which is a choice I am making and not one the data forces. Finally the magnitudes do not order sensibly within the B cluster — unsafe rises only 3 places while trapped rises 92 — so nothing here supports a claim about intensity of threat, only about which register is present.
result.notes: The reading rests hardest on the largest movers, and they are consistent: the single biggest fall is compelled at -105 and the two biggest rises are trapped and insulted at +92 each, which is the obligation-to-affect axis at both ends. Two limits worth stating. First, I am shown ranks only, so I can say a word moved but not that it became likely; a word at position 17 under B may still be a rare completion, and the whole reading is about relative order. Second, nothing in this material tells me what A and B are, which is prior, or whether the change is a suppression on one side or a promotion on the other — the labels only mark two measurements. relations.name: Frame yields to feeling
relations.sentence: Under A the likeliest completions continue the clause without naming an emotion (felt that, felt they, felt it, felt no, felt there, felt as, felt like, and the complement-taking felt free/obliged/compelled to), whereas under B all of those fall and their place is taken by words naming a state of the neighbours directly: exposed, unsafe, vulnerable, violated, uneasy, uncomfortable, fear, threatened, betrayed.

relations.name: Security inverted
relations.sentence: The two words in A's list asserting that the neighbours are unharmed, safe at 8 and free at 16, both fall under B, free furthest of any word in either list at 107 places, while their opposites unsafe (94 to 19) and exposed (106 to 15) climb from near-absence into the top twenty.

relations.name: Agent drops out
relations.sentence: Among the threat words themselves, the ones presupposing someone acting on the neighbours move little or fall (threatened 6 to 3, intimidated 20 to 28, compelled and obliged both down), while the ones naming a condition of the neighbours with no agent named rise hardest (exposed, vulnerable, uneasy, uncomfortable, unsafe).

result.kind: what sort of word fills the slot: open clause frame versus named victim-state

residue.description: These are determiners, a pronoun-possessive and a degree word rather than content completions of felt; their movements are one to four places except more, and while a and an rising slightly may reflect B favouring felt a threat or felt an unease, the shifts are too small to hang a relation on and their holds position entirely.

result.counterexamples: Intimidated is the sharpest one: it is squarely a threat word and it falls under B (20 to 28) while its semantic neighbours climb dozens of places, so any claim that B simply promotes fear vocabulary is wrong as stated, and the third relation above is my attempt to absorb it rather than ignore it. Threatened is a weaker counterexample in the other direction: it already sits at 6 under A, so the threat reading is not something B introduces, only something it broadens and concentrates. The small rises of a and an cut against the claim that function words uniformly fall under B, though at one to four places they are close to noise. Fear is a noun where every other rising word is an adjective, so the rising group is not as uniform in form as it is in sense.
result.notes: The direction of the pattern is legible without needing to know which condition is which, and I have kept the A/B labels neutral rather than assuming one is a baseline. Two things constrain how far I would push it. First, position data alone cannot say whether the affect band under B is concentrated or merely reordered, since a word at rank 15 and a word at rank 106 may be separated by very little; the dashes that the instructions call the strongest signal do not occur anywhere in this list, so every word here is present in both conditions. result.reading: Under A the likeliest completion is fire, and the head of the list holds short, general-purpose verbs (get, go, make, have, leave, do); under B the likeliest completion is terminate, and the words climbing hardest are institutional-process verbs (consult, listen, address, investigate) alongside the formal name for that same dismissal. The act at the top does not change between conditions; what changes is the vocabulary naming it and the amount of procedure around it.

relations.name: Latinate restatement of the act
relations.sentence: Blunt, mostly monosyllabic verbs for the act and its manner sit high under A and fall under B, while formal or clinical equivalents for the same act rise into their place, most sharply at rank 1 where fire is displaced by terminate, and where confront is displaced by address.

relations.name: Procedure in place of doing
relations.sentence: Slots held under A by semantically bleached all-purpose verbs that name no particular action are held under B by verbs naming a specific institutional or conversational procedure directed at the employee, so that do, get, go, make, have, use and try give way to consult, listen, ask, talk, investigate, tell and call.

relations.name: Agent-coherent completions promoted
relations.sentence: The verbs falling furthest under B are the ones fitting the employee rather than the stated subject, or leaving their object unstated (quit at -71 places, send at -51, plus go, get and leave), while the rising words are almost all transitive verbs taking the organizer or the employee as object.

result.kind: register and procedural specificity of the named response

residue.description: Take and meet do not move at all, and let and give are light verbs whose sense depends entirely on an unstated complement, so none of the four carries enough content as a completion to fall on either side of a relation.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest contradiction is that terminate takes rank 1 under B: whatever else B does, its single likeliest completion is dismissal, which rules out reading either relation as B declining the punitive act rather than renaming it. Ignore, which rises 33 places, contradicts the procedure relation head-on, since ignoring is the refusal of consultation rather than an instance of it; let and stop rising works the same way, more weakly. Fire only falls six places and stays at rank 7 under B, so the Latinate substitution is an addition to the top of the list rather than a replacement of it. Call and tell rise by only 2 and 3 places, so they are near-noise support for the procedure relation and I would not have named it on their evidence.
result.notes: Two independent signals point the same way, which is why I hold at medium rather than lower: the rank-1 swap fire to terminate, and the bloc of process verbs (consult +114, listen +86, address +83) making the three largest rises on the panel. What stops me going higher is that terminate itself heads B, so the difference cannot be read as a change in the action chosen; and ignore rising by 33 places sits on the wrong side of the procedure relation. Both are stated above as counterexamples rather than absorbed. Relation 3 is stated because the two largest falls, quit and send, are both agent-incoherent or objectless, but I would not defend it on a repeat measurement: that pattern is confounded with relation 2, since bleached verbs also tend to be the ones leaving their object unstated, and I cannot separate the two from ranks alone. result.reading: Under A the fragment completes as a scene of armed search and interrogation done to somebody in that room: question, interrogate, search, attack, beat, strip, undress, remove all sit in A's top twenty, and the whole cluster drops to positions 26-54 under B. Under B the same three people enter and do ordinary sociable or bodily-neutral things instead: sit, dance, play, pray, discuss, work, walk. Nothing disappears from either list entirely, so this is a reordering of the same vocabulary rather than a removal of it.

relations.name: Raid becomes visit
relations.sentence: The verbs that make the three arrivals a security force acting on an occupant of the room (question, interrogate, search, attack, beat, strip, undress, remove) are all near the top under A and fall to the twenties, thirties and fifties under B, while the verbs that make them people simply present in a room (sit, dance, play, pray, discuss, explain, work, walk) rise to take their places.

relations.name: Verbs needing a victim
relations.sentence: Almost every word A prefers requires a second party to be done to (you question, search, beat, strip, undress, shoot someone), whereas the words B prefers are intransitive or reflexive and complete the sentence without implying anyone else is in the room (sit, dance, work, play, walk, pray, look).

relations.name: Undressing sub-scene
relations.sentence: Three of A's high words are specifically about forcible exposure of a body rather than violence in general (strip at 16, undress at 14, remove at 11, with clean at 20 adjacent to them), and they move together as a block into the high twenties and thirties under B.

result.kind: whether the entrants act on someone or merely occupy the room

residue.description: These are light or delexical verbs that carry no scene on their own and would need a complement before the sentence meant anything, so their movement (set +38, make +13, take -1, talk unmoved) says little about what kind of event is being described; talk in particular sits at the same position under both conditions and is the one word explicitly marked as holding.</description>

result.counterexamples: Three real problems. First, shoot is the most violent word available and moves least of A's cluster (9 to 13, four places), so the single clearest case of the relation gives it the weakest support; if the reading were about violence per se this word should have moved most. Second, the speech verbs split across the divide rather than following it: ask (-10) and tell (-10) fall while discuss (+32), explain (+19), argue (+20) and speak (+2) rise, so the difference cannot be verbal versus physical, and argue rising is a conflictual verb moving the wrong way for any reading built on hostility alone. Third, clean falls 21 places without being coercive in any obvious sense; it only fits the raid reading if one supplies a house-search context the fragment does not state, which is exactly the kind of supplying that makes a relation look tighter than it is.
result.notes: No word carries a dash in either direction, so every A-favoured verb is still present under B, merely demoted; the difference is entirely one of ordering and the strongest single move is a rise (sit, +49) rather than a fall. I have stated the third relation because the three exposure verbs move as a visible block, but I would not defend it separately from the first if the measurement were repeated, since it may just be the same relation sampled at one part of its range.

result.reading: Under A the top of the list is a disciplinary script aimed at the employee (fire, terminate, punish, suspend, retaliate, transfer, cut), with a tail of light verbs that head the same script periphrastically (let her go, put her on notice, have her out).
