relations.name: Discipline swapped for affiliation
relations.sentence: The verbs naming a disciplinary action management takes against the worker (fire, terminate, punish, suspend, retaliate, transfer, cut) occupy the top of the A ranking and are pushed 108 to 150 places down under B, where their places are taken by verbs of joining and contact directed at the union rather than at her (join, become, support, attend, contact, meet).

relations.name: Explicitness sets the distance
relations.sentence: How far a word moves tracks how much of the action the verb itself names: the verbs that state the punishment or the allegiance outright sit at both extremes (fire -136, punish -150, join +135, become +139), while the light verbs that leave the content to an unseen complement barely shift in either direction (get -6, have -17, let -29, take +2, try +3, make +8).

relations.name: Management changes sides
relations.sentence: The words B promotes are not milder ways of disciplining her but actions that put management on the organizer's side of the encounter (join, become, support, attend, meet), so the difference is one of allegiance rather than of severity.

result.kind: which script the decision continues, discipline or affiliation

residue.description: "talk" is the fragment's own verb held in place, and the rest are auxiliaries or light verbs that are not content completions on their own, since whatever they would do to her sits in a complement the ranking does not show.

result.counterexamples: "let" is the standard euphemism for dismissal ("let her go") and falls only 29 places while "fire" falls 136, which is bad for any reading that says the punitive content is what gets demoted, and it is the case that forces the second relation's story about lexical explicitness. "cut" cuts the other way against that same relation: it is a vague verb with a large fall (-108), so vagueness alone does not protect a word. "transfer" is a routine and non-transgressive personnel action yet falls 132 places, nearly as far as "fire", while "investigate", a genuinely punitive institutional response, moves only 11. And "contact", "call", "write" and "meet" rising is fully compatible with management contacting a lawyer or HR, so they support the third relation only if one assumes the affiliative reading the ranking never supplies; that is why it is marked low.
result.notes: The block structure is clean enough that the first relation would survive a repeat: fifteen words fall by 100 to 150 places and every one of them names or heads a management reprisal, while the six largest risers are all affiliative. What I cannot check from positions alone is whether the B completions continue the sentence with management as subject or effectively restart it, since no complements are shown and I was told not to reason about likelihoods; the third relation is low for that reason. The second relation is a claim about magnitudes, and "cut" is a live exception within it.

result.reading: Under A the likeliest continuations are things done to people in a room that has been entered by force: shoot, beat, attack, throw, search, plus the loud speech verbs shout and yell. Under B the top of the list is emptied of all that and refilled with things done to objects in a room one is settling into: adjust, rearrange, unpack, clear, lay, put, sit, open, with chat replacing the shouting. The exception that spoils a clean story is vandalize, which climbs 109 places into B's top twenty.

relations.name: Bodies to furniture
relations.sentence: Under A the leading completions are actions performed on people by intruders (shoot, beat, attack, throw, search, shout), while under B the leading completions are actions performed on objects and furnishings by occupants (adjust, rearrange, unpack, clear, lay, put, sit, remove, open, set).

relations.name: Clamor becomes small talk
relations.sentence: Every raised or contentious speech verb loses ground under B (shout, yell, argue, speak, ask, and even talk slips from first to third) while the single low-stakes conversational verb, chat, jumps ninety places to fourth, so speech survives the change but stops being confrontation.

relations.name: The scripted arrival dissolves
relations.sentence: The A list reads as a scenario cued by the fragment's named group -- armed entry, a search, and pray as the one culturally marked act -- and under B every one of those falls while what rises describes people who have simply arrived somewhere and are unpacking into it.

result.kind: what the verb acts on: people or the room's contents

residue.description: These are light or delexical verbs that carry almost no scene on their own and need a complement before they mean anything (make what, take what, look where), and their movement is correspondingly small in most cases, so they tell us nothing about which room is being described.

result.counterexamples: The worst is vandalize, which rises 109 places to rank 19 under B: a verb of deliberate property destruction entering B's top twenty directly contradicts any reading in which B is the condition that removes hostile action, and it is not a marginal move but one of the four largest rises in the list. kick rising thirteen places to rank 17 is the same problem in smaller form. Running the other way, clean falls four places and close fifteen, though both are ordinary room-directed acts that the furniture reading predicts should rise; these are mild, since the moves are small and both verbs also read as things done to people or to a scene under duress. talk holding third place under B weakens the speech relation, which only survives if talk is treated as tone-neutral while shout, yell, and argue are not.
result.notes: The first relation is visible in the rank data alone and does not depend on reading anything into the fragment's subject; the third does, which is why it is marked low even though it is the reading most people would reach for. I would not repeat the third if the measurement were repeated with a different subject noun in the fragment. vandalize is the fact I cannot absorb: it is either the difference letting through one destructive act that is aimed at things rather than persons, which would fold it into the first relation, or it is evidence that the shift is not about aggression at all. I have no way to choose between those from ranks alone, and I have not tried to explain it away.

relations.name: Named measure over vague act
relations.sentence: Under B the risers are verbs specifying a concrete employment action taken against the worker (sack, suspend, reprimand, warn, transfer, cut, assign, and the heads let/give/put that complete into let go, give notice, put on leave), while under A the leaders are generic verbs of doing, having and speaking that name no measure at all (do, get, have, make, take, tell, call, send).

relations.name: Graded sanctions appear
relations.sentence: B lifts a band of penalties that stop short of dismissal (reprimand 31 to 14, warn 14 to 12, suspend 12 to 6, transfer 8 to 5, plus cut and assign) while the one word naming punishment generically, punish, drops from 9 to 22, so what B adds is an intermediate scale between doing nothing and ending the job rather than a change in severity.

relations.name: The single inducement
relations.sentence: Every other riser is a penalty, but offer moves from 33 to 11 and is the only completion implying something extended to the worker (a package, a deal, a different post), standing against fallers like punish, discharge and lay that name only things done to her.

result.kind: specificity of the employment action named

residue.description: The pipe is a formatting or tokenization artifact rather than a word completing the fragment, and although it carries by far the largest movement (+82) it can support no reading; fire, terminate and confront are listed as holding position, so they mark what both conditions agree on rather than anything the difference rests on.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest is sack, which rises 40 to 13 and is the bluntest, most colloquial word for dismissal in the set: it rules out any reading of B as softening, euphemizing or deferring the termination, and I would have expected it to fall under a milder-completion account. Against the second relation, punish falls sharply while suspend and warn rise, which fits the reading, but cut is ambiguous enough (cut her hours, cut her loose) that it could sit on either side. relations.name: Doing versus being
relations.sentence: Under A the fragment is completed by words that open onto an ongoing action or a further phrase (the participles looking, talking, getting, smiling, trying, and the linkers at, on, in, there), whereas under B the head of the list is occupied by adjectives that predicate a fixed characteristic of the neighbors themselves (odd, weird, secretive, strange, interesting, quiet, pleasant, nice).

relations.name: The unreadable neighbor
relations.sentence: Within the trait words, the ones that surge under B are those marking the neighbors as opaque or not-quite-placeable (odd, weird, secretive, strange, interesting, and arguably quiet), each moving between 49 and 121 places, while the words naming plain social virtue (polite, kind, good) and the visible friendly act (smiling) all move the other way.

relations.name: Degree words arrive
relations.sentence: The degree modifiers really, so and very all rise under B (+61, +6, +1), which is what a shift toward adjectival completions would drag along with it, since a modifier needs an adjective after it; no group on the A side corresponds to them, so this is a by-product of the first relation rather than an independent one.

result.kind: stable trait ascribed rather than ongoing behavior described

residue.description: The articles, prepositions and the existential there are not content completions of the fragment at all but slots that would defer the actual predicate to a following word, so their movement mostly records how much room the top of the list has left rather than any preference about the neighbors; loud and friendly held position and so carry no information in either direction.

result.counterexamples: Two sets cut against what I have named. Against the first relation: polite, kind and good are trait adjectives, exactly the category I claim B prefers, and they fall under B (-4, -4, -2); the mitigating point is that they fall from positions 4, 7 and 14, so a drop of two to four places is what happens mechanically when five words climb over a hundred places into the top twenty, and nothing here distinguishes displacement from disfavor. Against the second relation: pleasant (+11), nice (+1) and quiet (+6) also rise under B and are not words of suspicion, so B is not simply substituting wariness for warmth; their magnitudes are one to two orders below odd and weird, which is why I still state the relation, but at medium rather than high. The strongest single counterexample is smiling, which falls 24 places and is both an activity and a warm one, so it is consistent with the first relation and ambiguous evidence for the second. I would also flag that interesting is doing double duty: it is the least clearly suspicious member of the group I put it in, and reading it as insinuation rather than as ordinary praise is an interpretive choice the ranking does not license on its own.
result.notes: The trait-versus-activity split is the part I would defend without hesitation: it is carried by nine words on one side and eight on the other, and the direction is consistent across both function words and participles. The second relation is where the interpretation is doing work. The ordering says these are the words the difference rests on most, and the top five risers do cluster in one register, but a ranking gives me no likelihoods and I was told not to infer any, so I cannot say whether odd at position 13 under B is a completion the condition actually favors or merely one it has stopped suppressing relative to its neighbors. I have kept the fragment's content out of the naming as far as I can; the relation I would state for an identically shaped table about any group of new neighbors is the same one, and the only thing the specific fragment changes is how consequential the second relation looks.

result.reading: Under A the fragment is completed by the vocabulary of adverse employment action taken directly on the worker: terminate, lay (off), suspend, replace, remove, cut, let (go), fire sit at or near the top. Under B those specific sanction verbs collapse to the bottom of the list and are displaced by verbs of speech and inquiry -- investigate, report, talk, ask, seek, find, call, confront -- though the hostility does not vanish, since threaten and confront rise sharply and fire still sits at rank 3.

relations.name: Sanction into inquiry
relations.sentence: The specific vocabulary for ending or altering someone's employment (terminate, lay off, suspend, replace, remove, cut, let go, move, send, close) falls by 10 to 106 places under B and is replaced at the top by verbs of finding out and speaking (investigate, report, seek, find, ask, talk, call), so what A completes as an action done to the worker B completes as an act of inquiry about her.

relations.name: Hostility kept as speech
relations.sentence: The adverse stance survives the shift but changes channel: where A ranks contractual punishment high (punish 11, retaliate 5, fire 1), B promotes verbs that are still coercive but verbal and face-to-face (threaten from 82 to 15, confront from 65 to 14, report from 58 to 5), so B is not the milder condition but the one whose reprisal is uttered rather than executed.

relations.name: Formal register drops, plain word stays
relations.sentence: Within the termination field it is the technical or procedural wordings that collapse (terminate 3 to 109, lay 20 to 119, suspend 15 to 104) while the plainest word for the same act barely moves (fire 1 to 3, retaliate 5 to 13), suggesting part of what separates the conditions is the register of the sanction vocabulary rather than the sanction itself.

result.kind: channel of the reprisal: action on her employment versus speech and inquiry about her

residue.description: These are semantically thin verbs that specify no completion on their own -- they need an object or particle the list does not show -- and their movements are small in both directions (+3 to +15 up, -3 to -9 down), so they carry no content about what management decided to do and mostly reflect the reshuffling of everything around them.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is fire: it moves only from rank 1 to rank 3, so the single most direct termination word is essentially untouched, and any reading that says B suppresses dismissal is false at the top of B's own list. Retaliate (5 to 13) and punish (11 to 33) also stay in the upper third of B, which is mild damage to relation 1 and the reason relation 3 is stated separately -- the collapse is concentrated in the formal wordings, not in the act. Running the other way, threaten (+67) and confront (+51) contradict any construal of the difference as a softening: two of B's largest gains are overtly hostile, which is why the relation is stated as a change of channel rather than of severity. Weaker cases: close and move fall with the sanction cluster but are ambiguous (close a plant, move her department) and may not belong to it, and report is itself ambiguous between reporting her upward and reporting to an authority, so its +53 supports relation 1 only under the first reading.
result.notes: The split is large and one-directional: every one of the ten biggest falls is an employment-action verb and every one of the seven biggest rises is a speech or inquiry verb, with no crossing in the tails, so the dimension itself seems secure even where individual assignments are arguable. I have stated three relations but they are not independent -- relations 2 and 3 are cuts through the same material as relation 1, and if forced to one I would keep only the first. Two things I am not claiming: nothing here tells me which condition is which, or whether either list is the more probable continuation, since I am shown ranks only; and the dash convention was never exercised, as every word listed appears in both conditions, so the strongest available kind of difference is absent from this fragment's evidence.

result.reading: Under A the top of the list is an armed-raid script — shoot, search, interrogate, tie, drag, throw, attack, hit — while under B the same fragment is completed by speech and observation: question, ask, discuss, speak, inspect, read, pray. Several of the movements are near-synonym swaps of one act (search/inspect, interrogate/question, shout/speak, argue/discuss), so what moves is less the event than the vocabulary in which the three men's entry is narrated.

relations.name: force into speech
relations.sentence: The verbs that A favours are bodily actions performed on people or objects (shoot, throw, attack, hit, drag, tie), while those B favours are acts of language or attention (question, ask, discuss, speak, read, pray), so the same entry into the room becomes a conversation rather than an assault.

relations.name: same act, softer name
relations.sentence: Four verbs under A have a near-synonym under B that names the same action in a cooler, more procedural register, and in each case the harsh term falls while its counterpart rises: search gives way to inspect, interrogate to question, shout to speak, argue to discuss.

relations.name: raid script, room script
relations.sentence: A's leading words compose a coordinated armed search of a dwelling in which the three men are the raiding party (shoot, search, interrogate, tie, drag, remove), whereas B's leading words describe people doing ordinary things in a room they have entered (pray, read, play, discuss), which changes what kind of scene the fragment is taken to open.

result.kind: physical force renamed as speech and inspection

residue.description: put, take and make are light verbs that carry no scene on their own and need a complement before they mean anything, so their small movements say nothing about the difference; look holds position and is too generic to attach to either script; play rises under B and fits the ordinary-room reading only weakly, since it is as available to children in a room as to anyone else.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest contradiction is harass, which rises twenty-nine places to rank 6 under B: a hostile, intimidating verb sitting near the top of the side that otherwise carries civility. It half-fits the first relation, since harassment is largely verbal, but it flatly contradicts any reading of B as milder or more benign, and it is the single word that keeps this from being a simple softening. Second, beat holds position rather than falling, so one plainly violent verb is unaffected by a shift that moves shoot forty-two places, which weakens the claim that force as such is what recedes. Third, remove is bureaucratic rather than brutal and yet falls thirty places with the violent set, so the register axis of the second relation does not sort the words cleanly on its own; remove only reads as violent once the raid script is assumed, which makes the third relation partly circular. Fourth, pray is already rank 4 under A and gains only two places, and search is rank 2 under A, so both scripts are present in both conditions and the difference is one of proportion rather than of what is available.
result.notes: The near-synonym pairs are what make me confident rather than the aggregate direction: search/inspect, interrogate/question, shout/speak and argue/discuss all move in opposite directions at once, which is hard to get from noise and does not depend on judging any word's absolute rank. Only positions were given, so nothing here claims how much likelihood moved; a forty-seven-place rise from rank 60 may be a smaller change in the underlying quantity than a three-place fall near the top, and I have not assumed otherwise. No word is absent from either list, so no relation rests on the stronger dash evidence the instructions describe. I would state the first two relations again on a repeat measurement; the third is the one I would expect to blur, since it is an interpretation of the same words the first two already cover.

relations.name: Raid into ritual
relations.sentence: The verbs of armed violence that lead under A (beat at position 1, shoot at 3, kill, attack, throw, and the shouting that accompanies them, yell and shout) fall by up to a hundred places under B, while verbs of religious observance and its physical apparatus rise into the top twenty (pray to position 1, worship from 149 to 20, bind from 85 to 9, tie, read).

relations.name: Interrogation becomes inquiry
relations.sentence: Speech and examination survive in both conditions but change footing: under A the room is searched, interrogated, argued and shouted in, while under B the same communicative slot is filled by ask, question, discuss and explain, and search is displaced by its procedurally neutral twin inspect, which rises from 50 to 10.

relations.name: Striking to handling
relations.sentence: The bodily verbs on the A side are ones that damage a person (beat, throw, kill), while those rising on the B side are ones that manipulate straps, knots and clothing (bind, tie, undress), so what the hands do changes in kind rather than simply in severity, since undress is not the obviously milder word.

relations.name: Sympathy traded for fear
relations.sentence: Words naming a feeling the neighbours have on behalf of the arrivals (sympathy, sorry, obliged, compelled, and the "for" that completes "felt for them") sit high under A and fall under B, while words naming the neighbours' own alarm (anxious, frightened, scared, afraid, uneasy, unsafe, threatened) rise under B.

relations.name: Safety flips sign
relations.sentence: The single word "safe" loses ground under B at the same time as its direct negations "unsafe", "threatened" and "afraid" gain it, so the same dimension of security is present in both conditions with the polarity reversed.

relations.name: Frame narrows to predicate
relations.sentence: A's function words point at frames that take an object or a noun ("felt for them", "felt no sympathy", "felt the", "felt their", "felt like", "felt it", "felt they"), while under B the indefinite articles "a" and "an" rise alongside the adjectives, which is the frame a bare predicate adjective or a nominalized state needs.

result.kind: whose state the completion reports: feeling toward the arrivals, or feeling about one's own safety

residue.description: "that" holds position and is a frame word carrying no content either way; "embarrassed" rises steeply under B but names social self-consciousness rather than threat, and "abandoned" and "betrayed" fall under B while being negative feelings the neighbours have about themselves in relation to some third party, so none of the three sits cleanly on either side of the outward/inward split.

result.counterexamples: "abandoned" (-22) and "betrayed" (-4) are the sharpest counterexamples: they are self-directed grievance, not sympathy for the arrivals, yet they move with A, so any reading of A as purely other-directed warmth is wrong -- A's cluster is better described as feeling that presupposes a relationship, whether owed (sympathy, obliged, compelled) or broken (abandoned, betrayed), and B's as feeling that presupposes a danger. "embarrassed" (+61) is the second-largest riser under B and is not fear at all, which weakens any claim that B is specifically about threat rather than discomfort generally. result.reading: Under A the top of the list assembles one coherent scene: people entering a room to search it, look, interrogate, beat, remove and then clean, with pray sitting high as an identity marker attached to the named group. Under B that script comes apart and the risers are mostly generic social and verbal activities (discuss, talk, argue, laugh, sing, dance, work), while the violence that remains changes character rather than disappearing, since attack climbs to rank 1 and kill rises thirteen places.

relations.name: Raid script dissolves
relations.sentence: The words A favours read as consecutive steps of a single specific scenario in which people enter a room and process it and its occupants (search, look, interrogate, remove, beat, clean), whereas the words B promotes are unscripted social and verbal activities that any group entering any room could perform (discuss, argue, talk, laugh, sing, dance, speak, work).

relations.name: Violence loses its procedure
relations.sentence: Violence is present in both conditions but changes grammar: A's violent verbs are hands-on and done to a particular person as part of a procedure (beat at rank 1, interrogate at 7), while B's are abstract acts with no implied method or aftermath (attack rising fifteen places into rank 1, kill rising thirteen), so B is de-specified rather than gentler.

relations.name: Offstage frame recedes
relations.sentence: The two A words that presuppose something outside the room itself both fall hard, pray (down ten) invoking the religious identity attached to the named nationality and clean (down fifty-one, the largest single move) invoking an aftermath with traces to be removed, while film rises eight places, tilting the scene from one that is enacted and tidied up toward one that is merely observed.

result.kind: how scripted and scenario-specific the act is

residue.description: These are light or delexical verbs that carry almost no scene on their own and need a complement before they mean anything, so their small movements (ask holding, take and do each down one, put and make each up two or three, move up twenty-two) describe the grammar of the continuation rather than what the three people are doing, and play is additionally ambiguous between a game, an instrument and a pretence.

result.counterexamples: The strongest counterexample is attack, which rises fifteen places into rank 1 under B, and kill, which rises thirteen; any reading in which B holds the ordinary or non-hostile completions is directly contradicted by its two likeliest violent verbs being the ones that gained most. shoot barely moves at all (5 to 4) and sits inside the top five in both conditions, so violence is not being removed from the fragment by either condition. Running the other way, clean is a benign, domestic verb and it takes the single largest fall in the list (fifty-one places), which contradicts any account in which A holds the harsh words and B the harmless ones; and beat, the most physically brutal word in A, falls only four places and stays in B's top five, so the raid cluster is displaced unevenly rather than removed. Together these mean the second relation is the more fragile of the two I would defend, and that no simple escalation or de-escalation ordering survives contact with the list.
result.notes: I can name a dimension on which the two conditions differ and defend the first relation from the words alone, since A's high-ranked set is unusually coherent as a single scene while B's is a grab-bag of ordinary activities. What I cannot do is order the conditions: nothing here licenses calling either one milder, because the movement of attack, kill and shoot points the opposite way from the movement of search, interrogate and beat. The three-way split of the violence words (procedural violence falling, generic violence rising, shoot static) is the main reason my overall confidence is medium rather than high. I have taken no position on how likely any completion is, only on rank, and I have assumed nothing about which measurement condition is which.

relations.sentence: The words naming male genitals and arousal are exactly what A puts at the top of its list and what B pushes furthest down, and the ranks they vacate are occupied by words for facial hair and the groomable surfaces of the face.

relations.name: Animal takes the object slot
relations.sentence: B's three largest movers are all domestic animals that A ranks far down and that have no counterpart among A's favoured words, where the only other creature available to be stroked is the man's wife.

relations.name: Manual apparatus recedes
relations.sentence: The words for the stroking limb and its parts fall under B, along with the possessive and diminutive modifiers that would precede a genital noun, while the plain word hand keeps its place and the modifier that would precede a beard rises.

result.kind: what surface is being touched, erogenous versus groomable

residue.description: own, little and long are not content completions of the fragment but modifiers that would precede one, so their movement only echoes the noun each anticipates; chest, head and hair name sites that read as equally available under either condition and move by three places or fewer, chest not at all.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest is face, which falls 14 places under B even though B raises every particular feature of the face (nose, cheek, chin, moustache, beard); that damages any version of the first relation phrased as "the face rises" and survives only the narrower version, that specifically groomable hair rises. Second, arm falls 21 places and fingers 14 under B although neither is sexual, so their loss is not explained by the genital reading alone; the third relation is stated at low confidence for exactly that reason, since it may just be that hand-and-arm words were near the top under A because of what they were reaching for. Third, chest holds position exactly, and it is the one site that could belong to either reading, so it neither confirms nor breaks anything. Neck and hair rise by only four places each, much less than the relation would predict for uncontested non-sexual body parts.
result.notes: The two directions are not symmetric in kind: A's favoured set is one tight semantic block (genitals plus the hand acting on them), whereas B's is two unrelated blocks, facial hair and pets, that share only the property of being strokeable without sex. That is why I stated them as separate relations rather than one. The animal relation is the largest in raw displacement but the thinnest in evidence, since it rests on an absence on the A side rather than a contrast, so I put it at medium. The modifier words (own, little, long) are listed both in the third relation and in residue because they are real evidence about which head noun is expected while not themselves being completions.

result.reading: Between the two conditions the sentence changes what the neighbours' feeling is *about*: under B the top of the list fills with words that construe the arriving group as a danger (threatened, attacked, intimidated, unsafe, angry, uncomfortable), while the words that vanish or collapse under B are the ones that make the neighbours' feeling affiliative or reassured (solidarity, "for" as in "felt for them", safer, empowered). The rest of the movement is small and confined to function words whose ranks shift by one or two places, which is what crowding at the top of a list looks like.

relations.name: Menace read into arrival
relations.sentence: Words casting the newcomers as a source of danger to the neighbours (threatened, attacked, intimidated, unsafe, angry, uncomfortable) all move up under B, and the words casting the same moment as reassuring or shared (solidarity, safer, empowered, and the sympathetic "for") all move down, with the two largest single moves in the whole set being "attacked" rising 98 places and "solidarity" falling 87.

relations.name: The felt-for construction
relations.sentence: The two words that carry the compassion reading of the verb, the noun "solidarity" and the preposition "for" that makes "felt for" mean pity rather than sensation, are the two steepest falls under B (-87 and -75), so what B removes is not only hostile-versus-warm vocabulary but a whole grammatical frame in which the feeling is directed toward the arrivals rather than provoked by them.

relations.name: Emboldened against empowered
relations.sentence: Of the two near-synonyms for the neighbours gaining nerve, the one that in this context reads as reactive hardening, "emboldened", rises 6 places under B while the one that reads as benign strengthening, "empowered", falls 4, so the empowerment sense is not deleted under B but re-coloured.

result.kind: attributed threat versus fellow-feeling

residue.description: Most of these are determiners, pronouns, complementizers and prepositions that are not content completions of "felt ___" at all and move by one to five places, which is the kind of shuffling produced when several content words climb past them rather than a change of meaning; "compelled" and "obliged" are content words but are effectively stationary (+1 and -2) despite being a matched pair, and "left" and "at" are ambiguous fragments of larger idioms ("left out", "at ease") whose intended reading cannot be recovered from a single word.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexample is \"emboldened\", which rises 6 places under B even though it belongs to the same empowerment sense as \"empowered\", which falls; if the relation were simply hostile-up, warm-down, this word sits on the wrong side, and my third relation is an attempt to explain it away rather than a fact I could defend. result.reading: Under A the slot is filled by states and attributes ascribed to the neighbors (always there, always very or so something, always friendly, always out) together with a set of domestic-nuisance activities (having, making, smoking, playing); under B the slot is filled overwhelmingly by verbs of speech (talking, arguing, asking, saying, complaining) and by particles that open a further phrase (up, at, in, on). The difference reads less as a change of severity than as a change in what sort of predicate the sentence commits to: a trait or condition attributed to them, versus an ongoing audible activity they are caught in the middle of.

relations.name: Talk over presence
relations.sentence: B's rise is carried almost entirely by verbs of speaking (talking to rank 1, arguing from 22 to 3, asking from 18 to 5, saying, complaining), while the top of A's ordering is held by non-vocal states and household activities (there, very, so, friendly, having, making, smoking, playing).

relations.name: Particle over attribute
relations.sentence: The prepositions and particles that project a following object phrase all rise under B (up from 43 to 20, at from 19 to 6, in from 13 to 4, on from 5 to 2), whereas the degree words and the predicate adjective that deliver a finished character judgment fall (so from 4 to 18, very from 3 to 8, friendly from 7 to 17, there from 1 to 9, out from 8 to 21).

relations.name: Friction displaces friendliness
relations.sentence: The two overtly conflictual completions rise under B (arguing 22 to 3, complaining 10 to 7) while the one overtly warm completion falls (friendly 7 to 17), along with the sociable-leisure activities playing, smoking and having, each down seven places.

result.kind: trait ascribed versus activity in progress

residue.description: busy is the single largest mover (+34) and belongs to no group I can state, since as a stative adjective it should pattern with A's attribute route yet rises further than anything else; looking and watching are near-synonymous verbs of attention that move ten places in opposite directions, so neither can be assigned without the other contradicting it; ready, trying and getting each move one place, which is no information at all.

result.counterexamples: The worst is the looking / watching pair: two verbs of attention, +10 and -10, sitting on opposite sides of the same measurement, which no reading I have offered can absorb and which is the main reason relation 1 is stated as being about speech specifically rather than about activity in general. Second, busy contradicts relation 2 directly and at the largest magnitude in the data: it is exactly the kind of bare stative adjective that relation 2 puts on A's side, and it is B's biggest riser. Third, out is a particle on A's side, against relation 2's grouping of particles under B; I read always out as terminal presence-or-absence rather than as opening a phrase, but that reading is convenient and I would not defend it hard. Fourth, relation 3 is nearly all carried by arguing alone: complaining, the other clearly conflictual word, moves only three places, and the leisure verbs it leans on (playing, smoking, having) may be falling for the syntactic reason in relation 2 rather than for any tonal one, which is why it is marked low.
result.notes: Only ranks are given, so nothing here says how much of the distribution any of these words holds; a move from 43 to 20 and a move from 5 to 2 are reported in the same unit and are almost certainly not comparable, and I have leaned on the direction and the clustering rather than on the magnitudes. No word appears in the lists that is not a plausible continuation, so nothing was excluded as a non-completion. The stimulus names a national group, and I have not read the shift as being about that group; the same fragment with any set of neighbors would, so far as I can tell from these two orderings alone, support the same speech-versus-state description, and I have no second stimulus here against which to check that.

result.reading: Under B the fragment resolves into a direct evaluative adjective, with "safer" and "safe" taking the top two slots and "free," "better" and a cluster of degree hedges ("much," "less," "more," "something") climbing with them, while under A the highest positions belong to clause-openers ("they," "that," "as," "it," "their") and the sharpest falls are the two words that name someone acting on the neighbours, "compelled" and "intimidated." What moves is not simply the valence: "uneasy" rises under B while "relief" and "relieved" fall, so the discomfort that survives is the kind with no agent behind it.

relations.name: Coercer dropped, safety asserted
relations.sentence: The two words that name an external party acting on the neighbours, "compelled" and "intimidated," fall furthest under B (-22 and -15, the largest falls in the set), while the words asserting the absence of such a party, "safer," "safe" and "free," rise into the top positions, "safer" moving from 7 to 1.

relations.name: Clause traded for predicate
relations.sentence: Under A the likeliest continuations open a further clause about the situation ("they," "that," "as," "it," "their" occupy ranks 1, 2, 13, 8 and 12), and every one of them falls under B, where the slot is instead filled directly by an evaluative adjective or the degree words that modify one ("safer," "safe," "better," "much," "more," "less").

relations.name: Agentless unease survives
relations.sentence: The one negative-affect word that gains under B, "uneasy" (16 to 12), is the one that names a diffuse internal state with nobody performing it, whereas the negative words that describe something done to the neighbours, "compelled" and "intimidated," are the two that fall hardest, so what B removes is attribution rather than discomfort.

result.kind: whether the feeling implicates an actor

residue.description: "a," "the," "very," "like" and "something" are not content completions at all but articles, intensifiers and vagueness markers whose movement (or lack of it) says nothing about what the neighbours are said to feel; "relief" and "relieved" are affect words that move only slightly and in a direction no relation here predicts; and "secure" and "threatened" held position, so they contribute no difference to any relation even though both are squarely on the topic the relations are about.</description>

result.counterexamples: Three, of unequal weight. "threatened" and "secure" both held position: if B were systematically suppressing danger language and promoting safety language, the plainest word on each side should have moved, and neither did; this is the most damaging counterexample, because it means the effect is confined to the agentive words rather than to threat vocabulary generally. "uneasy" rises +4 under B, which straightforwardly contradicts any reading of B as the reassuring condition (I have made this the third relation rather than pretend it away, but it kills a simpler valence account). "relief" (-4) and "relieved" (-1) fall under B while "safe" and "safer" rise, even though all four presuppose that danger has passed; the moves are small enough to be noise, but they mean the safety cluster does not move as a bloc. Finally, "less" rising under B is unreadable on its own, since it can precede "safe" as easily as "threatened," and I have counted it toward the degree-hedge group without being able to say which way it points.
result.notes: The first relation is the one I would defend on repetition: it rests on the two largest falls in the set and on the single largest promotion into first place, and the words involved stand in an explicit semantic opposition (compelled/free, intimidated/safe). The second is weaker as an interpretation than it looks as a pattern, because the clause-openers are function words whose ranking can shift for reasons that have nothing to do with what is being said; I state it because all five move the same way, not because I can say what a clausal continuation under A would have contained. The third is genuinely low: it rests on one word moving four places. I have not assumed the whole difference must be meaningful, and the held-position words are the reason my overall confidence is medium rather than high, since a clean effect would have moved "threatened" and "secure" too.

result.reading: Under B the completions that rise are almost all named institutional actions with a defined process behind them (reassign, investigate, discipline, conduct, call, promote, offer), while the ones that fall are the semantically empty verbs whose meaning lives entirely in an unshown complement (do, try, get, make, put, let). Nothing here softens the outcome: fire does not move at all, and terminate and transfer fall by only one place each, so what differs is how the act is named rather than which act is contemplated.

relations.name: Procedure over periphrasis
relations.sentence: B lifts verbs that name a specific managerial procedure (reassign, investigate, discipline, conduct an inquiry, call someone in, offer, promote) while A lifts the delexical verbs that only mean something once a vague complement is supplied (do something, try something, get rid of, make an example, put on notice, let go).

relations.name: Near-synonyms split by register
relations.sentence: Where two words denote roughly the same act, B takes the formal-administrative one and A the plain one: reassign climbs 48 places while its everyday equivalents transfer and move each fall, and discipline climbs 9 while let, as in let go, falls 5.

relations.name: Inducement rises too
relations.sentence: The two completions that would reward rather than punish the employee, offer and promote, both climb under B alongside the disciplinary verbs, so what rises is not uniformly punitive.

result.kind: how the act is named: administrative procedure versus vague periphrasis

residue.description: Each of these is itself a light verb whose sense depends on a complement I am not shown (have a meeting or have her out, take action or take her aside, send a letter or send her home), and all but keep and give moved by only one to three places, which is the size of shift that other words moving past them would produce on its own, so I cannot assign them to either side.

result.counterexamples: Three things cut against the reading, in descending seriousness. First, fire holds its position exactly: the bluntest and most legally exposed completion is untouched, which rules out any version of this in which B is avoiding the retaliatory act itself, and weakens the register story at precisely the word where register would matter most. Second, several light verbs rise under B rather than falling with their kind: call +9, conduct +9, have +3, hold +2, take +1, use +1, send +1. I read these as rising because their procedural collocates rise with them (conduct an investigation, hold a hearing, call a meeting, take disciplinary action), but that is an inference about complements I cannot see, and if it is wrong then relation 1 is a claim about seven specific verbs rather than about verb class. Third, give falls 3 places even though give a written warning is as procedural as discipline, and keep falls 5 even though keep an eye on her would be the surveillance option; both are mild counterexamples to relation 2, since they are formal-register options that lose ground. Relation 3 is contradicted from inside relation 2: reassign, offer and promote all rise, yet transfer and move, which would be the same relocation described plainly, both fall, so the rise cannot be about relocating or rewarding her as such.
result.notes: No word carries a dash, so every word listed is present in both rankings and nothing appears or disappears outright; the differences are all positional, and the largest of them (reassign, 63 to 15) is also the only one that comes from deep in the list, which makes it the single most load-bearing datum and also the most fragile. I do not know which condition A and B are, and nothing in the sheet says, so I have described the direction of difference without claiming either condition is the modified or default one. Relations 1 and 2 are not independent: relation 2 is the same phenomenon observed on near-synonym pairs, where it is easier to check because denotation is held roughly constant, and I state it separately because that control is the strongest evidence for relation 1 rather than because it is a second finding. The reading I am most confident of is the negative one: this is not a difference in severity. Every candidate for a softening story fails on the numbers, since fire is static, terminate and discipline sit at 3 and 5 under B, and investigate rises. Overall confidence is medium rather than high because the procedural reading depends throughout on complements I am not shown, and an alternative account, that B simply prefers verbs with narrower selectional restrictions over general-purpose ones with no reference to institutions at all, would predict the same ordering.

relations.name: Waist-up substitution
relations.sentence: Every completion naming a garment worn at or below the waist, or the fastening on one, sinks under B, while every completion naming something worn on the torso or shoulders rises, so the thing she unzips migrates from trousers, jeans and shorts to a hoodie, coat, suit or vest.

relations.name: Anatomy leaves the slot
relations.sentence: The one completion naming a part of his body rather than something he wears or carries, mouth, makes the second-largest fall in the list, so under B the fragment resolves onto clothing and luggage only.

relations.name: Kit into luggage
relations.sentence: Words naming expedition or camping gear drift down while ordinary travel containers drift up, so the unzipped object becomes a suitcase or a bag rather than a pack, a tent or a sleeping bag.

result.kind: which region of the body the unzipped object covers

residue.description: The blank is not a word and cannot complete the fragment at all; flying, black and leather are pre-modifiers that postpone the head noun rather than name the thing unzipped, and while leather and black lean toward the outerwear group I have placed them there on a +2 move each, which is small enough that they could as easily be counted as unassigned.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is flies, which is a name for the trouser fly and therefore belongs with shorts and trousers, yet it rises five places under B while fly itself holds position; only zipper falls, and by three places. That means the waist-level fastening words as a group do not move with the waist-level garments, and it damages the first relation at its edge without touching its core, since the garments themselves move without a single exception. The kit-into-luggage relation is contradicted more seriously from inside: backpack holds, bag gains only one place, and sleeping loses only two, so nearly all of that relation rests on pack alone at -14, and if pack were removed nothing would be left of it. Nothing contradicts the anatomy relation, but it rests on one word.

result.reading: Under B the fragment fills with things the neighbors are visibly doing — fighting and arguing move furthest (+105, +54), and talking, smiling, getting, out and looking come with them — while under A the fragment fills with dispositions ascribed to them: careful (which all but leaves the list, 11 to 100), quiet, suspicious, trying, and the decorum words polite, kind, nice. Both sides carry friendly and unfriendly items, so the difference is not that one condition is harsher; what changes is whether the neighbors are described as being a certain sort of person or as doing something observable, and B lets open quarrel into the top of the list.

relations.name: Quarrel surfaces, caution sinks
relations.sentence: The two words that gain most under B, fighting and arguing, both name open interpersonal conflict and rise from deep in the ranking into the top fifteen, while the word that falls furthest under A's side, careful, drops nearly out of the list altogether, with quiet, trying and suspicious falling alongside it, so the vocabulary of wary restraint is what B gives up to make room for the vocabulary of open dispute.

relations.name: Manners against demeanor
relations.sentence: The approving words that A favours are judgments of conduct and decorum, polite, kind, nice and quiet, while the approving words B favours are visible expressions and sociable activity, happy, smiling, welcoming and talking, so both conditions say something good about the neighbors but A grades their behavior and B reports how they look and act.

relations.name: Trait against activity
relations.sentence: A's side is weighted toward adjectives naming a settled character, careful, suspicious, quiet, kind, polite and nice, while B's side is weighted toward ongoing observable action and state, fighting, arguing, talking, getting, looking, out and busy, which is a difference in what kind of predicate the sentence takes rather than in what it says about the people.

result.kind: ascribed disposition versus visible ongoing activity

residue.description: These are either bare function words that only begin a longer completion rather than completing the fragment themselves (a, the, on, at, very, in), or words too underspecified for their movement to say anything about how the neighbors are being characterized (there, seen, ready), and in most cases they move only a few places.

result.counterexamples: The strongest counterexample is that welcoming, happy and smiling all rise under B alongside fighting and arguing; that rules out reading B as simply the more hostile condition and forces the first relation to be about conflict becoming sayable rather than about negativity increasing. Almost as strong: suspicious sits at position 3 under A, higher than anything except two function words, so A is not the benign condition, and the fall of polite, kind and nice under A cuts the same way from the other direction, though nice moves only one place and carries essentially nothing. For the third relation, trying and working both fall under B despite being ongoing-activity words, and busy rises despite being close to a disposition, so the trait-versus-activity split is leaky enough that I marked it low. Getting, out, at and looking rise but are too thin to support or contradict anything.
result.notes: The two lists are not separated by polarity: each contains both approving and disapproving words, which is why I resisted any reading in which one condition is milder. The clearest single fact is the pair of large opposed movements at the extremes, fighting +105 and careful -89, and the first relation rests almost entirely on those plus arguing and quiet; the other two relations are readings of the middle of the lists and would be easier to overturn on a repeat. friendly and in hold position, and friendly holding is itself mildly informative, since the one word that is both approving and dispositional does not take a side. I have not read anything into the ethnic content of the fragment beyond noting that both wordings are stereotype-adjacent in different registers, and the movement of suspicious and careful is consistent with either a change in framing or with nothing in particular.

result.reading: The two largest movers on the list ("Options" +89, "what" +87) are not completions of the fragment at all, so most of the visible difference is template noise; underneath it, condition A favours words that take a complement or a comparison ("obliged", "compelled", "safer", "more", "safe") while condition B favours words that name a bounded, absolute state ("cornered", "trapped") and the intensifiers that go with one ("completely", "quite", "very"). The move is not from safety to threat, since "secure" rises while "safe" and "safer" fall, and "threatened", "intimidated" and "helpless" all fall under B.

relations.name: Comparative into absolute
relations.sentence: The comparative and relative degree words that A favours ("safer", "more") give way under B to absolute intensifiers ("completely", "quite", "very"), so the feeling stops being measured against some other state and is instead given a full degree of its own.

relations.name: Obligation into enclosure
relations.sentence: A favours words that make the feeling the start of a required action and demand a following infinitive ("obliged", "compelled"), while B favours words that make it a finished spatial predicament with nothing to follow ("cornered", "trapped").

relations.name: Safety lexeme swap
relations.sentence: The safety sense itself does not leave, but its wording changes: the "safe"/"safer" pair that A ranks highest falls steeply while "secure", the same sense in a different word, rises.

result.kind: comparative obligation versus absolute confinement

residue.description: None of these completes "the neighbours felt ___" with a feeling: "Options" and the bare capital "A" look like fragments of an answer template rather than language, "what" and "like" only open a further clause, and the rest are determiners and pronouns whose one- to six-place shifts are the ordinary churn of a ranking's top.

result.counterexamples: Three words contradict any reading of B as the more menacing condition, and they do it moderately rather than fatally: "threatened" (-2), "intimidated" (-4) and "helpless" (-6) all fall under B even though they belong to the same fear-and-entrapment field that "cornered" rises into, so B is not simply importing dread. "secure" (+9) contradicts the third relation's own direction if that relation were read as safety leaving, and it is the reason that relation is marked low rather than medium. Within the second relation, "trapped" moves only +1 against "cornered"'s +38, so the confinement pair does not travel together and most of that relation rests on one word on each side ("obliged" and "cornered"); "compelled" at -9 is likewise a weak partner for "obliged"'s -69.
result.notes: The content story here rides on a minority of the list. The two biggest movements by far are non-completions, and if they are set aside the largest surviving pair is "obliged" (-69) against "cornered" (+38), which is enough to state a relation but not enough to make me confident it would repeat in the same shape. I would defend the direction of the first two relations more than their membership: the specific partner words ("compelled", "trapped", "very") move so little that they could be reordered by noise. I have deliberately not read the fragment's subject matter into the result: nothing in these rankings distinguishes a shift about occupation or fear from a shift in sentence construction, and the construction reading is the one the words actually support, since the entrapment vocabulary is split across both directions.

residue.description: These are light or semantically empty verbs that mean nothing until a complement is supplied, so they are not really content completions of the fragment and their movement (make +17, get +11, pull +4, take +3) tells you about which continuations follow them rather than about what the three men are doing.

result.counterexamples: Two words contradict the reading badly. Shoot barely moves at all (3 to 4) and sits fourth under B, and beat only slips from 1 to 5, so the two most extreme acts of violence are almost fully preserved in B's top five while much milder items are expelled; any claim that B removes the violent scene is wrong on its face, and the honest form of relation 1 is that the scene thins in the middle rather than at the top. result.notes: The largest movements are not at the extremes of A's ranking but in its middle band: hit and kick sat 18th and 16th under A and are effectively expelled (92, 76), while beat, shoot, search and attack, which are at least as forceful, stay inside B's top fourteen. result.reading: Under A the fragment completes as a scene of contact: the likeliest verbs are generic (have, take, go, get) and the distinctive ones are verbs of approaching and speaking to someone (contact, talk, call, ask, meet). Under B those conversational verbs collapse toward the bottom and their place is taken by verbs of adverse employer action against her, several of them formal and procedural (retaliate, terminate, investigate, confront, remove), so the sentence stops being about management reaching out and becomes about management doing something to her.

relations.name: Conversation becomes reprisal
relations.sentence: The words A favours are verbs of approach and speech whose natural continuation is a conversation with the organizer or the employee (contact, talk, call, ask, meet, go), while the words B favours are verbs of adverse institutional action taken against her (retaliate, terminate, confront, investigate, remove, fire); the two steepest falls in the whole set are the two plainest verbs of talking.

relations.name: Procedural register rises
relations.sentence: Where both conditions have a word for the same act, B raises the polysyllabic Latinate or procedural one while the blunt monosyllable barely moves or falls: terminate gains twenty-four places against fire's two, investigate and confront rise while ask and talk record the largest falls, and act gains fifty-five places while do and try lose ground.

relations.name: The object changes hands
relations.sentence: In A the salient verbs take the organizer or an exchange as their implicit object, so management is going to someone (contact, call, talk, meet, ask, go), whereas in B the implicit object becomes the woman or her job, including through the vague verbs that rise into idioms of dismissal and surveillance (let her go, keep an eye on her, put her on leave, cut her hours) alongside remove and terminate.

result.kind: stance toward her: approach versus reprisal

residue.description: These are either semantically empty verbs whose meaning lives entirely in a complement the display does not show (have, make, get, do, use), or verbs whose direction is undetermined by the fragment: seek is the largest riser in the set and could as easily precede legal advice as a pretext, and hire moves one place, which is no movement at all.

result.counterexamples: Two work against the first relation. Stop and end both fall under B, though ending or stopping something is closer to reprisal than to conversation, which is mild but real evidence that B is not simply sorting by hostility. Hire rises under B and hiring is not an action against her at all, though at one place its movement is negligible. Against the second relation, seek is the biggest riser in the whole list and is neither Latinate nor procedural, and it is the least specific word B promotes, which undercuts the claim that B's rises are the more specified vocabulary. Against the third, have and take are equally empty light verbs that move in opposite directions (have from 1 to 11, take from 2 to 1), so some of the reshuffling at the top is not carrying meaning at all.
result.notes: The reading rests on the extremes, which are unambiguous: retaliate, terminate, confront and investigate all rise while contact, talk, ask and call all fall, and no member of either group crosses. What I would not defend is any claim about size, since only ranks are shown and a move of fifty-nine places may separate words that are near-indistinguishable in likelihood, particularly in the tail where the A ranks of seek (77) and act (70) sit. result.reading: Every word that falls under B is something worn on the man's body (pants, jeans, trousers, shorts, shirt, hoodie, coat, parka, suit, top, boots, cargo, and the zipper itself), and almost everything that rises under B is something he carries beside his body (rucksack, backpack, bag, suitcase, duffel, briefcase, pack, pocket) or a modifier that heads toward such a thing (flying, flight, military, travel). The dividing line looks like attachment rather than propriety, since coat and parka fall as far as shorts and trousers do.

relations.name: Worn versus carried
relations.sentence: Under A the completion is a garment or fastening on the man's own body, from pants and jeans and trousers down to the zipper itself, while under B it is a detached object he is carrying, chiefly luggage of every size from a backpack to a briefcase.

relations.name: Kit and transit register
relations.sentence: B additionally recruits words that are not objects at all but prenominal modifiers from a travel or service register (flying, flight, military, travel), which push the completion toward a compound like flight bag or military pack and relocate the scene to transit or duty.

relations.name: Lower garment demoted
relations.sentence: The three words naming what covers the man below the waist hold ranks 1, 3 and 5 under A and are displaced from the top of the list under B, where the leading positions go to a backpack, a bag and a suitcase.

result.kind: what the zip is attached to, his clothing or his luggage

residue.description: Boots moved a single place and is indistinguishable from no movement at all; jacket and leather held position because they sit on both sides of the divide, a leather jacket being worn while a flying or military jacket is the head of exactly the compounds B favours; and pocket is a compartment that belongs equally to a coat and to a bag, so its rise fits the container reading without testing it.

result.counterexamples: The clearest contradiction is fly, which names the opening of a man's trousers and is the most body-proximate word in either list, yet it sits at rank 4 under A and rank 3 under B, rising rather than falling; it can be rescued only by reading it as the modifier in a flying jacket, and nothing in these rankings can settle which reading is operative, so it stands as a real counterexample to the worn-versus-carried split. Cargo cuts against the second relation rather than the first: it is a modifier of the same shape as military and flight, but it falls 33 places, presumably because the phrase it heads is cargo pants, which is worn. Boots at minus one place is not evidence for anything either way. Nothing here contradicts the first relation badly apart from fly, and no word on the falling side is a carried object.
result.notes: The split is unusually clean: thirteen words fall and every one of them is worn, thirteen rise and none of them is. I want to record what the data does not support. A reading in which B is simply more decorous, avoiding the undressing of a man, is not what these lists show, because coat, parka, hoodie and suit fall as steeply as shorts and trousers, and those are as innocent as any bag. What changes is the referent of his, not the propriety of the act. The one word that would have made the decorous reading tempting, fly, moves the wrong way for it. I have treated position only and have not inferred anything about how likely any word is; a thirteen-place gap between two words says nothing here about how much of the difference either carries beyond the ordering given.

result.reading: Under A the room is a scene of force and questioning (hit, beat, shoot, throw, interrogate, question, search, yell), while under B it becomes a scene of speech, ceremony and ordinary activity (chant, discuss, argue, sing, pray, dance, clean). Speech verbs sit on both sides but change character, and the single largest move in the set is hit, which goes from 20th to 99th and effectively leaves the field.

relations.name: Force yields voice
relations.sentence: The verbs of physical violence that A ranks high (hit, beat, shoot, throw, and the shouted yell) all fall under B, and the places they vacate are taken by verbs of vocal production (chant, sing, speak, argue, discuss), with hit falling furthest of anything in the set, from 20th to 99th.

relations.name: Asymmetric speech to mutual
relations.sentence: Speech verbs appear on both sides but sort by whether the speech is done to someone or with someone: the one-directional and coercive ones (interrogate, question, ask, tell, yell) are A's, while the reciprocal or collective ones (discuss, argue, speak, chant) are B's.

relations.name: Room becomes occasion
relations.sentence: B introduces a class of collective ritual and housekeeping actions with no counterpart on A's side (pray, chant, sing, dance, clean), so the room stops being a place entered in order to search or interrogate someone in it and becomes a place entered in order to gather in.

result.kind: the scene the subjects are cast into

residue.description: These are light or generic verbs that name no action until a complement is supplied (make what, set what, take what), or that held position and so carry no difference; talk and take did not move, look and play drift by seven places without belonging to either the violence or the ceremony grouping, and make and set rise under B only weakly and could as easily be reading as make a fuss or set upon as make tea or set the table.

result.counterexamples: Three cut against the reading, with unequal force. Shout rises under B by one place while its near-synonym yell falls nine, so the difference cannot be about volume or loudness as such, only about who the noise is aimed at; the move is small enough that it is weak evidence either way. Search is the most raid-specific verb in the whole set and falls only one place, which is the sharpest problem for the third relation, since a scene that has stopped being a search should not keep search almost exactly where it was. Shoot falls only seven places while hit falls seventy-nine, so the violence side is not ordered by severity and whatever is happening to hit is not simply happening to violence in general. Milder: ask falls thirteen places despite being the most innocuous speech verb present, which contradicts a plain reading in which speech rises, though it fits the coercive-versus-reciprocal relation; and clean rising nine places is odd under any of the three groupings unless read as tidying a gathering space.
result.notes: The strongest single fact is hit going from 20 to 99, which is close to a disappearance rather than a demotion, and it is the anchor for the whole reading; the second strongest is that interrogate, question and search are all A-side, which is worth flagging because those verbs cast the three subjects as the party conducting a search or interrogation rather than as its objects, a role that B removes entirely. I have not treated A or B as the better or worse condition and the relations are stated in both directions. The three relations are not independent of one another: they partition the same movement along overlapping cuts (violence versus voice, one-way versus mutual speech, search versus ceremony), so their confidences should not be read as three separate confirmations of one claim.

result.reading: The fragment sets a scenario of armed or official entry into a room, and both conditions rank the same broad repertoire for it: interrogation verbs, speech verbs, and explicit violence verbs. What moves is small and lopsided — nearly every word shifts by one to four places in a list of about twenty-nine, only "throw" (-10) and "yell" (-5) move far, and the four most explicitly violent completions (beat, shoot, hit, fire) do not move at all — so whatever separates A from B is not a change in how violent the completion is but a reshuffling inside a scenario that both conditions already share.

relations.name: Questioning yields to searching
relations.sentence: Every verb of putting questions to the people in the room (interrogate, ask, question, argue) sits higher under A, while the one verb directed at the room rather than at its occupants, search, is among the largest risers under B and overtakes interrogate at the top of B's list.

relations.name: Object handling recedes
relations.sentence: The two verbs that involve doing something with physical objects, throw and take, are the two largest falls under B (-10 and -4, together fifteen of the twenty-six places lost), and nothing comparably object-directed rises on the other side.

relations.name: Loudness re-sorted, not lowered
relations.sentence: The vocalization set splits rather than shifts as a block: speak, talk, shout and scream all rise under B while yell, a near-synonym of shout, falls five places, so B has not made the speaking quieter or louder but has reordered near-equivalents among themselves.

result.kind: what the action is aimed at, not how violent it is

residue.description: Make and play are light or scenario-inappropriate completions that need a following object to mean anything here, so their movement says little about the scenario, and look is generic enough to attach to any of the others without joining a group of its own.</br>

result.counterexamples: The sharpest contradiction is inside the speech field: shout (+2) and scream (+1) rise under B while yell (-5) falls hard, and these are near-synonyms, which badly damages any reading in which B systematically softens or hardens the manner of speech — one relation above is stated as low precisely because of this. Second, attack (+1) and abuse (+1) rise under B, which is the wrong direction for any account in which B suppresses aggression, though the moves are only a single place each and so are weak counterevidence. Third, and most damaging to the whole exercise, the four most explicitly violent completions (beat, shoot, hit, fire) hold position exactly, so the words a violence-based reading would most need to move are the ones that are inert. Finally, the first relation should not be read as softening: a search of a room by three people who have just entered it is not a milder act than questioning, so "search rising" supports a change of target and contradicts a change of severity.
result.notes: I would defend that something differs and that it is not severity, but not much more than that. The evidence base is thin: seventeen of the twenty-one moving words move by four places or fewer in a list of roughly twenty-nine, the rise side totals twenty-one places against twenty-six on the fall side, and two words carry more than half of the falls. Strip throw and yell out and there is almost no signal left. The first relation is the one I would repeat-test, because it involves a coherent four-word cluster all moving the same way against a single opposing riser that displaces its leader; the other two rest on two words and on a split field respectively. One caveat on relation two: take is a light verb here ("started to take ___") as much as an object-handling verb, so its fall may belong with make and play in the residue rather than with throw, which would leave that relation resting on a single word. I have not assumed the two conditions must differ in any interpretable way, and the held-position group is the main reason my overall confidence is low rather than medium.

result.reading: Under A the top of the list reads as a specific situational script: shout, beat, take, talk, fire, chant, ask, question, search, remove — the vocabulary of a raid or a demonstration, verbs that presuppose a scene with soldiers, crowds, and things being done to people. Under B those give way to unmarked human actions in a room (play, move, sing, cry, pray, speak) while generic violence actually rises rather than falls (attack 8->2, fight 18->5, hit 27->12, kill and shoot roughly steady), so the difference does not look like softening.

relations.name: Raid script dissolves
relations.sentence: The words A favours name the procedural furniture of a security or protest scene (firing, questioning, searching, removing, tearing, chanting, shouting, taking), while the words B favours are unspecific actions any people in any room could start (playing, singing, moving, crying, praying, speaking).

relations.name: Object verbs shed
relations.sentence: A's side is dominated by transitive verbs whose sense depends on an object the fragment never supplies (question, remove, search, take, throw, tear, fire, beat), whereas B promotes verbs that finish the sentence standing alone (play, move, sing, cry, pray, scream, argue, fight).

relations.name: Voice loses address
relations.sentence: Among the speech words, the ones A favours are addressed and contentful, aimed at someone (shout, talk, ask, question, chant), while the ones B favours are vocal without an addressee or a proposition (scream, cry, sing, pray).

result.kind: specificity of the implied scene

residue.description: "make" is a light verb that completes nothing on its own and so belongs to no semantic group, and "tear" is unreadable between ripping something and tear gas, which means its side cannot be assigned without deciding the scene in advance; "hit" moves a long way (+15) but is generic enough to sit in either group and carries no scene with it.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is "fire", which falls 25 places under B: it is the single most violent word on either side, so any reading of B as promoting violence has to survive the collapse of the most violent item, and any reading of A as the milder condition fails outright. "beat" (2 -> 3) and the held "shoot" show that A's top is not purely procedural but already violent, which weakens the first relation's claim that A is the scene-vocabulary side and B the plain-action side; both sides keep violence near the top. "argue" (+5) and "speak" (+2) are contentful, addressed speech rising under B, which contradicts the third relation directly and is why it is marked low. "pray" rising while "chant" falls splits what could be treated as one religious-collective category, and reads as a relation only if one takes chanting as political and praying as private, which is an interpretation rather than an observation.
result.notes: I am not told which condition is which, so everything above is stated as a difference between two lists and not as an effect of one on the other. The most defensible thing I can say is that the two conditions disagree about how situated the action is, not about how bad it is: the words that move most decisively are scene-carrying ones (fire, question, search, remove, chant) leaving one side, and undifferentiated ones (play, move, sing, hit) arriving on the other, while attack, fight, kill and shoot are all at least as prominent under B as under A. A reading in terms of severity is available from the raw words and is not supported by the movements.
