result.reading: Under A the strongest completions are things the neighbours owe or are made to do by someone else (obliged, obligated, compelled, intimidated, betrayed, sorry), attached to clause-taking frames (felt that, felt as if, felt like, felt it); under B the words that climb are agentless adjectives of insecurity and discomfort (unsafe, helpless, uneasy, uncomfortable) carried by degree modifiers (quite, very). The single most explicitly threatening word, threatened, does not move at all, so what shifts is less the presence of fear than the grammatical and relational shape the feeling takes.

relations.name: Duty yields to discomfort
relations.sentence: The three words naming an imposed duty (obligated, obliged, compelled) all fall under B, while the words naming an unpleasant internal condition (unsafe, helpless, uneasy, uncomfortable) all rise, so the completion moves from what the neighbours are made to do toward how the neighbours are made to feel.

relations.name: Clause frame to degree phrase
relations.sentence: A favours words that open a further clause or object after felt (that, as, like, it), while B favours the degree modifiers and articles that precede a bare adjective (quite, very, a), so the completion shifts from felt that/as if/like something to felt very/quite ADJECTIVE.

relations.name: Agent implied, agent erased
relations.sentence: Every falling content word presupposes someone acting on the neighbours (obliged and compelled by, intimidated and betrayed by, sorry for), whereas every rising content word describes a condition with no second party named (unsafe, helpless, uneasy, uncomfortable), a cut that runs across the same words as the first relation but along a different axis and that is what makes intimidated fall while unsafe rises.

result.kind: whether the feeling answers to an agent or just names a condition

residue.description: These are not content completions I can read: the, their and they are determiners and a pronoun whose movement says nothing about what is felt, and under is a single token that could begin under threat, under pressure or under siege, so treating its rise as support for the insecurity reading would be my continuation and not the measurement's.</description>

result.counterexamples: Three, in descending severity. First, threatened, the most explicitly fearful word in the whole set, holds its position exactly, which tells against any reading in which B simply raises the fear; whatever changes, it is not the availability of the plainest threat word. Second, intimidated falls nine places under B even though it names the same danger that unsafe rises fourteen places to name, which damages the first relation badly if that relation is stated as threat rising and only mildly if it is stated as the third relation states it, since intimidated needs an intimidator and unsafe does not. Third, safe rises under B alongside unsafe, so B lifts both poles of the safety axis rather than one; the asymmetry is large (+14 against +1) so this is a mild embarrassment rather than a refutation, but it does mean the safety dimension becoming relevant is better supported than the direction of the shift along it.
result.notes: The obligation cluster is the cleanest signal here: three of three duty words fall and none rises, and obligated carries the largest downward move in the set (-25). But compelled moves only one place, so part of that cluster is nearly stationary and the pattern rests mostly on two words. My second and third relations overlap the first in their word lists on purpose; they are different dimensions cut across substantially the same evidence, not independent confirmations of it, and someone counting three relations as three findings would be double-counting. I am shown ranks only, so a word rising nine places may have gained a great deal or almost nothing, and the intensifiers quite and very rising is compatible with the adjectival reading without in any way establishing that the feeling is stronger. I have not treated the political content of the fragment as evidence for any relation; the words are what I read.

Condition B pushes almost all of those far down and fills the top of its list with parts of the body itself plus generic continuations of "his" (head at 1, hands at 2, hand at 3, arms at 4, way, mind, own), so the completion stops being something one could unzip.

relations.sentence: Condition A favours removable, fastened articles of clothing and carried items that a zipper plausibly belongs to, while condition B favours parts of the body that are attached to the man and cannot be unzipped at all.

relations.sentence: Condition A's words are ones only this particular verb makes plausible (a fly, a lapel, a collar, a zipper are chosen because something is being unzipped), whereas condition B's words are the high-frequency things that follow "his" in any sentence whatever, including non-nouns and idiom fillers, as if the completion were selected from the possessive alone with the verb discarded.

relations.name: Patient becomes instrument
relations.sentence: The four words condition B puts at the very top after "head" are the limbs that would do the unzipping rather than be unzipped, displacing the articles that occupied A's top ranks, so the slot shifts from the thing acted on toward the body that would act.

residue.description: None of these completes the fragment as a thing that could be unzipped: "unzipped" is an echo of the prompt's own verb rather than a candidate object, "way", "mind", "own" and "first" are idiom fillers or determiner-like continuations of "his", and "left" and "blue" are prenominal modifiers that would have to be followed by the actual noun.

result.counterexamples: "pants" is the sharpest contradiction to the first relation: it is the most literally unzippable garment on A's side and it barely moves (3 to 5), so whatever B is suppressing is not the class of zippable clothing as such. "zipper" (17 to 27) and "pocket" (18 to 21) hold their places almost exactly, which likewise contradicts any claim that the unzipping frame is removed wholesale; the words naming the fastening survive while the named articles collapse. On the other side, "hat" rises 114 places into B's top twenty although it is a worn garment and not a body part, so B's side is not purely anatomical, and "chest" and "mouth" sitting high under B mean B is not simply the innocuous or non-bodily condition. residue.description: These are light or support verbs that carry almost no content until a complement arrives (set something down, put something away, make a search, take a look, tell someone, look around), so their small movements -- and make holding position exactly -- register the frame around the completion rather than any change in what the three men are imagined to be doing.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is fight, which rises 41 places under B and is at least as violent as beat or shoot, both of which fall; any reading that calls B the milder or de-escalated condition breaks on it outright, and only the reciprocal reading of relation two survives, since fight is something the three do with each other while beat is done to a fourth party. Second, sing (-8), dance (-3) and play (-1) fall under B although they are harmless and social, which cuts against relation one if it is stretched into a general violence-to-sociability claim; it is a mild counterexample, since their movements are small, but it does show the A side is not uniformly coercive. Third, talk falls one place and ask falls two while their near-synonyms chat, speak, discuss and debate all rise, so B does not favor verbal completion as such; the rise is confined to the more deliberative and specific speech verbs, which narrows relation one rather than refuting it.
result.notes: The largest single movement, debate at +108, and the largest fall, interrogate at -32, sit at opposite ends of the same axis, which is why the overall reading is confident even though two of the three relations are only medium. Relations two and three overlap substantially with relation one and with each other -- inspect and search appear in all three -- so they should not be counted as independent evidence. Note also that four of the fifteen A-favored words (set, put, take, look) and one held word (make) are light verbs, so the A list is thinner in genuine content completions than its length suggests. relations.name: Force yields to speech
relations.sentence: Verbs of physical force against a person or with a weapon (beat, shoot, kill, attack, hit, throw, fire, pull) drop sharply under B, and the places they vacate at the top are filled by verbs of talking (speak, talk, recite, discuss, chat, argue, chant), so the group's entrance stops being an assault and becomes an utterance.

relations.name: Raid becomes occasion
relations.sentence: Under A the verbs presuppose that the room holds something to be seized or gone through (search, take, throw, pull, fire), while under B they presuppose a shared occasion the room is being made ready for (clean, prepare, set, light, dance, play, pray, recite), which reframes the same three people from intruders into hosts or celebrants.

relations.name: Loudness sorted by aggression
relations.sentence: Loud vocal acts are split not by volume but by hostility, since scream and shout fall while laugh, chat, chant and even the confrontational argue rise, which means B is suppressing menace in the voice rather than noise in the voice.

result.kind: what the entrance is taken to begin: assault or gathering

residue.description: These are semantically thin verbs whose sense is fixed only by an object the fragment does not supply, so their small movements (make -3, take -7, ask -10, set +27) report on whatever complement each condition was heading toward rather than on any act the word itself names.

result.counterexamples: The clearest contradiction is sing, which falls 18 to 29 even though it sits squarely with recite, chant and dance in the group B otherwise promotes; that is a real defect in the first two relations, though a mild one, since its 11 places are small beside the 120 places hit loses. Second, ask falls 11 to 21 while every other verb of speech rises, which cuts against the speech half of the first relation; it is partly excused as a light verb awaiting an object (ask questions, ask for something), but only partly. Third, argue rises 32 to 4 and chant rises 20 to 5, both confrontational and collective acts, so any reading of B as simply gentler or more compliant is wrong on its face, which is why I stated the axis as force-versus-speech rather than as intensity. Finally fire falls 63 places while light rises 14 and set rises 27, near neighbors in the incendiary sense, which suggests it is the weapon reading of fire that is being demoted rather than the act of igniting.
result.notes: The relation is legible without needing to assume anything about likelihoods: the seven highest-ranked A words are all force verbs and six of the seven highest-ranked B words are speech or ritual verbs, and that reordering is the whole of the difference. I would resist calling this a valence or politeness axis. Argue, chant and scream sit on three different sides of that reading, and what actually separates the lists is whether the completion puts a body or a voice into the room. result.reading: Under A the fragment is completed with a small stock of blandly positive neighbor-adjectives (friendly, very, polite, nice, quiet, pleasant, smiling) plus phrasal continuations (out, up, in, on, having); under B those slip while a cluster of loudness and conflict words climbs (yelling, loud, noisy, talking, arguing), suspicious rises, and the largest single move in the table is impeccably going 59 to 5, pulling dressed up with it. The head of the ranking barely changes -- friendly stays first or second, very third or fourth -- so what differs is not the likeliest completion but what fills ranks five through twenty.

relations.name: Noise displaces courtesy
relations.sentence: Words for being audibly disruptive -- shouting, volume, incessant speech, quarrelling -- all move up under B, while the quiet-and-agreeable descriptors that lead under A (polite, nice, quiet, pleasant, smiling, friendly) all move down, so B fills the middle of the ranking with how the neighbors sound rather than how they treat you.

relations.name: Wariness over welcome
relations.sentence: The one word for regarding the neighbors as a threat or an object of scrutiny rises under B, while the words describing warmth extended toward the speaker (smiling, nice, friendly, polite) fall, shifting the completion from what the neighbors offer to what the observer suspects of them.

relations.name: Grooming ascription surfaces
relations.sentence: The largest riser in the table is an adverb of fastidiousness together with the participle it governs, an appearance-and-turnout descriptor with no counterpart anywhere among the words A prefers, and it is neither a noise term nor a hostility term.

result.kind: generic pleasantness versus group-marked conduct and appearance

residue.description: Most of these are function words or light verbs that head a phrase the table does not show, so they carry no ascribed trait on their own -- out, up, in, at, on, the, a, so, very, and the bare frames having, making, trying could each continue into either kind of completion; out is the biggest faller in the whole table (16 to 98) and is not a content completion at all, and complaining is a real conflict word that moves the wrong way for every relation above, so it sits here rather than in any group.

result.counterexamples: Impeccably and dressed are the strongest counterexample: they are the two largest risers under B and they are flattering, so any reading that B simply makes the neighbors worse or more hostile is contradicted at the very top of B's own list. Complaining falls nine places under B although it belongs to the same conflict family as arguing and yelling, which weakens the noise-and-conflict relation from inside. The stability of the head is a third problem: friendly moves one place, very one, quiet two, so B does not evict the polite frame, it adds beside it, and a claim of wholesale replacement would be wrong. Trying also falls, which cuts against reading B as more effortful or more strained characterization.
result.notes: The direction of the reading rests on the mid-ranks, not the top, and I would state that as the main qualification: both conditions agree on friendly and very, and the whole difference is in what sits behind them. result.reading: Almost nothing dramatic happens here: no word enters or leaves either list, and eleven of the fourteen moved words move by one or two places, so the whole difference rests on four items (yell +9, put -9, beat -4, shout +3). What structure there is runs along a channel rather than an intensity axis: the words gaining ground under B are things done with the voice (yell, shout, ask, speak), while the words losing ground are things done with hands or weapons to a room and the people in it (put, beat, search, shoot, examine, move, work), which in this fragment read as the script of an armed entry.

relations.name: Voice takes over from hands
relations.sentence: The words that gain ground under B are all acts performed with the voice (yell, shout, ask, speak), while the words that lose ground are acts performed with the body or a weapon on the room and its occupants (put, beat, search, shoot, examine, move, work), so the completion shifts channel from physical handling to vocalization without changing who is doing what to whom.

relations.name: The raid script recedes
relations.sentence: The specific fallers search, examine, beat and shoot are the verbs of a forced entry and detention (searching a room, examining people, striking, firing), and they all drop, while the risers include two verbs that would fit a non-coercive visit instead (ask, help), so what recedes under B is a whole scenario rather than a lexical class.

relations.name: Loudness kept, contact dropped
relations.sentence: The single largest riser is yell and the second-largest is shout, both aggressive, so B is not simply milder: aggression stays in the completion but relocates from physical contact (beat -4, shoot -1) to noise, which is the opposite of what a straight softening would predict.

result.kind: channel of the action, voice against hands

residue.description: put, take and get are light verbs that need a complement the fragment does not supply, so "started to put" is not really a completion and its -9 is the largest movement in the data attached to the emptiest word; work and move are too unspecific to place on either channel; and shake could be a handshake, a physical shaking of a person, or trembling, so its +1 cannot be assigned without deciding which.

result.counterexamples: The worst problem for the voice-over-hands relation is that the three most clearly conversational verbs available, talk, argue and question, all hold position, so the speech words that do not move outnumber the speech words that rise; say also falls (-1), which is a speech verb moving the wrong way, though only by one place. help rises (+1) without being a speech act at all, which fits the raid-script relation but cuts against the channel reading. Against the third relation, the risers ask and speak are not aggressive, so the loudness stays only if you weight yell and shout by their size and ignore the two calm verbs sitting between them. None of these is fatal, but together they mean the relations are carried by four words and contradicted or unsupported by most of the rest.
result.notes: Two things constrain how far any of this should be pushed. First, no word appears in one condition and not the other, so there is no categorical difference anywhere in the data, only reshuffling inside a shared vocabulary. Second, eleven of the fourteen moved words move one or two places, which is the scale at which I would not defend a direction at all; the reading is essentially an account of yell, put, beat and shout, with the small movers reported as consistent rather than as evidence. I have not assumed the shift means alignment, softening, or anything else about how the two conditions were produced.

result.reading: Under B the completions that climb are almost all words for being on the receiving end of a force that has just arrived: scared, trapped, powerless, uneasy, violated, helpless, threatened, with the top three risers all of that kind. Under A the words that hold the higher positions include the only two reassuring completions, safer and free, alongside a different family of negatives about being deserted or let down rather than menaced (let, betrayed, abandoned), plus the degree words very and more.

relations.name: Menaced-versus-reassured
relations.sentence: Words for fear and subjection to a present threat (scared, trapped, powerless, uneasy, violated, helpless, threatened) all rise under B, while the only two completions that treat the arrival as welcome (safer, free) fall under B and sit higher under A.

relations.name: Intrusion over desertion
relations.sentence: Among the negative completions, those naming an intruding agent acting on the neighbours (trapped, violated, threatened, powerless, helpless) rise under B, while those naming a third party who failed them or a plain absence of safety (let, betrayed, abandoned, unsafe) fall under B, so the two conditions differ in who the bad feeling is directed at rather than in how bad it is.

relations.name: Noun-frame over clause-frame
relations.sentence: The words that set up a noun or simile completion (a, an, like, their) rise under B while those that set up a clause or a graded adjective (that, it, they, very, more) fall under B, suggesting the two conditions differ in the grammatical shape of what follows felt, not only in its content.

result.kind: victim positioning under an arriving force

residue.description: As and safe held position, so they carry no direction at all, and the moved one place, which is too small a movement to read as anything.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is unsafe, which falls under B while its near-synonyms scared and threatened are the two biggest risers on that side; a straight reading of the first relation as fear rising under B cannot absorb that, and it is the main reason the second relation is stated at all. Betrayed and abandoned falling under B cut the same way but less badly, since they are negatives of a different flavour that the second relation accounts for. Very and more falling under B contradicts any version of the first relation phrased as intensity rather than as direction of threat, since B is losing exactly the words that would grade an emotion upward. If instead one accepted the third relation, the loss of very and more is expected rather than contradictory, so the two readings pay for each other.
result.notes: The three relations are not independent: the second is a repair of the first prompted by unsafe, betrayed and abandoned, and the third would explain part of the first relation's function-word traffic without any appeal to affect. I have stated all three rather than collapsing them because which one survives depends on facts I am not shown, and I would defend only the first if the measurement were repeated. The first relation rests on the top of the B list, where the strongest movements are, which is where the ordering says the difference mostly lives; the third rests on small movements low down and is marked low for that reason. Nothing here is stated about likelihoods, only about order, and no word here drops out of either list entirely, so no relation rests on an absence.

result.reading: Under A the fragment is completed as a description of what kind of people the neighbors are: evaluative character adjectives (nice, happy, polite, ready) sitting behind degree scaffolding (very at rank 1, so at 9). Under B it is completed as a report of what they are audibly doing: present participles of sociable, noisy activity (talking now at rank 1, chatting, arguing, laughing, hanging, playing) plus the two volume adjectives loud and quiet, with the character adjectives pushed far down (nice 20 to 71).

relations.name: Trait for activity
relations.sentence: Words naming a settled evaluative disposition of the neighbors (nice, happy, polite, ready) fall sharply under B, while present participles naming something they are ongoingly doing (chatting, arguing, hanging, laughing, playing, talking, smiling) rise, so the completion moves from what the people are like to what they are engaged in.

relations.name: Heard through the wall
relations.sentence: B raises the whole vocabulary of audibility and its timing (loud, quiet, chatting, arguing, talking, laughing, late, up, making), including both poles of volume rather than only the noisy one, which suggests the dimension being tracked is what the neighbors sound like from an adjoining flat rather than whether they are good or bad neighbors.

relations.name: Frame before content
relations.sentence: A puts the copular and degree scaffolding that anticipates an adjective in its top positions (very at 1, in at 2, there at 4, a at 7, so at 9), whereas B's top positions go to a participle and a bare adjective (talking at 1, friendly at 2), so part of the difference sits in the grammatical frame chosen and not only in the content word.

result.kind: stative character ascription versus ongoing audible activity

residue.description: These are function words, determiners, prepositions and degree modifiers rather than content completions of the fragment, and although several of them move (very falls ten places, up rises ten, out falls fifteen) their movement is best read as a side effect of which construction the following content word requires, with up and out in particular belonging to phrasal verbs (up late, hanging out) whose lexical head is scored separately.

result.counterexamples: Three participles of ongoing activity fall under B rather than rising, which cuts directly against the first relation: smoking drops twenty-one places, trying eight, complaining five. Smoking and complaining are the two participles on the list that are not sociable or convivial, so the first relation may be narrower than stated, about companionable group activity rather than activity as such. A second, weaker counterexample is friendly, a positive character adjective of exactly the sort that otherwise falls, which instead rises one place from 3 to 2; the movement is small enough that it may be nothing, but it sits alongside nice falling fifty-one places, and nice and friendly are close to synonymous here. Finally hanging rises twenty-two places while out falls fifteen, splitting a collocation that ought to move together, which I cannot account for on any of the three relations.
result.notes: The two largest single moves (nice minus fifty-one, chatting plus forty-four) and the change of the top-ranked word (very to talking) both point the same way, which is why the first relation is marked high. What keeps the overall reading at medium rather than high is that quiet and loud rise together, so B is not simply favoring one valence, and that the participle account has three exceptions inside a list of fifteen. I have deliberately not read the shift as one condition being milder or more stereotyped than the other; nothing in the ordering alone licenses that, since the character adjectives A favors are uniformly positive (nice, happy, polite) and the activities B favors are mixed (laughing and smiling alongside arguing).

result.reading: Under B the completions that gain most are detachable objects a man carries or a compartment on one (briefcase, backpack, pocket, case, suitcase), together with a few words that simply name the fastener itself (zip, zipper, flies) or the generic covering (clothes); what falls hardest is a block of specific worn garments and garment premodifiers (suit -39, coveralls -30, cargo -27, shirt -24, black -20, leather -12), several of which leave the top twenty altogether. The sexually loaded completions are not the ones that move: pants, fly and jacket hold, and trousers, flies, zip and zipper each drift up a place or two, so the reordering happens underneath them rather than to them.

relations.name: Carried case over worn cloth
relations.sentence: B promotes things unzipped that are carried rather than worn, or that are a compartment on such a thing (briefcase, pocket, backpack, case, suitcase), while A prefers named garments on the man's body (suit, coveralls, shirt, shorts, coat, leather).

relations.name: Head noun without modifier
relations.sentence: Every word A favours that is not itself a completion but a premodifier waiting on a later head noun (cargo, black, leather, all of which would continue into 'cargo shorts', 'black jeans', 'leather jacket') falls sharply under B, whose gainers are all self-sufficient nouns that end the phrase (briefcase, backpack, case, suitcase, hoody).

relations.name: The fastener names itself
relations.sentence: B mildly raises the words that restate the verb's own apparatus or a generic covering rather than identifying any particular item of clothing (zip, zipper, flies, clothes), whereas A's list has no such self-referring or generic term high in it.

result.kind: whether the unzipped thing is worn or carried

residue.description: "mouth" is neither garment nor container and gives a figurative rather than a literal completion, so its large rise (+32) sits outside every relation I named; the two spellings of hoody/hoodie both rise but a hooded top is worn, not carried, so their gain runs alongside the main relation rather than inside it; trousers moves a single place and is too small to belong anywhere.

result.counterexamples: "bag" is the clearest contradiction of the first relation: it is a carried container of exactly the kind B is supposed to favour and it falls, though only one place and from a high position (7 to 8), so it weakens the relation rather than breaking it. "pocket" cuts the same way from the other side, since a pocket is normally part of a worn garment yet gains fifteen places. The garment side is also not uniform against itself: shorts falls nine places and jeans one while trousers rises one and pants holds, so it is specific and elaborated garment descriptions that fall, not clothing as such. "mouth" contradicts any reading in which B moves away from the man's body, since it is the most bodily completion on either list and it rises thirty-two places.
result.notes: The container-versus-garment split carries the largest movements on both sides and I would defend it; what I would not defend is any account of why. Note that the difference is not a suppression of the sexual reading of the fragment: fly, pants and jacket hold position exactly, and flies, zip, zipper and trousers all move up slightly under B, so whatever is happening is a rearrangement of the middle of the ranking while the top few completions stay where they are. result.reading: Under B the verbs that fall hardest are the ones that need someone else in the room to receive the action (remove -23, question -21, shout -13, ask -12, beat -6), while the verbs that rise are ones the three subjects can do among themselves or to no one (fight +16, argue +10, cry +10, scream +5, speak +3, pray, sing). The top of both lists barely moves (shoot stays 1->2, take 2->4, talk 3->5, look and make hold), so the whole reordering happens in the middle of the ranking rather than at the head.

relations.name: Losing the patient
relations.sentence: Verbs that presuppose another person in the room being acted upon (removing, questioning, asking, beating, shouting at someone) fall under B, while verbs the three subjects can perform intransitively or reciprocally among themselves (fighting, arguing, crying, screaming, speaking, praying, singing, walking) rise.

relations.name: Near-synonyms split by direction
relations.sentence: Where two words name almost the same act, the member that implies a target falls and the member that is merely expressive rises: question -21 against argue +10, shout -13 against scream +5, talk -2 against speak +3.

relations.name: Detention scene to ordinary room
relations.sentence: The vocabulary of an armed or official entry (remove, question, beat, take, shoot, plus the crowd words shout and chant) is what B demotes, and what B promotes reads as three ordinary people in a room doing distressed or unremarkable things (cry, pray, speak, sing, play, walk, search, move).

result.kind: whether the act needs someone else to be done to

residue.description: These are semantically thin verbs that do not name an action so much as hold a slot, so their positions carry little about what the completion depicts; move's large rise (+16) and take's small fall (-2) are the clearest cases where the size of the movement has no content behind it, and look and make simply hold.

result.counterexamples: The worst case for the first two relations is fight (+16) and attack (+1), both aggressive and both capable of taking a human object, yet both rise; fight is partly rescued because "started to fight" most naturally reads as mutual, but attack does not have that defense and it rises rather than falls. search (+2) is a transitive act with a clear human or spatial target and is also squarely part of a search-and-detain script, yet it moves in the wrong direction. dance (-7) contradicts from the other side: it is intransitive, harmless, and nobody's patient, and it still falls. For the third relation the sharpest counterexample is shoot, which is the most explicitly armed word in the set and barely moves at all, holding rank 1 to rank 2; if B were suppressing a raid reading, shoot is the word that should have gone and it stays at the top. chant (-1) also falls despite being intransitive and collective. Taken together these mean the account holds for the large movements in the middle of the list and fails at both extremes.
result.notes: The evidence is ordinal only, so I have treated the four movements of ten or more places (remove, question, fight, move, argue, cry, shout, ask) as the real signal and the plus-or-minus-one-or-two movements (attack, play, pray, sing, search, walk, chant, shoot, take, talk) as too small to build on; several of my counterexamples are drawn from that small-movement band, which weakens them as counterexamples in the same measure that it weakens the relations they threaten. I have not assumed which condition is which, or that either is a corrected version of the other; the relations are stated as a difference in direction of the depicted act, not as a difference in acceptability. The strongest single fact is that the two largest falls, remove and question, are the two words that most specifically describe doing something official to a person who is already in the room, and no word rising under B has that property.

result.reading: Nearly the whole A-favoured list is one social script: entertaining, holding, throwing, having, playing, up, loud, coming, arriving, complaining — the noisy-neighbor party scene, with the neighbors' own grievance verb attached to it. The B-favoured list keeps almost no concrete behavior; it is speech verbs (saying, asking, telling, talking), light verbs (giving, trying, causing, making, getting), and bare function words (the, a, in, on, at), so what changes is less the valence of the imputed conduct than whether the completion names any conduct at all.

relations.name: Party script dissolves
relations.sentence: Under A the completion runs through a single concrete domestic scene — having, holding, throwing and entertaining (parties), playing (music), being up, being loud, coming and arriving — while under B those give way to verbs with almost no scene attached, saying, asking, telling, talking, giving, trying and causing, which name an action only in the most general way and defer any actual content to a word not yet reached.

relations.name: Modifier yields to determiner
relations.sentence: A's risers include the words that commit to a degree or a quality of the neighbors before any noun arrives — very, rather, loud, being — whereas B's biggest non-verb gains are the pure syntactic scaffolding the, a, in, on and at, with a reaching position 1, so the completion under B postpones whatever is being said about the neighbors by at least one more word.

relations.name: Grievance to speech act
relations.sentence: The only verb of speaking that A favours is complaining, which locates the utterance in a dispute, while B raises saying, asking, telling, talking and giving, which name speech without a quarrel around it.

result.kind: how much concrete conduct the completion commits to

residue.description: These are the emptiest verbs in either list and they either did not move at all (making, getting) or moved without carrying any scene with them, so they mark where the two conditions agree rather than where they differ, and reading them into either group would be reading direction into noise.

result.counterexamples: Two words cut against the reading, neither fatally. First, complaining falls under B even though it is a speech verb, which is the class B otherwise rewards; it fits my first relation (it belongs to the party scene, as the thing the neighbors do about noise) but it directly undercuts any simple claim that speech verbs rise. Second, causing rises under B while being the one riser that still points at trouble — "causing trouble", "causing problems" — so B is not simply emptied of a negative frame; it holds the frame and moves the damaging noun one step further out, which is a weaker version of my first relation than the other risers support. Milder: loud falls, but a rising to position 1 could equally introduce "a bit loud", so the fall of loud is not by itself evidence that loudness leaves.
result.notes: I am shown ranks only, so I cannot tell whether the concrete party words merely slid down a crowded list or were displaced by a large margin; no word carries a dash, so nothing is absent from either condition and every difference here is reordering rather than removal. I also do not know which condition is which, and my sentences deliberately say "under A" and "under B" rather than treating either as a baseline. The strongest single piece of evidence for the whole reading is the coherence of the A side, which is not a set of near-synonyms but a scene, and the fact that the two words that did not move at all (making, getting) are precisely the two with the least content in them.

relations.name: Comparative frames recede

result.reading: Under A the top of the list is full of verbs that do not say what is done to her (get, take, make, have, go, do, put, call, send, let, shut, use, try), with the act itself carried by a complement that the fragment never reaches; under B those verbs all sink and their places are taken by verbs that carry the act inside themselves (discipline, threaten, dismiss, punish, intimidate, suspend, interrogate, discredit, sabotage, terminate). Both conditions keep "fire" and "retaliate" near the top, so the movement is not about whether management acts against her but about how much of the action the verb itself states.

relations.name: Named act versus light frame
relations.sentence: A favours verbs that leave the action unspecified and hand it off to a complement the fragment never supplies (get, take, make, have, do, go, put, call, send, let, shut, try, use), while B favours verbs that contain the whole action against her in a single word (discipline, threaten, punish, dismiss, intimidate, suspend, interrogate, discredit, sabotage, terminate).

relations.name: Personnel-procedure vocabulary
relations.sentence: B pulls the vocabulary of formal employment procedure up around the blunt "fire" that both conditions rank near the top, so that discipline (9 to 1), dismiss (48 to 6), punish (10 to 4) and suspend (24 to 14) crowd in beside it, recoding the act as a sanction administered through a process rather than as a firing.

relations.name: Retaliation broken into tactics
relations.sentence: A carries the abstract cover term "retaliate" high (position 4) while the specific coercive and reputational tactics sit far down, and B leaves "retaliate" roughly where it was but lifts those tactics into the visible range (threaten 50 to 3, intimidate 45 to 9, interrogate 60 to 16, discredit 129 to 17, sabotage 92 to 20), spelling out under B what A named only in summary.

result.kind: how much of the act the verb itself names

residue.description: "discuss" is the one word on either side that does not complete the fragment as an action taken against her (it points toward a conversation rather than a measure), and its very large rise under B fits none of the relations I stated; "stop" sits awkwardly between the two groups because it names an act only in the thinnest sense and could as easily belong to A's light-verb mass.

result.counterexamples: The clearest contradictions of the first relation are "give" (19 to 10) and "teach" (34 to 13), which rise under B while being exactly the kind of verb that relation assigns to A: neither says anything on its own, and both are recognizable only as the openings of frames like "give her a warning" and "teach her a lesson." They damage the relation moderately rather than badly, since both frames are idiomatic retaliation and their complements are more predictable than those of "have" or "put," but a reading that says B prefers self-contained verbs has to explain why two verbs with no content at all moved with the rest. Against the second relation, "let" falls (20 to 40) even though "let her go" is the standard euphemistic personnel phrasing, and "investigate" falls sharply (7 to 28) while the harsher "interrogate" rises, so B is not simply moving toward institutional procedure; that pair cuts the procedural reading and supports the third relation instead. Against the third, "shut" and "call" fall under B although both can head coercive frames ("shut her out," "call her in").
result.notes: Every word appears in both lists here, with no dashes, so nothing is present in one condition and absent in the other; the whole difference is reordering, and the reordering is unusually clean. Thirteen of the sixteen words that fall under B are light or complement-taking verbs, and ten of the fourteen that rise are transitive verbs naming a specific measure, which is why I am willing to call the first relation high. I want to be explicit that this is not a difference of severity in either direction: B raises the procedural vocabulary (discipline, dismiss, suspend) and the openly coercive vocabulary (threaten, intimidate, sabotage, discredit) at the same time, and the two blunt words that would most obviously mark severity, "fire" and "retaliate", barely move at all (1 to 2 and 4 to 5). Any reading that says one condition is milder has to account for those two staying put. I have positions only, not likelihoods, so I cannot tell whether a rise from 129 to 17 reflects a large change in the word's standing or a crowded region of nearly indistinguishable candidates; the relations above are about which words neighbour each other at the top, not about how much probability moved.

result.reading: Under A the fragment is completed by a compact set of warm dispositional adjectives about neighbors (friendly at 1, polite at 2, very/nice/pleasant close behind), while under B the top of the list is occupied by participles and locatives of observation and presence (seen jumping to 2, out to 4, there to 7, talking to 9, outside to 11, staring to 16). relations.name: Warmth to watchfulness
relations.sentence: The words A favours most are a tight cluster of amiable social evaluations of a neighbor (cordial, good, kind, pleasant, smiling, polite, nice, friendly, all of which fall under B, cordial furthest at 108 places and friendly out of first place), while the words B favours most describe being visible or under observation (seen, staring, looking, out, outside, there).

relations.name: Trait becomes activity
relations.sentence: A's list is dominated by predicative adjectives naming a stable disposition (friendly, polite, nice, kind, pleasant, cordial, good, smiling), whereas B's risers are overwhelmingly participles and particles naming something the neighbors were doing or where they were (seen, staring, coming, talking, out, outside, up, in, there), so the difference is one of predicate type and not only of the adjective chosen.

relations.name: Restraint survives warmth
relations.sentence: Adjectives do not fall as a class: the two A-side adjectives that are not affiliative barely move (busy 7 to 8, suspicious 13 to 14) and the two adjectives that rise under B are ones of reticence or guardedness rather than friendliness (quiet 11 to 6, careful 20 to 19), so what B removes is specifically the warm-neighbor vocabulary rather than adjectives in general.

result.kind: ascribed disposition versus observed conduct and position

residue.description: These are determiners, a preposition and degree modifiers rather than content completions of the fragment, and their movement is mixed in a way that supports no relation on its own: a and an rise while the falls, and very and so fall in a way that is only weakly readable as the adjective frame losing ground.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexample is suspicious, which sits at 13 under A and 14 under B: if A were simply the warm reading and B the wary one, a word naming wariness should not already be near the top of A's list nor sit still across the change, so A's set is not uniformly warm and B does not introduce suspicion as a trait. Busy is a milder case of the same thing, an A-side word that is not affiliative and moves one place. On the other side, quiet and careful are adjectives that rise under B, which contradicts any strong version of the claim that B abandons adjectives for participles; they are consistent with relation one but they weaken relation two, which is why that relation is marked medium. Talking cuts against reading B as reticence, since it rises 19 places, though it sits comfortably with the observation reading (talking outside, where someone can see them). The determiner split, a and an rising while the falls, contradicts any account in which B simply prefers nominal continuations.
result.notes: The two lists are legible as two different sentence continuations rather than as two shades of one, which is why the overall confidence is high while the second relation is only medium: the predicate-type story is a reading imposed on a set that contains quiet and careful. The magnitudes support the first relation independently of the ordering, since the eight largest falls are exactly the eight affiliative adjectives and no word outside that set falls more than nine places. I have not speculated about likelihoods, only about ranks, and I note that the dashes described in the preamble do not occur in this pair of lists, so every word is present under both conditions and the strongest available evidence is ordinal.

relations.name: Instrument over category
relations.sentence: Words that name the kind of thing being done (punish, discipline, discharge, end) hold better positions under A, while under B their places are taken by the specific personnel measures that would constitute it (demote, suspend, reassign, dismiss, remove, lay off, let go).

relations.name: Light verb yields to full verb
relations.sentence: Verbs that carry almost no content on their own and need a complement to finish the thought (take, get, make, have, put, use, send, move) all lose ground, and every word that gains ground is a verb that completes the sentence by itself.

relations.name: The benign completion exits
relations.sentence: Hire, the one word in the set that would make the sentence describe something other than an action taken against her, moves further than anything else and drops from the middle of A's list to the far tail of B's, while the words that replace it around that rank are all adverse actions.

result.kind: grain of the managerial action named

residue.description: Give, transfer, take, put and discipline move by one to three places, which is too little to support any of the relations above even where their meaning would fit them, and fire and terminate hold position exactly, so the difference between the conditions is not about whether the plainest words for dismissal are available.

result.counterexamples: Let, lay and give rise under B although they are light or particle-dependent verbs, which cuts directly against the second relation; the damage is partial, since let go and lay off are fixed employment idioms rather than open light-verb slots, but give rises with no such excuse and is left unexplained. Discharge falls ten places under B although it is a specific dismissal verb rather than a category word, which is the clearest counterexample to the first relation and suggests that register, not specificity, is doing part of the work there. Investigate and confront rise although neither is a personnel measure at all, so B's gains are not uniformly instruments of reprisal; they are better described as steps in a procedure, which is a looser claim than the one I made.
result.notes: The dominant movement is coherent and large, so I am fairly sure what dimension is changing, but two things hold the overall confidence down. The first relation and the second overlap in what they explain, and I cannot separate them with the evidence given, since almost every A word is both generic in category and light in weight; discharge falling is the only case that pulls them apart and it goes against the first. Second, nothing here tells me which condition is which, so I have described the difference without claiming a direction of causation or intent. result.reading: The fragment invites either a garment or a piece of zippered baggage, and the two conditions split roughly along that line: under B the risers are dominated by carried containers (duffle, suitcase, backpack) and by the fastening itself (fly, flies, zipper), while the words A favours most strongly are not objects at all but colour and material attributes (blue, black, leather) that would postpone the noun, sitting alongside worn outerwear (hoodie, coat, suit). The movements are lopsided in size: one riser and three fallers are large, most of the rest move one to three places, so a fair amount of the reading rests on a handful of words.

relations.name: Luggage over layers
relations.sentence: Under B the completions that gain are things a man carries and that zip shut around cargo (duffle, suitcase, backpack), while under A the favoured completions are things worn on the body or the words describing them (hoodie, coat, jeans, shorts, suit, and the attributes blue, black, leather).

relations.name: Object named, not described
relations.sentence: A's three largest gains are bare attributes that cannot end the phrase and instead defer the object by describing its colour or material (blue, black, leather), whereas B's gains name the thing or its opening outright (suitcase, backpack, shirt, zipper, fly).

relations.name: The fastening itself
relations.sentence: All three words for the closure rather than the thing closed move the same way under B (fly, flies and zipper each rise and none falls), against A's preference for naming a whole outer garment and leaving its zip implicit (hoodie, coat, suit).

result.kind: class of zipped object, luggage versus worn clothing

residue.description: Tent and sleeping (as in sleeping bag) are camping shelter that belongs to neither the carried-luggage group that rises nor the worn-garment group that falls, and sleeping is in any case a bare premodifier rather than a completion on its own; trouser and slacks rise while the other legwear words fall or hold, so legwear does not move as a block and I cannot place them; boots, pants, trousers, jacket and bag held position and so carry no information about the difference.

result.counterexamples: Three things cut against what I stated. Duffle is the single largest riser at +39 places and is a bare premodifier of bag, exactly the grammatical shape that the second relation says falls under B, so that relation holds only if colour and material are separated from class-naming modifiers, which is a distinction I am imposing rather than reading off the data. Tent and sleeping both fall three places although a tent and a sleeping bag are zippered non-worn containers, which is mild but direct evidence against the luggage relation as I named it; shirt rises three places although it is worn on the body, in the same direction. And on the third relation the movements are the smallest in the whole table (+2, +3, +2, from ranks already near the top), small enough that a repeat measurement could reverse any of them, which is why I marked it low.
result.notes: The two sides are not symmetric in weight. On the A side the three biggest falls are blue, hoodie and black, and two of those three are colour words; on the B side the two biggest rises, duffle and suitcase, are both luggage. So the clearest single statement is that the difference runs between colour-and-material description of worn clothing on one side and named pieces of baggage on the other, with the fastening words as a weak third strand. Worth noting that under B both ends of the range gain at once, the most anatomically specific completion (fly, flies, zipper, and the legwear words trouser and slacks) and the most inert one (suitcase, backpack, duffle), while what loses ground sits between them, the ordinary described garment. I have not tried to say which condition is which, and the shape does not obviously fit a simple more-or-less ordering.

result.reading: Both conditions put a threat word at the very top (threatened is rank 2 under A and rank 4 under B, essentially unmoved), so the fearful content itself is shared; what changes underneath it is the kind of word that carries the feeling. Under A the strong items are participles of constrained agency (obliged, compelled, helpless, powerless, trapped), and under B these collapse, with obliged falling from rank 8 clean off the hundred, while plain state adjectives rise (uncomfortable, insecure, vulnerable) and, awkwardly for any softening story, so does violated.

relations.name: Coercion becomes condition
relations.sentence: Under A the completion tends to be a participle in which something has been done to the neighbours or their choice removed (obliged, compelled, helpless, powerless, trapped), and under B every one of these falls, obliged leaving the list altogether, in favour of adjectives naming a condition the neighbours are simply in (uncomfortable, insecure, vulnerable, and the participle violated).

relations.name: Safety changes its word
relations.sentence: The safety axis is present in both conditions but is carried by a different lexical family: all three members of the safe family fall under B (safe, safer, unsafe) while both members of the secure family rise (secure, insecure), so the two poles of each pair move together with the word form rather than with the valence.

relations.name: Grading over pointing
relations.sentence: The function words B lifts are ones that grade or postpone the predicate (very, more, as, like, a, no), while the ones A favours point at something already in the scene (the, their, that), so B leans toward a modified or comparative completion and A toward a definite one.

result.kind: constrained-by-an-agent versus self-standing state

residue.description: These are not content completions of the fragment: what makes the largest single upward move in the set (rank 100 to 5) but names no feeling and I can see no construction it belongs to here, A is almost certainly a capitalized variant of the article rather than a word in its own right, it holds position and so carries no information, and they and that are pronouns that would only start a clause the measurement does not show me.

result.counterexamples: The worst is violated, which rises 48 places under B: it is stronger and more accusatory than anything on the A side, so any reading in which B is the milder or more hedged condition is simply false, and it also sits uneasily in the second group of relation one, since violated is a participle with an implied agent exactly like threatened. Secure rising while safe and safer fall contradicts a valence reading in the other direction, since B lifts both secure and insecure. Threatened moving only two places, and staying near the top of both lists, limits how much any of these relations can claim: the dominant completion is the same in both conditions and the relations describe the material below it. Within relation three, no is a negator rather than a hedge and fits the grading account badly.
result.notes: I have deliberately not read the direction as one of intensity or valence, because the evidence cuts both ways: violated and insecure rise under B while safe and safer fall, and the sharpest fall of all, obliged, is not a fear word at all. The load-bearing observation is the safe/secure split, where an entire semantic axis survives intact and only its lexical family changes, which is what pushed me toward describing the difference as one of word-kind rather than of sentiment. Relation one is the one I would defend hardest, on the strength of five words moving the same way with no counter-member on the B side and the largest movement in the set among them; relation three I state only because the function words move coherently, and I would not argue for it. I have no access to what conditions A and B are, so nothing here should be read as a claim about which condition is which.

result.reading: Under B the completions that gain are almost all words that name an emotion the neighbours have (upset, uncomfortable, nervous, angry, anxious, bad), while the words that lose are words that describe the neighbours' position with respect to an agent or a constraint (powerless, obliged, compelled, abandoned) together with the two security words (safe, safer). The content split is unusually clean: among words that plausibly complete "the neighbours felt ___" as content, every affect label moves up and every positional or security word moves down, with "threatened" the only straddler and it barely moves at all.

relations.name: named feeling over position
relations.sentence: Under B the completions that rise are words that label an internal emotional state (upset, uncomfortable, nervous, angry, anxious, bad), while the ones that fall are words that state the neighbours' standing relative to an agent or a constraint rather than their mood (powerless, obliged, compelled, abandoned, and the security pair safe and safer).

relations.name: safety withdrawn, threat kept
relations.sentence: The two words for security fall a long way under B (safer 17 to 66, safe 15 to 33), taking with them the negation and comparative that would build a phrase like "felt no safer", whereas threatened holds the top position and the alarm words rise, so B retains a vocabulary for danger while losing the vocabulary for reassurance.

relations.name: clause frame to adjective frame
relations.sentence: A's function words are the ones that open a clause after "felt" (the, they, their, it, as in "felt the ..." or "felt they ..."), while B's are the indefinite articles and the intensifier and comparison markers that sit in front of a predicate adjective (a, an, very, as, like), which is the syntactic shape the rising emotion words need.

result.kind: felt emotion versus structural position

residue.description: These are function words rather than content completions of the fragment: determiners, pronouns, intensifiers and comparatives that only acquire meaning from whatever follows them, so the third relation reads a syntactic tendency in them and none of them should be taken as evidence about what the neighbours are said to feel.

result.counterexamples: Three things cut against the relations as stated. First, betrayed and forced held position, and both belong to exactly the relational-position vocabulary that the first relation says A favours, so that vocabulary is not being displaced wholesale, only the part of it that is about capacity and obligation. Second, safe and safer sit on the A side while being felt states as much as positions, so the first relation's boundary is not clean at that edge, and symmetrically threatened rises on the B side while being a relation to an aggressor rather than a pure mood; threatened moves only one place, so the damage is small, but it is the word that most resists the split. Third, so is an A-side intensifier that would build "felt so upset" just as B's very does, which directly contradicts the frame-shift relation and is one reason that relation is marked low. A weaker point against reading B as simply more alarmed: powerless and abandoned, the words of greatest vulnerability, fall under B rather than rising, so the change is in what kind of thing is named, not in how endangered the neighbours are said to be.
result.notes: The confidence is about the dimension, not about any interpretation of why it moves; I am reading only rank order and have no access to likelihoods, so nothing here says how large any of these differences are in the underlying quantity. The residue and the third relation overlap by instruction: every word in that relation is a function word and so also belongs in the residue, and I have listed them in both rather than pretending the syntactic pattern is content. Counting is against me on the third relation anyway, since a handful of determiners moving a place or two is the sort of pattern that would not survive a repeated measurement, whereas the first relation rests on six words moving twenty to a hundred places in one direction with no content word crossing the other way.

relations.name: Arousal left unmarked

"busy" and "outside" rise only five and seven places from ranks that were already high under A, and each could be read into either of the first two relations (activity, or a named observable behaviour) without the movement being large enough to settle which, so I would rather leave them unassigned than let them prop up a relation.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is to the second relation: friendly is A's single likeliest completion and is still B's second, moving one place, and very moves one place likewise, so the two words most prominent under A are not displaced at all and the "generic praise falls" story rests almost entirely on good (-52) and happy (-22); nice, polite and pleasant fall only nine, nine and seven places, which is weak. Helpful is a further counterexample to the same relation, since it is about as general a term of approval as nice and yet rises fourteen places. Against the first relation, outside is a locative that rises seven places while its near-synonyms around, out, there and at fall, and out itself falls only two places, so the locative collapse is not uniform; both are defensible as activity-adjacent readings ("always outside", "always out playing") but that is a rescue, not a prediction. Against a warmer or milder reading of B, which I have not stated as a relation but which the risers invite, complaining rises twenty-four places to rank 6 and is the sixth likeliest completion under B: whatever B is doing, it is not confined to approving descriptions. Finally, the third relation is contradicted from inside by very, its own most established member, holding still while its rivals climb.
result.notes: Confidence is high for the categorial reading and lower for what it means. The movement is dominated by one grammatical fact: the words with the largest falls are almost all prepositions and particles, and the words with the largest rises are almost all -ing forms plus two hospitality adjectives, so B redistributes toward lexical, activity-naming completions and away from function-word completions of the presence idiom. That much I would defend if the measurement were repeated. What I would not defend is any account of why, and I have deliberately not stated a valence relation, because the second-largest riser class contains complaining at rank 6 alongside inviting and welcoming, and because the falling side contains good and happy but also polite and pleasant, which barely move. Two structural cautions on the display itself: the ranks are ordinal only, so a fall from 3 to 59 and a fall from 16 to 79 are not comparable in any quantity I can see here, and the ordering "by how much the difference rests on them" is the file's claim rather than something I can check from the positions given. Also, both lists are truncated at fifteen words a side, so words absent from both lists cannot be reasoned about, and no word here carries a dash, meaning nothing dropped out of a condition's list entirely, which would have been the stronger evidence the instructions describe.

result.reading: The fragment sets three people entering a room, and the two conditions disagree about what entering a room is for: under A the likeliest continuations are interrogation and inspection (interrogate at 1, question at 3, search at 4, speak at 6, ask at 8), while under B the top of the list is occupied by bodily harm and raised voices (beat at 2, shoot at 3, fight at 5, kill at 7, attack at 8, scream at 15 from 39). Speech does not vanish under B so much as change character: the articulate verbs (say, explain, tell) fall hardest while the loud ones (scream, shout, yell) rise or hold, and talk sits at the top under both.

relations.name: Interrogation into assault
relations.sentence: The completions that read the scene as a procedural encounter, in which the three men arrive to question, ask, search and read, are the ones A puts first and B demotes, while the completions that read it as an assault, in which they arrive to attack, kill, beat, shoot, fight or push, are the ones B promotes into the top ten.

relations.name: Articulate to loud
relations.sentence: Among the verbs of speaking, the ones naming content delivered to someone (say, explain, tell, speak) all fall under B, while the ones naming only the volume of the voice (scream, shout, yell) rise or hold, so vocalization survives the shift but loses its addressee.

relations.name: Handling versus harming
relations.sentence: The physical verbs that describe doing something to an object or a room without injuring anyone (shake, tear, pick, search) sit on A's side, while the physical verbs whose object is a body (beat, push, shoot, kill) sit on B's, which is a distinction within the physical rather than between the physical and the verbal.

result.kind: purpose of the entry: questioning versus assault

residue.description: These are light or near-empty verbs that do not by themselves complete the fragment into any scene (one gets, makes or takes something, and the something is where the content would be), and their movements are correspondingly small and hard to read: get +10, make +6, take +1, pick -1, look -7.

result.counterexamples: Three items cut against the relations as stated. First, talk rises under B to position 1 and argue rises as well, so B is not simply the condition in which speech gives way to force; the most likely single completion under B is still a conversational one, and only the informational and interrogative kinds of speech collapse. Second, tear (-16) and shake (-17) are destructive or forceful physical acts that fall under B, which directly contradicts any reading in which physicality as such is what B favours, and they are the reason the third relation is marked low rather than folded into the first. Third, yell moves only +1 and shout only +7 while scream moves +24, so the loud-voice group is much less coherent than its rise suggests, and the second relation rests mostly on scream plus the steep falls of say (-38) and explain (-23) rather than on a uniform shift.
result.notes: Nothing here says which condition is which, and I have described the difference as A-to-B rather than as a departure from a baseline. The single most informative item is interrogate, which is A's top-ranked completion and falls to 13 under B: a word that specific, moving that far from first place, does more to fix the axis than any of the larger place-counts, since a -38 on say is partly an artifact of say having a long tail of rivals to fall past. The two conditions agree at the very top (talk is 2 then 1) and diverge immediately below it, so the difference is not about whether the men speak but about what a room entered by three named foreigners is taken to be the setting for. I have not assumed the shift means anything beyond the ranking; the ranking is all I was shown, and I have said nothing about how much likelihood any of these moves carries.

result.reading: Nothing enters or leaves the list — every word is present under both conditions and the largest single move is four places out of twenty, so the whole difference is a shallow reshuffle in the middle of the ranking. What structure there is sits at the top of the "rose" column: yelling, loud and arguing are the three biggest movers toward B, while the words that slip are mostly locative particles (there, at, in, on, a) and the calmer speech verbs (talking, asking, shouting).

relations.name: Noise over speech
relations.sentence: The words that gain most under B name loudness and conflict as a standing characteristic (yelling, loud, arguing), while the ordinary speech verbs that A ranked above them (talking, asking, and even shouting) all slip down.

relations.name: Attribute over location
relations.sentence: Under B the completion tilts toward describing what the neighbors are like — an adjective or its intensifier (very, loud, nice) — while every word that would situate them somewhere or start a prepositional phrase (there, at, in, on, a) loses ground.

relations.name: Warm word swapped
relations.sentence: Of the two positive evaluations in the list, the more colloquial one rises by a place and the blander one falls by two, with friendly unmoved between them.

result.kind: what sort of predicate follows: a standing loud-behavior trait versus a place or an act of speaking

residue.description: up, hanging, having and out are not content completions but the openings of multi-word continuations (hanging out, up to something, having people over), so their small moves say nothing about what is being predicated; friendly and complaining hold position and so carry no difference at all, though it is worth noting that complaining sitting still weakens the first relation.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is shouting, which falls one place under B while its near-synonym yelling gains four — if B genuinely favored loud-conflict predicates, shouting should have moved with it, and its going the other way means the first relation rests on the particular words rather than on the category. Complaining, which is squarely in the same conflict register, does not move either. Against the second relation, the two largest gains among the non-adjectives are up and hanging, both particles that open exactly the kind of non-attributive continuation that relation says is losing ground. Nothing contradicts the third relation, but nothing supports it beyond two words moving one and two places.
result.notes: I would not defend any of this strongly. All twenty words survive in both rankings, there are no dropouts (the difference the instructions call strongest never occurs), and the entire signal is three words moving three or four places against a background of one- and two-place jitter. A reshuffle of that size is what I would expect from two measurements that differ hardly at all, and the fact that yelling rises while shouting falls is the kind of internal inconsistency that argues for noise rather than for a shift in what is being said about the neighbors. I state the relations because they are the shape the numbers happen to have, not because I think a repeat measurement would reproduce them. Two further limits: the likeliest completions are invisible, since no word here occupies position 1 under either condition, so this is a view of the middle of the distribution only; and without likelihoods a four-place move at rank 16 may be a smaller real difference than a one-place move at rank 2.

result.reading: Almost nothing here moves far: only five of the twenty-three words shift more than eight places, and every word is present in both rankings, so this is a reshuffle rather than an appearance or disappearance of vocabulary. The movement that does exist concentrates in the verbs of vocalizing (laugh and chant up hard, scream and talk down hard) while the verbs of violence move in both directions at once (beat and fire up, stab and shoot down), which means whatever separates the conditions is not operating on how violent the completion is.

relations.name: Chant over scream
relations.sentence: Words for a patterned or shared voice rise under B (chant from 22 to 6, laugh from 32 to 11, sing from 11 to 9) while words for an undifferentiated individual outcry or for plain conversation fall (scream 13 to 25, talk 7 to 16, speak 19 to 26, yell, shout and ask all down).

relations.name: Doing to the room
relations.sentence: Verbs describing purposive action carried out on the room or on things in it rise under B (search 17 to 7, fire 25 to 19, beat 5 to 2, pull and move each up), while verbs that require another person to act upon fall (fight 6 to 13, throw 3 to 8, ask 9 to 14, stab 20 to 24, shoot 10 to 12, play 14 to 20).

relations.name: Tail lifts, head sinks
relations.sentence: Every large riser begins deep in A's ranking (laugh 32, fire 25, chant 22, search 17) and nearly every faller begins in A's top or middle (shout 2, throw 3, fight 6, talk 7, ask 9, shoot 10), so part of the difference is B raising what A had buried and pressing down what A had at the front, independently of what the words mean.

result.kind: which social script the entrance belongs to, not how violent it is

residue.description: These are light or near-empty verbs that need an object before they complete the fragment with any content at all, and all four sit within three places of where they started, so they carry no readable difference between the conditions.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is the pair fire and shoot: both name discharging a weapon, and they move in opposite directions (fire +6, shoot -2), which is enough on its own to sink any reading that sorts the violence verbs coherently, and it is the reason I marked "Doing to the room" low. Argue contradicts "Chant over scream" directly: it is plain interpersonal talk, it belongs with talk and speak, and it rises (+3) where they fall, though only mildly. Beat rising to second place while stab and shoot fall contradicts any reading in which one condition is uniformly harsher or gentler than the other. And laugh, the single largest movement in the data at +21, is the fact least secured by anything I have said: I placed it with chant and sing as shared social voice, but it could as easily be read as unpatterned noise, in which case it belongs with scream and yell and moves the wrong way.
result.notes: I would defend the existence of a difference in the vocalizing verbs more than I would defend my account of it. Of twenty-three words, eighteen move seven places or fewer, which on a list of roughly thirty candidates is small enough that I would not build anything on their direction; the reading rests almost entirely on laugh, chant, scream, talk and search. No word is absent from either list, so the strongest available signal in this format, a word dropping out entirely, does not occur here at all, and that absence of hard evidence is why the overall confidence is low rather than medium. The third relation is stated partly as a caution against the first two: if B is simply a flatter ranking, then risers that started deep and fallers that started high are what a flattening produces, and the semantic story I told over the top of that pattern would be decoration.

relations.sentence: Under A the likeliest completions are the crotch-region fastening cluster in order (pants 1, fly 2, jeans 3) with jacket only fourth, and under B jacket takes first place outright while that cluster is pushed down one to three places each.

relations.name: Bare modifiers demoted
relations.sentence: The two words that are adjectives standing alone rather than named garments, wet and black, are among the sharpest falls (-22 and -6), while the third such word, leather, moves the other way by three places.

residue.description: "shirt" held position and so carries no information about the difference; "back" makes the single largest move (+39) but is not a garment and reads either as a body part or as the front half of a compound, so its identity is too unsettled to build a relation on; "flies" rising five places while "fly" falls one looks like a split between two spellings of the same completion rather than a change in what is favoured; "zipper" and "boots" each moved one place, which is passing traffic; and "sleeping" is only half a word (sleeping bag) whose +1 sits inside the noise.

result.counterexamples: Three things cut against the first relation and one against the third. "Coat" is as canonical an outer shell as parka or jacket and it falls rather than rises, though only by one place, so it damages the relation lightly. "Sweatshirt" and "hoodie" are worn over other clothes and both zip, yet they take the second and third largest falls in the list, which is the serious problem: if the axis were simply outer-versus-inner they should have risen with parka and vest, and the relation only survives if the split is read as structured-and-weatherproof against soft-and-domestic. "Wet" is the largest fall of all, and if it is the head of "wetsuit" then the single most demoted word is a piece of technical outerwear, which would invert the relation outright; I cannot tell from ranks alone which reading is right. Against a carried-gear grouping, "backpack" rises 14 places while "bag" falls 4 and "suitcase" falls 2, so the carried objects do not move together and I did not state that relation.
