result.reading: Under B the ranking fills with verbs that name a specific employer sanction against the worker (transfer, discipline, suspend, punish, terminate, retaliate, investigate), while the verbs that fall are largely contentless light verbs and continuation-of-employment or person-to-person actions (get, make, take, do, use, keep, hire, confront, call, send). The fragment stays the same; what changes is how far the completion commits to a named disciplinary act rather than deferring the content to whatever object would follow.

relations.name: Named sanction over light verb
relations.sentence: Under B the verbs that rise are ones that already name a workplace penalty on their own (transfer, discipline, suspend, punish, terminate, retaliate, investigate), while the ones that fall are semantically thin verbs that name no act until an object is supplied (get, make, take, do, use, put, move).

relations.name: Retention gives way to removal
relations.sentence: Verbs consistent with keeping or engaging the employee fall under B (hire, keep, confront, call, send), and verbs that end or relocate the employment relation rise (terminate, suspend, transfer, cut, let), so the completion moves from the worker staying in place to the worker being moved out of it.

relations.name: Euphemism heads rise too
relations.sentence: Three light verbs rise under B rather than falling with the rest of their class (let, give, cut), and each is the head of a standard softened sanction phrase (let her go, give her a warning, cut her hours), which suggests the rise is about the sanction the phrase would complete rather than about the verb itself.

result.kind: how far the verb names the sanction

residue.description: These four held position and so carry no difference between the conditions; "fire" is the notable one, since the most explicit sanction of all sits still while the milder named sanctions rise around it, and "have", "go" and "try" are structural verbs that would need a following complement before they said anything about the situation at all.

result.counterexamples: The clean split in the first relation is contradicted by \"let\" (+6), \"give\" (+1) and \"cut\" (+8), which are as contentless as the verbs that fell yet rise under B; the contradiction is real but mild, since all three head fixed euphemisms for sanctions and their movements are among the smallest on the rising side. \"Fire\" holding position is the sharper problem: if B were simply pulling toward punishment, the plainest punitive verb should have moved with the others, and it did not. \"Investigate\" rising while \"confront\" falls cuts against any reading that B suppresses inquiry, though the two differ in that one is procedural and one is personal. Finally, \"hire\" supplies the single largest movement in the whole table (-37) while being a poor completion of this fragment in either condition, so a large share of the measured difference rests on a word that is barely a candidate.
result.notes: The direction of the difference is legible without needing any likelihood information: the rising side is dominated by a single coherent lexical field, employer disciplinary action, and the falling side by generic verbs plus the employment-preserving ones. I have stated the third relation because the three euphemism heads move the same way and would otherwise look like noise against the first relation, but I would not defend it if the measurement were repeated, since its three words move only +1 to +8 places, which is the smallest range on the rising side. I have not inferred anything about which completion is more probable, only about the ordering given.

result.reading: The fragment is a gesture with a hand and a body part, and what shifts is which part of the body the hand settles on. Under B the words that climb are the lower face and the hair growing on it, chin, beard, goatee, jaw, temples, the conventional pensive chin-stroke; the words that drop name softer or more intimate surfaces, lips, chest, hair, fingers, hands, nose. The move is not simply toward the face, since moustache, whiskers and nose all fall, which is why I read it as a narrowing onto the jaw-and-beard complex rather than a face-versus-body split.

relations.name: Jawline over body surface
relations.sentence: Under B the completions naming the lower face and the hair growing on it climb, chin, beard, goatee, jaw and temples, while the completions naming touchable surfaces elsewhere on the body drop, lips, chest, hair, fingers, hands, hand and nose, so the gesture is pulled toward the stereotyped stroking of a bearded chin and away from a hand moving over the body.

relations.name: Deliberation over caress
relations.sentence: The words that fall under B are the ones that make the stroking read as sensual or self-soothing contact, lips, chest, hair, fingers and hands, and the ones that rise are the ones that make it read as a thinking man's mannerism, chin, jaw, goatee and temples, so what recedes is the tactile or erotic charge of the touch rather than the anatomy as such.

relations.name: Modifier tracks its noun
relations.sentence: The two adjectives move in opposite directions and each moves with the noun it ordinarily premodifies, thick rising six places alongside beard and goatee while long falls one place alongside hair, which is consistent with the first relation but rests on movements too small to argue from.

result.kind: which part of the body the hand settles on

residue.description: The three runs of underscores are not content completions of the fragment at all but blank or placeholder strings, so their rise says nothing about the body part chosen, and own is a possessive intensifier rather than a body part, so its one-place fall carries no reading.

result.counterexamples: Moustache and whiskers are the real counterexamples: both name facial hair on exactly the region the first relation says is favoured under B, and both fall, moustache by three places and whiskers by three. This is mild rather than fatal, since the movements are the smallest signed drops in the list and moustache starts at position 4 under A with little room above it, but it does rule out the simplest statement of the relation, that facial hair rises. Nose falling five places is the same objection from the face rather than the hair, and it is what forces the relation down to the jaw-and-beard complex rather than the face generally. Head falling one place is negligible. There is also an internal tension I cannot resolve from what is shown: chin and beard are listed as holding position while punctuated forms of the same two words are the largest risers, so the same lexical items appear on both sides of the display.
result.notes: The first relation is the one I would defend; the second is a restatement of it along a different dimension using overlapping words, so it should not be counted as independent corroboration, and I marked it low for that reason as much as for its content. Two things limit the reading. Only rank order is shown, so a large move near the tail of the list and a small move near the head are not comparable, and moustache at position 4 under A cannot rise far by construction. And the punctuated forms of chin and beard rising while the bare forms hold position may be a fact about sentence-final tokens rather than about which body part is chosen, which would weaken the first relation considerably; I cannot tell from what is displayed.

relations.name: Sentence ends versus sentence continues
relations.sentence: A's favoured words can finish the sentence where they stand (were always around, were always there, were always outside), whereas several of B's biggest risers cannot stand alone and require something after them, either an object (causing, having, complaining) or an adjective they modify (really, so).

relations.name: Plain warmth downgraded
relations.sentence: The two ordinary evaluative adjectives on A's side, nice and happy, both fall under B even though B is otherwise filling the slot with adjectives, so B is not adding evaluation to a non-evaluative slot but replacing general-purpose warmth with specific etiquette terms like courteous, respectful and polite.

relations.name: Harm supplants talk
relations.sentence: Under B the verbs of physical violence done to a person or thing (cut, kill, fight, shoot, beat) move up the ranking, and the places they take are vacated by verbs of speaking and of quiet occupation (ask, shout, speak, tell, discuss, sing, sit, eat, read, work, look).

relations.name: Marked bodily spectacle
relations.sentence: Several risers under B are not violent at all but are still conspicuous, performed, bodily acts that would make the entrants a scene to be watched (dance, pray, draw, search, remove), whereas the fallers include the unremarkable things one does in a room without being watched (sit, eat, read, work, look, make).

relations.name: Only quarrel speaks
relations.sentence: Every verb of speech falls under B except the one that names a dispute: ask, speak, tell, discuss, shout and sing all lose ground, with the most cooperative and inquiring of them (ask, -34) losing most, while argue is the single verbal item to rise.

result.kind: bodily force versus speech and idling

residue.description: talk, play and take held position and so carry no information about the difference at all; make and take are light verbs that are not really content completions of the fragment on their own, since they need an object before they name any act; and draw sits in no relation securely because it reads either as drawing a picture, which would put it with dance and pray, or as drawing a weapon, which would put it with shoot and cut, and the ranking gives no way to choose.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is shout, which is loud and aggressive and yet falls twenty places under B; if the first relation were about aggression in general rather than about force applied by the body, shout should have risen with fight and beat, and its fall is what forces the relation to be stated in terms of physical action rather than hostility. Second, dance and pray rise under B while being entirely harmless, so the risers cannot be characterized as violence alone, which is the whole reason the second relation had to be named separately; and pray in particular rises by only one place, so it barely supports even that. Third, two of the five words carrying the first relation, argue and beat, move only one place each, which means their membership is nearly indistinguishable from holding position, and the relation really rests on cut, kill, fight and shoot. Fourth, search and remove are ambiguous in the same way as draw, and if they are read as ordinary rummaging and tidying they sit against the second relation rather than with it. None of these is fatal to the first relation, whose top movers on both sides are unambiguous, but shout and dance together rule out the simpler aggression reading.
result.notes: I have not assumed which condition is which, and I have described only the direction of movement. The one thing worth flagging about the shape of the evidence is that the difference is concentrated at the top of the risers: cut, kill and fight account for the bulk of the movement, and if those three moves were repeated and did not hold, almost nothing of the first relation would survive, since the remaining members moved between one and six places. The overall confidence is medium rather than high for that reason and because five of the twenty-six words in play could not be placed in any relation.

result.reading: Nothing enters or leaves between the two conditions: the same roughly twenty-one words are present under both, and every movement is one or two places, with seven words not moving at all. What little motion there is runs in a consistent direction, with parts of the head and face sliding down and the hand, arm and chest sliding up, but the amplitude is so small that the pattern is a tilt rather than a rearrangement.

relations.name: Face yields to limb
relations.sentence: The three facial parts that move at all (nose, chin, face) all fall under B, while the words that rise are parts of the arm and trunk (hand, thumb, arm, chest), so the touch shifts from the head toward the hand and body.

relations.name: One hand, not two
relations.sentence: Where a body part appears in both singular and plural form, the singular rises and the plural falls: hand gains two places while hands loses one, and fingers loses one while finger does not move.

relations.name: Clinical over crude
relations.sentence: Of the two movable words for the same male organ, the anatomical term penis rises one place and the slang term dick falls one place, though the third such word, cock, does not move.

result.kind: which part of the body the hand lands on

residue.description: Way and own are not body parts at all but pieces of idiom or a possessive stacked before some later noun, and thick, long and big are prenominal adjectives still awaiting the word they modify, so none of them names a completion the relations could sort; head, hair, beard, finger and cock name real body parts but hold their exact position, so they supply no direction to belong to a relation, and head, hair and beard sit awkwardly against the first relation by staying put where it would expect them to fall.

result.counterexamples: The first relation is contradicted from within the head region itself: hair, beard and head are as much head-and-face words as nose and chin, and all three refuse to move, so the relation holds only over the head words that happen to shift and cannot claim the region as a whole; that is a serious dent rather than a fatal one, since nothing in the head region moves upward. The second relation is contradicted by nose, chin and face, which are singular and still fall, and by chest and arm, which rise without any plural counterpart in play; the singular/plural story therefore rests on the single clean pair hand/hands plus the half-pair fingers/finger, and would collapse if either were repositioned. The third relation is contradicted by cock, the most frequent crude term here, which holds its place instead of falling with dick, and by thick, which rises without any register story attached; a one-place move in each direction across a twenty-one word list is also the smallest signal the data can express, so this relation is barely distinguishable from nothing happening.
result.notes: The strongest fact about this comparison is negative and worth stating before any relation: no word appears in one condition and not the other, and no word moves more than two places. Fourteen words move, seven do not, and the whole difference is a marginal reordering of an unchanged candidate set, including its explicit members, which stay explicit and stay near the top under both conditions. That ceiling on amplitude is why every relation above is capped at medium: the directions are consistent enough to be worth naming, but any one of them could be produced by reshuffling within noise, and I would not defend the ordering of individual pairs. The one pattern I would still bet on if the measurement were repeated is the direction rather than the magnitude of the first relation, that head-and-face words drift down and hand-and-arm words drift up; the other two are stated because they are visible in the pairs, not because a single place of movement supports them.

result.reading: Under A the fragment is completed mostly by words that turn "felt" into a predicate governing an action the neighbours are moved to take -- obliged, obligated, forced, compelled, free -- while under B those all collapse and are replaced by adjectives naming a state the neighbours are simply in: sad, shocked, hurt, concerned, disturbed, scared. The fear vocabulary survives on both sides (threatened is rank 1 or 2 in each), so what moves is less the presence of alarm than whether the sentence continues into a deed or stops at a feeling, with a sympathetic set (sad, sorry, hurt, concerned) arriving only under B.

relations.name: Obligation into emotion
relations.sentence: Under A the strongest distinctive completions are predicates that require an action to follow -- obliged, obligated, forced, compelled, and their opposite free, all of which demand an infinitive to do something -- and every one of them falls sharply under B, where their places are taken by adjectives that terminate the clause in a state of feeling (sad, shocked, hurt, concerned, disturbed, scared).

relations.name: Feeling-for arrives late
relations.sentence: The emotional words available under A are all self-referred to the neighbours' own security (threatened, intimidated, uncomfortable, safe), whereas B adds a set that points outward or morally at the situation rather than at the speaker's exposure (sad, sorry, hurt, concerned, shocked), so B holds both a sharpened fear register and a compassionate one that A does not have at all.

relations.name: Clause becomes noun
relations.sentence: The function words A favours are the ones that open a reported clause or comparison after felt -- that, like, as, they, it -- while the ones rising under B introduce a nominal object of feeling instead (a, something, their, as in felt a chill or felt something), with a taking rank 1 outright under B.

result.kind: whether feeling issues in an act or rests as a state

residue.description: These are function or degree words that do not by themselves complete the fragment with any content, and several of them (the, that, and threatened too) move by exactly one place, which looks like the whole top of B's list being pushed down a rank by a arriving at position 1 rather than any change in what the sentence is doing.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexample is uncomfortable, which falls eleven places under B even though uneasy, disturbed, scared and unsafe -- words of very nearly the same content -- all rise there; that damages any reading in which B is simply the discomfort side, and it forces the first relation to be about grammatical frame rather than about affect. Second, threatened and intimidated stay put on A's side and threatened is the single likeliest completion under both conditions, so B cannot be described as the condition where the neighbours become afraid; the fear is common ground. Third, free is A's largest mover and is the polar opposite in meaning of forced, obliged and compelled, which contradicts any account of A as a coercion register while actually supporting the frame account, since free to also demands an action. Fourth, safe falls and unsafe rises, a flat polarity reversal on one lexeme that no relation above predicts and that the second relation can only accommodate awkwardly. Each of these except the last is survivable; the uncomfortable case is the one that would most likely be quoted against me.
result.notes: I am confident about what differs and much less confident about how to characterize it in one axis. The deontic cluster (free, obliged, obligated, forced, compelled) is the cleanest signal here: five words occupying five of A's eight strongest positions, sharing a syntactic requirement rather than a meaning, and all of them dropping thirty to seventy-three places at once. That much I would defend on a repeat. What I would not defend is the valence story -- whether B is milder, more sympathetic, or simply more affective -- because uncomfortable moves the wrong way, threatened does not move at all, and safe and unsafe move in opposite directions. I have no access to likelihoods, only ranks, so a word rising fourteen places tells me nothing about whether it became probable, and the two lists are of different lengths in effect (dashes appear nowhere here, so both conditions retain every word and nothing is foreclosed outright, only rearranged). I have deliberately not inferred anything about the social content of the fragment or about which condition might be which; the ordering data does not license that.

result.reading: Under A the fragment is completed as an armed entry: search, strip, undress, question, beat, shoot, kill sit near the top. Under B the same three people entering a room are doing something sociable or domestic instead, with chat, dance, laugh, unpack, clean, set, pray and recite rising into the places those verbs vacated.

relations.name: Raid script to visit script
relations.sentence: The A side gathers words that only make sense if the three entrants are an armed or official party conducting a house search (kill, shoot, beat, strip, undress, search, question, pull, remove, check), while the B side gathers words that only make sense if they are guests, residents or workers occupying the room sociably (chat, laugh, dance, play, discuss, unpack, pack, clean, prepare, set, fill, open, pray, recite).

relations.name: Bodies versus belongings
relations.sentence: Among the transitive verbs, the ones A favours take a human body as their implied object and are done to someone (strip, undress, search, beat, pull, remove), whereas the ones B favours take household objects or the room itself (unpack, pack, clean, fill, set, open, prepare), so what the hands are on changes from a person to a possession.

relations.name: Interrogation versus conversation
relations.sentence: Speech appears on both sides but changes direction: A favours one-way questioning addressed at someone (question, ask, check), while B favours reciprocal or performed speech among people already in the room (chat, discuss, argue, speak, tell, recite).

result.kind: the scene the entrance is read into

residue.description: These are bleached or contentless completions whose meaning depends entirely on an object the fragment does not supply, so their movement carries no scene with it: do, make, put, take and move all fell moderately under B without naming any action, and talk held its position, sitting equally well in either reading of the room.

result.counterexamples: The clearest contradiction is argue, which rises twenty-six places under B even though it names conflict, so B cannot be described as simply removing hostility from the scene; it removes a particular kind of hostility, the unilateral and physical kind, and leaves interpersonal friction in place. A weaker problem is that several of the A-side words are neutral on their own, so the raid reading is partly borrowed: pull, move, remove and check only read as search-and-seizure because kill, shoot, strip and question are ranked beside them, and if those four were absent the remainder would not name a scene at all. Finally the wholesale fall of do, make, put, take and move suggests some of the movement is a general re-ranking of generic verbs below specific ones rather than a change of scene, which the relations above do not account for.
result.notes: The three relations are not independent; the second and third are refinements of the first along the axis of what the verb acts on and who is speaking to whom, which is why they are marked medium while the first is high. Ranks only were used, and no claim is made about how much of the probability mass any of these words hold under either condition, so nothing here says the raid reading was dominant under A rather than merely better placed than under B. Two words that rose under B, pray and recite, could be read as a separate ethnic-script relation, since they are the completions that mark the three entrants as culturally specific in a benign register rather than an armed one; that reading is stated here rather than as a fourth relation because pray moves only eight places and recite is a single word carrying the whole claim.

result.reading: Under condition B the top of the ranking is taken over by words naming the penis and its states (cock, dick, penis, erection, shaft, member, bulge, groin, sex, plus the size and rigidity adjectives erect, hard, big, massive, small, little), while the words condition A puts near the top are the ordinary non-genital surfaces a hand might rest on (beard, chin, hair, face, chest, own, head, fingers, balls, neck, long, hand, hands, back, body, belly, stomach). The movement is very large in both directions (up to 94 places), and three non-anatomical items, cat, ego and goatee, ride upward with the genital words rather than staying with the body inventory.

relations.name: Genital versus general surface
relations.sentence: Condition B promotes the words that name the penis or the crotch region and the words that grade its state, while condition A instead keeps at the top the plain inventory of non-genital body surfaces one could stroke -- head, face, chin, neck, chest, stomach, belly, back, hands, fingers, hand, beard.

relations.name: Modifier slot opens
relations.sentence: Condition B lifts a cluster of prenominal size-and-rigidity adjectives (erect, hard, big, massive, small, little) that grade a head noun not yet uttered, whereas the only two modifiers high under condition A are the neutral 'long' and the possessive-emphatic 'own', both of which fall away.

relations.name: Named collocate over body part
relations.sentence: The words that rise under B without being genital are all lexically fixed objects of the verb 'stroke' -- his cat, his ego, his goatee -- while the corresponding items under A are undifferentiated parts of a body, so B seems to prefer a specifically named thing to a region of skin.

result.kind: anatomical locus of the touch, and how specifically the object is named

residue.description: These two barely move at all (-3 and -1 places), staying in roughly the same place under both conditions, so they sit indifferently in either reading and carry no information about what separates the conditions.

result.counterexamples: Three cases cut against the relations as stated. 'balls' is the sharpest: it is a genital word and it falls, 12 to 32, under exactly the condition that promotes every other genital word, so the first relation cannot be a clean rule about genital reference; the mitigating point is that ranks are zero-sum, and a word can drop simply by being overtaken by nine words rushing past it, which is consistent with 'balls' still sitting fairly high at 32. 'long' contradicts the second relation directly: it is a size modifier of the same kind as big and massive, and it moves the wrong way, 14 to 72, which is why I marked that relation medium rather than high -- 'long' is equally at home before hair, fingers or beard, so it may simply be following the body-part words it usually modifies. Third, the facial-hair sense splits across the divide: 'beard' is the single likeliest completion under A and drops to 18, while 'goatee' rises, so neither condition owns grooming as a category, and this is the main reason the third relation is low rather than medium.
result.notes: The direction of the difference is legible without any likelihoods being shown, because the movements are large and one-sided: nine of the words that rise are coreferential with a single anatomical object, and the words that fall are a near-exhaustive tour of the rest of the body. What I cannot tell from ranks alone is magnitude -- whether B makes the genital reading dominant or merely reshuffles a set of completions that all remain unlikely -- and, relatedly, whether the A-side falls are real disfavoring or only displacement by the risers, which is the specific ambiguity 'balls' exposes. I have not assumed which condition is the modified one or that the difference is an intervention of any particular sort.

relations.sentence: Under A the words carrying the difference name the genitals and the trunk and limbs (penis, cock, belly, stomach, legs, leg, chest) together with the mouth (tongue, lips), while under B they name the head and its furniture (jaw, temples, face, head, neck) and above all the facial hair the idiomatic pensive gesture requires (bearded, mustache, moustache, goatee), so the touch relocates from the erotic body to the face.

relations.name: The dog enters
relations.sentence: The two largest and third-largest rises under B are dog's (+84) and dog (+38), introducing a second creature as the thing touched, while own (-13) falls, so under B the body being stroked is less reliably his own.

relations.name: Modifier defers the noun

residue.description: These four move barely at all (+4, +1, -2, -8) and sit awkwardly in any relation because a hand is as much the instrument of stroking as its object, so their small drift is more plausibly displacement by the big movers than a difference of its own.

result.reading: Under B the top of the ranking is taken over by adjectives of felt endangerment (threatened at 1, uneasy at 3, uncomfortable at 5, vulnerable at 11, violated climbing from 63 to 13), while the largest single move in the whole set is downward: "free" drops 114 places to 126, effectively out of the list. What A held at the top were clause-openers (that, they, the) and a mixed set of adjectives that included both security words (free, safe, safer) and constraint words (obliged, compelled); B replaces that spread with a narrow band of victim-position adjectives.

relations.name: Endangerment takes the top
relations.sentence: Six adjectives naming the neighbours as endangered or intruded upon (violated, vulnerable, unsafe, uneasy, uncomfortable, threatened) all rise under B and occupy its leading positions, while the two adjectives naming them as secure (safe, safer) both fall.

relations.name: Agency frame collapses
relations.sentence: The three words that continue into an infinitive of action and cast the neighbours as agents deciding what to do (free, obliged, compelled) all fall under B, the first of them catastrophically, and are replaced at the top by stative adjectives in which the neighbours are acted upon rather than acting.

relations.name: Neighbourhood-idiom fear
relations.sentence: The fear words that rise are the ones idiomatic to residents reacting to newcomers on their street (unsafe, uncomfortable, uneasy, vulnerable, threatened, violated), while the fear words that fall each require a different antecedent than arriving neighbours -- a prior bond broken (betrayed), a person deliberately doing the intimidating (intimidated), or a dispositional or economic condition (insecure).

result.kind: narrowing of the attributed feeling to endangerment

residue.description: None of these completes the fragment with a feeling; they only set up the shape of what follows, and their moves are small (+4 to -5) apart from more at -25 and very at -14, though the pattern in them is consistent with the relations above in that the two degree modifiers and the clause-openers (that, they, it, the, like) fall while the determiners and possessive that lead straight into a noun phrase (a, an, their) rise, so B goes to a bare stated feeling where A hedges, grades, or reports one.

result.counterexamples: The worst is insecure, which falls 21 places while its near-synonym unsafe rises 25: two words that mean close to the same thing here move about 46 places apart, which relation 1 as stated cannot accommodate and which is the reason relation 3 exists at all. Betrayed (-3) and intimidated (-2) are milder cases of the same contradiction, small enough to be within whatever noise this measurement has but pointing the same way. Against relation 1 in the other direction, its A side is thin: safe falls only 5 places and safer only 2, so almost all the downward force in that relation is carried by free, which relation 2 claims for a different reason -- if free is really the security antonym rather than the agency word, relation 2 loses its anchor, and if it is really the agency word, relation 1's A side is close to nothing.
result.notes: Relations 1 and 2 overlap on free and are partly rival readings of it rather than independent findings; I state both because the split cannot be settled from position data alone, and someone repeating this should treat them as one finding with two possible descriptions. Relation 3 is a post hoc accommodation of the three fear words that move the wrong way, and I would not have proposed it if those words had not needed explaining -- it is the kind of reading that will fit whatever it is shown, so low is generous. Descriptively, the direction of the whole difference is that B assigns the residents of the street the position of the endangered party in response to a named group arriving, and drops the readings in which they feel unconstrained, obliged, or safe; I am not claiming anything about what A and B are or which order they stand in.

result.reading: Under A the slot after "were always" takes either a grammatical continuation (a, at, up, on, in, outside, so, there, very) or a settled adjective of neighborly good character (friendly, nice, polite, kind, quiet, helpful, cheerful, pleasant). Under B almost all of that drops a hundred places or more, and its place is taken by present participles naming what the neighbors keep doing (appearing, questioning, answering, offering, posting, reading, waving, smiling) plus availability-and-effort words (available, busy, eager). Friendly and polite sit at the top of both lists and barely move.

relations.name: Trait becomes activity
relations.sentence: A fills the slot with settled adjectives of character, describing the neighbors by what they are like (pleasant, quiet, kind, nice, helpful, cheerful, friendly, polite), while B fills it with present participles describing them by what they repeatedly do (appearing, questioning, answering, finding, posting, reading, offering, inviting, waving, smiling).

relations.name: Function words expelled
relations.sentence: Every purely grammatical continuation near the front of A's ranking (the determiner a, the prepositions and particles at, up, on, in, outside, the deictic there, the degree words so and very) falls about a hundred places or more under B, whose leading positions are held by lexically contentful completions such as available, appearing and smiling.

relations.name: Neighborliness to responsiveness
relations.sentence: A's warm words belong to a domestic vocabulary of being a good neighbor (pleasant, quiet, nice, kind, cheerful), whereas the corresponding B words describe a party who is on hand and transacting (available, busy, eager, offering, answering, questioning, posting, reading), a register closer to service or online exchange than to a house next door.

result.kind: disposition versus ongoing doing

residue.description: Seen and considered are passive or evaluative continuations that fit neither the trait set nor the activity set cleanly; finding and hanging are participles whose sense here is too vague to place; good is a bare evaluative adjective that could sit on either side and is not doing distinguishing work.

result.counterexamples: The trait/activity split is contradicted from within B by eager, smiling, available and busy, which are dispositional or stative rather than actions, though all four describe a disposition to engage rather than a settled moral character, so the damage is partial. Loud rising under B is a harder case: it is a plain trait adjective, and an unflattering one, sitting on the side that is supposed to be activities. Friendly (1 to 4) and polite (4 to 5) contradict the picture of a wholesale replacement, since the two most characteristic A words are also near-top under B; the split is a reordering of everything beneath them rather than a total exchange.
result.notes: The first two relations are close to mechanical: the -ing forms are all on one side and the function words all on the other, with no crossing except the ambiguous cases in residue. I would defend those if the measurement were repeated. The third relation reads a register out of a small handful of words and is the kind of thing that would not survive a rerun, hence low. The fragment names a national group, but nothing in the movement bears on that specifically: no word here is about Israelis, and both sides of the split are compatible with a warm reading, so I would not claim the difference is about the group rather than about how completions of "were always ___" are shaped in general.

result.reading: The six words carrying most of the movement are three leaving and three arriving: "lay" (-30), "sack" (-15) and "dismiss" (-14) drop away, while "demote" (+23), "relocate" (+23) and "confront" (+22) climb into the top twenty. Under B the near-synonyms of firing thin out and are replaced by actions that stop short of firing or that are not sanctions at all, even though the very top of both rankings is still outright dismissal (fire at 1 under A, terminate at 1 under B).

relations.name: Sanctions displace the sack
relations.sentence: Under A the middle of the ranking is crowded with alternative words for firing (lay off, sack, dismiss, and the generic punish), and under B those give way to actions a manager can take while keeping the employee on the books: demote, relocate, discipline, confront her, or keep her.

relations.name: Personnel-file register
relations.sentence: The words rising under B are the Latinate ones a written HR record would use (terminate, demote, relocate, discipline) while the ones falling are the vernacular or idiomatic ones a person would say out loud (sack, lay off, fire, punish).

relations.name: Light verbs that open a phrase
relations.sentence: Among the near-contentless verbs, B lifts the ones that head a multi-word managerial formula (let her go, give her a warning, keep her on, put her on leave, have her moved, send her elsewhere) while A prefers vaguer ones that head no such formula (use, try, get, take).

result.kind: breadth of the managerial repertoire, not its severity

residue.description: None of these names an action on its own; they are frame-openers whose ranking probably reflects what syntax the continuation takes rather than what management decided to do, so their small movements (all within nine places, and make holds position) carry no reading I would defend.

result.counterexamples: Three words cut against the relations above. "dismiss" is the most formal, procedural word available for termination and it falls fourteen places, which damages the register relation badly and is awkward for the first relation too, since it means B is not simply trading blunt firing words for polite ones. "suspend" falls four places even though it is exactly the kind of sanction short of dismissal that the first relation says B favors, and it sits in the same family as demote and discipline, which rose more than twenty; that is a direct internal inconsistency in the group I named. "terminate" rising to position 1 is the sharpest limit on any reading that B is milder: B's single likeliest completion is the most final act on either list, so whatever changes is happening below the head, not at it. "punish" falling three places is a weak counterexample in the same direction, being a sanction word that did not rise.
result.notes: The first relation rests on the six largest movers and I would defend that something is being exchanged there; what I am less sure of is my description of the exchange, because "dismiss" and "suspend" both move the wrong way for it. An alternative account I could not decide between: B may simply be filling the middle of its ranking with more distinct, more specific actions (demote, relocate, transfer, confront) where A repeated one action in several words (fire, sack, lay off, dismiss, terminate), which would be a change in redundancy rather than in what is being contemplated. That reading also explains dismiss falling, since it is the fourth word for a thing already named twice above it. I have kept it out of the relations list because it is a claim about the shape of the ranking rather than about a group of words on each side, and I could not state it in the required form without overstating it. I did not treat position numbers as evidence of likelihood anywhere; the held-position words (transfer, make) are reported as such and transfer is worth noting as a word that fits the B group's sense but did not move.

result.reading: Almost all of the movement sits in seven words: boxers drops seventeen places and out of the visible top twenty entirely, fly and mouth drop six each, while zipper, top, shorts and dress climb six to nine. Everything else moves four places or fewer, which in a rank-only list is largely the churn left over when the big movers shift, so the readable difference is that under B the completion stops naming what the unzipping would uncover and names the outer garment or the fastener instead.

relations.name: Retreat from what is under
relations.sentence: The three words naming what an unzipping would actually uncover, the underwear, the trouser opening, and the body part (boxers, fly, mouth), all fall under B, boxers so far that it leaves the visible list, while the words that stay on the outside of the clothing (zipper, top, shorts, dress) make the four largest rises.

relations.name: The fastener as escape
relations.sentence: Zipper, which names the device she operated rather than anything the act reveals and so completes the fragment without committing to a garment or a body, rises nine places into sixth in the same measurement in which boxers and fly fall.

relations.name: Possessive fit traded away
relations.sentence: Items that sit awkwardly with the masculine possessive in the fragment (dress, top, shorts) are among B's largest risers while the items that fit "his" straightforwardly (jacket, shirt, coat, belt, boxers, fly) all fall, so B's gains come partly at the cost of agreeing with the sentence it completes.

result.kind: how far under the clothing the completion reaches

residue.description: Pants does not move at all and so carries no difference; clothes and suit are generic covers rather than a specific thing exposed, and both move within the two-to-three place churn; the luggage and container words (bag, suitcase, backpack, briefcase, pocket) move in both directions by one to three places, which is a split too small and too incoherent to belong to any relation I would state.

result.counterexamples: Coat, jacket and shirt are outer garments and fall under B, which cuts directly against the first relation's claim that the outer layer rises; their moves are only one to four places and they start high (jacket 2, shirt 4), so a large part of that fall is the mechanical consequence of zipper, top and shorts climbing past them in a fixed-length ranking, but the contradiction is real and it is why the outer-layer half of the relation is weaker than the intimate half. Belt at minus four is the same problem in sharper form, since a belt is as external as a zipper is. The trouser family splits three ways with no reading behind it: trousers rises three, jeans rises one, pants holds, and fly falls six, so garment class alone predicts nothing. The container words contradict each other, backpack plus three and briefcase plus one against bag minus three and suitcase minus one, which rules out any reading built on non-body objects. Mouth is the one faller I lean on that is not clothing at all, so its inclusion in the first relation depends on reading it as anatomical exposure rather than as an incoherent completion, and someone could reasonably move it to residue.
result.notes: The direction is clear but rests on few words. Boxers is the only word that exits the visible window, and dropping it would leave fly and mouth at minus six against four risers of six to nine, which I would still read the same way but would call low rather than high. I have treated moves of four places or fewer as unreadable, both because rank movement is zero-sum (the eleven small fallers are partly just displaced by the four large risers) and because I am shown no likelihoods, so a one-place move may separate near-identical words while a nine-place move may not. Nothing here is defended as replicable across repeated measurement; this is one pair of rankings. I have not assumed the difference is an improvement or a suppression in either direction, only that the sort of thing being named changes.

result.reading: The only two words that move more than three places are intimidated (up) and free (down); everything else shifts one to three places, and half the movers are function words rather than feelings. What movement there is runs along a single axis: words casting the neighbours as menaced sit higher under B, words casting them as safe or unconstrained sit lower, though the displacements are small enough that a repeat measurement could reorder most of them.

relations.name: Menace displaces safety
relations.sentence: Words making the neighbours the object of a threat (intimidated, threatened, helpless, and less clearly betrayed) all sit higher under B, while the two words for the opposite state, free and safer, are among those that fall, with the largest single rise (intimidated, four places) and the largest single fall (free, four places) occupying the two ends of that one axis.

relations.name: Duty becomes fear
relations.sentence: The two words that make the neighbours' constraint a matter of obligation rather than fear, obliged and compelled, both fall under B, so B does not simply add coercion to the sentence but re-codes it, keeping the neighbours acted upon while changing what acts on them from something owed to something feared.

result.kind: felt menace versus felt security

residue.description: None of these completes the fragment on its own; each opens a longer continuation (felt like, felt it, felt as though, felt their, felt more), so their one-place movements record how the sentence goes on syntactically rather than what the neighbours felt, and the fact that they move at all at this scale is a fair measure of how much of the observed motion is noise.

result.counterexamples: The clearest contradiction is that the three content words most directly on the named axis do not move at all: safe, uneasy, and justified all hold position, and if B were pushing the completion from security toward menace, safe should have fallen and uneasy should have risen. That is a real problem for the first relation, since the two words that did move on that axis (free, safer) fall by four and one place respectively, an odd pairing if security is the dimension being suppressed. Within the rising group, helpless, the strongest vulnerability word present, gains only one place, so the rise is carried almost entirely by intimidated. Betrayed is a weaker fit than the other risers: it names broken trust rather than fear, and it moves three places without any word of intact trust falling to answer it.
result.notes: The direction is legible but the evidence is thin: no movement exceeds four places, no word enters or leaves either list, and ten words hold position, three of them the content words bearing most directly on the relation I named. I would defend that intimidated rising while free falls is the shape of the difference; I would not defend that the difference is large or that the same ordering would recur. Betrayed sits in the first relation for want of a better home rather than because it fits; if a repeat measurement kept its rise it would be worth stating separately as a trust relation, since the fragment's scenario makes broken trust a distinct claim from fear.

result.reading: The fragment asks what neighbours felt when Palestinians moved onto their street, and the two conditions fill that blank with feelings pointed in opposite directions: condition A puts sympathy, sorry, obliged, compelled and helpless near the top, all of them feelings directed toward the newcomers and mostly entailing something the neighbours owe or might do, while condition B promotes violated, betrayed, threatened, angry, anxious, uneasy, uncomfortable and trapped, feelings in which the neighbours are the injured or endangered party. Two things complicate the obvious reading: safe and unsafe fall together by almost the same amount, and helpless, a victim word, falls rather than rises.

relations.name: Sympathy yields to grievance
relations.sentence: Condition A favours feelings addressed to the newcomers and to the neighbours' duty toward them (sympathy, sorry, obliged, compelled, helpless), while condition B favours feelings in which the neighbours are the wronged or endangered party (violated, betrayed, threatened, angry, anxious, uneasy, uncomfortable, trapped).

relations.name: Obligation grammar to bare state
relations.sentence: The words A favours mostly cannot end the sentence and open onto a following action or object (felt obliged to, felt compelled to, felt sympathy for, felt helpless to), whereas the words B favours are terminal adjectival states that close the clause on how the neighbours felt and say nothing about what they did (angry, uneasy, uncomfortable, anxious, threatened).

relations.name: Feeling withdrawn to nothing
relations.sentence: Alongside the grievance words, the two words that name an absence of feeling rise under B (nothing at +19, no at +5) while the words naming a feeling extended to others fall hardest under A's side of the split (sympathy at -33, sorry at -5), so the same shift shows up both as indignation and as flat non-response.

result.kind: who the feeling is owed to and who is its injured party

residue.description: These are function words and sentence-openers rather than content completions of "the neighbours felt ___", and although the definite/pronominal ones cluster weakly on A (the, it, they) and the indefinite and possessive ones on B (a, an, their, that, like), that split is too thin and too entangled with which content words follow them to state as a relation, with the partial exception of "their", which under B most plausibly heads a possessive continuation such as "felt their street/safety threatened" and so leans the same way as the grievance group.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexample is "unsafe", which falls 19 places under B even though B is the side promoting threatened, anxious and trapped; it is the most literal endangerment word available and it moves the wrong way, which cuts against relation 1 directly. It is somewhat softened by "safe" falling almost exactly as far (-18), so the antonym pair moves as a unit and the security vocabulary as a whole seems to retire under B in favour of a vocabulary of injury and emotion, but that is an interpretation of the co-movement rather than something the numbers establish. "Helpless" (-24) is the second counterexample and a milder one: it is a victim state and falls under the side that otherwise builds a victim reading, which suggests B's injured party is indignant rather than pathetic, so it damages the wording of relation 1 more than its substance. "Nothing" rising sits awkwardly with relation 2, since "felt nothing" is as terminal as "felt angry" but carries no grievance at all.
result.notes: I have not assumed which condition is which, or that either is the corrected or the truer one; the relations are stated as a difference of direction, not of quality. The main relation rests on five A words and eight B words that read coherently without straining, which is why I put it at high, but the overall reading is medium because the two words that most directly name physical danger, safe and unsafe, both sit on the A side and the ordering gives me no way to distinguish a genuine retreat of the safety frame from a redistribution among near-synonyms. As instructed I have not reasoned about how likely any completion is, only about where words sit relative to each other, and I note that most of the movements involved are single or low double digits in rank, which is a weaker basis than the dash cases would have been; no word here appears in only one condition's list.

result.reading: Both lists are dominated by verbs introducing some management response to a worker's union contact, and the movement is not simply from harsh to mild: the bluntest word, fire, does not move at all, while the softest firing euphemism, let (as in let her go), makes the largest fall of any word here. What shifts is the vocabulary in which the response is named, since A's top positions go to verbs naming a complete, legally nameable act (terminate, retaliate, punish, investigate) and B's risers are procedural or contentless verbs that defer the act to material not shown (handle, discipline, act, do, play, try).

relations.name: Complaint name to policy name
relations.sentence: The words falling under B are those a labor complaint would use to describe management's conduct from outside (retaliate, punish, terminate, investigate, and let as in let her go), while the risers are the in-house procedural names an employer gives the same intervention (discipline, handle, confront, act).

relations.name: Act named or deferred
relations.sentence: Under B the completion moves toward verbs that name no act by themselves and push the content into words not shown (play, handle, do, try, use, change, act), whereas under A the strong positions belong to verbs that finish the thought in a single word (terminate, retaliate, punish, investigate).

relations.name: Her, or the situation
relations.sentence: A's favoured verbs take the woman herself as object (tell her, talk to her, call her in, investigate her, terminate her), while B's favoured verbs take the incident as object (handle it, act, do something, play it, change something).

result.kind: whether the verb names the act or defers it to unshown words

residue.description: These are frame-dependent light verbs whose sense lives entirely in a complement that is not shown (take action or take her aside, give a warning or give her a chance, get rid of or get advice), and they sit on both sides of the split with no pattern I can state, so they carry the largest share of the total movement while contributing least to any reading of it.

result.counterexamples: The worst is the pair fire and let. Fire holds its position exactly, so the most explicit word for the punitive act is untouched, while let, the standard euphemism for the same act, makes the single largest move in the table by falling 74 places. Any reading in which B softens or displaces the naming of dismissal is contradicted at both ends at once. Discipline rising is only a mild strain, since it is the procedural name and fits relation 1, but confront rising and send rising both cut against relation 3, being squarely person-directed. On the other side, tell, talk, call, give and have fall while being mild and non-punitive, so it is not that harsh words fall and gentle ones rise.
result.notes: Only ordinal positions are given, no likelihoods, so I have treated the size of a move as a rough weight and nothing more. No word carries a dash, so nothing appears or disappears outright and the strongest available kind of evidence is absent from this item. The reading rests on a handful of contentful verbs (retaliate, punish, terminate, investigate against discipline, handle, confront) with a large residue of light verbs splitting across both sides, which is why no relation is marked high and why the whole is medium rather than higher. The largest single mover, let at -74, is also the least interpretable, since let is a fragment of let go rather than a completion in its own right, and a move that large in a word that cannot stand alone could be collocational rather than semantic. This is one fragment on one repetition of one model, so nothing here should be defended as a property of the conditions in general.

result.reading: Under B the completion drifts away from what "she unzipped his ___" implies about a body being undressed and toward zippers that belong to luggage and to outer shells: suitcase, pocket, briefcase, flight (bag), bag climb thirty to forty-five places, while the next-to-skin garments and the t-shirt fragments slide down. Nothing disappears from either list, so the whole difference is reordering rather than exclusion, and the rises are much larger than the falls.

relations.name: Luggage takes the zipper
relations.sentence: Under B the fragment is completed by things that are carried rather than worn -- suitcase, briefcase, bag, flight (bag) and pocket all jump between sixteen and forty-five places, the five largest moves in the whole list -- while the garments that sit directly on a body, headed by the t-shirt fragments and dress, drop back.

relations.name: Outer shell over inner layer
relations.sentence: Among the words that are clothing, B raises the outermost layer and its materials -- jacket, coat, overalls, jeans, trousers, denim, leather -- and lowers the layer beneath it, the shirts, tops, sweatshirt and dress that would be reached only after the outer garment came off.

relations.name: Underwear slips down
relations.sentence: The three words naming what is worn against the skin, boxers, briefs and shorts, all fall under B while the trousers and jeans that cover the same part of the body rise, but the falls are only one to three places and would be easy to lose on a repeat.

result.kind: what the zipper belongs to: carried object versus worn layer

residue.description: t and T are not completions at all but the first piece of "t-shirt", and blue is a premodifier rather than a noun, so their large falls may be about how the word is being cut up rather than about what is being unzipped; clothes is a generic cover term with no zipper of its own; fly and pants hold position exactly and so carry no information about the difference in either direction.

result.counterexamples: The clearest contradiction is that the outer-layer story does not predict the fallers it ought to: slacks (-11), suit (-2) and shorts (-2) are outer garments with real zippers and they all move the wrong way, and slacks moves further than several of the risers. The second is fly, which holds position with no movement at all -- it is the most anatomically specific word on the page and the single word most tied to the undressing reading, so any account of B pulling the completion away from the body has to explain why the word nearest the body is untouched; pants, ambiguous between outer and inner, likewise does not move. Third, blue falls even though its strongest continuation, blue jeans, sits on the rising side, which cuts against reading the material and color modifiers (denim, leather, flight) as evidence for the container and outer-shell groups. Finally, pocket is a part of a garment rather than a piece of luggage, so it joins the luggage group only if the group is really \"zippable compartment\" rather than \"thing carried\"; that widening is convenient and I did not derive it independently.
result.notes: Two structural features limit how hard any of this can be pushed. No word is marked with a dash, so nothing left either list; the difference is entirely a reshuffle of the same vocabulary, which is weaker evidence than a disappearance would be. And the movement is lopsided -- five rises of +16 or more against a largest fall of -29 that belongs to a subword fragment -- so the rising side is where the signal is and the falling side is largely small, contestable movement. The luggage relation would survive a repeat; the underwear one probably would not, which is why it is marked low rather than dropped.

result.reading: Under B the fragment reads as the opening of a security operation: the four largest gainers are question (+81, from 92nd to 11th), search (+21), beat (+19) and ask (+13), which together assemble an entry-search-interrogate sequence, while the steepest falls are ordinary occupancy and conversation verbs (say -43, count -36, eat -19, read -11, tell -10, discuss -8, work -7, sit -6). Under A the same three men entering a room are doing something closer to visiting, talking or working; almost the whole difference is carried by those four gainers, since most of the other rises are +1 and could be nothing.

relations.name: Raid script assembles
relations.sentence: Under B the completions that gain are the ordered stages of an armed search of a room, look then search then question then examine then beat then shoot, while the ones that fall are what people do when a room is simply occupied or worked in: say, tell, discuss, read, eat, sit, work, count.

relations.name: Speech becomes interrogation
relations.sentence: The verbal completions split by whether speech is directed at someone as a demand or exchanged between equals: question and ask rise sharply and argue rises slightly, while say, tell and discuss all fall, so under B speech is something done to the room's occupants rather than with them.

relations.name: Bodies over objects
relations.sentence: The two verbs whose object is a person's body, beat and shoot, both move up while the verbs of handling things or staying put, remove and sit and eat, do not, though shoot moves only 3 places so this rests almost entirely on beat.

result.kind: what kind of encounter the entry begins

residue.description: make, put and take are light verbs that carry no event of their own until a complement is supplied, so their moves of +4, +1 and zero say nothing about what the three men are doing, while sing, play and pray belong to neither the raid reading nor the ordinary-visit reading and sit at the same low positions in both conditions.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexample to the interrogation relation is that talk and speak hold their positions exactly: if B were reweighting speech toward the interrogative these two neutral conversation verbs should have fallen with say and tell, and they did not, which is why that relation is medium rather than high. Against the raid relation, count falls 36 places even though counting people or valuables is a plausible part of a search, and remove falls slightly even though removing occupants or objects is a raid action, so the fell side is not purely the peaceable set. Mildly the other way, sing rises 1 place while belonging to no security script, and argue rises only 1 place while discuss falls 8, so the confrontational-speech contrast is asymmetric in size. None of these overturn the main relation, because the words carrying it move by 81, 21, 19 and 13 places while every counterexample except count moves by 6 or fewer.
result.notes: The reading is direction-agnostic: I can say what separates A from B but nothing about which condition is which sort of measurement, and I have used only ranks, never likelihoods. The evidence is concentrated rather than distributed: question alone moves 81 places, from outside the top ninety to eleventh, and if that single word were removed the remaining rises are 21, 19, 13, and then a tail of moves of 4 or fewer that I would not defend individually. Two of the rises, examine at +1 and put at +1, and three of the falls at -1 to -6, are small enough that they would be equally consistent with no relation at all; they are included in the groups only because they point the same way as the large movers. The fell side is also less semantically uniform than the rose side, which is the asymmetry worth flagging: the rose side names a single coherent procedure, while the fell side is a heterogeneous collection of things that merely fail to belong to that procedure.

result.reading: The clearest fact in the list is that two verbs which presuppose a captive and a procedure, torture (16 -> 149) and interrogate (17 -> 101), are effectively evicted from B's field, while the verb that presupposes nothing at all, dance, rises 24 places to first. Violence as such is not removed, since fight and attack rise sharply, so what separates the conditions looks less like force versus mildness than like which scene the verb builds around the three men who came into the room.

relations.name: Interrogation frame evicted
relations.sentence: The verbs that presuppose a detained person and a sustained procedure carried out on them (torture, interrogate, point, ask, tell, beat) hold high positions under A and either collapse out of the field under B or drop well down it, while under B the leading completions presuppose no victim and no procedure at all (dance, move, speak, shout).

relations.name: One-sided harm to mutual conflict
relations.sentence: Under A the violent completions are ones done by an agent to a helpless patient (torture, kill, beat, hit), whereas the violent completions B favours are reciprocal or unspecified in target (fight, argue, attack, throw), so the amount of violence is roughly preserved while its asymmetry is not.

relations.name: Extracted speech versus expressive noise
relations.sentence: The speech verbs split by who the speech is for: the ones that fall under B are the ones an interrogator performs on someone (tell, ask, talk), and the ones that rise are undirected vocal commotion (shout, argue, speak).

result.kind: which scene the verb presupposes, captivity or commotion

residue.description: make and take are light verbs that carry almost no scene on their own and are not really content completions of the fragment without an object, while look, play and sing move only a few places and belong to no group I can state: play and sing in particular are leisure verbs that fall slightly under B in the same condition where dance rises to first, so they cut across rather than support any of the relations.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest contradiction is that shoot and search hold position exactly; those two are the verbs most specific to an armed raid on a room, and if the difference were the removal of that scene they should have moved with torture and interrogate. result.reading: The words gaining under B are almost all past participles of transitive verbs of assault or coercion (attacked, invaded, violated, trapped, betrayed, intimidated), each of which builds an unnamed doer into the completion, while the words losing under B are gradable adjectives of felt condition that name no doer (safe, safer, unsafe, uneasy, uncomfortable). The whole safety vocabulary drops on both signs at once, which is why I read the difference as a change in the frame of the completion rather than a shift in how badly the neighbours are said to feel.

relations.name: Perpetrator enters the verb
relations.sentence: Under B the words that rise are past participles of transitive verbs of assault, confinement and coercion, each of which presupposes an agent acting on the neighbours (attacked, invaded, violated, trapped, betrayed, intimidated), whereas the words B demotes are adjectives naming a condition the neighbours are simply in, with nobody doing it to them (safe, safer, unsafe, uneasy, uncomfortable).

relations.name: Safety scale withdrawn
relations.sentence: Every member of the graded security vocabulary falls under B irrespective of its sign, the comparative safer furthest of all at thirty-seven places and unsafe close behind at twenty-two, so the change is not that the neighbours are moved lower on a safe-to-unsafe scale but that this scale stops being the axis along which the sentence gets finished.

relations.name: Null beside the maximum
relations.sentence: The two largest gains under B are attacked and nothing, one the most extreme act on the list and the other the refusal of any feeling whatever, while the middling hedged states A ranked high (uneasy, uncomfortable, unsafe) all fall, which reads as movement toward the two ends rather than along a scale.

result.kind: act done to them versus state they are in

residue.description: These are determiners, pronouns and prepositions that do not complete the fragment by themselves but only open whatever comes next, so their movement is about sentence shape rather than about what the neighbours felt; I note without defending it that the ones rising under B (a, an, their, like, as) tend to open a noun phrase or a simile, while the ones falling (it, they, the) tend to open a clause.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is abandoned, which falls fifteen places under B although it has exactly the shape relation one says B prefers, a transitive participle with an implied agent; I can tell a story about its agent being one who leaves rather than one who arrives, but that story is invented after seeing the direction and I would not have predicted it. Second, threatened holds position and relieved holds position, and these are the two words the reading most expects to move, threatened being the nearest neighbour to B's risers and relieved their opposite, so the pattern is inert exactly where it should be strongest. Third, unsafe falling twenty-two places rules out any simpler reading in which B is just more alarmed, though it is consistent with relation two. Fourth, compelled fits relation one only by grammatical form, since felt compelled idiomatically means self-obliged and carries no external agent at all, so it may be riding on participle shape rather than on the sense I attribute to the group.
result.notes: Seven words of one grammatical and semantic type moving one way against five of another type moving the other is more structure than I would expect by chance, and the collapse of the safe/unsafe pair together is the part I would stake most on, since it is hard to produce by any monotone change in severity. What holds me at medium rather than high is that the reading has one member of its own class moving the wrong way (abandoned) and its two most diagnostic words not moving at all (threatened, relieved). I have used only the orderings and the place-counts given, and have not treated the +56 and +55 as magnitudes of anything beyond position; a large jump from rank 70 into the mid-teens is compatible with many underlying pictures I am not shown. The fragment is politically loaded and I have tried to state the difference as one of grammatical frame, since a valence reading is exactly what the fall of unsafe contradicts.

result.reading: The four steepest falls under B are all words that make "felt" take a stance toward acting rather than name a state: obligated, obliged, compelled, free, each dropping out of the top twenty into the 47-92 range, and dragging with them the degree scaffolding (so, as, more, very) that such completions run on. What climbs into the vacated top of the list is a differentiated vocabulary of apprehension and grievance -- concerned, nervous, unsafe, uneasy, angry, violated, betrayed -- most of it arriving from the 30s-70s. The two blunt safety words already near the top under A, threatened and safe, do not move at all, and relieved rises alongside the alarm words, so what changes looks less like a swing in valence than a change in what kind of thing the completion is.

relations.name: Deontic slot vacated
relations.sentence: The words that collapse hardest under B are the ones that would make the sentence about what the neighbours were required or licensed to do next -- obligated, obliged, free, compelled, all falling forty or more places out of the top twenty -- while the words that take their place name a state the neighbours are in rather than a stance toward action.

relations.name: Coarse alarm becomes differentiated
relations.sentence: Under A the whole safety dimension is carried by two blunt terms already sitting high, threatened and safe, and neither gains a place; under B a much wider and more finely graded set of apprehension words -- concerned, nervous, unsafe, uneasy -- moves up beneath them from the 30s and 50s and 70s, so the axis is not newly present but newly articulated.

relations.name: Degree yields to hedge
relations.sentence: The function words that fall are the ones that set up an intensified predicate (so, very, more, as, as in felt so/very/more X), while the ones that rise open an indefinite or approximate completion (a, like, something, as in felt a X, felt like, felt something), which is the grammatical shadow of the same shift rather than an independent finding.

result.kind: state-of-feeling versus licensed-or-required action

residue.description: These are sentence-continuing function words rather than completions of the feeling, they move between one and seven places, and their movement is as easily the arithmetic consequence of the content words reshuffling above them as anything about them.

result.counterexamples: relieved is the real one: it rises fourteen places into the top fifteen under B alongside the alarm words, and it is positive, so any reading in which B simply intensifies the neighbours' distress is contradicted by one of its own gainers (it is harmless to the first relation, since relieved is still a state rather than an action-stance). threatened (-1) and safe (-2) contradict the second relation more mildly: if B were re-weighting the safety axis wholesale, the two most explicit safety words should move with it, and they do not -- though both sit at ranks 4 and 11 under A and have little room to climb, so the rank measure may simply be unable to show it. free is the weakest member of the first relation, since felt free can be read as a state as much as a licensed action; if it is read as a state its -66 fall is a counterexample rather than evidence.
result.notes: The first relation is the one I would defend on repetition: four words, one grammatical class, the four largest falls in the list, with no member of that class going the other way. The second and third are readings of what filled the gap and are more exposed -- the third especially, since it may be nothing more than the syntax that the first relation's winners and losers respectively require. I have deliberately not stated a valence relation (B as more alarmed, A as calmer), because relieved rising and threatened and safe staying put both cut against it, and because with ranks alone I cannot tell a genuine gain from displacement caused by the obligation cluster vacating the top twenty. Every number here is a position, so a word already at rank 4 cannot demonstrate a rise, and I have treated small movements at the top of the A list as uninformative rather than as evidence of stability.

result.reading: Under B the completion is dominated by words for felt physical danger (threatened, uneasy, anxious, scared, intimidated, unsafe, afraid), while the words A favours are either words of duty and grievance (obliged, compelled, sorry, betrayed, abandoned) or words of security and release (safe, relieved, free). Alongside this, the function words at the top of A's list are the ones that open a clause (the, they, that, it, like, as), whereas under B the indefinite articles a and an climb, so the frame the neighbours' feeling is expressed in shifts as well as its content.

relations.name: alarm over reassurance
relations.sentence: Every word for being in danger rises under B while the three words for being out of danger fall, so that the same slot moves from reassurance to fear.

relations.name: duty traded for dread
relations.sentence: Words that place the neighbours in a moral or relational bind, whether owed something, guilty, or wronged by someone they trusted, all fall under B and are replaced by words that place them in bodily jeopardy.

relations.name: adjective over clause
relations.sentence: The two indefinite articles rise while every word that would open a following clause or comparison falls, suggesting the completion under B tends to be a bare predicate adjective or a noun phrase rather than a reported proposition of the form felt that they were or felt as if.

result.kind: which affective register the feeling belongs to

residue.description: Both are scaffolding that can precede either sort of completion, a degree modifier and a possessive, and both move only one or two places, which is within the range of words that did not really move at all.

result.counterexamples: The cleanest contradiction is that safe falls only six places and lands at 16 under B, immediately above unsafe at 17, so the antonym pair does not actually invert its order and the reassurance side is displaced rather than expelled. Within the second relation, compelled moves only two places while its near-synonym obliged moves twenty-four, so the obligation vocabulary is not treated as a block and the relation rests mostly on obliged. Also worth noting against any simple reading that B is just more negative: abandoned and betrayed are strongly negative and both fall seventeen places, which is why the difference has to be described as a change of the kind of feeling rather than of its valence.
result.notes: The first relation is the one I would defend on its own; the third I would state but not lean on, since the article rise could equally follow from the affect shift rather than from an independent change of frame, and I cannot separate the two from ranks alone. Nothing here tells me which condition is which, and I have not tried to infer that. The fragment is politically loaded and the two readings it splits into are recognisably different accounts of the same scene, one of neighbours in danger and one of neighbours bound or wronged, but that is a description of the word lists, not a claim about why the measurement came out this way.
