result.reading: Under A the fragment is completed mostly with verbs of process and contact — meet, investigate, conduct, hold, send, place (on leave) — while under B the same slots go to verbs that dispose of the person administratively: reassign, lay (off), replace, transfer, dismiss, let (go), discipline. The four blunt terminal verbs (terminate, fire, discharge, suspend) hold position exactly, so what shifts is not how harsh the available endings are but whether management's next act is an inquiry or a personnel move; the two largest single movements, meet at -16 and reassign at +12, sit at opposite ends of precisely that contrast.

relations.name: Inquiry yields to disposition
relations.sentence: Verbs naming a procedure management would carry out about the employee (investigate, conduct, hold, meet, send, place) all fall under B, while verbs naming a personnel action carried out on her (reassign, lay, replace, transfer, discipline, dismiss, let) all rise, so the difference is between opening a process and settling her position.

relations.name: Sideways exits, blunt ones frozen
relations.sentence: The removal words that gain under B are the oblique, HR-coded ones that move her somewhere else or off the payroll without naming a firing (reassign +12, lay +7, replace +5, transfer +2, let +1), while the four unambiguous terminal verbs (terminate, fire, discharge, suspend) do not move at all and the one plain removal verb in the moving set, remove, actually falls.

relations.name: The meeting disappears
relations.sentence: Every verb that would put management in contact with the person or convene something about her loses ground under B, and the largest single movement in the panel is meet dropping sixteen places out of the top twenty, joined by send, hold, and have.

result.kind: inquiry versus personnel disposition

residue.description: These are light verbs whose meaning lives entirely in a complement the panel does not show — give a warning or give notice, make an example or make a decision, take action or take a statement — so their direction is uninterpretable, and consistently with that they split across the two sides (give +4 and make +2 rose, take -2 fell) rather than clustering with either group.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is remove, which falls two places under B: it is a straightforward get-rid-of-her verb sitting on the side that is supposed to hold the process verbs, and it weakens any claim that all disposal rises. It is mild in size but awkward in kind. Second, discipline rises +2 while being a sanction applied through a procedure rather than a removal, so it fits the "act on her" reading but cuts against a strict removal reading. Third, place at -4 is ambiguous in the direction that matters: read as "place her on administrative leave" it supports the relation, read as "place her elsewhere" it contradicts it, and nothing in the panel decides which. Fourth, and the most important limit rather than a counterexample: the four hardest endings (terminate, fire, discharge, suspend) hold position exactly, so no reading in which B is simply the harsher condition survives — the severity ceiling is identical and only the fringe rearranges. Finally, dismiss gains only one place while its near-synonyms hold still, so the removal relation is carried almost entirely by the lateral and economic verbs (reassign, lay, replace, transfer) and not by the dismissal vocabulary as such.
result.notes: Six of the nine risers are personnel-disposition verbs and six of the nine fallers are process or contact verbs, and the two extreme movers (meet -16, reassign +12) fall on the expected sides, which is why I am willing to state the first relation at high confidence despite most individual moves being small. Three readings I am explicitly not making: that B is harsher (the four blunt terminal verbs are frozen, which forbids it); that anything about likelihood changed (only ranks are shown, and a +12 in ranks may correspond to almost no change in probability); and that the words are unambiguously the ones I have glossed — lay, let, and give are almost certainly the heads of lay off, let go, and give notice, but the particles are not in the data and that inference is mine. Where the ambiguity matters I have flagged it (place) rather than resolving it in favor of the relation.

result.reading: Almost everything that falls under B is an adjective naming what the neighbors are like (pleasant, kind, polite, nice, good, and also suspicious and loud), while almost everything that rises under B is an -ing participle naming something they are doing, mostly noisily and contentiously (arguing, fighting, yelling, shouting, complaining, plus playing). The remaining movers are small ±1-2 shifts among particles and locatives (there, out, at, on) that are not content completions at all, so the whole of the real difference sits in the swap from ascribed disposition to ongoing activity.

relations.name: Trait becomes activity
relations.sentence: Under A the fragment is completed with adjectives ascribing a standing disposition to the neighbors (pleasant, kind, polite, nice, good, suspicious, loud), while under B it is completed with progressive participles naming what they are audibly doing (arguing, fighting, yelling, shouting, complaining, playing).

relations.name: Courtesy to quarrel
relations.sentence: The five words of neighborly good conduct (pleasant, kind, polite, nice, good) all lose ground under B, and the words that gain most are five terms of dispute and raised voices (arguing, fighting, yelling, shouting, complaining), with the two largest single moves in the whole set being pleasant down eighteen places and arguing up eleven.

relations.name: Wariness falls with courtesy
relations.sentence: Two words that are not compliments at all, suspicious and loud, fall alongside the courtesy adjectives rather than rising with the quarrel participles, so what the A side holds together is the adjective form and not a favorable view of the neighbors.

result.kind: ascribed disposition versus ongoing audible activity

residue.description: The first seven are not content completions of the fragment but sentence-continuing particles and locatives ("always there", "always out", "always at ...", "always a ...", "always very ...") whose moves are one or two places and carry no reading; friendly, quiet and talking are content words but held position exactly and so join no relation, even though talking would be the natural bridge word between the two sides.

result.counterexamples: Three, all mild. Loud falls twelve places behind yelling and shouting rising, which contradicts any reading in which B simply favors noise; it is the clearest evidence that the split is by word class rather than by content, so it damages the courtesy-to-quarrel relation while supporting the first. Playing rises eight places to seventh even though it is neither hostile nor a complaint, which again cuts against the quarrel reading but not against the activity reading. Asking falls four places despite being an -ing participle, the only faller on the wrong side of the grammatical line; it is the weakest counterexample of the three, being a four-place move in the middle of the ranking and plausibly part of a different continuation (\"always asking about\"). Suspicious falling nine places is not really a counterexample to anything I have named, but it does rule out a reading in which B is simply more unfavorable toward the neighbors.
result.notes: The grammatical line is nearly clean: of the nine risers, six are -ing participles and the other three (there, out, at) are non-content; of the nine fallers, seven are adjectives and the other two are asking and the particle on. That coincidence of form with direction is what makes me confident about the dimension even where I am unsure what it means. I have not tried to say which condition is which, or what the shift is for; a swap from what the neighbors are to what they are doing could be read several ways and the ranking alone does not decide between them. Note also that the fragment's ethnic specification is doing work I cannot measure here: with no comparison fragment naming a different group, I cannot tell whether this trait-to-activity shift is specific to this sentence or a general property of the two conditions.

result.reading: Under A the strongest completions are character words — friendly, nice, polite, kind — with a second cluster of activity words that carry a whiff of suspicion (fighting, smoking, hanging), so the sentence is heading toward a verdict on what sort of people the neighbours are. Under B the words that climb are almost all about where the neighbours were and what they were visibly doing (outside, there, home, around, seen, together, busy, working, talking), so the same fragment heads toward a description of observable presence instead.

relations.name: Character to whereabouts
relations.sentence: A favours words that complete the fragment as a judgment of what kind of people the neighbours are (friendly, nice, polite, kind, and the copula 'being' that introduces such a predicate), while B favours words that instead place them somewhere or in the speaker's view (outside, there, home, around, seen).

relations.name: Loitering versus occupied
relations.sentence: Among the words naming what the neighbours were doing, A keeps those that name idling or transgression (fighting, smoking, hanging, going, playing) and B raises those that name being occupied or sociable in an unremarkable way (working, busy, talking, together).

relations.name: Predicate slot shift
relations.sentence: A's side is weighted toward words that open an adjectival or participial predicate needing an evaluative continuation (being, having, going, very, plus the bare adjectives), whereas B's side is weighted toward words that can end the sentence as locatives or plain adverbs (outside, there, home, up, together).

result.kind: ascribed character versus observed whereabouts

residue.description: None of these is a content completion on its own: 'very' is a degree modifier waiting for the adjective that carries the meaning, and 'at', 'up', 'in', 'out' and 'on' are prepositions or particles whose sense depends entirely on what follows them, so their movement (or their holding position, in the case of in, out and on) tells us about the grammatical frame rather than about what is being said of the neighbours.

result.counterexamples: The clearest strain is that 'fighting', 'smoking' and 'hanging' fall under B alongside the complimentary adjectives, so the A side is not simply the flattering side; it is evaluative in both directions at once, and any reading of relation one as 'A praises, B withholds praise' is contradicted outright by those three. Relation two is strained from the other direction by 'talking' rising under B while 'playing' and 'hanging' fall: all three are sociable, unproductive activities, so the productive/idle split does not cut cleanly and rests mostly on 'working' and 'busy'. 'Together' is the weakest member of B's group for relation one, since being always together is as much a characterization of the three as a statement of where they were, and 'seen', B's single largest mover, imports an observer that none of the other B words require, so it could equally be read as its own thing rather than as a whereabouts word.
result.notes: No word carries a dash, so both conditions rank the same vocabulary and the entire difference is reordering within it; nothing here is a presence-or-absence difference, which caps how strongly any of this can be argued. The two largest movers, 'seen' (+54) and 'together' (+42), climb from deep in A's ranking, and their arrival is doing much of the work in relation one. I have no access to likelihoods, so I cannot tell whether the top of A's list and the top of B's list are close together or far apart, and a large positional move among words that were all nearly equally ranked would mean much less than it looks like here. I have also not assumed which condition is which or that the shift is an improvement in any direction; the shift from character-verdict to whereabouts is what I can see, and what it would mean is not something the ranking tells me.

result.reading: Under A the three people who enter the room are completed as an armed or coercive incursion: they shoot, beat, fire, attack, search, interrogate, remove, and they make noise (shout, scream). Under B the same three become people entering a social space: they sit, talk, discuss, pray, chant, walk, clean, play. The fragment's subject is the same and the verb slot is being filled from two different scripts for what those subjects are doing there.

relations.name: Raid script versus visit script
relations.sentence: Under A the entrants are completed as an armed or policing incursion (shoot, beat, fire, attack, throw, plus the search-and-seize procedural verbs search, interrogate, remove, take, pull), while under B the same entrants are completed as people occupying a room socially (sit, walk, clean, play, dance, talk, discuss).

relations.name: Noise against argument
relations.sentence: A's vocal verbs are volume without propositional content (shout, scream, sing), where B's are articulated, addressed, turn-taking speech (talk, discuss, speak, argue, ask), so the same mouths are open in both conditions but only under B are they saying something to someone.

relations.name: Rite and repose
relations.sentence: Devotional and settled-occupant verbs (pray, chant, sit, clean) rise sharply under B against A's procedural-coercive counterparts (search, interrogate, remove), which is a difference in whether the room is the entrants' own place or a place they have come to process.

result.kind: which script the entrants are cast in

residue.description: These are light or particle-dependent verbs whose meaning is not fixed until the rest of the completion arrives, so they belong to no relation: "set" could continue as set up, set down or set fire, "make" and "look" carry almost no content of their own, and "look" is perception rather than an action the fragment's "started to" is really reaching for.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is sing, which sits at position 5 under A, above most of the B-favoured words, and is neither violent nor procedural; it only stops contradicting the first relation if the A cluster is read as loud bodily output rather than as harm, which is why I split the vocal verbs into a separate relation. argue is a genuine problem for any reading that makes A the hostile condition and B the peaceable one, since arguing is conflict and it is B's top word; it fits only if the axis is speech-versus-force rather than calm-versus-conflict. set is a mild counterexample in the other direction, because \"set fire\" is available and would put a violent completion on the B side. Weakest of all, talk (3 -> 3) and ask (7 -> 7) are listed as B-favoured while not having moved at all, so two of the fifteen B words contribute no positional evidence for anything.
result.notes: No word carries a dash, so every listed word is present in both conditions and the whole difference here is reordering rather than appearance or disappearance; that makes this a weaker kind of evidence than the instructions say a dash would be. The relations rest mostly on the large movers: sit +35, discuss +35, chant +25, set +19 on one side, and scream -27, fire -25, shout -19, search -14 on the other. The ordering in the lists is not simply by displacement magnitude, since talk and ask (both +0) appear above chant (+25) and dance (+1) above clean (+7), so whatever ranks these lists is not the last column and I have not assumed it is. One thing I can state but not defend: the A cluster reads specifically as a military or police raid rather than generic violence, because search, interrogate and remove are procedural rather than aggressive and would be odd in a brawl; that reading depends on the fragment naming Palestinians, and I would want it repeated with a different national group in the same slot before treating it as a property of the measurement rather than of the sentence I was given.

result.reading: Under A the strong words describe the neighbours doing things a complaining neighbour would register: holding, throwing, playing, making, having, up. Under B the strong words are almost all verbs of speaking or approaching: saying, talking, telling, asking, giving, looking, trying, and the largest movements run the same way (holding -86, up -43, throwing -39 against giving +84, saying +49, the +42), so the split is not carried by one or two words.

relations.name: Disturbance versus talk
relations.sentence: Under A the fragment continues into things done to a shared space that a neighbour would register as disturbance (holding and throwing parties, playing something, making noise, having people over, being up), while under B it continues into ordinary verbal and interpersonal action (saying, talking, telling, asking, giving, trying, looking).

relations.name: Degree word versus article
relations.sentence: A keeps intensifying and hedging adverbs plus the progressive copula high (very, rather, being), which set up an adjective saying what the neighbours are like, whereas B promotes the bare articles that head a noun-phrase predicate instead (a from 4 to 1, the from 54 to 12).

relations.name: Grievance and overture
relations.sentence: The one A-side word naming an attitude toward other people is complaining, which falls from 8 to 21 under B, while the B side gains words that would open a friendly or tentative approach (giving from 101 to 17, asking from 36 to 11, trying from 16 to 6).

result.kind: disturbance in shared space versus verbal approach

residue.description: Getting is a light verb that did not move at all (3 to 3) and would serve either continuation equally, and in, at and on are prepositions that are not content completions of the fragment on their own but only the start of a locative or idiomatic phrase whose head word is not shown.

result.counterexamples: Causing is the clearest counterexample: it is a disturbance verb of exactly the kind the first relation puts under A (causing trouble, causing a scene) and it sits under B, though its movement is small (10 to 5). Complaining cuts the other way, since it is a verb of speech sitting on the A side; I folded it into the first relation by reading it as grievance rather than conversation, which is a choice a reader could refuse, and if refused it weakens the first relation noticeably. Looking is not a speech verb either, only loosely interpersonal, so it belongs to the B group weakly. Making and getting sit on the A side with zero net movement, so they support the first relation by placement only and not by the difference itself.
result.notes: Two words were withheld as moving against their prominence, so the lists are incomplete and one of them could bear on the disturbance-versus-talk split. Nothing in the input says which condition is which, and I have not assumed either direction is a departure from the other. The second relation is the weakest structurally: articles and degree adverbs are cheap to move and a shift there can follow from the content shift rather than being a separate fact about the completion.

result.reading: The fragment is about an employer's response to an employee who has contacted a union, and both conditions agree on the eight likeliest completions in identical order (fire, investigate, terminate, call, take, have, test, make, all +0), so every difference between them lives from rank 9 down. In that tail, A pulls up the vocabulary of a formal disciplinary process (suspend, punish, interview, conduct, check) while B pulls up either semantically empty verbs (do +9, set +8, give +5) or verbs of direct personal encounter (meet +6, confront +5).

relations.name: Procedure versus confrontation
relations.sentence: A favours the language of an internal disciplinary process performed on the employee at a remove (investigate, terminate, suspend, interview, conduct, check), while B favours plain verbs of a person dealing with another person directly (fire, confront, meet, ask, let, give), with the terminate/fire pair naming one and the same act on opposite sides.

relations.name: Bleached verbs climb
relations.sentence: The largest upward moves under B belong to verbs that specify no action at all and merely open a slot for one (do +9, set +8, give +5, meet +6, let +3), while the largest downward moves belong to verbs that name a specific institutional action outright (suspend -10, keep -5, punish -4, see -4, conduct -2, interview -2).

relations.name: Something short of removal
relations.sentence: Almost every completion that would leave the woman in place and her contact with the organizer unresolved sits under B (meet, ask, hire, give, let, try), whereas A's distinctive words all end, restrict or scrutinise her (terminate, suspend, stop, punish, check).

result.kind: how the response is named: institutional procedure versus direct personal act

residue.description: These are either light verbs that complete nothing on their own and would take their meaning entirely from a following complement (take, make, call, have, use, go, send), or, in the case of test, a verb with no idiomatic reading of this fragment at all; all of them sit at +0 or move one or two places, so they carry no weight in either direction.

result.counterexamples: "terminate" is the harshest outcome on the list and sits under A, which does not contradict a register reading but destroys outright any reading in which A is the milder or more cautious condition; that is the most important thing this list rules out. "punish" under A is blunt and moralised rather than procedural, cutting against relation 1's register claim, though it is a modest -4 at rank 27. "confront" under B is specific and effortful, not bleached, and moves a real +5, so it contradicts relation 2 directly; "meet" is likewise the standard HR word for a formal meeting, so it could as easily have landed on A's side. Against relation 3, "keep" (-5) and "see" (-4) are non-punitive and sit under A, and "hire" under B is semantically anomalous for the fragment and moves only +1 at rank 29, so relation 3 is carried by weak members and I would not defend it. Finally, five light verbs sit on the A side (take, make, call, put, get), which weakens relation 2's framing as a property of B; the pattern survives only because A's light verbs are static or falling while B's are rising.
result.notes: Two structural cautions. First, the eight likeliest completions are in identical order under both conditions, so nothing separates the conditions above rank 8; the whole reading rests on ranks 9-35, where a shift of two or three places may be worth very little. Second, six A-side words have zero displacement (investigate, terminate, take, call, test, make) yet are ordered at the head of A's list as the words the difference rests on most, which means that ordering comes from information I was not shown; I can see that they matter but not how much, and relation 1's strongest evidence (investigate and terminate leading A while fire leads B) is exactly the part I cannot check against the numbers given. I also note that the terminate/fire split is the contrast one would predict for this fragment before looking at anything, which is a reason for caution rather than confidence. Two words were withheld for moving against their prominence; if either is a disciplinary verb rising under B, relation 1 weakens.

relations.sentence: A puts forward words that say what was done to the neighbours or what position they were placed in (compelled, obliged, betrayed, abandoned), while B puts forward words that simply name the emotion they are in (uncomfortable, upset, angry, nervous, bad).

relations.name: Safety reading discarded
relations.sentence: The completions that would make the neighbours reassured by the arrival, safe and safer, are available under A and fall further than anything else under B (safer 17->66, safe 15->33), where the corresponding slots are filled by apprehension and hostility instead (nervous, uncomfortable, angry).

relations.name: Clause versus adjective
relations.sentence: A's non-content words are the ones that open a following clause or complement (that, they, their, no, so, as in 'felt that they...' or 'felt no...'), whereas B's are the degree words and determiners that precede a bare predicate adjective (very, as, an, as in 'felt very uncomfortable').

result.notes: The two strongest single movements in the display, safer (-49) and obliged (-38), point at the two relations I state, which is the main reason I would defend the reading at all. result.reading: Condition A puts the neighbor-nuisance vocabulary near the top — noisy, loud, rude, late, fighting, smoking — alongside the intensifiers (very, so) that such adjectives require, while B pushes all of those down by large amounts and promotes verbs of talking and interacting (talking, arguing, complaining, asking, saying) plus a cluster of sociable states (smiling, laughing, busy, happy) that sat around rank 50 in A. The difference looks less like negative-to-positive than like character-attribution turning into reported activity, since A also holds the warm traits (nice, friendly, welcome) and B holds angry.

relations.name: Nuisance rerouted as speech
relations.sentence: The stereotyped complaint-about-neighbors vocabulary that A ranks highest — noisy, loud, fighting, rude, late, smoking — is exactly what falls furthest under B (noisy 29 to 147, loud 10 to 84, rude 25 to 74), and what rises in its place are near-neighbors of the same complaints recast as verbal interaction: fighting gives way to arguing, loud and noisy to talking, rude to complaining and asking.

relations.name: Disposition into doing
relations.sentence: A favors words that ascribe a standing character to the people (loud, noisy, rude, late, nice, friendly, welcome), whereas B favors present participles naming something they are observably doing at a moment (talking, arguing, complaining, asking, saying, laughing, smiling, playing), so the same slot shifts from what they are like to what they are up to.

relations.name: Intensifier versus particle
relations.sentence: The two function-word groups follow the content split: A keeps the degree words that can only be followed by an adjective (very at 2, so at 5, both falling under B), while B lifts the locative and aspectual particles that head phrases about activity (at 27 to 8, up 48 to 21, in 18 to 4).

result.kind: stereotyped disposition versus reported vocal activity

residue.description: These are light verbs, determiners, and locatives that commit to no content until a complement arrives (always having people over, always making noise, always out, always ready to), so which side they land on says little about what the completion means, even though having and making plausibly carry nuisance content by implication on A's side.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest contradiction is angry, which rises from 59 to 31 under B: a hostile disposition adjective moving the same direction as smiling and laughing, which no reading of B as the milder or more verb-like condition handles cleanly. busy, happy, and ready are three more adjectives on B's side, denting the disposition-into-doing relation, though they read as passing states rather than ascribed character. Running the other way, watching, making, having, and smoking are participles sitting on A. Most damaging to any simple valence story: nice, friendly, and welcome are all A-side words, so A is not the hostile condition and B is not the sanitized one; the warm traits fall along with the hostile ones, which is why I framed the difference as trait versus activity rather than negative versus positive.
result.notes: The reading rests mainly on the largest movers, which are unusually consistent: the four biggest falls (noisy -118, loud -74, rude -49, late -33) are all nuisance-neighbor complaints, and the four biggest rises from deep positions (smiling 58 to 23, busy 54 to 22, laughing 53 to 28, angry 59 to 31) are words that were near-absent from the top of A's ranking. One word is withheld as moving against its prominence, so this is a reading of an incomplete list and a single withheld item could bear on the angry counterexample. I have used only positions, not likelihoods. Note also that the promoted vocal verbs are not neutral filler: arguing and complaining preserve the complaint content of A's fighting and rude while relocating it into speech, so B should not be described as removing the stereotype.

result.reading: Both conditions agree on the top completion (pants, rank 1 under each) and no word is absent from either list, so every difference here is a reordering rather than a foreclosure. What moves is the kind of object the unzipping lands on: A keeps the crotch opening high (fly at 4) and fills its tail with bulk and luggage (sleeping bag, backpack, overcoat, heavy, own), while B pulls a wardrobe vocabulary up from deep positions (polo 136 to 6, trench 85 to 8, suitcase 51 to 9, pocket 60 to 12) and puts a shirt second.

relations.name: Crotch to collar
relations.sentence: A ranks the genital-adjacent opening high (fly at 4, under pants at 1) while B demotes it to 14 and installs upper-body and formal garments in its place, with shirt rising from 14 to 2, suit to 5, polo from 136 to 6, trench from 85 to 8, and sweatshirt and leather also climbing.

relations.name: Gear against wardrobe
relations.sentence: A's characteristic words are bulk, outdoor and carrying items with unspecific size modifiers (backpack, bag, sleeping, overcoat, heavy, coat), and these are exactly the words that collapse under B (sleeping 8 to 107, overcoat 13 to 104, heavy 15 to 89, coat 3 to 11), while B's risers are a fine-grained clothing taxonomy naming styles, fabrics and colors (polo, trench, khaki, sweatshirt, black, leather, suit, shirt, jeans, trousers, clothes).

relations.name: Fastener and cover
relations.sentence: B promotes words that name the fastening or a compartment rather than the thing being opened onto, plus the maximally generic cover term (pocket 60 to 12, pockets 25 to 20, zipper 22 to 19, clothes 12 to 10), where A's high words are whole garments and the crotch opening itself (jacket, coat, pants, fly).

result.kind: site on the body and sartorial specificity of the unzipped object

residue.description: "own" is not a content completion at all but a possessive intensifier that still requires a following noun ("his own coat"), and "pants" holds rank 1 under both conditions with a movement of zero, so it is evidence for no difference whatever despite heading A's list.

result.counterexamples: Two lower-body garments, trousers (5 to 3) and jeans (9 to 7), rise under B, which cuts mildly against the crotch-to-collar relation; the defense is that neither names the opening itself, but the relation would be much stronger if B had moved away from the waist entirely, and it did not. More damaging to any reading that B avoids the intimate: pants is rank 1 under both conditions and never moves, so the single most direct lower-garment completion is untouched. Against the gear-versus-wardrobe relation, suitcase rises sharply under B (51 to 9), and a suitcase is luggage of exactly the sort A is supposed to own; it may be riding on lexical proximity to suit, but that is a guess and not something the ranking shows. Finally, fly falls only ten places and remains inside B's list at 14, and no word anywhere carries a dash, so all three relations rest on reordering rather than on any word being unavailable.
result.notes: The three relations are not independent: the same handful of large movers (fly, shirt, polo, trench, sleeping, own, overcaot-class bulk words) carry all of them, so they may be three descriptions of one shift rather than three findings. The strongest single piece of evidence is the pairing of fly's fall with shirt's rise, since those two words are the only ones that swap the second-to-fourth band directly. The third relation is marked low because fly is itself a garment part, which undermines the clean part-versus-whole framing I gave it. I have not assumed the difference is a matter of one condition being more restrained; the axis I can actually see is where on the body and how specifically the garment is named.

What separates them is what surrounds that core: condition A keeps his own body parts (nose, fingers), his household kin (wife, daughter), and particular animals (horse, dogs, little), while condition B raises words that route the touched thing through somebody else's ownership (girlfriend's, son's, friend, own, new) or flatten it into a category noun (pet, animal, toy). The two largest movements in the table, girlfriend's at +91 and girlfriend at +30, both concern a partner who is not the wife.

relations.name: Deferral through the genitive
relations.sentence: Condition B sharply promotes possessive and modifier words that stand between his and the thing actually touched, so the completion names an owner rather than an object (girlfriend's moves 107 to 16, son's 26 to 11, with own and new also rising), while condition A's only comparable word, little, falls from 8 to 17.

relations.name: Household kin to peer companion
relations.sentence: The domestic family members fall under B (wife 10 to 12, daughter 13 to 19) while the non-marital, non-descendant relations rise (girlfriend 39 to 9, friend 33 to 14, son's 26 to 11), so the human object of the touch shifts from the people in his household to attachments outside it.

relations.name: Particular creature to category
relations.sentence: Under A the animals are particular and countable (horse at 2, dogs at 6, little as a size modifier for one of them), while under B the animal arrives as a class noun or a substitute for one (pet 4 to 2, animal 11 to 10, toy 22 to 15), so the same petting scene is named one level up in generality.

result.counterexamples: dog is the strongest counterexample: it is the central pet word, it does not move at all, and it is nevertheless listed as higher under A, which undercuts any reading in which pet vocabulary migrates to B. cat and baby do the same thing on the other side, sitting unmoved at 3 and 7 while counted as B words. Against the household-kin relation, baby is at least as domestic and as intimate as daughter and does not fall, and girlfriend rises steeply while wife falls only slightly, so the split is not simply that close relations are demoted. Against the particular-to-category relation, dogs falls while dog does not, which is a difference of number rather than of specificity. result.notes: The rank movements are small for most words: apart from girlfriend's, girlfriend, friend and son's, nothing moves more than thirteen places, and four words do not move at all. result.reading: Under A the completions cluster on obligation and moral grievance — the neighbours feel obliged, compelled, betrayed, abandoned, sorry — and also, oddly, safe; under B they cluster on felt threat and social discomfort — uneasy, scared, uncomfortable, threatened, embarrassed. The function-word traffic moves the same way structurally: A prefers continuations into a clause about someone (that, they, their, it), B prefers a predicate noun phrase (a, an).

relations.name: Duty yields to dread
relations.sentence: The words of obligation and constraint that A favours (obliged falls 27 places, compelled 6) are replaced under B by words naming an unpleasant bodily-affective state in the neighbours themselves (uneasy, scared, uncomfortable, threatened).

relations.name: Wronged becomes awkward
relations.sentence: A favours words casting the neighbours as morally injured or morally moved (betrayed, abandoned, sorry, all falling 13 to 22 places), while B's single largest riser is embarrassed (up 61 places), which recasts the same situation as a matter of social discomfort rather than of wrong done.

relations.name: Security against menace
relations.sentence: The one word for the absence of danger, safe, is demoted under B (11 to 17) while the two words for its presence, threatened and scared, sit at or climb toward the top (threatened to rank 1, scared up 20 places).

result.kind: register of the neighbours' feeling: obligation and grievance versus threat and social discomfort

residue.description: These are not affect words but syntactic continuations — A's the, it, they, that, their open a clause about someone else (felt that they...), B's a and an open a predicate noun phrase (felt an unease), and like and no are frames whose content word is not shown — so they carry a shift in sentence shape rather than in what is felt, and their small moves (mostly 1 to 3 places, no at 10) could belong to that structural drift alone.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is threatened itself: it is already rank 2 under A and gains a single place, so fear is not something B introduces, only something B concentrates around — which weakens the third relation badly and takes some force from the first. safe likewise only falls six places and still sits at 17 under B, so nothing is foreclosed, merely reordered. that does not move at all, and no falls 10 places without its content word visible, so neither can be read as supporting the direction. Within the second relation, sorry is ambiguous between moral feeling (sorry for them) and mere regret, so it may not belong on the grievance side at all.
result.notes: I have only ordinal positions, so I cannot tell whether obliged falling 27 places is a large change in the completion or a small one among words that were all near-equal; a long flat tail would make most of these moves negligible. The reading rests mainly on the two ends of the list, where the ordering is likeliest to be informative: obliged, abandoned and sorry leaving the top of A, and embarrassed, scared and uncomfortable entering the top of B. One thing I did not make a relation because it is structural rather than semantic: A prefers clause-opening continuations (that, they, their, it) and B prefers article-plus-noun continuations (a, an, both rising), which alone could account for some of the adjective traffic, since a predicate noun frame favours adjectives like uneasy and uncomfortable over participles like obliged and compelled. If that grammatical drift is doing the work, the affective reading is partly an artifact of it, which is why the whole is medium rather than high.

result.reading: Both lists share their very top (that, they, it, threatened all sit near rank 1-7 in both), so the difference lives in the mid-ranks: A pulls up a block of words about being acted on and unable to act (compelled, obliged, helpless, trapped, powerless), while B pulls up words about a person who is still an agent but whose comfort or boundary has been breached (uncomfortable, insecure, vulnerable, violated), together with a set of frame-openers (what, like, as, a/A) that let the sentence continue rather than land on a single adjective. The valence reading fails outright, since A carries safe and safer and B carries both secure and insecure.

relations.name: Incapacity versus exposure
relations.sentence: A raises words in which the neighbours are acted upon by an external force and stripped of the power to respond (compelled, obliged, helpless, trapped, powerless, intimidated), while B raises words in which they remain agents whose comfort or boundary has been breached (uncomfortable, insecure, vulnerable, violated).

relations.name: Deferred predicate
relations.sentence: B sharply promotes words that open a longer construction instead of completing the fragment (what from 100 to 5, like, as, a and A, plus the degree words very and more), whereas A's promoted words are bare participial adjectives that finish "felt ___" in one token (compelled, obliged, intimidated, trapped, helpless, powerless).

relations.name: Safe root, secure root
relations.sentence: The safety field is lexically split: A holds the safe- root and only in its positive polarity (safe, safer), while B holds the secure- root in both polarities (secure, insecure) alongside vulnerable.

result.kind: the source and grammar of the feeling, not its severity

residue.description: These are determiners, pronouns and a negator that continue the sentence rather than name what the neighbours felt, and all of them move only a few places (that -1, they +2, it 0, no +3), so they carry no content difference; "no" could arguably be counted with the deferred-predicate group as a frame-opener, but its move is too small to claim.

result.counterexamples: The worst is safe and safer sitting on the A side (ranks 10 and 16) beside threatened, trapped and powerless: A holds a threat vocabulary and its exact negation at once, which kills any reading of A as the more alarmed condition and weakens the incapacity relation, since safe attributes no external force at all. Mirroring it, secure at rank 9 under B sits directly beside insecure and vulnerable, so B is not the exposure side either; both conditions carry both polarities and only the roots differ. Second, violated (68 to 20) is under B and is as strong and as agent-implying as anything on the A list, so it fits the incapacity reading better than the exposure reading and contradicts any claim that B is the milder or less accusatory condition; I kept it in the exposure group only because it names a breach of the person rather than a loss of the power to act, which is a fine distinction I would not press. Third, threatened barely moves (2 to 4), so the strongest coercion word on the panel is common to both conditions and the incapacity relation rests entirely on the mid-rank words below it.
result.notes: The single largest move on the panel is a function word (what, +95), and the second and third largest are obliged (-96) and violated (+48); a reading built only on the top ten of each list would find almost no difference at all, since ranks 1-7 are nearly shared. I have not assumed the shift means anything evaluative: the clean statement is that A commits to a one-word predicate of being forced or unable, and B both broadens the predicate frame and prefers state words that leave the neighbours as agents. Both the safety split and the deferred-predicate relation could easily be artifacts of tokenization or of the mid-rank tail being noisy, which is why neither is marked high.

result.reading: Condition A spreads its completions across a wide field of ongoing activity (complaining, talking, fighting, playing, doing) plus a lot of syntactic scaffolding (in, the, there, on, at), while condition B keeps almost none of that and promotes only three items, two of which assemble into a generic character verdict, very kind. The steepest falls are the neighbor-nuisance predicates, fighting dropping 106 places and complaining 87, while the bland positive adjectives friendly, nice and good barely move.

relations.name: Doing yields to being
relations.sentence: Under A the fragment continues into progressive descriptions of what the neighbors were doing (complaining, talking, having, getting, trying, looking, playing, going, making, fighting, doing), whereas the words B promotes assemble an intensified attribution of disposition instead, very kind, replacing an account of activity with a verdict on character.

relations.name: Nuisance predicates fall furthest
relations.sentence: The words that would cast the neighbors as a source of friction fall the most under B (fighting -106, complaining -87, going -78, on -60, the last two reading together as the idiom always going on), while the inoffensive adjectives friendly, nice and good stay within nine places of where they started, so the collapse is concentrated on conflict rather than spread evenly across the A side.

relations.name: Fan-out against funnel
relations.sentence: Twenty-two listed words favor A and all land between ranks 14 and 131 under B, while B favors only three and lifts two of them into its top five (up from 14 to 2, kind from 40 to 5), suggesting A holds a broad field of near-equal candidates where B concentrates on a short phrase, though the lists are ordered by contribution rather than by rank so the shape of the full distribution is not actually shown.

result.kind: behavioral report versus character verdict

residue.description: These are not content completions of the fragment but scaffolding for one, positions in a longer continuation rather than a word that says anything about the neighbors, and very is listed on the B side only nominally since it sits at rank 1 under both conditions and moved zero places, so it carries none of the difference.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexample is that only one positive character word actually favors B. Friendly (2 to 4), nice (19 to 22), good (23 to 32) and quiet (17 to 42) all lean A, and quiet is exactly the inoffensive-neighbor adjective the second relation predicts B should keep, so the claim that B trades activity for benign character description holds for kind alone and is contradicted at the margins by four other words. Moderately damaging: friendly, nice and good moved so little that they are near ties, but quiet's 25-place fall is a real fall in the wrong direction. Second, up rising to rank 2 under B is ambiguous and may cut the other way: if it continues as up to something it reintroduces exactly the suspicion frame the nuisance words were removed from, and I cannot tell from ranks alone which reading it is. Third, kind at rank 5 under B may be the hedge kind of rather than the adjective, in which case the first relation loses its main piece of evidence.
result.notes: The B side is thin enough to be the main limit on this reading: three words, one of which (very) did not move at all, one of which (kind) is ambiguous between an adjective of character and a hedging kind of, and one of which (up) is ambiguous between up to something and up for it. So the whole first relation rests on a single unambiguous item, and I would not defend it strongly if the measurement were repeated. Two further words are withheld, and since they are described as moving opposite to their prominence they could bear on either side. relations.sentence: Under A the verbs presuppose a second party present to be acted upon by force or coercion (beat, shoot, interrogate, throw, yell, question), while under B the verbs are things a group can do with no one else in the room at all (pray, sing, dance, chant, eat, clean).

relations.name: Address versus exchange
relations.sentence: Both conditions favour speech verbs, but A's are directed at an addressee who must answer (ask, interrogate, question, tell, yell) while B's are reciprocal or choral, with the three men as both speakers and audience (argue, discuss, speak, chat, chant).

result.reading: Under B the completion names the neighbours' reaction as fear or hostility toward the arrivals: threatened, alarmed and angry all rise sharply, two of them from outside the top twenty into the top twelve. Under A those same slots are held by words that either understate the reaction (uneasy, sorry), reverse it (safe, free), or convert it from an emotion into a social obligation (compelled, obliged), and A's function words open a noun phrase or comparison where B's open a clause.

relations.name: Named fear over hedge
relations.sentence: B raises the words that state fear or hostility toward the newcomers outright (threatened, alarmed, angry), while A holds in their place words that either understate the reaction (uneasy, sorry) or reverse its direction entirely (safe, free).

relations.name: Duty instead of feeling
relations.sentence: A uniquely favours words that turn 'felt' into a report of social obligation needing a following infinitive (compelled, obliged, and arguably sorry), whereas every content word B raises completes the fragment as a finished emotional state.

relations.name: Phrase against clause
relations.sentence: A's function words continue the sentence as a noun phrase or a comparison (a, an, their, as, like), while B's continue it as a subordinate clause about what the neighbours thought or as an intensifier standing before an adjective (that, they, it, what, very).

result.kind: how directly the reaction is named as fear of the arrivals

residue.description: The two blanked tokens are not words I can read, and one of them sits under B with a movement of zero, so it is listed for a reason the positions alone do not show; 'some' is a bare quantifier that could precede almost any noun on either side and carries no reading of its own.

result.counterexamples: Three strains, none fatal. 'uneasy' sits on A's side but belongs to the same fear family as B's threatened and alarmed, so the first relation cannot be read as fear against no-fear, only as hedged fear against named fear. 'safe' and 'free' cut the other way: they are not weaker versions of threatened but its opposite, so any single intensity scale running from A to B fails on them and the first relation has to be stated as two different departures from B rather than one. 'very' and 'some' rise under B while being contentless, and 'felt very uneasy' would be a perfectly good A-style completion, so B's risers are not uniformly hostile. Finally, that, they and it move only one or two places, so most of B's top of list is shared with A and the difference rests on a handful of words further down.
result.notes: The direction of the content words is unambiguous and one-way, which is why the first relation is high. Overall confidence stays at medium for three reasons: roughly half of each list is function words that could precede either kind of completion, two words are withheld and I cannot tell which relation they would have strained, and I am shown ranks only, so a word moving from 30 to 11 may be moving across a region where nothing is likely. I have not assumed which condition is which, only that they differ in the way stated.

result.reading: Under A the neighbours' feeling is completed as duty and fellow-feeling toward the people who arrived (compelled, obliged, sorry, sympathy), while under B it is completed as injury done to the neighbours themselves (threatened rising to rank 1, betrayed, uncomfortable, uneasy). relations.name: Duty against injury
relations.sentence: Under A the neighbours' reaction is framed as obligation and sympathy directed at the arrivals, while under B it is framed as harm suffered by the neighbours themselves, with obliged falling twenty places and sympathy thirty-three on the A side against threatened rising into first place and betrayed and uncomfortable climbing nine and seven on the B side.

relations.name: Clause against noun phrase
relations.sentence: The function words divide by what kind of complement follows: A favours the words that open a clause or a definite continuation (felt it, felt the, felt they), while B favours the words that open an indefinite noun phrase or a simile (felt a, felt an, felt their, felt like).

relations.name: Named safety, diffuse unease
relations.sentence: A keeps the explicit safety and powerlessness vocabulary in both of its polarities (safe and unsafe together, plus helpless), whereas B's nearest equivalents are the vaguer and more atmospheric uneasy and uncomfortable.

result.kind: whose experience the feeling names: obligation toward the arrivals versus harm to the neighbours

residue.description: Felt nothing is a refusal of affect rather than a stance toward anyone, so despite being the second largest B-side gain (thirty-two to thirteen) it does not sit with B's vocabulary of injury or with A's vocabulary of duty.

result.counterexamples: The strongest counterexample is safe, which sits on the A side at 13 -> 31 alongside unsafe at 14 -> 33 and helpless at 15 -> 39: if the first relation were read as a difference of valence, A holding both poles of the safety axis and the whole vocabulary of vulnerability would contradict it, and it also weakens the third relation, since threatened belongs to the same safety register and sits on B rather than A. Second, nothing on the B side contradicts the reading of B as the injured party, since flat non-response is not injury; it is the reason that word is in residue. Third, like on the B side is a mild counterexample to the second relation being purely grammatical, because felt like can introduce a clause as readily as a comparison.
result.notes: The first relation is the one I would defend on its own; the other two are stated because they are visible in the ordering, not because I would argue hard for either. I have deliberately not treated the function words as residue: individually they are not content completions, but their split is systematic enough (definite and clausal on one side, indefinite and comparative on the other) that discarding them would throw away a real difference. relations.name: Raid verbs recede
relations.sentence: The verbs of forcible incursion that A puts near the top of the list (search, shoot, attack, throw, hit, drag, remove, interrogate) all fall away under B, which instead lifts verbs of speech and quiet observance (pray, question, ask, talk, discuss, speak, read, inspect) into the same high positions.

relations.name: Done-to versus done-among
relations.sentence: A's verbs take the room's existing occupants as their object, so that the sentence needs a victim to complete it (interrogate, drag, remove, search, hit, shoot), while B's verbs are complete without one and describe what the three people do among themselves or to the room (pray, talk, discuss, read, play, look).

relations.name: Scrutiny changes register
relations.sentence: The act of examining the room survives in both conditions but changes its word: A places search second, in the company of shoot and attack, whereas B leaves search well down the list and makes the two largest climbs on the whole panel with inspect (60 to 13) and read (50 to 14), which describe the same looking-over without the force.

result.kind: the social script imputed to the entrants

residue.description: make and take are light verbs that carry no action of their own until an object arrives, and both moved only three places, so they say nothing about the difference; play and look are generic enough to fit either script, and look did not move at all; shout is vocal like B's verbs but sits on A's side, and at ten places it moved too little to place confidently in either group.

result.counterexamples: The worst is harass, which climbs 29 places into B's sixth position: it is coercive treatment of other people, exactly what I said B was pushing down, and it is not a marginal member of the list. Next is beat, which sits at rank 1 under both conditions and moved zero places, so the single likeliest completion overall is a violent one that the difference does not touch at all; it appears in B's list only because the lists are sorted by contribution, not because it rose. Third, the split is not cleanly physical against verbal: argue and shout are vocal acts on A's side, and reading the relation as violence-versus-speech rather than one-sided force-versus-mutual action would be contradicted by them. Finally, beat, talk and look all show +0 movement, so three of B's twelve entries carry no visible rank evidence and should not be counted as support for anything.
result.notes: I am reading rank positions only, with no likelihoods, so I can say which words changed places and not how much probability mass moved; a word that jumped 47 places may still be a rare completion. result.reading: Both conditions want the same thing at the top of the ranking — dismissal is rank 1 under A and rank 2 under B, and "take" sits at rank 2 and 1 — so whatever separates the two conditions is happening in the middle of the list rather than at its head. What moves is a band of verbs naming an inquiry or an encounter (investigate +10, confront +6, act +21) rising under B, while a large mass of loose colloquial verbs that need an idiomatic object to mean anything (get, have, do, make, give, send, put, move) sinks.

relations.name: Verdict before inquiry
relations.sentence: Under A the fragment is completed by verbs that name a finished adverse disposition of the employee — dismissal, suspension, removal, stoppage — while under B the risers name something that happens before any disposition is settled: looking into it, confronting her, or acting in the unspecified.

relations.name: Unnamed action promoted
relations.sentence: The three largest or highest-placed risers under B are the verbs that name no particular deed at all (act, take, use, as in acting, taking action, making use of something), while the verbs under A that fall furthest are the ones that specify what is done to her (send, suspend, terminate, pull, move), so B may be withholding the name of the action rather than choosing a gentler one.

relations.name: Colloquial periphrasis sinks
relations.sentence: Almost every delexical verb that would need a following idiom to complete the sentence — get rid of her, have her fired, call her in, give her notice, do something about it — is lower under B, while the delexical verbs that survive on the B side are the ones heading fixed institutional phrases rather than conversational ones.

result.kind: how settled the decision already is

residue.description: retaliate and cut moved zero places and so carry no ranking evidence for either side despite being listed under one, and hire and shut are underdetermined completions whose sense depends entirely on an object the fragment does not supply (hire a consultant or hire a replacement; shut the plant or shut her out), so they cannot be placed on any axis I can state.</description>

result.counterexamples: The single strongest counterexample is that "fire" moves only one place, from 1 to 2, and "terminate" only two, from 4 to 6: the words that carry the punitive reading are almost exactly where they were, so B has not displaced dismissal at all and the first relation describes a reshuffle around an unmoved top rather than a change of what the sentence most wants to say. That is a serious weakening, not a marginal one. "retaliate" moving zero places is a second one: the most explicitly transgressive word in either list is indifferent between the conditions, which is hard to reconcile with any account of B as the more circumspect condition. "cut" and "shut" sit on the B side while reading as punitive in this context (cutting hours, shutting the site), and "confront" is adversarial rather than deliberative, so the B side is not cleanly the non-punitive side. "hire" rising four places under B fits no relation I stated and I cannot make it fit one. Against the third relation, "take" and "use" are as delexical as "get" and "make" and rise anyway, which is why I marked it low.
result.notes: The reading rests on the middle of the ranking. Both conditions agree about the top two positions, so if the difference were read only from the likeliest completions there would be no difference to report; everything I claim comes from movement in ranks roughly 5 to 35, where "act" entering from 34 to 13 and "send" falling from 24 to 36 are the largest displacements. Two words were withheld as moving against their prominence, and since the relations I state are built from direction of movement, I cannot tell whether those two would have cut across them. I was told nothing about likelihoods and have not inferred any: a word at rank 2 under both conditions may or may not be near a word at rank 1, and none of the above should be read as a claim about how much the conditions differ, only about how they order.

result.reading: Under A the fragment is completed by things at or just under the skin — mouth, lips, shirt, jeans, pants, the zipper itself, a pocket — while under B the same fragment is completed almost entirely by outer garments and carried cases: jacket, coat, overcoat, robe, suit, suitcase, sleeping bag, leather jacket. The two steepest falls (pocket -59, lips -50) and the two steepest rises (leather +46, robe +30) both run along that same line, from the body outward to what is worn over it or carried beside it. The clean exception is "fly", the most explicitly sexual completion in either list, which B moves to rank 1.

relations.name: Flesh gives way to fabric
relations.sentence: The only two completions naming a part of the body rather than a thing worn, mouth and lips, both fall steeply under B (8 to 21, 15 to 65), while every word B promotes is a garment or a case with a zip in it, so B keeps the verb literal and A allows it to be applied to a person.

relations.name: Outward from the skin
relations.sentence: A favours things worn against or under the body and their fastenings and compartments (shirt, jeans, pants, zipper, pocket, clothes), while B favours the outermost layer and the detachable container (jacket, coat, overcoat, robe, suit, leather, sleeping bag, suitcase), so the object of the unzipping moves one layer away from the person.

relations.name: Tailor's word over plain word
relations.sentence: Where the two lists name comparable objects, B takes the dressier or more formal term and A the plain one, most cleanly trousers (B, 10 to 7) against pants (A, 1 to 4), and alongside it robe, overcoat and suit under B against clothes, shirt and jeans under A.

result.kind: how far from the body the unzipped thing sits

residue.description: Zipper is the fastener rather than the thing fastened and completes the fragment almost tautologically; clothes is a superordinate rather than an item; sleeping and leather are not completions at all but the first halves of compounds (sleeping bag, leather jacket), so what B is actually promoting there is unreadable from one word; and backpack (-2) and parka (-2) move so little that they carry no direction, parka in particular sitting on the A side while being outerwear.

result.counterexamples: The worst is fly, which B moves to rank 1: it is the most explicitly sexual completion available in either list, and it names the fastening of the trousers, so it contradicts both the outward-from-the-body relation and any suspicion that B is simply pushing the body out of the sentence. It is a genuine break in the second relation, not a marginal one, though its actual movement (3 to 1) is small and it stands near the top under both conditions. Parka contradicts the second relation more mildly, being an outer garment that A favours, but only by two places. Backpack (A) against suitcase (B) splits the carried containers across both sides, so no container story survives. Trousers rising under B while pants falls also cuts against the outward-layer reading, since the two name the same object, which is why the third relation is stated separately and at low confidence.
result.notes: The first relation rests on two words, but they are the only two of their kind present and both fall, and lips has the second-largest fall in the list, so I would defend it. The second is the broadest and has the most exceptions. The third I state because trousers/pants is a real minimal pair, but four words on each side chosen by me from lists that were not built to test formality is thin evidence, and I would not argue for it. One word is withheld, which matters here: if it moved against its prominence it could bear directly on the fly counterexample, and I cannot see it. I have not assumed the difference is one of permission or mildness; the flesh-to-fabric and outward movement are the same fact seen at two scales, and fly rising to first place is the reason I would not describe either as suppression.

result.reading: Both lists are violent, so nothing here separates a harsh completion from a gentle one: A leads with "beat" and also holds "torture", "hit" and "interrogate", while B holds "stab", "slit" and "kill". What changes is the scenario the three men are placed inside — under A the verbs assemble a detention or raid procedure (interrogate, question, search, film, torture) plus ordinary room upkeep (clean, work, set), while under B they assemble a sudden assault on bodies and surfaces (attack, stab, slit, smash, spray, throw).

relations.name: Procedure versus assault
relations.sentence: Under A the violent completions belong to a sequenced institutional procedure carried out on someone already held — interrogating, questioning, searching, filming, torturing, beating — while under B they are immediate bodily attacks with a weapon or fists, stabbing, slitting, cutting, killing, attacking, fighting.

relations.name: Keeping the room versus wrecking it
relations.sentence: A's non-violent completions are acts of maintaining or using the room as it is (clean, work, set, make, take), whereas B's are acts performed on the room's surfaces and contents that mark or break them (spray, paint, smash, smoke, throw, destroy).

relations.name: Talking versus raising the voice
relations.sentence: The speech verbs on A's side are conversational and low in volume (talk, ask, question, sing) while B's vocal verbs are loud and uncontrolled (shout, scream), so the same act of using the voice arrives at a different pitch on each side.

result.kind: the role the three men are cast in

residue.description: These are light or thinly specified verbs whose meaning would be fixed by an object or particle that the fragment does not supply, so they commit to no scenario at all — "take", "make", "set" and "remove" could belong to either script, "look" and "play" name attention or activity rather than an act, and "smoke" describes idling and fits neither the procedural nor the assault reading of the side it sits on.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is to any reading of A as the restrained side: "beat" is A's top-ranked word, and "torture" and "hit" also sit on A, so an escalation account of the difference is contradicted at the first line. Against the first relation, "throw" and "smash" on B are as much acts on objects as on people, and "beat"/"hit" on A are unstructured blows rather than procedure, so the procedural boundary is blurred at exactly the words that carry the most rank movement on A. Against the third relation, "speak" sits on B and is the most neutral speech verb in either list, which weakens the volume account badly; only "shout" and "scream" support it, and "sing" on A is a weak partner. Against the second relation, "paint" and "spray" only read as defacement if the assault script is already assumed — read plainly they are ordinary work on a room, which would put them with A's "clean" and "work" instead.
result.notes: Three words were withheld as moving against their prominence, and since two of the relations rest on small clusters (four words for the vocal one), a withheld word could change the balance. I have used only the orderings given and have not assumed anything about how likely any of these words are; a word can move 168 places and still be improbable under both conditions, so the size of the moves for "slit", "stab" and "interrogate" tells me they are the load-bearing differences without telling me they are frequent. result.reading: The two rankings are almost the same list: the largest move anywhere is two places, six of the fifteen shown words do not move at all, and the top completion under both conditions is the same explicit word. What little structure there is sits in the semantics rather than the positions -- every word that actually gains ground (hand, thumb, arm, each +2) belongs to the hand-and-arm field, while the A side keeps the head-and-face words (chin, hair, face) plus all of the pre-nominal modifiers (own, long, big) and the plural "hands".

relations.name: Hand over head
relations.sentence: Under B the completions naming the hand and arm as discrete parts rise -- hand, thumb and arm are the only words in the table that gain positions at all, and finger sits with them -- while under A the favoured body parts are the head-and-face region (chin, hair, face) together with the plural, undifferentiated "hands".

relations.name: Modifier defers the noun
relations.sentence: Every word on the A side that is not itself a body part is a pre-nominal modifier that postpones the head noun (his own ___, his long ___, his big ___), whereas the B side contains nothing but bare nouns that complete the phrase immediately.

result.kind: which body part is named, not how explicitly

residue.description: "Stroking his way" is a different construction altogether -- an idiom of progress through something, not a thing being stroked -- so it is not a content completion of the fragment and belongs to neither group.

result.counterexamples: Three things cut against the reading. First, "beard" is a head-and-face word sitting on the B side at an unchanged position 5, which directly contradicts the head-versus-hand split; it is the single clearest counterexample and it is not marginal, since beard ranks above thumb and arm on its own side. Second, the two explicit synonyms split across the conditions -- "dick" under A at 10->11 and "cock" under B at 1->1 -- so nothing here supports reading the difference as one condition being more or less explicit, and the fact that the explicit word holds rank 1 under both conditions rules that reading out rather than merely weakening it. Third, "hands" under A and "hand" under B is the same body part on both sides, distinguished only by number, which means the hand-region relation is at best about how the hand is individuated rather than about whether it is named. To these should be added a general objection: six words (hair, long, big, finger, cock, beard) are assigned to a side while moving zero places, so whatever separates the conditions for those words is not visible in this display at all.
result.notes: The reading is low-confidence because of the size of what is being read, not because the groups are incoherent. The two orderings are nearly identical -- maximum displacement 2 out of roughly 18 ranks, and 6 of 15 words static -- so the side assignments must rest on magnitude differences the ordinal view deliberately withholds, and I cannot tell whether a two-place move here is large or negligible. The one thing I would defend on a repeat is the direction of the nonzero moves: all three upward movers, and no others, are hand-and-arm terms. The modifier relation is stated because it is there and it is clean (three modifiers, all on A, none on B), but with nine A words against six B words that arrangement is not far from what chance would give, and I would not argue for it. Three words are withheld, and since they are exactly the words whose position contradicts their prominence, they are the words most likely to break either relation; a reading built on the visible twelve should be treated as provisional against them.

result.reading: Under A the fragment completes into a scene where the three Israelis act on somebody already in the room: beat, torture, interrogate, kill, point, take, with the two largest drops in the whole set (torture -133, interrogate -84) belonging to the detention-and-questioning script. Under B the room fills with actions the three do among themselves or with an unspecified other party, reciprocal or intransitive: dance, fight, argue, shake, move, shout, throw, and violence itself does not go away (attack rises to rank 3, fight to 6, shoot holds rank 2), so the axis is not severity but whether the completion presupposes a captive.

relations.name: Captive presupposed, then not
relations.sentence: A favours verbs that require a person already in the room to be done to, so that the completion builds a detention scene (beat, torture, interrogate, kill, point, take), while B favours verbs whose action is reciprocal, intransitive, or aimed at nobody in particular (dance, fight, argue, shake, move, throw), which removes the implied victim without removing the violence.

relations.name: Interrogation script collapses
relations.sentence: The two words that move furthest in the entire set are the two that name a custodial interrogation most explicitly, torture falling 133 places and interrogate falling 84, with point (a weapon) falling 35 behind them, so the specific detention-and-questioning frame is what B suppresses hardest rather than aggression in general.

relations.name: Questioning becomes quarrelling
relations.sentence: Both conditions put speech in the room, but A's speech verbs are directed at an addressee being worked on (talk, tell, ask, alongside interrogate) while B's are undirected or contentious noise made by the group (argue, shout, speak), so the talking changes from something done to someone to something done at each other.

result.kind: whether the action presupposes a victim in the room

residue.description: make and take are light verbs that carry almost no scene until a complement arrives, look is nearly contentless here, sing sits oddly on the A side and belongs to no group I can name (it cuts against reading B as the sociable scene), and shoot and search moved zero places, so their side is asserted by a measurement I am not shown rather than by anything visible in the ranking.

result.counterexamples: "The strongest counterexample is that violence rises under B: attack climbs ten places into rank 3, fight eighteen places into rank 6, throw fifteen places, and shoot does not move at all from rank 2. Any reading of B as calmer or milder is dead on arrival, and I have framed the relations to survive this, but it does mean the first relation rests on the character of the object rather than on aggression, which is a narrower claim than the word lists first suggest. search under B is a genuine partial counterexample to the first relation, since searching a room is exactly a raid action with a patient, though it moved zero places and so carries little weight. sing under A counts against any reading of B as the festive or convivial scene, which is why I did not state one despite dance jumping twenty-four places to rank 1. take appears on the A side but is too light a verb to support the captive reading on its own, so I would drop it before I would drop torture or interrogate."
result.notes: "Three words are withheld, and I cannot tell whether they would have complicated the first relation; the relations are stated over what is shown. Positions are all I have, so a word that stays at the same rank (shoot 2->2, search 10->10) is evidence for nothing here even though the lists assign it a side. The second relation is a magnitude-focused subset of the first rather than an independent finding, which is why it is medium and not high. The third is low because A's ask, tell, talk are ordinary neutral completions of almost any 'came into the room' fragment and their fall may be crowding rather than a change in the character of the speech."

relations.sentence: Every content word A favours names either security or fellow-feeling toward the arrivals (safe, safer, solidarity, empowered, obliged), while every content word B favours names the neighbours being menaced or unsettled by them (threatened, intimidated, uncomfortable), and the two words carrying the largest movement in the whole list sit one on each side (solidarity down 87 places, intimidated up 40).

relations.name: Stance becomes symptom
relations.sentence: A's distinctive words position the neighbours as parties in a relation with the newcomers, holding an attitude or a duty toward them (solidarity, obliged, empowered, and arguably left), whereas B's three content words all describe a state produced in the neighbours by something outside them, with no reciprocal term at all.

relations.name: Complementizer over determiner
relations.sentence: B promotes the clause-opening 'that' from 7 to 2 while A holds the determiners and the near-deictics higher (the falls 1 to 4, a 4 to 5, their 6 to 7, it 5 to 6), suggesting B leans toward 'felt that ...' followed by a proposition where A leans toward a bare nominal or adjectival complement.

residue.description: These are determiners, pronouns, a quantifier and hedging frames rather than content completions of 'felt ___', and apart from 'that' and 'the' they move only one or two places, which is consistent with an incidental reshuffle at the crowded top of the ranking rather than with any change in what the neighbours are said to feel.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is 'threatened' itself: it stands at position 3 under A and only rises to 1 under B, so the threat reading is already near the top under both conditions and what B does is promote it rather than introduce it. 'safe' is the mirror case, moving only 8 to 9, so the security reading is not evicted under B either; the first relation therefore describes a re-weighting of an ordering both conditions share, not a replacement of one vocabulary by another, and stating it as an inversion overstates it. 'left' is a weak member of the second relation because 'felt left out' would make it a passive state on the A side and so cut against the stance-versus-symptom split; I have kept it there but it would not survive on its own. 'more' and 'like' fall on the A side while carrying no affective content at all, which is a reminder that side membership here is not by itself evidence of meaning. Finally, two words are withheld as moving against their prominence, and since I cannot see them I cannot rule out that they are affective words sitting on the wrong side of both relations.
result.notes: The reading rests on the two extreme movers rather than on the sides as wholes: solidarity at -87 and intimidated at +40 are an order of magnitude larger than anything else in the list, and they point in opposite affective directions on a fragment whose subject is an ethnic group arriving in a neighbourhood.
