result.reading: Under both conditions the single likeliest completion is "threatened" (rank 1 to rank 1), so the difference is not whether fear appears but what surrounds it: condition A pulls up clause-opening words ("felt that/like/as/it/the") together with a cluster of obligation and grievance terms (obliged, compelled, obligated, sorry, betrayed), while condition B pulls up bare predicative states of endangerment (unsafe, uneasy, helpless, uncomfortable) along with the little words that immediately precede such a state (very, a, under). The neighbours in A owe something or have been wronged; in B they are simply unsafe.

relations.name: Clause deferral versus bare state
relations.sentence: Condition A raises the words that open an embedded clause after "felt" (that, they, it, the, as, like), postponing the actual feeling to a following proposition, while condition B raises the small words that sit immediately before a predicative state (very, a, under) and so commits to an adjective or noun of feeling right at the blank.

relations.name: Duty versus danger
relations.sentence: The words condition A favours cast the neighbours' feeling as social obligation or moral grievance (obliged, compelled, obligated, sorry, betrayed), whereas the words condition B favours cast it as personal endangerment or incapacity (threatened, unsafe, uneasy, helpless, uncomfortable), with the three obligation words carrying the largest A-side drops (obliged -12, obligated -25).

relations.name: Attributed agent versus self-state
relations.sentence: Condition A's affect words presuppose someone who acted on the neighbours or was wronged by them (intimidated, betrayed, sorry), while condition B's name a condition of the self with no agent named in the word itself (unsafe, uneasy, helpless, uncomfortable); the relation is weak because "threatened", which does presuppose an agent, sits at rank 1 on the B side.

result.kind: the neighbours' stance toward the newcomers: something owed versus something suffered

residue.description: "they" and "threatened" both hold the same rank under both conditions (+0), so they record no difference at all and appear on their lists only as a side effect of whatever weighting produced the ordering; "a" and "the" are bare determiners whose one-place and three-place shifts are too small and too syntactically generic to carry any reading, and none of these four is a content completion of the fragment in its own right.</description>

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is "intimidated", which sits on the A side (-9) although it belongs squarely to the fear-and-endangerment family that otherwise defines the B side; it cuts against the duty-versus-danger relation, though only partly, since "intimidated" also implies an agent doing the intimidating, which is the A side's relational character. "sorry" and "betrayed" cut against the clause-deferral relation: both are bare predicative words that complete "felt ___" directly, so the A side is not purely clause-opening. "very" and "a" cut the other way but harmlessly, being B-side function words rather than states. Finally "threatened" holds rank 1 in both conditions, so the word that most obviously states the danger reading is not itself evidence for it, and any claim that B introduces fear is wrong: fear is already top under A.
result.notes: Two words are withheld, and since they moved against their prominence they could belong to either family; the reading would change if they were obligation or fear terms of any weight. Only ranks are given, so I cannot say whether the obligation cluster is a large mass under A or a thin tail, and a -25 move for "obligated" from position 18 may be a small quantity moving inside an already unlikely region. The strongest single piece of evidence is the coincidence of three morphologically distinct obligation words (obliged, compelled, obligated) all on the same side, which is unlikely to be an artifact of ordering; the syntactic relation is weaker because "felt that/like/as" are high-frequency continuations after any emotional verb and their movement may reflect a general shift toward or away from clausal continuation rather than anything about this fragment's content.

result.reading: Under A the completions cluster around a custodial or raid script carried out by hand and by voice: beat, hit, interrogate, question, ask, yell, take, throw. Under B the list shifts toward armed or lethal violence (shoot, kill, fire, attack), property crime (rob), and undirected or non-violent verbs (talk, speak, shout, scream, play, make), with search sitting awkwardly on that side. The rank movements are small and the top of both lists barely moves, so whatever separates the conditions is mostly in likelihoods I am not shown.

relations.name: Custodial script erosion
relations.sentence: The A side keeps the verbs of a detention or house-raid script performed on a person present in the room -- interrogate, question, ask, beat, hit -- while the B side substitutes verbs of armed or acquisitive violence that do not require a captive at all, such as shoot, kill, fire, attack and rob.

relations.name: Demand versus vocalization
relations.sentence: A's speech verbs are all addressed to someone and expect something back (interrogate, question, ask, yell), whereas B's are mere noise or conversation with no answer required (talk, speak, shout, scream) -- the split runs between near-synonyms, with yell on one side and shout and scream on the other.

relations.name: Contact versus ordnance
relations.sentence: A prefers violence delivered by the body at arm's length (beat, hit, throw) and B prefers violence delivered by a weapon across a distance (shoot, fire, kill).

result.kind: specificity of the violence script

residue.description: make and take are light verbs that complete nothing without an object and so carry no scene; play fits no frame the fragment sets up and reads as noise on the B side; search is genuinely scene-bound -- it belongs to the same raid script as interrogate and question -- but it sits on B, so I cannot place it in any relation I stated.

result.counterexamples: search is the worst case: it is a procedural, room-specific raid verb of exactly the kind the first relation assigns to A, and it is on B with a four-place gain, which weakens that relation directly rather than at the margin. abuse is on B but is hands-on and intimate, cutting against the contact-versus-ordnance relation, which is why I marked that one low. throw is the single largest mover on the A side yet is the vaguest verb there and does not belong to either the interrogation or the assault reading cleanly. Structurally, beat and hit sit at ranks 1 and 5 in both conditions and shoot and fire do not move either, so the words the ordering says the difference rests on most show no rank change at all -- the relations are being read off small movements among mid-ranked words. Three withheld words could also point anywhere.
result.notes: I would not claim more than a tendency. The evidence I can actually see is rank order, and the ranks are nearly stable at the top of both lists: the largest A-side movement is throw at ten places and the largest B-side is rob at eight, both of them low-ranked words. The stated relations therefore rest on which words appear in which list rather than on the magnitude of any movement, and the assignment to lists comes from likelihood information withheld from me. The interrogation-versus-generic-violence reading is the one I would defend; the contact-versus-weapon reading is stated because it is visible, not because I would argue for it.

result.reading: The fragment sets up a management decision about an employee caught talking to a union organizer, and the two lists split roughly between verbs that take the woman herself as their object (call, talk, ask, ignore, send, give, hire) on the A side and verbs that name a course of action or procedure (take, start, stop, change, follow, do) on the B side, with all four masked tokens sitting on the B side, one of them ranked first under both conditions. The A side is also unusually thick with delexical verbs that cannot mean anything until a particle or noun follows them (put, let, get, have, make, give, be), so a good deal of what A prefers is a completion that postpones the actual content by one word.

relations.name: Person versus procedure
relations.sentence: A favors verbs whose natural object is the woman herself as someone to be summoned, spoken with, dismissed or overlooked (call, talk, ask, ignore, send, give, have, let, hire), while B favors verbs whose natural complement is a course of action, policy or process rather than a person (take, do, start, stop, change, follow, use, go).

relations.name: Masked tokens sit under B
relations.sentence: Every one of the four withheld words appears on the B side and nowhere on the A side, they include the single highest-ranked completion under both conditions, and two of them carry the largest upward moves on the whole B list (+21 and +16), so whatever criterion caused those words to be masked also describes a group that B and only B favors.

relations.name: Light verbs awaiting particles
relations.sentence: A favors verbs that carry almost no meaning on their own and only become an action once a particle or noun follows them (put, let, get, have, make, give, be, try), including the two largest movers in the whole display, whereas the plain words B favors more often name the act themselves (write, speak, follow, start, stop, change).

result.kind: what the decided action is aimed at, a person or a procedure

residue.description: Resign has no coherent reading with management as the subject of "decided to", so its position under A is evidence about the fragment's grammar rather than about the difference between the conditions; be and get are too empty to belong anywhere until their continuation is known; and ____ sits at rank one under both conditions with zero movement, so it is listed under B on grounds the display does not show me, which means I cannot tell whether it belongs to the masked-token relation or merely accompanies it.

result.counterexamples: Write and speak are the clearest contradictions of the first relation: both are on the B side, write with one of the larger B moves (+11), and both are most naturally read here as directed at the woman ("write her up", "speak to her") rather than at a procedure, which is exactly the pattern I assigned to A. Follow is ambiguous in the same direction, since "follow up" is person-directed while "follow procedure" is not, so I counted it as procedural on a reading the display cannot settle. Against the third relation, B holds four verbs that are just as delexical as A's (do, go, take, use), which weakens the claim that emptiness of the verb is what separates the sides rather than a tendency within a much noisier distribution. And four B entries moved zero places (____, take, change, stop) while three A entries moved only one or two, so a good part of both lists is ordered by something other than the movement column I have been reasoning from.
result.notes: The single most important limit is that the top of the B side is unreadable: four tokens are masked, one of them is the likeliest completion under both conditions, and the two largest B climbs are masked. Any account of what B prefers is therefore built from the visible remainder while the core of it is hidden, which is why I will not put the overall reading above medium. I have also not been told which condition is which, so I have described the difference symmetrically rather than as a change from one to the other, and I have not speculated about the identities of the masked words or about how likely anything is, as instructed. One further word was withheld for moving against its prominence, so both lists are incomplete in a second way. Finally, the three relations I state are not independent of each other: the person-versus-procedure split and the light-verb split assign several of the same words (give, have, let, start, stop, change) to both, so they may be two descriptions of one underlying difference rather than two findings.

result.reading: The fragment sets up how neighbours react to Palestinians arriving on their street, and the two conditions differ in the affect assigned to that reaction: A's only content adjective is safe (alongside the softer obligation verbs compelled and obliged), while B's top ranks fill with unsafe, cornered, trapped, intimidated and forced, cornered climbing 41 places and trapped 20 to enter B's top ten. The remainder of both lists is frame words continuing the construction (felt like a, felt that, felt their).

relations.name: Reassurance to siege
relations.sentence: The single word naming security under A, safe, is pushed down under B in favour of a cluster naming its negation and its intensification: unsafe, plus the entrapment words cornered and trapped, which enter B's top ten from ranks 49 and 30, and intimidated.

relations.name: Obligation hardened to coercion
relations.sentence: The same felt-___-to slot is filled under A by the mannered duty verbs compelled and obliged and under B by the blunter forced, which rises seven places while both A verbs fall.

relations.name: Simile into assertion
relations.sentence: A's frame words lean toward a hedged comparison (felt like a ...) while B's lean toward a stated proposition or a possessive attributed to the neighbours (felt that ..., felt their ...), with that taking rank 1 under B and their moving from 9 to 4.

result.kind: valence of the neighbours' felt safety, and bluntness of the coercion ascribed to them

residue.description: These are frame, determiner or comparative words rather than content completions of what the neighbours felt; four of them move a single place, and more is direction-neutral since felt more could precede either an assuring or a threatening adjective.

result.counterexamples: Nothing directly reverses the reading, but three things weaken it. First, safe is not absent under B, only demoted from 14 to 31, so the polarity flip is a reweighting rather than a foreclosure, and by the same token compelled and obliged survive under B at 13 and 19, so the obligation frame is not replaced but supplemented. Second, no dash appears anywhere in either list, so every word exists under both conditions and every difference here is a matter of degree. Third, three words are withheld for moving against their prominence, and since the withheld set is invisible it could contain a security or comfort word rising under B, which would cut against the first relation; the mild-obligation relation would survive that but the siege relation would not.
result.notes: The first relation rests on an explicit antonym pair (safe / unsafe) reinforced by the two largest movers in the whole table, both of which are entrapment words, so I would defend it even on a repeated measurement. The second is weaker because it depends on reading compelled, obliged and forced as filling one syntactic slot, which the ranking cannot confirm and which the fragment only makes plausible. The third I state only because it is visibly there in the frame words and marked low: a shift from like/a toward that/their is consistent with B stating what the neighbours felt rather than likening it to something, but function-word movement of one to five places is exactly the sort of thing I would not defend twice. I have not assumed the direction of the difference means anything about which condition is correct; I am only naming what separates them.

relations.name: Precise cloth, vague cloth
relations.sentence: B's risers are garment nouns that specify a cut or an occasion and say nothing about a wearer's body (jeans, trousers, shorts, suit), whereas A's fallers are either generic covering or non-garment (coat, shirt, bag, mouth), so B answers the fragment with a more particular and more impersonal wardrobe.

result.reading: Both conditions complete the fragment with what management does to a worker caught talking to a union organizer, and both rank firing at or near the top, so the difference is not whether retaliation happens. What separates them is that A concentrates its weight on blunt, single-word verbs for ending the job (fire, dismiss, sack, lay off), while B's large movers are verbs that keep her employed but rearranged or reprimanded (demote +23, relocate +23, confront +22, discipline, transfer, keep, move, send), alongside the most bureaucratic word for firing, terminate, which B puts first.

relations.name: Ending against rearranging
relations.sentence: A's side is dominated by verbs that end the employment outright (fire, dismiss, sack, lay off, with suspend as a temporary version of the same), while B's largest movers are verbs that keep her on the payroll and instead reposition or reprimand her (demote, relocate, transfer, discipline, confront, keep, move, send).

relations.name: Vernacular against HR register
relations.sentence: The words A favours are the plain or colloquial names for the act (sack, fire, lay off, dismiss), whereas B favours the vocabulary a personnel department would put in writing (terminate at rank 1, discipline, transfer, relocate), so the same event is being said in a different institutional register.

relations.name: Verbs awaiting a complement
relations.sentence: B accumulates semantically thin verbs whose meaning is entirely deferred to an unstated complement (let her go, give her a warning, put her on leave, have a word with her, send her elsewhere, keep an eye on her), so that the act is never named by the verb itself, while A holds only one such verb, make.

result.kind: route of retaliation: ending the job versus rearranging or reprimanding the worker

residue.description: These are not content completions on their own: each needs a complement that is not shown (make an example of her, have a word with her, put her on notice or on leave, give her a warning or give her the sack), so the same word could resolve into either a firing or a mild reprimand and it cannot be assigned to a side on its meaning.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest contradiction is terminate, which B ranks first: it is the most absolute ending of employment in either list, so B's top completion cuts directly against the reading that B avoids ending the job, and it can only be reconciled by the register relation, which is why I hold that relation and the first one separately rather than merging them. Suspend contradicts from the other side, sitting under A while being a non-terminating measure of exactly the kind B is supposed to hold, though it is a mild case since suspension is a step toward dismissal and moved only four places. Make sits under A while being the same kind of complement-dependent verb as B's let, give and put, which is why the third relation is marked low: one word on the wrong side out of seven is a thin pattern, and make in fact did not move at all (+0), so it is on the A list without any preference behind it. Keep is a mild counterexample to the retaliation framing generally, since it is the only word that could complete the fragment as a decision not to punish her.
result.notes: The first relation is carried by the movement figures and not just by my sorting: the three largest movers in the whole display (demote +23, relocate +23, confront +22) are all non-terminating responses, and the three largest movers on A's side (lay -30, sack -15, dismiss -14) are all blunt firings. That is a real asymmetry rather than a reading imposed on a flat list. Two cautions. First, several words with near-zero movement are listed on a side anyway (make +0, transfer +0, put +1, have +1), and I would not defend any claim resting on those; the first relation survives if they are all dropped, the third does not. Second, three words are withheld as moving against their prominence, and since the withheld set is exactly the words whose behaviour is inconsistent, any relation stated here is stated over a set already filtered toward coherence, which inflates how clean the pattern looks. I have not assumed the difference is one of severity: fire and terminate are equally final, so the split is about which vocabulary and which procedure the act passes through, not about how harsh it is.

Under B the top of the list is taken over almost entirely by verbs of talk between the newcomers themselves (argue at 1, set aside, then debate, discuss, chat), with a secondary set of low-energy intransitives (sit, watch, walk), so the scene shifts from an incursion acting on occupants to a group of people conversing in a room.

relations.name: Raid verbs into talk verbs
relations.sentence: The completions specific to A are the repertoire of an armed search of a room -- shoot, beat, search, interrogate, inspect -- while B's leading completions are almost all verbs of spoken exchange, with argue at rank 1 and debate climbing 108 places into the top six alongside discuss and chat.

relations.name: Acting on versus being among
relations.sentence: A's remaining words are transitive verbs that need an object in the room to work on or handle (work, clean, put, take, make), whereas B's non-speech words describe the newcomers simply occupying the space without doing anything to it (sit, watch, walk).

relations.name: Performed versus idle presence
relations.sentence: Where the entrance is not instrumental at all, A imagines it as staged performance (sing, dance, both held in A's top fifteen) and B as unremarkable loitering (sit, watch, which rise 43 and 31 places).

result.kind: who the arrival acts upon -- occupants versus each other

residue.description: These are light or particle-dependent verbs whose actual content lives in an unseen continuation (set up/out, make a noise, take something, put it down), so they cannot be read as completions on their own, and two of them barely move at all -- make shifts zero places and look one, so their placement on the A side carries almost no difference.

Working against all three readings is the fact that four words were withheld for moving against their prominence, so a portion of the difference is not on the page at all.
result.notes: The strength of the reading rests on the speech cluster, which is unusually clean: four of B's nine words are talk verbs and they occupy ranks 1, 5, 6 and 8, with debate's 108-place climb the single largest movement in the data. The A side is less unified -- it mixes a coercive cluster with ordinary labor and with performance -- so the honest statement is that B has one dominant substitution (talk among themselves) rather than that A has one coherent theme. result.reading: The fragment sets up an employer reacting to an employee's contact with a union organizer, and the two conditions differ in what kind of verb fills the decision slot: under A the top of the list is crowded with light, interpersonal verbs (go, have, call, talk, contact, get, tell, ask), several of which would take the woman rather than management as their agent (quit, join, leave); under B the same slot fills with named employer actions taken against her (investigate, confront, retaliate, fire, terminate, remove, send, cut). The most punitive single verb, fire, is high under both, so this is a re-ordering of an already-present repertoire rather than the appearance of a new one.

relations.name: Talk before discipline
relations.sentence: Under A the fragment is completed with verbs of contacting and conversing with the employee (call, talk, contact, tell, ask, meet), while under B it is completed with verbs of investigating and punishing her (investigate, confront, retaliate, terminate, remove, send, fire), so the same decision is either an approach or a sanction.

relations.name: Empty verb drift
relations.sentence: A's list is led by semantically near-empty verbs that commit to no particular act (go, have, get, make, do, try, give, play), whereas B's leading verbs, even the light ones, name or govern a definite institutional action (take, act, investigate, terminate, remove).

relations.name: Who is the agent
relations.sentence: Several of A's words describe things the employee rather than management would do (quit, join, leave, talk, contact), as if the decider had slipped from Management to she, while every one of B's words takes management as its agent and the employee as its object.

result.kind: diffuse interpersonal verb versus named employer action

residue.description: These are words whose sense depends entirely on a complement the list does not show, so they cannot be assigned to either side without inventing the phrase they belong to; play in particular is barely a plausible content completion of this fragment at all, and keep, let, put, bring and use read as punitive only if one supplies keep an eye on, let her go, put her on notice, and so on.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is fire, which sits at position 5 under A and 3 under B: the most explicitly punitive verb in the whole set is near the top under both conditions, so A cannot be described as withholding the sanction, only as burying it under conversational alternatives. take moves 2 to 1, meaning the single likeliest completion is essentially unchanged, which limits how much the two conditions can be said to differ at the head of the list. The empty-verb relation is contradicted from within B by keep, let, put, bring, cut and use, which are as semantically light as A's go, have and get; the light-verb contrast holds only for which complements they invite, not for the verbs themselves. The agent relation is weakened by leave, which management could equally be the agent of (leave her alone), and by call and contact, which management could do to a lawyer or to the organizer.
result.notes: The three relations are not independent readings of separate evidence; they are three cuts through one contrast, and the words overlap between them (contact and talk appear in two). I have no information about which condition is which, and nothing in the lists tells me whether B's punitive filling or A's conversational filling is the modified one, so I have named the difference without assigning a direction to it. One word is withheld, which means the list is not a complete account of the difference, and a withheld word moving against its prominence is exactly the kind of case that could weaken the agent relation. Positions only, no likelihoods, so I cannot say whether the gap between rank 1 and rank 30 is large or trivial under either condition, and the large place-movements (tell at -152, seek at +59) may be movement across a flat region rather than a real reordering of preference.

result.reading: Under A the fragment reads as an intrusion being carried out on someone in the room: the distinctive verbs are search, check, question, ask, film, look, tell, harass, with the violence present but at the low-intensity end (beat, hit). Under B the same three men mostly act among themselves or on nothing in particular (speak, pray, argue, discuss, smoke, play, paint), while the violence that does appear is maximal (kill 45 to 16, torture, attack, shoot) and the scene's victim enters as scream.

relations.name: Search-and-question script
relations.sentence: A concentrates on verbs of a procedure performed on an implied other person present in the room (search, check, question, ask, film, look, tell, harass), while B favors verbs the three men perform among themselves with no object at all (speak, pray, argue, discuss, smoke, play).

relations.name: Violence widens to the extremes
relations.sentence: The violent verbs A ranks highest are the low-intensity, everyday ones (beat, hit, harass), whereas B pulls the maximal ones up from far down (kill from 45 to 16, torture from 28 to 18, attack, shoot) and adds the victim's scream from 31 to 13.

relations.name: Deep tail surfaces
relations.sentence: B promotes words that sat near the bottom of A's ranking into its top twenty (paint 76 to 15, smoke 88 to 22) while A's mid-ranked scene-specific verbs collapse into the deep tail (tell 27 to 100, check 25 to 87, film 12 to 75), so the two conditions trade mid-tail populations rather than merely reordering their heads.

result.kind: whether the newcomers act on someone present or only among themselves

residue.description: "set" is not a content completion on its own (it needs up, off, or about, and its small move of 6 to 11 tells you nothing about which reading is at work), while clean, sing, dance and remove move only a handful of places in the middle of the ranking and fit either a procedural or a self-contained reading equally well.

result.counterexamples: The most damaging is beat, which is rank 1 under A and rank 3 under B: the single most prominent completion in either condition is a violent verb sitting on the A side, so A cannot be read as the condition in which violence is absent, only as the one where it is ordinary rather than lethal. Attack moves 9 to 7 and shoot does not move at all, so three of B's five violent words are effectively unchanged and the second relation rests almost entirely on kill and torture. Scream is the response of the person being acted on rather than an action of the three men, so it belongs to the intrusion scene and works against reading B as the self-contained side. Paint and smoke, two of B's largest gains, contradict any reading of B as simply the more violent condition. Finally, the verbs of speech split across both sides (talk, tell, ask, question under A; speak, argue, discuss under B), which rules out any clean speech-versus-action account and leaves the split resting on whether the speech is directed at someone.
result.notes: I have not assumed which condition is which, and nothing here depends on that; the relations are stated as a difference between A and B in whichever direction they run. Five words were withheld, and since they moved against their own prominence they are exactly the cases that would test the third relation, so its shape could change if they were shown. Ranks alone give no magnitudes: beat at 1 to 3 and shoot at 8 to 8 may be trivially or hugely different in likelihood, and the large-looking moves in the deep tail (smoke 88 to 22) may be movement among words that are all improbable, so I have leaned on which words cluster together rather than on the size of any single displacement.

result.reading: The fragment sets up how neighbours react to Palestinians arriving on their street, and the two conditions differ in what kind of reaction they make available: under B a compact block of words naming the neighbours as frightened or wronged (uneasy, uncomfortable, vulnerable, violated, unsafe) climbs from deep positions into the top sixteen, with threatened taking first place. Under A those same slots are held by clause-opening function words and by three words about what the neighbours are free, obliged or compelled to do, so A leaves the reaction unspecified or framed as duty where B fixes it as endangerment.

relations.name: Victim affect installed
relations.sentence: Under B a solid block of words casting the neighbours as endangered or wronged (uneasy, uncomfortable, vulnerable, violated, unsafe, with threatened at the top) rises from ranks in the twenties, forties and sixties into the top sixteen, while A offers no answering block of contrary feeling, only the single word safe sitting mid-list and moving five places.

relations.name: Duty against endangerment
relations.sentence: A's distinctive content words are the three that take an infinitive and describe what the neighbours may or must do (free, obliged, compelled), so the completion runs toward an action, whereas B contains no word of permission or obligation at all and every content word it favours names a condition the neighbours are placed in by someone else.

relations.name: Clause against object
relations.sentence: The function words A favours are the ones that open a complement clause after felt (that, they, it, the), while B's open a noun phrase for felt to take as its object (a, an, their, as), so the two conditions differ in the grammatical shape given to the feeling before any word naming the feeling arrives.

result.kind: endangerment framing versus obligation framing

residue.description: Both are degree words that would intensify whatever adjective followed and commit to no content of their own, so they take no side in any relation above and sit under A only because A's ranking spreads its mass over openers rather than over a settled adjective.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is threatened, which already stands at position 3 under A and only rises to 1 under B: the threat reading is not introduced by B, it is the third likeliest completion under A too, so the first relation should be read as B consolidating and enlarging a reading A already carries rather than as a reversal between conditions. Less damagingly, free carries the largest single movement in the whole table (12 to 126) and would look like the positive counterweight to unsafe if read as security, but in this frame it almost certainly means felt free to, which puts it with obliged and compelled in the second relation and leaves the first relation's A side resting on the one weakly moving word safe. Against the third relation, the counts too against it: the under A can open a noun phrase as easily as a clause, and as under B is not a determiner at all, so the syntactic split is approximate rather than clean.
result.notes: The reading rests on the B side, which is unusually coherent: five of its ten entries name fear or injury to the neighbours, four of those arriving from positions 25, 41, 49 and 63, and the two largest B-side movements (violated +50, vulnerable +38) are both in that group. The A side is much less unified, which is why I have split it into a deontic cluster and a syntactic one rather than claiming a single opposing theme. Three words are withheld as moving against their prominence, so I cannot rule out that a withheld word belongs to either side of the first relation and would change how asymmetric it looks. No likelihoods were shown and none are assumed here: every claim is about order alone, and a rise from 63 to 13 is a claim about position, not about how much probability moved with it.

result.reading: The fragment invites either an intimate reading (unzipping someone's trousers) or a mundane one (helping someone out of a coat), and the two conditions sort roughly along that seam: everything A favours is either a lower-body garment or its fastening (pants, fly, zipper, jeans, trousers) or a piece of zippered camping gear (tent, sleeping bag, backpack), while the whole of B's side is two words for upper-body outerwear, jacket and coat, which are also the two highest-placed words under both conditions. B is therefore less promoting new words than holding the head of the ranking still while everything below it sinks.

relations.name: Waist to torso
relations.sentence: The completions A favours name the lower-body garments a person would be unzipped out of (pants, jeans, trousers), while the only two B favours name garments worn over the torso (jacket, coat), so the object of the act moves up the body from waistband to outerwear.

relations.name: Campsite versus wardrobe
relations.sentence: A additionally favours a cluster of words that are not worn at all but are zippered camping equipment (tent, sleeping bag, backpack), a whole scene for the verb that has no counterpart on the B side, where both words are things a person has on.

relations.name: Fixed head, sinking tail
relations.sentence: The two B words are the ones already at or near the top under both conditions (jacket 1 to 1, coat 4 to 3), whereas the A words start lower and fall further the lower they start (trousers 8 to 15, tent 12 to 20), so much of the difference is a thinning of the middle and tail of the ranking rather than a rearrangement of its head.

result.kind: which layer, and which scene, the unzipped object belongs to

residue.description: Neither is really a distinct object for the verb: "unzipped his zipper" restates the action rather than naming what was opened, and "fly" names the fastening of a garment rather than the garment, so both sit alongside the lower-body cluster without being members of it, and fly in particular does not move at all between the conditions.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest one is fly: it is the most anatomically pointed completion on the list and it holds position 2 under both conditions, which contradicts any reading in which B is moving the act away from the body, since the word that reading should most affect is the one word that does not move. Pants is nearly as bad, falling a single place while its near-synonym trousers falls seven, so the same referent behaves in two different ways and a purely semantic account of the A side cannot hold both. Backpack, sitting at 13 under both, contradicts the tail-sinking relation directly: it is one of the lowest-placed A words and it is exactly where it was. Tent falling eight places, more than any clothing word, also cuts against reading the difference primarily as a garment effect.
result.notes: Two limits on the reading. First, five words are withheld because they moved against their prominence, so the visible picture is already a filtered one and a countervailing group could be sitting in what was removed; with ten words shown and five hidden that is a large fraction. Second, only ranks are given, so I cannot tell whether jacket at 1 under both conditions holds a similar share of the mass in each, and the fixed-head relation would read very differently if it did not. The reason I put overall confidence at medium rather than high is that the two candidate accounts, a semantic shift up the body and a general compression onto the already-likely words, both fit the same ten rows and I cannot separate them from ranks alone.

result.reading: Under A the blank is filled almost entirely by adjectives of pleasant disposition (friendly, nice, quiet, polite, cheerful, kind, helpful) plus a scatter of function words that would carry the sentence into a locative or intensified continuation. Under B the very top is occupied by present participles (causing, being, creating, making) that cannot end the sentence on their own but require an object, alongside two adjectives of disturbance (busy, loud), so the completion shifts from a standing character trait to an ongoing act with something after it.

relations.name: Trait against ongoing act
relations.sentence: Under A the fragment is completed by a single adjective that closes the sentence as a settled character trait (friendly, nice, quiet, polite, cheerful, kind), whereas the words B lifts to the top are present participles (causing, creating, making, being) that cannot finish the sentence and demand a following object naming what the neighbors were doing.

relations.name: Neighborly praise to nuisance
relations.sentence: A's ranking is led by words of warmth and good conduct toward neighbors (friendly, nice, polite, cheerful, pleasant, kind, helpful, smiling), while the words B raises name disturbance or the production of it (loud, busy, and the causing/creating/making that most naturally take trouble or noise as their object).

relations.name: Noise vocabulary resited
relations.sentence: Disturbance words are present under both conditions but sit differently: A carries the quiet/noisy pair as ordinary adjectival description with noisy barely moving between conditions (15 to 18), while B promotes loud and busy into its top six, so the theme is not introduced by B so much as pushed forward and recast as something the neighbors actively produce.

result.kind: trait-adjective versus act-in-progress

residue.description: These are not content completions of the fragment but syntactic hinges that defer the actual word: intensifiers (very, so), an article awaiting a noun, prepositions and a deictic that would open a locative continuation (in, on, at, there), and a participle needing a passive complement (seen), so their fall under B tells us the shape of the continuation changed rather than that any meaning did.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexample is noisy, which is a disturbance word sitting high on the A side at rank 15 and moving only three places, so the valence split in the second relation cannot be clean: A already had the nuisance reading available near the top and B did not have to supply it. It damages the second relation moderately but leaves the first untouched, since noisy is still a trait adjective. Milder counterexamples run the other way: busy is not obviously negative, and causing, creating, making and being are contentless without the object we are not shown, so the negative valence attributed to them in the second relation is inferred from their company rather than read off the words. Quiet on the A side is also awkward, since it belongs to the warmth cluster only by convention and is as much a description of low disturbance as of good character.
result.notes: The grammatical relation is the one I would defend hardest: four of B's six words are present participles, and three of them (causing, creating, making) are near-empty verbs whose whole function is to introduce a following noun, while A's leaders are terminal adjectives. That difference is visible without any interpretation of valence. The second relation depends on guessing what those participles would take as objects, which the data does not show, and noisy's near-immobility argues against reading the shift as a simple positive-to-negative flip. I have deliberately not speculated about probabilities, only positions; note also that several of B's promotions come from deep in A's list (creating 115 to 3), which is a larger structural change than any of A's leaders falling to the fifties and eighties.

residue.description: These are degree words, prepositions and determiners that open a construction rather than complete the fragment with content, so which side they fall on records the grammatical frame each condition is heading into (very/so before an adjective under A, a/the before a noun phrase under B) rather than anything about the neighbors themselves.

result.counterexamples: Three A-side words are participles of exactly the kind relation 1 assigns to B: playing, smiling and laughing. result.reading: The fragment puts three named people into a room, and the two conditions disagree about what kind of scene that is: under A the likely continuations are a raid script performed on someone already there (beat, interrogate, search, question, strip, shoot), while under B they are things the three do among themselves or with the occupants as equals (talk, discuss, play, sit, dance, pray). The single top completion, "talk", is rank 1 in both, so the difference is not about the head of the distribution but about what fills the space just below it.

relations.name: Raid script versus visit
relations.sentence: Under A the three entrants are completed as armed agents running a search-and-detain sequence on someone in the room (beat, interrogate, search, question, attack, strip, undress, shoot, remove), while under B they are completed as people who have simply arrived somewhere and begun an ordinary activity (play, dance, sit, work, pray, talk).

relations.name: Victim implied or absent
relations.sentence: A's words are transitive verbs that require a human patient in the room to be done to, so the completion presupposes someone at the receiving end (beat, interrogate, search, strip, undress, shoot, take, remove, attack), whereas B's words are intransitive or reciprocal and need no such person (sit, dance, play, work, talk, speak, argue, discuss, pray).

relations.name: Interrogation versus conversation
relations.sentence: Speech verbs appear on both sides but in two different modes: A prefers asymmetric speech in which one party extracts or issues (interrogate, question, ask, tell), and B prefers symmetric speech among parties of equal standing (talk, speak, discuss, explain, argue).

result.kind: what role the three entrants are cast in

residue.description: These are light or complement-hungry verbs that carry almost no scene on their own: "set", "get", "do" and "make" only mean something once a particle or object follows, "take" barely moves at all (3 to 4), and "clean" and "look" could belong to either reading depending on what is being cleaned or looked at, so none of them is really a content completion that could support a relation.

result.counterexamples: "argue" is the sharpest one: it sits under B and is conflictual, so it cuts against any reading in which B is simply the peaceable or de-escalated side, though it survives the reciprocity relation because arguing is something parties do with each other rather than to each other. "ask" cuts the other way, sitting under A while being the mildest speech verb on either list; it is only recoverable as A-typed if read as the opening move of questioning rather than as a request. "clean" under A is a genuine oddity that none of the three relations accounts for, since it fits neither the raid script nor the victim-taking pattern. "pray" under B is not a counterexample to the relations but is a different sort of word from the rest of its side: it types the three by identity rather than by activity, which is closer to what A does than the other B words are.
result.notes: The three relations are not independent; they are one difference cut three ways (scene, argument structure, speech mode), and the transitivity relation is the most mechanical statement of it. Two things constrain the reading. First, "talk" is rank 1 under both conditions, so the difference lies entirely in the body of the ranking and not at its head; a summary saying "A completes with violence and B with conversation" would overstate what the top of either list shows. Second, one word is withheld, and because it is a word whose movement ran opposite to its prominence I cannot know whether it would sit against the pattern, so the relations above are stated over an incomplete list. I have not reasoned about how much likelihood any of these movements carries, only about ordering.

Under B the same slot fills with disturbance and scrutiny words (loud, noisy, yelling, arguing, suspicious), with intensifying frames (a, so) that set up a predicate adjective, and with one very large riser, impeccably, which drags the fixed collocation "impeccably dressed" into fifth place from fifty-ninth.

relations.name: Amiable versus abrasive
relations.sentence: Condition A puts the warm-neighbor adjectives (friendly, nice, polite, smiling, kind, pleasant, quiet) at or near the top, while condition B promotes words for noise and friction (loud, noisy, yelling, arguing) together with suspicious, so that the same neighbors are characterized as congenial in one condition and as disruptive or untrustworthy in the other.

relations.name: Grooming cliche imported
relations.sentence: Condition B pulls in a fixed appearance collocation, impeccably rising fifty-four places into the top five and dressed rising twenty-six, whereas condition A's descriptors are bare temperament adjectives (nice, polite, pleasant, kind) with no appearance term anywhere in its list.

relations.name: Whereabouts over character
relations.sentence: Condition A ranks a spread of place and particle continuations high (in, out, up, outside, there, on, at), which would finish the sentence with where the neighbors were or what they were doing, while condition B's rising function words (a, so) are the intensifier and determiner frames that force a characterizing predicate instead.

result.kind: what sort of neighbor the sentence is about to assert: sociable temperament versus conspicuous disturbance and appearance

residue.description: These are determiners and light or aspectual verbs that commit to no content at all (getting did not move, and having, making, trying only open a further complement), so they carry no reading of the neighbors either way.

result.counterexamples: complaining is the worst case: it is a grievance word sitting fifteenth under A, on the side I called amiable, and it belongs by sense with B's arguing and yelling, so the warm-versus-abrasive split is a tendency of the top of each list rather than a clean partition. talking under B is neutral rather than abrasive and only reads as noise by the company it keeps. in and out both sit on the A side while pointing opposite directions on the same axis, which shows the third relation is about the availability of a locative frame, not about any direction within it; if that frame is what matters, the third relation is weaker than its confidence suggests. Nothing contradicts the appearance relation, but it rests on two words.
result.notes: I have taken the two conditions as unlabelled and made no assumption about which is which or which is prior. The two B-side movements are not obviously one thing: the noise cluster and the impeccably-dressed cluster are opposite stereotypes of the same group, one slovenly-disruptive and one over-groomed, and I have kept them as separate relations rather than merging them into a single claim about stereotyping, which the data does not license on its own. result.reading: Under A the slot closes with an adjective naming what the neighbors are like: friendly at rank 1, polite and nice behind it, and the intensifiers very and so ranked high because they anticipate that kind of completion, plus function words and participles that place the neighbors relative to an observer (there, on, at, around, watching, looking, coming, asking, hanging). Under B the slot fills with participles of self-contained activity: up and busy at the top, then talking, working, doing, helping, studying, chatting, playing.

relations.name: Trait against occupation
relations.sentence: A fills the slot with adjectives of ascribed character (friendly, polite, nice) plus the intensifiers such adjectives require, while B fills it with participles naming an ongoing occupation (busy, working, studying, helping, playing, chatting), so the neighbors are characterized under A and shown at work or at play under B.

relations.name: Watched versus self-occupied
relations.sentence: Among participles alone, A favours ones that read the neighbors from an observer's vantage next door (watching, looking, coming, asking, hanging, around, there), while B favours activities that imply nobody watching (working, studying, helping, chatting, laughing, playing, smiling).

relations.name: Standing there, up to something
relations.sentence: A's bare function words build continuations of mere presence (always there, always on the, always at the, always around) while B's build idioms of unspecified action (always up to, always in and out, always going, always getting), a split that rests on words too syntactically light to carry much on their own.

result.kind: ascribed disposition versus depicted activity

residue.description: a is a bare determiner and making, trying, getting and doing are light verbs that need a complement, so none of them completes the fragment with any content of its own; wearing and dressed form a small appearance cluster on the B side that neither the occupation reading nor the observer reading covers; in barely moves at all (rank 2 under both), so it is on the B list without being a B word.

result.counterexamples: The adjective-versus-participle split is not clean: watching, looking, coming, asking, hanging, making and trying are ordinary activity participles sitting on the A side, which is why relation 1 needs relation 2 to absorb them rather than standing alone. Against relation 2, smiling and laughing are pleasant, socially facing words on the B side, so A does not monopolize warmth; and playing (+2) and talking (+2) hardly move, so they are weak members of any B group. Against relation 3, in moves zero places. The strongest single counterexample is the wearing/dressed pair, which is neither a trait nor an occupation and moves a long way (+34, +18).
result.notes: Two words were withheld, so the A side of any relation may be missing members. I have not tried to say which condition is which.

result.reading: Two words dominate the movement: boasting climbs from 93 to 6 and bragging from 84 to 18, by a wide margin the largest shifts in the set, and they arrive alongside telling, saying, talking, shouting, loud and very, so the B side reads as a cluster of verbal self-display. The A side is mostly domestic-nuisance activity plus the grammatical scaffolding that would carry it: fighting, arguing, complaining, up, late, having, playing, and the prepositions and light verbs of "up late", "having a", "at it".

relations.name: Boast words surfacing
relations.sentence: Two words for self-praise that sat near the bottom of A's ranking, boasting at 93 and bragging at 84, move into B's top twenty alongside telling, saying and talking, so B completes the fragment with speech about oneself where A had those options buried.

relations.name: Quarrel versus utterance
relations.sentence: A prefers words naming disturbance conducted as activity in the house next door (fighting, arguing, up, late, playing, having), while B prefers words naming acts of speech and their volume (talking, telling, asking, saying, shouting, loud), so the same nuisance is located in conduct under A and in the mouth under B.

relations.name: Deferred versus named trait
relations.sentence: A's favoured items are largely function words and light verbs that postpone the characterizing term (a, at, in, on, up, having, getting, going, being), whereas B's include the intensifier-plus-adjective route (very, loud) and finished trait verbs (boasting, bragging), so B commits to a description one word earlier than A does.

result.kind: where the noisiness is placed: household conduct versus vocal self-display

residue.description: These are not content completions of the fragment but grammatical scaffolding or maximally generic light verbs whose direction of movement carries no readable meaning on its own: a, in, on, at and being are only the first word of a completion that has not yet been chosen, and coming, leaving, looking, trying and getting could head almost any predicate, with being sitting exactly still at 20 in both conditions.

result.counterexamples: Three words cut against the relations as stated. "complaining" is a speech act and it is firmly on the A side (8 to 23), which directly contradicts the quarrel-versus-utterance split, since A is supposed to be the non-verbal side; that is the worst of the three because complaining is a fairly prominent A word rather than a straggler. "shouting" is the mirror problem, a conflict-and-volume word landing on B (22 to 15), though it is at least also an act of speech and so partly rescued by the first relation. "friendly" on the A side (12 to 24) contradicts any reading of A as the hostile or negative side, and shows that whatever A is doing is not simply imputing conflict. Milder: "late" and "loud" are both noise-nuisance descriptors and they split across the two sides, which is awkward for the deferred-versus-named-trait relation, and "making" on the B side is a light verb of the kind I assigned to A.
result.notes: The reading rests almost entirely on two words. If boasting and bragging are removed, what is left is a modest tilt from activity verbs toward speech verbs that I would not have called a relation at all, and would have reported as medium-to-low. Those two jumps are large enough (87 and 66 places, into positions 6 and 18) that I am willing to call the first relation high, but the whole thing is one fragment, one model, one direction, with ranks only and no likelihoods, so I cannot tell whether boasting arriving at rank 6 is a near-tie with rank 5 or a decisive preference. I have also avoided speculating about why a group-referring subject would draw a self-praise completion under one condition; the measurement shows the shift and does not license a mechanism. The third relation is stated because the function-word asymmetry is visibly there (nearly every bare preposition and article is on the A side), but it may be an artifact of the first two: if B commits to boasting or loud, the tokens that would have introduced a longer completion necessarily fall.

relations.sentence: The largest rises under B are contentless pro-verbs that defer the action to an object never shown (do, get, make, try, handle, act), whereas A's comparable light verbs are ones that head a fixed disciplinary phrase in this frame (take action, put on notice, give a warning, have a word).

relations.name: Contact versus confrontation
relations.sentence: The two communication verbs favoured by A describe neutral contact with her (call, talk), while the two favoured by B describe a one-directional or adversarial approach (confront, send).

result.kind: naming of the act: deed versus procedure

residue.description: Each of these depends entirely on a particle or object that is not shown, so on its own none names an action taken toward the employee, and the two largest movers among them (play +55, change +22) cannot be assigned a reading without inventing the missing continuation.

result.counterexamples: The worst is "fire" itself: it sits at position 1 under both conditions with zero movement, so the bluntest possible naming of the act is equally the likeliest completion either way, which rules out any reading in which B suppresses the punitive outcome rather than its paraphrases. Second worst is "let" (-74, the largest single move in the list), because "let her go" is the softest available euphemism for dismissal and it is A that favours it, directly against a reading of A as blunt and B as sanitized. "investigate" (A, -12) is a lawful procedural step sitting on the side I called deed-naming, and "discipline" (+6) and "confront" (+13) are overtly punitive and adversarial words sitting on the side I called procedural, so relation 1 has a defector in each direction. result.notes: Relations 1 and 3 are close to being one relation sliced twice, and I state relation 3 separately only because it is about who is addressed rather than about how the act is named; if it were repeated I would expect relation 1 to survive and relation 3 not to, which is why it carries low. result.reading: Under A the fragment is completed mostly by verbs of bodily force directed at people or things (beat, attack, hit, shoot, throw, plus the object-handling search, take, remove), while under B the same fragment is completed mostly by verbs of voice and address (argue, yell, shout, scream, talk, speak, ask, cry). The split is not a change of intensity within one kind of act so much as a change of what channel the act happens in, and it is clean enough that the few crossings (chant on the A side, push and tear on the B side) stand out as exceptions rather than as noise.

relations.name: Fist into voice
relations.sentence: A favours completions in which the three men do something with their bodies to a person or object (beat, attack, hit, shoot, throw), while B favours completions in which they produce sound aimed at someone (yell, shout, scream, argue, talk, speak, ask, cry), so the same entrance into the room becomes an outbreak of noise rather than of force.

relations.name: Room versus interlocutor
relations.sentence: The non-violent A words are still directed at the contents of the room (search, take, remove, throw are things done to objects), whereas the corresponding B words are directed at another person as an addressee (argue, talk, ask, speak), so A keeps the room as the target of the action and B substitutes a person being spoken to.

relations.name: Aggressor to distressed
relations.sentence: Where A's leading words cast the three as agents of harm (beat, attack, shoot, hit), two of B's risers cast them as people in distress rather than sources of it (cry and scream, which moved +5 and +3, the two largest gains on the B side), which is a change in who is doing what to whom and not merely in the loudness of the act.

result.kind: channel of the act: bodily force versus voice

residue.description: Both sit at zero movement and belong to neither the force nor the voice grouping: play is a generic low-ranked filler that names no determinate act in this scene, and look is perception rather than an action performed on anyone, so neither tells us anything about the difference between the conditions.

result.counterexamples: Three words cut against the force/voice split, and one of them cuts hard. chant is a vocal act and it sits on the A side, which is the clearest contradiction of relation 1; it is partly recoverable if what A favours is collective and politically coded vocalization rather than force as such, but that is a rescue, not a prediction. push and tear are on the B side and are plainly physical and forceful, so the B list is not purely vocal; tear at least admits a non-violent object reading and push is a small mover (+1), which softens but does not remove the problem. Against relation 3, the two furthest B risers are cry and scream, but scream is equally readable as aggressive shouting, so the distressed-subject reading rests almost entirely on cry alone. A weaker caution against all three: beat, play, talk, speak and look moved zero places, so for those words the position columns supply no evidence at all and their grouping rests entirely on which list they were placed in.
result.notes: The high overall confidence is about relation 1 only; relations 2 and 3 are stated because they are visible in the lists, not because I would argue for them. Two limits worth recording. First, six words were withheld as moving against their prominence, and since the force/voice split is a claim about the completion set rather than about the twenty-one words shown, a withheld set containing violent B-favoured words or vocal A-favoured ones would damage relation 1 without anything in what I was given signalling it. Second, I was shown positions and not likelihoods, and five of the twenty-one words did not move at all, so the ordering within each list, which I was told reflects where the difference rests, is doing work the position columns cannot corroborate: beat is position 1 under both conditions and is nonetheless named as A's leading word. I have taken that ordering at face value because I was instructed to, but relation 1 would look considerably weaker if it were built from the movement column alone.

result.reading: Both conditions read the fragment the same way at the top: attack is rank 1 in both and take is rank 4 in both, so the reshuffling happens in the middle of the list, not at its head. What moves is that A spreads weight across individual utterance (talk, speak, ask, shout, scream, yell) and across options where nothing happens to anyone (sit, leave, play), while B pulls up verbs that take the room and its contents or occupants as an object (search, drag, pull, tear, remove, beat) plus a few collective, patterned vocalizations (chant, sing, laugh, argue).

relations.name: Utterance versus chorus
relations.sentence: The vocal completions split by whether the speaking is individual and unshaped (talk, speak, ask, shout, scream, yell, all falling under B) or collective and patterned (chant, sing, argue, laugh, all rising under B, chant by sixteen places and laugh by twenty-one).

relations.name: Handling the room
relations.sentence: B raises verbs that need the room, its contents or its occupants as an object and describe sustained handling of them (search, drag, pull, tear, remove, beat), whereas A's physical verbs are self-contained bursts or weapon acts that need no room at all (throw, fight, shoot, stab).

relations.name: The uneventful option
relations.sentence: Completions under which nothing is done to anybody (sit, falling twenty-two places, with leave and play) are available under A and give way under B to verbs that presuppose someone or something being acted upon (search, drag, take, remove).

result.kind: acting on the room versus speaking in it

residue.description: move is a near-contentless light verb that fits any continuation and carries no scene of its own; fire is lexically ambiguous between discharging a weapon, setting alight and dismissing someone, so its rise cannot be assigned to either side; throw is incomplete without an object and could belong to a fight or to ransacking a room equally.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is that A holds shoot and stab, the two most lethal and most explicitly weapon-bearing words in either list, while B's rises include laugh and sing. That kills any reading in which B is simply the more violent or hostile condition, and it strains the handling relation too, since shoot and stab are as directed at occupants as beat or drag are. Within the vocal relation, argue and laugh are weak members: neither is choreographed the way chant and sing are, so the collective-patterning gloss holds for two of the four B words and is stretched for the other two. Finally, fight sits under A while attack and beat sit under B, close synonyms distributed across the split, so the difference is not about aggression as a category.
result.notes: The stability of attack at rank 1 and take at rank 4 in both conditions is the main check on this reading: whatever differs, it is not the top of the distribution, and both conditions frame the entrance as an intrusion. I would defend the direction of the split (B toward transitive handling and collective voicing, A toward individual speech and non-events) more than any particular grouping of words within it. One word was withheld, so the list is not the whole difference, and I have not tried to guess what kind of word would move against its own prominence.

result.reading: The fragment invites a management decision about an employee caught talking to a union organizer, and both conditions agree completely on the headline: fire is rank 1 and terminate rank 2 under A and under B alike. What differs sits underneath that shared top, where one side pulls up generic verbs that leave the act unstated until a complement arrives (have, get, make, take, do) together with the two words naming the act as correction or encounter (punish, confront), while the other side pulls up specific employment actions, three of which stop short of expulsion (suspend, transfer, assign, the last moving fourteen places).

relations.name: Deferred act, named act
relations.sentence: Under A the upper ranks fill with light verbs that complete the syntax but not the decision, postponing the actual measure to a complement not shown here (have, get, make, take, do), whereas under B those positions are occupied by verbs that are themselves the measure and need nothing added (fire, terminate, suspend, transfer, assign).

relations.name: Correction versus personnel action
relations.sentence: A carries the only two words that construe the decision as something people do to a person, one as moral correction and one as a face-to-face encounter (punish, confront), while B's words construe it as a change of employment status of the kind an institution records (terminate, suspend, transfer, assign).

relations.name: Alternatives short of expulsion
relations.sentence: The non-dismissal options B raises keep the employee inside the organization and move her within it (suspend up six places, transfer up three, assign up fourteen, the largest movement anywhere in the set), whereas the one word A raises as an alternative to firing is simply another word for firing (discharge).

result.kind: deferred generic act versus named personnel action

residue.description: Call is not a completed action on its own and could head anything from calling her in to calling a lawyer or calling security, so it neither defers to a complement in the way the light verbs do nor names an employment measure, and I cannot place it on either side of any relation I would defend.

result.counterexamples: Three, in rising order of damage. First, give sits on the B side and is a light verb, which cuts against the claim that A owns the unspecified verbs; the damage is mild, since give in this frame most likely heads a specified sanction such as a warning or notice, but that reading is supplied by me and not by the data. Second, discharge sits on the A side and is as formal and administrative a term as terminate, which contradicts the correction-versus-personnel-action relation directly; I read it as the archaic, more juridical register rather than the personnel-file register, but that is a distinction I am imposing, and it is the one word that most weakens relation 2. Third and worst, fire and terminate are ranked 1 and 2 under both conditions and moved zero places, so the two words that would carry any claim that one condition reaches for dismissal and the other does not are identical in position across the conditions. Any reading that says B is harsher, or that A softens the outcome, is refuted on the face of the list: the likeliest completion is the same word in both. Whatever separates the conditions happens below the top two, and since I am shown only order and not likelihood, I cannot tell whether the shared top-two ranking conceals a large difference in weight or a negligible one.
result.notes: The relations are legible but the evidence is thin in ways that should be stated. Only fifteen words are shown, three more were withheld for moving against their prominence, and those three could belong to any of the groups above, so each list may be missing its most awkward member. Positions are all I have; a word moving from 23 to 9 and a word moving from 4 to 17 are not obviously comparable amounts of difference, and the dash case that the instructions call the strongest difference does not occur anywhere here, so nothing entered or left either condition's list. Relations 1 and 2 rest on the same underlying observation seen from two angles (what the A words leave unsaid, and what the two A words that do say something say), and someone could reasonably collapse them into one; I kept them apart because the light verbs and punish/confront differ in kind, the former specifying nothing and the latter specifying a register. Relation 3 has the cleanest arithmetic behind it, all three words moving the same way with the largest single movement in the set, but the smallest semantic footing, since suspend, transfer and assign are three words and assign in particular could be an ordinary work-allocation verb rather than a sanction at all.

result.reading: Both conditions put the same act at the top of the list, with 'fire' at rank 1 and 'terminate' at rank 2 under A and under B alike, so the movement is not about what management decided to do but about how the deciding word is phrased. Under A the ground is held by plain, syntactically incomplete verbs that need something after them (get, make, have, send), while under B it is held by single Latinate words that carry the whole action by themselves (remove, dismiss, terminate, transfer, retaliate).

relations.name: Latinate ejection vocabulary
relations.sentence: B favours formal, personnel-department words for getting rid of an employee, with 'remove' climbing twenty-three places from thirtieth to seventh and 'dismiss' ten places to ninth alongside 'transfer' and 'terminate', while A's side is held by blunt or generic verbs such as 'fire', 'get', 'send' and 'make'.

relations.name: Named act versus deferred act
relations.sentence: The words A loses hardest are all light verbs that cannot complete the sentence on their own and defer the real action to an unstated continuation, with 'have' falling fourteen places, 'make' twelve, 'send' nine and 'get' six, whereas the words B gains name a completed action in a single word.

relations.name: Motive spoken aloud
relations.sentence: B is the only side where a word naming the legal character of the decision rather than its content sits high, 'retaliate' rising six places to fifth, and it sits there beside that same side's softest evasions, 'let' as in let go and 'transfer'.

result.kind: register of the act-word, institutional single-word naming against plain periphrasis

residue.description: Both are listed as favoured by a side yet neither moves at all, holding rank 1 and rank 2 under both conditions, so whatever separates the conditions is not visible in these two words and they cannot be evidence for any relation.

result.counterexamples: Two words cut against the register split. 'discipline' sits on A's side yet is itself a bureaucratic personnel term, exactly the vocabulary I claimed belongs to B; the damage is small because it moves only two places, so it barely carries the difference either way. 'let' sits on B's side yet is the plainest light verb in the whole set and only completes as the idiom 'let go', which belongs with A's 'get' and 'have' rather than with 'dismiss'; against this, 'let go' is itself standard workplace euphemism, so it partly rescues the reading it contradicts. 'transfer' supports the relation in vocabulary but moves only one place, so it adds a name to B's side without adding evidence.
result.notes: The reading rests almost entirely on four large movements (remove +23, have -14, make -12, dismiss +10) and those four point the same way, which is why I am willing to state a relation at all; the remaining eight words move two places or fewer, or not at all, and would not on their own tell me the conditions differed. Because only rank order is shown, I cannot tell whether B's promoted words became likely or merely became less unlikely than the words below them, and 'remove' arriving from rank 30 is the case where that matters most. One word is withheld, and since the withheld word is by definition one whose movement runs against its prominence, its absence could only weaken the account given here, not strengthen it.

result.reading: Both conditions describe the same basic scene, a man touching his own face or hair, with beard, chin, hair and chest at or near the top under each. What changes sits at the fringe of that scene: under B the explicit genital nouns lose ground (dick falls 37 places, penis 10) and the possessive "wife's", which would make another person's body the thing touched, collapses 34 places, while "partner" climbs 28 into the top ten and "wife" edges up one.

relations.name: Genitals down, face steady
relations.sentence: The nouns naming male genitals drop under B (dick from 15 to 52, penis from 8 to 18) while the facial-grooming nouns that dominate both lists hold or improve (beard stays first, chin rises from 4 to 2).

relations.name: Possessed part to named person
relations.sentence: Under A the other person enters as a possessive modifier awaiting a further noun (wife's, rank 9), and under B that construction collapses to rank 43 while the person appears instead as the direct object of the touch, partner leaping from 36 to 8 and wife edging from 7 to 6.

relations.name: Stable grooming core
relations.sentence: The hair-and-face vocabulary barely reorders between the conditions (mustache 11 to 11, head 12 to 12, moustache 13 to 15, hair 2 to 3, chest 3 to 4), so whatever separates A from B operates only on the sexual and relational words at the edges of an otherwise fixed scene.

result.kind: which body part, and whose

residue.description: "own" and "long" are not content completions but modifiers that still require a noun after them, and neither moves (5 to 5, 14 to 10), while neck is an ordinary neutral body part that nonetheless falls nine places, which none of the relations above accounts for.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is cock, which is the most explicit item on the list and barely moves at all (6 to 7), sitting above penis in both conditions; if B were demoting explicit genital nouns as a class it should have fallen furthest, and instead the two words that fall are the clinical penis and the crude dick while the equally crude cock stays put. That is bad enough to keep the first relation at medium rather than high, since the effect then rests on two of three members. Second, neck falls nine places while carrying no sexual or relational content, which shows that appreciable movement is not confined to the words the relations single out and that some of the smaller falls may be reordering rather than signal. Third, wife rises by one while wife's collapses by 34; this is consistent with the second relation but rules out any simpler reading in which references to the man's wife are being pushed down as such.
result.notes: Two of the three relations rest on single large movements (dick at -37, wife's at -34, partner at +28) rather than on a coordinated shift across many words, and most of the list is nearly static, so I am confident that something differs between the conditions and much less confident about which of the two candidate dimensions, anatomical explicitness or grammatical/relational framing, is primary. They may not be separable here: "wife's" is the one item that both introduces another person and implies a further, unstated body part, so its fall could belong to either relation. Two words were withheld for moving against their prominence, and since only sixteen are shown a withheld item could sit anywhere in the ordering, which limits how far any of these groups can be treated as complete. Ranks only, no likelihoods, so I have avoided saying how large any of these shifts are in effect and only how far each word moved relative to the others.
