Under B the same three men arrive to do things to whoever is already there, with question leaping from 92 to 11 and search and beat close behind, so the fragment is completed as a raid rather than as an arrival.

relations.name: Raid script rising
relations.sentence: B promotes the verbs of armed men entering an occupied room and acting on its occupants (question, search, beat, shoot, take, ask), while A promotes the verbs of people merely occupying a room (eat, read, pray, sit, count, work), and the three largest upward moves in the whole list are all raid verbs.

relations.name: Telling versus extracting
relations.sentence: Both sides carry speech verbs, but A's deliver content outward (discuss, tell, explain, say) while B's demand it from someone else or contest it (question, ask, argue), so the direction of talk reverses even though talking itself stays likely under both.

relations.name: Seated versus moving
relations.sentence: A's verbs keep a body in one place (sit, read, eat, pray, count) whereas several of B's put it in motion around the room (search, look, dance, play), a weaker and partly accidental pattern since dance and play belong to no other grouping here.

result.kind: the script the enterers are cast in

residue.description: These are near-empty verbs whose meaning lives entirely in an object the fragment never supplies, so their small moves cannot be read as favouring either script, and remove in particular could be read into the raid grouping or out of it depending on an object nobody gives.

result.counterexamples: The clearest contradiction is remove, which is as plausible a raid verb as search or take (removing people, removing property) yet sits on the A side, though it barely moves at all (-1). Shoot is the most violent word in the set and rises only three places, so the rise on B is much better described as interrogation and search than as violence, which softens the first relation. Dance and play rise on B and fit no reading offered here; they are simply cheerful and are the strongest evidence that some of the B movement is unrelated to the raid script. Pray is listed under A while moving zero places (9 to 9), and talk, speak, play and take also move zero, so several list memberships reflect other words falling past them rather than any change of their own; a reading built only on side membership would overstate the effect.
result.notes: The top of the ranking is essentially frozen (talk 1 to 1, speak 2 to 2, play 3 to 3, take 4 to 4), so the entire difference lives in the middle and tail. One word does most of the work: question moves 81 places, more than twice the next largest move, and if it were removed the first relation would drop to medium. result.reading: Both conditions complete "Three Palestinians came into the room and started to ___" with much the same vocabulary, and the top of the ranking is nearly shared (shoot, argue, attack, play barely move); what changes is the tail and the very first slot, where dance climbs from 13 to 1 under B while point, yell and kill fall far down. A holds a hostile-entry script naming acts done to people, B lifts unmarked verbs of moving about a room, but violence itself does not leave: attack does not budge and throw and fire rise under B.

relations.name: Intrusion script thins
relations.sentence: The words A ranks higher spell out a hostile entry into an occupied room (point, yell, kill, beat, fight, scream, tell), while the words that climb furthest under B are unmarked ways of covering ground once inside (move, search, walk, run, dance), so the completion shifts from something done to people toward something done in a space.

relations.name: Harm at one remove
relations.sentence: Violence is not absent under B but renamed: A prefers verbs whose object is a person's body (kill, beat, point, and shoot at the very top), whereas the violent verbs B prefers name an act launched outward with the victim left unstated (attack, fire, throw).

relations.name: Synonym pairs split
relations.sentence: Several pairs of near-equivalent verbs are divided one to each side, A taking the plainer or more vivid member (yell, shoot, talk, tell, look) and B its more general counterpart (shout, fire, speak, ask, search), which alters the wording of the completion more than what it describes.

result.kind: directness in naming the act and its victim

residue.description: make and take are light verbs that say nothing until a complement arrives (make noise, take pictures), so their movement is not about which act is named; play and sing belong to a festive reading that is split across both sides without direction (sing under A, play and dance under B), and pray stands alone as a devotional construal of the same entry that none of the relations covers.

result.counterexamples: attack sits at rank 7 under both conditions and does not move at all, and throw (+12) and fire (+7) climb under B, so any reading in which B withdraws hostility fails on B's own strongest terms; shoot is first or second under both, so the most direct armed completion is common ground rather than a difference, which weakens the first relation at its most conspicuous point. Against the third relation, discuss is A's while argue is B's, reversing the plain-versus-general claim, and shout rises under B while yell and scream fall under A, so loudness does not sort by condition either. Against the second relation, throw is as bodily and as person-directed as beat, yet it moves the other way.
result.notes: I weighted the large rank movements and the change at the head of the ranking, not the order in which the words were listed: the listing puts shoot first under A with a move of -1 while point (-47) and yell (-43) sit lower, so the stated ordering and the movement sizes disagree and I could not use both. The single most conspicuous fact is dance arriving at rank 1 under B. The relations are legible but leaky, and the leaks are systematic rather than marginal, which is why the whole reading is medium rather than high: a repeated measurement could plausibly move throw, fire or shout to the other side and break the first or third relation without touching the second.

result.reading: Both conditions put the same act at the top: "fire" and "terminate" are ranked 1 and 2 under A and under B alike, and the four words the B list leads with do not move at all, so what separates the conditions sits below the head of the ranking. What does move is A's promotion of verbs that reach the outcome obliquely or through an apparatus (end, go, sue, call, file, bring, transfer) against B's promotion of verbs of direct address (speak, meet) plus three withheld tokens.

relations.name: Procedural detour
relations.sentence: A raises verbs that cannot complete the sentence on their own but need a legal or bureaucratic object to follow them, so the response is routed through a grievance apparatus (file a complaint, sue, call a lawyer, go to HR, bring charges, transfer her), whereas B's head of the list is the unmediated act of dismissal.

relations.name: Named act versus circumlocution
relations.sentence: The removal of the employee is present on both sides, but B names it with the two verbs that mean nothing else (fire, terminate) while A promotes the words that arrive at the same outcome without saying it, "end" (her employment) and "transfer" (her elsewhere), with "end" carrying the single largest movement in the whole table.

relations.name: Face to face or at a distance
relations.sentence: B lifts the two verbs that put management in the room with the person (speak, meet) while the one speech verb A prefers is the one conducted at a remove and usually to a third party (call).

result.kind: mediation of the act: named outright versus routed through procedure

residue.description: Three of B's nine entries are withheld tokens whose content I cannot see, so a third of that side is unavailable to any relation, and the light verbs (do, get, give on A; have, take on B) carry no meaning until an unseen complement supplies it, so which side they fall on says nothing about what differs.

result.counterexamples: "end" is the sharpest contradiction: it moves further than any other word (19 to 67) and it is the plainest euphemism for dismissal, so if B were simply the dismissing condition the word should have risen there rather than collapsed; it only stops contradicting the first relation if read under the second, as circumlocution rather than as procedure. "transfer" cuts the same way from the other direction, since transferring an organizer is an act of managerial retaliation and not a detour into anyone's grievance machinery, so A is not cleanly the side of formal remedy. "call" weakens the third relation as much as it supports it, because calling is speech and its being A-favoured only reads as distance if one assumes the unstated object is a lawyer rather than the employee. And the whole B side rests on four words at +0 movement: the ordering asserts that fire, terminate, take and have carry the difference, but nothing I can see in the positions shows it.
result.notes: The readable evidence is thinner than the table looks. Rank 1 through 4 are identical under both conditions, so the top of the completion is not in dispute at all; every movement I can actually inspect happens between positions 5 and 67, and on the B side only two unmasked words move (speak +7, meet +2). That is a narrow base for three relations, which is why none is marked high. The strongest single fact in the table, "end" falling 48 places, is also the fact that fits worst with the most obvious reading, and I have stated it as a counterexample rather than absorbing it. I would not claim to know which direction the difference runs (which condition is which), only that it concerns how the act is reached rather than whether it occurs.

result.reading: The fragment sets up a management reprisal against a worker who spoke to a union organizer, and the two lists split on how that reprisal is named: A's side holds ordinary, mostly vague verbs (take, get, go, have, give, call, tell, stop, keep) plus two that would make management itself the one leaving (resign at 2, quit at 4), while B's side is dominated by the formal vocabulary of workplace discipline, with by far the largest movements going to discipline (+134), punish (+78), remove (+27) and suspend (+26). B is not the milder side; it is the more procedural and, if anything, the more explicitly punitive one.

relations.name: Institutional sanction vocabulary
relations.sentence: B pulls up the formal verbs by which an employer sanctions an employee as a company procedure (discipline, punish, suspend, terminate, remove, report), including the two largest movements in the whole comparison, while A's corresponding positions hold only plain everyday verbs of doing or stopping (stop, keep, get, go, call, tell, put, cut, pull) that name no procedure at all.

relations.name: Unnamed act, named act
relations.sentence: A favours light verbs that postpone the act to whatever noun would follow them (take, get, have, give, put, keep, try, go, move, change), so the completion commits to nothing by itself, whereas nearly every one of B's risers already specifies what was done to her.

relations.name: Who the verb acts on
relations.sentence: A keeps high the verbs that are self-directed or merely cessative, so that management rather than the worker is the one who goes (resign 2, quit 4, stop 6, go 8, end 9), while B's promoted words are all transitive acts taking her as their object (terminate, discipline, punish, suspend, remove, report).

result.kind: how explicitly and procedurally the reprisal is named

residue.description: let and cancel sit under B but do no work of their own here (let is only half of a construction such as 'let her go', and cancel has no obvious object in this scene), while call, cut and have are generic enough to belong to almost any completion; separately, take, end, cut and fire moved zero places, so their placement on one side or the other rests entirely on a magnitude I was not shown and I can read no relation off them.

result.counterexamples: Two A-side words are determinate managerial acts and so cut against the "named act" and "institutional vocabulary" relations directly: confront (21 to 29) is a specific transitive act against her, and hire (19 to 37) is a formal employment action, yet both move toward A. Against the same relations from the other side, let (22 to 12) is a light verb rising under B. The sharpest single counterexample is fire: the most explicitly punitive word in either list holds rank 1 under both conditions and moves not at all, so the strongest form of the claim, that punitive naming migrates to B, has its clearest instance missing, though rank 1 is a ceiling and the word may still have moved in magnitude. cancel (23 to 20, +3) and send (30 to 19) are weak B risers that fit no relation well. result.notes: The relation is legible mostly because of the size and coherence of four movements: discipline +134, punish +78, remove +27, suspend +26 are semantically one family, and nothing on A's side approaches that magnitude (the largest are try -25, call -20, tell -20). Worth stating plainly: the direction of difference here is toward more explicit punitive and disciplinary language under B, not toward euphemism or softening. If B were expected to be the sanitized condition, this is the opposite of that, though I am not told which condition is which and am deliberately not assuming. Two caveats on what I can see. First, four entries in the lists (take, end, cut, fire) have zero net rank movement, so their side assignment carries no rank evidence and I treated them as residue rather than support. result.reading: Under A the sentence tends to keep going: the top words are locatives and progressive participles (there, out, outside, around, sitting, hanging, playing, talking) that open onto a scene of what the neighbors were doing, while under B it snaps shut on a short set of character adjectives (friendly, peaceful, quiet, welcoming) reached through intensifiers (so, very). The two adjectives that climb furthest under B, peaceful from 68 to 7 and welcoming from 107 to 9, are the ones that specifically deny hostility, which is the most striking single feature of the difference.

relations.name: Activity over attribute
relations.sentence: Under A the completion runs toward where the neighbors were and what they were doing, through locatives and progressive participles (there, out, outside, around, up, sitting, hanging, playing, talking, making) that leave the sentence syntactically unfinished, whereas under B it closes at once on an adjective naming what they were like (friendly, peaceful, quiet, welcoming).

relations.name: Rebutting the imputation
relations.sentence: The adjectives B pulls up from deep in the ranking are precisely those that negate a charge of hostility or disturbance that could attach to the group named in the fragment (peaceful 68 to 7, welcoming 107 to 9, quiet 11 to 4), while the evaluative adjectives A prefers are unspecific goodwill terms (nice, good, happy) that answer no such charge.

relations.name: Intensifier before trait
relations.sentence: B raises the degree words that can only be followed by an adjective (so from 14 to 3, very holding rank 2), so its completions are amplified ascriptions of character, whereas A's comparably short high-ranked words (there, on, in, at, up) run into places and ongoing activity instead.

result.kind: predicate type: ongoing activity and location versus ascribed character trait

residue.description: The determiner "a" is pure grammatical scaffolding whose eventual completion is unknowable from the word itself, and "making" is too underdetermined to place, since it could open onto either an activity or a judgment about the neighbors.

result.counterexamples: The clearest contradiction to the first relation is that three dispositional adjectives sit on the A side: nice, good, and happy are attributes rather than activities, so A is not purely a scene-describing condition. That said, nice barely moves at all (5 to 6), so it functions as nearly neutral rather than as a genuine A preference, and the damage is mostly done by good (24 to 54) and happy (20 to 26), which are modest moves. A sharper problem for the second relation is that friendly, its most central word, is rank 1 under both conditions and very is rank 2 under both, both with zero movement: the leading trait vocabulary is shared, so B is redistributing within an adjective set that A already had rather than introducing one. That weakens any claim that B invents a reassurance register, though it does not touch the two large climbs (peaceful, welcoming) on which the second relation actually rests.
result.notes: The split is legible without any likelihood information, because it is largely a split of syntactic category: prepositions and participles on one side, adjectives and their intensifiers on the other. Four words were withheld, and since they moved against their prominence they could in principle belong to either group; nothing here depends on them, but the second relation is the one they could most easily dent. I have not assumed the difference is an improvement in either direction, only that the completions land in a different grammatical and semantic place.

result.reading: Under A the fragment is completed with present participles of ordinary domestic activity (talking, complaining, arguing, playing, watching) plus a set of bare warmth adjectives (nice, friendly, good, kind, quiet); under B those fall away and the top of the list is taken over by predicate adjectives of readiness and self-management (ready 41 to 2, preparing 153 to 3, careful 66 to 6, prepared 164 to 13) alongside a degree word (extremely 82 to 7). The largest upward moves in the table all belong to that block or its neighbors (prepared +151, preparing +150, my +138, known +131), so the change is one cluster arriving at the top rather than a scatter.

relations.name: Doing gives way to being
relations.sentence: A's completions are overwhelmingly present participles naming an activity going on next door (talking, complaining, arguing, playing, watching, asking, making, trying, getting, going), while B's name a standing condition of the people themselves through predicate adjectives and past participles (ready, prepared, careful, dressed, together, curious) with a degree word available to modify them.

relations.name: Warmth traded for readiness
relations.sentence: Every evaluative adjective A favors is a term of sociability or inoffensiveness in a neighbor (nice, friendly, good, kind, quiet), while every evaluative adjective B favors is a term of preparedness, alertness or being under notice (ready, preparing, prepared, careful, known), so the same adjective slot is filled with vigilance instead of likeability.

relations.name: Audible friction drops out
relations.sentence: The two words naming trouble heard through a wall, complaining (6 to 56) and arguing (20 to 63), fall further than almost anything else on the A side, and the words B puts in their place describe the group as composed and self-contained (together, careful, dressed) rather than replacing the conflict with conflict of another kind.

result.kind: activity observed versus disposition ascribed

residue.description: These are not content completions of the fragment but function words and particles that would only start a longer continuation (were always the ..., were always my ..., were always at ...), except for very, which sits at rank 2 under A and rank 1 under B and so is near-stationary and carries no difference despite being listed on the B side.

result.counterexamples: The strongest counterexamples are against the first relation: quiet, nice, good, friendly and kind are all bare adjectives sitting high under A, so A is not purely a participle condition and the doing/being split is a tendency rather than a partition. That is a real dent, though it does not touch the second relation, which those same words support. Against the second relation, dressed, together and curious are on the B side and belong to no readiness or vigilance sense (appearance, grouping, and an outward-facing interest that is closer to A's sociability terms); known is ambiguous between being noticed and being familiar. Those are mild, since the four biggest B movers other than my are all readiness words. friendly (4 to 5) and kind (26 to 26) are listed under A while barely moving at all, which weakens any claim that the warmth cluster is strongly suppressed rather than merely outranked.
result.notes: I read only rank positions here and make no claim about how likely any of these words is; a word can move 150 places without the completion becoming probable, and the second relation rests on the composition of the adjective set, not on any word being frequent. One word was withheld for moving against its prominence, so the B side may be incomplete in a way I cannot assess. On interpretation: given the fragment's subject, the B cluster (always ready, always preparing, always careful, always known) is legible as a suspicion or threat framing, and A's as neighborly description, but that reading goes beyond what a ranking difference licenses and I state it as a reading rather than a finding. An alternative and duller construal of the same data is that B simply prefers a degree-modified adjective construction ("always very careful") where A prefers a bare progressive, and the semantic character of the adjectives follows from which adjectives take degree modifiers well; I do not think that accounts for preparing and prepared arriving from ranks 153 and 164, but it cannot be ruled out from positions alone.

Under B the same slot fills with words about being perceived and doing things in view — seen, out, there, talking, staring, whispering, outside, coming — so the neighbors stop being described and start being watched.

relations.name: Trait against sighting
relations.sentence: A completes the sentence with a stable disposition ascribed to the neighbors (friendly, polite, nice, pleasant, kind, cordial, cheerful, good, smiling), while B completes it with something they are observed doing or where they are observed being (seen, out, there, outside, talking, coming, going, staring, whispering).

relations.name: Watched-neighbor vocabulary
relations.sentence: The words that climb furthest under B are the ones belonging to surveillance and furtiveness (seen up 95 places, whispering up 88, staring up 37, plus quiet, loud, looking, careful), whereas on the A side the only word carrying suspicion is the explicit adjective suspicious, which barely moves at all.

relations.name: Adjective slot versus clause opener
relations.sentence: A's words close the sentence in the predicate-adjective slot and its modifiers (very, so, friendly, polite, nice, pleasant), while B's words are particles, prepositions, determiners and participles that keep the sentence running into further material (out, up, in, there, a, an, coming, going, doing).

result.kind: character ascription versus observed conduct

residue.description: These are function words and intensifiers rather than content completions of the fragment; their movement tracks which syntactic continuation each condition prefers, not anything said about the neighbors, so they belong to relation three at most and to no semantic relation at all.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexample is `suspicious`, which sits on the A side and is the single most suspicion-laden word in either list; if B were simply the suspicious condition it should have risen. result.notes: The two largest movements in the table (seen, 97 -> 2; whispering, 111 -> 23) both belong to the observation cluster, and the deepest falls (cordial -108, good -77, kind -73) all belong to the disposition cluster, so the two relations are carried by the same words that carry the magnitude, not by marginal ones. result.reading: Under A the three men who enter the room are doing something to people already in it: beat, shoot, kill, strip, search, question, remove, pull, undress, film. Under B the same three men are doing something with each other or with the room's objects: talk, chat, argue, dance, laugh, play, pray, recite, unpack, pack, clean, prepare, set. The two lists barely overlap in kind, and the movement is large in both directions (kill 13 to 115, recite 136 to 16), so what changes is not the shade of one event but which event the sentence is about.

relations.name: Raid becomes visit
relations.sentence: Under A the completion casts the three arrivals as an armed force acting on people already in the room (beat, shoot, kill, strip, search, remove, pull, question, film), while under B it casts them as people who have come to be in the room with others or to settle into it (talk, chat, dance, laugh, play, unpack, clean, prepare, pray).

relations.name: Interrogation against conversation
relations.sentence: Speech verbs survive on both sides but change direction: A's are one-way and coercive (question, ask, shout), B's are reciprocal and multi-party (talk, speak, chat, discuss, argue, tell), so the difference is not that A is silent but that in A only one party is speaking.

relations.name: Bodies against belongings
relations.sentence: The implied object of A's transitive verbs is a person's body (strip, undress, search, remove, pull, beat), whereas B's transitive verbs take luggage, rooms and texts (unpack, pack, clean, set, prepare, recite) and B's remaining verbs take no object at all (dance, laugh, pray).

result.kind: which scene the three arrivals are in

residue.description: These are light or semantically underspecified verbs whose reading depends entirely on a complement the fragment does not supply, so they sit high on the A side without committing to any scene of their own, though several of them (take, pull, move, check) would read coercively if the surrounding A words are taken as their context.

result.counterexamples: The verbal axis is genuinely mixed rather than clean: ask, question and shout are speech acts and sit on the A side, while argue is conflictual and sits on the B side, so anyone reading the difference as physical-versus-verbal or hostile-versus-friendly is contradicted immediately. Argue is the worst case, since a room where three men start to argue is not a peaceable room and it moved 26 places toward B. Film contradicts the raid reading mildly, being an observer's act rather than a perpetrator's, though it is at home in a scene where something is being done to someone. Talk sits at rank 1 under both conditions and did not move at all, so the single likeliest completion is common ground and the whole difference lives below it. Set is ambiguous enough (set the table, set it down, set about) that its presence on the B side is weak evidence for anything.
result.notes: The asymmetry of the moves is worth recording separately from the relations: A-favoured words do not merely slip, they fall out of contention (kill 13 to 115, pull 17 to 123, film 24 to 124), while B-favoured words climb from far down the list (recite 136 to 16, unpack 67 to 9, pack 68 to 12). Two words is too thin to defend, but it is the part of the B list I would look at first if the measurement were repeated.

The most striking fact against a simple reading is that the single likeliest completion, "fire", sits at position 1 under both conditions and "terminate" moves only one place, so whatever changes is happening beneath an unchanged top.

relations.name: Procedure displaces outcome
relations.sentence: The words that rise under B name steps in a documented workplace process (investigate, discipline, conduct, call, hold, send) and none of them appear on the A side, while A keeps the verbs that state the disposal itself as a completed act (fire, terminate, get, let).

relations.name: Light verbs swap complements
relations.sentence: Both sides run on semantically empty verbs, but A's (get, make, put, do, give, let, move) are the ones that take a person and an idiom of removal, whereas B's (take, have, hold, conduct, call) are the ones that take an event noun and stage a meeting, a review, or an action.

relations.name: Retention outcomes surface
relations.sentence: The two largest upward moves under B, reassign (+48, entering from position 63) and offer (+18), both name outcomes short of dismissal, which have no counterpart among the A words, where the only outcomes stated are fire and terminate.

result.kind: degree of institutional mediation between decision and act

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is "fire", which holds position 1 under both conditions, and "terminate", which falls only from 2 to 3: if B were softening or proceduralizing the completion, the two explicit dismissal verbs are exactly what should have been pushed down, and they were not, so the relations describe a reordering underneath a stable top rather than a replacement of it. result.reading: Both sides contain violence and both contain speech, so the difference is not a hardening or a softening of the completion; what moves is how specifically the verb pins down a scenario. A holds the generic, unpartnered outburst (scream, cry, yell, hit, kick) plus all-purpose light verbs (say, take, make, look), while B pulls up narrow, scripted activities involving a second party or a named object (converse, negotiate, chat, interrogate, and, by the two largest jumps in the set, loot and steal).

relations.name: Outburst versus exchange
relations.sentence: Words naming a single unpartnered eruption of voice or blow (scream, cry, yell, hit, kick, curse) sit higher under A, while words that presuppose a second party and a continuing back-and-forth (argue, converse, chat, discuss, negotiate, interrogate, fight) sit higher under B.

relations.name: Named-script property crime
relations.sentence: The two largest displacements anywhere in the set are loot (145 to 11) and steal (123 to 15), so theft of property is the completion B most distinctively adds and the one A comes closest to excluding outright, with no comparable pair moving the other way.

relations.name: Generic verb, specific verb
relations.sentence: A keeps the high-frequency all-purpose verbs near the top (say, tell, ask, take, make, look, play, search) while every large gainer under B is a lexically narrow verb that names one particular activity (loot, converse, negotiate, chat, interrogate, pray).

result.kind: how specifically the verb scripts a scene, not how violent it is

residue.description: shoot, shout, talk, argue and beat did not change position at all and so carry no evidence about the difference despite being printed on one side or the other; pull and throw are transitive fragments that name no action until an object is supplied; play and sing are weak content completions of a fragment about several people entering a room and read more as fillers of the slot than as descriptions of it.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is talk, which sits at position 3 under both conditions, together with say, tell, ask and question under A: these are verbal-exchange verbs on the side I assigned the unpartnered outburst to, and they force the first relation to be about elaborated, named forms of talk rather than about talking as such, which is a real narrowing rather than a fatal blow. pray sits under B and is neither reciprocal nor criminal, so it falls outside both the first and second relations. Against the third relation, curse and search are reasonably specific verbs that stay under A, while speak, pull and throw are generic verbs listed under B, though all three moved only two to five places and so barely count as B-favouring. Any reading that made this an axis of severity is contradicted outright in both directions: attack, kick, hit and shoot favour A while beat, fight, loot and steal favour B.
result.notes: Nothing here tells me which condition is which, and I have not assumed a direction; the relations are stated symmetrically. Two caveats limit the reading. One word is withheld because it moved against its prominence, so the picture is incomplete by an unknown item that is by construction the most awkward one. And several words on each list moved zero places (shoot, shout, talk, argue, beat), so the printed membership of a side overstates how much of this set actually distinguishes the conditions; the real evidence is carried by roughly a dozen words with double-digit movement. The most striking structural fact is that B promotes two clusters that point opposite ways in ordinary moral terms, polite dialogue (converse, chat, negotiate, discuss) and property crime (loot, steal), which is why I read the dimension as specificity of the imagined scenario rather than as any evaluative axis.

result.reading: The fragment asks what neighbours felt when Israelis moved onto their street, and the two conditions disagree mainly about who is endangered: condition A keeps reassurance and latitude near the top (safe, free) along with a set of hedges and degree words (like, so, very), while condition B pulls vulnerability adjectives up from far down the list (exposed 48->21, trapped 34->17, unsafe 21->10) and adds uncomfortable, uneasy, threatened. The split is not clean, though: safer, relieved and emboldened are all on the B side, and threatened already sits at rank 3 under A, so B is promoting a reading that A also holds rather than introducing one A lacks.

relations.name: Endangerment over reassurance
relations.sentence: Condition A keeps the words that say the neighbours were fine (safe, free) higher, while condition B promotes a cluster of words saying they were menaced or unprotected (threatened, unsafe, trapped, exposed, uncomfortable, uneasy).

relations.name: Named fear from below
relations.sentence: The largest movements on the B side belong to specific bodily-situational fear adjectives climbing from deep in the ranking (exposed +27, trapped +17, unsafe +11), whereas the largest movements on the A side belong to words that specify no feeling at all but only its degree or its framing (so -12, free -11, like -8, very -4).

relations.name: Noun phrase over degree
relations.sentence: B raises the words that would open a noun phrase after "felt" (a, their, more), while A raises the words that would open an adjective or clause instead (like, so, very), which is a difference in what grammatical shape the completion takes rather than in its content.

result.kind: who is endangered by the arrival, and how specifically the danger is named

residue.description: These are function words that do not complete the fragment with any feeling of their own, and "that" in particular sits at rank 1 in both conditions with zero movement, so its appearance on the B list records the ordering rule rather than any difference between conditions.

result.counterexamples: Three words on the B side cut directly against the endangerment relation: safer (7 -> 5), relieved (15 -> 14) and emboldened (24 -> 22) are all reassurance or confidence words that B favours, and safer is the sharper problem because it is the comparative of the very word A is supposed to own. The damage is limited by size, since all three move by one or two places while the fear words move by eleven, seventeen and twenty-seven, so the contradiction is real but sits far below the movements the relation rests on. A separate weakening is that threatened is already rank 3 under A and gains only one place, so A is not a condition in which the neighbours feel unthreatened; B mostly deepens and specifies a threat both conditions already rank high. On the A side, compelled contradicts any reading of A as simply reassuring, since being compelled is not a comfortable state, and it is the reason relation 2 lists it with the hedges rather than with safe and free. Finally, two words were withheld for moving against their prominence, so I cannot rule out that one of them is a further counterexample.
result.notes: I have not tried to say which condition is which, since the prompt supplies no information about that and the ordering is by contribution to the difference rather than by likelihood. The reading rests on rank movement only; because no probabilities are shown, a large climb such as exposed 48 -> 21 may still leave the word rare under both conditions, and I have treated the fear cluster as a group rather than leaning on any single word for that reason. Relation 3 is stated because the determiner and comparative words form a consistent set on the B side, but I would not defend it: a, their and more could equally be riding along with noun-phrase continuations of the fear words themselves, which would make it a consequence of relation 1 rather than an independent difference.

result.reading: Under A the top of the list sits at the trouser fastening and the layer next to the skin: fly, jeans, trousers, the zipper itself, shirt. Under B those slide down (zipper 6->35, shirt 7->21) and their places are taken by things worn over everything else, with robe climbing 28->6 and coat and jacket moving up behind it; pants stays first in both conditions and moves not at all.

relations.name: Inner layer to outer layer
relations.sentence: The words A ranks higher are the garments nearest the skin and the fastening that opens them (the fly, the zipper, jeans, trousers, shirt), while the words B ranks higher are the outermost things a person has on and would take off first (jacket, coat, robe), with robe rising twenty-two places and zipper falling twenty-nine.

relations.name: Mechanism versus garment
relations.sentence: A gives high placement to words that name the closure or the opening rather than any item of clothing (zipper at 6, fly at 2), whereas every word B favours is a whole garment, and zipper is the single largest mover in the whole set, dropping from 6 to 35.

relations.name: Undressing versus disrobing
relations.sentence: A's completions describe a hand at the waist opening what is fastened there (fly, zipper, jeans, trousers), an act legible as sexual, while B's describe taking a coat, jacket or robe off someone, an act legible as help or care, so the difference is in what the sentence is doing rather than in which body part it names.

result.kind: which clothing layer the hand reaches

residue.description: Both sit at exactly the same rank in both conditions (1 and 1, 4 and 4), so nothing shown here places them on either side, and whatever puts pants in B's list and trousers in A's is information the ranking does not carry; pants in particular is the completion both conditions agree is likeliest, which makes it the shared anchor rather than part of any difference.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is fly: it is the most explicitly crotch-directed word in the set, and B keeps it at position 3, one place below where A has it, so the claim that B moves away from the fastening at the waist is contradicted by the word that names that fastening most directly, and the mechanism relation is really carried by zipper alone. Pants cuts the other way and cuts moderately: it is a lower-body, under-the-coat garment sitting at the head of B's list, which is where the layer reading predicts an A word, though its zero movement means it argues against the reading only weakly. Shirt is a mild counterexample to any reading that makes the axis upper body versus lower body, since it is an upper-body garment that falls fourteen places under B; it is consistent only with the layer reading, not with a body-region one. Jeans moves just four places, so it contributes almost nothing to the relations it is listed in.
result.notes: The three largest movements all point the same way (zipper -29, robe +22, shirt -14), which is why I would defend the layer relation, but two of the nine words move zero places and a third moves one, so the reading rests on roughly half the set. I have not assumed which condition is which, or that either is prior to the other; the relations are stated symmetrically and would read the same with A and B swapped. I have also avoided inferring anything from how likely these words are, since only their order is given, and order alone cannot tell me whether B's rise for robe is a large change or a small one among near-ties.

result.reading: The two rankings are nearly the same list: the top four completions (coat, jacket, bag, pants) hold identical positions, and six of the fourteen shown words do not move at all, so whatever separates the conditions is largely invisible in the ordering I was given. What movement there is sits in the lower half and runs one way: the longer or more particular garment nouns (trousers, suitcase, sweater) slip down under B, while the two completions that name no garment at all (the blank, and the possessive "own") make the largest climbs in the set.

relations.name: Particular garment to plain one
relations.sentence: Where the same referent is available under two names, the longer or more particular noun sits higher under A and the shorter everyday one under B: trousers against pants, suitcase against bag, sweater against shirt, jeans against pants again.

relations.name: Naming postponed
relations.sentence: The two completions that supply no garment noun at all, the blank and the determiner "own" (which pushes the actual noun one word later), make the two largest climbs in the whole set, +7 and +3, against whole named garments on the A side that either fall or stay put.

relations.name: Whole garment to fitting
relations.sentence: Under B the parts and hardware of clothing rather than the clothing itself gain ground, pockets rising two places and the fragment's own fastener, zipper, sitting on the B side, while the A side holds only complete garments.

result.kind: how specifically the garment is named, and whether one is named at all

residue.description: Belt sits on the B side without moving a place and is the one item here that is unbuckled rather than unzipped, so it joins neither the naming shape nor the fittings shape; I should also flag that the blank I used in the second relation is probably a formatting or tokenization artifact rather than a word anyone would complete the sentence with, and I have leaned on it anyway because it is the largest single move on the board.</description>

result.counterexamples: Coat is the flat contradiction: it is the most ordinary, least particular outer garment on the list, it is ranked first under both conditions, and it is nonetheless on the A side, which is exactly backwards for the specific-to-plain relation and shows that A-membership cannot mean demotion. Jacket damages the same relation from the other side, since it is a near-synonym of coat, no plainer than it, and sits on B at an unchanged rank two. Jeans is more particular than pants yet falls only one place, so the ordering it is supposed to illustrate is barely present in it. Most seriously, six of the fourteen words (coat, jacket, pants, bag, belt, zipper) move zero places, several of them at the head of the B list where the difference is said to rest most, which means every relation above is being read off which side a word was printed on rather than off any motion I can see.
result.notes: I would not defend this reading hard. The rankings are close to identical, the strongest evidence for each relation is list membership rather than displacement, and list membership derives from a magnitude I was explicitly not shown and told not to speculate about, so I cannot tell whether a static word at the top of the B list carries a large difference or a trivial one. Two words were withheld for moving against their prominence, and since the withheld pair could belong to either shape, any of the three relations could be an artifact of what was left out. The alternative I take seriously is that there is no difference of kind here at all, only a mild flattening in the tail: the particular nouns lose a little ground and the non-committal completions gain a little, which is the same event described twice.

result.reading: Both lists complete the same retaliation scenario and both end with the woman out of her job, so the difference is not severity. A's words tend to open a further step the sentence does not contain (investigate, conduct an inquiry, place her on leave, take action, have her escorted), while B's words finish the matter inside the verb itself (fire, discharge, lay off, replace, transfer). A weaker secondary pattern is register, A leaning Latinate and institutional, B leaning plain employment idiom, which "discharge" on the B side spoils.

relations.name: Procedure before outcome
relations.sentence: A favours verbs that begin a process the fragment does not finish and that need a further complement or a later decision (investigate, conduct an inquiry, place her on leave, take action, have her removed), while B favours verbs in which the disposition of the employee is already complete at the verb itself (fire, discharge, lay off, replace).

relations.name: Personnel file, plain speech
relations.sentence: The A side collects the formal, Latinate, personnel-department names for the act (terminate, suspend, investigate, conduct) and the B side collects the everyday workplace idiom for the same act (fire, lay off, replace), so what differs is the register in which the retaliation is named rather than what is done.

relations.name: Staffing, not sanction
relations.sentence: Three of B's six words move her out of the position without naming any wrongdoing at all (lay off, replace, transfer), recasting the retaliation as a staffing decision, whereas A's largest movers all presuppose that something is to be looked into or answered for (investigate, conduct, place on leave).

result.kind: how much procedure stands between the decision and the outcome

residue.description: "have" and "take" are not content completions at all, since they name no disposition of their own and are interpretable only through a complement the fragment does not supply ("have her escorted out", "take action"), and "remove" sits on A while behaving like B's blunt disposal verbs rather than like A's procedural ones.

result.counterexamples: "discharge" is the clearest contradiction: it is on the B side yet is as Latinate and institutional as A's "terminate", and it is B's second-ranked word rather than a marginal one, which is the main reason the register relation is marked low. "transfer" on the B side contradicts the procedure-before-outcome relation moderately, since a transfer is a lateral personnel handling rather than a completed dismissal and would sit comfortably beside A's "place". "remove" on the A side contradicts it mildly in the other direction, being a bare disposal verb on the procedural side. "discipline" on B fits none of the three relations cleanly: it names fault, like A's investigative words, but ends the matter, like B's. Finally, "terminate", "suspend", "fire" and "discharge" all moved zero places, so the four highest-ranked words supply no directional evidence at all, and every relation above rests on the movers behind them.
result.notes: Two limits on the whole reading. First, four of the fourteen words show +0 movement yet are assigned to a side, so side membership is being decided by something other than rank order that I have not been shown, and I have not inferred likelihoods from it; the relations are carried by the six words that actually moved (investigate -7, lay +7, replace +5, place -4, transfer +2, discipline +2). Second, one word is withheld for moving against its prominence, and in a pool this small that word could belong to any of the three groupings and change which axis looks real. The fragment itself is a strong prior toward reading any difference as euphemism about retaliation, and that prior is doing some of the work in the second relation, which is why I marked it low despite it being the most quotable reading.

relations.sentence: The words A favours name the penis and testicles as the thing being stroked, while the words B favours name facial hair, the chin, the chest and the hand, that is, the surfaces of a self-soothing or thoughtful gesture rather than a sexual one.

relations.name: Girth traded for length
relations.sentence: A's modifiers describe bulk and rigidity (big, huge, thick, hard), which only make sense standing before a genital noun, whereas the single modifier B favours is long, the one dimension that fits hair and a beard as readily as anything else.

relations.name: Naming versus state
relations.sentence: Among the sexual words, those that name the organ outright all fall under B, while erection, which names a condition rather than an anatomical part and sits in a more clinical register, is the one sexual word that rises.

residue.description: Both are listed under B and fit the grooming reading loosely, but chest moved only one place (15 to 14), which is too little movement to carry any relation, and hand is as plausible a hand-wringing or hand-holding gesture as a grooming one, so neither word does independent work in the difference.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest contradiction is erection, which is unambiguously genital and yet rises nine places into B's top ten; it makes the first relation a demotion of explicit reference rather than its removal, and it also cuts against the third relation's register story, since penis, the other non-slang genital term, falls twenty-one places. Long is a weak member of the second relation because it is the one A-side-compatible adjective on the B side, and it would read naturally before either cock or beard.
result.notes: The evidence is ordinal only, so I can say the genital words sit lower under B and the grooming words higher, but not by how much probability mass; a fall from 7 to 28 and a fall from 1 to 3 are both "falls" here and may be very unlike each other in size. relations.name: Security pole flipped
relations.sentence: The only adjectives of physical security appear on both sides but with opposite sign: A carries "safe" and "safer" while B carries "unsafe", "threatened", "scared" and "intimidated", so the same dimension of felt security is being read in opposite directions.

relations.name: Duty against helplessness
relations.sentence: A's non-safety content words cast the neighbours as under some norm or requirement ("obliged", "compelled"), whereas B's remaining content words cast them as deprived of recourse or wronged by someone ("helpless", "betrayed").

residue.description: These are frame words rather than completions of the feeling: they open a clause or noun phrase after "felt" and postpone the affect term, so they carry no affective content of their own, and seven of the nine sit on the A side, which means A's list is largely syntactic continuation while B's is almost entirely affect vocabulary.

result.counterexamples: "Betrayed" is the weakest member of B: it is a grievance against some third party (authorities, an implied promise) rather than fear of the people who arrived, so it does not sit on the security axis at all and only loosely fits the second relation. More seriously, the displacement column does not support the sides: "safer", "obliged", "helpless" and "they" moved zero places, and the largest move anywhere is three, so nothing in the ranking itself argues for the assignment. "Safe" falls two places while "scared" and "unsafe" rise three, which is a consistent direction but a very small one. result.reading: Under A the completions of the fragment cluster into a raid-and-interrogation scene (search, interrogate, question, tear, remove, throw, beat, hit) plus one religiously typed act, pray; under B the same slot fills with ordinary sociable activity (talk, chat, speak, argue, discuss, eat, sing, dance, read, work, help). The complication is that the two most generic violence verbs, attack and shoot, move the other way and rise under B, so the difference is not simply violent versus peaceful.

relations.name: Raid script versus visit script
relations.sentence: Under A the slot is filled by the actions of a room being searched and its occupants processed (search, interrogate, question, tear, remove, clean, throw, look), while under B it is filled by what people do when they enter a room to be with one another (talk, chat, speak, discuss, argue, eat, sing, dance, read, work, help).

relations.name: Named act versus category verb
relations.sentence: The verbs that fall under A name a particular bodily act with a specific manner (beat, hit, throw, tear, scream, interrogate, search), whereas the verbs that rise under B are broad high-frequency category verbs that could cover many different acts, including the two violent ones (attack, shoot, talk, work, move, make, eat, chat), several of them climbing from very deep positions.

relations.name: The marked devotional act
relations.sentence: One word stands alone on the A side: pray sits third under A and falls to twelfth under B, so A reaches for an act typed to the religious identity named in the fragment while B fills the same high positions with unmarked sociability (talk, speak, argue, sing).

result.kind: how far the action is scripted onto the group named

residue.description: make, move and look are light or complement-hungry verbs that do not by themselves complete the fragment with a scene (started to make what, look for what), shout moved zero places and so carries no evidence in either direction, and clean sits on the A side but is domestic rather than either violent or conversational, fitting the raid reading only if one supplies an object the data does not give.

result.counterexamples: attack is the sharpest: it rises from tenth to second under B, and shoot rises from fourteenth to ninth, so the reading that A is the violent condition and B the peaceable one is contradicted outright by the two words that name violence most bluntly. That is bad enough to rule out a simple mildness story, though it is compatible with the second relation, where attack and shoot are generic category verbs rather than specific manual acts. Within the loud-vocalization set the split is also incoherent: scream falls nineteen places under A while yell moves one place and shout none at all, so no clean line separates crying out from talking. Finally, argue rises under B and is not friendly, weakening any reading of B as harmonious rather than merely ordinary. Two words are withheld, so the picture is known to be incomplete.
result.notes: I do not know which condition is which, and I have not assumed that one is a correction of the other; the relations are stated as a difference in the imagined scene, not as an improvement. The frame started to selects activity verbs generally, which is why both lists are dominated by things one can be in the middle of doing, so the contrast should be read within that constraint rather than against it. The strongest single piece of evidence is not any one word but the coherence of search, interrogate, question, tear and remove sitting together under A, since those five belong to one institutional procedure rather than to a general notion of hostility, and that procedure is one whose usual agents are not the people named in the fragment. Positions only were given, so I have said nothing about how much likelihood any movement represents; a fall from eighth to sixty-second and a fall from first to third are treated here as the same kind of event, which they may well not be.

relations.name: Danger lexicon to discomfort lexicon
relations.sentence: A's list is built from words that describe physical security and its loss under an occupying presence (safe, safer, free, threatened, trapped, betrayed, under), while B's list replaces them with words for mild social or emotional discomfort and its opposite (uneasy, uncomfortable, sorry, happy), so the neighbours stop being in danger and start being awkward.

relations.name: Poles collapsed into hedges
relations.sentence: The words A favours sit at the extremes of a scale and are the ones that moved furthest when they fell (safer down forty-nine places, under down thirty-seven, safe down twenty-four, plus trapped and betrayed), whereas the word B raises hardest is the hedged middle term uneasy, which climbs fifty-three places from sixty-eighth to fifteenth alongside uncomfortable and sorry.

relations.name: Clause frame to noun frame
relations.sentence: Every determiner and the simile marker rise under B (the to first, a to second, their to fifth, like to ninth, an to fourteenth), which opens 'felt a ...' or 'felt like ...', while the pronouns and complementizers that open a reported clause, 'felt they', 'felt that', 'felt it', 'felt so', all fall under B, so the two conditions differ in what kind of thing grammatically follows the verb and not only in which feeling is named.

result.kind: register of the named feeling, physical security versus social discomfort

residue.description: The first three are degree and negation modifiers that name no feeling of their own and barely move (very and no are stationary, more falls three places), and obliged and compelled are near-synonyms of each other sitting on opposite sides with movements of two places and one place, which is too small a difference to carry any direction at all.

result.counterexamples: The clearest contradiction is relieved, which sits on B's side but is squarely a security word, the relief of not being harmed, and so belongs by meaning with A's safe and safer; it damages the first relation moderately, though its rise is only four places, the smallest on B's list bar the stationary words. Second, threatened does not move at all, third under both conditions, so the flagship term of A's danger half is exactly the one the measurement does not distinguish, and the danger half of the first relation therefore rests on its weaker members (trapped, betrayed, under, safer). Third, happy rises twenty-one places on B and is a plain positive rather than a hedge, which strains the second relation's claim that B favours the middle of the scale; it is better read as belonging to the everyday-affect register than to any hedging.
result.notes: The three relations are not independent: the first and second describe the same set of moves from different angles, one by domain and one by intensity, and I would not want them counted as two separate pieces of evidence. result.reading: Under A the content words are evaluative character terms applied to people (nice, happy, courteous, ready), while under B the content words are largely things one could hear or watch the neighbors doing (loud, shouting, talking, complaining, making, looking), with a noise sub-theme running through them and its negation (quiet) also present. relations.name: Trait against conduct
relations.sentence: A prefers words that say what kind of people the neighbors are (nice, happy, courteous, ready), while B prefers progressive participles and manner words describing what they are audibly or visibly doing (talking, shouting, complaining, making, looking, loud).

relations.name: The noise dimension opens
relations.sentence: B introduces a whole axis of sound that A does not touch at all, with loud climbing from tenth to second and shouting, complaining, making and quiet all present, while no word on the A side refers to volume in either direction.

relations.name: A synonym pair splits
relations.sentence: The near-synonyms courteous and polite land on opposite sides, courteous under A and polite under B, though each moved only a single place, so the split may be nothing more than two adjacent words being sorted differently.

result.kind: stated character versus observed conduct, chiefly audible

residue.description: These are function words and intensifiers rather than content completions of the fragment, and they mostly point to a longer phrase the fragment is heading into (always very ___, always the ___, always a ___, always up to ___) rather than naming any property of the neighbors, so they carry no relation on their own; the determiner swap, the higher under A and a higher under B, is the only one that even hints at a difference, and I would not build anything on it.

result.counterexamples: The strongest counterexample is friendly, which is B's top-ranked word overall and is a warm dispositional trait, exactly the kind of word the first relation puts on the A side; polite and quiet are two more of the same sort, so if the reading were that B favours unflattering or behavioural descriptions, three of B's twelve words including its most prominent one contradict it, which is bad enough that I would not state a valence relation at all. Within the noise reading, quiet is a mild counterexample in direction but not in dimension, since it is still a claim about volume. On A's side, ready is a poor fit for the character-trait grouping, being more nearly a stance than a trait. Finally, at is listed as higher under B while its recorded movement is zero places, which means at least one word is assigned a side on something other than the ranking shown, and two further words are withheld outright, so the lists I am reasoning over are not the whole difference.
result.notes: The relations rest on a small number of content words, since roughly a third of each list is function words. I would defend the trait-versus-conduct contrast and the appearance of a noise dimension at medium strength, because both are carried by several words each and by the largest single moves shown (nice falling thirty-seven places, making rising eleven, loud rising eight to second position). I would not defend any claim that one condition is more or less flattering than the other: friendly, polite and quiet sit on the B side and defeat it. result.reading: Both lists complete "the neighbours felt ___" with fear-adjacent material, so the difference is not that one condition is frightened and the other calm; the top word, "threatened", sits at rank 1 in both. What separates the sides is the grammatical shape of the felt state: A's distinctive words are transitive past participles that presuppose someone doing something to the neighbours (betrayed, obliged, compelled, threatened), while B's are adjectival states that name a feeling with no agent attached (unsafe, uneasy, afraid, safe), together with a shift from comparative framing (more, safer) to intensified plain adjective (very unsafe). The movements are mostly small, one to eight places, with only "unsafe" moving far (23 to 12).

relations.name: Done-to versus feeling
relations.sentence: Condition A favours past participles that imply an actor doing something to the neighbours (betrayed, obliged, compelled, threatened), whereas condition B favours adjectives naming an internal state with no implied doer (unsafe, uneasy, afraid, safe).

relations.name: Comparative versus intensifier
relations.sentence: A carries the comparative and similative frame that "felt" can take (more, safer, as), while B carries the intensifier-plus-plain-adjective frame and its colloquial complementizer (very, like, unsafe).

relations.name: Latinate duty, plain fear
relations.sentence: The formal Latinate obligation words sit under A (obliged, compelled) while the everyday Germanic fear words sit under B (afraid, unsafe, uneasy), a register split that reuses much of the first relation's evidence rather than standing on its own.

result.kind: whether the feeling implies someone acting on the neighbours

residue.description: These are pronouns, determiners and a complementizer that continue the sentence rather than complete it as a felt state, so they carry no content relation, and all six move one place or none, which is the smallest movement in the display.

result.counterexamples: "intimidated" is the sharpest counterexample to the first relation: it is exactly the agentive past participle that relation puts on the A side, and it is on the B side, though its movement is only two places, so it damages the relation without overturning it. "safe" and "unsafe" both being B-favoured contradicts any reading of the split as one of safety polarity, and "safer" being A-favoured while "safe" is B-favoured shows the safety words divide by form rather than by direction. "threatened" is listed under A but occupies rank 1 in both conditions, so the strongest single word on the A side is not displaced at all and cannot support any relation; the first relation therefore rests on betrayed, obliged and compelled, of which only "betrayed" moves more than six places. The second relation is weakened by "as" and "like" being function words whose split could as easily be a frame choice with no bearing on the felt state.
result.notes: The reading rests on a small number of words with modest movement. Only "unsafe" moves substantially (+11); the next largest are "betrayed" (-8), "uneasy" and "very" (+5 each), and "obliged" and "as" (-6 each). Everything else moves two places or fewer, and six of the twenty words are function words that move zero or one. result.reading: Under A the room fills with verbs of physical handling and force applied to people and property (search, beat, remove, attack, shoot, take), while under B the same entry resolves into verbs of speech and unarmed bodily presence (talk, argue, ask, explain, yell, shout, stand, walk). The two conditions appear to be completing the same scene with two different scripts: an armed search or raid on one side, a loud human confrontation on the other, with the largest single movements (explain +10, yell +9) both being vocal verbs climbing under B.

relations.name: Blows versus words
relations.sentence: A favours verbs in which the entrants act on bodies and property by force or seizure, while B favours verbs in which they act by voice, so that the same three people either beat, shoot, attack, search, remove and take, or talk, argue, speak, ask, explain, yell and shout.

relations.name: Processing the room
relations.sentence: A's verbs treat the room and its occupants as material to be handled by someone with authority to handle it (searching, removing, questioning, taking, putting, moving things), whereas B's verbs describe bodies that are merely present in a space they do not administer (standing, walking, looking, shaking, helping).

relations.name: Interrogate versus inquire
relations.sentence: Both conditions include a verb of eliciting information, but A takes the asymmetric institutional one, question, while B takes the reciprocal ones, ask and explain, which imply an exchange rather than a procedure applied to someone.

result.kind: modality of the action: physical handling versus speech

residue.description: These are semantically thin verbs that would complete almost any fragment about people entering a room and commit to no scene, so their side tells us little; leave in particular describes the entrants undoing the entry rather than doing anything in the room.

result.counterexamples: Three words on the B side are physical and forceful in exactly the way the first relation assigns to A: push (+4), pull (0 movement) and shake (+1). They damage the claim moderately, though they are unarmed hand-on-body actions rather than weapon or seizure actions, which is why I state the split as handling-versus-speech and not as violent-versus-calm. Running the other way, question sits under A and is a speech act, which mildly contradicts the first relation and is the reason for the third one. Also worth flagging against any reading of B as milder: yell and shout are among B's biggest climbers, so B is not the quiet condition, only the vocal one. Finally, look ranks first under both conditions and pull, take, remove, get, talk, argue and question moved zero places, so several words sit on a side without any change of order to justify it.
result.notes: The split is legible enough that I would defend the first relation on a repeat, but two cautions attach to the evidence rather than the reading. First, eight of the twenty-seven listed words moved zero places, so their assignment to a side rests on something I am not shown; if the ordering is all I have, those words carry no weight and I have used them only as scene-filling, not as evidence. Second, four words are withheld precisely because they behaved inconsistently, and I cannot tell whether they would have thickened the physical side, the vocal side, or the residue. The strongest evidence is the movement column, and it is one-directional in a useful way: the largest climbs under B are explain (+10) and yell (+9), both vocal, and the largest falls under A are put (-9), leave (-7) and attack (-7).

result.reading: Under A the risers assemble into one recognizable procedure carried out on people and things already in the room: searching, questioning, removing, tying, tearing, opening, firing, beating. Under B the risers split two ways, into bare category-names for violence (attack, destroy, kill, fight) and into unaccompanied bodily or vocal acts needing no object at all (pray, sing, cry, scream, play, speak). Four near-synonym pairs sit astride the divide, which is enough to make me hold the reading loosely.

relations.name: Raid script, room noise
relations.sentence: The A side assembles into a single coherent search-and-detain procedure performed on people and objects already present, covering searching, questioning, removing, tying, tearing, opening and taking, while the B side collects acts a body performs audibly or physically with nobody to perform them upon: praying, singing, crying, screaming, playing, speaking, looking.

relations.name: Instrument versus category
relations.sentence: Both conditions raise violence, but A raises it at instrument level as particular physical acts (firing, beating, tearing, throwing) whereas B raises it as category names for violence in general (attacking, destroying, killing, fighting, hitting), the largest single move in the whole set belonging to the most category-like word of all, destroy, which climbs seventy-three places from ninety-sixth into the low twenties.

relations.name: Contentless verbs drift
relations.sentence: Three verbs that commit to almost nothing about what actually happens, play, move and look, all rise under B, two of them from outside the top thirty into the top twenty, whereas the thinnest verbs on the A side hold roughly still or slip.

result.kind: specificity of the enacted script

residue.description: Shoot sits at position one under both conditions and moved zero places, so its appearance in the B column reflects the ordering of the list rather than any difference between the measurements, and make is not a content completion at all since started to make requires a complement the fragment never supplies.

result.counterexamples: The worst damage comes from near-synonym pairs split across the two sides with no semantic distance between the members. Talk sits on A and falls six places while speak sits on B and rises two, and nothing about the meaning of the completion distinguishes them, only register. Shout falls fifteen places on A while scream rises six on B, though both name the same vocal outburst, which undercuts any account in which A holds the audible and B the procedural or vice versa. Beat on A and hit on B are likewise a minimal pair. Fire falls twenty-five places on A while shoot is pinned at position one under both, so the instrument-level reading in relation two survives only if fire is read as igniting or dismissing rather than discharging a weapon. Chant, a collective vocal and liturgical act, belongs with pray and sing but sits on A, and argue on B is as interpersonal and object-directed as question on A. Fight and attack on B implicate people in the room just as much as beat and search do on A, which is a direct strain on relation one.
result.notes: I read only positions, not likelihoods, and did not treat either condition as the correct or the milder one. The aggregate clusters that hold are about ten words strong (search, question, remove, tie, tear, open on one side; pray, sing, cry, play on the other) and they are what keeps this above low. Against them stand at least four split synonym pairs, which is the signature of a difference that is not tracking word meaning cleanly, so I would not defend any of the three relations at the level of an individual word, only as tendencies over the groups named. Relation three is stated because it is visible in the movement numbers and not because I would argue for it; play at plus twenty-six and move at plus fifteen could equally be noise in a low-ranked tail. Note also that the two largest movers in the set, destroy at plus seventy-three and play at plus twenty-six, both start from far down the A ranking, so both relations that lean on them are leaning on words that were marginal under A to begin with.

result.reading: The A list is dominated by verbs of articulate, addressed speech (say, tell, ask, question, interrogate, speak, argue) plus a few physical verbs whose objects are things rather than people (throw, tear, shake), while the B list is dominated by verbs of assault on a person (attack, beat, kill, shoot, abuse, kick, push, fight) and by inarticulate or collective vocalizing (cry, sing, scream, chant). The biggest movers on each side follow that pattern rather than cutting across it: say and interrogate fall furthest under B, and cry, sing, abuse and kill rise furthest.

relations.name: Addressed speech to bare voicing
relations.sentence: Verbs of speech that require someone spoken to or something said (say, tell, ask, question, interrogate, argue, speak) sit high under A and drop under B, while under B the speech verbs that rise are ones that need no addressee and no content at all (cry, sing, chant, scream, talk).

relations.name: Objects become victims
relations.sentence: The physical verbs A favours act on things or are non-specific about what is acted on (throw, tear, shake, walk), whereas the physical verbs B favours all presuppose a human target and several of them a lethal or degrading one (attack, beat, kill, shoot, abuse, kick, push, fight).

relations.name: Room scene to crowd scene
relations.sentence: A's words describe things three people could do to each other inside a room (interrogate, question, tell, hug, speak), while several of B's rising words belong to a public or massed scene that the fragment's room does not contain (chant, sing, scream, attack).

result.kind: articulate address versus bodily assault and undirected noise

residue.description: Make and take are light verbs that carry no action until a complement is supplied, so they are not really content completions of the fragment; hug moved one place and is the only affiliative word anywhere in either list, so it is a lone outlier rather than a member of a group; walk and shake are generic enough (walk where, shake what or shake with what) that they could be read into either side and so support neither.

result.counterexamples: The worst is the near-synonym split: shout and yell stay high under A while scream rises under B, and there is no semantic difference between them large enough to carry the second relation, which suggests the ordering can separate words that mean the same thing. Second worst is hit, which sits on the A side while attack, beat and kick sit on the B side, directly contradicting the claim that A's physical verbs lack a human victim (mitigated only by its small move of four places). Talk is the highest-ranked word under B and is a speech verb, which looks like a contradiction of the first relation, though it is the one speech verb that takes neither addressee nor content and so is arguably evidence for it. Throw and tear on the A side are aggressive enough to blunt the second relation, though both take inanimate objects.
result.notes: Two independent cuts (speech transitivity, and whether a physical verb needs a human victim) partition most of the thirty words the same way and are backed by the largest movements on both sides, which is why I did not return an empty list. What holds me at medium rather than high is that the shout/yell/scream split shows the ranking can put synonyms on opposite sides, so some of the apparent structure may be arbitrary ordering noise dressed up as a distinction, and roughly a third of the words (make, take, walk, shake, hug, push) carry no clear membership. Worth recording without speculating about cause: the fragment names an ethnic group, and the words that rise under B are kill, abuse, attack, shoot, kick, chant and scream while the words that fall are say, interrogate, tell and question. That is a statement about which words moved, not about why. One word was withheld, so no relation here is stated over the complete difference.
