The generic verbs that specify no errand at all (take, say, talk, ask, look) hold near the top of both lists, so the change is concentrated on the words that say what the three men came into the room to do.

relations.name: Raid script withdrawn
relations.sentence: The verbs that make the entry an armed or custodial operation on the people already in the room fall furthest under B, with interrogate dropping 133 places, search 110, shoot 90, attack 78 and beat 44, while the only two words that rise, help and sit, put the entrants in the room as callers rather than as a force.

relations.name: Errandless verbs survive
relations.sentence: Verbs that name an action without committing to any errand keep high placement under B (take at 7, say at 11, talk at 15, ask at 16, look at 17, moving between one and thirteen places) while every verb that specifies what the entry is for moves thirty to a hundred and thirty places down, so B's list reads as help and sit followed by whatever was too unspecific to fix a scene.

relations.name: Innocent casualties too
relations.sentence: Two words naming nothing coercive also fall, play by 95 places and pray by 12, and play's fall is larger than beat's or attack's, which suggests the demotion catches more of the scene than its violence alone rather than excising only the harmful completions.

result.kind: what errand the entry is on

residue.description: These verbs are not content completions on their own, since make, open, tell and throw all need an object that the fragment does not supply and walk needs a direction, so each could belong to a raid or to a visit depending on a word that is not shown, and their movement cannot be read as being about any particular scene.

result.counterexamples: The worst is play, which falls 95 places, further than beat (-44), attack (-78) or shoot (-90), even though nothing about playing fits a raid; on the first relation it should have been indifferent to the change and on the second it is specific but harmless, so it sits badly with both. Pray (-12) is a milder version of the same problem, and it is a word the ethnic framing of the fragment makes salient. Talk (-13), ask (-13), look (-13), speak (-38) and argue (-12) also fall despite naming ordinary conversation, which weakens the claim that only the coercive words were demoted; speak at -38 is the one I would not have predicted. Against all of this stands a structural caution rather than a counterexample: only two words are listed as higher under B, so a downward move is close to guaranteed for everything else, and the size of a fall carries more information here than its direction.
result.notes: The reading rests on the ordering of the falls rather than on the falls themselves, for the reason given in the counterexamples: with only help and sit listed on the B side, almost every other word must move down. What is not forced is that the four largest falls are interrogate, search, play and shoot, three of which name a search-and-detain operation, and that the words nearest the top under B are two verbs of guest-like conduct. One word is withheld as moving opposite to its prominence, so a word that would bear on this is missing and I cannot tell which side it would have helped. No likelihoods are shown, so I have not treated a fall from 12 to 145 as more than a fall in rank; the gap between rank 97 and rank 145 may be negligible or large and nothing here says which.

result.reading: Under A the blank fills with character adjectives ascribed to the neighbors (friendly, nice, kind, polite, cordial, welcoming, and alongside them willing, eager, careful, suspicious, curious), while under B it fills with participles and locatives describing what they were doing or where they were (out, outside, at, busy, working, talking, smiling, coming, doing, looking, seen). Both sides are compatible with the habitual "always," so the shift is not one of warmth or of judgment but of what sort of predicate is being attached to the three people: an inward disposition under A, an observable activity or position under B.

relations.name: Trait against activity
relations.sentence: Words A favours name a standing disposition of the neighbors (friendly, nice, kind, polite, cordial, welcoming, willing, trying, eager, careful, interested, curious, suspicious), while words B favours name what they were doing or where they were at the time (out, outside, at, busy, working, talking, smiling, coming, doing, looking, seen).

relations.name: Civility thesaurus thins
relations.sentence: A carries a dense set of near-synonymous civility terms (friendly, nice, kind, polite, cordial, welcoming), where B keeps only smiling and happy as sociable descriptors plus welcome, which reverses the direction of the hospitality so the neighbors receive it rather than extend it.

relations.name: Watching versus being seen
relations.sentence: A holds words casting the neighbors as scrutinizing or being scrutinized in an interior way (curious, interested, asking, careful, suspicious), where B holds words about their visibility to an onlooker (seen, out, outside, coming).

result.kind: trait ascription versus observed activity

residue.description: These are determiners, a degree word and prepositions that defer the content of the completion to a following word rather than supplying it, so they carry no relation on their own; that A ranks "on" second and B ranks "very" fourth means high-prominence positions on both sides are occupied by slots rather than by predicates.

result.counterexamples: Three words cut against relation 1. "happy" (B, 12 to 5) is an affective disposition sitting high on the activity side, and "ready" (B, 29 to 9) is likewise a stance rather than an act; together they show B has not abandoned dispositional predicates, only demoted the social-evaluative ones, which is the most damaging objection here. "very" holding rank 4 unchanged under both conditions makes the same point structurally: B still leads into an intensified adjective. Against relation 2, "careful" and "suspicious" on the A side show A is not simply a warmth cluster, so the civility reading covers part of A rather than A as such. Against relation 3, "looking" under B is an observing verb, not a visibility one, which weakens the observer/observed inversion enough that I marked that relation low. "busy" and "working" on B are mild counterexamples in the other direction, since an unfriendly reading of the fragment would expect them on A.
result.notes: The predicate-type split is the one thing I would defend without qualification; the two finer relations are readings of subsets of A rather than of the whole difference. Nothing in the lists licenses a claim about tone toward the three people: both sides are ordinary and neither is hostile, and the largest single moves (curious -103, cordial -78, careful -76, seen +38, coming +29) are all consistent with the type shift rather than with any change of stance. One word was withheld, and since the withheld word is by construction one whose rank and prominence disagree, it could belong to either group and I cannot bound its effect. Ranks alone are shown, so a large positional move may correspond to a small difference in likelihood and I have not treated the ordering as a magnitude.

relations.name: trait becomes activity
relations.sentence: A's leading completions are predicate adjectives naming a settled disposition (friendly, nice, pleasant, kind, quiet, cheerful), while B's leading completions are present participles that turn the predicate into an ongoing action or appearance (appearing, smiling, offering, seeming, answering, questioning, inviting, reading, hanging), several of which sit near the bottom of A's ranking or outside it.

relations.name: warmth versus availability
relations.sentence: The evaluative adjectives A prefers rate the neighbours' character as agreeable (friendly, nice, pleasant, kind, cheerful), whereas the adjectives B prefers rate their accessibility or state of occupation instead (available, busy, eager, good), so the judgment shifts from what they are like to whether they are on hand.

relations.name: scaffolding versus content
relations.sentence: Almost all the non-content material sits on the A side, where articles, particles, locatives and degree words (a, in, on, at, up, there, outside, very, so) occupy nine of the fifteen slots and defer the actual completion, while every word on the B side is a content word.

result.kind: predicate form: settled attribute versus ongoing conduct

result.counterexamples: The grammatical relation is contradicted from both directions. On the B side, available, eager, busy and good are plain adjectives, not participles, and available is B's top word, so the participle account cannot be the whole of the difference; those four are the reason the second relation is stated at all. On the A side, smiling is a participle already ranked 7 under A and only moves four places, which shows participles were not absent from A but merely subordinate, and its presence in the B list is weak evidence. Boundary cases weaken things further: cheerful moves only 25 places and still sits at 42 under B, so the warmth cluster is not evacuated; quiet is an observational rather than an evaluative-warmth term and fits the second relation badly. relations.name: Warmth drops, noise level stays

result.kind: attributed disposition versus observed activity

result.reading: Under A the top of the list is a run of lower-body garments and the opening in them (pants, jeans, fly, trousers, shorts), and under B the highest position is taken by jacket, with leather rising behind it and backpack climbing fourteen places out of the low twenties into the top ten. The reordering at the very top is small in absolute terms (pants 1 to 2, fly 2 to 3, jacket 4 to 1), so most of the reading rests on two large movers, shorts falling ten and backpack rising fourteen, which both point the same way: away from what is worn over the crotch and toward outerwear or a thing carried.

relations.name: Crotch to outerwear
relations.sentence: The words A holds highest are the garments that cover the hips and groin together with the opening in them (pants, jeans, trousers, shorts, fly), while B promotes an upper-body garment and its material (jacket takes first position, leather rises three places), so the zipper moves from the front of the trousers to the front of a coat.

relations.name: Worn versus carried
relations.sentence: B's single largest movement takes backpack from twenty-second into the top ten, putting a container that is carried rather than worn among the likeliest completions, while every word A keeps high is an item of clothing on the body.

relations.name: Fly becomes flies
relations.sentence: The same referent appears on both sides in two forms, with the singular fly slightly higher under A and the plural flies rising five places under B, which is a change of wording rather than a change of what is unzipped.

result.kind: where on or off the body the zipper sits

residue.description: Zipper names the fastener itself rather than any garment, so it completes the fragment almost tautologically and its one-place slip carries no information about what is being opened; shirt does not move at all between the conditions, so it belongs to no difference; and bag sits on A while its near-synonym backpack is B's biggest riser, which leaves it anchoring nothing.

result.counterexamples: Flies is the clearest contradiction of the first relation: it is the same trouser opening as fly, it is as lower-body as anything on A's side, and it rises five places under B, so B is not uniformly moving away from the crotch. Bag against backpack contradicts the second relation almost as badly, since two words for a carried container sit on opposite sides and move opposite ways (bag down four, backpack up fourteen), which means the worn-versus-carried line cannot be drawn through the data cleanly. Shirt is a mild counterexample to the first relation from A's side, being an upper-body garment that A supposedly favours, though its movement of zero makes it weak evidence either way. Finally, the small size of most A-side movements (five of the eight move one or two places) means the first relation is carried by shorts and by the promotion of jacket rather than by the group as a whole.
result.notes: The two conditions agree far more than they differ at the top: pants, fly and jacket occupy the first three or four positions under both, and the difference is which of them leads. One word is withheld for moving against its prominence, so the picture is incomplete by construction, and I have no likelihood information, only ranks, so I cannot tell whether jacket taking first position reflects a large change or a near-tie resolving the other way. Leather is a pre-nominal modifier rather than a standalone completion, and I have kept it with jacket only because the two rise together and leather jacket is the obvious phrase; read alone it would be residue. The reading I would defend is the first relation stated at medium, and I would not defend the other two if the measurement were repeated.

result.reading: On the A side the neighbours' feeling is named as something done to them — betrayed, trapped, obliged — while on the B side the feeling is named in the vocabulary of security itself, and in both directions at once: safe, safer, relieved, but also unsafe and intimidated, with unsafe (+10) and relieved (+8) the two largest movers anywhere in the list. So the difference does not look like a swing from negative to positive; it looks like a swing from a lexicon of grievance and confinement to a lexicon that says explicitly whether one is safe or not.

relations.name: Safety lexicon surfaces
relations.sentence: Condition B pulls up the words that state a security condition outright, in both polarities (safe, safer, unsafe, relieved, intimidated), while condition A prefers words that describe the same situation without ever using the vocabulary of safety (betrayed, trapped, obliged).

relations.name: Wrong done, danger felt
relations.sentence: A's negative words attribute an injury with an implied agent behind it (betrayed by someone, trapped by something, obliged to do something), whereas B's negative words report a bare state of the person feeling them (unsafe, intimidated) with no wrong named.

relations.name: Obliged becomes compelled
relations.sentence: The one near-synonym pair in the data is split across the conditions, obliged falling under B (9 -> 14) while compelled rises (11 -> 10), so a single sense of coerced duty is present in both conditions and only its wording changes.

result.kind: explicitness of the security frame

residue.description: These are function words, determiners and degree modifiers that open a longer clause ("felt that...", "felt like...", "felt very...") rather than completing the fragment with a feeling, so their movement says something about sentence shape and nothing about what the neighbours felt.

result.counterexamples: The worst is unsafe: it is the single largest mover in the whole list (+10) and it sits on the B side alongside safe and relieved, which destroys any reading in which B is the calmer or more reassuring condition and is the reason I framed relation 1 around whether safety is named rather than around valence. Intimidated (+3) on the same side compounds this. Compelled on B against obliged on A contradicts relation 1's implication that the coercion sense belongs to A, and it is why relation 3 is stated separately and rated low. Softer counterexamples: they, that, the and safer are listed as favoured by one side while having moved zero places, so the two lists are not ordered by displacement alone and I cannot tell how much of any grouping is prominence rather than difference.
result.notes: Five words are withheld, and they are withheld on a criterion (movement opposing prominence) that could easily have removed further affect words, so the affective picture here is a filtered one. No likelihoods are shown, only ranks, so a word moving from 28 to 18 may still be very unlikely under both conditions and I have not treated large rank movement as large change in the completion. The fragment names a specific political situation; the safest thing I can say is what the words do, and I am not inferring from safe/unsafe rising together that either condition takes a position on it, since a condition that raises both poles of an axis is raising the axis, not a side of it.

result.reading: Both lists are dominated by syntactic continuations ("that", "the", "it", "they", "a", "like"), and once those are set aside the remaining content words split fairly cleanly: A carries reassurance and duty ("safe", "safer", "obliged", "compelled") plus one mild negative ("uneasy"), while B carries named injury with an implied agent ("threatened", "betrayed", "helpless"). What makes me cautious is that almost nothing actually moves — the largest displacement in the whole table is +3 and most entries are +0 or ±1, with no word dropping out of either list — so the relation is read off which side a word was placed on, not off any visible reordering.

relations.name: Safety against exposure
relations.sentence: The two words describing the neighbours as protected sit on the A side while the two describing them as exposed to attack sit on the B side, an almost antonymic pairing of the same affective slot.

relations.name: Duty against injury
relations.sentence: A favours words in which the neighbours are placed under an obligation to act, while B favours words in which something has been done to them by someone else, so the same constraint is felt as a demand on one side and as harm on the other.

relations.name: Diffuse against named
relations.sentence: The single unambiguously negative word on the A side is a low-intensity mood with no agent attached, whereas every negative word on the B side names a specific injury that presupposes someone who inflicted it.

result.kind: whether the feeling names harm and an agent for it

residue.description: These are function words that defer the actual affect term to a later position ('felt that...', 'felt like...', 'felt more...', 'felt their...') rather than completing the fragment with any feeling, so they carry no content that could join either group, and they make up the majority of both lists including the item each list leads with.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexample is "uneasy", which sits on the A side yet is a negative affect word of exactly the family B is supposed to own; it does not break the relations badly, since it is much milder and agentless than "betrayed" or "helpless", but it does rule out reading A as simply the reassuring side. "obliged" and "compelled" cut the other way with less force: they are constraint words on the side I have also called the safe side, so the safety relation and the duty relation cannot both be describing all of A at once. Weakest but worth stating, "more" on the A side is compatible with any adjective at all, including B's, so it is evidence for nothing. The broadest counterexample is the table itself: no word moves more than three places and no word appears in one condition and not the other, which is the pattern one would expect if the two conditions barely differ here.
result.notes: The relations are stated from which side each word was assigned to, not from displacement, because displacement is essentially absent: the largest move is betrayed at +3, the leading word of each list ("that" for A, "threatened" for B) moved +0, and there are no dashes at all. That means the ordering criterion given in the header ('the words the difference rests on most come first') is not rank movement, and I cannot see the quantity it is actually using, so I have not treated list position as evidence of strength. I would not defend any of these relations on the rank data alone; what I am reading is the partition, and the partition is legible.

relations.sentence: The participles that make the fragment a report of something the neighbours were moved to do (felt compelled, felt obliged, felt like) fall far under B, by seventeen, twenty-five and thirteen places, whereas B's risers (as, something) leave the neighbours as the site of an unspecified experience rather than as people about to act.

relations.name: Intensifier scaffolding lost
relations.sentence: The word carrying by far the largest movement, so, collapses sixty-nine places out of A's frame of intensified predication (felt so threatened that), and the word that takes over the top position under B is as, which builds a comparison instead of an intensity.

result.kind: whether the feeling gets named or is deferred

residue.description: These are determiners, pronouns and complementizers rather than content completions of "felt ___", and all of them move between zero and three places, which is too little to read anything from; "it" is listed as B-favoured on a rise of two, the same size band as "the" falling by two on the other side.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is internal to relation one: the fear adjectives are the words that move least, threatened by five and uneasy by one, while the words that actually carry the difference in magnitude are so, obliged and compelled. If the reading were that B suppresses named fear, the fear words should be the ones displaced, and they are not; they merely slip a little while a much larger rearrangement happens around obligation and intensification. Second, "an" and "they" are placed on the A side while having moved zero places, and "uneasy" and "their" only one, so side membership here is not a function of movement and cannot on its own support any grouping. Third, "it" contradicts the clean split by sitting on the B side while being the same grammatical kind of thing as A's "the" and "a". Fourth, nothing in B's promotion of "as" excludes the fear reading, since "felt as though they were in danger" names the same state one clause later; the deferral I am describing is syntactic and I cannot tell from ranks alone whether the affect returns downstream. result.notes: I would defend the direction of the difference (B's top ranks go to frame words that postpone the predicate, A's to words that supply it) more than I would defend any account of why. The fragment's content invites a reading about threat being softened, and that is the reading I am most suspicious of in myself, because the evidence for it is weak on its own terms: the threat words are the least displaced words in the list. The obligation pair (compelled, obliged) is the cleanest cluster here, two words of one construction moving seventeen and twenty-five places in the same direction, and it is the one I would bet on surviving a repeat. Relation three is stated because "so" is the single largest number on the page and it would be dishonest to leave the largest movement unremarked, but a sixty-nine place fall out of position seventeen tells me little without likelihoods, which I was not shown.

result.reading: Under A the top of the list is held by grammatical continuations of "felt" (the, that, they, it) plus a small set of participles naming something done to the neighbours by an agent (threatened, betrayed, compelled, obliged), while under B a dense band of ordinary emotional-state adjectives (uncomfortable, upset, annoyed, nervous, angry, alarmed, worried, scared) climbs from ranks 24-104 into the top 25 and pushes A's mid-band words down. The function words themselves barely move, so what actually changes is which content words occupy positions roughly 6 through 27.

relations.name: Done-to versus felt
relations.sentence: The content words A favours are past participles that presuppose an external agent acting on the neighbours (threatened, betrayed, compelled, obliged), whereas the words B promotes name internal emotional states that require no agent at all (uncomfortable, upset, annoyed, nervous, angry, alarmed, worried, scared).

relations.name: Mid-band adjective arrival
relations.sentence: A whole vocabulary of everyday gradable discomfort adjectives that sits deep in A's ranking (upset at 104, nervous at 76, annoyed at 71, scared at 55, worried at 53, uncomfortable at 47) rises into positions 6 to 24 under B, displacing the words A had in that band (obliged 10 to 38, safe 15 to 27) downward.

relations.name: Valence held open
relations.sentence: A's list contains both a threat reading and its opposite (threatened and betrayed alongside safe), while every content word B promotes is negative, so B narrows the range of feelings on offer even as it lowers their intensity.

result.kind: implied agency behind the feeling

residue.description: None of these completes "felt ___" with a feeling: the, that, they and it open a clausal continuation ("felt that they..."), their and no are determiners, so and as are scaffolding, and very is an intensifier awaiting an adjective; the first four are effectively fixed across conditions (moves of +0 to -2) and appear on A's side only by a place or two, while their, no and so drop 10 to 28 places without that drop being about their meaning, and very and as rise on B's side only because the adjectives they modify have risen.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is "forced," which sits on B's list at rank 20 under both conditions: it is a coercion participle of exactly the kind relation 1 assigns to A, so if the agentive/non-agentive split were clean it should not be on that side at all. Its +0 movement softens the damage, since B does not actually raise it, but it shows the split is a tendency among the moving words rather than a property of the two lists. "Safe" damages any simpler reading that A is the threat-laden condition: A ranks safe at 15 and B pushes it to 27, so the condition favouring "threatened" also favours its opposite. "Angry" and "annoyed" on B's side are outward-directed and reactive, and can be read as responses to something done, which weakens the agent/no-agent contrast at its edges. Finally, four words are withheld for moving against their prominence, and any of them could belong to either grouping; none of the relations above has been tested against them.
result.notes: I would defend the positional claim (relation 2) at high confidence because the movements are large, consistent in direction, and confined to one contiguous band; the interpretation of what the two vocabularies mean (relation 1) is the part I would expect to be argued with, mainly because of "forced." Relation 3 is stated because "safe" is genuinely there on A's side, but one word carrying a claim about valence range is not something I would defend if the measurement were repeated. I have not speculated about how likely any word is, only about order, and the withheld four are a real gap: if they include coercion words that rose under B, relation 1 would be in trouble.

result.reading: Under A the three men are simply people who have entered a room and begun doing things among themselves: talking, telling, eating, sitting, praying, walking, singing, shouting. Under B the top of the list is occupied by attack, shoot, question and search, and the words that gain most are the ones that need somebody else present to be done to, so the same three men are recast from occupants of the room into a party carrying out a raid or an interrogation on whoever was already there.

relations.name: Raid script surfacing
relations.sentence: Under B the completions that rise to the top and gain the most ground are all acts performed on some other person or place present in the room (attack, search, question, shoot, beat, fire, pull), while A prefers acts the three men perform among themselves with no second party implied (talk, tell, eat, sit, pray, walk, sing, play, ask).

relations.name: Aggression is not the axis
relations.sentence: The aggressive words A keeps barely move at all (yell -1, scream -3, fight -7, shout -9), so what separates the conditions is not how violent the completion is but whether the violence has a target: undirected noise and brawling stay roughly where they were under both, while directed force (attack, shoot, beat, fire) is what climbs.

relations.name: Outcry becomes chant
relations.sentence: The vocal completions change character rather than disappearing: A's are individual outbursts (shout, scream, yell) and B's are collective or derisive (chant +21, laugh +11), which are vocal acts performed at somebody rather than under duress.

result.kind: whether the action takes an outside target

residue.description: These are semantically empty or underspecified on their own -- make and get are light verbs that carry no action until a complement arrives (and make moved zero places, appearing on B's side only by listing), while look, pull and work could belong to either reading depending on what follows them, so I would not build any relation on their movement.</description>

result.counterexamples: Three words cut against the reading. Laugh (+11 under B) is not a coercive or targeted act at all and sits in B's upper half, which weakens the raid framing more than the chant reading repairs. Fight (-7) is on A's side despite being the most obviously violent word there; this is mild damage, since fight is mutual and untargeted and so fits the directedness relation even while embarrassing a simple violence reading. Sing (-5) and play (-1) moving very little also blunt the claim that ordinary-life verbs are what B drives out, since the largest A-side falls are eat, sit, pray, walk and get rather than the whole domestic set.
result.notes: The strongest signal is positional rather than compositional: B's first four ranks are attack, shoot, question, search, and three of those four also carry large gains, so the reading rests on the head of B's list and not on the tail. result.reading: Both conditions put the same explicit words at the top (fire 1 under both, retaliate 3 under both, terminate 2 and take 5 under A against take 2 and terminate 4 under B), so the change is not at the head of the list but in its middle: under B a procedural verb, investigate, climbs eleven places into fifth, discipline and take rise slightly, and what falls is the set of named penalties (terminate, punish, suspend) together with the causative light verbs (let, have, make). relations.name: Process over penalty
relations.sentence: Under B the completion leans toward verbs that open an institutional procedure rather than name its outcome, with investigate rising eleven places into fifth and discipline and take rising slightly, while the verbs that state a specific penalty outright, terminate, punish and suspend, all fall.

relations.name: Which light verb rises
relations.sentence: Both conditions favour verbs that name no action by themselves and need a complement, but the ones that fall under B are the causative-permissive ones that project colloquial dismissal phrases such as let her go, have her fired, make an example of her (let -4, have -5, make -5), while the one that rises is take, which collocates with an institutional object such as action or disciplinary measures (+3).

relations.name: Blunt words sit still
relations.sentence: The two most explicit words in the set, fire and retaliate, hold ranks 1 and 3 under both conditions and move zero places, so whatever separates the conditions leaves the naming of dismissal and of reprisal untouched and rearranges only the words below them, including the euphemistic terminate, which is the one word near the top that does move.

result.kind: whether the verb opens a process or names a penalty

residue.description: Give does not move at all (9 to 9) and get moves a single place (7 to 8), so their assignment to the A side rests on something the positions do not show, and as bare verbs neither completes the fragment with an action at all until a complement arrives (give her a warning, get rid of her), which makes them poor evidence for any direction.

Take is also weak evidence for the procedural reading on its own, since take rid of, take her aside and take action are all available and the ranking cannot tell them apart.

Investigate's +11 is the only movement larger than five places, and if it were removed the remaining pattern would be a set of small shuffles that I would not defend. result.reading: Both lists complete the same sentence about three Israelis entering a room, but they seem to be entering for different reasons: side A's verbs assemble a hands-on search-and-detain sequence (search, interrogate, question, look, remove, clean, beat, hit, throw), while side B's are dominated by talk and sociality (talk, speak, discuss, argue, ask, laugh, dance, film) with a small block of armed, lethal action on top of it (attack jumping 16 to 1, plus shoot and kill). So the difference is not that one side is violent and the other is not; violence sits on both sides in different forms, and what changes is the script the room is being entered under.

relations.name: Raid script versus encounter
relations.sentence: Under A the completions assemble the procedural sequence of a room being searched and its occupants handled (search, interrogate, question, look, remove, clean), while under B they assemble people meeting and speaking in a room (talk, speak, discuss, argue, ask, laugh, dance, film).

relations.name: Hands against weapons
relations.sentence: The violence on A's side is manual, close, and non-lethal (beat at rank 1, hit, throw), whereas B's violence is armed, distanced and lethal (attack rising from 16 to 1, shoot, kill), so the two conditions differ in the instrument and finality of harm rather than in whether harm appears.

relations.name: Devotion beside spectacle
relations.sentence: A places a religious act high in the ranking (pray at 4) with no counterpart on the other side, while B raises verbs of being watched or performing (film, dance, laugh), which is a difference in what the three men are imagined to be doing for their own sake rather than to anyone in the room.

residue.description: These are light or near-contentless verbs that need a complement before they say anything about the scene, so their side assignment carries no reading; play is a genuine content verb but fits neither the search sequence nor the conversation, and it sits on A where nothing else supports it.

result.counterexamples: The strongest counterexample is that kill, shoot and attack sit under B while beat, hit and throw sit under A: any reading in which A is the harsher or B the milder condition is directly contradicted, and attack moving to rank 1 means B's single likeliest completion is an assault. This is why the second relation is stated as a difference of instrument rather than of degree, and someone could reasonably say that distinction is too fine to carry the weight. Within the first relation, question moved +0 and ask moved +0, so two of the verbs closest to the talk/interrogate contrast barely moved at all and their placement on opposite sides is close to arbitrary. Pray under A cuts against the raid reading, since praying is what occupants of a room do rather than what searchers do, and laugh and dance under B cut against reading B as the hostile condition. Clean is the largest single move on the page (-51) and is the least interpretable word in either list: it fits a raid only through the idiom of clearing a place out, and it would fit a domestic scene equally well.
result.notes: Two cautions about the display itself. The header says the lists are ordered so that the words the difference rests on most come first, but that ordering does not track the printed movement: pray leads A with -10 while clean, at -51, is sixth, and attack leads B with +15 while discuss, at +31, is sixth. So the ranking column and the ordering are two different measurements and I have read the ordering as the more authoritative one about weight, without knowing what it weighs. Second, three words are withheld for moving against their prominence, and since the whole reading here turns on which kind of violence lands on which side, a withheld verb of harm would matter more than any word shown; I cannot tell whether the pattern survives them. Nothing in the two lists is shown as a dash, so no word is absent from either condition, which means every difference here is a reordering rather than an appearance or disappearance, and reorderings of this size are the weaker evidence.

result.reading: Under A the fragment is completed mostly by very high-frequency, semantically thin verbs (get, go, make, have, do, use, give, put, try, leave) together with one blunt punitive verb, fire, at rank 1; under B the top of the list is filled by verbs that name a determinate institutional action in a single word (terminate, consult, listen, talk, ask, end, stop, address, investigate, dismiss, postpone). The movement is not from harsh to gentle, since terminate rises to rank 1 and ignore, dismiss, cancel and postpone all rise as well, but from a vague or colloquial way of saying what management did to a specific, procedural, largely Latinate one.

relations.name: Plain word, procedural synonym
relations.sentence: The blunt everyday verb for dismissing an employee is demoted while its formal workplace synonyms are promoted to the very top: fire falls from 1 to 7 while terminate rises from 38 to 1 and dismiss from 107 to 22, so the same act is still being named but in the vocabulary of a personnel file rather than of speech.

relations.name: Empty verb, named act
relations.sentence: A's favoured completions are light, near-contentless verbs that only work as the first word of a longer phrase (get, go, make, have, do, use, give, put, try, leave, send), while B's favoured completions are verbs that carry the whole action by themselves (terminate, consult, investigate, address, contact, postpone, engage, dismiss, respond, cancel), so the difference is between deferring the content to a complement and stating it in one word.

relations.name: Unilateral act, dialogic procedure
relations.sentence: A keeps the verbs in which management acts on the woman directly and alone (fire, confront, send), while B promotes, often from very deep in the list, verbs of talking to somebody about it (consult from 123 to 9, listen from 96 to 10, address from 99 to 16, engage from 158 to 28, plus talk, ask, contact, meet, respond, tell), so the decision becomes a communicative or consultative step rather than an act performed on her.

result.kind: register and specificity of the named managerial act

residue.description: quit and let are not coherent completions with management as the subject of decided to (management deciding to quit, or to let, needs a complement the list cannot supply), and quit's enormous fall from 11 to 82 may simply be the removal of a bad parse rather than any shift in how the act is named; take, meet and file sit in the B list while barely moving (take 2 to 2, meet 19 to 19, file 30 to 24), so they are carried by the lists rather than by any difference between the conditions; change is too unspecified about its object to say which relation it belongs to; try, have and do are pure auxiliaries of intention with no content of their own.

result.counterexamples: The third relation is the weak one and its counterexamples are numerous: B does not only promote consultation, it also promotes ignore (48 to 15), postpone (156 to 25), cancel (74 to 27), stop (12 to 5), end (15 to 6) and above all terminate (38 to 1), none of which involve talking to her and several of which are more decisive against her than anything on A's side, so a reading of B as conciliatory would be wrong and only the narrower reading, that B names procedures of any temperature, survives. The second relation is contradicted from inside B by take (rank 2 under both) and let (24 to 18), which are exactly the light verbs the relation assigns to A, and by A's confront and fire, which are specific verbs sitting on the light-verb side; take is the worst of these because it is near the top of both lists and unmoved, so it shows the light-verb pattern is a tendency in the ordering rather than a partition. The first relation has no counterexample within these lists, since fire is the only colloquial term for the act present and both of its formal synonyms move the other way.
result.notes: The dimension is legible without needing to decide which condition is preferable, and I have deliberately not treated B as milder: terminate at rank 1 under B is at least as severe as fire at rank 1 under A, which is why I named the kind as register and specificity rather than severity. The first relation is the one I would defend on a repeat measurement, because it rests on three words moving in a coordinated way with very large displacements and no word contradicting it. The second is safe as a statement about the shape of the ordering but not as a partition, given take and let. The third I would state and not argue for at full strength; it is stated at medium because the communicative verbs make the largest single jumps in the whole table (engage +130, postpone +131, consult +114), but postpone sitting among them is a sign that the jump size is tracking how far down the list a word started rather than what kind of word it is. Words deep in a ranking have more room to rise, so the largest positive movements are partly an artifact of the starting position and I have not leaned on them. No claim here rests on likelihoods, only on order.

result.reading: Every word shown occupies the same rank under both conditions except `suit`, which slips one place (8 -> 9), so the ordinal evidence for any A/B difference is essentially null: the two conditions agree on the ordering of these eight completions almost exactly. What signal exists is not in the positions but in the list ordering the prompt supplies (words the difference rests on most come first), where `trousers` heads the A side and `pants` heads the B side -- the same garment under two names -- while the B set is otherwise scattered through the ranking (positions 1 and 5) rather than forming a band.

relations.name: Same garment, rival name
relations.sentence: The word the A side rests on most and the word the B side rests on most denote the identical article of clothing under two dialect names, so the leading contrast is `trousers` against `pants` rather than one garment against another.

relations.name: Torso outlier among waistlines
relations.sentence: Every garment on the A side fastens at or below the waist (`trousers`, `jeans`, `shorts`, `suit`, and `fly`, the fastening itself), while the B side contributes the only upper-body garment in the set, `jacket`.

result.kind: which name for the same garment, not which garment

residue.description: `bag` is not clothing at all and belongs to no garment relation; `fly` is a part of a garment rather than a garment, so it can be read either as the fastening or as a metonym for trousers; and `suit`, `shorts` and `jeans` are ordinary lower-body completions that sit on the A side without distinguishing it from `pants` on the B side, so they carry no relation of their own.

result.counterexamples: The region reading (relation 2) is contradicted head-on by `pants` itself: it is a waist-fastening lower-body garment, a synonym of `trousers` and a co-hyponym of `jeans` and `shorts`, yet it sits on the B side, so the same semantic category straddles the split and `jacket` is left as a single word doing all the work. That is a severe contradiction, and it is the reason relation 2 is marked low. Relation 1 is contradicted more mildly by the fact that `jeans` and `shorts` -- also lower-body, also ordinary -- stay on the A side rather than following `pants`, so the split is not a clean dialect sort. Against both relations stands the ordinal evidence: with seven of eight words frozen in place and the eighth moving one rank, nothing in the positions favours any grouping over any other.
result.notes: Two structural observations that bear on how much any of the above should be trusted. First, the movement column is almost entirely zero: the only nonzero entry is `suit` at -1, and no shown word rises to fill rank 8 under B, which means at least one word not displayed here is involved in that swap (rank 9 under A and rank 8 under B are both occupied by words outside this list). A difference that leaves the visible ordering intact is either very small or lives entirely in magnitudes I have not been shown, and I was told not to speculate about likelihoods. Second, no word is absent from either condition's list, so the strongest available kind of difference -- presence against absence -- does not occur anywhere in this set. Given that, I would not have stated any relation from the ranks alone; relation 1 rests wholly on the prompt's statement that each list is ordered by how much the difference rests on the word, which puts `trousers` and `pants` at the two heads. If that ordering guarantee is weak, relation 1 goes with it and the correct answer to question 1 becomes the empty list.

relations.sentence: Every speech verb A favours carries a raised voice or open conflict (shout, yell, argue) and each falls, while the speech verbs that rise under B name the same act of addressing the people in the room with the loudness and antagonism taken out (talk, ask, discuss, explain).

relations.sentence: Two verbs naming what an armed force does to persons under its control fall (interrogate, search) while their bureaucratically neutral near-synonyms rise into almost exactly the slots they vacate (question to 3, inspect to 10, read to 13), so the procedure is renamed rather than dropped.

relations.name: Trait against activity
relations.sentence: Condition A puts stative adjectives naming a durable disposition of the three people at the top, while condition B puts present participles naming an ongoing observable activity at the top, so that A completes the fragment with what they are like and B with what they are doing.

relations.name: Courtesy praise against plain report
relations.sentence: Nearly every content word A favours is a term of approval drawn from the vocabulary of good manners and welcome (friendly, polite, nice, kind, respectful, welcome), whereas B's words carry no verdict on the neighbours at all and include one openly negative one (arguing), so A reads as a character reference and B as a description.

relations.name: Unobtrusive against audible
relations.sentence: A's single most neighbour-specific word is quiet, while B's leading words are all things one hears through a wall (talking, laughing, chatting, arguing), so the two conditions disagree about whether these neighbours register on the senses.

result.kind: character ascription versus observable ongoing activity

residue.description: These are not content completions of the fragment but words that defer the completion by one more slot ("always on time", "always at home", "always a bit", "always so", "always very", "always up to"), and their side is mostly determined by which continuation type each condition is heading toward rather than by any meaning of their own.

result.counterexamples: Four items cut against the relations, in descending order of damage. result.reading: Under A the three people who enter the room are treated as arriving to do something to it or to someone in it, and the completions are the verbs of an armed incursion: beat, shoot, kill, attack, hit, fire, throw. Under B the same entrance is read as people arriving to be together in a room, and the completions are speech and shared occasion: speak, talk, recite, argue, chant, pray, dance, prepare, clean, light. The shift is not a softening of one act but a substitution of one scene for another, and the deepest movers on each side (hit -120, kill -55 against recite +82, clean +67) are the words that belong to only one of the two scenes.

relations.name: Striking becomes speaking
relations.sentence: The verbs of physical assault on a person present in the room fall away under B and are replaced at the top of the ranking by verbs of talk, so that what the entrants do to bodies under A they do with voices under B.

relations.name: Raid recast as gathering
relations.sentence: Words that under A cast the entry as a search or an intrusion give way under B to words for a ceremony or a domestic occasion held in the room, several of which climb from far outside the top forty (recite from 85, clean from 84, prepare from 75, dance from 52) as though a different event were being narrated.

relations.name: Object-hungry verbs resorted
relations.sentence: Verbs whose meaning is fixed only by the object they take split by which object each condition supplies: under A pull, fire, hit and throw are the ones that rise, which are those completable by a weapon or a stone, and under B it is set, light, clean and prepare, which are those completable by a table, a candle or a room.

result.kind: imputed scene of the entrance: incursion or assembly

residue.description: Take and make are the two smallest movers on either side (-7 and -3) and carry no scene of their own until an object is named, so their position says nothing about which reading is in force; ask sits on A while being a plain verbal act, and belongs to neither the assault group nor the gathering group it would otherwise fit.

Ask and sing are the mirror problem on the other side, both verbal or expressive acts that sit at 11 and 18 under A and fall under B, which the first relation predicts should not happen, though both move only ten and eleven places and neither is near the top. Scream is ambiguous rather than contradictory: it is a vocalization, so it reads against the striking-becomes-speaking split, but it is the vocalization of someone being harmed and so belongs to A's scene anyway. Search under A is not violence and only weakly supports the raid reading on its own. One word is withheld, so a counterexample may be missing from the list I was given.

result.reading: The two lists swap the scenario rather than soften it: under A the top completions are employer discipline (fire, terminate, suspend, punish, retaliate), under B they are affiliation with the union (join, become, attend, support, organize). Fire goes 1 to 137 and join 136 to 1, while the thin verbs shared by both lists stay high in both.

relations.name: Retaliation against enlistment
relations.sentence: A completes the sentence with disciplinary acts an employer performs on the employee, while B completes it with acts of joining or backing the union, so the same fragment reads once as a punishment and once as a recruitment.

relations.name: Disposal against address
relations.sentence: A's words dispose of the woman administratively and none of them involves speaking to anyone, whereas B's second tier is made of verbs of contact and correspondence aimed at the organizer, a channel with no A-side member at all.

relations.name: Thin verbs hold still
relations.sentence: Verbs committed to one script or the other move a hundred places or more, while semantically empty verbs that could head either script stay near the top of both rankings and move only single digits.

result.kind: which party the decided act serves

residue.description: Talk sits at 18 under both conditions and moves zero places, so it is listed while carrying none of the difference; use, find, cut and follow need an unstated object before they mean anything (cut hours, follow up), so they cannot be assigned a side on their own.

result.counterexamples: Take (+2), make (+8) and go (+31) sit on B's side yet read naturally in A's direction (take action against her, make an example of her, go after her), so the split is clean only among the lexically specific verbs and blurs among the generic ones. Investigate is on A but is procedural rather than punitive, and it moved only 11 places where its punitive neighbours moved 130 or more; let is ambiguous in the same way (let her go). None of this is fatal, since no B word is unambiguously punitive and no A word is unambiguously pro-union.
result.notes: I do not know which condition is which and have not guessed. The strongest evidence is the near-total exchange of the two top ranks and the hundred-place moves of the lexically specific verbs; the weakest is the light-verb group, which is a claim about what did not move rather than about what did.

result.reading: Under A the blank is filled by what these neighbors ARE — a disposition ascribed to them (nice, friendly, polite, kind), with the intensifiers (very, so) that such adjectives take; under B it is filled by where they are and what they are seen doing (outside, there, at, home, together, seen, busy, talking, working). The two biggest climbers, seen (+54) and together (+42), point the completion toward a witness's report of the household from the street rather than a verdict on its character.

relations.name: Character verdict to whereabouts
relations.sentence: Condition A completes the fragment with a judgment of what the neighbors are like as people (nice, friendly, polite, kind) together with the degree adverbs those adjectives require (very, so), while condition B completes it with their location or presence in space (outside, there, at, home, around, up, in, out).

relations.name: Warm regard cooled to observation
relations.sentence: The evaluative vocabulary does not vanish under B but changes temperature and stance: the words of personal warmth and interpersonal contact (nice, friendly, kind, polite) fall, while the detached appraisals a neighbor makes from a distance (pleasant, quiet) and the vocabulary of being watched (seen, together) rise sharply.

relations.name: Fighting becomes arguing
relations.sentence: Both conditions allow the neighbors to be in conflict, but A places the physical and vice-marked terms higher (fighting, smoking) while B raises the verbal and domestic term for the same trouble (arguing) alongside other ordinary household activity (talking, working, busy).

result.kind: ascribed disposition versus observed presence

residue.description: The intensifiers (very, so) and the light or auxiliary verbs (being, having, getting, going, coming) are not content completions at all but grammatical scaffolding for a word that would follow, and the bare prepositions in, out and on moved zero places, so they carry no difference between the conditions even though they sit on the B list.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexample to the first relation is pleasant, a disposition adjective of exactly the kind A is supposed to monopolize, sitting on the B side and climbing thirteen places; quiet does the same, though quiet reads more easily as a report of noise than of character, so the damage is partial and both are absorbed by the second relation. Running the other way, playing, hanging, smoking and fighting are activity words on the A side, so the split is not trait-versus-activity but trait-versus-location-and-observed-activity; anyone reading the first relation as A-holds-no-verbs would be wrong. Finally, arguing on the B side blocks any reading in which B is simply the more agreeable completion, and its presence is why the third relation is stated as a change of register rather than a removal of conflict.
result.notes: The two clusters are legible without straining, and the fragment supports both grammatically ('were always nice' and 'were always outside' are equally well formed), so the difference is a choice between two available frames rather than one condition failing to complete the sentence. I have not tried to say which condition is which or why they differ. The third relation rests on three words and one of them (smoking) is a vice term rather than a conflict term, which is why it is marked low; a repeat measurement moving fighting or arguing a dozen places would dissolve it, whereas the first relation would survive substantial reshuffling because it rests on fourteen words and on the largest movements in both directions.

result.reading: Under A the top of the list is mostly semantically empty verbs (get, take, make, use, have, do, put, go) that defer the actual act to a complement the fragment never shows, alongside a few contentful ones (fire, investigate, shut, retaliate); under B four specific Latinate verbs naming an employer sanction on the worker (discipline, threaten, dismiss, punish) are pulled to the very top, two of them from ranks 50 and 48. The difference looks less like a change of severity than a change in whether the verb names the managerial act at all, though "fire" sits at rank 1 or 2 under both and "retaliate" barely moves, which cuts against reading B as a sanitizing move.

relations.name: Deferred act versus named act
relations.sentence: A favours light, contentless verbs whose meaning would have to be carried by an unstated complement (get, take, make, use, have, do, put, keep, let, move), while each of B's four promoted words is a single verb that names the managerial act outright as a sanction on the worker.

relations.name: Personnel-process vocabulary
relations.sentence: The words B promotes are the Latinate register of formal employment procedure (discipline, dismiss, punish), whereas A's contentful verbs are either blunt Anglo-Saxon (fire, shut) or name responses that are not sanctions on her person at all (investigate, call, send, move).

relations.name: Firing without the word
relations.sentence: A holds the pieces of the multiword euphemism for firing, let and go as in 'let her go', both falling steeply under B (-20 and -57), while B supplies the single formal word for the same act, dismiss, promoted from 48 to 6.

result.kind: specificity of the act the verb names

residue.description: These are so contentless that their movement is presumably carried by whatever would follow them, which is not shown, so they support no reading beyond the general light-verb pattern; 'have' in particular could be causative ('have her fired') and is therefore unreadable on its own.

result.counterexamples: The worst is "retaliate", which sits at 4 under A and 5 under B, essentially unmoved: it is the most explicit and most legally loaded description of the act, so any reading in which B suppresses naming what management did, or in which A monopolises the transgressive vocabulary, fails outright. "fire" is nearly as bad, at 1 under A and 2 under B, meaning the bluntest punitive verb is at the top under both conditions and B's promotion of "dismiss" cannot be a substitution of a formal word for a forbidden one. "threaten", promoted from 50 to 3, contradicts the personnel-process reading in the other direction, since threatening a union organizer is a coercive and unlawful act rather than a procedure. Contentful A-favoured words (investigate, shut, call, send) contradict the light-verb characterization of the A side, though they are consistent with the second relation. Two words are withheld, so the A side as shown is incomplete.
result.notes: The three relations are not independent: the second and third are refinements of the first, and if the first is an artifact of light verbs being generally frequent, all three go together. Rankings alone are shown, so I cannot tell whether B's promotions reflect a large redistribution or small shifts among near-ties, and I have not assumed either. The strongest single observation is that discipline moves 9 to 1 and threaten 50 to 3 while the plain verbs that need a complement fall by 44 to 87 places; the strongest thing against a tidy reading is that fire and retaliate, the two words a severity or sanitization account would most expect to move, do not move.

result.reading: The two rankings share a head that does not move at all: "pants" sits at 1 under both conditions and "fly" at 2 under both, so the most intimate completions of "She unzipped his ___" are not displaced. All the movement is in the middle and tail, where a lower-body garment falls hard (shorts, 6 to 15) and a zippered container climbs hard (backpack, 16 to 6), with suitcase, hoodie and zipper drifting the same way. The picture is of a mid-list reweighting from clothing worn on the lower body toward objects and outerwear that merely have zips, rather than any suppression at the top.

relations.name: Body to baggage
relations.sentence: Under A the completions that fall away are garments worn below the waist, whose unzipping undresses the man (shorts drops nine places, jeans one), while under B the risers are zippered containers and outer layers that can be opened without touching a body at all (backpack climbs ten places from sixteenth to sixth, suitcase two, hoodie three, jacket holding fifth).

relations.name: Zip named, not worn
relations.sentence: B pulls up the words that name the fastening itself rather than the thing fastened, so "zipper" rises from ninth to seventh and "flies" from eleventh to tenth alongside "fly", shifting the completion from the garment to its mechanism.

relations.name: Hemline moves up
relations.sentence: Ordering the garment words by where they sit on the body, the ones below the waist lose ground under B (shorts sixth to fifteenth, jeans third to fourth) while the ones above it gain or hold (hoodie twelfth to ninth, jacket fifth to fifth), which is the same movement as the container relation but measured only over clothing.

result.kind: what the zip belongs to, a body or a bag

residue.description: "flies" is a morphological variant of "fly", already present two places above it in the same list, so it adds an inflectional duplicate rather than an independent completion, and its single place of movement carries almost no evidence; "trousers" is a near-synonym of the stationary "pants" and I could not place it on either side without contradicting one of my own relations, so I have left it out of all of them and reported it below instead.

result.counterexamples: Three, of unequal weight. "Trousers" is the worst: it is a lower-body garment, exactly the class relations one and three say B demotes, and it rises from fourth to third under B, which flatly reverses the direction I claimed for shorts and jeans; the move is only one place, but its sign is wrong and it sits high in the list where the evidence should be strongest. "Fly" is the second: it is the most explicitly bodily completion available here, and it holds second place under both conditions while appearing on the B side, so any reading in which B avoids the intimate is contradicted at the head of the ranking, and this is why I confined relation one to the middle and tail. "Pants" is the third and mildest: it is a below-the-waist garment that does not move at all from first place, so the single likeliest completion is common ground between the conditions and none of my relations explains it. Taken together these mean the reading survives only as a claim about mid-list reweighting, not about what either condition most expects.
result.notes: The evidence is entirely ordinal, and two entries assigned to the B side, "fly" and "jacket", have zero rank movement, so whatever makes them B-favoured is a difference in likelihood I am not shown and cannot check; I have used them only as supporting members of groups whose other members do move. Two further words are withheld as moving against their prominence, and since the withheld set is precisely the incoherent one, I cannot tell whether it would strengthen or break the container reading. The two largest moves in the table, backpack at plus ten and shorts at minus nine, point in opposite directions and are the whole basis of my first relation; strip those two out and there is little left but drift of one to three places. Relation two is marked low because it rests on moves of two and one place and because "fly" would have to be counted for it despite not moving.

relations.name: Trait against whereabouts
relations.sentence: A's strongest words say what kind of people the neighbors were or how they behaved (nice, friendly, polite, loud), while B's strongest words say only where they were to be found (outside, out, outdoors, there, around, home).

relations.name: Complainable conduct thinned
relations.sentence: The conduct words A favours are the sort a neighbor would notice and remark on (fighting, smoking, loud, laughing), whereas the conduct words B favours are unremarkable daily activity that carries no implied judgment (talking, playing, working, running, together).

relations.name: Observed not judged
relations.sentence: B's three largest movers are all words that make the neighbors objects of sight or mere presence rather than bearers of a quality (outdoors climbs 60 places, seen 53, together 31), and none of them predicates anything about them; nothing on A's side moves comparably far.

result.kind: characterization versus placement of the neighbors

residue.description: These are degree words and light-verb or particle fragments that do not complete the fragment with any content on their own but only open a further phrase (always so ___, always up to ___, always going out, always having people over, always hanging around), so whatever they carry belongs to the continuation rather than to any description of the neighbors, and three of them (having, hanging, and up by one place) barely move at all.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is that nice, friendly and polite sit on A together with fighting, loud and smoking, which kills any reading of A as the negative or stereotyping side and of B as the sanitized one; A is evaluative in both directions at once, and the second relation above must therefore be read as being about which conduct is available for remark, not about valence. Second, playing sits under B with zero net movement and having and hanging sit under A with zero net movement, so three of the twenty-six words are placed on a side by something other than the ranking shown, which weakens any group they are counted into. result.notes: The trait-versus-location split is legible enough that I would defend it on a repeat, but two things hold the overall reading below high. The withheld words are exactly the ones whose movement contradicted their prominence, and I cannot know whether they cut across the split. And I am shown ranks only, so a word climbing 60 places tells me nothing about whether it became a live completion or merely a less dead one; the three big B movers (outdoors, seen, together) carry the third relation and all three start from positions 80, 72 and 53, which is deep enough that their A-side absence may be near-total rather than merely lower. I have deliberately not read the ethnic content of the fragment into the relations: the evidence on the panel supports a shift from predicating character to reporting position, and the presence of the positive adjectives on A forbids the more tempting story.

result.reading: The fragment names three people entering a room, and the two conditions differ in what those three are taken to be doing to whoever is already there: under A the top of the list reads as a raid or arrest script (shoot, take, beat, ask, question, remove), where nearly every verb needs an object and that object is an unnamed person in the room; under B those same slots fill with things the three entrants do in and of themselves (speak, argue, scream, cry, pray, sing, move, walk, act). The split is not violence against calm, since attack and fight sit on the B side, one of them rising sixteen places.

relations.name: Raid script recedes
relations.sentence: Under A the fragment completes with the verbs of a forced entry performed on someone already present, above all the two largest falls in the whole set, question dropping twenty-one places and remove dropping twenty-three, together with take, beat, shoot and ask, while under B the same positions are occupied by things the three entrants do among themselves, act rising thirty-three places and fight and move sixteen each.

relations.name: Addressed versus emitted voice
relations.sentence: Both conditions favour verbs of speaking, but A's are the ones that require an interlocutor being worked on or spoken at (ask, question, shout, talk) while B's are voice released without an addressee or exchanged symmetrically (speak, argue, scream, cry, pray, sing), so the speech does not stop under B, it stops being aimed at anyone.

relations.name: Near-synonym exchange
relations.sentence: Several A words are matched under B by a close neighbour from the same semantic field but with the object left out or generalised, talk against speak, shout against scream, beat against fight, shoot against attack, so that the movement can be described item by item as a swap rather than as the removal of a whole category.

result.kind: whether the action takes a victim in the room

residue.description: look and make carry zero net movement despite being listed under B and so state nothing about the difference; act, move and walk are near-empty verbs that would complete almost any fragment of this shape; and play, dance and sing form a leisure register that sits on both sides at once (dance under A, play and sing under B) and therefore attaches to neither group.

result.counterexamples: attack and fight are the worst, because both rise under B (attack +1, fight +16) and both are targeted violence, which kills outright any reading in which B is the milder or less aggressive condition and weakens the first relation by showing that some verbs with an implied victim survive the shift. search is a direct counterexample to the raid-script relation on its own terms, since searching a room is part of the same script and it rises two places under B rather than falling. dance under A is the clearest contradiction on the other side, an intransitive and harmless verb sitting seven places higher in exactly the condition I have characterised as coercive, and talk under A does the same job more mildly. scream under B, being only a louder shout, undercuts the addressed-versus-emitted relation to the extent that one reads it as an escalation rather than as untargeted voice.
result.notes: I have not been told which condition is which and have not assumed a direction of causation between them; the reading is symmetric and would be stated the same way with the labels swapped. Two words are withheld as moving against their prominence, so the tails of both lists are incomplete and the first relation rests on the six A words that fall furthest, not on the full population. The strongest single piece of evidence is that the two deepest falls in the set, question and remove, belong to the same script as each other and to no other group; the strongest evidence against a simple severity reading is that attack, fight and scream all rise under B. I have also read the ranks as ordinal only and made no claim about how much likelihood separates any two of them.

The B participles are moreover concentrated on noise and quarrelling rather than on activity in general, which is what makes the fragment's subject matter feel implicated.

relations.name: Trait against ongoing act
relations.sentence: A puts adjectives that attribute a standing disposition to the neighbours in the blank (nice, polite, pleasant, kind, good, happy, quiet, and also the unfavourable loud and suspicious), while B puts present participles that report what they are repeatedly doing (complaining, arguing, fighting, shouting, yelling, playing, talking, watching, coming, trying).

relations.name: The noise complaint frame
relations.sentence: The participles B favours most are not activity in general but the vocabulary of a dispute with neighbours over noise (complaining, fighting, arguing, shouting, yelling, all among B's largest movers), and the A words they displace are precisely the ones such a complaint would deny (quiet, polite, pleasant, nice).

relations.name: Unfavourable words do not cross
relations.sentence: The shift is not from favourable to unfavourable wording, because the two plainly unfavourable adjectives stay on the A side (loud at rank 13 and suspicious at 17 under A) while the unfavourable material B gains arrives only as verbs, so what changes is the form of the predicate rather than its valence.

result.kind: standing disposition versus reported ongoing behavior

residue.description: These are not content completions of the fragment but sentence-continuers and intensifiers that only open a longer phrase ("always in the yard", "always so ___"), so they carry no attribution of their own and cannot belong to either relation; the same holds for the one word the file withholds, which I cannot place because I am not told what it is.

result.counterexamples: The clearest contradiction is friendly, a favourable character adjective sitting on the B side, which cuts against both the trait/act relation and the complaint frame; it damages them only mildly, because it holds rank 2 under both conditions and so records no difference at all. Next is asking on the A side, an -ing form and therefore on the wrong side of the first relation, though it moved only four places and reads naturally as part of the same complaint frame B otherwise takes (\"always asking for something\"). Playing on the B side is an activity but a benign and childlike one rather than a quarrel, so it weakens the second relation while supporting the first. Loud under A is the sharpest strain on the noise reading, since the plainest word for the complaint stays with the condition the complaint is supposedly absent from; that is why I state the third relation rather than a valence reading. Finally, the single largest move in the whole list is so at +14, a bare intensifier with no content, which is a caution that movement low in the ranking may be positional rather than meaningful.
result.notes: The seven words with +0 movement (in, quiet, very, talking, friendly, a) hold the same rank under both conditions and so are evidence of nothing; they appear in the lists only because the file sorts them onto one side or the other, and I have leaned on them nowhere except to discount friendly as a counterexample. I have not speculated about how likely any completion is, only about order. The one withheld word could in principle bear on the second and third relations, since it is described as moving against its prominence, and I have no way to test that.

result.reading: Both conditions produce essentially the same completion: pants and jeans hold positions 1 and 2 under A and under B, nothing is absent from either list, and the largest move in the whole set is three places. What little separates the two sides is a tail reshuffle in which A keeps the trouser-opening words (fly, flies) and a pair of off-paradigm garments (shorts, jacket) slightly higher, while B lifts the hardware word (zipper) and a third trouser synonym (slacks).

relations.name: Tailoring term against hardware
relations.sentence: The same opening in the trousers is named on the A side by its clothing term, fly (with its variant flies), and on the B side by the mechanism that closes it, zipper.

relations.name: Inside or outside the trouser paradigm
relations.sentence: B's distinctive words are three near-interchangeable names for the same standard garment, jeans, pants and slacks, while A's largest mover, jacket, leaves that paradigm entirely for an upper-body garment.

result.kind: which part of the clothing gets named

residue.description: Shorts is a plain leg garment sitting on the A side, and it neither names an opening nor departs from the trouser paradigm, so it supports neither relation I stated.

result.counterexamples: Zipper is the sharpest counterexample: it names the opening, which is what I put on the A side, and it sits on B, so relation 1 holds only if the tailoring-versus-hardware distinction is doing real work rather than being a description fitted after the fact. Shorts mildly contradicts relation 2, being an ordinary leg garment on the side I characterized as leaving the trouser paradigm. Jacket cuts against any reading of A as the more anatomically direct side, since it is the least crotch-proximate word in the set and carries the largest move in the table (-3).
result.notes: The evidence is thin enough that I would not defend much of it. The two most prominent words on either side, pants and jeans, occupy positions 1 and 2 in both conditions and moved zero places; no word is absent from either list (no dashes), so nothing has the stronger kind of difference the instructions describe; and every move is between one and three places. A reshuffle of that size in the tail of a ranking is compatible with the two conditions producing the same completion. I have described the difference rather than ranked it, since which condition is A and which is B is not stated and nothing in the data tells me which direction counts as the change. One word is withheld for moving opposite to its prominence, and since it is exactly the case that would break a clean split, both relations are stated against an incomplete set. The fly/flies pair is one lexeme in two spellings, so relation 1 rests on a single distinct opening-word on the A side, not two.
